abstract: In this study, we investigate the way people perceive physical characteristics as they relate to sexual orientation. Physical characteristics include appearance, mannerisms, and voice. Specifically, how do voice and movement of a potential partner influence people’s judgments about that partner’s attractiveness? 65 male and 52 female participants were recruited for this study, about equally split between sexual orientation and ethnicity (White and non-White). Participants engaged in a videotaped interview. Afterwards, experimenters rated the participants on sex typicality of speech, movement, appearance, and also gave ratings on their desire to have a romantic affair with the participant and willingness to be friends with them. Gay men and women, on average, are more sex atypical than straight people, but men more so on voice and movement, women more soon physical appearance. In men, sex atypicality negatively impacts their perceived attractiveness. However, in both sexes sex atypicality has no influence on the desire for friendship.

While much research evaluates existing psychotherapies, less focus is given to specific characteristics of certain psychopathologies and how that informs or explains psychotherapeutic improvement. As we come to know what the active ingredients of psychotherapies are and more specifically what affective, cognitive, and behavioral components are of different pathologies, we need to be able to further evaluate the appropriateness of matching certain psychopathologies with certain therapies. This study attempted to look at a cognitive aspect of depression, specifically logical consistency – consistency within a small set of beliefs. By measuring depression levels and consistency, I was able to explore the relationship between these two variables in a way that informs us about depression. I further was able to look at the effects of persuasion on people’s consistency and depression level to examine the potential effects of persuasion as a factor in reducing inconsistencies.

Breastfeeding is one manner in which a mother can transfer HIV to her infant. In the industrialized world, the current recommendation is for mothers with HIV/AIDS to use formula to feed their feed their infants. This recommendation is more problematic for infected mothers in developing countries. Factors such as availability, cost and sanitation make it very difficult for infants to be formula-fed safely. Consequently, additional work is needed to develop appropriate infant feeding recommendations for HIV-infected mothers of the developing world. Anthropology has contributed greatly to research on the relative merits of breastfeeding in different social and ecological conditions. Previous anthropological research has demonstrated the tradeoffs associated with prolonged breastfeeding. Breast milk provides many immunological and nutritional properties that are important to an infant’s health; however, it can be energetically demanding for mothers, especially if they are undernourished. This paper will examine current breastfeeding recommendations for women in both developed and developing countries in light of the recent literature on maternal-infant HIV transmission through breast milk. The integration of the breastfeeding and HIV literature is critical for developing recommendations that are safe and beneficial for both the mother and child. This integrative perspective also illustrates the importance of the anthropological perspective for this particular area of AIDS research.

I will have completed two senior theses by May 1st, each centered on the topic of political participation and the political attitudes and beliefs among contemporary young adults (under 30 years of age). My sociology thesis addresses youth political participation through focus group methodology. After conducting an extensive literature review on youth political activists, social movements, political socialization (e.g. the media, family, peers, school, and college), youth culture, and political participation, I formulated my research design. Two of the three focus groups were recruited from student political organizations on campus, one drawn from a liberal-leaning group and the other drawn from a conservative-leaning group. The final focus group was selected to mirror the Northwestern undergraduate population demographically. Each participant completed a questionnaire to assess their political socialization before the start of the focus group, in order to contextualize their focus group responses. The thesis concludes from the research and the focus group responses that the differing levels of youth political participation between the late 1960s and early 1970s and now relates directly to the absence of a rallying issue of immediate, day-to-day importance to young adults. The draft, for instance, served as a strong motivating force for political activity and generated an entire youth culture promoting political participation for the Vietnam War generation. My political science thesis explores youth political attitudes and beliefs through a statistical analysis of National Election Study data. I predict that youth political opinion has become increasingly more cohesive since the 1950s, as a result of the changing nature of the agents of political socialization. Primarily, the homogenizing influence of the mass media has increased, primary and secondary school curriculums have become more and more standardized, greater numbers of young adults attend college and pursue graduate degrees, delaying their entrance into the workforce (research has shown that people crystallize their political beliefs and increase their political participation when they enter the work world) and increasing the number of years during which they are surrounded primarily by their own age cohorts. Thus, I contend that these societal forces, coupled with the declining influence of the family on political beliefs and the increasing influence of the peer group, have served to create a more cohesive political beliefs and attitudes framework among young adults. I have termed this a ‘national youth culture.’

title: Molecular Power Lines: Design and Nanofabrication of Electrically-Isolated Molecular Wires on the Silicon Surface.
abstract: The scanning tunneling microscope (STM) is the world's highest resolution microscope, capable not only of imaging individual surface atoms, but also of patterning individual molecules anywhere on a suface with atomic precision. It is one of the most sophisticated tools for imaging and fabricating on the nanoscale. As the size of electronic devices rapidly continues to decrease, the prospect of using individual molecules as active electronic components (e.g. wires, switches, transistors) becomes increasingly attractive. Unfortunately, STM-based patterning of molecules is incompatible with long polymer wires. The second problem is that the electrical current traveling through a molecular wire laying directly on top of a semiconductor will be limited by leakage current going into the substrate. My project circumvents these limitations by imitating the real-world powerline structures and replicating them on the nanoscale. The first step involves strategically patterning individual tin-porphyrine molecules (idealized as the poles of the power lines) on the hydrogen-passivated Si(100)-2x1 surface at specified distances from each other, by utilizing the atomic precision of the UHV-STM. The second requires that the surface be taken out of UHV and into ambient atmosphere, where it will be dipped into a wet chemical solution containing polymer molecular wires (idealized as the wires). Ultimately, a power line structure should result, wherein a wire molecule, bound at each end to the tops of two adjacent poles, is suspended above and isolated from the silicon substrate.

Previous work in our laboratory has revealed a large difference in the way that men and women process erotic stimuli. Men have a target-specific pattern of sexual arousal. Heterosexual men respond, subjectively and physiologically (i.e., genitally) much more to female sexual stimuli than to male sexual stimuli, while homosexual men show an opposite pattern. In contrast, women of all sexual orientations tend to respond similarly to both male and female stimuli. Thus, women have a bisexual arousal pattern. The current research will investigate brain differences underlying these physiological and mental differences. Homosexual and heterosexual men viewed sexual stimuli depicting either men or women, and their brain activity was monitored using fMRI. By studying similarities between homosexual men?s responses to male (female) stimuli and heterosexual men?s responses to female (male) stimuli, we will identify brain regions involved in male sexual arousal. In the future, we will test female subjects, in order to look for differences in brain activation compared with male subjects.

This paper examines the relationship between gender and spirituality in the fiction of Miguel de Unamuno. Specifically, it deals with the role of female characters in the spiritual development of male characters. It studies how spiritual salvation can be obtained by the men in Unamuno’s novels, and examines the issue of whether women are responsible when salvation is never achieved. The paper considers the archetype of the Virgin Mary in defining the spiritual responsibilities of the female characters. This Christian model of femininity is contrasted with the models provided by pagan religions. The paper examines the pagan characteristics of the female characters in order to identify the ways in which these characters deviated from the ideal of the Virgin. The paper analyzes two works by Unamuno, La Tía Tula [Aunt Tula] and Abel Sánchez [Abel Sánchez]. Both were chosen because of the increasing moral corruption of the major male characters throughout the novel. The narrators as well as the characters themselves offer opinions on who is to blame for this corruption, and whether the females failed to offer sufficient support in the males’ quests for salvation. This paper builds on previous articles which examine the concept of Christian sacrifice in Unamuno’s fiction. I believe that these articles do not fully explore the conflict between Christian and pagan archetypes. I draw from the literature on Greek, Roman, and Egyptian mythology to examine the pagan traits of the female characters. I use citations from the Bible as well as academic writings on Christianity to define the archetype of the Virgin Mary. The paper concludes that Unamuno portrays women as largely responsible for the spiritual salvation of men. His novels suggest that women who do not sacrifice themselves for the spiritual well-being of men fail to fulfill their Christian obligation to embody the ideals of the Virgin. By making certain female characters reminiscent of pagan goddesses, Unamuno defines these characters’ actions as anti-Christian, and the unhappy endings of the novels present a threat of destruction to all women who do not properly provide for the spiritual health of men. In my opinion, Unamuno’s perspective implies a denial of the female’s autonomous existence by defining her through the spiritual assistance that she provides the male. His perspective also diminishes the autonomy of the male, who is portrayed as unable to independently reach salvation. This paper was originally written in Spanish, but an English translation is available.

This winter I was in a classes called 'Writing Women's Lives'. I chose to interview women from an organization called Murder Victims' Families for Reconciliation. It is an organization of people who have had a family member murdered but are now working against the death penalty and victims rights. My piece is an art installation exploring their transition from loss to activism. It requires three TV/VCR-VHS monitors which I can provide. I just need outlets! IT also requires a 8x8 space if possible. The TVs are showing three execution scenes from popular movies, but on the ground in front of the TVs is a chalked outline of what appears to be a murder victim. The victim is juxtaposed with those being murdered on TV. Next to the chalking lies a heart made from red paper, viewers are invited to take a piece. The papers have a quote from the voice over which is played during the piece. The voice over contains a series of quotes from the interviews with the women. It is a powerful and moving piece as was noted this past Wednesday during it's viewing.

My research, part of a three-part project funded by the United States Department of Education, is a psychological study of the effects of concrete representations on children’s developing symbolic awareness. My study focuses on children’s emergent literacy skills and the impact of exposure to concrete letter objects on two distinct components of early literacy: alphabetic knowledge and symbolic understanding. The theoretical basis for this research is the dual representation hypothesis, which asserts that to gain symbolic knowledge from a concrete object, a child must understand it simultaneously as an independent object and as a symbol. Therefore, young children often have difficulty in effectively using concrete representations of symbols, such as letters. This difficulty is mediated by factors such as the object’s attractiveness, similarity of the object to the symbolic referent, and tactile interaction with the object. My experiment will compare a group of children exposed heavily to the object properties of letter toys to a control group where the physical properties are not as salient. This research has real world relevance in our culture, in which educational programs often promote the use of concrete objects based on a belief that children will learn more easily from something they can manipulate directly. Research on young children’s use of symbols suggests that this may not be the case, and my study explores the possibility that attractive letter toys will impede children’s understanding of the symbolic function of letters. Currently we are in the process of pilot testing subjects, and will begin studying in children’s homes in late spring.

From Fall 2000 through Spring 2002, we worked with Professor David Abrahamson in a statistical study of the magazine industry. We analyzed the differences between the a new data set and one David compiled 10 years ago, looking at the advertising rates, circulation and cover prices of 300 magazines. With the help of a Northwestern research grant, we accompanied David to the Association for Education in Journalism and Mass Communication convention in Miami last August, where we shared in the presentation of the paper and accepted an award within our division for our efforts. The abstract of the paper, titled 'A Quantitative Analysis of U.S. Consumer Magazines: A Ten-Year Longitudinal Study of Transformation,' follows: In an effort to examine a number of fundamental questions about the U.S. consumer magazine publishing industry in a historical context, the research of a baseline 1990 quantitative study was duplicated exactly 10 years later employing the same research methodology. It is evident that a number of the defining economic business parameters, such as levels of circulation, cover price, and advertising rates (in cost-per-thousand and page rates), have undergone significant change in the last decade. The periodical industry's responses to these changes reflect not only a variety of economic pressures – specifically, those related to cost management and the optimization of revenue within the framework decade's market conditions – but also, perhaps speculatively, the ways in which magazines may continue to reflect the on-going sociocultural reality of American society.

For the last two years I have worked on a project involving the synthesis, characterization, and application of a novel class of polymers. These polymers incorporate macrocycle compounds, cyclodextrins and calixarenes, onto a silicon backbone. This arrangement combines the known extraction capabilities of the macrocycles with the chemical and thermodynamic stability of silicon polymers, leading to potential applications in drug delivery, separations, environmental remediation, and catalysis. Currently, I am working with one of the cyclodextrin based polymers. Cyclodextrins, cyclic oligomers of glucose, are known to form inclusion complexes with small organic molecules absorbing them into their hydrophobic inner cavity. Since cyclodextrins are chiral, it follows that they may be used to resolve a racemic mixture of a compound. Previous work by Armstrong et al has shown that cyclodextrins covalently bonded to silica gel can resolve racemic mixtures with high performance liquid chromatography. However, the cyclodextrin or its linkage to silica gel must be modified for the column to work with different racemates. The focus of my work is to demonstrate the feasible of separating racemic mixtures with liquid chromatograph without having to modify the cyclodextrins. For more detailed information see: Lambert, J.B.; Liu, C.Q.; Boyne, M.T.; Zhang, A.P.; Yin, Y.X. ' Solid phase host-guest properties of cyclodextrins and calixarenes covalently attached to a polysilsesquioxane matrix ', Chem. Mater. 2003,15 (1), 131.

This project explores the topic of American presidential authority during wartime. For instance, how have American presidents abused their constitutional authority by acting without Congressional approval to initiate conflicts since World War II? After analyzing some of the major international conflicts, I will then suggest changes in the law to resolve this problem. The historical examples that I will discuss include: Harry S. Truman in Korea, Lyndon B. Johnson in Vietnam, Richard M. Nixon in Laos and Cambodia, Ronald W. Reagan in Grenada, George H.W. Bush in the Persian Gulf. Lastly, I will also discuss implications for this research in present society; by examining President George W. Bush's constitutional authority in taking military action in Iraq.

title: Sustainable Food and Community
abstract: The industrialization of agriculture and food production in America has disconnected most of us from our food sources, leading to devastating consequences for human health, communities, local economies, and the environment. The consolidation of food production has also threatened many rich and diverse local food traditions across the country. However, some communities have begun to re-establish these connections between farmers, producers, and consumers with very positive results. Last spring, we received a summer undergraduate research grant to study this growing sustainable food movement and how it is strengthening various communities. We worked on a community supported farm near Buffalo, NY, attended the American Community Garden Association conference in NYC, volunteered at the Rodale Agricultural Research Institute in PA, attended the Northeast Organic Farmers Association conference in MA, went to the International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements in Victoria, BC, and took part in a Slow Foods symposium in Iowa City. We also studied local food paradigms in other towns including Burlington, VT, Washington, D.C., and Omaha, NE. We discovered marked similarities in how local food movements were benefiting these very different communities. Upon returning to Northwestern, we became involved in the Illinois sustainable foods movement. On a state level, we were the only students invited to take part in a meeting aimed at creating a Sustainable Food Council of Illinois. Here at Northwestern, we have been working with the dining services committee to bring local organic food to campus. We are currently teaching a student-organized-seminar based on our research.

I have been working with Professor Smilowitz and former Mercedes Benz co-workers (summer internship 2002) on developing a method to analyze the transportation system of company cars. Currently Mercedes transports their vehicles from Germany by shipping to three main ports and then directly distributing to their dealerships. My research explores the possibility of optimally adding warehouses to first store vehicles and then redistribute to only nearby dealerships. My hope is that the system I am developing will efficiently cut down on cost and money. Using actual dealership locations, sales, and cost estimates, I am able to apply my IE studies to a real life problem. My research is primarily based on mathematical programing in AMPL and various routing heuristics.

Nanotechnology is rapidly evolving into a revolutionary field of science. In particular, the synthesis and application of nanoporous materials including molecular sieves such as zeolites and other silicates have been identified as areas possessing immense potential. Zeolites have been used regularly to refine petroleum, separate chemicals, and catalyze reactions. These materials are comprised mostly of silicon, oxygen, and aluminium atoms but can be modified to include other elements. Our project consists of synthesis and characterization of silicalites containing framework titanium atoms (TS-1) that can be used as a catalyst for liquid phase oxidation reactions. To characterize these nanoporous materials, we will utilize the following techniques: scanning electron microscopy, x-ray diffraction, infrared and ultraviolet spectroscopy, inductively coupled plasma spectroscopy, and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. These techniques will allow us to determine the structural and the physical makeup of the synthesized material. A successful synthesis leading to a high quality TS-1 catalyst will also allow us to further examine the physical and catalytic properties of this unique nanoporous material. The purpose of our research is to explore the possibilities that molecular sieves hold for the nanotech industry.

I’ve taken a number of classes on Youth related drama with Rives Collins. I also am a two-time winner of the Agnes Nixon Playwriting Contest, a member of the Creative Writing for the Media program, and a 2002 winner of the T Stephen May Scriptwriting contest. After taking Children’s Theater, Rives and I took on and independent study together during which I wrote a Theater for Youth Play called “Skye Blue.” It is a one-act play aimed towards ages 8-15. It addresses the topic of religious discrimination, while also addressing Paganism as a benevolent and valid religious path. It follows the journey of Skye, a thirteen-year-old girl, who, like many real young people, faces religious discrimination and intolerance from both her classmates and her school principal. However, during her wrongful suspension from her school, she befriends a Jewish girl who’s father studies the Kabbalah, and begins to teach her magicks. My first proposal is to present a scene between the two, discuss the basics of Skye’s faith and become friends. Two theater majors would act, and Rives would direct it. I am the playwright and do not wish to either or act or direct this piece. I understand that this would differ from the other performance proposals, because I am not the one performing. Therefore my second proposal would be to enter this as a reading, and either read the whole thing myself, or read the stage directions, and have actresses say the dialogue, in order to reduce confusion.

Two aspects of Mexicali, Mexico, have not changed in its 100-year history. The first is a perennial summer heat that could wilt a cactus. The second is the pervasive presence of Chinese. Before the Chinese established itself in Mexicali, the scorching climate made the dust bowl of a region so unbearable that hardly any group—including Mexicans— had migrated to the area en masse. But in the early 20th Century, the opportunity for work just south of the U.S.-Mexico border and harsh economic and political conditions in Southern China made Baja California’s Mexicali Valley a particularly appealing option for Chinese immigrants. Some scholars estimate that the Chinese of Mexicali reached at least 40 percent of the population while others say that they once outnumbered Mexicans 14:1. Yet, why did the Chinese thrive in Mexicali? Why did they settle in a desert region where temperatures frequently reach 125 degrees? Why did the Chinese community maintain its strongest presence during the Mexican Revolution (1910-1920), the most nationalistic and tumultuous time in Mexico’s history? And how did the Mexicali Chinese thrive while entire Chinese communities in other Mexican states and cities were ransacked, expelled and even mass-murdered? These questions constitute the heart of my thesis, which focuses on 1902-1931, the most vibrant period of Mexicali’s Chinese community. The answers to these questions matter because the magnitude of the Chinese population in Mexicali, its economic foothold and its fundamental constitution of Mexicali’s mosaic have not been replicated in any other city in Mexico.

The Chinatown Square Project’s goal was to construct attractive housing and recreational facilities to lure middle-class Chinese away from metropolitan suburbs back into Chinatown to reduce its residents’ social isolation from mainstream society. My study evaluated whether or not the Chinatown Square Redevelopment Project was successful in bringing more middleclass Chinese to live in Chinatown, whether or not changes in the middleclass population affected the community’s overall level of social isolation, and whether or not changes in the middleclass population affected the viability of Chinatown’s established social organizations. I used data from the 1980, 1990, and 2000 Census and interviewed leaders from Chinatown’s prominent community organizations to determine whether or not there was an increase in the middleclass population residing in Chinatown and whether or not the community was less socially isolated than before the Redevelopment Project. I analyzed interview responses for Roland Warren’s horizontal and vertical ties to see how the Redevelopment Project affected the viability of Chinatown’s community organizations. I will use graphs of Census data, interview responses, photos of the Redevelopment Project, and maps of the geographic Chinatown community to show that the Chinatown Square Project succeeded in reducing Chinatown’s social isolation. I will also include profiles of other redevelopment projects to give viewers a greater understanding of how redevelopment affects urban communities and how differences between Chicago’s Chinatown and other urban communities contributed to Chicago’s Chinatown’s success and their failure.

Our project is the design and implementation of a fully functional first-of-its-kind broadcast communication network capable of integrating data content delivery with pre-recorded media on portable electronic devices. In other words, we have created a system in which, as an example, 'Discman' style portable CD players can wirelessly receive new audio or data content and integrate that new content with the audio on the listener's CD. Consider listening to a Dave Matthews CD and, at the end of the disc, hearing a brand new unreleased track that has been wirelessly delivered to your player. Here's how it works: Every FM radio station can transmit a secondary signal, called the sub-carrier channel, which is multiplexed onto the baseband, or main program signal. The sub-carrier can contain audio information or data but can only be picked up by special receivers. Our system begins by sending messages of our choosing (such as a new Dave Matthews song) in a digital form via the sub-carrier of one or more local FM stations. A CD player integrated with our hardware - consisting of a radio receiver, memory and control circuitry - receives and stores the messages we send over the sub-carrier. We can code players and messages so that different groups of players receive different messages (in a large scale deployment of our technology). Instructions that control the playback of messages are also sent to the player. We believe our project is nothing short of an enabling technology for a revolution in music listening.

Non-volatile memory requires the ability of a material to retain the data written, which in ferroelectrics refers to the polarization direction of each domain. For data storage, there is the need for considerable remnant polarization and for data writing the need for polarization saturation or in other words low coercive fields. Conducting measurements and determining hysteresis loops can therefore select ferroelectrics of interest. However, the low yield on current ferroelectric random access memory wafers shows the demand for submicron structures. This implies being able to be develop techniques to be able to “write” domains and perform direct hysteretic measurements at the nanometer scale. This paper highlights a part of the Dravid Research Group’s ongoing project in patterning functional architecture of inorganic and bio-organic-inorganic complexes at the nanoscale, characterize their nanostructural attributes and exploit the site- and shape-specificity of nanopatterning to create proof-of-concept novel bio-diagnostic, electronic and sensing devices. The method selected in this project is to use a Pb(Zr0.52Ti0.48)O3 precursor solution which is stable in the ambient. This is used to pattern on Si[111] substrate by Dip-pen Nanolithography using an AFM tip and is subsequently heat treated. The characterization of the pattern is twofold. First, both electron microscopy (SEM, TEM) and scanning probe microscopy (AFM) are used to confirm that the pattern is exactly what was intended. Second, the ferroelectric properties, such as polarization, domain structure and surface charge density, are investigated using techniques such as EFM and NSOM. Direct hysteretic measurements are also made using a biased AFM tip.

The goal of this project is to design an SUV that would appeal to environmentally-conscientious consumers by challenging the modern stereotype of an SUV. The target generation is the Millennials in the technological context of 2013. The proposed transformation is done on four levels: engine, exterior, materials, and interior. To combat SUV’s poor fuel economy and higher exhaust emissions, the engine will be replaced with biodiesel/electric hybrid, which combines a renewable fuel source resulting in cleaner emissions. At the same time, the hybrid also improves mileage by a factor of nearly two. The exterior will be designed to reduce air resistance, further improving fuel economy. This will be done by emphasizing curves rather than straight lines as well as incorporating a variable ground clearance into the chassis design. To further the idea of eco-friendliness, the materials used would be organically based and/or recyclable. Floor matting and plastics will be substituted with newer and more environmentally-friendly alternatives including thermoplastic composites, metallic foam, and industrial hemp. Finally, the interior design will reinforce the ecofriendly image by combining organic elements with the technology of 2013. In addition to the standard heads-up display, voice-activated controls, and central LCD control screen, a naturalistic environment will be added, consisting of extra large-windows, a completely retractable roof, and a simulated water flow throughout the car. The end product is the ultimate environmentally-friendly SUV.

The Interactive Chef, or IChef, is a two-year on-going project Computer Science 399 project consisting of 3 undergraduate students and 1 graduate student. IChef is a software application to provide voice-enabled cooking assistance. IChef walks users through recipes step-by-step providing answering questions in the form of basic instruction, photograph or video. Designed with the intent of improving the user's experience from talking to a machine to talking to another person, IChef is able to understand unstructured and untrained speech meaning that anyone can simply pick up the microphone and begin talking to it.

We have developed an experimental setup to measure interfacial adhesion forces using the contact between an oil/water interface and a coated glass hemisphere. This geometry is very sensitive to small deformations from which the contact angle and adhesion energy between the interface and surface can be calculated. Fnctionalized molecules are placed at the interface to interact with the treated hemispherical surface. This way, we can examine the specific bonding forces between biological molecules, particularly biotin and streptavidin. Initially however, we need to understand the background interactions between the oil/water interface and several contact surfaces. Prior to testing our technique on different systems, we need to understand the basic contact behavior of water on the various surfaces of interest. Changes in the pH of the liquid and the hydrophilicity of the contact surface are important parameters in determining contact behavior. We used a goniometer to measure the contact angle between droplets of varying pH and our coatings on flat glass slides. To determine limiting contact behavior, we have investigated both hydrophobic and hydrophilic surfaces. The hydrophilic surfaces are glass and a layer of a triblock copolymer with a hydrophilic midblock and hydrophobic endblocks, while the hydrophobic surface is a layer of poly(methyl methacrylate). We are also investigating the contact angle of water on 3-aminoproplytriethoxylane, used to attach streptavidin to glass, and streptavidin. Contact angle measurements will give us an idea of the behavior we should expect in our oil/water interface experiments. After a basic understanding of interfacial interactions is achieved, we can proceed towards more complicated systems involving functionalized amphiphiles specifically interacting with a functionalized surface.

Robotic manipulators currently play a major role in manufacturing systems by assembling parts together. However, with the trend of parts becoming smaller and smaller, it becomes economically unfeasible to have robots individually manipulate and assemble parts that may be on the micron, even nano scales. Underactuated self assembly is a paradigm shift from traditional robotic prehensile manipulation that can allow for this miniaturization. My research project involves determining control methods for assembling two parts together without feedback. The experimental setup involves throwing plastic parts with a one degree of freedom arm. The parts glide on a nearly frictionless air hockey table with an adjustable angle of incline to vary the gravitational force. Previous work done by Dr. Lynch has shown that for parts with non-trivial geometries, repeated throws and catches of parts with an arm causes the parts to demonstrate a unique cyclic pattern from a large set of initial conditions. Using this knowledge, self assembly can be achieved by implementing the correct geometry for both the parts and the arm.

Long term total parenteral nutrition (TPN) treatment of patients with permanent intestinal dysfunction risks infection and may result in liver failure. Patients with a history of complications resulting from TPN are considered for small bowel transplants to relieve their dependency on TPN. Even with the emergence of FK506 (tacrolimus) in the early 1990s, small bowel transplantation patients still face high risk of rejection compared with grafts of other solid organs, necessitating high dose acute and chronic immunosuppression. An improved understanding of the mechanisms that result in such rejection processes may result in improved patient survival. Using an orthotopic murine model, we observe replacement in the mesenteric lymph nodes of donor t-lymphocytes by host lymphocytes in both isograft and allograft. However we also observe this replacement in the small bowel lamina propria even in the isograft. FCM staining of these infiltrating lymphocytes in the SB and MLN suggest that within the allograft there a significant increase in expression of the CXCR3 receptor while there is no comparable increase in the isograft. Realtime PCR demonstrates that in the allograft there is significantly increased induction of mRNA encoding IP-10 and Mig, both of which are CXCR3 ligands. Also realtime PCR shows an increased induction of IFN-? when comparing the allograft with the isograft. There is little change in IL-4 induction. The combination of this data suggests to us that rejection processes with the small bowel likely is a Th1 mediated mechanism involving the receptor CXCR3. The working theory of this laboratory is that small bowel transplants occur more frequently because immune cells will traffic to it even without infection or an allograft. We thus have attempted to examine directly the role of CXCR3 in trafficking to the small bowel using CXCR3 knockout mice.

title: Transverse Vibrating Modes of a Resonance Wire Loop
abstract: The Resonance Wire Loop is a common demonstration apparatus whose resonance structure is more complex than that of a vibrating string. The apparatus consists of a wire loop supported at a single point that also serves as the point of excitation. The resonance modes are easily demonstrable and are often used in the classroom to loosely represent standing waves of electrons in orbitals of the Bohr model for an atom. The frequency structure of these modes is such that the harmonic frequencies go as the square of odd integers. The wavelengths of the standing waves are proportional to the inverse of the circumference. These characteristics are more closely related to the transverse vibration modes of a straight stiff bar. CONCLUSION: If the basic relationship between frequency f, wavelength λ and wave speed v is to hold for resonance mode n, then fnλn = vn. The velocity must therefore be strongly frequency dependent vn = k^(fn) where k is a constant which depends on the wire size and other factors. This is very similar to what is seen in a stiff straight bar. In that case both tension along the bar and the stiffness of the bar contribute to the restoring force that is responsible for the velocity of the wave. The observed proportional relationship between fundamental frequency f1 and the inverse square of the circumference is also similar to the relationship between frequency and length of a stiff straight bar. Why the wire loop would behave more closely to the frequency of a stiff straight bar is not understood currently.

Functional study of the Bag-1 ortholog Snl-1 (suppressor of Nup-116C lethal 1) in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Bcl-2 associated athanogene (Bag) class proteins participate in a wide variety of cellular functions ranging from cell growth to cell death. A single novel Bag class protein was identified in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae as the protein Snl1. Snl1 was isolated in a high copy suppressor screen for temperature sensitive nuclear pore mutants; it contains a transmembrane domain and localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membrane. Snl1 suppresses 4 different temperature sensitive nuclear pore mutations and I have chosen to focus on the temperature sensitive mutation in Nup57, a nuclear pore protein involved in nuclear pore assembly. With the contribution of the Bag domain and the transmembrane domain to Snl1’s ability to rescue the Nup57 temperature sensitive mutant currently unclear, three basic questions must be asked in order to elucidate the function of Snl1. First, is the Bag domain necessary to save S. cerevisiae from its temperature sensitive nuclear pore defect at nonpermissive temperatures? Second, is the transmembrane domain of Snl1 and hence Snl1’s localization to the nuclear envelope necessary to save the temperature sensitive phenotype? Finally, are other proteins involved in Snl1’s rescue of the temperature sensitive nuclear pore defects? Through an analysis of Snl1’s functional domains and the roles that they play in the rescue of the Nup57 temperature sensitive mutant insight can be gained into the role that Snl1 plays in the assembly and stability of the nuclear pore as well as the functions of Bag class proteins in higher organisms.

Estrogen, traditionally known as a sex hormone, has also been shown to affect cognitive function. Specifically, estrogen increases working memory in the hippocampus, a part of the brain involved in the learning and formation of new memories. An anatomical correlate of the estrogen-induced memory increase is an increase in the density of hippocampal spines, the site of excitatory input to hippocampal neurons. Prior to the increase in excitatory input to hippocampal neurons, these cells experience an estrogen-induced decrease in inhibitory input. Currently, this disinhibition has only been characterized functionally, using electrophysiology. This project utilizes transmission electron microscopy to investigate possible anatomical correlates of estrogen-induced functional disinhibition. The pyramidal cell plasma membrane surface and its inputs have been reconstructed in three dimensions to provide highly detailed information. This project has revealed a novel correlation between neuronal structure and function.

title: Hyaluronic Acid/Collagen Scaffolds for Tissue Regeneration
abstract: Guided tissue regeneration aims to regenerate tissue at sites damaged by trauma or disease. Biodegradable scaffolds serve a central role in regeneration as a mechanical support to guide tissue formation. Recently, these scaffolds have been designed to deliver biologically active molecules, such as DNA. We have designed a scaffold that is composed of hyaluronic acid and collagen, two naturally-occurring polymers in the body, with the ability to bind bioactive molecules to its surface. Hyaluronic acid and collagen are attractive polymers for scaffold fabrication, as they have important biological functions and can be modified for drug delivery. Scaffolds were formed by crosslinking hyaluronic acid and/or collagen chains with a diepoxide crosslinker. The percent water of the hydrogels ranged from 98% to 60% depending on the degree of crosslinking and collagen content. The degradation rate of the gels in hyaluronidase was found to range from 1 to 13 days depending on the degree of crosslinking. Cells cultured on these gels were able to attach and proliferate. Interestingly, the hydrogel surface can be patterned to induce contact guidance with cells growing along the pattern. Current project directions include adding biological functionality to the hyaluronic acid; specifically, DNA will be immobilized to the gel surface to direct cell functions. Ultimately, the attachment of DNA encoding for tissue-inductive factors may enhance and direct regeneration in vivo.

I coordinated a content analysis of news coverage for HIV/AIDS in Chicago and Cape Town media during the last five weeks of 2002. This project was done by nine journalism students (eight who are in South Africa on journalism internships right now)who were assigned to analyze one of 10 newspapers, magazines,and broadcast channels in Chicago (in Cape Town, three newspapers, one radio station and broadcast channel were looked at - different comparison points because of different media culturea)looking at how HIV/AIDS is portrayed in the media. This is the first cross-cultural comparison of HIV/AIDS media analysis done. The Columbia Journalism Review conducted a media analysis of HIV/AIDS for 1985-1996, which is the only other study done on this. (For South Africa, media analysis of HIV/AIDS is limited with a few reports done on neighboring countries.) The project is composed of two parts: 1.) an analysis of stories mentioning HIV/AIDS in Chicago and Cape Town. 2.) Interviews with journalists in more than a dozen newsrooms to understand the culture of how HIV/AIDS is made into news and understood.

This project focuses on the impact of particle size in mixed-phase titanium dioxide photocatalysis. Degussa P25 titanium dioxide was chosen as the mixed-phase catalyst. This particular commercial catalyst blends two phases of titanium dioxide with two different structures: anatase and rutile. In photocatalysis, the titanium dioxide is first exposed to a light source. Then, the two structures cooperate to cause chemical reactions that can remove organic materials from solution by converting them to carbon dioxide gas. Developed as a paint pigment, titanium dioxide is currently used in many products including sunscreen and Oreo™ cookies. Because of its photocatalytic and environmentally friendly properties, mixed-phase titanium dioxide has excellent potential as a catalyst in wastewater remediation. To simulate industrial wastewater, batches of water polluted with 4-chlorophenol were created. Then, portions of different size-fraction Degussa P25 titanium dioxide catalyst were added to each batch of wastewater. Water was treated with ultraviolet light for two hours, taking samples every twenty minutes. Finally, the 4-chlorophenol concentrations in the samples were analyzed using HPLC. The smallest particles, present in the lightest fraction, removed the 4-chlorophenol from the water much faster than any other size fraction. This initial discovery prompts further research into photocatalysis with light fraction mixed-phase titanium dioxide as an effective, environmentally benign new way to treat wastewater.

title: Development of Room Temperature Continuous Wave Quantum Cascade Lasers
abstract: The ultimate goal of this project is to develop the existing technology of mid-infrared quantum cascade lasers (QCL) to perform at continuous wave. Currently, the Center for Quantum Devices (CQD) has research being performed under Dr. Steve Slivken who, as a result of his research, achieved high power, low threshold current, room temperature pulsed mode, QCLs. These devices can be used for a multitude of different applications ranging from military to medical to everyday life. The wavelengths we utilize fit within the strategic 3-12 micron range. This range encompasses two important atmospheric transmission windows and other regions of high absorption. Unlike standard near-infrared lasers, this laser transmitter technology promises longer-range detection in adverse weather conditions. The same properties make it useful for free-space optical Internet interconnects. The telecom industry would find this of interest in developing better Internet interconnects for phones which can remotely access the Internet. In terms of chemical detection, almost every chemical has some absorption lines in this wavelength range. Already, a system is being commercialized to analyze Nitrous Oxide emission levels in vehicle exhaust. Currently, the QCL is the only un-cooled semiconductor laser in this wavelength range, and is in high demand by many military and industrial companies due to its compact and robust nature. This project is seen as three steps, which will be run in a continuous loop to speed up production and research time. The first step will be to theorize and model a prototype structure whose conditions will facilitate continuous wave operation. The next step will be the growth and characterization of the structure on the Gas Source MBE (GSMBE). The material quality is at the heart of the project because of the great dependence of device performance on the quality of the material. The last step in the loop is the processing and testing of the lasers themselves. The testing is vital in the experimental procedure requiring both high quality equipment and high quality technical skills. The results from the testing will be the connection to the beginning of the process so as to improve and better the performance of our lasers. While room temperature pulsed QCL performance has been successfully demonstrated, we are now pushing forward to get continuous wave operation. Currently, this goal is limited by the intrinsic device efficiency and thermal resistance (ability to dissipate heat). By improving the material quality, device fabrication, and packaging technologies, room temperature continuous wave QCLs are an eminently achievable goal. The purpose of this project is to analyze the limiting factors for continuous wave laser operation and design a workable solution. In addition to the design, the experimental work will help confirm the validity and repeatability of this approach.

I have spent over five months in Belize, Central America over the last three years studying archaeology. Much of that time has been spent in the rural Western part of the country working in cave sites deep in the jungle. While I have always been interested in Mesoamerican archaeology and the ruins of the ancient Maya civilization, I became aware of more pressing matters while I was in Belize. I found that I was more interested in the stories of the people that currently live in that country, a vivid mixture of people that are having to find new ways to live in a nation caught between its rich history and modern industrialization. The people of Belize constantly carry with them the a dark legacy of colonialism and slavery, and yet they must also struggle to come into their own as a new country in Central America. My thesis is a collection of fiction stories about the people in Western Belize that are living through this time of great change. These stories are about everything from machete fights to Belizean funerals, bus riots to a man who makes kites for children. The characters in these stories are inspired by the real Belizeans that I have met during my travels. Through writing fiction, I hope to distill the often contradictory realities of their lives in this strange but beautiful country into a meaningful glimpse of Belize today. I plan to give a dramatic reading of one of my stories for my presentation for the Undergraduate Research Symposium.

Alcohol abuse is a significant problem among college students, and peer intervention can be an effective tool for early intervention and prevention of more serious alcohol abuse. Unfortunately, college students are often reluctant about confronting their peers about alcohol abuse, or do not know enough about how to approach them. Though much research has focused on how to approach the drinker, not much has been done on enabling the peer on confrontation. One way to reach a large number of college students and promoting confrontation is through mass media. Media messages, such as newspaper articles, can be very effective in promoting health and increasing awareness of societal dangers (Heath, 1984; Tyler & Cook, 1984). Content of the message is crucial to convincing and enabling a person to confront a peer with a drinking problem. Both mood and efficacy have been proven to affect helping and confrontation (Isen & Levin, 1972; Bandura, 1999). In this 2X2 study, we presented 75 college students with newspaper articles on alcohol issues, and manipulated mood (positive or negative affect) and efficacy (self-efficacy or outcome-efficacy) within the articles in order to test which conditions will most effectively incite helping behaviors among peers.

My thesis looks at the mechanism for trait inheritance, as perceived by children. There has been much controversy whether children understand inheritance as a concept to begin with and further whether they follow the concept of 'genetic' inheritance, attributing physical traits to the birth parent, even if the baby had no further contact with her. My study builds on this concept, exploring whether children in fact have an understanding of inheritance, and if so, what is the mechanism needed for the inheritance of traits. In other words, what part of 'giving birth' process passes down the traits. I have tested 88 subjects from Chicago and Evanston schools, in two age groups: second graders and preschoolers. I provided a child with one of four scenarios wherein a baby is born to a mother, of one kind and gets adopted by a new mother immediately. The scenarios change with regard to what happens next. In the control mechanism, the baby simply grows up with the new mother; in the language mechanism, the baby hears only the language of the adoptive mother and learns to speak that language; in the blood mechanism the baby receive a blood transfusion from the adoptive mother and finally, in the nursing mechanism, the adoptive mother nurses the baby. The subjects are then asked to attribute either the birth or adoptive parent’s traits to the baby after she grows up. There seems to be a trend pointing to the fact that children perceive nursing as the mechanism for the transference of traits. Furthermore, some of my findings suggest that second graders may consider language as a possible mechanism for trait transference. This has many implications both in the educational and cultural spheres.

My project is focused on using the animal remains from an archaeological site to determine if there social control was exacted by means of feasting. Feasting has been observed in archaeological and ethnological contexts as a mode of control. The thought is that there are two kinds of feasting, elite-sponsored feasts and competitive feasts. Elite-sponsored feasts are used to create a cohesive whole of the group and promote unity and equality. This type of feast may be utilized under a corporate strategy, which emphasizes the group rather than individuals. The other type of feasting is competitive feasting which involves the differential giving and receiving of food in order to gain prestige and demarcate individuals as superior. This type of feast is utilized in the network strategy of power. My study involves looking at the animal bones of an archaeological site from Late Bronze Age (1500-1150BC) Armenia to determine whether or not feasting was being utilized. There has been little research into detecting feasting by means of the faunal record, making this study rather unique. I will present the paper in poster format, including pictures of bones, maps, and statistical charts to help illustrate the conclusion came to in the paper, namely that the people of Late Bronze Age, Armenia (site name: Tsakahovit) were indeed using feasting as a means of gaining or maintaining power.

Phenotypic Radiation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Biofilms Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a ubiquitous bacterium that is clinically important because of its presence in burn wounds, catheters, and the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients. P. aeruginosa PAO1 wild type (PAO1 wt) biofilms, which are surface-attached populations, were grown in silicone tubing in our laboratory. After several days of growth, a colony morphology subpopulation was observed; this morphology, which accounts for about 15 percent of the biofilm, has rough, cohesive colonies and is referred to as the sticky morphology (PAO1 st). I have characterized the stability of PAO1 st and have found that it has a very low reversion rate to PAO1 wt. To understand how and why the sticky morphology occurs, I am studying the genetic basis for this phenotype. I am generating a library of mutants using transposon mutagenesis, which randomly inserts a transposon to the P. aeruginosa genome; then, the resulting insertional mutants are screened for the sticky morphology phenotype. Once I generate PAO1 st transposon mutants, I will sequence the gene flanking the transposon, thereby determining which gene or genes are responsible for the sticky morphology. This research is important because PAO1 st is particularly persistent in biofilms; by understanding the nature of its occurrence, I can investigate ways to decrease its persistence in unwanted biofilms.

My research consists of the analysis of the suburban drug market with a focus on the organization of the supply side. I argue that current drug control strategy used in suburbs is developed within the context of the urban drug market and is misapplied to the suburban market. Because the markets operate within such a vastly different social context, a control strategy developed in an urban area is ineffective in a more affluent town. This is brought to light with an in depth look at the attributes and operations of suburban drug dealer from their driving motivation for selling drugs to logistical questions like how they store and transport the illicit good. With an understanding of the suburban drug market, the misalignment of suburban policing efforts to the actual problem becomes evident and so does the need for the development of suburban specific drug control strategies. The end of the paper suggests new drug control strategies that have a better fit to the actual problem. My methodology consisted of interviews with suburban drug dealers and suburban police departments.

Broadcast television is a medium aimed at the common interests of a viewing audience. The level of depth and breadth associated with any topic is the same for all viewers. In a very real sense, the nature of the medium is such that all viewers get the same picture. Imagine instead, that a viewer has access to a system that is actually watching with him, in tandem, noting the kind of show, the content of the show, and the details of what is being discussed. If this system was also capable of translating its understanding of the show into a set of information queries, it would make it possible for a viewer to say “tell me more” and have that information immediately presented. The viewer wouldn’t have to know where the information resides, how to search for it, or even how to build a query. He would only have to push a button and the information comes to him. InteracTV is implemented within the context of the TiVo digital television recorder. It tracks user choices and does an ongoing capture of the closed captioning information of shows as they are being viewed, either from a real time feed or from a recording. When asked to do so, the system hands its understanding of the current context to an information server, which crafts specialized queries based on the context (what kind of show is being watched) and content (what is in the closed-captioning) of the current show. The results are then sorted, organized, and presented to the user, either on the TV or an external device.

We have researched the development of deployable mirrors for NASA and the United States Air Force. We have helped in developing the mirrors by using electroforming, vaccum depostion, and composite materials. Our project will present a mirror made by electroforming mounted on a lightweight honeycomb structure. This should represent the time and weight decrease instead of making the mirror out of glass which can take over a year on a large scale. Also, we will present our lab in which we have set up a bath for electroforming to help us continue with our work.

Carbon nanotubes have excellent mechanical and electrical properties. Multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWNT) can withstand electrical current densities as large as 109 A/cm2 – larger than any other known material, and recently transistors have been fabricated from single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNT), which have outperformed their silicon counterparts. Ropes of SWNT have been shown to have an average tensile strength of 30GPa – many times the tensile strength of high strength steel. Carbon nanotubes are expected to have interesting optical properties. In a recent study, the Smalley group at Rice University observed band-gap absorption and fluorescence in unbundled carbon nanotubes encapsulated in surfactants. Through my research, I hope to gain a better understanding of these optical properties by studying the band-gap absorbance of encapsulated nanotubes.

title: Distribution of Pores in Schlemm's Canal of the Eye
abstract: The aqueous humor outflow pathway in the eye has been studied for almost 100 years in an attempt to find the source of the pressure increase found in glaucoma. Regions of the pathway have been identified that contribute to this pressure increase, but the full pressure increase has not been accounted for. In the outflow pathway, the aqeous humor flows radially across the inner wall of Schlemm's canal through pores which pass between or through cells. The fluid exits through collector channels along the outer wall of the canal, which feed into the aqueous veins. The inner wall of Schlemm's canal is thought to contribute a large fraction of the pressure increase seen in glaucoma. In this study, we investigated the hypothesis that more pores may be found closer to the collector channel because the greatest pressure drop occurs there. To test this hypothesis, micrographs of the inner and outer wall were taken of normal human eyes fixed at 8 mmHg. The collector channel locations from the outer wall were mapped onto the micrographs of the inner wall, where pores were identified. The distance from each pore to the collector channel was measured, and the area at each distance was measured, to determine the local pore density. An analysis of the data showed that the pores were not randomly distributed as a function of distance and that the pores were more dense near the collector channel. The techniques used in this experiment can be used to analyze the pore distribution in glaucomatous eyes to see if the pore distribution differs from normal eyes.

title: Advanced Packaging Techniques and Performance Improvements for Quantum Cascade Semiconductor Lasers
abstract: Laser sources are preferred to broadband sources for spectroscopic and chemical detection systems because they produce a higher definition response and can detect trace amounts of substances. However, practical long wavelength laser sources are not currently available. An excellent candidate for improved long wavelength laser spectroscopy sources is the Quantum Cascade semiconductor Laser (QCL) because of its high output powers and wide range of tunable wavelengths (l~3-25mm). The best mid- to far-infrared semiconductor lasers on the market today still require large cryogenic cooling systems to produce continuous-wave (CW) operation, however, the QCL has demonstrated the potential for CW operation at room temperature. This project demonstrates improvements in device performance aimed at producing high power CW operation at room temperature. Simulated device improvements due to epilayer-side bonding, semiconductor re-growth, and other advanced packaging are demonstrated and a portable proof-of-concept mid-infrared laser module prototype is realized.

title: DNA Gyrase Function and Form in Various Organisms
abstract: The long term goal of this project is to decipher the quaternary structure of DNA Gyrase in atomic detail. We will attempt to solve the three dimensional structure of the two domains using X-ray crystallography. To maximize the chances of success, gyrase from different organisms will be studied. Sub-domains of DNA Gyrase have been previously crystallized and solved. However, a structure of the intact heterotetramer has yet to be determined. To maximize the chances of successful overproduction, purification, and crystallization, I will study gyrase from eight different organisms in parallel. The genes for both domains of DNA Gyrase have been successfully amplified using PCR from all eight organisms. From two of these organisms, Haemophilus Influenzae and Bacillus Subtillis both domains of DNA Gyrase have been cloned into the pGEX 5T-1 vector. Additional cloning of gyrase subunits from the other organisms is also in progress. Furthermore, we will also clone the same subunits using the MCSG-7 expression vector. Protein production using either IPTG or phage induction in BL21 cells is planned for each protein, followed by purification with a GS-sepharose affinity column and His-tag affinity column for pGEX 5T-1 and MCSG-7 vectors respectively for each subunit. The subunits will be mixed together at the appropriate ratios to reconstitute the heterotetramer and purified by size exclusion chromatography. Upon production of a stable heterotetramer, attempts to further characterize and crystallize the protein will be made using standard procedures. Following crystallization, X-ray diffraction crystallographic studies at the Advanced Photon Source will help to determine the structure of the molecule and will provide an atomic picture of how this important molecule is made.

It is well known that fighting HIV/AIDS is one of the most significant challenges facing the African continent today. Uganda’s multi-sectoral approach to AIDS education and prevention programs and subsequent success in reducing country-wide infection rates generated by a proactive government and President has placed the country in the international spotlight for HIV/AIDS prevention efforts. One under-studied aspect of HIV/AIDS prevention is that of the role of religious organizations in HIV/AIDS awareness creation among their communities. How do religious communities differ in their approaches toward HIV prevention? What are the implications of these differing approaches to HIV/AIDS education in what people are told about using condoms to prevent HIV/AIDS transmission? By studying different angles religious groups take in addressing HIV/AIDS prevention education, and observing how religious groups put their HIV/AIDS prevention education programs into action, I have found stark differences in the ways in which different faith-based organizations approach HIV/AIDS prevention education, particularly in the manner by which these different religious groups address condom use as a means of HIV transmission prevention. The aim of my study is to concentrate on the transmission of knowledge about HIV prevention, rather than focusing on the transmission of the disease itself. Specifically, I examine how faith-based organizations transmit knowledge about the disease, looking at education and awareness programs from an organizational perspective, rather than from an individual decision-making or behavioral model. I focus on how religious organizations design and implement their HIV/AIDS educations programs, as well as on how religious community members conceptualize condom use as a means for HIV/AIDS prevention.

All optical fibers are not manufactured and installed equally. Slight imperfections and asymmetries cause the fibers to be birefringent, which means that the speed of light depends on its polarization state. A pulse sent into an optical fiber with arbitrary polarization will be projected into two orthogonal polarization states known as the principal states of polarization (PSPs), which correspond to the fastest and slowest transit speeds. These different speeds result in temporal pulse splitting known as differential group delay (DGD). Polarization Mode Dispersion (PMD) is the name given to this and other effects that broaden a pulse in a polarization dependant manner. A simple measure of the PMD is provided in the PMD Vector, which points in the direction of the fast PSP with a magnitude equal to the DGD. More complex impairments are measured by the frequency derivatives of this vector. The birefringence of fiber varies randomly with distance and time, and thus so does the PMD. While standard methods exist to simulate random events, it is difficult to obtain results accurate at extremely low probability levels. My research has focused on ways to numerically model fibers with large PMD effects without resorting to billions of Monte Carlo simulations.

I am engaged in a threefold project in the area of computational chemistry, the goal of which is the computational analysis of the effects of various peptide nucleic acid (PNA) monomers on the stability of DNA/PNA and RNA/PNA duplexes. Primarily, the effect of substitution of a typical ethylenediamine-based PNA monomer with a cyclopentyl-based PNA monomer (as synthesized in the Appella lab) was examined. A free energy perturbation was performed using the AMBER force-field, in which the PNA molecules in explicitly solvated PNA/DNA and PNA/RNA duplexes were perturbed to a polymer in which the middle monomer was replaced with a cyclopentyl based monomer. An improved method of generating the initial structure has already been worked out, although the perfection of the free energy perturbation is ongoing (may be complete w/in a week from today). As a secondary aspect of this project, a method of generating free energy profiles of dihedral angles was developed, as we believe a preference for certain dihedral angles may induce selectivity in PNA monomers. Finally, as a third aspect of this project, a method of generating photographic quality ball and stick animations of molecules was completed. If you desire more information, please contact me, as I have a 3 page paper about my recent work I would gladly send to you. I will need a poster board for basic charts, graphs, and math, as well as a method of displaying computer animations (quicktime). I can bring a laptop if neccessary.

title: ‘Plus cubiste que le cubisme'
abstract: Cubism is, in addition to an art historical movement led by Picasso, Braque and Gris, a literary movement led by poets like Apollinaire and fostered by writers such as the Vorticists, and, according to Picasso scholar Douglas Cooper, the defining aesthetic of an entire Epoch. If Cubism can cross the boundary from the canvas to the page, what does it become on the stage? This interdisciplinary thesis focuses on the two ballets which, critically and historically, have most often been granted the designation of “Cubist.” One is Parade of Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, with choreography by Léonide Massine, libretto by Jean Cocteau, music by Erik Satie, and designs by Picasso. The second, called Skating Rink belongs to the repertoire of the Ballet Suédois, the Ballets Russes’ more avant-garde counterpart. Based on a poem by Canudo aligned with Futurism, it was choreographed by Jean Börlin and designed by later Cubist Ferdinand Léger, with music by Arthur Honegger. The appellation of “Cubist” in describing these works is shifty, from review to revival. The loaded word is dropped casually, often by dance writers whose necessarily journalistic criticisms cannot afford involved explanations. Therefore, what is actually meant by calling a ballet Cubist has become ambiguous. The designation could, and does, mean everything from mere association of a ballet with the school of its designer, to a more complex comment about the nature of its formal structure. In attempting to relocate the Cubist formal process within these ballets--in the workings of their choreographies especially--this thesis ultimately argues that dance is actually a more appropriate medium than Cubism’s traditional two-dimensional media to express the idiom’s formal project. Cocteau theorized Cubism as an art “plus vrai que le vrai,” more real than reality. Thanks in part to their fourth, temporal dimensions, Parade and Skating Rink are arguably “plus cubiste que le cubisme,” more Cubist than that which has been upheld as the (painted/pasted) pinnacle of Cubism.

This paper deals with the notion of 'truth' in ancient historical writing: what did writers of the ancient world consider to be 'true,' and what liberties did they take in their expression of that truth? Modern historiography is rooted in positivist scientific doctrine and tirelessly seeks non-subjective descriptions of historical events, their causes, and their consequences. Modern research on the ancient world, however, suggests that for the ancient Greeks and Romans such an ideology was nonexistent, and that rhetorical devices such as character slandering, historical rumor, and divine intervention were commonly employed. The ancients themselves were aware of this phenomenon and constantly in search of claims to objectivity; however, such claims seem never to have reflected a genuine impartiality. In recent years even historians such as Thucidydes, long-praised for their 'modern' and objective pursuit of knowledge, have come under attack, and famous testimonies to the belief in objective historiography, such as Cicero's De Oratore 2.62, are being systematically revealed as rhetoric-inspired works. This paper examines ancient claims to impartiality as well as modern criticism, which itself is sharply divided. Synthesizing both one can see that the notion of what was 'true' in an historical document, and how that truth was expressed, changes from the dawn of the Greek classical age until the beginning of the Roman Empire. The historiographical construct of 'truth' is consistently subject to literary and sociological trends which include oral history, an increased use of rhetoric, and the changing function of the author.

Our work focuses on how chromium—commonly found in contaminated soil and aquatic environments—interacts with aqueous-solid interfaces. The experiments are carried out with surface selectivity and molecular specificity using environmentally relevant chromium concentrations and the interfaces are probed at environmentally representative temperature and pH conditions. To study these heterogeneous processes in real time we use the nonlinear optical laser spectroscopy second harmonic generation. Among toxic metals that contaminate the environment, chromium is second in abundance after lead, and its sources in the environment are both natural and anthropogenic, resulting from such industries as chromite ore processing, petrochemical cooling towers, electroplating, and lumber treating. It is, in fact, the species which devastated the health of countless residents around Hinkley, California in the 1960’s-80’s via a groundwater leak from the nearby Pacific Gas and Electric Company as depicted in the film Erin Brockovich. Since the binding of toxic metal species at geosorbent surfaces is controlled by mechanisms operating at the surface via adsorption, desorption and redox processes, our experiments have been achieving a detailed kinetic and thermodynamic understanding of pollutant binding to geosorbent surfaces for predicting migration potentials of heavy metal ions and toxic chemicals released into the environment. Interface specific kinetic and thermodynamic information is essential for effective toxic spill control and the management of contaminated ground water and soils. Our poster presents recently acquired data on this crucial interaction between chromium and a sample quartz interface including adsorption isotherms, polarization data, and how pH affects the adsorption process.

The judiciary is considered by many to be the most important branch of American government because it has been entrusted with the Herculean task of protecting the people from tyranny by both their government and each other. In this role as protector there is significant power and the threat from other political forces that would be eager to control or exert influence over the judicial branch. The potential for outside political influence is one of central points in contemporary state judicial debate about whether or not there is a best method of selection from among the diverse plans represented in the fifty states. One source of the contentious and controversial nature of discussion surrounding state judicial selection is the deeper philosophical dispute over the desirability of the judicial branch to be independent of other elements in the political process, and therefore able to make unpopular decisions that are found to be unfavorable to the other branches of government, the people or both, versus the desirability of accountability, which values the popular will and appears more aligned with Americas democratic principles. The purpose of this research is to examine the continuation of an elected state judiciary within the framework of Americas founding principles, the independence and accountability debate, and will answer the question: why have systems of elected judiciaries survived if they are incompatible with the ideal role of the judiciary as the protector of minority rights? This involves both a historical analysis of the development of the elected judiciary as well a review of the practical problems that the elected judiciary faced today.

We conducted the following research project for the Junior Tutorial in Applied Microeconomics with Professor Leon Moses (Econ 395) in Spring 2002. Our goal was to establish a relationship between the percentage a minority consitutes in a specific U.S. metropolitan area and the level of racial wage discrimination in that area. We looked at the black and Hispanic populations in over 300 metropolitan areas. Using econometric analysis we established a significant relationship between the wage gap and the minority population proportion for African-Americans. We find that blacks do not benefit from living in a city with a relatively large black population. The analysis did not yield statistically significant results for the Hispanic population due to data limitations. The findings contradict the idea that a large group will be able to use its political power to improve its own economic situation. They support Gary Becker's model of discrimination. The results also provide evidence for more comprehensive socio-economic explanations of the persistence of wage differentials, which, for instance, incorporate the quality of schooling, and occupational crowding. We believe our project would make for an excellent presentation because: it provides a contemporary insight into the current labor market conditions for minorities in the U.S.;it supports a well-established economic model introduced by Gary Becker; it is understandable and interesting for students in the social sciences in general, and lends itself to further investigation; the project is a motivating example of how regular course work can lead to independent undergraduate research, and of what resources are available at Northwestern; and the results can be effectively presented in a poster presentation.

In the 1850's, the fate of a 6 year-old boy shook the foundations of national, international, and religious politics. When he was still an infant, Edgardo Mortara's family housekeeper changed his fate-- and that of church/state relations in Italy-- forever. Anna Morisi did the unthinkable, and yet all too common-- she baptized a Jewish baby. During the rampant conservatism of the Catholic Church in the 19th century, papal policy toward the Jews is a striking precendent for later Nazi racial laws. The papacy created and maintained the first Jewish ghettos, forbid interracial marriage, and adopted the use of the yellow emblem. Perhaps the most disturbing example of the pontific opinion of the Jews, however, was the great honor and prestige bestowed on those Catholic citizens of Italy who took it upon themselves to baptize Jewish children. According to Papal law, the baptism of a Jewish child was the irreversible work of God, resulting in an immediate conversion. This child could not live with his parents-- the Jews would rather murder their own babies than to allow them to lead Christian lives. The result was the regular forced baptism and kidnapping of Jewish children with the hope that, once converted, they may be used to as tools to ensure the conversion of all Judaism.
