My paper examines the effects the Edgardo Mortara case (the results of which included the weakening of Papal power and Napoleon III's increased desire to assist in the unification of Italy), the role of the Houses of Catechism (where the children were held as ransom) as a means of creating a 'currency of souls', and the implications of baptism on the definition and conceptualization of the social identites of 'the Catholic,' 'the Jew,' and 'the Convert.'

95% percent of reported cases of breast cancer start as mammary duct carcinomas. Ductal Lavage may prove to be an important tool in assessing risk for breast cancer. Ductal Lavage involves catheterizing mammary ducts, passing a saline solution through the catheter, and recollecting the solution. The saline solution collects cells, which are screened for malignancy, as well as hormones. This study focuses on the relationship between different hormones in the lavage fluid and their impact on methods for breast cancer detection. Under the guidance of Dr. Robert Chatterton, my work has been to assay the collected saline solutions to find the concentration of different hormones. Before running tests, the cells are removed from solution, and then the solution is purified. High estrogen levels increase a person’s risk of developing breast cancer. The objective of this research is to develop a method for measurement of estradiol (the main form of estrogen in the body), potential precursors of estradiol and products of estradiol actions in the breast. Tests to assay estradiol in blood and saliva already exist, but research suggests that testing breast fluid may provide a more accurate diagnosis for a person’s risk. Extracted samples are assayed for nine analytes that all contribute to the production or marking of estradiol. Preliminary results have shown links between certain analytes that may be important in finding biomarkers for high risk of breast cancer.

Abstract Previous researchers (Clark & Wells, 1995) have constructed a model of how negatively biased cognitive processes both before and after social situations perpetuate social anxiety. There is support for negatively biased memories in the literature, as well as correlations between the onset and maintenance of anxious symptoms and rumination. The current study, based on Catherine Garrett’s (2000) study, examines anticipatory processing in Clark and Wells’ model by looking at the causal role of memories and rumination in social anxiety. High and low socially anxious participants were asked to recall either a negative or positive memory before interacting with another study participant. Anxious behaviors during the interaction were videotaped, and participants were asked to report their anxious feelings before and after the interaction. I predict that participants who recalled a negative memory would show more anxious behavior and feel more anxious during the interaction than participants asked to recall a positive memory, but especially so for high socially anxious participants. Also, I predict that highly anxious individuals who are high on trait rumination and who recall a negative social memory will be the most anxious group. The results will be reported when the study is completed, in Spring Quarter 2003.

The electrical signals transmitted through neurons are generated by the actions of ion channels, and differences in the properties of ion channels among neurons result in different signal processing capabilities. Cerebellar Purkinje cells contain a set of intrinsic ion channels through which ionic currents flow to produce spontaneous, high-frequency action potentials. In this study, electrophysiological recordings of action potentials and ionic currents were made in acutely dissociated Purkinje cells. These data were used to develop computer models of these ion channels, which were then incorporated into a single-compartment simulation of a Purkinje cell body. This simulation was used determine the roles of particular ionic currents in spontaneous high-frequency firing. Also, some strains of ataxic mice possess mutations in the sodium channel gene NaV1.6 and have been shown to have a disruption in an unusual ionic current called resurgent sodium current. The Purkinje neurons of these mice also show disruptions in their ability to generate spontaneous action potentials. Therefore, the model of resurgent sodium current was altered to reflect the differences observed in mutant mice. These changes in the sodium current model were introduced into the simulation of a Purkinje cell body to determine their influence on spontaneous high-frequency firing. This study clarifies the nature of resurgent sodium current in mice with mutations in the NaV1.6 sodium channel gene and supports a role for resurgent sodium current in promoting and accelerating high-frequency spontaneous firing in cerebellar Purkinje cells.

My work was an analysis of blood vessel diameter in the cat retina. Professor Linsenmeier's team performed the experiments and took magnified pictures of the retinal blood vessels. I then used these pictures from each specimen to compare the diamters using a statistical approach. The results yielded a negative trend which is depicted in a series of graphs.

Creating a tool to measure the effects of anesthetics on the drosophila fruit fly. Using the results to test mutant fruit flies inorder to discover what the anesthetics are actually effecting. Give a person one advil and they feel less pain. Give a person two advils and their headache is completely gone. Give a person one dose of anesthetics and they feel no pain. Give a person two doses of anesthetics and they die. This poster presentation will shine light on the future of anesthetics and how we can creat a more perfect drug.

On the synthesis optimization of Barium Ferrite nanoparticles: The desire for ferromagnetic nanoparticle systems with increased magnetic capabilities has become common to many advanced technological applications, including non-surgical cancer therapy and high-density recording media. It has been shown that the Barium Ferrite (BaFe12O19) system demonstrates magnetic capabilities far exceeding those of traditional ferromagnetic nanoparticle systems such as Fe3O4. To maximize the magnetic capability aforementioned, the synthesis conditions must be optimized so that the presence antiferromagnetic matter, such that that a-Fe2O3, be reduced to a minimum. Through the variance of both the Iron/Barium precursor stoicheometric ratio and the preheating and heating schedules, the optimal synthesis conditions are obtained by comparing relative intensities of X-ray diffraction peaks for each combination of variables tested. It is concluded that the system with an Iron:Barium ratio of 11.5:1 preheated at 450 C for 4 hours and heated at 950 C 2 hours yields the least antiferromagnetic matter, making it the best synthesis method to date for the Barium Ferrite system.

My project is a performance ethnography dealing with media portrayals and public perceptions of midwives and homebirths in America today. It is a one-person show based on ethnographic interviews with parents and midwives, as well as cultural texts, medical information, and media studies theory. It explores how the media, as a reporting outlet portrays midwives in times of tragedy, giving a false overall sense of their incompetence. By presenting diverse opinions and information, the performance seeks to both identify this innate problem, and begin to remedy it by presenting midwives in a more unbiased light. The performance aesthetics are low key, but the content is rich. Performance as a way of presenting ethnography is particularly beneficial because it both reaches a wide audience, and gives a voice to the informants and subjects of research. I believe it is an innovative way to present information, while maintaining academic integrity.

When human beings discuss the concept of irrationality, they very frequently refer to their own perspectives of other people's decisions. This sort of 'subjective' irrationality is always open to perspectival interpretation and, therefore, rarely agreed upon collectively. Conversely, a much more pervasive and dangerous 'internal' irrationality can be objectively recognized and, with few exceptions, philosophers since Plato have confirmed and described its existence. These same philosophers, however, disagree with an almost stunning regularity over the psychological mechanisms at work in the objectively irrational mind. Donald Davidson, in a series of articles, has written the standard contemporary explanation for weakness of the will (akrasia), perhaps the most commonly discussed and debated form of internal irrationality. In his explanation, he adopts what he believes are Freudian concepts in order to explain how a human being can defy rationality, which he believes is constitutive of thought. Upon examination, however, the principles Davidson adopts are not Freudian at all; instead, when taken to their logical extreme, they point to the homuncular (or rationally divided) mind as the primary mechanism of irrationality, a concept anathema to psychoanalytic theory. In an examination of both contemporary and Freudian explanations of weakness of the will, I point out Davidson's error in assuming a homuncular mind; I continue to examine and argue for Freud's explanations of irrationality, noting that they provide a far smoother and more rational explanation for the everyday psychological phenomenon of akrasia. In conclusion, I argue that, while the Freudian mind looks quite different from contemporary perspectives, it offers a number of explanatory advantages for both internal irrationality and, more generally, human motivation.

As a co-op at the ITW Technology Center, I worked with Wilsonart International on a project involving their laminate flooring. In preparation for marketing their new glueless flooring product, Wilsonart needed to find a sealer that could be applied to the edge profile of the laminate planks in order to prevent swell upon incidental water contact. While glueless floors offer an unparalleled ease of installation, they do not necessarily provide the water protection that a glued floor has. This poster presentation examines the steps taken to identify and test the edge sealer that is currently in production with Wilsonart’s glueless floor products.

There is very strong evidence that some stars orbit black holes. Gas can be stripped off the star and spiral around the black hole, forming an accretion disk. These disks are heated to thousands of degrees by viscous heating and glow in the x-ray spectrum. Most of these x-ray systems can be explained by a normal star orbiting a stellar mass black hole--one formed at the end of a single normal star’s evolution. Certain sources-- known as ultra luminous x-ray sources, or ULXs--are too luminous to be explained by stellar mass black holes. One explanation is that the black holes in these systems have masses between stellar mass black holes and supermassive black holes found in the center of galaxies. Computer simulations of these intermediate mass black holes (IMBHs) have been made, and their radiative properties compared with observation to determine if these IMBHs are valid candidates for ULXs. If they are not found to be a viable explanation, it will lend support to the theory that ULXs are not abnormally luminous, but that their x-rays are focused into beams, making the sources appear brighter. Because ULXs are observed to be transient--having both bright phases and dim phases, the models are tested to see if they also exhibit transience. By determining which models are transient and for how long, many parameters of the system can be estimated. Such properties include masses of IMBHs, masses of companion stars, lifetimes of the systems, and formation rates of the systems.

title: Imaging of the Supernova Remnant G352.7-0.1 with the Very Large Array (VLA) of Radio Telescopes
abstract: Supernovae are the violent, explosive deaths of massive stars - some of the most energetic events in our universe. As the star exhausts it's nuclear fuel, the core can no longer support itself against the grip of enormous gravitational forces. The collapse of the star results in a powerful blast wave that ejects the envelope of a star into interstellar space. A supernova remnant (SNR) forms as the explosion spreads out into the surrounding medium. When the supernova remnant propagate into a dense molecular cloud, a shock wave is driven into the cloud. Intense stimulated emission from OH molecular at 1720MHz are known as MASERs (the microwave counterpart to LASERS). These MASERs act as very bright 'signposts' of the interaction between the SNR shock wave and the adjacent molecular cloud. Here, we examine the VLA image of the SNR G352.7-0.1 to determine if this remnant is interacting with a molecular cloud, and how this knowledge improves our understanding of the physical processes the SNR is undergoing.

title: Nanostructures and Surface Passivation Techniques for Type II InAs/GaSb Infrared Superlattice Detectors
abstract: Infrared detection shows promise in improving applications such as missile and target tracking, free space communications, non-invasive examination in medical and industrial settings, and space radiometry and spectroscopy. Recent developments in highly sensitive quantum well infrared detectors have allowed scientists and researchers to build more sensitive detection and control systems based on these devices. Today, commercially available infrared photodetectors generally consist of interband HgCdTe and InAsSb materials or utilize intersubband transitions with quantum well infrared photodetectors (QWIP). Disadvantages to these devices include high Auger recombination and thermal generation rates. As an alternative to the conventional infrared detector, Type II superlattices were first suggested by L. Esaki, et. al. in 1977 due to their misaligned band alignment, which results in lower Auger recombination and higher device detectivity. These materials are also attractive because they may potentially allow room temperature and low power operation. The term ‘misaligned band alignment’ refers to the broken gap where the conduction band edge of InAs has a lower energy than the valence band of the GaSb (in the InAs/GaSb material system). Recently, researchers at the Center for Quantum Devices have demonstrated high-performance Type II InAs/GaSb superlattice photon detectors operating in the very long wavelength infrared range (VLWIR). These detectors have cutoff wavelengths of 18.8 and over 30 um. Type II detectors with 32 um cutoff wavelength were the first demonstrated in this material system. The InAs/GaSb superlattice band gap can be engineered to vary through the range of 0 to approximately .3 eV.

Funded by the Circumnavigator's Club, this past summer I traveled to eight countries of the developing world, studying how American factories impacted the development of the communities they operated in. I conducted numerous interviews, both formal ones with factory managers, economists, journalists and trade union organizers as well as more informal ones with factory workers, community residents, street vendors and other small scale entrepreneurs. I took photos, kept copious notes, and made many audio recordings of the sounds and songs of the places I visited. I have already put together a audio/visual presentation, and I am now working on creating a performance based on my experiences integrating these source materials with character sketches and monologues. Through the combination of media and the intimacy of personal narration, I hope to recreate some of what I saw and learned and in doing so, create a dialogue about some of the social issues of our generation and the globalized world it is our privelege and responsibility to explore.

Circadian rhythms act to synchronize an organism’s internal environment to the daily 24-hour changes in the external environment. The internal circadian clock has been localized to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the brain, which serves as the master oscillator for the circadian system. In the past ten years, researchers have begun to unravel the molecular mechanisms underlying circadian rhythms in the SCN, such as the monumental discovery of the Clock gene in 1997 by the Takahashi Lab. In this molecular mechanism, the casein kinase I (CKI) plays a pivotal role in circadian rhythm regulation. A natural, spontaneous mutation was discovered for CKI in Syrian hamsters, known as the tau mutation. This tau mutation delays phosphorylation activity of CKI, which results in a shortened circadian rhythm as measured by the locomotor activity rhythm. Further DNA analysis revealed the specific site of the tau mutation in the CKI gene, where a thymidine base replaces a cytosine base, thus causing an amino acid substitution of arginine to cysteine. Because the tau mutation in CKI is expressed in Syrian hamsters, a mammalian species, I hypothesize that the mutation would also be expressed in mice due to DNA sequence similarity. Therefore, my current research project is to insert the tau mutation into mice and observe their circadian rhythms. In the future, I hope to breed tau mutant mice with mice containing other circadian gene mutations, such as the Clock mutation, and observe the combinatory effects.

The student will research methods and design techniques of minimizing power usage of driving a solar car to a destination. In order to save energy, the student will study the effects of car drag to determine the amount of power needed for various scenarios. Three types of drag forces, aerodynamic, rotational, and rolling, combine to prevent the car from maintaining constant speed once a certain momentum is achieved. In addition, the student will find the best layout of solar cells so that more average power can be charged to the battery pack. Various parameters in solar cell layout include bypass diodes, power-point trackers, and shape of vehicle shell. Besides the shape and orientation of the solar array, solar energy input depends on diurnal variation, seasonal variation, and annual variation of the sun. From the research, an efficient control strategy will be developed to regulate the vehicle’s speed under various terrain conditions for better solar-power management. Furthermore, other methods of power generation will be explored, such as magnetic generation of power through mechanical force.

Psychologists and linguists have for many years extensively examined the development of language and categorization in young children. Past studies investigating the types of strategies used by children in the rapid acquisition of word meanings and concepts have found that they display distinct patterns in their extension of labels to novel objects. Some researchers have explained the origins of these biases as learned associations between perceptual information. This Dumb Attentional Mechanism means that children form word meanings based upon similarities in physical appearances. However, it is also possible that children employ intelligent strategies to determine whether new objects belong in the same categories. Perhaps children at an early age possess a complex understanding about categories that go beyond simple perceptual similarities but are ultimately bound by commonality in conceptual ontology. Implied in this hypothesis is that perceptual cues are merely gateways into the conceptual knowledge possessed by children and not the sole determiners of categorization patterns. This study attempts to examine whether children’s existing conceptual information of target objects would affect their categorization of new objects. The effects children’s conceptual knowledge is explored through the introduction of target objects labeled with animate and artifact information and the extension of labels to novel test objects differing by size, shape, and texture. Since objects are identical between the two conditions, differences in word extension patterns must result from children’s ability to process and use conceptual knowledge specific to the category described.

Within the southern Peruvian Andean highlands there is an interesting mix of histories. Several ancient civilizations occupied this region, some overlapping in chronology. The Torata Valley, which lies in the upper reaches of the Moquegua River drainage basin, is an excellent example with which to study these interactions. This region of Peru is representative of the many powers involved in building and maintaining empires in the Andes. Its harsh climate and rugged terrain proved to be an element that was essential to tame in order to ensure societal success. Here, the agricultural techniques each society employed shaped the social fabric and destiny of the region and beyond. The introduction of farming to this high sierra region began with the Wari influence. Their irrigation and terracing techniques provided the framework for agricultural success during their occupation and for future cultures. This introduction was a turning point for the southern Peruvian Andes, as no other culture had attempted agricultural endeavors at such high elevations. Using existing archeological information from the Torata Valley, I utilized the ArcView 3.2 GIS program to create maps and statistics analyzing the slope stability indexes of the high sierra farming efforts employed by the Wari, Tiwanaku, Estiquiña, and the Inca. Using aerial photographs and existing topographic information as a basis for interpretation, I was able to produce a numerical framework with which to compare these agricultural systems. Within ArcView 3.2, I primarily utilized an extension called SINMAP (Stability Index MAPping). This program allowed me to manipulate digital elevation models (DEMs) to calculate the numerical results of the slope stability analysis. The purpose of this study is to expand on the research in the Torata Valley and to provide important statistical data relating to ancient agricultural systems. The numerical index of slope stability provides the basis to determine which systems were best suited to high sierra slopeland farming. As a result, I am able to give an approximation as to which systems were constructed and/or maintained to optimum levels based on their current conditions. The findings will also relate to tectonic vulnerability of individual agricultural systems. Offering evidence in support of terrace reclamation in southern Peru is an application of these findings. Using the most stable ancient terraces as a model, I am able to provide numerical data in support of sustainable terrace farming in southern Peru.

The project I am working on is entitled 'The Computational Discovery of Novel Metabolic Pathways'. My work mainly consists of analyzing enzyme databases to recognize patterns and modifying existing computer code to model biological pathways. Concerning the enzyme databases, a four-digit system is currently used to classify enzymes. For example, the number 1.1.1.1 classifies a specific enzyme. The fourth number indicates which specific substrate is used in a reaction, while the first three numbers make more general classifications. However, we know that all fourth level reactions within a third level are usually the same. In other words, enzymes 1.1.1.1 through 1.1.1.251 all perform the same reaction on the same functional group, but they do this on different substrates. Therefore, we can generalize enzyme reactions according to their third level classifications. There are over 4,000 fourth level reactions, while there are only about 250 third level categories; consequently, generalizing the enzyme reactions facilitates our job. Occasional problems arise when generalizing the enzyme reactions. There are many fourth level reactions that do not exactly fit with the other reactions in the same third level category, and this is one of the main reasons why I analyze the enzyme databases. For each step of a biological pathway, a general reaction will give us the next expected product in the pathway along with many other unexpected products because the general reactions work on all functional groups in a molecule. This fact will hopefully allow us to discover novel metabolic pathways.

The Gaber Lab studies the Hsp90 protein and its associated co-chaperones in Yeast. Hsp90 is typically the most abundant chaperone in eukaryotic cytoplasm, and its expression is essential for life. Based on studies in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that examined the function of Hsp90 in vivo, Hsp90 is required for nascent chain folding of a subset of proteins and refolding of denatured proteins. It also has regulatory interactions with a variety of important signal transduction proteins. Hsp90 exists in the cytosol as a diamer and functions by binding to several other co-chaperones in a complex pathway. These associated co-chaperones include immunophilins like Cpr6 and Cpr7 that bind to Hsp90 through three units of the tetratricopeptide repeat or TPR domain. Hsp90 also binds other cellular proteins including Cns 1, a TPR domain containing cyclophilin (also essential for life), and Sti 1. My project involves screening a yeast multi-copy genomic library and searching for suppresors of lethal mutations in known genes/proteins that are already associated with the Hsp90 pathways. Using genetics, I have created a Cns1TS and Cpr7 delete genotype. Cns1TS is a temperature sensitive mutation in the Cns 1 gene that confers slow growth to cells at high temperatures. Cpr7 delete cells have slow growth at all temperatures. These mutations together provide conditional inviability that can then be used in a genetic screen to look for suppressors of this synthetically lethal double mutant. My poster will deal mostly with the process of genetic screening and the results obtained to date in my own particular multi-copy screening experiment.

PocketClassmate is an integrated software suite that addresses a problem common to note takers in the classroom or the conference room: notes taken in one context often lose their meaning when reviewed at a later time. Using PocketClassmate, a user can take notes that are dynamically linked to active presentation slides, enabling subsequent viewing within the context of the presentation. Because the presentation and note taking applications are linked, speakers are also able to get immediate and ongoing feedback from their audience as to interest levels and possible confusion. Students using PocketClassmate can engage in more effective note taking and use the system as a means of sharing information with others. Instructors, utilizing the feedback provided by PocketClassmate, can identify areas where greater explanation is warranted and tailor a presentation to the needs of that particular group of students. They can also use the information gathered by the system to assess the overall effectiveness of their presentations. While designed for the classroom, PocketClassmate is the first step in developing technologies to support ongoing interaction between information providers and consumers. In effect, the system turns a one-time presentation into a living document through which communication is mediated and contextualized. In any situation where there is a presentation and an audience, this technology can be used to provide an exciting new level of interaction and communication.

With his 1999 paper, “Algorithms for Selfish Agents”, computer scientist Noam Nisan of Hebrew University introduced a new area of theoretical computer science later termed “algorithmic mechanism design” (AMD). A combination of mechanism design from microeconomic literature and algorithm design, AMD is an acknowledgment of the of selfish motives of many agents in modern computation, especially over the Internet. A few well-studied applications of this idea is for sharing the cost of multicast transmissions, task allocation, and network routing. My research with Professor Ming-Yang Kao involves selfish network routing using the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). The problem with network routing among selfish agents is that the cost of network traffic, i.e. latency, is only known locally. The source, however, would like to minimize the latency to its destination. It therefore must provide incentives to the participating nodes to tell the truth. In “A BGP-Based Mechanism for Lowest-Cost Routing” Feigenbaum, et al., introduced a distributed algorithm for routing between networks that provides such incentives, in the form of payments, and runs on top of BGP. The algorithm is not practical for realistic BGP networks, though, because: 1. It assumes a uniform routing policy, which is not the case on the Internet. 2. The payments may be arbitrarily high, which may not be acceptable to source nodes. 3. There is still some opportunity and incentive for lying. My work explores these problems, in an attempt to design more practical incentive-compatible routing algorithms.

In his life and work, Samuel Beckett engages a foundational nothingness, a void which underlies language and identity. This 'aporia' recurs throughout his work, manifested by alienation, disintegration, solitude, silence, absurdity, and doubt. In the volume and range of his writings, for which he ultimately won the Nobel Prize in 1969, his deeply human vision elevates tenacity above all. He represents a hope that is only possible with the recognition of hopelessness, and a compassion that lies beyond the extremity of degradation. As a writer, actor, and director, I was drawn to Beckett's challenging worldview and his revolutionary use of the empty space. I approach this material with the tools of a critic and an actor, seeking both deeper readings of his work and understanding of the author. Following two years of research in Paris, Dublin, Reading, New Haven, and Evanston, I crafted 'On Going On,' a one-person non-fiction performance of Beckett adapted from his complete works. That performance, produced at Northwestern in November, is the subject of my thesis paper, a segment of which I wish to present at the Symposium. Examining both the work of Beckett and my own subsequent creation, I will explore the question: what is the meaning and implication of aporia as a worldview for the artist? I pose a paradox: how can the nothingness of language be expressed through the prolific production or performance of words? What is the meaning of the choice to 'go on,' when one 'can't go on'?

My project is based on a settlement survey done in Chan, Belize. The project, led by Cynthia Robin was geared towards analyzing the peripheral settlments of a major Maya civic center. In this case, we looked at a small peripheral village near the site of Xunantunich. Xunantunich is a typical civic center with substantial pyramid structures and a plaza. My thesis specifically looks at the agricultural system of this village and analyzes the relationship between the subsistence technology and the settlement pattern. For the most part, I am concentrating on the terrace structures which are found in large quantities within our surveyed region. The main goal of this paper is to show that intensive agriculture was practiced to a major extent in the Maya region.

One's generativity represents one's concern for and commitment to promoting the well-being of the next generation. Erikson (1963) saw generativity as the main psychosocial task of middle adulthood. Yet, adults differ substantially with respect to the strength and scope of their generative attitudes and behaviors (McAdams, 2001a). The purpose of this study is to examine the relationship between individual differences in generativity on the one hand and midlife narratives of parenting on the other. Secondarily, the study also examines gender differences in narratives of parenting. The first hypothesis is that highly generative adults will have significantly more developmental themes in their life stories. The concept of generativity implies, by definition, a preoccupation with growth and progress. Developmental themes address this. Looking for examples of active involvement in their children's' lives, subject's narratives have been scrutinized in order to test whether or not highly generative people convey proportionately more developmental themes in their narratives than those who scored lower on generativity. A second hypothesis is that female gender roles, which are revealed through parenting narratives, will emphasize nurturing themes for their children. More specifically, self-actualization on the part of their progeny may be revealed as a goal of these women. These expectations often lead to women being more expressive and nurturing than males. Hypothesis 3 states that as a result of male gender roles they will have more socialization themes in their parenting narratives. These themes concern expectations, standards as well as an emphasis on learning through role modeling.

This past Winter quarter, I conducted an independant research project (ESAM 399) with Professor David Chopp. The work was based upon previous research by Professor Chopp and several professors from various other scientific and engineering disciplines. During the quarter, I developed a mathematical model for the growth of a Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm in a spherical shape. The work is based on a previous paper describing the one-dimensional growth of a biofilm on a flat surface. Since both papers model P. aeruginosa, the kinetics of growth are the same. However, the model of the system dynamics and diffusing equations had to be re-derived for the new geometry. Once the model was complete and boundary conditions derived, the system of equations was solved using a finite difference approximation method. I constructed a MATLAB program to solve this system. Currently, Professor Chopp and I are working out the few remaining bugs in the program. Finally, the results of the spherical model will be compared to the results of the previous flat-film model.

I will be presenting my senior thesis which is on Navajo Grassroots Organizations and their construction of Leetso, the Navajo word for Uranium. I will start with a brief history of uranium mining on the Navajo Nation and then give current statistics from community based health risk assessment surveys the Uranium Education Program at Dine College is currently working on. My paper will focus on Grassroots Activism on the Navajo Nation, set within the context of past and present uranium mining, by looking at the Navajo's struggle to identify a community problem, name it, organize themselves, draw up resolutions, and attack the identified problem, working within the Navajo Nation government, as well as the United States Government. Three main issues at the heart of their progress are funding, inability to form a united front (there are many grassroots organizations involved in lobbying the US government but as one of my consultants said, they aren't all singing the same song), and a general lack of hard evidence/research on the subject of Uranium Mining and Milling, its effects on the environment and populations, past, present, and future. My analysis will look these issues within the larger context of Iron Triangle politics, comparing the grassroots organizations' approach to lobbying Congress to other environmental activist groups that have gone before them; i.e. the Wolf Fund and its fight to reintroduce the wolf to Yellowstone, activist groups trying to stop logging in the Northwest to save an endangered species, the Spotted Owl, and many other political/economic/environmental battles through out the history of the United States.

This study draws from and expands on several previous studies on lying and personal relationships. Specifically, the study examines lying between same-sex friends in a laboratory setting. A main objective of the study is to compare the frequency and nature of lies in male/male versus female/female friendships. Furthermore, the experiment examines the predictors of everyday lying in college students. With these objectives, the research attempts to use a more comprehensive and reliable approach to studying lying in close friendships. It was hypothesized that males will use more self-oriented lies (lies told to benefit themselves), while females will use more other-oriented lies (lies told to benefit others) in their interactions with same-sex friends. It was also predicted that social anxiety, social potency, aggression, traditionalism, and parental control would all predict rates of lying. In the study, participants were asked to complete a math task as well as a short-essay on a social problem. Also, participants completed several personality and personal background questionnaires. After receiving feedback for both tasks (all feedback was false), participants discussed their performances on the tasks with each other. In discussing the math task, participants only had access to their own evaluations. However, when discussing the results of the essay task, they only had access to their partner’s evaluation. In relaying feedback to each other, the pairs of friends were observed to see how much information from the evaluations they chose to reveal and how they presented this information to their friends (ie. fabrications, exaggerations etc.). Males were predicted to tell more self-serving lies when discussing their performance on the math task; whereas, females were predicted to tell more other-oriented lies when relaying feedback from the essay task to their friends.

Perceptual priming refers to the phenomenon whereby experience with a stimulus induces systematic changes in subsequent processing of that same stimulus. Looking at a face, for example, alters how that person’s face is recognized when viewed subsequently, as indexed by increased accuracy or reduced response time. Perceptual priming can be disrupted by various stimulus transformations. Priming would be reduced, for example, if a very different image or view of the same face was initially presented, or if only the person’s name was initially presented. Here, we measured event-related potentials (ERPs) associated with perceptual priming of faces. Participants first attempted to memorize 80 pre-experimentally unknown faces. The next day they viewed faces and judged each according to whether or not they remembered it from the learning session. Half of the faces were familiar (i.e., from the learning session) and half were unfamiliar. Each face was presented twice in the task; half of the initial face presentations were inverted and half were upright; all second presentations were upright. We observed a positive-going ERP modulation for second versus first presentations of familiar faces around 250 ms occipitally. This positivity was apparent only for faces presented upright both times. A similar topography was observed for second versus first presentations of unfamiliar faces. The sensitivity of this ERP modulation to the stimulus transformation from first to second presentation suggests that it reflects primed perceptual processing (i.e. structural encoding). This ERP modulation thus specifically indexes the time course of priming-induced changes in perceptual processing.

title: An Internet-Enabled Remote Monitoring System for Civil Infrastructure
abstract: Owners and operators of civil infrastructure systems - roads, bridges, tunnels, mines, quarries, and so forth - are often faced with the task of monitoring the health of a large number of complex facilities. Remote data acquisition systems have emerged as a means of providing some insight on the health of the facility without having to have engineers on site at all times. However, these remote monitoring systems produce copious amounts of data, and the engineers responsible for analysis of the data are often overwhelmed by the tedious tasks of data archiving and processing. To mitigate this problem, I have developed an Internet-enabled remote monitoring system which automatically collects, archives, processes, and displays data from remote monitoring systems. The data are displayed in near-real time in a graphical format on a Web site accessible to concerned parties- engineers, managers, and, where appropriate, the traveling public.

Energy plays a significant role in our economy, but exactly how significant it is an ongoing debate. On one hand, over the past fifty years, energy intensity (energy per dollar of GDP) on average has been declining. This statistic causes people to believe that energy is not important to the economy, or at least diminishes the importance of energy’s role. On the other hand, information and other electrically powered technologies have been spreading exponentially fast. Our economy is more interconnected and automated now than it has ever been before. Energy intensity is thus a limited and inaccurate proxy statistic for energy importance. I would like to explore the statistic of elasticity. Energy elasticities are measurements of sensitivity between energy and other factors, such as price, income, and various other substitution sources. I am looking at own price elasticity, a statistic which answers the question “If the price of energy increased by one percent, by how many percent would use decrease?” If this number is less then one, then energy would be considered an inelastic good, therefore we cannot easily substitute it for other goods and it is indeed very important. I am looking at both long and short run elasticities, and so far, my results are consistent with my expectations. I am using GLS regression analysis on panel data from 30 years across 50 states, and the data shows energy to be an inelastic good in both, the short and the long run.

This presentation outlines a project testing the generative ability of a cognitive model of musical improvisation presented by Jeff Pressing (in his chapter in Generative Processes in Music, 1988). The model attempts to describe the way in which an improvising musician makes musical decisions--that is, how the musician decides what to play and how to play it. Pressing's model requires that one take into consideration the performer's musical vocabulary, technical considerations brought about by the type of instrument being played (saxophone, trumpet, drums, etc.) and also the musical context: what the other musicians in the group are playing, the genre of music and the basic rules that go along with it, and other such factors. By demonstrating that these factors influence the musical choices of a performer, Pressing's model presents a very plausible case for the type of processes underlying creative or improvised behavior. My project tests whether or not Pressing's model can result in technically and stylistically appropriate improvisations. Since the author is a jazz bassist, the model is being used to create jazz bass lines. The project creates a representative vocabulary, designs a musical context, and then applies the model to generate some bass lines. The vocabulary was created from transcriptions of Paul Chambers' bass lines. All of the transcribed lines come from 12-bar blues tunes from the late 1950s and early 60s, thus defining the musical context within a type of song and a coherent style. Finally, the project compares these artificially generated lines with real ones to examine the success of the model in creating a characteristic improvisation.

title: When Good Ideas Make Bad Policy
abstract: My paper uncovers the detrimental effects of criminalizing intentional/reckless HIV-transmission on America's health epidemic. Although criminalization may appear congruent with the purposes American criminal law (specifically retribution, utilitarianism, and deterrence), idiosyncrasies specific to HIV-transmission ultimately render this legal approach an ineffectual waste of gravely scarce resources. So while criminalizing reckless/intentional HIV-transmission may seem like a very good idea, it is in fact very bad policy. Understanding this discrepancy requires assessing criminalization at both academic and grass roots levels. It requires understanding why criminalization arose as a response to this public health crisis in the first place, how it has been practiced, how and why strategies have been revised, and whether or not it ultimately hits its intended targets. This paper will address all of these things in order to explain why criminalization is an ineffective tool with which to fight America’s AIDS epidemic, and consequently why it threatens, not protects Americans from the danger of this devastating virus. Chapter Two will examine the appeal of criminalization, why it seems to fit so well within our political and legal infrastructure—essentially, what makes it seem like such a good idea. Chapter Three will follow the evolution of criminalization from prosecution under traditional criminal, leading to an examination of HIV-Specific Statutes in Chapter Four. These two chapters will explain not only why these transitions occurred, but also why none of them met tremendous success. Looking on the practice of criminalization in Chapters Three and Four, Chapter Five will present overarching criticisms of this method, highlighting its problems and deficits. While Chapters Two through Five stem from fairly traditional academic sources, such as law review, journal, newspaper, and other articles, Chapter Six offers a more intimate, grass roots look at the issue through several interest group interviews. From the real-life criminalization front, representatives from these groups provide an invaluable insight to the practical impact of criminalization on our domestic AIDS epidemic. Considering their answers to questions and problems posed in Chapters Two through Five, I will use Chapter Seven to reconcile scholarly accounts, policy initiatives, and interest group experiences in addressing my thesis’ focus. By the end, I will argue that a good idea can translate to bad policy because an idea doesn’t live on the ground—something that makes a lot of sense in theory can take a serious beating on the streets. Looking at the real-life consequences of the somewhat abstract idea of criminalization exposes its inability to effectively combat the real problem: curbing the spread of HIV. If we decrease the number of people with HIV, we will inevitably decrease our chances of transmitting the virus. Because criminalization’s unintended consequences may actually increase the spread of HIV, it exacerbates, not emasculates the underlying problem.

One of the largest challenges impeding a proper route of breast cancer treatment is metastasis of the tumor. If the cancerous cells did not spread throughout the body, surgery at the primary site would be an effective treatment option. To solve this problem of metastasis, a thorough understanding of breast tumor interaction with surrounding tissues is needed. What are possible pathways for the tumor cells to use in development and what signals might be used for that purpose? One important protein that may have a role is Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-C. This protein was originally thought to be a lymphatic network marker. However, its receptor, VEGFR3, has been found on various other cell types of the body recently, such as breast duct epithelial cells. What role might these receptors have on these ducts and what might the role of VEGF-C exactly be? A possible explanation might be that VEGF-C/VEGFR3 interactions are used to induce breast duct formation. This led to the hypothesis that breast tumor cells might induce breast duct formation and use this as a possible route for metastasis. A tumor might release VEGF-C to induce duct formation and through some other interactions, use this duct network as a spreading pathway. My project deals with the role of VEGF-C/VEGFR3 in tumor cell – epithelial cell interactions and in what ways tumors might possibly use the breast duct as a pathway to metastasis using VEGF-C. The project is a preliminary study on a new hypothesis that has many direct physiological implications.

My research project compares the ethical projects of the philosopher Charles Taylor in Sources of the Self and the Radical Orthodoxy theologian John Milbank in Theology and Social Theory as each characterizes a ‘playing field’ for ethical debate, the space in which different contemporary theories interact, but also a space that possesses boundaries that limit who the competitors are. Describing the playing field rewrites what a valid argument entails, and hence, Taylor and Milbank redefine the rules and the playing field to adjust which theories are legitimate contenders. As well as utilizing similar methods, both hope, through a project of historical recovery, to reincorporate religion as a major player on the ethical field. My comparison of the two yields the relative successes of each in this wider project of restoring religious ethics as a potential player within the wider philosophical debate. The result of my project is that Taylor’s phenomenological approach is superior to Milbank’s metanarrative realism, thereby suggesting that Taylor’s method captures both the clearer understanding of agency and the more compelling description of the playing field. Milbank’s system undermines itself because of his insufficiently cautious use of post-modern, secular tools and the baggage they carry, whereas Taylor successfully reincorporates religious discourse as a valid contender without having to deny the successes of secular humanism. Thus, Taylor has accomplished Milbank’s ostensive goal of making theology its own autonomous discipline more successfully than Milbank himself. My conclusions from the project explicate some little discussed ramifications of Taylor’s work, point to serious flaws in Milbank’s work and Radical Orthodoxy, and offer a more thorough understanding of the relationship between the religious and the secular in ethics.

It is clear that Japan is in a state of transition. This transition for Japan can be seen in many aspects of Japanese life, but the strongest visible affects of this transition are played out by the youngest generation. In particular, the consumption of secondhand and English language clothing reflects one aspect of the transformation and shows the interaction between individualism and collectivism within modern Japanese society. Clothing is a special commodity as it mediates the self and society. Consumption of secondhand and English language clothing reveals Japanese ideas about fashion and consumerism and it also tells a story about globalization, capitalism and the interaction between Japan and the West through cultural hegemony.

India and China, both among the most populous nations in the world, are currently experiencing HIV/AIDS epidemics of massive proportions. UNAIDS predictions estimate that both nations will have over 20 million cases of HIV/AIDS by the year 2010. One major difference between India and China are their political systems. While both nations share many geographic and demographic similarities, one main difference is their political systems. While India’s political system is a democracy with regular national elections and liberal values, China’s political structure is very authoritarian with a one party system lacking any form of popular elections. This thesis will explain how the different political systems in India and China affect their responses to the HIV/AIDS epidemic in each respective country. I will answer the question of why India and China's responses to the AIDS epidemic within their borders have been so different, and what is causing both nations policies to fail.

The family is a central unit within the social structure of society, making understanding the family important to sociological study. One theoretical model of relationships between family members is the bargaining model. The military family is an example of an arrangement that limits the ability and function of bargaining. Employment by the military places many constraints on active-duty personnel that affect the family structure and power relationship between marriage partners. The theoretical framework for this project is based on the conflict between the greedy institutions of the military and the family, with emphasis on gender role negotiation and the trend away from the military as a two-person career. I conducted interviews with eight couples in which one spouse was an active duty officer in the United States Navy. The initial anticipation was that the respondents would report that the demands the military makes on its families, including frequent movement, loss of career opportunities, impact on children, separation, and unpaid work on the part of the spouses, would lead to conflict and dissatisfaction. The data collected, however, did not support this hypothesis. There was little conflict reported, either between the spouses or between the family and the military. Rather than establishing the family and the military as greedy institutions with separate goals, the successful Navy family combines them, dividing the labor between the two spouses. As a result, there is little conflict between the spouses, provided that both are committed to their respective role within the family-military arrangement.

This is an interview-based ethnographic study about the generation gap. A concept heavily studied in America throughout the 1970s, the generation gap has now filtered into the Navajo culture. By researching the detailed causes behind this phenomena known as the generation gap on the Navajo Nation, I will discuss the similarities and differences between the Navajo and American generation gaps. Although the Navajo use the same term as was used in America, are they actually speaking of the same idea? If so, perhaps solutions and advice offered in these American studies may be useful to the Navajo people when finding solutions to their generation gap.

title: Towards Androgyny? An Analysis of Content in Gender-Specific Magazines Over the Last Ten Years
abstract: The topic of this report is the changes gender-oriented consumer magazines have undergone in the last decade, specifically with respect to the trend of men's magazines becoming more like women's magazines and vice-versa. In an effort to qualitatively examine how each gender audience adopted topics and styles traditionally associated with the opposite gender audience, a content analysis of four magazines was conducted. Hard-copies or microfilm of the January, June, and December issues of Esquire, Cosmopolitan, Men’s Health, and Shape from 1992 to 2001 were studied as primary sources because they are marketed specifically for men (in the case of Esquire and Men’s Health) or women (in the case of Cosmopolitan and Shape). Indications of trends were gathered from observations of the covers, headlines, photographs and article content in each of the nearly 120 magazines reviewed. In the context of this report, female magazines are those which include topics such as fashion, food, dating, and self-improvement. Conversely, male magazines are those centering on topics like business, politics, travel, and sports/fitness. Thus, whether or not, and to what degree, magazines are holding to their gender-defined content and style is paramount to this paper’s qualitative analysis. The report analyzes the magazines in two pairs. General adult audience magazines Esquire and Cosmopolitan are first compared and contrasted, followed by general adult/high school audience magazines Men’s Health and Shape. Review of a decade's worth of four magazines targeted to specific gender audiences provides corroboration for the notion that men’s and women’s magazines are increasingly adopting each other’s attributes. However, conclusions also delve into how and why this trend is somewhat stronger for the tendency of men’s magazines to incorporate traditionally feminine topics of interest.

The main goal of our research is to study and characterize what happens when small amounts of Carbon Nanotubes are added to polymers. We are currently studying unprocessed single walled nanotubes, functionalized nanotubes, and various polymers. We have been doing testing and analyses in the Keck II Laboratory using the XPS and SIMS to fully understand the surface microstructures and compositions. We have also been researching in the EPIC laboratory using scanning electron microscopes including the LEO. We plan to display our progress at the Undergraduate Research Symposium including high magnification micrographs and positive results about strengthened Carbon Nanotube reinforced polymers.

Speciation affects the fate, bioavailability, and toxicity of metals in aquatic systems. It is therefore important to accurately determine this speciation and assess which species are bioavailable. In this work we are correlating the response of a biosensor to the determination of the electrochemically labile fraction of the metal. An E. Coli biosensor with merR-luxcdabe transposon was exposed to mercury concentrations in the 0-4mM range in the presence of a minimally complexing medium. Cathodic square wave voltammetry using an Ir microarray plated with Au was used to measure Hg speciation. The luminescense response of the biosensor was linear within the 0-280nM range after an exposure time of 4 hours. A drop-off in luminescence was observed at higher concentrations. The experiment was repeated in the presence of EDTA, and the response of the biosensor remained virtually identical. In contrast, the voltammetric signal illustrated that the electrochemically labile metal fraction was reduced due to metal complexation with EDTA. Toxicity was not ameliorated when bacteria was grown in the presence of EDTA proving that the Hg-EDTA complex is labile. Additional experiments will look at toxicity of Cd and Zn and will attempt to ameliorate the toxic effect through addition of other ligands.

This project was conceived when I learned in my human sexuality class (with Professor Michael Bailey) that Americans could distinguish voices of gay people from those of straight people. Even if gay and straight people say the same sentences, they are distinguishable on average. I am a native speaker of Mandarin, and I was curious about whether native Mandarin-speaking gay and straight speakers were also distinguishable. Furthermore, would someone have to be a native Mandarin speaker in order to distinguish gay and straight Mandarin speakers? Thus, I carried out the project as an Advanced Supervised Research (C97 in the Psychology Department) and recruited thirty native Mandarin-speaking subjects, half of whom were straight and half of whom were gay. The subjects were asked to read a passage in Mandarin, about a minute in length, and their voices were recorded. A different group of subjects, consisting of native English and native Mandarin speakers, were recruited to listen to these voices. Results so far indicate that on average, people can distinguish gay versus straight Mandarin speakers. Furthermore, this ability does not seem to depend on knowledge of Mandarin. For the undergraduate research symposium, I will share my findings in more detail and bring voice samples to demonstrate the difference between a typical gay and straight voice, in both English and Mandarin. The study suggests a cross-cultural trend that people can distinguish gay-sounding voices from straight-sounding ones.

The CFA Franc Zone is the world’s largest monetary union whose members share a fully convertible common currency issued by a supranational central bank. Composed of 14 West and Central African nations, this currency union presents a unique opportunity to analyze the effects of specific institutional arrangements on economic growth and development. One would expect that a fixed and externally guaranteed exchange rate together with a supranational central bank would cause low inflation, increase savings and investment, and ultimately lead to economic growth greater than that of otherwise similar countries. A cost inherent in joining a currency union arises from the fact that member governments lose the ability to pursue individual monetary policy. The monetary policy employed in the CFA zone seeks to maximize some aggregate welfare function as opposed to that of any individual country. The CFA zone countries are very small open economies that suffer from large shocks. Consequently, the correlation of the shocks faced by these countries is an important determinant of whether zone membership is a worthwhile endeavor for an individual country. Shock correlation can also provide insight into drawing optimal boundaries within the zone to group countries together that experience similar shocks, and thus lower the cost of the loss of monetary policy autonomy. I will examine the observed shock correlations and seek to explain them using econometric models. My focus is on the role of fiscal policy in shock dissipation.

A new ethynylbiphenyl cyclization reaction was characterized using photochemical techniques. The fluorescence lifetimes, fluorescence quantum yields and photocyclization quantum yields were measured in various solvents and at various temperatures to elucidate the pathway of the reaction. NMR spectroscopy, mass spectroscopy, and gas chromatography were used to identify the structures of the cyclization products.

This project is a biography of a 20th century American woman's life who experienced the century's history very intimately, including the Great Depression and World War II. She is my grandmother, Ruth Boyle, an ordinary woman with extraordinary insight and character. A series of narrative vignettes give an account of her life, incorporating elements of fiction and storytelling to elucidate actual events as revealed by family interviews and her detailed correspondence with her husband (my grandfather) during World War II when he served in the air force. Focusing largely on Ruth's life in the early 1940s, this biography fills a gap in historical accounts of World War II that largely leave out the perspective and experiences of the women at home (save for women who joined the work force in the war effort)-- women who were forced to reconstitute home life as husbands and relatives left for the war. Ruth's story reveals the feelings the war created for a young woman, married not even two years, left alone while her husband serves his country. Nine months pregnant with her first child, Ruth gives birth alone in the hospital, without the support or much contact from her husband. She watches as all of her male friends and relatives leave one by one for the service. Her everyday life offers a poignant and unique testimony to the vast scale that war pervaded the national consciousness and changed the family landscape.

Like so many other instances involving imperial powers and native populations, the question of British intervention during the Persian Constitutional Revolution (1905-1911) was a classic case of real politick versus morality. The British had the full knowledge of Russian military intervention in the counter-revolution, and of Russian atrocities in northern Persia. British statesmen had been receiving countless pleas from Professor E. G. Browne of Cambridge University, and other scholars and activists to intervene on behalf of the constitutionalists. Browne’s argument was that as the epitome of progress and liberalism, Britain had a moral obligation to help Persia find her path to progress and not let anyone (Russia) unjustly stand in the way of that path. But to ask the Russians to stop was no simple matter: the Russians and British had been allies since 1905 – an alliance that Britain desperately needed in face of a powerful and aggressive German Empire. Furthermore, the reply of many conservative British statesmen was that the Persians were not ready for democracy because they were too backwards. But did the British really believe that the Persians could not achieve democracy even in light of recent organized, peaceful mass demonstrations – events that demonstrate a vibrant, educated, and organized public sphere – which are undeniable seeds of democracy? Or was their rhetoric really cloaking their own calculated, naked self-interest? In this paper, I intend to assess the morality of British inactivity, and to investigate whether or not democracy was possible in Persia at turn of the century.

Worrying is a common process that is well utilized yet often despised among the general population. “Don’t worry,” people usually say to someone feeling anxious. “Try not to think about it.” The majority of people do indeed overcome moderate amounts of worries to continue living in a functional, satisfactory manner. Yet for a certain portion of the population, worrying is a process of immense interference. Sufferers of intense anxiety frequently experience thought intrusions which impair everyday functioning and often find dismissing their worries extraordinarily problematic. A line of research begun by Daniel Wegner has demonstrated that by attempting to suppress a thought, a person may actually incur an ironic rebound of the unwanted thought. Trying to rid oneself of a thought can lead to an ironic increase in intrusions under certain conditions. Highly anxious people meet several important criteria described by Wegner as causing unsuccessful thought suppression; my experiment sought to investigate whether highly anxious subjects would have a special difficulty suppressing thoughts as compared to a low anxiety control group. As expected, the results of the experiment have shown highly anxious subjects to possess an impairment of suppression abilities within threatening situations. When confronted with threatening information, it seems that highly anxious people first experience an influx of unpleasant thought intrusions and subsequently resort to thought suppression as a tactic to avoid the intrusions. Unfortunately, the evidence provided by this study suggests that such a strategy will often backfire, causing thought intrusions to proliferate.

title: Effects of Flow Velocity on Quorum Sensing in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Biofilms
abstract: Planktonic (i.e., free-swimming) and biofilm (i.e., surface-attached) bacteria communicate through the secretion of diffusible signaling molecules, called acyl-homoserine lactones (acyl-HSLs). When enough bacteria are present to produce the critical acyl-HSL concentration, the bacteria have a "quorum." Hence, this cell-cell signaling process is called quorum sensing. The induction of quorum sensing leads to the expression of quorum sensing controlled genes, such as those encoding virulence factors and those necessary for biofilm formation. The ability of biofilms to upregulate such genes make them more of a challenge to combat in situ. My research objective is to determine how velocity affects quorum size, which is the number of cells required for the induction of quorum sensing, in a Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm. My hypothesis is that the quorum size will decrease as the velocity increases, because increased flow velocity has been correlated with increased biofilm density. Biofilms were grown in silicone tubing with medium flowing at different velocities. The experiments were inoculated with a strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa containing a transcriptional fusion between gfp (green fluorescent protein) and lasB (a quorum sensing controlled gene). When quorum sensing is induced, gfp is expressed, and the bacterium fluoresces. For each velocity, quorum sensing induction was monitored as a function of biomass surface coverage. Thus far, two flow velocities have been examined: 0.1 mm/s and 1.0 mm/s, and the quorum sizes appear to be similar. To obtain more definitive results, I am currently running biofilm experiments with a velocity of 10 mm/s.

In the last decade, the ways that people use media have changed in response to expanding options, which include the possibility of creating avatars and handles which the media user can play as they navigate virtual spaces. Media use researchers as well as developmental psychologists such as Sherry Turkle and Kenneth Gergen have responded to this development by researching how individuals, particularly adolescents, construct their identity in virtual spaces. This paper will address how the creation of and the ability to play the roles of avatars can influence one’s off-screen identity. Specifically, this paper will investigate three questions. 1. What are the criteria to define the environments and venues which do and do not affect identity formation? 2. Do mastery of the medium and/or participation in a social group affect users’ identity formation? 3. Do created characters exist residually in the non-virtual lives of this kind of media users? In order to begin to answer these questions, it will be necessary to critically review both research on identity formation generally as well as recent research in identity formation on the internet. The paper will examine the research on a macro level and attempt to sort out the major contradictions in current research which relate to these questions. This research is timely and relevant because the changing uses of media and the consequential influence it has on the way people understand and define themselves must be understood in order to inform the public about the effect these uses could have on their children.

title: Elastic Modulus and Friction of Indium at Elevated Temperatures
abstract: Metals with low melting points, such as indium (156.6 C), are used in a variety of applications. For example, indium-tin alloys are used as solder joint materials in electronic circuits. The elastic modulus low melting point metals changes significantly at temperatures greater than 80 C, the operating temperature of many electronics. There is experimental and theoretical evidence indicating that surface melting may occur at substantially lower temperature than the bulk. Thus, it is important to investigate the friction properties of indium as a function of temperature. The purpose of this project is to explore how the elastic modulus and friction properties of indium vary from room temperature to its melting point. The traditional methods to measure these properties do not work at or near the melting point, because they do not have the precision to detect surface melting. The above problems can be overcome by using a high-temperature nanoindentation instrument that operates from room temperature to 250 C. The instrument can obtain the elastic modulus by measuring the penetration of a sharp diamond indentor as a function of load. Second, the friction force can be determined by sliding the indentor across the sample surface at a given load. With this instrument, one can measure the elastic modulus and friction coefficient as a function of temperature and depth into the sample. The depth is easily controlled by setting the applied load of the indentor. Results of these measurements provide one with insight into the phenomenon of surface melting in these metals. These measurements have never been done previously.

The purpose of Leaders Research is to find a tool that will improve the effectiveness of the process used to select a company's next CEO. Our team is attempting to identify a correlation between certain behavioral tendencies of people in corporate leadership roles and the overall success of the company. We have developed an online test that uses a seven-point scale to evaluate and assess how often management exhibits a particular behavior. Our test is designed to report the frequency that a person exhibits various identified behaviors. To increase statistical significance, the survey includes numerous questions correlating to each behavior. Thus, there are a variety of indications regarding each aspect of the executive's habits. Our research lends itself to use by several groups of people such as board selection committees and corporate recruiters, the training community, academics and social behavior scientists, and perhaps even investors. Our conclusions could impact managers at many levels, not just to CEOs. Our research team plans to put up a poster explaining our research concept and the expected conclusions of our data. We will also have a computer for the visitors to take the online test and get their personal behavioral evaluation. This 15 minute test will effectively exhibit the seven-point scale and the behaviors that we are observing.

title: Designing an Outreach Project that Trains Both Future Faculty and Future Engineers
abstract: Few K-12 engineering outreach projects aim to benefit the project developers and instructors as much as the target recipients of the instructional materials. We have created an outreach project in which the developers are university engineering students (both undergraduate and graduate), and our primary objectives included increasing these developers’ abilities to design instruction that is consistent with modern research on how people learn as well as increasing the depth of their biomedical engineering (BME) content knowledge. This idea grew out of our experience with BME faculty members having gained these same tremendous benefits when collaborating with learning scientists, assessment experts, and other content experts to develop instructional modules for undergraduate and graduate students as part of the VaNTH project. Believing that students might similarly benefit from this experience, we challenged them to develop an instructional module for middle school students on some aspect of biomedical engineering. The students rose to the challenge and have nearly completed a module on artificial limb design, designed in collaboration with Chicago public school (CPS) teachers, BME faculty, learning scientists, and content experts at the Center for International Rehabilitation. The benefits to the university engineering students resulting from their participation in this project have been more far-reaching than originally anticipated. We have observed additional gains beyond our stated objectives, including: 1) development of student leadership and communication skills, 2) development of a community in the department among undergraduate and graduate students, and 3) creation of a sustainable outreach effort to CPS schools. This module has been successful in benefiting the target recipients as well. By virtue of being based on education research, the module provides the middle school students a program in which to apply their basic sciences and social studies background to a task in biomedical engineering design.

The objective of designing polymeric derived drug delivery scaffolds is to allow for the effective and controlled release of bioactive factors to desired locations within the body. The structural integrity and composition of the constructed scaffold are thus of utmost importance because they determine the release kinetics of the bioactive factors as well as the polymeric scaffold’s rate of decay within the body. Through the conclusions of previous research projects, the polymer Poly (D, L-Lactic-co-Glycolic) Acid, also known as PLG, was the biodegradable material selected to construct the scaffolds. Because the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the use of this polymer for biomedical applications and because this polymer has the desired scaffold properties, it was the material selected to generate drug delivery scaffolds. Because the existing problems facing physicians are how to effectively stimulate nerve growth in spinal cord injury victims, much research interest has been directed toward developing an engineering approach to promoting the regeneration of severed axons. Thus, the motivation behind engineering such scaffolds is to induce nerve regeneration of severed axons via the release of a protein, Nerve Growth Factor (NGF). Through the conclusions of previous research projects, a cylindrical shaped scaffold was selected for nerve regeneration applications. Because the goals of this research project are to only determine what factors influence the successful and efficient production of scaffolds with consistent shape, properties, and structure, none of the PLG used in the laboratory protocol was drug loaded. The current research conducted at the Shea Lab at Northwestern University is directed towards understanding how to efficiently and effectively produce these scaffolds derived from PLG via a three step process.

The endpoint stiffness of the human arm fully describes its mechanical properties at the point of contact with its environment. It has been proposed that the central nervous system regulates these mechanics in a task-dependent manner to provide optimal control of the arm-environment interface. Recently, two independent experiments tested this hypothesis, yielding differing results. The results of one experiment suggested that control of endpoint stiffness is quite limited (Perreault et al. 2002), whereas the other showed that a great degree of control could be obtained (Burdet et al. 2001). These experiments differed in a number of respects including the task given to the subject and the methods used to investigate endpoint stiffness. The purpose of this study was to investigate if the differing conclusions obtained in these experimental studies may result from the methodologies employed in each. To accomplish this task the results of the second (Burdet) experiment were simulated utilizing MATLAB/Simulink and a second order, two-degrees-of-freedom model to represent arm motion through a diverging force field. System identification techniques were used to determine the parameters for inertia, viscosity, and elasticity that characterize the behavior of the arm for a simple 1-D system. In a 2-D simulation, a vector profiling the movement of the arm was obtained based on its response to a moving offset given an expected bell-shaped velocity profile. Both of these simulations were successful, and once combined, will be used to determine how the mechanics of arm motion influence the range of endpoint stiffness in a human arm.

I am attempting to determine if Neuropeptide Y (NPY) plays a significant role in the response of the reproductive hormonal axis to food restriction. Through examination of Potassium ATP (K+ATP) channel subunit expression I will try to determine if these channels are the mechanism through with NPY conveys inhibitory signals to the gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) neuron. Specifically, the expression of the Kir6.2 and SUR1 subunits of the K+ATP channel will be determined through reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). I will take food restricted and fed NPY knock-out mice and wildtype mice and first measure the leutenizing hormone (LH) levels to determine the state of the reproductive axis. Subsequently, the hypothalamus will be removed and RT-PCR analysis will test for the expression levels of the Kir6.2 and SUR1 subunit mRNA expression. In light of the background information and the anticipated mechanism of the GnRH pulse generator, I expect the expression of the subunits to increase in the food restricted wildtype mice as NPY release is increased in response to the negative energy balance. Correspondingly, I expect subunit expression for the food restricted NPY KO mice to remain the same as in non-food restricted wildtype mice. Previous studies show a shutdown of the reproductive axis in wildtype food restricted animals and a lack of response to food restriction in NPY KO mice.
