I anticipate a repeat of these results as well.

I am writing a thesis that investigates the influence of peer groups on an adolescent’s success. Success at this age is generally measured by achievement in school, how the adolescent views himself, and the types of behaviors he engages in. I am using total of nine standard outcomes. The causal variables that I am investigating attempt to measure various aspects of an adolescent’s friendship group. The adolescents in my dataset named their friends, and I am using this to construct measures of the adolescents’ friendship groups. Therefore, unlike in many studies, I am using the friends’ self-reports, rather than the adolescents’ perceptions of their friends. Previous studies suggest that adolescents may often overestimate the similarities between themselves and their friends. The measures of the friendship group I am considering include items such as behavior and math score. I am also looking at items about the groups, such as number of friends named, having continuing friends, and the extent to which friends are oriented towards their peers. This final measure deals with whether or not the adolescent’s friends turn to other friends, rather than parents or other adults, for advice. I hope that my analysis will shed some light on which aspects of an adolescent’s friendship groups are important for successful development and achievement.

My Senior thesis explores the performance art of Mexican-American artist Guillermo Gomez-Pena, and focuses specifically on the way he uses images and metaphors from 19th and early 20th century American freak shows. Over the past ten years, Gomez-Pena has been involved in a series of "living diorama" projects, in which he seeks to challenge and question the way that American mainstream media and popular culture portray Mexicans and Latinos. In order to achieve his powerful cultural critique, Gomez-Pena operates according to a unique creative strategy of "reverse anthropolgy." By alluding to the historical practice of exhibiting non-Western peoples as "freaks" in his performances, Gomez-Pena encourages his audience to recall the oppression and racism that fueled such displays. In his work Gomez-Pena utilizes and appropriates a variety of structural elements from the American freak show (staging, costume, choreography), and yet he uses the genre as a way to showcase contemporary racial issues. In this way, he is able to infuse today's problems with an incredible gravity and urgency. Through his performances, Gomez-Pena attempts to unleash the "colonial demons" of the past that he still sees present in contemporary America. Forcing his audiences to deal with this reality, according to Gomez-Pena, is the first step to overcoming it.

In 1936, geographer Derwent Whittlesey published a map of agricultural regions of the world. It is still the authoritative map of both subsistence and commercial agriculture. For my thesis, I am updating the parts of this map that are most likely to have drastically changed: areas where the predominant occupation is non-sedentary. I chose three categories for these groups: pastoralists, hunters and gatherers, and shifting cultivators. While these groups undoubtedly still exist, they are fewer in number and cover a smaller land area now than Whittlesey’s map indicates. Shifting cultivation no longer is the dominant form of agriculture in Bolivia, but would seem to be according to Whittlesey’s map. The Bantu pygmies of the Congolese rainforest still exist, but have been passed over in Whittlesey’s map (as have all hunter-gatherer groups). Due to increasing infrastructure, pastoralists in Saharan Africa have been pushed to the fringes of habitable land; areas that Whittlesey showed as empty. These groups are difficult to map given the limited available literature about them. Surprisingly, web sites, maintained either by or on behalf of many of these groups, are available that give insight into the culture and geography of little-known groups. Once I determined the accuracy of the information in each site, I developed a map of the groups I found using Atlas GIS version 4.0 software. My thesis will include the process of making the map, information on all of the groups contained in it, and how this new map differs from Whittlesey’s 1936 version.

In the fall of 2001, as city after city in Afghanistan fell from Taliban control, and the Northern Alliance and the U.S. military overtook the country, the West rejoiced. Tyranny had fallen. Newspapers and television networks celebrated the newfound freedom enjoyed by Afghan citizens. Americans grasped the immediate meaning of this freedom: Men shaved their beards. Women walked in the streets without their burqas. Throughout the next year, girls returned to schools, the Loya Jirga assembly convened to draft a new constitution, and the interim government--inclusive of all ethnic groups-- took control of day-to-day administration. But after the initial liberation of Kabul, Kandahar, Mazir-e-Sharif and other cities, American media demonstrated a tendency to deal with the complex issues swirling around Afghanistan in a superficial way--if at all. A selection of seven newspaper articles and broadcast reports from late 2001 and 2002 reflects a remarkable misunderstanding of, or lack of understanding about, Afghanistan’s history, culture, politics and ethnic structure. Mainstream reporters writing about freedom in Afghanistan rarely traveled beyond Kabul, which has more experience with liberal democracy and exposure to Western cultural influences than the rest of the country. Geopolitics and American interests in the region received even less scrutiny. Instead, as this study shows, reports about freedom after the Taliban often--but not always--focused on a narrowly defined conception of liberty that resonates better with Americans than Afghanis.

Systemic corruption encumbers and often precludes private enterprise, aid, and investment in struggling economies. Still, little is known about the causes of corruption at the micro level, where corruption actually occurs. Utilizing data from the World Bank Group’s World Business Environment Survey 2000, this study tests existing theories of corruption at the firm level in a sample of over 1100 firms from 40 countries in Latin America and Transition Europe. Results show a significant positive relationship between the business constraints caused by corruption and government intervention.

I am undertaking two related research projects under the faculty members listed above. The first project, under Professor Bill Kath, consists of numerical simulations of a fiber-optic system. Recent experimental findings have shown that power distribution over a broad frequency range can be generated under certain conditions. While the general physical phenomena contributing to this generation are known, exactly how the phenomena interact to produce this generation is unknown. Using analysis to derive appropriate equations, I have developed numerical code that models the system and hope to be able to provide insight into how this so-called supercontinuum generation is achieved. With knowledge of how the system works, refinements and improvements can be made to this fiber-optic system with the most notable application being a possible optical source over a relatively large tunable frequency range. My second project, under Professor Allen Taflove, deals with numerical simulations of spatial solitons, which are beams of light that are self-confining in space (i.e. no waveguide is needed for confinement as the light propagates). More specifically, I am interested in the interactions of spatial solitons with one another. I have developed techniques that effectively model such species of light and have conducted simulations with implemented code. Studying the simulation results, it becomes apparent that the interaction of these solitons provides a mechanism for which an all-optical switch can be constructed. What makes this proposed switch so attractive is that it has the potential of operating on a time scale of one hundred femtoseconds (10^-13 seconds).

A presentation of my paper on how the eugenics movement led to the creation of intelligence testing. In the late 19th century, eugenicists were ready to institute programs to sterilize individuals they believed unfit to reproduce. But previous criteria used to evaluate individuals' intelligence/social worth, like cranial measurements, had been invalidated. IQ tests were created to meet the eugenicists' demand for a new (though arbitrary) standard for intelligence. This paved the way for sterilization laws to be passed in 30 states. I will give a brief talk on my paper, supplemented with slides if desired.

Gravitational waves are predicted by General Relativity, but have yet to be directly observed. The most promising source for emission of these gravity waves is a merger event (collision) of a binary pair of extremely dense stars (black holes or neutron stars). In hopes of finding the first detections of these events, LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory) was recently built, and has begun taking in observational data. The project has explored the various properties of the sources and how these properties affect LIGO's ability to detect the gravity waves the sources emit. Our project has focused, in particular, on the affect of the true spatial distribution of such sources on LIGO's detection capabilities. The results of such a focus are highlighted by precise probability functions (eg., the probability that a detection would be due to waves coming from a given segment of the sky, or coming from a given distance from Earth), and the most accurate, yet, predicted rate for expected detections (per year) by LIGO.

title: Gender and Dating at Northwestern
abstract: This Gender Studies independent study in sociology explores the stereotype that Northwestern students do not date. With a historical perspective of dating at Northwestern since the 1920s, the project uses data from 18 interviews with current undergraduate students or recent graduates to analyze the social systems that regulate dating pratices on campus. The data reveals that student discontent with the dating scene is largely a product of larger cultural movements and less an issue endemic to Northwestern.

title: The Effects of Prenatal Androgen Exposure on Expression and Localization of ATP-sensitive K+ Channel (KATP) Subunits in the Male Rat
abstract: Prenatal exposure to certain steroid hormones can have organizational effects on brain circuitries. Gonadal steroid hormones present perinatally, particularly testosterone (T), contribute to the sexual differentiation of the brain. Recent studies in the Levine laboratory suggest that the expression of ATP-sensitive K+ channels (KATP) in the rodent brain could be regulated by exposure to T in utero. KATP channels couple cellular metabolism to membrane excitability and neurotransmitter release by sensing glucose availability. An increase in intracellular ATP causes channel inactivation (closure), which results in membrane depolarization and an increased firing rate. These glucose-responsive neurons are comprised of an inwardly rectifying pore-forming unit (Kir6.1 or Kir6.2) and a sulphonylurea receptor (SUR1 or SUR2), a member of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily. Both proteins are necessary for channel function. We hypothesize that androgen exposure in utero can affect the expression of KATP channels, and that these actions may give rise to sex differences. We predict androgens program neuronal populations to exhibit reduced channel expression, rendering those circuitries more prone to hyperactivity. Therefore, we will determine the quantity and location of KATP channels (Kir6.2 and SUR1) in the brains of T-treated and 5a-dihydrotestosterone (DHT)-treated male rats versus those of control via in situ hybridization. If the hypothesis is correct, we will see a decrease in channel expression in rats exposed to excess androgens in utero.

While taking ECE 223, Professor Razeghi offered me the unique undergraduate opportunity as a result of my motivation, grade point average (3.91), and academic dedication to continue to study topics of my choice within the Center for Quantum Devices (CQD). Solid state engineering is a truly challenging field and research in this area contributed to the widespread use of cell phones and continues to inspire more devices. Of the projects at CQD, I chose to assist the research of infrared cameras. This subject is important because infrared light is a portion of the electromagnetic spectrum not seen by human eyes. Today, especially, thermal and night-vision imaging is seen on the evening news and I am working to make these cameras more efficient and versatile. Infrared cameras show great usefulness in many military (target tracking, night vision, etc) and commercial applications (medical, civil, industrial, environmental, etc). At CQD, my research is leading me to partially carry out the growth and processing of the QWIP structure with a detection wavelength of 8.1 micron. I assist the production of 256 x 256 pixel focal plane arrays through photolithography, dry etching, and other fabrication steps. I observed successful imaging of objects using the QWIPs. This was the first demonstration of infrared imaging from an Al-free QWIP and will be shown in a video clip during my presentation.

My research is based on my experience in the Ethnographic Field School through the Anthropology Department in the Summer of 2002. I spent the summer doing ethnographic research on the Navajo reservation in a school for individuals with developmental disabilities. I followed up with a literature review of the anthropology of disability upon returning to Northwestern. The resulting research paper considers individual incompetence/competence within the Navajo culture and the ideas surrounding what it means to be different. The concept of being human is something that has different meaning across different cultures depending on various factors such as world view, ideas of body/mind, and other cultural elements such as kinship traditions. The line between competence and incompetence is evident in local social structures and in the daily interactions of people. Cultures incorporate people who are different into their understanding of human nature in diverse ways. To the existing body of literature on the anthropology of disability, I add my own observations of the Navajo understanding of “disability” which come from ethnographic field work completed on the Navajo reservation in the summer of ’02. I look at the implications of the cultural constructions of disability and (in)competence for the treatment and support of people with disabilities, focusing on my case study of the Navajo. This discussion includes a consideration of the dominating presence of Western medical knowledge in indigenous communities, and the nature of the reservation area and its implications. Keeping in mind the role of anthropology in the burgeoning field of disability studies, I examine what it means to be different in diverse cultural contexts, and how culture and environment determine the understanding and treatment of disability.

title: The e2-Seat
abstract: The problem faced by our team was to design a second row module for a pickup truck that maximizes functionality and utility without sacrificing comfort and practicality. A survey of current options available for the second row of trucks as well as strong user feedback revealed the need to increase storage room without sacrificing seating room or comfort. Strong user feedback towards the implementation of electrical outlets and Internet access in the second row of the truck lead us to adopt three features in our design. Key features of this design are: 1) Increased storage space, via the seat bottom storage compartments (2.4 cubic feet), without having to sacrifice seating room. 2) Electrical outlets (AC power) allow users to power a variety of devices in or outside of the truck. 3) Wireless Internet access allows users to connect to the world and communicate while on the go. We are confident that the e2-Seat will appeal to a large demographic of potential buyers. The increased storage room will prove beneficial to everyone from construction workers to soccer-moms. The electrical outlets will make the driving experience more enjoyable for children who want to use electrical devices and will make the second row of the truck more useful to construction workers, the outdoor aficionado, or anyone in between. The ability to connect to the Internet revolutionizes the meaning of mobile communication. The e2-Seat embodies twenty-first century technology with timeless practicality and utility.

title: Fabrication and Classification of Carbon Nanotube Circuits
abstract: Nanoelectric devices have been presented as a replacement to the MOSFET technology. It is hoped that these new technologies will provide a new method of fabricating IC’s that will allow scaling to continue at the current rate. For this project we will start by familiarizing ourselves with the processes that are used to make electronic circuits on the nanometer scale. We will acquire carbon nanotubes in powder form, then use of the electron beam lithography system in the Electron Probe Instrumentation Center to mill the contacts for a circuit. We will then use the atomic force microscope probe stations to observe and manipulate carbon nanotubes to finalize the production of simple circuits, consisting of nanotube transistors and nanotube interconnects. We will use the scanning tunneling microscope from Keck-II to create images of our circuits. Finally, we will test the circuits and evaluate their performance and the effects of varying methods of fabrication and structure. The conclusion that will be drawn from this research is a comparison of the carbon nanotube - used as a transistor and as an interconnect - with the equivalent CMOS technology. This will serve as a basic classification and will provide empirical evidence as to the effectiveness of the carbon nanotube in IC technology.

A new wheelchair seat design characterized by unloading the ischia and supporting the lumbar spine was investigated. The back part of the seat could be tilted downward, so as to decrease the pressure under the ischia while shifting the contact area anteriorly towards the thighs. Additional lumbar support was also added on the backrest. The purpose of the study was to investigate the pressure changes, oxygen and carbon dioxide transcutaneous perfusion, muscle activity, and temperature effects related with the new wheelchair design. In addition, the effects of adjusting the knee extension angle on the seat pad and backrest pressure with and without ischial support were investigated. Moreover, a comparison of alternating between the postures the chair offers and the clinical method of using a push up to relieve pressure are compared. The basis is to help treat patients with spinal cord injuries that as a population suffer greatly from lower back pain and pressure sores due to there inability to move and the large amounts of constant time they spend in wheelchairs.

Cells, the basic functional units of living organisms, need to communicate with their environment in order to work properly. If certain cell types cannot respond to external signals, there can be severe consequences: diseases like hypertension or other physical abnormalities. Those external signals are biological molecules, like pheromones. To react to those signals, cells need to recognize them at the cells’ outer surfaces. There are proteins on the cell surface that uniquely attach to those signaling molecules. After the signal is attached, then the cell reacts. For instance, if the signaling molecule is a growth factor, then the cell will grow. Then the cell has to deactivate or “downregulate” the effect of the signal. Using the growth factor example, after the cell grows, it needs to stop growing at some point; otherwise, it will die. The downregulation of the signal, in turn, is achieved through the process of endocytosis, during which the cell swallows (internalizes) the signal, and the protein that attached it. I am researching endocytosis in yeast as it relates to a protein called Cos16. We already know that yeast cells that have a mutated version of the Cos16 protein are severely defective in endocytosis. My work involves finding out the role of the Cos16 protein by characterizing it several ways. To find it’s location in the cell, I use the molecular technique of fluorescent labeling. In yeast cells without Cos16, I try to see if inserting normal Cos16 protein will allow endocytosis to work again. Also, I work to see if a structural protein, actin, has an effect on endocytosis.

Editorial opinion is a newspaper's way of combating those who try to dominate, deceive, or mislead public opinion. Editorial writing isn't easy, but it is crucial in helping people to see their way through difficult times by providing thoughtful analysis of the daily flow of information. Editorials are a particularly vital part of free elections, through which newspapers can persuade people to vote for the betterment of the community. However, sometimes the choice between disappointing candidates is not clear, and the fallout can mean disaster. What does a newspaper owe its community when both candidates are undesirable? In the 1991 Louisiana Gubernatorial runoff, the New Orleans Times-Picayune helped its readers through a nightmarish choice between the crook and the racist (Edwin Edwards and David Duke). My paper combines primary sources (such as original Times-Picayune editorials, news articles, and interviews with Time- Picayune staff) with secondary sources analyzing the coverage of the nightmarish election. I conclude that in an election where neither candidate was desirable, the Times-Picayune’s leadership rose to new heights. Through the use of front-page editorials, the Times-Picayune took an in depth look at both candidates and showed Louisiana the possible consequences of each as governor. I think their professional adherence to the highest standards of editorial writing saved Louisiana from sinking into swamp.

What is at stake when law collides with art? Should the arts be funded and how can we reconcile public perceptions with specialist views of controversial art? My thesis answers these questions by analyzing the 1998 Supreme Court case National Endowment for the Arts v. Karen Finley. The United States began funding artists during the Cold War, encouraging artists to break from the state-sponsored models of art supported by communism. As the Cold War ended, the lawmakers were unwilling to face the consequences of the diverse art world they helped shape. Controversial exhibits funded in part by the NEA prompted Congress to pass an amendment in 1990 requiring the NEA to consider “general standards of decency and respect for the diverse beliefs and values of the American public.” Four performance artists sued the NEA for withdrawing previously awarded grants and challenged the constitutionality of the “decency clause.” The Supreme Court upheld the clause’s constitutionality by ignoring precedent and incorrectly applying standards for funding regulation. I will explore the subjectivity of constitutional law and the consequences for contemporary artists. This decision not only harms artists, but it also sets a very dangerous precedent for regulating government funding. This study provides an interdisciplinary approach to an event that will have a far-reaching impact on the arts and other publicly funded institutions.

Human-computer interfaces can be evaluated in 4 ways: automatically, empirically, formally, and informally. The most popular method is the empirical method, where real users are used to test the interface and respond with feedback. But it is also one of the most expensive methods. Automatic analysis would be the cheapest method because the programmer could get feedback on the interface in terms that they could understand without any sort of second-party expenses. But automatic methods fail again and again to obtain accurate results because of poorly defined heuristics. GOMS analysis of a system presents an interesting theory: That an interface can be evaluated by evaluating its most fundamental components. Actual GOMS implementation, though, does not reach any sort of accurate analysis in many situations. This is mostly due to rigid units of analyses and nonscalability. But, if one were combine the best of all three analysis methods listed? This project takes the true feedback of the human, couples it with the simplicity of GOMS, adds automates it. The user is presented with a questionnaire of 'which one is better' interface questions. From this random sampling and a knowledge of the fundamental differences between the interfaces presented, a previously-unidentifiable heuristic is developed. This heuristic can then be applied to similar interfaces, or revisions of a current interface, automatically comparing in a reverse method than what was used to capture the sampling data. The end result is a quantitative departure (of the interface evaluated) from the user's heuristics. This project analyses only the visual components of the interfaces through digital image analysis, but is abstracted in such a way that other methods can be added in the future.

High nitrate concentrations in our nation’s waters cause adverse effects to ecosystems, human health, and the economy. Nitrogen is often the primary causes of eutrophication in estuarine and marine ecosystems. Agriculture has also modified the landscape dramatically. Although agricultural drainage practices have nearly doubled yields, it has also eliminated or degraded the bulk of the wetlands in this region. Modern agricultural drains move water from fields to streams in a matter of hours, so that nitrate-laden agricultural runoff is rapidly delivered to surface water systems. This, coupled with the near-elimination of riparian wetlands, has drastically impaired natural pathways of nitrogen removal. Currently, Professors Kimberly Gray and Aaron Packman in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering have a project funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to examine the development of constructed wetlands for the purpose of decreasing nitrate export from agricultural lands. This work involves both field work to examine the functioning of constructed wetlands and laboratory experiments to examine the nitrate removal process in detail. One major goal of this effort is to examine nitrogen transformation in periphyton, which are surface-attached microbial communities. The field work involves considerable sampling of periphyton in wetlands throughout north-eastern Illinois, along with general characterization of these wetland systems. My project involves assisting graduate students with the collection of these field samples and with later sample processing and analysis. I help collect periphyton samples and measure water flows and other environmental parameters such as temperature. I also help prepare periphyton samples for analysis of microbial populations and nitrate transformation rates.

Due to the brittleness of MgB2, its use in superconducting wires requires the higher ductility often gained by making a composite with a ductile phase. David Dunand and John DeFouw infiltrated MgB2 powder with Mg to achieve a composite with higher ductility using a liquid-metal infiltration process. The resulting Mg/MgB2 composite was pore-free with no reaction between Mg and MgB2. The work was later developed by Cedric von Grundigen who produced Al/MgB2 and Zn/MgB2 superconductors. However, these composites exhibited significant porosity. This work is an attempt to improve the quality of infiltration by controlling solidification and improving the MgB2 powder perform. Thermally conductive crucibles and cooled graphite post was used to enhance the directionality of solidification. The MgB2 powder was packed in a powder press to obtain more connectivity between particles and to better measure the density before infiltration. In addition to Al and Zn, Ag was also employed due it its combination of electrical and thermal properties

In my project I will be exploring how race-of-examiner effects function in Dr. Lindsay Chase-Lansdale’s study Welfare, Children, and Families: A Three City Study. In her longitudinal investigation, Dr. Chase-Lansdale has looked at how changes in welfare law since the 1996 switch to TANF have affected child and family outcomes. The Three City Study assesses children and their families from three different racial backgrounds: African American, Hispanic, and non-Hispanic White. Those going into the homes of the participants to administer surveys and measures, know as the examiners, are representative of the same three racial backgrounds. Since the 1940s, researchers have expressed concern that interviews taking place between a subject and an examiner of different races are biased. For example, an African American subject’s lack of comfort and trust with Whites may translate to the interview situation, and as a result his responses to questions posed by the White examiner may be inhibited. In my project I will use statistical analysis to explore the presence of race-of-examiner effects in the Three City Study. While past studies of race-of-examiner effects have only looked at how Whites and African Americans interact in the interview situation, I will go further by adding Hispanic examiners and subjects to the equation. This project serves two purposes: 1.) to further establish the validity of the Three City Study, which has recently received much acclaim in its study of welfare reform; 2.) to further gain understanding of the communication with examiners and subjects of different racial backgrounds in the interview situation.

This is the third story I wrote for the first half of the Creative Writing Sequence in the Writing Major of the English Department, entitled '5% Redford'. I worked under the instruction of not only Sheila Donohue but also Brian Bouldrey, another professor in the department.

With the improvement of highways and interstates, road trips have become more popular among families. However, the design of the car has not evolved quickly enough to accommodate this new trend. Cars were never intended to provide sleeping space for children and therefore discomfort and safety issues arise. In order to design a solution to this problem, we interviewed children and parents while reviewing current Sport Utility Vehicle (SUV) and minivan models for possible areas of improvement in comfort and safety. Through our research, we determined seat features that we could modify to make children more comfortable and safe while they sleep in minivans and Sport Utility Vehicles. In our design concept, we propose the following additions to bucket and bench seats: • Cushioned headrest with adjustable sides to provide head support • Double-wide cushioned armrests to provide arm support • Footrests with various positioning for children and for adults to provide leg support • Canvas pullouts as privacy screens • Four-point padded seatbelts to provide safety and additional comfort • Storage compartments in the armrests and footrests to stow extra blankets and pillows • Controllable electro-tint windows The conceptual seat design makes sleeping in cars much easier by providing full body support, increased safety, and maximum comfort while providing extra storage space for blankets and other sleep items.

My English 399 independent study tutorial project, The Bruise, is an original manuscript of fourteen poems written over the course of the last six months under the guidance of Professor Mary Kinzie. The collection is a poetic exploration in fourteen figures, which seeks to engage with readings by a broad range of writers from Anne Carson to Jorge Luis Borges to Kafka. Central to the poems that comprise The Bruise is Ovid’s Metamorphoses, that seamless text of change in which seduction often manifests itself as distrust and predation, with catastrophic personal ends. As with the original Ovid text that inspired them, these poems explore the darker themes of classical mythology, but in a transposed and humanized form: Apollo as a depressed factory worker, Orpheus as a street musician, Icarus as a young airman of the second world war. Each poem questions what it means for the divine to live among us and to what end their emotions can be matched to our own through physical, emotional, or temporal transformation. Myth is used as a filter through which to pass modern life and all of its complications: desire, hatred, war, racism, and beauty, that perplexing abstraction that accumulates from the most unlikely sources. For each experience, we have a mark, a bruise. They are the innumerable imprints of memory.

My research with Dean John Birge has been focused on developing a financial model to maximize wealth through investment in stocks, bonds, and private equity. The model takes into account details such as the number of assets held, number of periods the assets are held, how often and when trading is allowed and transaction costs. The models are created using the Matlab programming language. I am using these models to examine the options for Northwestern University to invest its endowment over an infinite horizon. Taking into consideration the many possibilities for investment in the three assets, I will use the models to determine the effects of different trading strategies on the future value of the Northwestern University endowment.

The goal of this research is to develop a platform for imaging a diverse range of samples with resolution of 10 nanometers or less. The proposed system borrows from computationally intensive techniques used in exploratory seismology. Whereas geologists use source waveforms that range from 10 Hz to 10kHz to obtrain an inverse solution to a structure using source/reciever waveforms, this research aims to create a source that will generate acoustic waves on the order of 100 GHz. Such a waveform should be able to accurately image internal structures of incredibly small size within any material. The primary application for this technology would be for quality control in nanotechnology manufacturing.

In For Whom the Bell Tolls Ernest Hemingway creates “a literary dialect” by manipulating Spanish and English languages in order to depict an American’s engagement in the Spanish Civil War. Similarly, Sandra Cisneros chooses not to preference one language in “Bien Pretty.” Like Hemingway, Cisneros employs a bilingual hybrid dialect as her means of expressing a Mexican-American love story. Whereas the fluidity of language problematizes traditional translation methodology, the dialects of Hemingway and Cisneros are able to accommodate the myriad colloquialism, slang, familiar, and other nonstandard usages that force language into a non-static state. Here, the language performs its own translation, by finding approximations through synthesis rather than unequal substitutions. For Whom the Bell Tolls and “Bien Pretty” exhibit a fundamental trend in post-modernist literature: self-conscious awareness of multiculturalism, and subsequently the ways in which language enacts cultural representations in a modern society. In response to these movements, Hemingway and Cisneros manipulate Spanish and English language to better represent the complex cultural relationships they portray. The result is an effect of instantaneous and reciprocal translation of Spanish and English in the moments of intersection between the two languages. This essay will prove that at these junctions of language the texts also engage in the transaction of the cultures that are represented – and constructed – by these languages. Furthermore, Hemingway and Cisneros conceive of the boundaries of translation, and the power of language in this new way: to include the capacity of language translation in the contact zone also to translate culture.

In January of 1999 Kendra Webdale, a New York State resident, was killed by a mentally ill man named Andrew Goldstein with a history of non-compliance to treatment. Andrew Goldstein pushed Kendra Webdale in front of a moving New York City subway train. The result of this gruesome act was that on August 9, 1999, Governor Pataki signed “Kendra’s Law”. Legislation described by Governor Pataki as being “designed to protect the public and individuals living with mental illness by ensuring potentially dangerous mentally ill outpatients are safely and effectively treated.” (Governors Press Release 08/03/99) Kendra’s Law provides for non-voluntary care of the mentally ill who fit certain criteria. This provision that headlined in the media and in press releases ostensibly implies that if the state could have forced Andrew Goldstein to comply with treatment, Kendra Webdale would not have died. However, if one closely examines Kendra’s Law, the relevant debates from the New York House, Senate, and the press, it becomes clear that the bulk of Kendra’s Law is in fact not aimed at the safety concerns of the public but rather at long desired improvements in the mental health system of New York. This paper seeks to prove that the New York State Government used outrage over the death of Kendra Webdale as a political misdirection. Misdirection that was used to pass long desired improvements to the mental health system that only minimally increases public safety from mentally ill individuals.

title: Constructing Divergence
abstract: One often hears the phrase “Play is Children’s Work”. Some take this statement to mean that children have little else to do with their time than play. However, the true meaning of these words is that children learn a great deal about our world through the vehicle of play. With little control over the “real” events and circumstances in their lives, the child’s imagination is a practice arena of sorts through which one can build and test his or her mental representations of the world and how it works. Moreover, psychologists studying play over the past forty years have come to highlight a number of cognitive skills that children develop specifically through play. Among other benefits, these skills lead to improvements in divergent thought, an integral part of one’s creative abilities. Considering these findings, this study looks to determine whether children play more creatively when they construct their own toys than when they are given toys with which to play. To answer this question, I have designed and arranged a weekly puppet workshop at the Kohl Children’s Museum in Wilmette, IL. In this workshop, small groups of children will design and perform puppet shows with puppets that, according to their variable group, they will have either constructed themselves or been given. Their performances are videotaped and analyzed in hopes of better understanding the impact of such an affect on the imaginativeness and creativity of their play.

The following project was undertaken as independent research in the Mugnaini lab at the Northwestern University Institute of Neuroscience. The unipolar brush cell (UBC), a glutamergic interneuron of the vestibulocerebellum, forms an intrinsic network for the distribution of extrinsic excitatory signals throughout the granular layer of the cerebellum. It has been shown that two distinct subsets of UBC exist and are characterized by their chemical phenotypes: one subset is positive for the calcium-binding protein, calretinin, while the other is positive for metabotropic glutamate receptor 1alpha. The recent discovery of two isoforms of vesicular glutamate transporter (VGluT1 and VGluT2) has prompted the question of whether the transporters are differentially expressed over each of the UBC subsets. This question was addressed using techniques of immunocytochemistry and fluorescence microscopy on organotypic slice cultures, in which all extrinsic input to the UBC network has been severed. The results demonstrate that VGluT1 is expressed by both UBC subsets, but VGluT2 is expressed exclusively by the calretinin-positive population. This further elucidates the phenotypic distinction of the two microcircuits, and is suggestive of potential functional differences between VGluT1 and VGluT2. The coexpression of VGluT2 and calretinin may be linked to the possible role of calretinin-positive UBCs as neuroendocrine releasing cells.

Colombia suffers the worst political violence and most dire human rights situation in the Western Hemisphere. Engaged in a nearly four decade-long civil war, Colombia’s armed internal conflict is active, with differing degrees of intensity, in every part of the country. It claims approximately twenty to thirty lives per day and has displaced more than two million people, making Colombia the world’s fourth-largest host of internally displaced persons, and forcing refugees to pour into neighboring countries or congregate in urban centers. Although the protagonists of the civil war are the guerrilla rebel groups, the paramilitaries, and the Colombian government and military, the overwhelming majority of the victims are innocent civilians caught in the line of fire. Attempts to negotiate peaceful settlements between the warring groups have endured a lengthy and tumultuous history. Beginning with President Belisario Betancur in 1982, Colombia has made five successive attempts at peaceful resolution under five different presidents. Despite widely varying strategies and tactics, all five peace processes ultimately ended in frustration, failure, and increased violence. Some evidence suggests that negotiated settlements have grown more common since the end of the Cold War. If this is true, why, after over two decades of peace talks pursued through different strategies, has negotiated settlement in Colombia consistently failed? This thesis argues that Colombia embodies distinctive factors that differentiate its situation from that of other intrastate armed conflicts and undermine its potential for successful negotiated settlement. These factors include: 1) a tradition of politically motivated violence; 2) a historically weak Colombian state; 3) a closed political system; 4) U.S. foreign policy; and 5) the changing interests of the actors involved, partially as a result of the meteoric expansion of the drug trade since the 1970s.

title: Risky Choice Selection in Small Group Scenarios
abstract: Framing effect studies show when positive words are used to describe 2 outcomes, 1 definitive and 1 probabilistic, participants have a greater tendency to choose the definitive outcome (risk aversion). They want to ensure some of the positive outcome is realized/maintained. Conversely, when negative words are used, participants choose the probabilistic option (risk seeking), as they presumably do not want to be responsible for loss. We aimed to see how framing effects operate in small group scenarios. We used a variation of the Asian Disease problem, where participants are told 6 people (instead of 600) are infected with a fatal disease and to select between saving 2 people for sure or a 1/3 chance of saving them all. There were 8 conditions, a positive and negative frame of 4 scenarios where each scenario described the 6 people differently (6 people/6 of your friends who don’t know each other/6 of your immediate family members/6 of someone else’s family members). We hypothesized that as the amount of infected people described has been decreased, the level of interdependence in a scenario is increased and, thus, the greater the risk seeking behavior. Further, the greater the interdependence there is, the greater the potency of the framing effect. Roughly 240 NU participants were tested individually. Participants received a consent form. Upon agreeing to participate, they were given a sheet that describes a scenario and asks them to choose a plan. They were then given a demographic and study response questionnaire.

Organisms code spatial locations in a variety of ways, and the redundancy in forms of spatial coding may provide evolutionary advantages. My focus is on the development of a particular type of spatial coding which involves taking into account the relations among landmarks. Researchers disagree about when relational coding develops in children (Overman, Pate, Moore, & Peuster, 1996; Huttenlocher, Newcombe, & Sandberg, 1994). This study aimed to clarify at what age children are able to utilize more than one landmark object to code location in space. The experimental procedure is adapted in part from prior work on spatial cognition in gerbils (Collett, Cartwright, & Smith, 1986). Thirty-two (16M, 16F) 4 and 5-year olds searched for the location of a hidden object. On different trials we manipulated (a) the number of landmarks, and (b) the distance between landmarks or between landmarks and the target. The most important manipulation involved training children with two landmarks relatively close together and then moving them apart. If children search on the basis of the relation of the landmarks, then the accuracy of searches will not be affected by this manipulationin both cases, the location is in the middle of the two landmarks. If, however, children search only on the basis of relation between the target and a single landmark, then they should search the original distance from the landmark. Our results indicate that 4-year-olds, unlike gerbils, do code relationally; when we placed two landmarks, their performance was not affected by the distance between these landmarks. However, when only one landmark was available, they did code the distance between the hidden object and the single landmark. These results suggest that both relational and landmark coding is present in young children and that coding strategy use depends on the initial cues given.

Our project is assessing the clinical effects of a class of short-acting migraine drugs, the triptans, using a number of MRI-based neuroimaging techniques. These drugs usually reach their peak level of effect approximately one hour after oral administration and significantly reduce migraine symptoms for between 10 and 12 hours. Specifically, rizatriptan, commercially known as Maxalt, will be administered to patients who have moderate to severe migraine and are already taking the drug on a daily basis for alleviation of their symptoms. Patients are scanned for the first time before taking the drug and after the onset of their symptoms. The rizatriptan is then orally administered and another scan taken approximately one hour later once the drug has taken effect. Imaging is being conducted on the 3.0T scanner at Highland Park Hospital. Functional MRI will be used to assess changes in activation of brain regions due to the drug. Diffusion-tensor imaging will also be used to assess for changes in the diffusivity of neuronal axon membranes as well as possible white matter abnormalities in the brains of the migraine patients. It is predicted that analysis of the scans will show alterations in the regional activation of the trigeminal pain centers in the brainstem, the cingulate cortex, and the sensory association cortex after administration of rizatriptan. Findings may shed light not only on the neurological effects of the triptans, but also on the aberrant mechanisms that underlie migraine pathology.

title: Application of the Zirconium-Phosphonate Multilayer Technique to the Field of Nanotechnology
abstract: One discipline of nanotechnology involves controlling the assembly of molecules in an attempt to construct molecular architectures at the nanometer scale. Thin-molecular films prepared via direct assembly are an attractive way to build molecular architectures on surfaces. Thin-molecular films have been used for a wide variety of purposes and depending on the substrate and molecular structure of the scaffold molecules, these nanoframeworks could be used for a wide variety of tasks such as sensors, catalysis, and controlling molecular architecture. Due to the ease of preparation and synthesis of zirconium-phosphonate multilayers (ZPM) thin-films, they have been used for a wide variety of applications. ZPMs prepared using diphosphonated oligothiophenes have been used to produce novel materials to study electron and energy transfer, while thin-films of porous materials have been used as enantiomerically selective sensors, and thin-films of diphosphonated asymmetric molecules have demonstrated nonlinear optical responses on the same order of lithium niobate. Recently, our interests focused on using these porous films as molecular sieves, high sensitivity chemical sensors and use in heterogeneous catalysis. Our current efforts test the potential of applying the ZPM thin-film technique to assemble larger nanoarchitectures on surfaces in highly controlled, directed fashion to test the potential applicability of ZPM technique to the field of nanotechnology.

The human ability to perceive whether different frequency components of a complex sound begin synchronously or asynchronously aids in the identification of speech sounds and the grouping together of frequencies that arise from the same sound source. We are interested in the plasticity and organization of the mechanisms that underlie such asynchrony detection in humans. We previously observed that listeners trained to detect asynchrony at sound onset improved significantly on the trained condition, but did not generalize that learning to sound offset [1]. To determine whether learning was actually possible at sound offset, we performed the converse experiment. We trained 9 listeners one hour per day for 8 days to determine whether two tones at 0.25 and 4 kHz ended synchronously or asynchronously. Before and after training we tested these listeners and 15-25 untrained controls on the trained offset condition and a parallel onset condition. The trained listeners improved significantly on the trained condition during the training period, and learned markedly more than controls on both the trained offset condition and the untrained onset condition. Their improvement on the onset condition actually matched that of listeners trained on that condition. Thus, the mechanism(s) underlying asynchrony detection at both sound onset and sound offset are malleable in human listeners. Further, the fact that listeners trained at sound onset could have improved at sound offset, but did not, and that listeners trained at sound offset did improve at sound onset indicates that there is an asymmetric relationship between the two mechanisms. [1] Wright, B.A., Fitzgerald, M.B., Mossbridge, J.A. (2001). Specificity of learning in an auditory asynchrony-detection task, J. Acoust. Soc. Am., 109, 2289 (A). Supported by NIH and a Northwestern University Undergraduate Summer Research Grant.

The frequencies of domestic violence and sexual assault in South Africa are alarmingly and uncommonly high. My project examines the direct role the presence of the apartheid government system has played and is still playing in facilitating the high frequencies of such violence against women in South Africa. It demonstrates how, during the time the apartheid government was in place, the system made tolerance of abusive husbands necessary for women’s economic survival. My research also shows that in addition to making women financially unable to fight violent partners, apartheid also induced a social atmosphere of sub ordinance to ill treatment by men. I have also found that during the apartheid resistance movement, the fight to end abuse and subordination of women was put aside as unimportant compared to the fight for equality for the races. In the years following the fall of apartheid, women found many more opportunities for employment outside the home, which the project shows sometimes let to hostility and violence from their spouses. Just as with domestic violence, the influence of apartheid on rape is seen during the system, the struggle against it, and after it was abolished. My project examines the ways in which the apartheid legal system bred apathy for sex crimes against women. During the political turmoil of the resistance, both black and white men were frequent rape aggressors. As was the case with domestic violence, my project demonstrates how apartheid continues to be a factor in high sex crime rates in South Africa.

Researchers have found a linear relationship between the incidence of schizophrenia and paternal age. This relationship may be due to the increased likelihood of random germ-line mutations associated with advancing paternal age. The objective of my research project is to determine how much such random mutations contribute to the overall incidence of schizophrenia. This is interesting because it would explain the stable incidence of schizophrenia even though the low fertility of schizophrenic individuals leads one to expect that the incidence would gradually decrease. The fact that it remains stable might be explained by the hypothesis that such random mutations might contribute to the infusion of 'new' cases of schizophrenia (cases that are not inherited). For the study, we re-analyze and combine data to obtain the maximum possible contribution of random mutations to the incidence of schizophrenia.

This thesis explores the role of ritual in the mythopoetic men’s movement (MPMM). The MPMM gained popularity and media attention with the success of Robert Bly’s Iron John: A Book About Men (1990), but the analytical literature of the mythopoetic movement is scant. This thesis adds to that literature by examining the men’s group Spiritual Warfare Effectiveness Training (SWET) based in Bryn Athyn, PA. Recognizing that a purely textual analysis of the men’s movement is insufficient, this thesis combines participant-observation as an uninitiated and initiated member of SWET, interviews of SWET members, a review of contemporary literature on the men’s movement, and classical anthropological theory on ritual. Several themes for understanding the role of ritual in SWET (and more broadly, the Men’s Movement) are developed and evaluated. The role of secrecy, the potential for ritual to engender community and social bonding, and the use of ritual for individual growth work is examined. By understanding these themes one comes to better understand the content and aims of MPMM.

The sun emits a broad spectrum of electromagnetic radiation, including everything from far infrared to short wavelength ultraviolet. The ozone layer protects us from the shortest, most damaging, wavelengths, however a great deal of UV light in the UVA (400 - 315nm) and UVB(315 - 280nm) reaches the earth. Prolonged exposure to these high-energy photons can be harmful to humans. Based upon knowledge of a user’s skin type and the sunscreen being used, this personal UV detector warns the user when their exposure to UV radiation reaches potentially harmful levels. This project uses a wide-bandgap III-Nitride semiconductor photodetector grown at the Center for Quantum Devices capable of recording a person’s UV dosage. This detector has a peak responsivity at 365 nm which roughly corresponds to the threshold below which human skin is most sensitive to the damaging effects of UV radiation, and shows a flat response out to 280 nm where the ozone layer absorbs completely. The device’s electronic layout consists of a three-stage high precision op-amp circuit controlled by a digital potentiometer to allow varying of the gain over three orders of magnitude. These analog components are then interfaced to a PIC microcontroller which manages the analog/digital conversion. The microcontroller also displays the instantaneous measurement of UV light, the elapsed exposure time, the integrated UV dose, the skin type chosen, and the SPF setting on an LCD.

Since my freshman year (March 2000) I have been employed as a research assistant in Professor Allen Taflove’s Computational Electromagnetics Laboratory developing both two- and three-dimensional (2-D and 3-D) finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) codes. Under his personal instruction, I have been using the FDTD solution of Maxwell’s equations to model global extremely low frequency (ELF) electromagnetic wave propagation. This work has the potential to provide the physics basis of remote-sensing investigations of lightning and sprites, global temperature change, subsurface structures, and even earthquake precursors. My first step was to construct a 2-D FDTD grid mapped onto the surface of the Earth. This grid incorporated periodic boundary conditions, regular trapezoidal and triangular cells, and cell-merging. It exhibited a high degree of isotropic numerical wave propagation despite the nonuniform nature of the grid, and yielded results for antipodal propagation consistent with those obtained by J. R. Wait in 1969. This work resulted in my publication in IEEE Antennas and Wireless Propagation Letters. Next I constructed a 3-D ELF wave-propagation model in spherical coordinates for the entire Earth-ionosphere volume within ±100 km of sea level. It included the characteristics of the lithosphere, oceans, and ionosphere at a resolution of 40 × 40 × 5 km and yielded results for ELF propagation attenuation from 50 - 500 Hz within ±1 dB of data reported in the literature. I have submitted as first author a full paper on this research to IEEE Trans. Antennas and Propagation. I am now porting my code to a teraflops supercomputer.

My project is a piece of fiction that I have written under the direction of Professor Morson. I have written an alternative ending to one of the greatest novels of all time, Crime and Punishment. Dostoevsky has been criticized for his ending, primarily because he fails to give a psychologically plausible account of the main characters conversion from evil to Christian love. Although Dostoevsky is one of the greatest psychologists to ever live, one thing he was unable to do throughout his career was describe this conversion from evil to good. The goal of my alternative ending is to describe this conversion in Dostoevsky’s style, and to give it the psychological plausibility that it lacks. My ending continues the themes found earlier in the book and mimics his style and form of writing, while giving it new content with the hope of accomplishing what he could not. My presentation will consist of nothing more than a reading of the text I have written, with a small introduction and interpretation of the novel as well.

title: The Role of Domestic Politics and the Kyoto Protocol
abstract: Domestic politics play an extremely important role in determining a state’s response to international environmental issues. A primary example of this is the way the United States and Germany have addressed climate change and the Kyoto Protocol to the FCCC. Factors such as legislative processes, interest group participation, public opinion and electoral processes have great influence over how the issue will be addressed by the state. In the United States, domestic factors have led to foot-dragging, whereas in Germany, swift and comprehensive action has been widely supported by the public and government. I intend to analyze the role of domestic politics in both countries and ascertain which domestic political factor(s) is most significant in determining state action or non-action.

In animal models of early life stress, neonatal stress can cause long lasting impairments in many physiological functions. In my project, I used neonatal maternal separation to determine how postnatal stress impacts the sleep-wake cycle and stress response of neonatal and adult mice. I studied the effects of maternal separation on sleep and plasma corticosterone (CORT) levels under baseline and acute stress conditions in three groups of mice. At nine days of age, the maternally separated (MS) mice (separated from their litter for 3 hours per day for the first 2 weeks after birth) had more rapid eye movement (REM) sleep compared to handled (H) (separated for 1 minute for the first 2 weeks after birth) and control (C) undisturbed mice. As adults, MS mice show an abnormal sleep response to a stress challenge relative to H and C mice. All groups exhibited an initial decrease in both non-REM and REM sleep time in the light phase followed by increased amounts of non-REM and REM sleep time in the dark phase, but these effects were more pronounced in the MS group. Additionally, stress-induced CORT secretion differed between the groups of adult mice. Compared to baseline levels, higher CORT values were observed in all groups of mice following a stress challenge. However, MS mice did not maintain high CORT levels compared to C mice. My project elucidates possible connections between neonatal stress, early detection of sleep abnormalities and adulthood behavioral and endocrine disturbances.

Efforts have been made to develop a microparticle-based glucose biosensor that is to be utilized to measure vitreous glucose concentrations. Monitoring the concentration of glucose in the vitreous is significant because the vitreous serves as one of the primary sources of glucose for the metabolically active retina. The mircoparticle-based glucose biosensor utilizes molecular recognition and fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) as its sensing mechanism. Due to competitive binding, the strength of the fluorescent signal is indicative of the level of glucose present. The suitability of the biosensor and its effectiveness for in vivo use is addressed by performing sensor validation experiments in vitro using a vitreous-like fluid. Utilization of a vitreous-like fluid allows for variation of the viscosity and consequently the diffusion coefficient of the fluid, which addresses the dynamic nature of the vitreous. As a result of the sensor validation experiments, the diffusion coefficient of the vitreous-like fluid can be experimentally derived and compared with what would be predicted theoretically. Knowledge of the diffusion coefficient of the vitreous-like fluid will be useful in determining the sensitivity of the glucose biosensor when employed in the vitreous.

My research is on accurately modeling wireless channels for the somewhat specialized context of wireless video communication. The bulk of my project is designing simulations based on the models with an eye towards runtime efficiency to allow for longer simulations. Although it is mostly a programming and number crunching project the part I will present will be mostly conceptual, with an emphasis on applications of wireless video, the effects of the lossy wireless channel on applications, and some coding methods meant specifically for wireless mediums. I will include data generated from my simulations in my presentation, which will be a high-level summary of the conceptual portion of my research. I will give my presentation using MS PowerPoint, and will entertain questions at the end. I will present simulation data in the form of graphs interspersed throughout my talk, and if I get any detail questions about my data I will be ready to go into finer detail.

My paper will describe the work I have completed under the direction of Dean Barbara O'Keefe. Specifically, I have focused on the interactive gaming industry and the interplay between its three largest console maker corporations: Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo. The development of the modern system, the current state of the industry, and the future trends and innovations will all be considered. My paper will combine economic, communication, and computer science data and analysis to reach conclusions about how corporations position themselves in the industry and their intentions for future development.

title: SPIT and NS-Tools for /proc Counter Collectors
abstract: Spit and Ns are both counter collectors. They both access the /proc directory on a Unix machine and collect all the numbers present there. Spit simply outputs a vector of all the numbers in /proc, separating them by a tab. Ns on the other hand, has all (depends on machine's /proc design) the numbers mapped to a suitable namespace. The idea behind counter collectors is to be able to do all sorts or resource measurements which in turn could be used for example for an intrusion detection system. Here Spit's output vector could be used for principal component analysis of the data while Ns would allow us to concentrate on one or more specific counters (such as data packets lost durung a denial of service attack). Both of them are perl scripts, thus the user should have perl installed. The script also uses the GetOpt :: Long library from CSPAN. Scripts will not work without it. SPIT Usage: % spit [-max i] [-rate f] [-period f] If none of these numbers are defined, max becomes a big (infinite) number, while rate’s default setting is 1 and period is calculated as reciprocal of the rate in this case. All these options affect a single snapshot. Snapshot is a single image of the /proc number data in a given time period. Thus for example % spit -max 100 will take 100 snapshots of the entire /proc numerical image. NS Usage: % ns [-max i] [-rate f] [-period f] [-name s] [-timestamp]. The first three function identically to the options in spit. Name is used to specify the namespace of the desired number. Multiple names are supported Timestamp is simply a trigger, which, when typed, will cause the script to print a timestamp at the beginning of each run. Ns will print results from counters (if there are more than one counter being collected, then the results will be printed side by side, separated by tab) in a column ordered fashion, one counter state in time per line. To compare free and total physical memory and stop at one-hundredth-line, one would type: % perl ns -max 100 - name mem/physical/free - name mem/physical/total. Ns currently supports most of /proc counters except process/process_id/status, drive/scsi and tty/driver/serial.

Prior research has indicated systematic cultural differences in concepts of illness, which may account for communication problems between doctors and minority patients. Though addressing these issues would help physicians better treat their patients, little work has focused on the cognitive structure of mental representations. This study investigates how causal models of illness vary across cultures. The three groups included in the study (Hispanic highschool educated, Caucasian highschool educated, and Caucasian college educated) allowed us to isolate the effects of education and cultural background on cognitive models of illness. All participants listed symptoms and causes of alcoholism, asthma, AIDS, cold, depression, and diabetes. The symptoms listed did not vary significantly, indicating that all three groups were referring to the same illnesses. However, the causes of illnesses varied between groups as a function of both education and culture. With regard to education, participants with higher education cite biological internal causes across illnesses as opposed to participants with lower education. For example, college educated Caucasians name virus and bacteria whereas the two highschool educated groups attribute external causes, such as sneezing, to contagious illnesses. Culture, rather than education, seems to increase attributions of heredity. That is, Caucasians of both levels of education mentioned hereditary causes more frequently than Hispanic participants. This study utilizes qualitative and quantitative methods to distinguish the cultural and educational factors of illness representation.

While studying abroad with the School for International Training, I completed a month-long anthropological research project in a village located in the mountains of Chapada Diamantina, Bahia, Brazil. My objective was to study the effects of an alternative intentional community, a ten-year-old commune of roughly 30 members, on the surrounding society. Until 1980, the village had been a closed society of plantation farmers, without many modern amenities. In the past 25 years, an influx of newcomers, including the founding members of the commune, has drastically altered village culture. Most noticeably, the overall view towards environmental policy has nearly reversed from traditional crop farming and clear-burning cattle ranching to passionate environmental protectionism. There is some dissent, evidenced by a plague of deliberately set forest fires in and around the farm and newly created national park, which natives, newcomers and experts alike attribute to the former ranchers who depended on fire to create pasture land. The majority of the villagers now join volunteer firefighting squads and activist groups to help prevent this practice. Through interviews, observations and photographs, I explore the influence of the commune, which has an environmental mission and members active in controlling the fires and publicly teaching their own environmental methods, in the reversal of the village’s overall view towards environmental policy.

I am working to develop in-situ scanning probe and electron microscopy testing of nanomaterials by employing a MEMS device developed using the MUMPS process. The microdevice has three well-defined elements, a thermal actuator, a specimen, and a load sensor based on differential capacitance measurement. A set of slanted beams connected to a trunk provides the actuation displacement when a current is circulated between the fixed pads. Thermal expansion of the doped polysilicon beams results in a displacement of the trunk and consequently loading of the sample. The device works in displacement control. The differential capacitor attached serves as a load sensor after proper calibration. I will employ this device to load a nanocrystalline specimen and simultaneously image its surface with the purpose of measuring its deformation. Therefore, the focus of my research will be the development of imaging techniques for deformation mapping. The Park CP-R AFM possessing closed loop feedback control will be used to scan the central part of the specimen at various loads. The images will then be analyzed using digital image correlation (DIC) software to obtain the deformation field with nanometer resolution. Two type of surface patterns will be investigated: i) surface roughness arising from the microfabrication process and delineated grain boundaries, and ii) patterns of dots produced with dip pen nanolithography (DPN). In-situ SEM experiments using the same MEMS loading device will be performed by employing the FEG SEM LEO instrument. In this case the surface of the specimen will be interrogated using images produced by secondary electrons.

Piaget’s early studies of spatial cognition suggested that children had rather poor mental representations of space – representations that did not include the relationships between places, but rather more route-specific beads-on-a-string type knowledge. A new string of research in the seventies suggested that children did have some configurational knowledge, but that it was mostly centered on landmarks and was not very flexible to mental manipulations. At this point in their development (around age 7), we ask ourselves if exposure to maps would allow children to develop a more integrated mental structure of the space. This would mean increased performance not on distance rankings and route descriptions, but on inferences and calculations that could take place as a result of a more complex spatial understanding. This study was designed to measure children’s learning from maps of their own neighborhoods. The children were divided into a verbal group (which functioned as the control group) and a map group. Over the first two sessions they were given tasks relating to landmarks in their neighborhood. In the third session, the children used photographs to create a representation of the way these and other landmarks existed in 'real space.' This mapping procedure was used to force the children to create relationships not only between landmarks learned in the tasks, but also new landmarks, representing the integration of their mental representations. It was hypothesized that children who had completed tasks with maps would have more success at placing the landmarks with novel relationships. Results are not at this point completed, but will be ready by the time of presentation.

My project encompasses organic synthetic chemistry and nanotechnology. The goal of my project has been to synthesize novel molecules that will self-assemble to encapsulate a carbon nanotube. Applications of the carbon nanotube to nanotechnology are currently hot areas of research. These nanotubes are small tube-shaped structures that have certain electrical and mechanical properties that makes them potentially very useful in microscopy, hydrogen storage, building of nanoscale transitors, bio-sensing, etc. However, there are certain challenges that must be overcome. First, nanotubes group together in bundles, but they are generally useful only as single nanotubes. Second, the nanotubes are not water soluble, which poses a problem, especially when the nanotube is needed in a biological system. Third, for use in transistors, nanotubes need a stable insulating coating, much as a copper wire needs insulation by plastic. Finally, functional molecular groups used as sensors for other molecules can be attached to the nanotube covalently, but this can alter the electrical properties of the nanotube. My research has focused on creating molecules that will solve all of these problems by assembling and cross-linking on the nanotube to form a stable, water-soluble coating that can be functionalized without drastically changing the electrical properties of the nanotube and that will separate individual nanotubes from bundles. Size, charge, shape, and hydrophilicity were varied to create molecules that would prefer to assemble on and encapsulate the nanotube rather than assemble into micelles that do not interact very well with the nanotubes.

An impressive increase in the immunization rates among the indigenous population of the South American Andes has been reported since 1990. While the communities remain relatively isolated in terms of geography, languages, and traditions, the healthcare conventions of the people have been integrated with Western medicine and vaccinations. The general health of the indigenous population in this region is inferior to that of the urban population, as well as health in terms of vaccine-preventable diseases. Vaccine-preventable disease in the children of the Quechua, Aymara, and the indigenous population at large is an issue at the forefront of many national and non-governmental agencies’ agendas. A multitude of vaccination and disease eradication programs have been implemented, the technique for doing so has no formal structure. This greatly impacts the effectiveness of such programs based both on willingness to participate and continued adherence to such programs. In order to ensure the health of the region and the eradication of vaccine-preventable disease, it is imperative to have a cultural context in which to place the disease in order to create an understanding within the community. This paper will review the current literature and studies on the health of the indigenous peoples of the region, the disease rates within the population and the techniques used in the existing vaccination programs focusing on children. A comparison of both methods in this region and in others around the world will bring to light effects of culture on the health of a population and recommend techniques to integrate the indigenous health techniques with the Western model.

title: Metal-binding studies of mutant DNA-binding domains of the glucocorticoid receptor
abstract: It has been observed that the symptoms of lead poisoning in children differ from those of adults. This suggests that lead affects proteins important in development. One group of proteins important in development is the nuclear hormone receptor superfamily. These proteins can be divided into six functional domains, one of which is the DNA--binding domain (DBD). The DBD contains two zinc--binding regions similar to 'zinc fingers' but each contain four cysteine residues (Cys4-zinc sites). Of the proteins in the nuclear hormone receptor superfamily, the DNA-binding domain of the glucocorticoid receptor (DBD/GR) has been extensively studied in our lab. Zinc--binding studies of the DBD/GR indicate that two equivalents of zinc bind, whereas lead-binding studies seem to indicate that three equivalents of lead bind. Upon closer examination of the amino acid sequence of the DBD/GR, two additional cysteine residues outside of the Cys4-zinc sites exist. It is hypothesized that these extra cysteine residues are responsible for the third equivalent of lead binding in the DBD/GR. To test this, we have begun preparing mutants by systematically mutating the cysteine residues to alanine, and performing lead-binding studies on these mutants. Details and progress will be presented.

We are working in conjunction with the Naval Research Lab to model dialectics with negative permittivity and permeability using Finite Difference Time Domain methods. A scientist at the lab has tried to solve Maxwell’s equations for a rectangular wave-guide consisting of this type of dielectric and has been unable to find satisfying results in the frequency domain. We are using a three dimensional Fortran code to model his geometry in the time domain so that more can be known about how these strange materials work. In the course of this project we have encountered hurdles from both the inherent limitations of FDTD and also from the lack of knowledge in this area. However, we have persevered because of the unknown benefits this knowledge could have for electrical engineering.

title: Struggling Students at a Prestigious University: Exploring the Impact of Social Class and Self-support
abstract: This is a qualitative analysis of in-depth interviews with fifteen undergraduates and three high-ranking administrators at a prestigious private university. I spoke with students who felt that they were “struggling with money due to their parents’ situation.” Two variables, social class and level of self-support, emerged as important determinants of student experience. These two concepts were used to divide the sample into six groups for further analysis. The research also examined university administrators’ conceptions of social class, views of self-support, and the corresponding institutional practices relating to each group. Also included are suggestions for improvement of student services from respondents in each group. This study attempted to escape the confines of the “liberal model” that is present in other research of this kind. This model often disregards the self-reported experiences of the individual, obscures the variation within social groups by attempting to define individual experience based on group membership, and collapses the concepts of social class and parental/self support into one variable. Reflected in my methodology is an effort to allow participants to define their own perceived advantages and disadvantages. I also chose to not focus on a particular category but rather on all students who believe they are struggling and to distinguish the effects of social class and parental/self support.
