I hope this study helps to create a more nuanced dialogue about education and advantage. I will also be submitting an application for a group project. I was told to state this in both applications.

The achievement gap between black and white students is of increasing concern in this country. Based on the Minority Student Achievement Network survey administered to 2,640 Evanston Township High School students, this project was designed to examine one explanation for this gap – Signithia Fordham and John Ogbu’s theory of oppositional culture. In accordance with this theory, we looked at racial group differences in perceptions of returns to education, resistance to school, and various aspects of peer culture; we then looked to see how strongly these factors affected students’ grade point averages. Our quantitative methods included comparing group means for each variable and performing regression analyses for each race and gender group. If the data fit this theory, we would expect to find that black students have higher levels of oppositional culture than their white counterparts and that this difference explains the lower average achievement of black students. However, our data do not support the existence of an oppositional culture at the high school. Racial differences in oppositional culture pale in comparison to gender differences; instead, males on average have much higher levels of oppositional culture than females do. The predictive value of the theory is also lacking. The relationship between academic achievement and oppositional culture changes according to what measure is used and affects males, females, and each racial group differently. A powerpoint presentation has already been created. Kimberly Tester will also be submitting an application for her senior thesis project. She was told to state this in both applications.

My research project is done in a specialized field of Electrical Engineering called VLSI. VLSI stands for Very Large Scale Integration and involves the lowest level in the design of microchips used in computers and electronics. Modern trends in computing and user demands are always pushing for faster and faster machines. This in turn dictates speed as being the single most important factor in all elements of computer hardware and integrated circuits. The relatively recent explosion of laptop use and mobile communications has made power an important consideration. However, speed has still dominated integrated circuit design methodologies. Newer technologies have been used so far purely to generate faster circuits. My research is in attempting to assess the potential for value added by scaling this technology without increasing the frequency. By not increasing the frequency there is ability to reduce the power consumption used by transistors, the fundamental unit of computer hardware. Many portable and micro devices nowadays use VLSI circuits where speed is not as great an issue to them as it is to the computing world. Cell phones, pagers, and watches are just a few devices that would greatly benefit from lower and lower power consumption. Cellular phone battery life is a much greater issue today than is the speed of the programs it runs. This lower power consumption will in effect create longer battery life for the electronics that will use it. My research also addresses costs and cost savings associated with all of the above.

My project was a case of athletic identity from a Symbolic Interactionist Perspective. I interviewed 12 athletes about their athletic experiences. I then examined the responses for patterns and looked to explain the results. I used previous work on symbolic interactionism (Mead, Goffman, Turner, Stryker) to establish a theoretical framework. My focus was the relationship between the individual who is actively making and taking different roles, and the athletic institution which contrains role making and role taking. I compared the confining nature of collegiate athletics to what Erving Goffman refers to as a 'total institution' and found many parralells. In addition, I comfirmed earlier studies that asserted that the nature of college athletics creates a salient athletic identity amongst the participants. However, I departed from earlier studies that claimed that this salient athletic identity creates inherent conflict and strain between the multiple roles individuals must assume. Rather, I argue that the athletic institution is structed in such a way as to allow to avoid role conflict. The encompassing nature of athletics makes it so that if an athlete chooses they can stay in an athletic role while in a social and academic setting, thus avoiding conflict. This study has importance as it raises issue about the experiences of college athletes. As collegiate athletics becomes a more and more lucrative business, it becomes more important to re-evaluate the demands placed on the athletes, and the experiences they endure.

Production of high quality materials is a fundamental building block for creating state of the art electronics. The quaternary semiconductor material consisting of gallium, indium, arsenic, and phosphorous (GaInAsP) is one such material. At the Center for Quantum Devices at NU we use this material in the development of laser diodes and waveguides for telecommunications applications. One method of producing or growing this material is a method called Metalorganic Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD). For my research I am investigating ways to grow high quality GaInAsP material using MOCVD. Some requirements of high quality material are that it should be free from physical defects, have low amounts of impurities, and achieve certain performance measures (i.e. respond to a certain wavelength of light). As a part of creating these high quality materials it is necessary to test these indicators of quality using scanning electron microscopes, x-ray diffraction, photoluminescence testing, and atomic force microscopy. MOCVD growth is a very complex process with numerous variables and even today there are certain aspects that are more of art than a science. The MOCVD process involves electrical engineering, chemistry, and quantum physics. Finding out how to manipulate these variables is intriguing, multidisciplinary research that is at the cutting edge of science. In the lab I carry out both the growth and testing of the material and work with other researchers in the lab to figure out the optimal growth conditions for producing the high quality GaInAsP material necessary for the devices we produce.

Using data taken from Kitt Peak National Observatory and the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer, I examine features in the interstellar medium toward the star system HD206267 (including stars A, C, and D) concentrating on molecular hydrogen.

Based on qualitative and quantitative analysis, this research project was designed to examine the existence of a glass ceiling – the name given to the subtle barriers that inhibit women and minorities from reaching the upper echelons of corporate America, government and academia – inherent in a university student newspaper. Specifically, the study looked at reasons why the student newspaper has not seen a woman editor in chief in 10 years when women comprise nearly 75 percent of the university’s journalism majors. The data suggests that the glass ceiling exists at the university newspaper for reasons similar to why it exists in the U.S. labor force – choices made by individuals and constraints inherent in institutions cause men and women to make different choices about labor force participation. Existing research that attempts to explain the existence of the glass ceiling attributes the phenomenon to human capital theory, to social role theory and to a male-dominated and inhospitable workplace culture. Most important to why the glass ceiling exists at this institution, however, is its male-dominating and inhospitable workplace culture, which includes an informal social network among men, the assumed authority of men and the existence of sexual harassment.

My project concerns Yttria powder-loaded screen printing inks used as electroyte layers in Solid Oxide Fuel Cells. Specifically, I experimented with powder loading levels and their effects on electrolyte characteristics and performance. The project includes rheometry data for the inks, as well as single fuel cell test results and Scanning Electron Microscope chracterizations of the screen printed electrolyte layers.

In the thesis I am writing for the Economics Honors Program, I would like to examine how the quality of care in United States non-profit nursing homes compares with that in for-profits; I would then like to explore what factors determine the variable “quality of care.” Quality of care is extremely difficult to measure because of its subjectivity. In my analysis, I have decided to take a novel approach and use the variable “percentage of residents with bedsores” as a proxy for quality of care. Bedsores have a direct correlation with how much time you spend in bed and also with the degree of medical treatment you receive. A general outline of my analysis: 1) Examine all the nursing homes in Rhode Island, chosen simply because of its manageable number of nursing homes (103). These will be representative of the 13,000+ nursing homes in the U.S. 2) Separate them into profit and non-profit types and compare their respective qualities including # of certified beds, # of residents, % of residents with bedsores, % of residents with loss of ability in basic daily tasks, % of residents in pain, # of health deficiencies, and RN hours per resident per day. Hypothesis: there will be a smaller percentage of patients with bedsores in the non-profit sector--quality of care is higher in non-profit nursing homes. 3) Compare RN hours/patient/day ratio with bedsore variable. Hypothesis: there will be an inverse relationship between % of patients with bedsores and nurse hours/patient/day.

title: Three-dimensional atom-probe investigation of the evolution of the composition and structure of nanoscale precipitates in model Ni-Al-Cr superalloys
abstract: In this project, I employ the three-dimensional atom probe (3DAP) microscope to follow the temporal evolution of Ni3Al (gamma prime) precipitation at 600 C of the superalloy Ni-7.5 Al-8.5 Cr at. % from nucleation to coarser development. I will compare my results with previous results from Ni-5.2 Al-14.2 Cr, an alloy containing a lower Al-supersaturation. After minutes of aging at this temperature, precipitation is evident in both alloys, with precipitates (clusters) as small as 0.5 nm in radius detected by the 3DAP microscope. In particular, I will report the composition of the matrix and precipitate phases, precipitate dimensions and morphologies, and kinetics of decomposition as a function of aging time.

Our research examined young children’s understanding of object size and of scale relations between objects. The motivation for this research originated from parents’ reports that their child has attempted to sit in a chair that is obviously too small for the child to fit in. These scale errors are intriguing since prior research and theory on children’s cognitive, perceptual, and motor abilities suggest that these kinds of errors should not occur (Adolph and Avolio, 2000). We investigated whether young children (twenty-four 16-24 month-olds and twenty-four 29-32 month-olds), would make scale errors both with their own bodies and when playing with a doll. An example of a body scale error would be a young child making a serious attempt to lie on a doll bed that is too small for him or her. An example of a doll scale error would be a child attempting to place a rather large doll (approximately 30 inches long) in a miniature chair. Our research was primarily aimed at the investigation of the occurrence of doll scale errors. Our results indicate that young children make scale errors frequently and with a variety of objects. Our study provides evidence for the occurrence of both body and doll scale errors. These findings suggest that scale errors are caused by something other than children’s body scaling abilities. It seems as though young children’s knowledge of the function of objects (e.g., chairs are for sitting) sometimes predominates or is not inhibited by their knowledge of size constraints. Children may know about objects in two separate ways: in terms of their functions and in terms of their sizes.

In recent years there has been significant interest in conducting business research and particularly in learning about chief executive officers (CEO). Several studies have been conducted on CEOs and their backgrounds, but none have tried to determine the relationship, if any, between the career paths of CEOs and their ability to successfully lead their companies to higher returns. This study examines the relationship between functional areas of experience and shareholder returns. It is hypothesized that all areas of functional experience will positively impact a CEO’s success, but that in the energy and utilities industries, the more structured areas of experience, such as finance and operations, will have the largest impact. These industries were chosen because they are large long standing-industries with inelastic product demand. The independent variable is the number of years of experience in each of ten functional categories. The dependent variable is the percentage change in the company’s stock price between July 1, 1998, and June 29, 2001. In an attempt to eliminate many parameters, restrictions were placed on the period of analysis, the size of the companies, the industry in which the companies operate and the amount of time the CEO has held the current position. The data were analyzed in two sections: the key antecedent statistics and the relationship between the antecedent statistics and success. Analyzing the antecedent statistics revealed several predictable phenomena. Many CEOs had experience in general management, finance, operations and engineering but few had experience in marketing, legal, non-profit and entrepreneurial areas. Several categories had skewed distributions because a few CEOs had several years of experience in a certain area. The key findings came in the analysis of the relationship between the antecedent statistics and the change in stock price. While no relationship could be determined from analyzing the years of functional experience, two statistically significant relationships were present when analyzing the binomial data. With 95% confidence, a CEO with marketing/sales experience led his company to a 101% higher return on average over a three year period than a CEO without such experience and with 90% confidence, a CEO with entrepreneurial experience led his company to a 65% higher return on average over a three year period than a CEO without such experience. It also appeared that increasing the years of experience in these two areas yields diminishing returns. Based on this study, conclusions cannot be drawn about the relationship between the other areas of functional experience and the change in a company’s stock price. The market conditions during the period of analysis, sample size and broad definition of the general management category present some risk to the conclusions drawn in this study. Nonetheless, this study provides a foundation for future research that could further explore the relationship between the functional areas of experience of a CEO and the ability to generate higher returns for company shareholders.

It has been suggested by Abraham Tesser (2000) that repair mechanisms for the self work best when operating in the same domain as that of the rejection experience. That is, if one’s self-esteem is threatened, it must be reassured in order for the self-esteem to return to salient levels. Since our lab is concerned with the need to belong, our basic hypothesis was that a repair to a participant’s mood could not ameliorate a perceived social threat but a specific repair addressing the invalidity of that threat (e.g. the participant is shown acceptance) could return social belonging levels back to baseline. Participants were divided into two main conditions: (a) social threat, and (b) individual threat. Within these two categories, two further categories were used in order to assess repair strategies: (a) mood repair, and (b) social-self repair. Participants were placed in individual computer stations where they were given a false rejection situation—either they were told they would be working on a project alone, or they were told that they were not creative enough to participate in a follow-up task. Their moods and self-esteem were then assessed and a repair mechanism was administered. Following the repair session, the mood and self-esteem was reassessed. Preliminary analysis suggests that our hypothesis is true to significance. When the participant's was rejected socially, only a social repair was able to raise their social-self scores back to normal levels; mood repair was unable to do this.

title: The Role of Gender in Mental Illness Stigma
abstract: The basic issue at the heart of this project concerns the factors that determine whether or not an individual feels sympathetic toward, and motivated to help, a person with a mental illness. The psychological factors governing the decision to help are captured in the attribution-affect-action theory of behavior. This model states that characteristics of actors and their behavior elicit attributions about the causes of the behavior, which in turn elicit affective reactions and action tendencies. The goal of this study is to better understand some of the psychological determinants of these attributions, in particular the role of gender. Most obviously, gender stereotypes may influence the attributions that people make about mental illness. Gender stereotypes appear to arise in an effort to explain the perceived behavioral differences between men and women. Thus, the present study will examine not only the sex of the target person but also the gender stereotypicality of the person’s mental illness symptoms. People are assumed to represent psychological disorders as prototypes having specific features or symptoms. By examining the attributional and affective underpinnings of perceivers’ reactions can we begin to understand how gender (a)typicality influences overall favorability of reactions to persons with mental illnesses. Little is known about how these two forms of stereotyping interact to determine reactions to the men and women who experience serious mental illnesses. This current study will clarify the nature of this interaction.

I propose to present the research which I have conducted and been involved with over the four quarters that I have co-oped as a research biomedical engineer in the R&D Orthobiologics department at DePuy Orthopaedics, Inc., A Johnson & Johnson Company. A fellow co-op student, (Northwestern undergraduate biomedical engineering student) who works in the same research department as myself, also plans to participate in the presentation. The research group that I work with concentrates on tissue engineering, with a special emphasis on the design and fabrication of knee meniscus tissue implants for meniscal tissue repair. The biomaterial utilized in many of the research group's products and projects is SIS (Small Intestine Submucosa), of which DePuy owns the exclusive orthopaedic application intellectual property rights. I plan on using two posters that I created and used during the past co-op student poster contest for presentation during the undergraduate research symposium. The posters depict my involvement in the conceptualization, design, fabrication, and mechanical testing processes associated with researching the tissue repair implants. The company that I co-op for, DePuy Orthopaedics, Inc., A Johnson & Johnson Company, is the leading designer, manufacturer and distributor of orthopaedic devices and supplies including hip, knee, ankle, shoulder, wrist, elbow, and finger replacements, and operating room products.

title: Performing Ambiguous Identity: The Problem of Resource Acquisition in Santiago
abstract: In the past 100 years almost half of the Mapuche indigenous population of Chile has migrated to Santiago from the Southern rural areas of Chile. This has changed their cultural identity, in that land no longer epitomizes the people nor the culture. In Chile, because the state has not been successful in helping the Mapuche preserve their culture and achieve a better standard of living, these indigenous peoples have migrated to the cities in search of new resources in order to survive. For these people, preserving culture is secondary. In Santiago the Mapuche try to hide their identity in order to avoid discrimination, and paradoxically, in order to obtain a better standard of living. Because they hide their identity and try to assimilate, they are not organized as a community, and the government has no way of recognizing them as Mapuche. They have become tourists at their own cultural events. The new urban Mapuche society has different priorities, such receiving aid for education and housing. However, access to this aid for the Mapuche is restricted because of the way they perform their identity. The idea that identity is something that is performed is key in understanding the Mapuche dilemma. (Barth 1969). This directly affects the relationship and interaction of Indians, states, and cultures. (Urban and Sherzer 1997). The Mapuche are at a critical juncture where the environment, culture, and relationship within the state are changing. However, many people are not acknowledging this change. This creates problems for the acquisition of resources and makes the Mapuche a permanent lower class.

title: The Dynamics of Extrasolar Planetary Systems
abstract: The dynamical theory of star systems with multiple planets plays an important role in the theory of solar system formation and is key to the understanding of the stability of our own solar system, as well as to the understanding of and search for extrasolar planetary systems. In a solar system of two planets, there exist analytical criteria for determining the stability of the system based on the initial orbital properties. No such criteria exist in systems with 3 or more planets, and thus analytical predictions of final orbital properties of systems and evolutionary timescales are difficult when the number of planets is greater than 2. The 3 planet system represents a qualitatively different type of dynamical system, and understanding the evolution of 3 planet systems is crucial to an understanding of the dynamical evolution of planetary systems in general. Through numerical integrations of the Hamiltonian equations of motion that describe 3 planet systems, this project investigates the statistical properties of 3 planet systems and enables a probabilistic prediction of the distribution of orbital properties from the initial orbital conditions.

I have been working on the characerization of factors involved in the process of limb specification, or how fore and hind limbs develop differently during vertebrate development. For two years I have investigated the expression of several proteins involved in limb specification during chicken development, using several techniques including in situ hybridization and RT-PCR. One such protein is a novel factor identified by our laboratory which seems to be involved in the cell localization of important Tbx family transcription factors. These Tbx proteins have been previously shown to be crucial in limb specification, and our work may be an important first step in understanding how their functions are regulated in the cells of developing animals.

The 3D structure of a protein, which determines its biological function, results from its sequence of amino acids. Mutating an amino acid of a protein can alter its structure and function. The 'secondary structure' of a protein, which is the collection of characteristic structures determined by short stretches of amino acids (i.e. a group of adjacent amino acids may form a helix or a flat sheet), can be accurately predicted. The ability to design proteins with a given structure is an important area of research especially for advancements in drug design. I have developed an algorithm for detecting the mutational constraints of a family of structurally similar proteins; this tells us which amino acids should not be mutated in order to preserve the structure. I have also developed a novel algorithm that uses this data to fully-automatically generate a new primary amino acid sequence. Using secondary structure prediction methods, I have verified that this de novo sequence has the same secondary structure as the family I used to create it. This is a novel and significant approach to protein design. In summary, I can take a group of proteins with the same structure and fully-automatically generate a new protein that also has the same structure. I have implemented this methodology into a computer program and have made the results publicly available on the Internet. This methodology has only used on families with very simple structure and the results remain to be further verified in a 'wet lab.'

title: The Role of the Vastus Medialis and Vastus Lateralis in Medial-Lateral Knee Joint Stability
abstract: The purpose of this research study was to improve understanding of stability of the patellofemoral joint in the medial-lateral direction. It has been shown that changing the background activation levels of the quadriceps may influence the quadriceps moment exerted at the knee (Lafortune and Cavanagh, 1987). This study examines the effect of different quadriceps background activation levels on the role of individual quadriceps muscles in the medial-lateral direction. Different background activation levels of all the quadriceps muscles are provided prior to electrical stimulation of an individual quadriceps muscle. The two quadriceps muscles examined in the experiment were the vastus lateralis (VL) and the vastus medialis oblique (VMO). The VL is the traditional abductor of the patellofemoral joint, while the VMO is the traditional adductor. Electrical stimulation of either the VL or VMO resulted in an abduction/adduction to extension moment ratio, which was used to determine the role of the VMO or VL in each subject. The results of the study showed that the role of the VL was consistently an abductor of the patellofemoral joint for all subjects, while the VMO surprisingly functioned as either an adductor or an abductor of the patellofemoral joint for different subjects. A trend was observed between the role of the VMO and the magnitude of the moment ratio of the VL. The VL was a significantly stronger abductor when the VMO served as an abductor, and the VL was a weaker abductor when the VMO functioned as an adductor.

title: Concreteness and Symbolic Development in Early Literacy
abstract: The purpose of the present study is to empirically investigate the effects of playing with concrete representations of letters on the two components of the alphabetic principle—letter knowledge and symbolic knowledge. In order to do this, we have compared the effects of playing with two different types of toys—symbolic letter toys versus non-symbolic toys—on preschool children’s acquisition of the alphabetic principle. Parents often give their children symbolic toys because they believe these will help their children achieve literacy. However, recent research on children’s developing understanding of symbolic relations suggests potential disadvantages of using concrete letter toys to help children learn alphabetic principles. This research suggests that symbols have a dual nature: They are simultaneously objects in their own right and a representation of something else. If children are to focus more on the tangible features of the object (e.g., the salient properties of the concrete letter), it may be at the expense of the symbolic relation between the object and its symbolic meaning. Our findings have shown that while non-symbolic play does not have an effect on children’s understanding of the symbolic properties of letters, playing with letter manipulatives in a symbolic manner does have a positive effect on children’s ability to use letters as symbolic representations.

title: Dynamics of a Bouncing Ball
abstract: A steel ball, when dropped into the appropriate magnetic field, will accelerate due to both the gravitational and magnetic field. Appropriate timing of an electromagnet in conjunction with a hard bouncing surface can therefore create the appearance of a ball bouncing in perpetual motion. This system has been modeled and built through LIMS (Laboratory for Intelligent Mechanical Systems) in the Department of Mechanical Engineering. Alternative methods and control systems for achieving stability will be discussed in an exhibition-booth style poster, and will accompany a working prototype ball bouncer. This project has potential application in several separate areas of study. First, as an educational tool, this project is a clear application of energy conservation and basic kinematics for basic physics. Second, it explores control strategy for optimization of different variables. And finally, as an example of an under-actuated system, this project explores under what circumstances the application of a single actuator can create multiple stability modes.

title: Determinants of Female Autonomy and its Demographic Implications
abstract: Amartya Sen argues that “the extensive reach of women’s agency is one of the more neglected areas of development studies, and most urgently in need of correction.” It has been suggested that women’s agency has important implications for demographic transition in developing nations, with higher female autonomy encouraging lower fertility and lower child mortality. However, the precise definition of female “agency” or “autonomy” has often been unclear, and although there has been extensive speculation about the determinants of female autonomy, there is little empirical research to support these claims. This study analyzes female autonomy according to the definition of Dyson and Moore (1983): “the ability. . . to obtain information and use it as the basis for making decisions about one’s private concerns and those of one’s intimates. Thus equality of autonomy between the sexes. . . implies equal decision-making ability with regard to personal affairs.” My project uses data from the 1998-1999 National Family Health Survey (NFHS) in India, a survey in which 90,303 ever-married women ages 15-49 throughout the country were interviewed regarding their decision-making power and other freedoms within the household. The subjects provided detailed information on their own socioeconomic backgrounds as well as those of their spouses, permitting an analysis of the factors that influence female autonomy. The Survey also contains detailed maternal history data and questions regarding the “ideal” number of sons and daughters, allowing for observation of fertility, child mortality, and son preference. This project uses NFHS data to better understand the determinants of female autonomy, and then examines the relationship of women’s autonomy to fertility, child mortality, and son preference.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility in the 21st Century: Examining the Link between Corporate Social Performance and Financial Performance
abstract: In this study I test the hypothesis that corporate social performance, the measure of a corporation’s relationships with its stakeholders (customers, suppliers, employees, investors, and the community), has a positive impact on the financial performance of corporations. I analyze the validity of the social performance (SP)-financial performance (FP) link by using suggested methods of controlling for variables. By including factors such as quality of management, innovativeness, organization size, and industry, I attempt to improve internal validity of the SP-FP correlation and explain other internal factors of management that contribute to this link.

title: McHenry County Ku Klux Klan: Populist or Violent?
abstract: Most Americans probably envision the average Klansman as an ignorant, hooded redneck who burns crosses on behalf of white supremacy. Although this image is often accurate, the Ku Klux Klan (KKK) of the 1920s did not resemble the Klan of later eras. The 1920’s Klan encompassed a large number of middle-class white men with stable families and a strong Protestant religious faith. These men were driven by a number of economic, political, and cultural tensions during the early 1920s that increased nation-wide support for “pure Americanism.” With mainstream backing, the KKK’s membership during this era soared into the millions as it became one of the most influential secret societies that America has ever formed. This honors project seeks to understand the tactics, motivations, and social base of the 1920s Klan. I will test the generalizations of a number of historians of the 1920s Ku Klux Klan against data from the McHenry County, Illinois Klan provides to determine what really drove chapters in the Midwest to participate in Klan activities. Was it primarily a movement based on civic activism, as historians Leonard Moore and Alan Goldberg argue, or an attempt to subordinate entire groups of people as Nancy MacLean contends? Were Klansmen in northern Illinois largely populist, reactionary, religious extremists, racists, or a combination of all of these things? Comprising Seventeen townships with a rich history of Klan related activities that peaked into the 1920s and existed beyond the mid-1990s, the McHenry County, Illinois chapter of the Klan will be a test case against a number of theories on the 1920s Ku Klux Klan.

title: Self-Awareness and Aggression
abstract: Duval and Wicklund’s 1972 “Theory of Self-Awareness” hypothesized that when attention is directed towards the self, internal personal standards are activated and behavior changes to conform with these standards. For example, if people disapprove of aggression, but are provoked, increased self-awareness will cause them to control their aggression. Adding to this theory, Carver and Scheier found that self-awareness may activate not only standards, but can also increase the intensity of emotions. For example, when participants were angered, those in the mirror condition of high self-awareness behaved more aggressively than those in the non-mirror condition of low self-awareness. Carver and Scheier proposed that when self-awareness is high, there is a competition between standards and emotion, to influence behavior. The present study attempts to determine when standards overpower emotions, or vice versa, when self-awareness is high. We propose that the salience of aggressive standards is dependent upon situation conditions, such as intent of provocation. When people are intentionally provoked, the emotion of anger will overwhelm standards, and aggressive behavior will increase. However, in an unintentionally provoked situation, standards against retaliation will be increased with self-awareness, overpowering the influence of emotion, thus resulting in decreased aggression.

title: Perceptions of Asian Ethnicities by the Internet Community: The Politics of Personal Ads on Craigslist
abstract: This study was conducted in order to understand the stereotypes and assumptions that lie in the Internet community about Asian ethnicities. By posting 25 ads, consisting of 5 ethnicities, 5 personalities, and 5 cities, I was able to collect over 1,000 responses and glean what perceptions men have of Asian and Asian-American women. This study was able to understand what the hyphenated-American identity means to both men and women, as well as the ways in which ethnicities are clumped together or separated (e.g. Japanese by culture and Thai by food). General trends were found, such as the use of food as a cultural marker and the abundance of Asian men who feel emasculated by society. These trends, along with numerical data, were used to better understand the cultural implications of these ad responses. There were also instances of white privilege, "Asian fetishes," the confusion of South Asian men’s identity, as well as a substantial presence of multiracial children, who are a significantly small minority that represented themselves more aggressively in these responses.

title: Inhibition of Donor-derived NF- B Dependent Mucosal Inflammation Mitigates Small Bowel Allograft Rejection
abstract: Small bowel transplantation is the only remaining option for people on total parenteral nutrition experiencing liver failure. But even with immunosuppression, acute allograft rejection remains a major impediment. The augmented rejection responses may be due to continuous interactions with resident bacteria, often characterized by an activated phenotype in mucosal T cells and higher levels of inflammatory mediators when compared to solid organs. This baseline state of activation can be further increased in a SB allograft that has been challenged by specific pathogenic bacteria. NF B is a pleiotropic transcriptional activator involved most notably in inflammatory responses, apoptosis, differentiation, and growth. Activation of NF B requires the ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis of its repressor, the I B subunit. Our hypothesis is that NF B activation in donor intestinal epithelium augments the rejection response in a SB allograft by promoting epithelial inflammatory responses. To support this, we used a mouse model to demonstrate significantly higher levels of activated NF B in the SB allograft compared to SB isograft controls. mRNA expression of selected NF B dependent cytokines and chemokines in the allograft became increased as early as Day 3 after transplantation and continued to increase until at least day 8. Using small bowel donors from double transgenic mice with proteolysis-resistant I B localized only to intestinal epithelium, we observe a significant decrease in T cell-activation induced inflammatory mediators in the intestine. More importantly, this epithelial inhibition of NF B prolonged allograft survival. These data suggest that controlling NF B dependent inflammation in the graft itself can inhibit rejection in a SB allograft.

title: Unveiled: The Headscarf in Turkey
abstract: One of the main factors that has differentiated Turkey from other countries in the Middle East is the high degree of freedoms granted to women. Turkish women received the right to vote, among other privileges, a considerable time before their counterparts in the Middle East and even in some European countries. Perhaps even more importantly, Turkish women have made great inroads into the areas of literacy and education. The number of female students in Turkish Universities has grown exponentially over the past fifty years to a point where, as of 1997, more than a third of all faculty members in Turkish academia were comprised of women. In spite of these extraordinary accomplishments in the area of women’s rights, Turkey has witnessed a formidable Islamist backlash against secularization and Westernization that analysts have labeled a U-turn in Turkey’s road to modernization. By donning the socially banned veil and adopting a newly constructed, all-encompassing view of Islamic practice, many highly educated, urban Muslim women are taking part in a movement to broaden the role of Islam in Turkish society. Therefore, the purpose of my project is to research the integral role of Turkish women in the Islamist movement, with the goal of elucidating the paradox of how those benefiting most from Ataturk’s secularization policies, namely educated women, have instead advocated a return to the very system that is argued to have previously resisted their ascension to public life.

title: Fatto in Italia
abstract: In 1964, Italian filmmaker and poet Pier Paolo Pasolini directed “Comizi d’Amore” (“Love Meetings”), the first documentary in the history of Italy. He interviewed Italians across the entire country for their thoughts on taboo questions of love, sex, marriage, divorce, homosexuality, prostitution, and gender equality. Writer Alberto Moravia and psychologist Cesare Musatti analyze these responses of the Italian people, which range from inflexibly Medieval to self-censoring. In the end, Pasolini’s ambitious goal was to capture the “real Italy.” What were the shape, size, and essence of love according to Italy in the booming post-war economy as the seeds of feminism begin to sprout? Forty years have passed and the identity of Pasolini’s Italy has changed significantly, yet not surprisingly. Italy's demographics possess one of the lowest fertility rates (1.21) in the world, making it the oldest country in the world. This research aims to follow Pasolini's documentary with a documentary on what comes after the love between a man and a woman—the decision to have a child. Why has Italy decided to become a childless society and what consequences will it suffer in the future? Italians across the entire country have been interviewed in a style similar to Pasolini's. Interviewees range from politicians, children, elderly, fashion models, professors, immigrants, and especially the future mothers of Italy.

title: Intentions, Rules and Norms
abstract: In this project, I am defending the claim that rational agency is founded in linguistic practice. For this purpose, agency is analyzed in terms of the way we talk about and attribute intentions. Our practices of expressing our intentions are discussed in terms of their circumstances of application, their justification, and their consequences— that is, in terms of the difference such moves make for the speaker. Within this framework of reformulating questions of agency in terms of statements expressing intentions, such statements are interpreted as counterfactual assertions on the model of promises. The basic idea is that, by stating her intention publicly, a speaker explicitly acknowledges the undertaking of a commitment to act in a certain way, as if she is making a public promise, and therefore licenses other speakers to make corresponding assumptions about her behavior. On the basis of this model, I further defend the view that private intentions are best understood analogously to overtly stated intentions as commitments that make a difference to the behavior of an agent. I will proceed in two steps: first, I will interpret private intentions as self-given rules. Second, I will argue that we don't have another paradigm available for understanding intentions. I conclude that like rule-following, promising and other such normative behavior, our self-understanding as individual rational agents is parasitic on our understanding and following social and linguistic conventions.

title: Characterization of Ferroelectric Domains by Piezoresponse Force Microscopy (PFM)
abstract: In recent years, ferroelectrics (FE) have attracted considerable technological interest because of their switchable static polarizations and high dielectric constants. The existence of a direct relationship between properties (such as dielectric constant, electro-optic coefficient, device efficiency, aging) and FE domain structure, it is important to be able to accurately characterize the domain structure and its evolution under bias. The following proposed research will develop and utilize a technique called piezoresponse atomic force microscopy (PFM) to understand ferroelectric domain dynamics. PFM operates on the basics of contact mode scanning force microscopy (SFM), but utilizes the special properties of piezoelectrics to determine the domain structure. An electric field is applied in the form of an AC bias between the bottom electrode and AFM tip. This causes the piezoelectric sample to oscillate in response to the bias such that the different polarization states respond differently to the applied electric field. The phase of the oscillations forms the piezoelectric signal that allows the accurate determination of the polarization state of particular domains. The polarization of particular domains can also be manipulated by applying a localized DC bias. The AC bias applied to the tip results in cantilever deflection. The lock-in amplifier detects the phase and amplitude of the oscillations, the phase producing the piezoresponse.

title: Wayback: A User-level Versioning File System for Linux
abstract: Wayback is an implementation of a versioning file system for Linux. This means that when you use a Wayback file system, old versions of files are never lost. No matter how much you change a file or directory, everything is always kept in a versioning file so that you never lose important data. Wayback provides the ability to remount any already mounted file system with versioning support under a different directory. Because of this, you can use Wayback on any block device with any base file system (ext3, ReiserFS, FAT, etc).

title: Infant Reaching as an Indicator of Support Knowledge
abstract: The purpose of this project is to determine whether infant reaching measures indicate support knowledge. I want to know if the knowledge of support affects object-directed reaching in infants. Looking time studies, including those by Needham, show that support knowledge affects looking time measures. Infants, ages 5.5-11.5 months, are being recruited to participate. Each infant will see and reach for four trials of all four conditions in a randomized order. We expect to see a difference in reaching across the trials if the infants have and use knowledge of physical support.

title: Separation of DNA-Wrapped Carbon Nanotubes by Chirality Using Anion-Exchange Chromatography
abstract: The purpose of this project is to reproduce an existing method used for separating DNA-wrapped single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) by electronic type. This method of separation takes advantage of the charge induced on SWNTs by the negatively charged DNA. Since different types of nanotubes will have different surface charges due to the disparity in the dielectric constant of metals and semiconductors, one can use ion-exchange chromatography for separation. This follows the methods of Zheng et al. [1,2]. Using this method, SWNTs are produced in bulk with randomized chiralities and dimensions. First, raw SWNTs are wrapped by single-strand DNA in solution. Individually wrapped nanotubes are then separated from nanotube bundles by ultracentrifugation and additionally separated by electronic type using a salt gradient in an anion-exchange chromatography column. By fine tuning the chromatography, we can attempt to collect fractions of SWNTs with a single chirality. These fractions of a single chirality are essential in the study of the optical properties of SWNTs and are a major step in the introduction of carbon nanotubes into real-world applications. One specific interest is the creation of nanotube opto-electronic devices, for which a single chirality of nanotubes would be necessary. 1. Zheng, M. et al. DNA-assisted dispersion and separation carbon nanotubes. Nature Mater. 2, 338-342 (2003). 2. Zheng, M. et al. Structure-based carbon nanotube sorting by sequence-dependent DNA assembly. Science. 302, 1545-1548 (2003).

title: Laryngeal Sensation and Normal Sensory Responses to Penetration of Substances into the Airway
abstract: In the past, there has been very little research conducted on laryngeal sensation in subjects with normal swallowing function; however, in the future it could prove to provide valuable information to researchers studying dysphagia. Most of the literature on normal laryngeal sensation indicates that if a substance penetrates the larynx at any level then the subject will cough. However, during normal swallow, clinical researchers find that penetration into the larynx occurs with no cough or throat clearing. It appears that what the literature states is not consistent with what is seen during radiographic studies of normal swallowing. It is evident that we do not have a clear understanding of normal sensory responses in the larynx, so if clinicians use a cough as an indicator of penetration or aspiration they could misinterpret a patient’s condition. Thus, research on normal swallowing function and the sensory responses of the larynx during penetration could prove to be crucial in the future development of dysphagia research and diagnosis. The main goals of this project are to define the frequency of penetration into the airway during videofluoroscopic studies of normal swallow, to score the level of penetration using the penetration-aspiration scale (Rosenbek, et al), and to describe the body’s sensory response to the penetration based on audible coughs or throat clearing on the audible channel of the videotaped fluoroscopic study. This will be defined in normal subjects of various ages (20-90 years of age) so a comparison to the data in the most recent literature on normal swallow function can be made.

title: Electronic Interactions in Donor-Bridge-Acceptor Pi-Stacked Polyarylurea Systems: Naphthalene Donors and Fluorophenyl Acceptors
abstract: The absorbtion spectra at room temperature and the fluorescence spectra at room temperature and 77 K in 2-methyltetrahydrofuran for a series of donor-bridge-acceptor systems containing a naphthalene donor and polyfluorinated acceptors have been investigated. The fluorescence properties of the system are dependent upon the nature of the donor and acceptor and the number of linkers. Studies at 77 K showed that conformational restrictions cause the localization of the excited state on the naphthalene ring. Room temperature studies showed that the pentafluorinated acceptor group stabilizes the ground state relative to the excited state for both the di and triarylureas to a greater extent than do the difluorinated and phenyl acceptors. In addition, further ground state stabilization is afforded by adding a spacer p-phenylene. The absorption and fluorescence solvent studies showed that the excited state is stabilized relative to the ground state with increasing solvent polarity. However, the solvation must not interfere with the pi-stacked interactions in order for this stabilization to occur.

title: The Changing Face of Broadcast Journalism: A Study of the Relationship Between Diversity in the Newsroom and Audience Demographics
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between diversity in the newsroom and the diversity within the audience and to what degree this relationship exists. Twenty-three stations from eight cities were examined (ABC, CBS and NBC affiliate stations). Each city was chosen for its ethnic demographic characteristics and geographic location. This process ensured that the collection of cities used represented a wide variety of minority populations. All on-camera personalities from each station were classified in one of four ethnic groups (white, black, Hispanic and Asian) and recorded. Using 2003 census information, the percentages of minority on-camera anchors and reporters were compared to the minority populations of that particular city. After examination of the data, it was found that those cities with a higher minority population consistently had higher percentage of minority reporters as members of their on-camera news team. A correlation is also found among the various minority groups. Cities with a dominant Asian population had a higher percentage of Asian anchors and reporters on camera than those cities that had lower Asian populations. In addition, I look at the possible explanations for this relationship between diversity in the newsroom and city demographics. FCC regulations and the desire to produce quality journalism are among some of the suggested causes.

title: A Room at Night: Poems
abstract: My project, completed and awarded honors for an independent study in the Creative Writing program, is a series of poems related to dreams and visions. The poetry encompasses a wide range of themes and forms, from complexly interlocked formal poems (such as the villanelle) to free verse lyrics. All of the poems completed for the project, though, have in common both the poignant emotional content of dream-life and the peculiar insights that can be garnered from this state of consciousness in which we spend one-third of our lives. The poems in the project have undergone numerous revisions under the guidance of Professor Pugh, and are the result of many hours of refinement and careful consideration. Insofar as it is ever possible for poetry to be fixed or “finished,” this project certainly is, having turned from assorted musings on the vast subjects of dreams and visions into a concerted (if multi-toned) examination of and meditation upon them. All poetry is best described through a reading of it, but failing that it may also be described by its intent. The intent of my project is to explore a dimension which, although examined by many poets before me, has not and cannot be exhausted, for it differs depending on the individual life and consciousness. The intent of my project is to detail and to present what I have found there, in the most accurate and truthful way that I know how.

title: Irish Fenianism and Monroe Doctrine Diplomacy: Patrick Egan, James Blaine, and the Baltimore Affair
abstract: To establish the United States as a world superpower, foreign policy makers began to implement the aggressive diplomacy outlined in the Monroe Doctrine at the close of the nineteenth century. James G. Blaine, U.S. Secretary of State under Presidents Garfield and Harrison, played an instrumental role in shaping this policy. The movement for Irish Nationalism, meanwhile, encompassed fervent and resolute idealism: Fenian leaders manifested hatred for Britain, their commitment to intense notions of honor, and their willingness to act on principles before pragmatics as cornerstone values of the movement. My paper examines the relationship between Irish Nationalism and the emergence of Monroe Doctrine diplomacy through the diplomatic work of Patrick Egan. Egan was a devoted Irish Nationalist who after feeling Ireland assumed the post of U.S. Minister to Chile in 1888. He was at the center or the diplomatic crisis that nearly resulted in War between Chile and the U.S. following a riot in Valparaiso, Chile that involved sailors from the USS Baltimore. I trace Egan’s diplomatic conduct to his roots in Irish Nationalism, showing how Fenianism became reconcilable with Monroe Doctrine Diplomacy in Chile in 1891-92. I establish the Baltimore Affair as foundational to a major shift in U.S. foreign policy and argue that this transition was underway years before most diplomatic historians claim.

title: The Impact of Divorce on Communication Patterns in Sibling Relationships
abstract: As rates of divorce have risen over the last few decades, research on the impact of divorce on the family system has increased. Past research examines both the negative and positive effects of divorce on the parents, the parent-child relationship, and on the child (Hetherington, 1989, 2002; Westman, 1983). Although the sibling relationship is the longest-lasting family relationship due to similarity in age (Galvin, 2003), and remains one of the more influential relationships (Tucker, 2001), most research often neglects to acknowledge the significance that divorce may have on sibling communication. Previous work mentions that according to the social learning theory, positivity in parent-child relationships is generally linked to positivity in sibling relationship experiences (Brody 1992; Seigner, 98). Other work has shown that a sibling may serve to substitute for the inadequacies of a parent during a divorce (Boer et al 92; Hetherington, 88; Tucker 2001). This research takes an in-depth approach examining sibling communication prior, during, and two years following parental divorce. Specifically, this study will examine the conflict behaviors, perceived closeness, and divorce-related topics of conversation that may have changed as a result of parental divorce. All primary research for this study comes from confidential interviews with students from the Northwestern student body.

title: Savior to Saboteur: Anti-Americanism in South Korea
abstract: Anti-Americanism has been an emerging force in many countries and has been unfolding within the Republic of Korea for many decades. At the close of 2002, the US media frequently published articles about the anti-American protests of up to one hundred thousand South Koreans that were taking place in Seoul. Simultaneously, the election of the current South Korean President Roh Moo Hyun, a public anti-American, seemed to confirm that South Korea and the US had begun growing apart in a dangerous way. The reality of this anti-Americanism became muddled by several Pro-American rallies held by South Koreans in a demonstration against the anti-American population in Seoul. We were very intrigued to find out the true beliefs of the South Korean people. Was South Korea moving from ally to enemy? Would the ROK become a dangerous place for Americans to visit or were these claims an inaccurate media portrayal of some other more complicated sentiments? This paper discusses the state of anti-Americanism in South Korea and its underlying causes and effects on US-ROK relations.

title: Free Speech in Oregon: Can an “Original Intent” Framework Be Used to Adequately Determine the Validity of Laws Regulating Modern Speech Issues?
abstract: This paper will examine the rise in autonomy of state constitutions following the onset of the increased conservatism of the U.S. Supreme Court under Chief Justice Warren Burger. I will survey how states that chose to build more extensive protections of free speech into their constitutions use their free speech clauses to assess the constitutionality of laws dealing with modern speech issues such as urban zoning and telecommunications. Oregon is one such state. Since 1982, the Oregon Supreme Court has protected all speech for which there is not an “historical exception” outlining the possibility of its regulation. I propose to study the history of the protection of commercial speech in Oregon as compared to the protection of commercial speech required by the U.S. Constitution, as well as the constitutions of other states. I will examine cases decided on this issue by the Oregon Supreme Court between 1982 and the present. I will look for federal rulings as well as ruling from other state courts on similar issues during this time period for comparison, and to test the following hypothesis: The technology and concerns of modern society pose free-speech related problems unforeseen in mid-19th-century Oregon; thus the “historical exception” standard by which free speech in Oregon can be limited is no longer a sufficient way to determine the constitutionality of statutes restricting speech.

title: Understanding the Outbreak of Militancy in Indian-held Kashmir
abstract: There are numerous debates that shape the political landscape of South Asia, but few of these touch as many political fault lines as the debate surrounding the state of Jammu and Kashmir. The “Kashmir-issue” accordingly deals with class and caste divisions, religious tensions, the failures of democracy, the legacy of Partition, and the specter of regionalism and sub-nationalism in South Asia. Kashmir has been the cause of two out of three wars between India and Pakistan, as well as the recent “Kargil conflict” in 1999, during which time both nations were nuclear-armed. With the nuclearization of South Asia, the issue of Kashmir has moved away from being a mere regional problem, and its resolution has assumed an international importance for global stability. But a resolution of a conflict is impossible to achieve if one does not first understand its origins. Why then did Kashmiris, who had at one point participated in the democratic arrangements of their state, abandon legitimate political channels and resort to violence on a mass-scale to redress their political grievances? There are ultimately two central questions that drive my analysis on the outbreak of militancy in Kashmir. First, why did a violent revolution occur in 1989 in Kashmir at all? Second, why did this revolution take on a nationalist flavor? To answer the first question, we must turn to the already vast body of revolutionary theory. Those theorists who are most relevant to the case of Kashmir are Samuel Huntington, Theda Skocpol, Ted Gurr, Chalmers Johnson, and Charles Tilly. To answer the second question, regarding the nationalist quality of the Kashmiri insurgency, I have turned to an Instrumentalist approach: focusing on the role of political actors in fostering ethnic and religious nationalism. Here I have borrowed largely from the nationalist theories of Benedict Anderson and Ronald Suny, both of whom emphasize the confluence of institutional and instrumental factors in the formation of nationalist sentiment.

title: The Verb Mutability Effect: Noun and Verb Semantics in English and Japanese
abstract: The study of human representations of meaning has led to debates about influences of language on semantic systems. One line of research has investigated the combinatorial semantics of nouns and verbs in adult sentence processing, finding that English-speaking adults change the meaning of verbs more than nouns when asked to paraphrase semantically odd sentences (e.g., “The lizard worshipped”). This verb mutability effect suggests that verb meaning is less stable than noun meaning for English speakers. Unlike research in noun and verb acquisition, the verb mutability effect has not been thoroughly investigated in languages where linguistic features and input patterns might bias speakers away from noun stability. The present project investigates verb mutability in Japanese, a language in which linguistic features, such as word order and argument dropping, and input factors such as heavier emphases on verbs than on nouns in mother-child discourse, may result in semantic systems that differ from English. A double paraphrase paradigm is used, in which participants paraphrase semantically odd sentences and another set of participants paraphrases the paraphrases. Double paraphrases are examined for reappearance of original nouns or verbs. The project will highlight similarities and differences in the combinatorial semantics of English and of a language that emphasizes verb relative to noun meaning in linguistic features and input.

title: Learning in Spanish and English: Language-Dependent Memory in Bilinguals
abstract: The academic and cognitive performance of bilingual students may be impacted by their linguistic background and the relationship between language and learning. Previous investigations of bilingual episodic memory support the hypothesis of language-dependent memory, suggesting that memories become more accessible when the language of retrieval matches the language of encoding. The present study examined the effect of language on semantic memory by testing learning in fluent bilingual speakers of Chilean Spanish and English. Academic-type information was taught in either Spanish or English and memory was tested in the two languages. Participants produced more correct responses and responded faster when the language of retrieval matched the language of encoding than when the two did not match. Proficiency understanding and speaking English influenced participants’ ability to encode and retrieve new information. These findings support the idea that reinstating the linguistic environment present at encoding at the time of retrieval facilitates memory for semantic and lexical information in bilinguals and underscore the need for sensitivity to linguistic background and contexts when testing cognitive abilities of bilinguals.

title: Gunpowder: An Examination of Antonio Negri's Writings
abstract: My project will present the implications of the enigmatic figure Antonio Negri. Recently, Negri has been idolized as the intellectual who best understands globalization, the international best-selling author of Empire, and one of Time Magazine’s “Seven Most Innovative People” in 2001. Yet, twenty years earlier, Negri was arrested on charges of terrorism against the state. And, in many of the same American periodicals in which he currently is glorified, he was then demonized. The New York Times, for example, which commissioned him for an editorial immediately after the publication of his most recent work, had twenty years prior called him the mastermind behind Italy's most notorious terrorist organization, the Red Brigades. Thus, this dilemma poses the question: Who really is Antonio Negri? My project will present an original answer to this question by comparing and contrasting his pre-arrest writings to his most recent work Empire. I will show how Negri's ideology has transformed over time and conclude with what implications that has on the No Global Movement, Internet Political Activism, and the moral responsibility of political idealogues. My research has been guided as part of my senior honors thesis seminar in the History Department. Professor Hayes instructed the class, while Professor Muir has acted as my advisor.

title: Belonging Illusions
abstract: The need to belong within groups is a fundamental human motivation and can be almost as compelling a need as food. When deprived of human relationships, a person experiences negative affect, low self-esteem and in some cases poor physical and mental health. Evidence regarding self-enhancing illusions (i.e. Dismissing in-group failure, evaluating in-group members more positively) suggests that people have illusions about their social world to avoid the negative states associated with isolation. The purpose of this experiment is to document the presence of “belonging illusions” after a perceived threat to belonging. Participants wrote essays and answered questions relating to their in-groups after reliving a rejection experience. Our hypothesis is that socially rejected individuals will buffer themselves against perceived slights by rating their groups as more meaningful, positive and cohesive than controls. In addition, we believe rejected people will be more likely to recall family or group events with a higher degree of togetherness. The control conditions for this experiment included a negative non-social (illness or injury) and a neutral stimuli. Although there has been extensive work to date on this project, this quarter’s work focused on adding a fourth control: a positive social condition (acceptance). Before adding the acceptance condition, the study showed some evidence for belonging illusions, yet afterwards the results became more robust. One major finding was that the rejected group had significantly higher correlations between their perceived group outcome and attributions of success to the group. In other words, rejected people attributed group success to the team‚s effort rather than to individual effort. Another finding, though unexpected, was that the acceptance group showed significantly lower collective self-esteem than all other conditions. This phenomenon could be explained because accepted individuals feel satiated with their level of inclusion and do not have as much need for belonging illusions. In summary, there appears to be some evidence for the presence of belonging illusions.

title: The Role of Relational Language in the Development of Relational Analogical Reasoning
abstract: Previous research has suggested that language may play a role in the development of analogical reasoning. The present study was designed to test the role of relational language in a difficult relational mapping task. A total of 64 children, divided into two age groups (5.5 years and 7 years), participated in this task. Children were presented with cross-mapped pairs of drawings: that is, drawings that depicted similar events but in which the target object in drawing A (e.g. a cat that is chasing a mouse) matched at the object level with one item in drawing B (e.g. a cat) and at the relational level with another item (e.g. a dog that is chasing a cat). The experimenter pointed to the target object in drawing A and asked the child what it went with in drawing B. Half of the children received neutral language instruction while the other half were given relational language instruction, where the relevant relation was included in the task instructions. Results indicated that those in the relational language condition picked significantly more relational matches on average than those in the neutral language condition. There was also a trend of age, as the older children picked marginally more relational matches than the younger children. This supports the Relational Shift hypothesis that relational language plays a key role in the development of relational analogical reasoning, along with domain-knowledge and experience.

title: Estrogen and Excitotoxic Cell Death
abstract: This study poses to ascertain the effect, or lack thereof, that estrogen treatment may have on glutamate excitotoxicity in a novel way. Because it will be conducted in adult organotypic slices, it poses to be more indicative of phenomena in the in vivo rat brain than past studies. To investigate a possible effect of estrogen upon glutamate excitotoxicity, first a quantification of glutamate excitotoxicity must be completed for comparison with previous baseline data. For the presently progressing glutamate study, 20 female Sprague-Dawley aged 65-73 days were ovariectomized and sacrificed 7 days later. Their brains were fixed and sectioned, and incubated with glutamate 7 days prior to labeling and imaging. Using a live/dead kit, live and dead neurons were labeled green and red, respectively. Stacks of photomicrographs of the CA1 pyramidal cell layer were taken using fluorescence microscopy, and will be counted, using MetaMorph imaging software, in slices of three treatment types: 1) baseline, or untreated slices, 2) slices treated with glutamate, or 3) slices treated with glutamate and estrogen. Analysis will compare the percentage of live to dead cells, cell density, and relative area of the sections of CA1 pyramidal cell layer. We expect that higher concentrations of glutamate, longer exposure times, and longer delay times before observation will coincide with a higher prevalence of cell death. Likewise, we anticipate treatment with estrogen to correlate with lower cell death rates in slices pretreated with glutamate. Christine Lauay, Post Doctoral Fellow (Trainee), Neurobiology & Physiology

title: Leaders Research
abstract: The purpose of Leaders Research is to find a tool that will improve the effectiveness of the process used to select a company's next CEO. Our team is attempting to identify a correlation between certain behavioral tendencies of people in corporate leadership roles and the overall success of the company. We have developed an online test that uses a seven-point scale to evaluate and assess how often management exhibits a particular behavior. Our test is designed to report the frequency that a person exhibits various identified behaviors. To increase statistical significance, the survey includes numerous questions correlating to each behavior. Thus, there are a variety of indications regarding each aspect of the executive's habits. Our research lends itself to use by several groups of people such as board selection committees and corporate recruiters, the training community, academics and social behavior scientists, and perhaps even investors. Our conclusions could impact managers at many levels, not just CEOs. Our research team plans to put up a poster explaining our research concept and the expected conclusions of our data. We will also have a computer for the visitors to take the online test and get their personal behavioral evaluation. This 15-minute test will effectively exhibit the seven-point scale and the behaviors that we are observing.

title: HIV/AIDS in Mozambique
abstract: We rented a car and drove from Johannesburg, South Africa, to Maputo, Mozambique. After a successful border crossing, we arrived in Maputo to begin our research project on the state of HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment in Mozambique. During our six days in Maputo, we met with representatives from a number of organizations, including AMODEFA, an association that coordinates youth education projects with schools and government agencies around Maputo; Kindlimuka, a member organization for people with HIV/AIDS and sympathizers; Population Studies International, which runs condom social marketing programs in Maputo and other parts of the country; and the World Food Program, which delivers food parcels in impoverished regions. Additionally, we received nearly a three-hour personal lecture about the state of HIV/AIDS in Mozambique during dinner with a former UNAIDS director who has since moved into private consulting. We delved into numerous aspects of the pandemic, but we will focus in our poster presentation on patterns of infection, funding and staffing issues, and educational materials and approaches.

title: Parental Temperament as a Partial Mediator of the Relationship between Parental Mood Disorder Symptoms and Child Temperament Traits
abstract: This study tested the hypothesis that temperament acts as a diathesis for the development of mood and anxiety disorders. Twenty-two mothers and eighteen fathers completed a series of inventories designed to measure parental and child temperament and to assess current parental internalizing disorder symptoms. Parental lifetime internalizing disorder diagnoses were also assessed through a structured clinical interview. Bivariate correlational analyses were conducted to investigate the nature of the relationships between parental internalizing disorders, parental temperament and child temperament. Additionally, this study employed partial correlational analyses and determined that, in certain cases, parental temperament acts as a partial mediator of the relationship between parental internalizing disorder symptoms and child temperament traits.

title: University Newspapers and the University Community
abstract: Most American universities have student-staffed and often student-run campus newspapers. These newspapers serve as an important medium and report on a variety of campus issues, from crime to coverage of guest speakers. The papers also have a function as watchdogs of their surrounding communities, writing about the decisions, triumphs, missteps, scandals and performance of the university administration, student government, faculty and other authoritative groups around campus. The presence of a faculty adviser on the newspaper staff, an element that varies from college to college, could add a factor into the decisions that the editors face when putting together an issue. Through research, I attempted to answer two critical questions: (1) Do college newspapers criticize more than they compliment their surrounding university community? (2) How does the addition of a faculty adviser affect the content of the newspapers in respect to the question above? In addition to surveying literature related to this topic and interviewing experts on campus publications, I inspected and categorized the content of eight daily college newspapers for a period of four weeks.

title: The Wealth and Portfolio Choice of Immigrants to the United States

people.affiliation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

abstract: This paper uses SIPP data from the late Nineties to investigate the role portfolio choice plays in the large observed differences in wealth between foreign and native-born households. By extending the discrete-continuous portfolio choice methods to the immigrant wealth gap literature, this paper examines how differences in asset ownership decisions and asset demand conditional on ownership can explain the wealth gap. For financial assets, this paper demonstrates that the observed differences in asset ownership between natives and immigrants can explain a large portion of the observable gap in wealth held in financial assets. Therefore, efforts to improve the financial knowledge and participation of immigrants can play an important role in improving immigrant wealth and overall well-being. MMSS Thesis Seminar Faculty Supervisor: Joseph Ferrie

title: Queer Mourning and the Art of Felix Gonzalez-Torres
abstract: My project explores the work of conceptual artist Felix Gonzalez-Torres (1957-1996). The installations of Gonzalez-Torres suggest an implicit paradox. While utilizing a Minimalist vocabulary of bareness and absence, the artworks simultaneously explode in content and meaning. A large body of Gonzalez-Torres’ art either directly or indirectly alludes to the illness and loss of his lover and friend, Ross Laycock, to AIDS-related causes in 1991. And yet, amidst the personal and collective losses of the AIDS epidemic, Gonzalez-Torres’ art conveys a powerful sense of hope, joy, rejuvenation, and generosity. In contrast to traditional medicalized models of grief, mourning, and loss, the artwork of Gonzalez-Torres suggests a way of addressing loss that is hopeful instead of destructive, communal rather than privatized, and fluid instead of stagnant. To conduct research for this project I was fortunate to receive funding from the Undergraduate Research Grants Committee. This gave me the opportunity to travel to view Gonzalez-Torres' artwork and to speak with two individuals who knew the artist personally--Anne Umland, curator with the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, and Andrea Rosen, owner of the Andrea Rosen Gallery in New York City.

title: Godspeak: Defending God in the Rhetoric of American Civil Religion
abstract: This paper examines the role of religion in American political rhetoric. This paper argues that religious rhetoric in political discourse should be viewed within the rubric of civil religion as described by Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Robert Bellah. This civil religion, which is the system of beliefs about America held to with ardor and faith by the American people, manifests itself most clearly in political rhetoric. The rhetoric of the civil religion, or Godspeak, has three foundational tenants: the existence of an undefined higher power from which humans derive their natural rights, the exclusion of religious intolerance, and the concept or responsible liberty, which balances the values of freedom and obligation. This paper argues that, not only has this model been used by political leaders since the inception of the nation, it is also crucially important as a tool for challenging government authority and majority rule. [Morning Session]

title: The Freedom Model: A Theory of Free Speech
abstract: The Freedom Model proposes a comprehensive theory of free speech jurisprudence. The Freedom Model posits that all behavior includes elements of expression. This expression, once properly separated from action, should be stringently protected from government restriction. The only exception to protecting this speech is when the speech coerces or deceptively coerces others to take harmful action. This paper examines free speech jurisprudence in the light of Lockean political theory and then applies the Freedom Model theory to various areas of free speech case law. [Afternoon Session]

title: Does Transgenically Overexpressed GAP-43 Impact Actin Distribution in the Hippocampus?
