abstract: My study focuses on molecular mechanisms of memory formation. I targeted the hippocampus since the hippocampus is crucial for spatial learning. A previous study demonstrated mossy fiber sprouting in rat hippocampi after performance in a spatial learning task. I studied how this could occur using the three different proteins GAP-43, actin and zinc transporter. Because mossy fibers have the unique property in the hippocampus of containing zinc, I used the protein stain of zinc transporter to differentially stain the mossy fibers in the hippocampus. In order for sprouting to occur, both GAP-43 and actin have crucial roles. Growth from a presynaptic terminal requires polymerization of filamentous actin. Also, GAP-43, a plasticity-related protein, promotes axonal growth. Thus, the distribution of both GAP-43 and actin has implications for the ability of axons to sprout. I present a model for how GAP-43 and actin may directly interact based on evidence obtained through literature. My research has also explored how overexpression of GAP-43 in transgenic mice affects distribution of both actin and zinc transporter. Because transgenic mice for GAP-43 exhibit a strong amount of GAP-43 labeling in the stratum lucidum, which contains mossy fibers, I focused my research on this area in the hippocampus. This research has allowed a more cohesive, molecular understanding of functional plasticity of the mossy fiber terminals in the hippocampus.

title: A Study of Hydroxyl Maser Lines Toward Supernova Remnants at 1.7 GHz
abstract: When a star exhausts its nuclear fuel, the core collapses under the grip of enormous gravitational forces. The collapse of the star results in a violent, explosive death, called a supernova. As the blast wave ejects the envelope of the star into the surrounding interstellar medium a supernova remnant (SNR) forms. When the SNR propagates into a dense molecular cloud a shock is driven into the cloud. At the interaction sight, intense stimulated emission, known as MASERs, occurs as hydroxyl (OH) molecules in the cloud suffer a population inversion and emit radiation at 1.720 GHz. A MASER is similar to a LASER, but operates in the microwave regime of the electromagnetic spectrum. Using the 100m Green Bank Radio Telescope, we observed OH MASER emission from a number of galactic sources to identify the signature of the interaction between SNRs and molecular clouds. This research explores the morphology of this emission, as well as the geometry and physical conditions present at the SNR-molecular cloud interaction site. A case study of one observed SNR will be presented in detail.

title: Baker in Between: A study of Josephine Baker's representation in Djibril Diop Mambety's “Touki Bouki”
abstract: Josephine Baker’s entrance onto the Parisian dance scene in 1925 with her hit act, Revue Negre, precipitated not only her immediate stardom but also a hotly contested debate over the construction of “blackness” in Europe. Many have since argued whether her performance was an affirmation of African inferiority or if Baker’s overtly sexual dance numbers were a social critique of those stereotypes. In evaluating Baker’s role in France, one must examine the function of the medium of dance and performance and what exactly the black body constituted on stage during the interwar period in Europe. Djibril Mambety in his seminal film, “Touki Bouki,” connects Baker’s life in Paris in the 1920s and the symbol that she became with postcolonial Senegal in the late 1970s and 1980s. Mambety uses Baker’s voice as the basis of the movie’s soundtrack and is persistently in dialogue with the script to confound notions of Europeanness and Africanness, progress and primitiveness. What are the implications of Mambety’s use of an African American European star in his social commentary on modern Senegal? How does Baker figure into the political context of West Africa, particularly the emergence of a film industry in a post-colonial era? Addressing these question necessitate examining such highly contentious issues as Africanness in art, the complex relationship between the French and their colonial “other,” and the agency of the black artist in contributing to modernity and interpreting tradition. My research will culminate in a close reading of Mambety’s use of Baker in “Touki Bouki.”

title: World War II VD Training Films: Disease, Gender, and American Wartime Culture
abstract: Ask any American male World War II veteran about the military training films he had to watch about venereal disease and you’re likely to get a strong reaction. The VD military training films shown to troops during World War II have become infamous for their scare tactics and use of shocking, graphic imagery. However, the training films are equally remarkable for their representations of sex and gender in American wartime culture. In this presentation, I examine the venereal disease training films as products of culture, rather than science or biology. Venereal disease is certainly a biological entity, but any understanding or representation of the disease is profoundly informed by the culture that produced it. The military made several dozen training films about VD during World War II, but I have limited my study to three: the Army’s “Sex Hygiene” (1941), the Navy’s “Sex Hygiene” (1942), and “Pick Up” (1944). Collectively, these three films tell us much about the social construction of venereal disease, cultural attitudes about gender, and the role of film as an educational medium during World War II. The films, which were made at different times during the war, expressed a gradual shift in the military’s thinking about where VD originated and how it spread. The films participated in the construction of a new image of the American woman. As the films focused less on prostitutes and more on “amateurs,” wartime women became imagined as powerful, dangerous, duplicitous, and unknowable—similar to the femme fatale characters in film noir.

title: Doctors, Detectives, and Pretty Women: Feminist and Postfeminist Discourses on NYPD Blue and ER
abstract: Representations of women on prime-time television have made great progress since the 1950s. Beginning in the 1990s, many female characters on prime- time television have been cited as postfeminist icons, implicitly assuming that feminism on television is no longer needed or relevant. Frequent examples of postfeminist icons include Buffy Summers of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Samantha Jones of Sex and the City, and of course the short skirt wearing attorney Ally of Ally McBeal. While these characters are certainly significant, I am more interested in women on television who emerge in the context of prime-time drama as "ordinary" or "routine." What does prime-time drama consider "normal" for women? My analysis of programs in this vein suggests that feminist analysis of the 1970s and 1980s still applies to mid-1990s programming---that critics calling for postfeminist icons might have stepped forward a little too fast. Feminism is still relevant, highly applicable, and even needed to effectively analyze prime-time television. I will be focusing on the first seasons of NYPD Blue and ER, broadcast in the 1993-94 and the 1994-95 seasons, respectively. Upon a closer look at the construction of these series, specifically concentrating on the characterization of women on the series, its narrative structures, and televisual style, it appears that the women of television in a supposedly postfeminist era are still held back by elements of sexism in the narrative and construction of the program as a whole.

title: Heparin Binding Peptide Amphiphile and Transforming Growth Factor: A Novel Approach to Anti-angiogenic Drug Delivery
abstract: Transforming Growth Factor Beta (TGFβ) has been shown to inhibit the proliferation of smooth muscle cells and endothelial cells. The growth inhibition signaling pathway involves the phosphorylation of the activin receptor-like kinase 5 (ALK5) and receptor regulated R-Smads. In high concentrations, TGFβ may also disturb the activity of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), two primary promoters of angiogenesis. TGF is inactive when complexed with 2-macroglobulin. Heparin, which is known to bind to TGF and potentiate its anti-proliferative effect, acts on this complex to dissociate and release TGF hence triggering the anti-proliferative pathway. The specific binding of TGFβ to its receptor is also enhanced by this interaction. Potentially, the heparin binding properties of TGFβ will allow self-assembling peptide amphiphiles (PA) to be used as a form of drug delivery. The Consensus 1 (Con1) PA sequence consists of a putative heparin binding peptide head group (LRKKLGKA) and linking sequence (AAAAGGG) attached to a hydrophobic palmitic acid tail. When heparin is added, the nanofibers self-assemble into a cross-linked self-supporting gel. A passive heparin release mechanism is currently under study. Recent work has shown that large amounts of heparin are quickly released from the gel during the first five days. Progressing days show a decrease in the amount released. Thus, the Con1 PA may possibly be used as a passive anti-angiogenic drug delivery device. The heparin bound within the PA would complex with the TGFβ and provide a means of delivering it. Contained within a gel, TGF could be readily transferred into targeted areas. When transplanted, this passive release would provide an environment of continual and gradual drug exposure. In effect, this may slow or prevent unregulated angiogenesis. Possible applications of this growth inhibiting gel (GIG) include administration to malignant sites of vessel proliferation (ie. retinopathic outgrowths, tumors).

title: The American Law Institute's Model Penal Code and Sodomy Law Reform in the 1950s and 1960s
abstract: In 1955, while drafting the sex offenses section of the Model Penal Code, the American Law Institute broke with centuries of legal precedent and aligned itself with Dr. Alfred Kinsey’s sex research, which supported the decriminalization of private adult consensual sodomy. This was a radical decision because it required defending homosexuals in a time period that particularly repressed them. Not only was sodomy illegal in all 50 states, sex crimes panics were sweeping the nation and the government was firing thousands of employees suspected of homosexual behavior. Given that antigay repression was ratcheting up in so many arenas, including the law, why did the ALI chose this moment to propose a policy sympathetic to homosexuals? My thesis argues that Kinsey’s findings formed the basis of a new approach to morals legislation that emphasized the disparately small influence of private acts on the general welfare and called for their decriminalization. Thus, while the ALI’s decision decriminalizing private consensual adult sodomy was drastically out of step with American public opinion, it was consistent with the conclusions of a small but influential group of elites who held the social sciences and personal privacy in high regard. As a direct result of the MPC, 23 states decriminalized sodomy in the 1970s. This knowledge changes our understanding of antigay sentiment, community formation, and American history generally by challenging the dominant historiography, which attributes sodomy law reform to post-Stonewall gay organizing, and demonstrating that developments in legal and moral defenses of homosexuality began decades before gay liberation.

title: Domestic Violence among the South Asian Community of Kampala, Uganda
abstract: My project concerns the study of domestic violence among the Asian community of Kampala, Uganda. I spent a total of six weeks in Uganda, from mid-August until late September 2003. My methodological approach was to interview battered women and learn about the abuse of South Asian women via interviewing community members, NGOs, and physicians at hospitals where battered women may have gone if they were injured. These interviews were conducted in hospital rooms, offices, workplaces, and homes of women. In the case of interviewing abused women, the women were always living separately from their abusers in the homes of friends and relatives and were safe. My case study is based on a total of 30 South Asian women of Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi and Sri Lankan descent. I interviewed six abuse survivors and discovered 19 cases of domestic violence. Upon returning to the U.S. and analyzing my research, I was able to delineate the specific causes of the heightened abuse of South Asian women in Kampala, Uganda. I posit that South Asian women’s experiences of domestic violence in Uganda have been intensified by: (1) the marginalized position of South Asians as a community within Ugandan society; (2) the combined negative effects of migration, isolation and male dominance; (3) a sexually non-egalitarian legal infrastructure (characterized by rife corruption and cultural toleration of domestic violence); and finally (4) the disruption of South Asian women’s mobilizing and organizing efforts due to the Asian Expulsion of 1972, culminating in a contemporary lack of access to resources that potentially could provide battered women with protection and rehabilitation. My research has allowed me to develop a model depicting the various interacting factors that can be applied to each of the lives of the women I interviewed in Kampala.

title: Human Rights, Power, and Control in China: The Dynamic Policy Persuasion of Hong Kong's Article 23
abstract: Human Rights seems to be one of most difficult forms of domestic policy to externally influence. Thus if studies of successful and failed attempts to influence such types of policy yields an understanding of the most potent tools, this can be exercised not only in human rights negotiations and relations, but other contentions that seem impenetrable. China relations stand as a prominent candidate for such analysis. As the world‚s largest emerging market and population, China is of great interest to the global community. Yet, the comprehensive control of the Chinese Communist Party Government over domestic policy has proven vastly impenetrable to outside pressure. China has followed a modernization progression of its own designs, only offering concessions and compromises when its rewards greatly outweigh its loss of complete legislative and persecutory supremacy and control. Yet in August 2003, China suddenly tarnished this record by allowing the rescinding of Article 23 anti-subversion legislation in Hong Kong, its semi-autonomous region. This shocking reversal marked one of the first times the CCPG allowed a government endorsed policy to be changed due to outside pressures. How and why was the CCPG so acutely influenced to allow the complete reversal of such powerful legislation? For the first time China seems to have taken steps that do not immediately fulfill the interests of complete domestic control and power. Identification of the influences that forced the shelving of Article 23 legislation will better allow the actions and reasoning of China and prove valuable for future international relations dealings.

title: Transportation
abstract: This is a short story that I wrote during my time as a student in the English Major in Writing 394 Theory & Practice of Fiction sequence. The story is a milestone for me because it is the first time in my life that have dealt with the two most important aspects of my life simultaneously: my religion and my art.

title: Emerging from the CAVE: Attributional Style and the Narrative Study of Identity in Midlife Adults
abstract: It has been widely documented that individuals who explain negative life events with a depressogenic attributional style (stable, global attributions) tend to have increased rates of depression and other poor outcomes. The Content Analysis of Verbatim Explanations (CAVE) is a method of assessing attributional style in spontaneously generated causal attributions appearing in accounts of real events (Peterson & Seligman, 1984). 70 life story interviews obtained from a diverse sample of midlife adults were coded for attributional style with the CAVE technique and also the theme of contamination (scenes in which good events turn to bad outcomes, McAdams et al., 2001). While depressogenic attributional style and contamination sequences were unrelated to each other, both were shown to independently predict self-reported depression, low life satisfaction, low self-esteem, and poor physical health. In addition, while the observed relationships between depressogenic attributional style and these self-report variables were no longer significant after controlling for Neuroticism, a similar pattern was not observed for contamination sequences. This study forges possible connections between cognitive theories of depression and the narrative study of adult identity.

title: Asian American Political Coalition Building “On the Ground”
abstract: Americans of Asian descent are the fastest growing minority group in the United States. Their unparalleled jump in population size has led to an increased visibility of Asian Americans in all aspects of American life. As Asian Americans become more incorporated into the domestic political system, it is increasingly important to understand how that incorporation occurs. The current literature on the field of Asian American political participation exclusively focuses on two areas: the participation of ethnic/national Asian American groups or the participation of Asian Americans as a unified panethnic "Asian American" political body. There is very little, if any, literature specifically examining the implications of the political use of "Asian American", a term constructed by an extremely small segment of Asian Americans in the 1960s. This term though creates both the manner in which Americans of Asian descent are politically mobilized and how their political participation is analyzed. This paper specifically explores the state of Asian American panethnicity "on the ground" by examining Asian American activists and Americans of Asian descent in terms of how their political participation is affected by panethnic organizing. New York City, the home to more Asian Americans than any other American city, will be used as the specific place in which Asian American panethnic organizing is critiqued. The methods used to examine this research question are an analysis of current literature in the field, national identity surveys of Asian Americans, exit polls, and field research/formal interviews conducted by the author.

title: The Politics of Biotechnology: The Transatlantic Divide Between the US and EU
abstract: Since its inception in the early 1970s, agricultural and food biotechnology has had “the most rapid adoption of new technology in the history of agriculture” say Lowell Hill and Sophia Battle, researchers at the University of Illinois. But this new technology of genetically modifying organisms also has had far-reaching economic, social and political reverberations. As public administration Prof. Christopher L. Plein of the University of Missouri, Columbia noted, “The development of biotechnology as a science and technology has laid the foundations of enduring and often controversial public and policy debate.” So far, the outcome in the United States is that the nation is for genetically modified organisms, while the outcome in the European Union is it is against them. My thesis looks to answer the question: Why do the United States and the European Union have diametrically opposing laws towards genetically modified organisms? To examine why the EU and U.S. have diametrically opposed laws in regards to biotechnology, a three-level approach will be utilized. The hypothesis of this paper will first be supported by an investigation of the power struggle over who defines biotechnology. Next, it will be supported by using Patterson’s work (2000) on the three major domains in society that affect biotechnology policy: the market domain, the environmental domain and the scientific domain. Finally, the biotechnology issue will be applied to Yatagana’s (2001) comparative study of the American system of independent regulatory agencies and the emergence of similar bodies in the European Union. I assert that the United States and European Union hold different opinions on genetically modified organisms because of the structure of these governments, specifically in regards to their regulatory agencies, and how the political actors get their views across through these structures.

title: Casual Swearing: An Examination of How Gender Impacts the Breaching of Social Norms in Regards to In-Group Solidarity
abstract: My research was on how casual swearing functions between in and out group members in society, including the frequency of the words and how much of a social norm are swear words in society. This research examines how casual swearing functions in society, specifically in relation to group solidarity and gender. Past literature indicates that swear words may serve as a tool to promote in-group solidarity. This study proposes that when an out-group member casually swears to an in-group, his/her behavior will violate a social norm; however, the gender of the stranger will influence the severity of the group‚s reaction to the breach of a social norm. Further, same-gender strangers of a group will be more tolerated than those of an opposite gender. Using a “three-tier” methodology (i.e., observations, social breaching experiments, and interviews), a convenience sample of 10 groups of Northwestern University undergraduates was examined. Patterns in the data support both parts of the hypothesis. Out-group members who casually swear to in-group members were observed to breach a social norm, while the formers’ gender was found to influence the severity of in-group members’ reactions to the breach.

title: Is Court Packing effective?
abstract: My thesis explores the practice of court packing as it has been used by the executive branch of government. Specifically, I ask the question of whether court packing when used by Presidents to fill positions in the Supreme Court is effective in fulfilling ideological goals. Starting with FDR's famed attempt to pack the court in 1937 to as recent as the conservative court packing campaign of Reagan and Bush, Presidents have often been disappointed with the actions of decisions made by the Supreme Court and tried to change the composition of the court in order to bring about changes in policy. This calls into question the independence of the Supreme Court, and what role it can play in deciding crucial issues.

title: An Internet Study of Authoritarianism
abstract: This study discusses the results of an online survey measuring six personality traits, Right Wing Authoritarianism (RWA), and the lexical Big 5 (extraversion, emotional stability. openness to experience, agreeableness, and conscientiousness.) The study has three goals. First, it evaluates claims that RWA is truly a personality trait rather than a learned political orientation. At over 1,000 participants, the present study is currently the largest study comparing RWA with known personality measures. Second, the study explores the fruitfulness of using the Internet to collect psychological data and explores methods of screening data for bias. In addition, by using open-source and free software, as well as public-domain personality inventories, the study makes headway in the direction away from expensive proprietary tests and software and drastically reduces the cost of experimentation. The third goal of the study is to educate the public about the Big 5 model, by providing instantaneous and custom feedback to all respondents.

title: Investigating the Cross-race Recognition Error Through the Lens of Racial Identity
abstract: Cross-race Recognition Error (CRE) is a phenomenon in which individuals have shown reliable deficits in recognizing members of other races, as compared to members of their own race. Past literature has debated the source of this phenomenon, often presenting evidence for either differential experience or differential motivation caused by racial identity. Previous studies have been restricted to monoracial participants. This study focuses on biracial participants to analyze the role of racial identity in cross-race recognition. Participants were randomly assigned to two experimental conditions such that they each included an equal number of the three racial groups (Black, White, biracial). Participants spent five minutes writing an essay about their mother or father, including a physical description of the parent, an account of their relationship and of their similarities. For biracial participants this should have caused them to identify with the race of the parent, thus making that racial identity temporarily more salient to them. Participants then completed a face recognition task with Black and White faces as well as an explicit and an implicit manipulation check. Results are predicted to show that the cross-race recognition of biracial participants is influenced by their salient identity; they will recognize faces from the salient racial group significantly better than faces from the other racial group. These results would suggest that group membership plays a role in CRE. This study could also shed light on the nature of biracial identity as well as the dangers of using the “one drop rule” to categorize biracial participants.

title: Terminal Illness in Physician-Assisted Suicide and Oregon's Death with Dignity Act: Tensions, Frames, and Losses
abstract: Oregon's Death with Dignity Act is inherently interesting because of its status as the only act passed in the United States that legalizes physician-assisted suicide (PAS). The criterion of terminal illness plays a critical role in the Oregon law. Yet much of the heated public debate regarding PAS in the United States seems to revolve around issues that are not dependent on terminal illness, and that might even be undermined by a terminal illness focus. However, terminal illness seems to be generally accepted as an automatic presumption in the debate, rarely coming into question. The purpose of my research is to 1) substantively and concretely define the issues at stake in the PAS debate, and 2) examine the role of terminal illness in those issues to allow for a better understanding of that criterion in Oregon's law. I explore the issues in the debate by examining arguments that arise in 1) the medical professional community, 2) the philosophic community, 3) the legal community, and 4) interest groups which are involved in the debate. My research demonstrates that the primary issues at stake in the PAS debate are autonomy, suffering, dignity, slippery slope, role of doctors, equality, and sanctity of life. Through close analysis of those categories, I show that terminal illness is not critical for any of those issues and is actually inconsistent with many of the issues when extended to their logical conclusions. Having reached this conclusion, I argue that while Oregon's law is able to address the PAS debate in one context, the PAS debate has been poorly framed by being verbalized in terms of secondary issues. The PAS debate has been characterized as a continuation of the end-of-life care discussion. But by limiting the framing of the PAS discussion to end-of-life care and including terminal illness as a stipulation, my research shows that it trivializes and sidesteps the issues that are truly at stake in the PAS debate.

title: Friend or Foe? Predicting the Future Role of the EU in the Transatlantic Marketplace
abstract: In today's global economy, the European Union market share is an important opportunity for growth by United States companies who have saturated other markets domestically. The EU constitutes one fifth of global trade; however, success in the market it difficult. While cultural and political barriers play a role in limiting the success of US multinational corporations with operations in the EU, my argument is that laws limiting transatlantic market liberalization and regulations by which American companies feel constrained are also prevalent and act as a barrier to trade. As evidence for my thesis, I interviewed a diverse group of experts regarding their perceptions of difficulties American multinationals face in the EU. The categories of people included heads of American companies with operations in the EU, European Union officials, Non-government Organizations who help American companies set up operations in the EU, academics from the EU who specialize in US-EU relations, and government agencies and NGOs in the US that seek to alleviate difficulties for US companies in the EU. In addition to other barriers, the majority of interviewees pointed to laws within the EU and within member-states that limit the performances of US companies operating in the EU. Applying the responses of the interviewees to a more theoretical framework, I discuss the implications laws within the EU have on the functioning of the transatlantic marketplace. Market liberalization and harmonization of laws will be to the benefit of both the US and the EU. A revitalized cooperative partnership between the two regions is a necessary component of economic stability and growth.

title: Decay
abstract: This story, written for the Writing Major’s Theory & Practice of Fiction sequence, is based on the style of Flannery O'Connor. It centers around a very young boy's relationship with his depressed mother after they have moved to a new town to await his father, whom the boy has never met. From the very limited viewpoint of the child, a Southern-gothic narrative unfolds.

title: Children of World War II GIs and Japanese War Brides in Postwar America
abstract: The American occupation of Japan after World War II led to thousands of marriages between U.S. soldiers and Japanese women and to the birth of even more of interracial children, who form the subject of my honors thesis in History. My goal is to explore issues of identity and historical memory among these children. I seek to find out whether and in what ways they came to see themselves as American and/or Japanese, and what kind of cultural and social conflicts they had to endure. Studies of these marriages and the racially mixed children they produced have not received serious historical scrutiny. Only a few published studies include interviews with these children. However, these studies have examined my subjects from the viewpoint of sociology, psychology, and education. These children have never been put in historical perspective. I will analyze these children’s experience of growing up in postwar America (approx. 1952-1968). The children of World War II GIs and Japanese war brides were physically and socially isolated due to the pressure to assimilate into the dominant white culture of postwar America. They were only able to begin to connect with their heritage and accept themselves as they came into adulthood and left their white, middle class communities during the 1960s youth and social movements.

title: Britain and the Rise of Reza Shah
abstract: In my senior thesis in history, I intend to illuminate the rise of Reza Shah, in the context of Britain's role in the process. I intend to answer several questions. To what degree did the British government control the course of events in Iran between the coup in 1921 and Reza Shah’s accession to throne in 1925? Was Reza Khan a tool of the British or were the British a tool of Reza Khan? Did the rise of Reza Shah more closely resemble a democratic mandate or a tyrannical seizure of power? A brief synopsis of Reza Khan’s rise to power illuminates some of the goals of my research. The Iran of Reza Khan’s generation was ripe for radical change. Following the crushing failure of the 1905-1911 constitutional movement, the First World War ravaged Iran leaving it weak and unstable, and acutely susceptible to British influence. On a cold February morning in 1921, rumors of a British engineered coup were apparently confirmed. Citizens of Tehran awoke to learn that an obscure Cossack Colonel named Reza Khan and co-putschist Seyyed Zia had seized the city and forcefully installed a new Parliamentary cabinet. Through a complex amalgam of British support, popular mandate, and strong-arm tactics of the Iranian army, Reza Khan steadily rose through the ranks of high office and was eventually elected Prime Minister. By 1925, Reza Khan abolished the formerly ruling Qajar dynasty and was elected by the Parliament to become Reza Shah Pahlavi, Shah of Iran. The answers to these questions have large implications. Many scholars and Iranians themselves regard the establishment of the Pahlavi dynasty as one of several tragic endings of the democratic movement that started after the Constitutional Revolution of 1905. Although Reza Shah considerably modernized Iran, he was also a ruthless dictator who censored the press, marginalized Parliament, and violently stifled opposition. Learning from precedents set by his father, Mohammad Reza Shah followed similar patterns of autocracy during his rule from 1941 to 1979. Sixty years of repressive rule culminated in the Revolution of 1979, which rejected Pahlavi legacies of authoritarianism, industrialism, secularism, and cordiality toward the West.

title: Creating an Information Technology Subculture of “Privateers”: University Administrators and Students
abstract: Northwestern University Information Technology (NUIT) is a human service organization that has more recently become a covert agent of social control. This paper focuses on the possible reasons why NUIT exerts social control, and on whom the control is exerted. The methods used for the research include literature concerning the behavior of complex organizations, such as newer organizations whose role has become the processing of people, and reasons why organizations seek to reduce reactive risk. Even though NUIT proposes overtly that the reason for their reduction in bandwidth is for the purpose of deterring on-campus media piracy, I contend that their primary motive is reducing overage costs due to large amounts of bandwidth used for this transfer, regardless of its morality. I have also interviewed students that have been caught by NUIT for excessive use of bandwidth, and discovered an information technology subculture that exists within this group, whose motive is simply to download as much data as possible to incur financial damages to NUIT. My findings as pertaining to the practices of NUIT seem to indicate that my hypothesis is correct, and NUIT is concerned with reducing the use of bandwidth as their primary concern, and thus rationalize their restriction of bandwidth as a means of social control.

title: Validation of Real-Time PCR and Melt Curve Analysis for the Detection and Speciation of Plasmodium
abstract: This study involved designing a real-time assay for identifying the species of Malarial infections. This research was conducted as a general push toward designing clinical tests for microbiological assays so as to use current DNA based procedures in molecular biology for quicker and more effective diagnosis.

title: Children’s Talent and Community Involvement as Predictors of Psychological Functioning
abstract: This paper relates the methods and results of a quantitative analysis of the effects of strengths-based mental health treatment on the psychological functioning and well being of foster children. Data were gathered from 762 foster children receiving mental health care through Illinois Department of Child and Family Services' System of Care program. System of Care provides wraparound mental health services including, but not limited to, psychiatry, counseling, and community service linkage, all administered with the goal of building the child's strengths to promote better functioning and increased resiliency. My analyses examined whether an improvement or regression in level of two personal strengths, talent and community inclusion, predicted a similar effect on the child's psychological functioning.

title: The Role of Tbx5 and LMP in Cardiac Cell Migration
abstract: Extensive studies have been carried out to describe the temporal and spatial expression of the T-box genes Tbx4 and Tbx5 during development. Currently, it is thought that these genes function in cell specification, differentiation, and growth in the limbs and heart. However, little investigation has been made to elucidate how these genes act to regulate molecular and cellular activities during development. Our lab has identified a new member of the PDZ-LIM protein family, called LMP, which has overlapping expression with Tbx4 and Tbx5. It is possible that LMP plays an important role in the function of these transcription factors. The correlation between Tbx4, Tbx5, LMP and cardiac cell migration was explored in stage 25 chick embryos through an in vitro model of epicardial migration. Tbx4 and Tbx5 expression appeared primarily in the nucleus of these migrated cells but also weakly in the cytoplasm. Other results to follow.

title: Synthesis and Study of Regular and Cyclopentane Modified PNA Oligomers to Determine Minimal Length for DNA Binding
abstract: Peptide nucleic acids (PNAs) are a unique class of antisense molecules that exhibit high binding affinity and sequence specificity for DNA targets. Poly-thymine PNA oligomers were synthesized and tested to determine the minimum length requirement for DNA binding. Further studies were done to determine the effect of structural rigidification by incorporation of a diasteromerically pure trans-(S,S)-cyclopentane modified monomer at various positions. First, an efficient and economical synthesis of a protected aeg-PNA monomer was established utilizing a reductive amination between Boc-glycinal and ethyl glycinate. Poly-thymine heptamers (1 and 2) and other oligomers were prepared using this monomer and previously synthesized cyclopentane modified monomer. The DNA binding properties established by thermal denaturation and Job’s plot analyses will be discussed. Graduate Student Co-Researchers: Michael C. Myers, Jonathan Pokorski

title: Random Drug-Testing in Illinois Public Schools
abstract: During his 2004 State of the Union Address, President Bush argued that the government must continue to support “aggressive education, treatment, and law enforcement” programs that reduce drug consumption amongst America’s youth. Citing the goal of “helping children make right choices,” President Bush announced that his 2005 budget proposal would include an additional $23 million for schools to implement student drug testing programs, a substantial increase from the previous year’s $2 million. The Bush administration’s recent support of student drug testing has resulted from the Supreme Court’s 2003 ruling in Board of Education v. Earls which allowed for all students involved in any competitive extracurricular activity, ranging from the chess team to Future Farmers of America, to be subjected to random drug testing. In the wake of the Bush administration’s push for drug testing, and the Earls decision, this research will further examine random-drug-testing programs within the state of Illinois. The research will not only identify the school districts within the state of Illinois which have chosen to implement drug testing policies, but will examine the motivation behind implementation. Furthermore, this article will demonstrate that geographic and demographic discrepancies exist between districts choosing to implement drug testing policies, and those not choosing to. In analyzing the given discrepancies, one can better understand the motivation for implementation, and therefore predict the effectiveness of the Bush administration’s new push for student drug testing.

title: The Effects of Gender Atypical Behavior on Sexual Attraction in Heterosexual and Homosexual Populations
abstract: How do masculinity and femininity affect the perceived attractiveness of an individual? Are those who deviate from gender typical behavior (i.e., societal norms of masculine and feminine behavior) found less attractive than individuals who conform to society’s behavioral norms? Do these standards of attractiveness hold true for both the heterosexual and homosexual communities? Research has shown that the tendency exists for gay men to look for “straight-acting” qualities in potential mates (Laner et al., 1977; Bailey et al., 1997) and that lesbians also tend to prefer either feminine partners (Bailey et al., 1997) or androgynous ones (Laner, 1978). If this is true, then effeminate gay men and masculine lesbians (a significant portion of the homosexual community) would most likely have to continue to fight prejudice within their own communities when looking for potential mates. In order to study this issue, I will be looked at ratings of perceived attractiveness to masculine and feminine behavior in both heterosexual and homosexual men and women. I used videotapes of men and women acting in either a gender typical or atypical manner. Each videotaped individual was asked to act out a neutral sentence in a stereotypically feminine, masculine, and neutral way. Raters watched these videotapes on a computer and answered a series of questions that evaluated their level of attraction to each individual. Heterosexual men and homosexual women viewed videotapes of women, and homosexual men and heterosexual women viewed the men. Each rater saw each videotaped individual only once, in either the feminine, masculine, or neutral condition. Participants were a combination of undergraduate students and community members between the ages of 18 and 30.

title: NetLogo 3D: A Simple Three-Dimensional Multi-Agent Modeling Environment
abstract: Since my sophomore year (March 2002) I have been doing project work for Uri Wilensky's Center for Connected Learning and Computer-based Modeling whose flagship application is NetLogo. NetLogo is a descendent of the Logo family of programs, and has the goal of providing an environment and language capable of presenting emerging results from complex multi-agent systems in a concise and simple manner. It is straightforward enough to be used as a teaching-aid by many schools, yet is powerful enough to be used by researchers. The project I have been working on for the past two quarters involved extending NetLogo to a three-dimensional environment while still preserving the user-friendly nature of the application. This work involves many aspects of computer science including graphics, computer languages, human-computer interaction, and software engineering. Furthermore, a small suite of three-dimensional models was developed to provide examples of how the tool can be used. This includes models such as Conway's Game of Life and Boid's Flocking Model. Previously, there has been a minimal effort to create a widely-used three-dimensional multi-agent modeling environment. Therefore, many of the issues that arose during development revolved around issues of design and observer perception. The purpose of this project was to tackle many of these issues and produce an experimental version of NetLogo 3D that will provide the foundation for general use by the teaching and research community within a year or two.

title: Combating Narrative Determinism: Malory, White, and the Arthurian Tradition
abstract: Sir Thomas Malory’s Medieval work, Le Morte D’Arthur is known as the last definitive interpretation of the Arthurian myth before the dawn of the English Renaissance, and is the literary basis for modern Arthurian writings such as T.H. White’s 1958 novel, The Once and Future King. While separated by nearly five hundred years, these two books represent two of the most influential works in the Arthurian tradition. Both works center on the notion of destiny, a critical function of the tradition, but if the Arthurian genre is so steeped in destiny, how can an author, reader, or character escape the fate dictated to them? In this paper I question why and how we hope for change in a literary world that is clearly predetermined. It is with this paradox in mind that authors and readers alike must question the ways in which a story is retold and reread. We must ask ourselves, how does an author tell a story that everyone already knows? And how does a reader read a story that he or she already knows? These are the questions at the heart of my work. I examine the determinism of the borrowed plot and illustrate the ways in which author, reader, and character resist the narrative destiny that seeks to contain them. The paper (which is also my senior honors thesis) analyzes these two Arthurian works, but on a greater scale, examines issues of reception theory, reader-response criticism, and the philosophical notion of determinism as applied to narrative.

title: The Effect of a Sibling's Diabetes on a Non-Diabetic Sibling: A Communicative Approach
abstract: As recent research indicates, there has been a significant increase in the prevalence of newly diagnosed diabetic children, resulting in extensive literature on the subject. However, this literature has been limited to the disease's impact on the inflicted child, their parents, and their family as a whole; it has failed to acknowledge the disease's impact on the non-diabetic sibling(s). Since the sibling relationship is one of the most influential relationships in a person's life (Tucker, 2001), coping with a disease of this nature could have the potential to significantly affect their relationship. The limited writing on the impact of a child's disability on siblings suggests there are impacts on sibling's identity, the sibling bond, the sibling's need for information, as well as future career choices (Seligman & Darling, 1997). This research study takes an in-depth look at the dynamics of this sibling relationship, focusing on the ways the non-diabetic sibling is impacted by his/her sibling's diabetes and the way their communication is impacted based on Petronio's Communication Privacy Management Theory. All primary research for this study came from confidential 30 minute personal interviews with participants from the Northwestern University student body.

title: Corporation Conglomeration in the Radio Industry and the Politics of Popular Music: A Case Study of the Chicago Radio Market
abstract: In the summer of 2003, I studied radio airplay on stations owned by corporate conglomerates in order to determine if the political biases of the ownership were being expressed in broadcast choices to include and exclude politically relevant artists and songs. This was in response to claims about the existence of such bias made in the press and in the Senate Commerce Committee after a controversy arose involving the country group The Dixie Chicks. After their lead singer publicly castigated President Bush over the impending war in Iraq, some conglomerates pulled the band's songs off their country stations. I set out to investigate whether or not such actions were part of a larger pattern of behavior by corporate media entities, or if there were other social forces at work determining the radio airplay of politically active musicians. To do so, I designed a research project monitoring airplay of conservative/pro-war and liberal/anti-war artists and songs on stations in the Chicago market, and compared the data to the political affiliations of the stations' corporate executives. Interestingly, I found absolutely no correlation between politics in radio ownership and in radio airplay in the 10-week sample I conducted. To explain the politically neutral behavior of media companies, I looked beyond the idea that radio conglomerates are actively pushing their political agendas into their broadcast products. Instead, I explored the nature of corporate culture industry itself, which seeks to reap profits from Americans with a wide spectrum of political beliefs.

title: A Rhetorical Analysis of Public Education in America: Communicating the Paradigm Shift
abstract: This paper is principally about public education in America. I analyze education in both the realm of political rhetoric and in the realm of functional reality. I begin with the historical foundations of education and the background behind specific American political policies and education legislation. This affords the reader an appropriate understanding for the establishment of the major themes and educational philosophies upon which the American education system is built. The foundations of communication rhetoric are also outlined to present the reader with a global historical context concerning education and communication and how they are tied together. I focus the analysis on President George W. Bush, his leadership position, and the political rhetoric and communication initiatives he uses to connect the audience (America) with the mission of the No Child Left Behind Act. The writer also considers George W. Bush's compassionate conservative approach and the rhetoric behind America's education paradigm shift. Thesis Statement: George W. Bush, through his strong understanding of communication, uses political rhetoric to champion his educational platform through the formation and implementation of the No Child Left Behind Act, effectively shifting the paradigm of America's long-established, time-honored educational system form the simple right of equal access to a free public education for all students to a policy requiring and thus guaranteeing student success through a demand for and verification of concrete student data.

title: Unbinding: Recovering Self
abstract: This project primarily consists of a performance of a woman struggling with her identity mainly through a battle with eating disorders. It is a one-woman show about an hour in length. I will be performing a segment of this work. The text results from my reading of several texts dealing with women, identity, eating disorders, cultural influences on women's health and my own writing. The actual script is a combination of excerpts from these texts woven into a single story. The texts used as background for the script, and as actual pieces of the script, include Naomi Wolf's The Beauty Myth, Marya Hornbacher's Wasted, and Dr. Mary Pipher's Reviving Ophelia: Saving the Selves of Adolescent Girls. The purpose of the project was to explore several ways in which women struggle with their identities and specifically the ways women harm themselves in order to control or change their identities. The performance looks into the pain of the destruction caused by identity control through an eating disorder as well as the pain, hope, and never ending positive battle required to escape such self-destruction. There is a written component to the project beyond the performance text documenting the creation process focusing on changes in the performance vision and reality throughout the research, writing and rehearsal periods. There will also be a discussion of where to take the performance in the future to act as a tool for discussion of identity issues for women and men.

title: Cuentitos Caóticos
abstract: I wrote the novella “Cuentitos Caóticos” during my 399 Independent Study for honors in the English Major in Writing. It is a series of humorous stories that are tied together not only through the reappearance of its characters by also by its setting, which is a fictional town called Caos in northern New Mexico. The piece is set mostly in the present day, but there are also sections that take place many years in the past, and so it has elements of historical fiction as well. The primary language of the work is English, but with a heavy Spanish influence. In presenting my project, I will read several excerpts and use an overhead projector to show some of the photographs that I have incorporated into the piece. I intend to make this novella into a full-length novel in the coming year.

title: Cultural Competency: Turning an Imagined Ideal into a Reality
abstract: Cultural Competence within the healthcare system has become a significant area of concern as our nation becomes more diverse. By 2050, ethnic minorities are projected to constitute nearly 50 percent of the American population. Current research has indicated that many healthcare disparities amongst ethnic groups are attributable to culturally incompetent healthcare providers and culturally incompetent healthcare systems. Much focus has been on defining what it means to be culturally competent without considering what factors contribute to cultural competency. For the purposes of this research, it was determined that the factors that contribute the most to cultural competency are a person‚s demographic background, preexisting attitudes towards cultural competency, training experiences, motivations and organizational environment in which they work. This research seeks to determine which of these factors are most important to individual cultural competency, with the idea that training will contribute the most towards building cultural competence. This was done through surveying people who participated in a cultural-competency training program. However, the research found that though training was important, preexisting attitudes towards cultural competency were better predictors of cultural competence. The research then sought to further examine the effect preexisting attitudes and training experiences had on the participants. Determining which factors are most significant and which ones are the least significant will be useful as policymakers pour resources into making both people and organizations more culturally competent in hopes of moving towards a more equitable healthcare system.

title: Dilute Magnetic Semiconductor (DMS) Nanowires
abstract: Dilute magnetic semiconductors (DMS) have become an active research area because one might exploit the charge and spin of electrons in DMS to create useful devices in data processing and data storage. DMS may also be used to create spin-polarized carrier sources that would be particularly useful for spintronic applications. DMS can be made by alloying nonmagnetic semiconductors and magnetic elements. For instance, the addition of manganese as an acceptor to indium arsenide makes InAs a ferromagnetic p-type semiconductor. The excess carriers (holes) align the Mn atoms provide the magnetism in the semiconductor. We are interested in making DMS nanowires to analyze the size dependent magnetic properties of the material. In a nanostructure, the energy spectrum of the free carriers can be affected by quantum confinement. Hence, the size dependent quantum confinement in DMS nanowires may affect the magnetism of the material in interesting ways. It is also important for us to understand how the size of DMS material can affect its magnetic properties when considering device miniaturization.

title: Callings
abstract: This project is a 62-page novella, which was written in the fall quarter of 2003 for my honors project in the English Department's Writing Major. The novella follows the protagonist, who is the goddess figure of a minor cult in Chicago. The action takes place over one night, after she has been released from prison and meets up with an estranged friend who helped her begin the cult. During the course of the night, she has various encounters that compel her to analyze her ethical and moral role as the cult leader, specifically the racial, class, and sexual power dynamics of her group. The protagonist establishes herself as a goddess figure and ultimately comes to grips with the limitations of her own power, and submits to a power higher than her own. Her estranged friend, the leader of a splinter group, undergoes a similar analysis of his own group. Through these conflicts, the novella explores contemporary religious faith through the dimensions of race, sexuality, class, and the relationship between popular and religious cultures. Snippets of popular romantic ballads throughout the novella complicate the separation of secular and religious devotion.

title: Mad Song to Madrigals
abstract: I will be reading some works--sonnets, madsongs, ballads--of mine and will explain their structure (namely the intricate functions of the rhyme) and how it works to convey the poem's music, style, and emphasis. I will also try to relate the rhyming structure in today's popular songs and show why some rhymes work and others don't.

title: How Our Relationships Affect Us: The Effects of High-Maintenance Interactions between Dating Partners on Self-Regulatory Success
abstract: Why do difficult relationships seem to take such a huge toll on our lives? The present research seeks to clarify how engaging in a frustrating interaction with a significant other affects unrelated aspects of life. Previous research on self-regulation suggests that many seemingly unrelated acts of higher-level cognition (such as exerting will power, doing logic, and controlling emotions), all draw from one, depletable resource. We propose that a frustrating or high-maintenance interaction between dating partners is depleting enough to produce adverse effects on self-regulation and subsequent performance on unrelated tasks. Correlational analyses of 40 couples revealed that participants who experienced a lab-based interaction with their partner as high-maintenance exhibited impaired GRE performance, but they were not more likely to rely on the correspondence bias when judging a peer. These findings suggest some intriguing implications for how a high-maintenance interaction affects subsequent efforts at self-regulation.

title: AFM Liquid Cell Development
abstract: The goal of my project is to design and build a liquid cell for the conductive probe atomic force microscope (CP-AFM) in Professor Hersam’s research group. This liquid cell is to be used for liquid phase nanolithography (LPN) experiments that involve patterning molecules on hydrogen-passivated silicon surfaces in the absence of oxygen and other ambient molecules. In order to complete these experiments in an efficient time scale a new and more robust liquid cell would need to be made that incorporates features that the original liquid cell lacked, i.e. in-situ flow capabilities. Through my time working in the group I have designed and built a working prototype for a new liquid cell that incorporates many desired features required for future LPN experiments. Currently, further design modifications are being made as I have started running preliminary LPN experiments.

title: Effects of Benevolent Sexism in a Military Context
abstract: After taking a variety of courses in social and gender psychology, I became interested in the cultural motivations and expectations of soldiers in war. Historically, war has been a very masculine endeavor. However, as legal sanctions against female participation in the military have been removed in the recent past, America has witnessed an upsurge in female enlistees whereby women now constitute 15% of active-duty military. Further, the institution of incentives such as the G.I. Bill has provided potential recruits with more gender-neutral reasons for enlisting. Yet, the male-female participation in the military remains unequal. Why would this be the case? Up until now, the gender difference has been attributed largely to discrimination against women due to their stereotypical inability to perform masculine tasks of war. However, Peter Glick and Susan Fiske (2001) have asserted that discrimination can be viewed in terms of benevolent sexism (a belief in the protection of women) and hostile sexism (a belief that women are inferior to men). The project utilizes questionnaire data to investigate the possibility that both benevolent and hostile sexism contribute to a cultural belief that a military context is inappropriate for women. The findings may point to cultural reasoning that believes not only that women are physically incapable of performing military duties, but that they should be protected from the dangerous situations that these duties require.

title: Further Dimensions of Perfectionism: Influential Factors of Independent and Interdependent Perfectionism
abstract: Perfectionism has been widely studied, and the focus of perfectionism research has mainly concerned the negative consequences of perfectionism. Researchers have linked perfectionism to depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, eating disorders, and low self-esteem. Perfectionism has also been analyzed as a multivariate construct, as demonstrated in Hewitt and Flett's (1991) study describing self-oriented, other-oriented, and socially prescribed perfectionism. However, researchers have not examined the focus of perfectionism within a social realm. The present research investigates whether some perfectionists have unrealistic ideals concerning their individual achievements, while others have unrealistic ideals concerning their social relationships and interactions (termed independent and interdependent perfectionism, respectively). In order to measure the differences between interdependent and independent perfectionism, there were two conditions in the study: social rejection and individual failure. After mass-testing at the beginning of the quarter, participants were invited to the lab and asked to complete a story-writing task. After completion, they were either told that their creativity score was not high enough to participate in the next task, or that others did not rank their story highly, so they could not participate in the next task. After receiving their feedback, the participants completed a questionnaire that included a state self-esteem scale, an independent perfectionism scale, the interdependent perfectionism scale, a mood scale, and various other measures. The newly developed Interdependent Perfectionism Scale (IPS) was factor analyzed, and three distinct factors emerged: motivation-focused, criticism-focused, and favoritism-focused interdependent perfectionism. The influence that each type of threat had on each type of perfectionism was also examined.

title: The Circumference: A Collection of Poems
abstract: This year, I completed an independent study for departmental honors in the English Major in Writing with Professor Mary Kinzie. The finished project was a collection of poems that integrated scientific concepts into poems about family and other interpersonal situations. In many cases I used trope in order to compare broad and complex scientific concepts to very tangible and real human situations. For example, in one poem I had a man use chaos theory as a way of talking to his daughter about his sister's death. The collection spanned roughly twenty pages, and used theories and data from such subjects as mathematics, geology, and cosmology.

title: Underactuated Motion and Path Tracking: The Snakeboard
abstract: Conservation of momentum tells us that all momentum is conserved about a point. Sometimes, systems can take advantage of this principle to locomote. For example, if an astronaut is floating free in space, he can swing his arms around to reorient himself. However, since his momentum is conserved only about his center of mass, he will always remain centered on the same point. This project demonstrates how conservation of momentum can be used to move through space. There are two basic elements to the robot: a pair of coupled steering wheels and a large rotating flywheel. Unlike the astronaut, this robot can change its center of rotation by changing the angle of the steering wheels. Conservation of momentum means that rotating the flywheel in one direction will cause the robot to rotate about this point in the opposite direction. Through a series of arc motions, the robot can wind its way through space, earning its name, The Snakeboard. In this project, the Snakeboard will not only move through space, but will follow a predefined path. Since it can perform this task only by steering and rotating the flywheel, it is classified as underactuated.

title: Taking on Uncle Sam
abstract: In 1996 President Bill Clinton signed into law a welfare reform bill that dramatically changed the American welfare system. As a result of this bill, members of advocacy groups, labor union officials, welfare-to-work participants and lawyers for legal aid societies took action to reverse and change parts of the new legislation. My research analyzes the collective actions and social movements in New York City from 1994 to 2000 that developed to protest the 1996 welfare reform. For my research, I have collected original empirical data from newspaper articles, which I used to code and categorize the different actions according to the type and nature of each event. From my research and preliminary analysis, I have found that most events have remained non-disruptive and nonviolent and each event can fit into one of four main categories of protest: lawsuits and legal actions, unionization efforts, advocacy work, and rallies and demonstrations. I completed most of my data collection last quarter. This quarter I am continuing some research, but I am mainly analyzing my empirical data as part of an independent study with sociology professor, Maryjane Osa.

title: The Destruction and Reconstruction of Bosnian Cultural Heritage Sites
abstract: My project traces Bosnians' ideas about and connections to three cultural heritage sites that were damaged in the 1992-1996 war. My conclusions are drawn from thirty-five informant interviews conducted with Bosnians in three cities about three different sites. The first site examined is the City Hall and National Library of Sarajevo, destroyed during the four-year siege on the city. 600,000 volumes that recorded Bosnia's multicultural history were destroyed in the flames. The second site examined is the Stari Most in Mostar, a 16th-Century Ottoman bridge destroyed in 1992 by Croatian forces because of its Islamic qualities. The third site examined is the Ferhadija Mosque in Banja Luka, dynamited and turned into a parking lot by Bosnian Serbs. In all cases, informants compared the loss of these structures to the death of family members and injury to the body. The three sites were destroyed in an attack on the Bosnian culture; informants feel the loss of these structures so strongly because they have come to symbolize the Bosnian nation. My research reveals that reconstruction could demonstrate a positive commitment to ethnic coexistence and reestablish the symbolic resources that the Bosnian community needs to heal.

title: Polybius and the Cultural Divide Between Greeks and Romans
abstract: Polybius, a Greek writing in the second century BC, wrote a history of Rome's conquest of Greece. His purpose was to explain the Romans to the Greeks (and vice versa) and to educate generals and statesmen on both sides. One facet of this education involved dealing with the clash of alien cultures. This clash causes cultural misunderstandings, which perform an important function in the narrative. They occur exclusively during peace negotiations and lead to further conflict. Moments of crisis such as these are when the contours of cultural difference are greatest and most obvious, so we can assume that these will be natural focal points for his analysis of cultural difference. This leads to the conclusion that his text is designed to alleviate cultural misunderstandings and thereby prevent conflict. Polybius himself, late in his life, actually played an active role in the historical events that he later described. Here we see him following his own advice by actively mediating between Greeks and Romans.

title: The Positive Side of Negative Scenes: Patterns of Life Narrative and their Relation to Healthy Functioning During Midlife
abstract: The present study analyzed a pre-existing archival data set from the National Survey of Midlife Development in the United States (MIDUS: Brim, et al. 1995-96), a large-scale study sponsored by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation Network on Successful Midlife Development. The MIDUS includes results from measures of physical health, emotional well-being, psychological health, personality, and other social, cultural, and demographic issues. A life story interview was given to a subset of participants in the MIDUS. It is this subset of individuals who comprise the sample for this study (n=48). The study compared growth that results from negative scenes within life story interviews and compared it to this same theme resulting from positive life story scenes. Growth themes and characteristics were coded for in the life story interview and then related to the objective indices of well being and generativity obtained from the MIDUS assessment.

title: The Reconstruction of Iraq and the Marshall Plan: A Comparative Study
abstract: This paper is a comparison of current United States efforts to reconstruct Iraq with U.S. efforts to reconstruct Western Europe following World War II. Through comparing the aid given, the processes through which reconstruction efforts were undertaken, and the outcomes produced by American aid, this paper finds that the current efforts in Iraq cannot be called a modern Marshall Plan because while the real dollar amounts of aid given are comparable, the current efforts in Iraq have not accomplished the necessary intangible goals that made the Marshall Plan a success. Instead, current U.S. efforts are consistent with initial U.S. efforts to reconstruct Western Europe, between 1945 and 1947, which lacked cohesion much as current efforts in Iraq do. Current U.S. efforts in Iraq are not yet successful, but are on a path that could lead to success if the U.S. remains committed in Iraq, achieves the intangible goals of reconstruction, and solves the security problems in Iraq.

title: The Perception of Angry and Calm Speech in English, Spanish, and Arabic
abstract: The study explores whether or not English listeners will perceive calm Arabic speech as angry because of its glottalized elements, I have collected data for a project analyzing native English speakers‚ perceptions of calm and angry speech in English, Spanish and Arabic. Studies in phonetics have shown a correlation between emotional speech and the sound patterns of such speech; such exploration has reported that angry speech in English demonstrates increased glottalization as part of this acoustic phonetic correlation. Glottalization occurs when a consonant is pronounced with a simultaneous catch in the throat from the closing of the vocal cords (also known as a glottal stop). Because Arabic has a prevalence of glottalized sounds, it is a potentially useful language to explore in studying the perception of emotions based on the acoustic phonetic correlation. I have studied the phonetic cues native English speakers use to identify angry speech by having subjects listen to English, Spanish, and Arabic two-word phrases which have been recorded as angry and calm with glottal and non-glottal target words. Arabic is used as the target language, while Spanish is used as a foreign language which does not present glottalization in order to determine if responses are the result of bias toward a foreign language.

title: The Bay of Pigs, Cuban Missile Crisis and The New York Times
abstract: In the 1960s, The New York Times censored its stories about the Bay of Pigs invasion and the Cuban Missile Crisis in order to “protect national security.” The research aims to explain how and why the Times printed certain information. It contrasts what was printed with what the Times actually knew by using the accounts of Times reporters and editors from the era and declassified government documents about the events. The paper also examines how the editorial decisions affected President Kennedy's actions and what happened in the Caribbean.

title: News Corporation: Process Behind Global Diversification of iTV
abstract: With the help of digital satellite technology, News Corporation is distributing interactive television in only a few parts of the world. Rupert Murdoch wants to one day introduce this technology to the rest of the world. Interactive television (iTV) technology combines television and the Internet so that the viewer is given individual choices about what he/she watches. The newest versions of this convergent digital technology gives consumers new options such as picking different camera angles to watch a soccer match or incorporating email and text messaging into the television. In the past few years News Corp. has used satellite technology instead of cable to distribute iTV in Britain, Australia and Italy. More recently, Murdoch purchased DirecTV in the United States, so there has been speculation of New Corp. distributing iTV in America. The thesis analyzes News Corporation’s global diversification strategy in the distribution of interactive television. It explains how New Corporation has decided on distribution strategies for its satellite broadcasters like BSkyB, Foxtel, and Sky Italia. The thesis tries to draw the line between where these strategies are standardized and where adaptation has been necessary. This is accomplished by comparing and contrasting the different technology and companies currently involved in Murdoch’s distribution of iTV. This will help explain if the standardization or adaptation of technology and mergers is a reason for News Corporation introducing iTV to Britain, Australia and Italy before the United States.

title: Convergent and Predictive Validity of Child Self-Report Measures: Links to Risks for Psychopathology
abstract: Over the last few decades, the number of individuals diagnosed with depressive disorders has significantly increased (Solomon, 2001; Kessler et al., 1994). The present study took a multi-method approach to understand children’s emotions in an effort to identify risk factors for these disorders. The primary goal of this study was to test the relative validity of various measures of emotional states in young children, including parental, observational, and child self-report measures of the child’s emotional state. It is important to investigate the validity of emotion report methods other than parental report, since several studies indicate that parental reports show poorer predictive validity for later adjustment problems and evidence of bias (Mesman & Koot, 2000; Youngstrom, Izard, & Ackerman, 1999). We also investigated the convergence between children’s self-reports of their emotional state and objective coding of their emotional behavior during a structured laboratory visit. The visit was composed of 10 previously validated emotion-eliciting tasks designed to tap major temperamental traits and emotionality. After each task, children reported how they felt during the task, using pictorial aides. Videos of the children during each task were coded for facial, bodily, and vocal indicators of emotional states. Convergence between these codes and each of the three reporters (parent, observer, and child) was examined.

title: The Abuse of Diplomatic Privileges
abstract: The Vienna Convention of 1961 explicitly states that diplomatic privileges are not intended to “benefit individuals but to ensure the efficient performance of functions.” In spite of the original intentions of the right to diplomatic immunity, there has been a considerable rise in the number of cases of diplomatic abuse in the last half of the twentieth century, meriting a critical reevaluation of these privileges. It is important that the immunities granted diplomats be reassessed because the rise in the number of highly publicized cases of diplomatic abuse has the potential of undermining the credibility of both the U.S. government and the United Nations. The abuse of privileges by some diplomats has cast aspersions on the talented and dedicated diplomats who employ their privileges in a way that benefits U.S. citizens. Scholars around the world have proposed several suggestions for dealing with the current rise in flagrant abuses of diplomatic immunities. These suggestions include amending the Vienna Convention to give power to the International Court of Justice to suspend non-complying countries from the UN, isolating disobedient nations, creating a fund to compensate victims, and enforcing more strictly the provisions of the Convention. The most promising solution for attenuating the abuse of diplomatic privileges in the U.S. is for the government to issue a law mandating the purchase of insurance by countries operating embassies in the U.S. and to more stringently enforce the Diplomatic Relations Act of 1978 requiring the purchase of auto liability insurance by diplomats. These actions would not require amending the Vienna Convention, but would oblige the U.S. government to adhere to rights already delineated in the Convention to host states to more strictly implement such a policy.

title: Human Language: The Exploration of Archetype through Fiction
abstract: My project consists of a short-story sequence involving three different works, each approximately 18 pages in length. The three pieces each involve an exploration of historical themes through the techniques of modern fiction-- that is, while the writing strives to maintain a modern style, the subject matter involves the co-mingling of different eras and cultural aesthetics. It is the intention of the work to map the ways in which certain myths, religious stories, and histories can still be made relevant and emotionally powerful within a modern setting. The goal is to make evident the smaller aspects of humanity that make a mythic figure epic: that it is the ways in which Samson fails, or the ways in which Achilles is vulnerable, that make them great and universal figures. There are ways in which Roland on the plain is the same as Ephialtes at Thermopylae is the same as Nero at the fiddle is the same as Pyrrhus surveying the field, and this is what is interesting to me: the ways that myths create heroes, and the ways in which heroes are ordinary men—ordinary in a sense that is not mundane but universal. This project required a large amount of both historical and literary research, which I believe is evident in the material. It is the goal of the writer for these pieces to resonate on more levels than traditional fiction might, and for the depth of the subject and the intention to come across through the execution of those elements which make up good fiction.

title: The Harlem Renaissance: Black Theatre and the Performance of Black Identity
abstract: This is a short performance piece that is a reflection of my research done in an eight-week program here at NU— The Summer Research Opportunity Program in the Summer of 2003. The research undertakes an exploration into the souls of Harlem’s Black folk in the 1920s and 1930s. Guided by the assumption that the “keepers of the word” or writers of the time gave voice to the sentiments of this Black community crammed inside white New York, I view this period with the idea that Black theatre set the stage for the reconfiguration of Black identity. Theatre must act as a venue that simultaneously educates Blacks and Whites about Black identity and voices the frustrations and immediate realities of the Black plight. Closely examining a single work by Langston Hughes, I pose the following questions: What is the purpose of theatrical works? Are these works of art or propaganda?
