title: Bowling for Budapest: Social Structure and Ceramics at the Hungarian Bronze Age Site of Százhalombatta
abstract: The emergence of social stratification in the Carpathian Basin, Hungary, occurred during the European Bronze Age (2500-800 b.c.e.), when dramatic increases in settlement size and fortification document social aggregation. Craft production specialized as these previously agrarian communities increasingly diversified their subsistence and technological bases. Centralization of power is apparent within the fortified areas, which seem inhabited by a distinct warrior class, who rather than engaging in agrarian activities appear to have protected the community from outside attack, as well as control trade along the Danube River. Recent excavation has defined the Bronze Age tell settlement of Százhalombatta-Foldvár, situated along the Benta River Valley, a Danube tributary. The region was occupied extensively by the Vatya culture of the Middle Bronze Age (1700-1200 b.c.e.). This settlement provides insight into the development of labor and craft specialization; such differences are evident in the emerging patterns from the ceramic evidence. Two sets of categories were considered in the analysis: Down Valley, the region most closely associated with the Danube River, and the Up Valley sites emphasize economic trends and region foci; and a Tell and Non-tell (agricultural sites) site comparison which concentrates on the question of social identity and the emergence of class. An ongoing Phase II surface collection has provided the numerous ceramic sherds, from which functional and surface treatment analyses have indicated particular social and economic behaviors that express class distinction. The daily interactions and habits performed using ceramics have helped reconstruct the everyday experiences in the sociopolitical landscape.

title: The Development of Protein-Repellant Microparticle Probes for Immunodiagnostic Assays
abstract: A critical issue in the use of blood-contacting immunodiagnostic biosensors involves the high level of non-specific binding caused by serum proteins adhering to the probe surface. To eliminate such non-specific adsorption, we engineered surface-modified magnetic microparticle probes that exhibit complete resistance to common serum proteins such as human serum albumin (HSA) and Immunoglobulin G (IgG). Polystyrene (PS) magnetic microparticles were surface-coated with a Pluronic™ triblock copolymer, (PEO)a(PPO)b(PEO)a (where PEO is polyethylene oxide and PPO is polypropylene oxide) and exposed to high concentrations of fluorescein-labeled HSA and IgG. The modified probes were left in the concentrated protein solutions for time periods that simulate standard immunodiagnostic assays. Protein adsorption was then quantified through the use of flow cytometry. With this strategy, we were able to demonstrate the complete resistance of the coated microparticles to HSA and IgG, compared with uncoated PS probes. Significantly, the success of our microparticle probes in resisting protein adsorption allows the targeting of low concentration disease proteins like Prostate-Specific Antigen in blood serum without the need for lengthy pre-purifications of patient blood samples.

title: Ganglioside GM3 Triggers Urokinase Plasminogen Activator Receptor (uPAR) Signaling to Facilitate Melanoma Growth and Metastasis
abstract: Overexpression of ganglioside GM3, a sialylated glycosphingolipid, correlates with increased metastasis of melanomas. Anti-GM3 antibody and GM3-related vaccine have been used to treat melanoma, lung cancer and breast cancer at Stage III and IV in clinical trials. However, neither active vaccination nor antibody administration appears to be sufficient to completely clear melanomas or prevent their metastases. Determining the mechanism of elevated GM3 on cancer cell metastasis may offer a rationale to improve GM3-related cancer treatment. GM3 is able to cosegregate with uPAR at the leading edge of migrating cells and GM3 overexpression facilitates squamous carcinoma cell proliferation when uPAR is activated. To address the role of uPAR signaling on GM3 elevated melanoma metastasis, I used a mouse melanoma cell (B16F1). I found that (1) increases in the expression of GM3 facilitated B16F1 cell proliferation without affecting uPAR expression; (2) disruption of the uPAR expression prevents the stimulatory effect of elevated GM3 on cell proliferation; (3) disruption of uPAR expression or treatment of cells with anti-GM3 IgG antibody reduced the stimulatory effect of elevated GM3 on cell spreading, while functional blockade of both uPAR and GM3 eliminated cell spreading. These results suggest therapeutic modalities that target GM3 may require concomitant treatment that suppresses uPAR signaling to control neoplastic cell proliferation.

title: Solution 1H-NMR Reveals Distinctions among Genera within the Family Pinaceae
abstract: Recent studies have used spectral distinctions among exudate-producing plant species to classify samples between families, but have failed to distinguish below this mark, particularly at the levels of genus and species. Such work examined taxonomic relationships throughout the Kingdom Plantae via solid-state carbon-13 (13C) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The present study utilizes solution proton (1H) NMR to determine if intrafamilial differences are detectable. Previous examinations have dealt with a wide variety of exudates, many of which were insoluble in any type of deuterated solvent. Since high-resolution 1H-NMR is limited to solutions, this study focuses on the family Pinaceae, which produces resins that are highly soluble in deuterated chloroform (CDCl3), a common NMR solvent. Representing seven of the eleven genera of the family, the Pinaceae test samples were shown to display distinctiveness in their one- and two-dimensional proton spectra. The 1H-NMR technique was found to be a sufficient means of identification at the familial and generic levels. Moreover, a particular set of one-dimensional traits and eleven, two-dimensional cross-peaks were found to typify the family Pinaceae, setting it apart from other families within Plantae. Thus, both one- and two-dimensional proton spectra can distinguish among test samples at the generic level. These results highlight the power of the 1H-NMR technique and offer many practical applications in archaeology and botany, such as creating a more complete description of primitive economic activity from resins at dig sites or confirming the taxonomy of a contested plant species.

title: Improved Wastewater Treatment in Portobelo, Panama
abstract: The Northwestern University chapter of Engineers for a Sustainable World (ESW-NU) is an interdisciplinary student group focused on the challenges of long-term, sustainable development. Following a scoping trip to Panama in December 2005, ESW-NU began collaborating with the Panamanian NGO Foundation of Support for Social Development on an engineering research project to address the problem of raw sewage running through the town of Portobelo. The raw sewage endangers a historical monument, detracts from tourism, and threatens public health. In winter 2005 under the design course IDEA 298, four students researched the best way to improve the receiving water stream quality by treatment schemes that use aerobic or anaerobic process units with various post-treatment solids capture processes. Several treatment alternatives for the community were identified, and each was systematically evaluated based on feasibility, performance, cost, sustainability (20 year life-cycle), and aesthetics. The research process utilized existing research and design work, as well as feedback from professional engineers and wastewater treatment authorities. The principal research findings are documented in a preliminary engineering report, and recommend an aerated septic tank and slow sand filter as the treatment alternative. The project is an ongoing initiative, and research into methane recovery and sustainable sludge disposal options has continued into spring quarter 2006. The research findings provide crucial insight into the universal challenges of sustainable development, as well as innovative and efficient means of wastewater treatment subject to the needs and priorities of developing communities.

title: Neural Bases of Listening to Speech in Noise
abstract: Background noise occurs everywhere, and discerning speech in the context of a noisy environment is a part of daily life. An impaired ability to comprehend speech in noise is a common symptom of a variety of developmental disorders, particularly Auditory Processing Disorder, currently understood only from behavioral observations. These disorders are believed to arise from neuroanatomic and neurophysiologic abnormalities. However, it is not known how such abnormalities work to impair the neural processes of listening to speech in noise. Using a sparse sampling fMRI method, this study investigates the neural mechanisms involved in perceiving speech in noise. Subjects were asked to match auditorily presented words with three picture choices. The auditory stimuli were either heard in quiet or embedded in multi-talker babble noise, the MRI scanner noise absent in both conditions. Behaviorally, subjects were slower and less accurate in identifying words presented in noise. Comparison of hemodynamic responses associated with listening to the two types of stimuli revealed increased activation in a network of brain regions when subjects listened to speech in noise. The data suggest that an individual must exert greater cognitive and/or auditory effort when background auditory distractions are present than when they are absent. Identifying the neural components of listening to and comprehending speech in noise lends a much-needed empirical aspect to the current understanding of auditory processing. The continuation of this type of research will aid in further understanding and ultimately treating individuals who suffer from neurophysiologic disorders that impair their auditory comprehension.

title: Analysis of the 1.8 Å Resolution Crystal Structure of [2Fe-2S] Ferredoxin Domain of CopZ from Archaeoglobus fulgidus
abstract: Copper is an essential micronutrient to all known organisms, but can cause oxidative damage if left unchecked. To minimize this damage, chaperone proteins are responsible for the transport of copper from its entry at the membrane to its appropriate sites within the cell. CopZ, in concert with CopA and Cop B, is a putative chaperone for prokaryotic and archaeal copper homeostasis. Sequence analysis revealed that the hyperthermophile Archaeoglobus fulgidus possesses a unique member of the CopZ family with a CopZ-like domain located on the C-terminus and a 15 kDa previously uncharacterized N-terminus containing nine conserved cysteines. In this study, the structure of the N-terminus domain of CopZ was determined via X-ray crystallography to 1.8 Å resolution. The novel structure reveals the presence of a [2Fe-2S] cluster and mononuclear zinc site. These metal sites were further analyzed through various spectroscopic techniques. A small pocket of approximately 60 Å3 in close proximity to the Fe-S cluster suggests the domain may perform an unidentified catalytic function. Cysteine 118, the only conserved cysteines that is not bound to a metal, could be involved in this process. It was shown that the ferredoxin domain has the ability to reduce Cu2+ to Cu1+, although this may not be its physiological role. Finally, the results of this study provide a basis for elucidating copper homeostatic mechanisms.

title: Jazz, Blues and the Language of Harmony
abstract: In many ways, harmonic structure in music parallels syntactic structure in language (Sloboda, 1985). Recent studies (Besson et al., 1998; Koelsch et al., 2003; Patel et al., 1998) using this analogy provide interesting insights into harmony’s cognitive function. Results from these studies suggest the cognitive function of harmony and illustrate similarities underlying the processing of musical and linguistic structure. The current study probes the abstract, transformational, rule-based properties of harmony focusing on the importance of harmonic context and online processing capabilities within the harmonic context of the 12-bar blues form. Analyzing the harmonic content of songs in this style, we identified three important, defining events. From this statistical analysis, we developed a set of graded expectations characterizing the harmonic content at those locations and created stimuli with target chords that correspond to three categories (e.g., “expected”, “acceptable”, or “unacceptable”). To test the psychological relevance of these expectations, we asked participants for immediate and retroactive judgments of the chord’s appropriateness at that location, and participants used a button box to respond. We expect responses to reveal graded expectations following the target-chord categories (i.e., “expected”, “acceptable”, and “unacceptable”). Current pilot data anticipates a statistically significant difference between the response times for chords belonging to the three categories suggesting people accommodate certain chord substitutions while rejecting others, as they would allow certain substitutions in linguistic examples. These results provide insight into the nature of harmonic expectations and the cognitive relevance of musical structure while shedding light on the psychological similarities between musical and linguistic structure.

title: Shakira Body, Qur'anic Propriety: What Notions of Beauty and Respectability Tell Us About Cairo's Changing Gender Roles
abstract: In this study I draw on recent research on the anthropology of the body, which has become increasingly central to understanding the interaction between the individual and society. Specifically, I explore the ways in which young unmarried women in Cairo shape and present their bodies in pursuit of the twin goals of beauty and respectability in an era in which older sex roles are being overturned and new ones are still emerging. Egyptian women have recently entered the public realm en masse for education and salaried employment. In addition, they increasingly view new possibilities for the self through globalization in the form of movies, television, and magazines. The particular stratum of women I worked with, young unmarried women, is also breaking new ground as marriage ages are being pushed back and they find themselves in a demographic category without clear precedents or behavioral norms. Because none of the established image models are completely relevant in Cairo’s current circumstances, women pick and choose desirable elements from available models and improvise when necessary, with the outcomes of their individual attempts at image construction varying widely. The apparently trivial nature of these young women’s efforts at beautification obscures their broad implications. Intentionally or otherwise, the aggregate decisions of these young women about self-presentation have the potential to rework the rules of the cultural system in which they are embedded.

title: The Influence of Social Proof on Motivation to Pursue Relationships and the Perceived Value of a Potential Partner
abstract: Previous research in psychology has made extensive efforts to understand how various systems of motivation and value facilitate the development of intimate interactions and relationships. However, there has been a lack of empirical research regarding how the motivational mechanisms associated with social proof contribute to the pursuit of intimate relationships. This current study advances utilizes the behavioral model of social proof to further understand why people are motivated to engage in particular relationships and which factors contribute to the perception of a valuable partner. More specifically, in an effort to connect the different sources of human motivation, this investigation focused on how sexual differences in mate preference and individual differences in the Behavioral Inhibition and Approach Systems moderated the effects of social proof on the perceived value of a potential partner and the motivation to engage in a relationship. It was predicted that females and individuals with high levels of Behavioral Approach would be more sensitive to social proof when making value judgments of potential partners whereas males and individuals with high levels of Behavioral Inhibition would be unaffected. Through the assessments of 99 university students, Behavioral Inhibition and Behavioral Approach sensitivity did not moderate the effects of social proof. Sexual differences remained a moderating variable, as females were influenced by social proof when making value judgments regarding willingness to date and talk to a potential partner. These results suggest that females utilize implicit, socially reinforced cues, such as status, to assess the value of mates.

title: A Public-Domain Assessment of Music Preference as a Function of Personality and General Intelligence
abstract: Various studies within psychology have examined how the ubiquitous social phenomenon of music relates to aspects of personality and specific facets of intelligence. In particular, recent studies within personality psychology, such as Litle and Zuckerman (1986) and Rentfrow and Gosling (2003), have attempted to understand how musical preferences serve as manifestations of individual differences. Accordingly, the current study attempts to expand beyond previous research regarding the relationship between musical preferences and personality by modernizing as well as validating the Musical Preference Scale (Litle & Zuckerman, 1986) and the Short Test of Musical Preferences (Rentfrow & Gosling, 2003). Furthermore, extensive research has examined how the short-term effects of listening to music and the long-term effects of formal music training may enhance intelligence. However, there have been limited studies within psychology that analyze how personal preferences for particular genres directly relate to factors of general intelligence. Thus, this project examines the structural relationship between musical preferences and general intelligence by developing of an exploratory measurement of various cognitive abilities. Moreover, in order to conceptualize the underlying manifestations of musical preferences, the study utilizes the internet as a collaborative, data collection tool through the use of the Synthetic Aperture Personality Assessment (SAPA) technique, which builds large correlation matrices, in addition to the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP).

title: The Economics of Same Sex Couples
abstract: The family is a basic social institution, where individual members make choices in regard to allocation of time and human capital accumulation. These choices could be made based on members of the family’s relative comparative advantage. According to Becker (1981), if members of a household that share home and market production have different comparative advantages, then they would choose to allocate their time to household work and/or market work, based on their respective comparative advantage, to maximize the family’s utility. Lesbian, gay, and cohabitating heterosexual couples are differently constrained in choices than married heterosexual families due to institutional factors. In the absence of legal protection that marriage can offer, such individuals would be less likely to specialize in production based on comparative advantage and in particular, to risk doing all or a larger share of home production since in doing so, the individual forgoes market capital. This study uses data from the 2000 Census 5% Public-Use Microdata to examine how domestic partnership benefits offered by state and city governments to its employees act as a social safety net. If all the individual characteristics are held constant, cohabitating couples (including same sex and heterosexual couples) with domestic partnership benefits would be expected to act more like married couples. Hence, after controlling for all other productive characteristics, cohabitating individuals employed without such benefits would be expected to earn less since these individuals would be less likely to specialize in market production as defined in the Becker model of the family. Since household work data is not available in the Census data, the effect of domestic partnership benefits is measured through the individual’s hourly wages. Only full-time workers are included in the sample assuming that such members of the respective family unit are specializing in market work with their partner doing the same or larger share of home production, with relatively less market work.

title: Magnetoresistance of UPt3
abstract: Anomalous magnetic behavior near 5 K has been observed in some samples of the unconventional superconductor UPt3. An antiferromagnetic transition near 5 K was first observed in µSR and later confirmed by neutron scattering. However, a subsequent µSR study on a different sample showed no anomalies near 5 K, and the transition remains unseen in thermodynamic measurements. To explore this, we have performed measurements of the temperature dependence of the transverse magnetoresistance (up to 9 T) in bulk single crystals, with the field along both the easy and hard magnetization axes, the b- and c-axes, respectively. Our results with the current along the c-axis confirm previous results by Behnia et al (K. Behnia, O. Laborde, L. Taillefer, and J. Flouquet, Physica B, 165 & 166, 431, 1990). We observe an onset of a linear term in the c-axis transverse magnetoresistance with respect to field near 5.5 K, which provides evidence for bulk magnetic ordering.

title: Genetic Screens for the Identification of E3 Ubiquitin Ligases that Regulate LIN-12/Notch Activity in Caenorhabditis elegans
abstract: The Notch signaling pathway is highly conserved among diverse multicellular animals and mediates many cell-fate decisions during animal development. In Caenorhabditis elegans, LIN-12/Notch is important for normal vulval and gondanal development. It is well known that misregulation of Notch activity is linked to many developmental disorders and cancer. Recent findings suggest that more than 50% of human patients with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia have gain-of-function mutations in the Notch receptor. It is therefore important to identify key regulators of the canonical Notch signaling pathway. Here, we employed the C. elegans model system to identify specific E3 ubiquitin ligases (E3s), which are suggested to be involved in the ubiquitination of Notch and signaling attenuation. We performed an RNA-interference (RNAi) feeding screen in C. elegans to deplete individual putative E3s and scored for defects in vulval and skin cell development. From approximately one hundred E3s that we scored, we identified three E3s that caused enhanced skin developmental defects (molting defects). Our result suggests that these specific E3s genetically interact with the C. elegans LIN-12/Notch pathway and that these interactions may be conserved in higher organisms including humans.

title: Institutionalizing Unassimilation: Education Policy and Second-Generation North African Immigrants in France
abstract: Has the French universalist model of assimilation failed? With the increased salience of the “immigration problem” on a worldwide scale, debates have been raging about the merits of different forms of integration. France, as a self-consciously Universal and color-blind state, has been central to these debates. France’s “difficulty” integrating its North African immigrant population, it is argued, is more proof that in the battle between “multiculturalism” and “assimilation”, the latter has failed. I challenge this claim. I argue that the French model of assimilation has not failed in regard to North African immigrants, precisely because it was not applied to them. I show this by comparing the efforts to assimilate North African immigrants since the 1970s with the French peasants of the late 19th century. Analyzing education policy, the French government’s legal and institutional practices have diverged significantly in the two cases while publicly and rhetorically remaining the same. When these practices are placed in the context of the debates around family reunification, repatriation, limitations on access to citizenship, and deportation since the 1970s, one can begin to understand the French government’s role in creating a separate and increasingly expendable immigrant community- a community that contains immigrants and Frenchmen alike.

title: Same Boat, Different Waters: Explaining the Difficulties Facing the Hawaiian Sovereignty Movement
abstract: The success of the African-American Civil Rights Movement (CRM) opened the door for other rights-based movements that hoped to emulate its success. One such movement, the Hawaiian Sovereignty Movement (HSM), has imitated the non-violent tactics of the Civil Rights Movement toward the end of restoring sovereignty to Native Hawaiians. Four factors have kept the HSM's similar tactics from achieving comparable legislative success. First, while both movements experienced infighting, competing definitions of the word “sovereignty” fractured the goals of the HSM from the beginning, hampering legislative agreement. By contrast the CRM’s main schism, over the issue of “black power” separation, came only after it had realized key legislative victories. Second, the CRM received comparatively more material support, in large part because “black” was easily defined, allowing every potential black participant to benefit from the movement’s success. Within the HSM, though, different definitions of who is “Hawaiian” create potential winners and losers within the native population, to say nothing of those outside of it. Obtaining support is thus made more difficult. Third, the contrast between the CRM’s peaceful action and segregationists’ violent responses earned black American protesters broad sympathy. The opponents of the HSM are instead taking a legal approach to defeat it, making the struggle more technocratic and less politically salient. Fourth, the CRM could build upon a pre-existing network (black churches), which provided roster lists, meeting space, and Sunday sermons, which could mobilize the population. The HSM, by contrast, does not have a prior network to aid in mobilization, and thus does not have the benefits (listed above) that a church or university network could provide. In examining these four crucial differences, this thesis uses the Hawaiian Sovereignty Movement to further discussion of the reasons why some social movements succeed and others fail.

title: Solid Phase Synthesis of N-Methylsansalvamide A Analogues
abstract: N-Methylsansalvamide A is a natural product that was isolated from a marine microorganism in the Bahamas in 1999. The compound showed cell toxicity activity against the National Cancer Institute’s 60-cell line during preliminary tests, which pointed to the possibility of its use as an antitumor drug. A catalogue of 12 N-methylsansalvamide A analogues was then created in an attempt to find a more potent chemical. These analogues varied form the natural product in that an oxygen atom was replaced with a nitrogen atom, and as a whole the analogues showed decreased activity from the initial compound. The goal of this research is then to synthesize a new catalogue of compounds that retain the oxygen atom found in the natural product, while varying the functionality of the amino acids that constitute the compound. A number of new analogues have been synthesized and will be tested for anticancer properties while the rest of the catalogue is being created. The future of this project will then be to design new analogues, using non-natural amino acids, based upon the results of these tests, with the ultimate goal of discovering a potent drug that is also biologically safe for the human body.

title: The Metra as a Model of Group Homogeneity and Social Distance in Public Interaction
abstract: The research applies theories of social interaction in an attempt to bridge the gap between what we know about the unequal transit opportunities for minorities and what we need to know about the interaction patterns between people of different race and gender onboard public transit. This study of interaction on the Metra train consisted of observing the passengers for a month, performing a statistical test on the seat-pairs generated, and conducting interviews to uncover the rationale behind their seat selection. The findings show that the frequency of individuals who paired up with someone of the same gender and race is significantly different from the expected number of pairs that would have been generated randomly. This is consistent with Bruce Mayhew’s study of homogeneity in group formation and further supports Bogardus’s social distance studies. By selecting to sit with someone of the same race and gender, the passengers revealed a preference for a homogeneous social environment. Moreover, the interviewees’ adamant denial of race as a significant factor in seat selection also mimics the more recent findings of Christopher Donoghue and Vincent N. Parrillo, who updated the Bogardus study in 2001. This paper reveals both the passengers’ cognizance of the people surrounding them and their denial of this very fact. The study emphasizes the strength of group homogeneity as well as the persistence of social distance in public interaction, both of which highlight the troubling state of race relations today.

title: The Associations of Agreeableness and Dominance with Attractiveness to Potential Romantic Partners in a Speed-Dating Event
abstract: “Neither men nor women prefer all members of the opposite sex equally” (Buss & Barnes, 1986). Research into what causes one person to become romantically interested in another to the exclusion of many fascinates academics and non-academics alike. In the current project we studied the impacts of agreeableness (friendly and responsive qualities) and dominance (confident and ambitious qualities) on romantic attraction using data collected in a speed-dating event at Northwestern University. Participants completed 4-minute speed-dates with 11 to 13 people. Each participant rated his or her speed-dating partners individually on several measures both during and following the event. Each participant’s final score for a measure was the average of 11 to 13 scores given to that participant by other participants. Collecting ratings made by 11 to 13 participants for each individual participant in many measures enabled us to calculate consensus data for each participant in several dimensions. We measured initial romantic attraction through items that asked participants to rate each of their speed-dating partners in measures of romantic interest, perceived physical attractiveness, and interest in further interaction. Our project focused on both men and women’s preferences. Data revealed that women were more attracted to both men who were more agreeable and men who were more dominant. Men, too, were more attracted to more agreeable and more dominant partners, but a woman’s agreeableness was a more important predictor of men’s attraction to her to the degree that she was especially dominant.

title: The Piquetero Effect: Examining the Argentine Government's Response to the Piquetero Movement
abstract: Beginning in the late 1990s, large groups of unemployed workers in Argentina called piqueteros began illegally protesting their precarious situation, hoping for some combination of employment and social benefits. This paper seeks to understand how and why long-standing leaders of the current Argentine political establishment embraced the piqueteros. Through strategic cooptation, President Néstor Kirchner successfully has managed the piqueteros by using them as his own political shock troops to accomplish both his objectives as President and as a party politician. Kirchner's strategy is congruent with historical Peronist tendencies of absorbing new social actors, supporting Peronist scholar Steven Levitsky's belief that the party's flexibility allows it to adapt to changes in the political environment. However, whereas Levitsky predicts that reliance on machine politics will weaken the party, Kirchner's strategy has increased Peronist hegemony, thereby adversely affecting the quality of Argentine democracy.

title: Multiplying, Splitting, Connecting: The Self in the Fictions of Katherine Mansfield
abstract: Though she is generally considered a Modernist British writer, in many ways such a label does not suit Katherine Mansfield (1888-1923). Born in New Zealand, Mansfield moved to London only in her late teens, and even then spent large portions of her life abroad. More significantly, the Modernist tenets that were beginning to take hold of art in Europe did not always appeal to her. In the research, I investigated Mansfield’s short stories to determine accurately her relationship with Modernism. I closely examined her treatment of self and identity within her fictions, using her letters and notebooks as well as critical studies on her work as secondary resources. Overall, I found Mansfield’s literature to contain two rather distinct notions of self. Many of her works suggest that identity is split between a false outer self that is a product of social expectations, including gender and sexual norms, and an inner, true self. These instances correspond with earlier, nineteenth century ideas of the split self a la Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. However, several of her stories present characters who possess multiple identities, who wear mask after artificial mask. This concept of multiple identity is generally associated with Modernism. I thus determined that Mansfield sits at a liminal position between Modernism and earlier artistic movements. While her regular use of a split self suggests that she never wholly embraced all Modernist tenets, Mansfield’s early experimentation with the multiple self nonetheless secures her fictions as foundational forerunners to the genre.

title: Dating Christians: Muslim and Jewish Young Adults’ Experiences with Interfaith Relationships
abstract: While interfaith relationships have been fairly common among American Jews, especially those who are Reform or Conservative, since the latter part of the 1990s, they are relatively new and increasingly frequent among American Muslims. This research looks at the various challenges, benefits and themes found for Jewish and Muslim individuals who have dated Christians. In-depth interviews were conducted with eight Muslim and eight Jewish young adults (19-22 years of age) in the Chicago area. The interview explored religious and cultural identity, dating history, family relationships, benefits and challenges of interfaith dating, gender roles, and future plans. Although Jewish and Muslim participants described similar challenges, benefits, and identity formation issues, half of the Muslim participants shared stories regarding the stress of keeping their interfaith relationships hidden from their families. Muslim participants were also more likely to be first generation Americans, adding interesting themes about the intersections of faith and culture. Significant gender differences emerged based upon the religious traditions’ history of descent: more challenges were noted for Jewish men in matrilineal Judaism and for Muslim women in patrilineal Islam. This study has implications for understanding young adults’ identity development in this multicultural society, as interfaith relationships as well as non-Christian religions continue to grow in size.

title: Marital Conflict’s Effects on Child’s Peer Relationship by Gender
abstract: With the rise in divorce, there has been an increasing interest in the effects marital conflict has on children. Most studies have found support for the association between marital conflict and child maladjustment. Among the maladjustments found are problematic peer relationships. In addition, there is some evidence indicating gender differences in the reaction to marital conflict, with boys displaying externalizing problems and girls displaying internalizing problems. The reason for these differences may have to do with their different perceptions of marital conflict, with boys seeing marital conflict as a threat and girls seeing marital conflict as their fault. Differing emotional dispositions would seem to account for this difference, with an angry disposition leading to aggressive behavior and a sad disposition leading to reclusive behavior. In this study, to gain further understanding of marital conflict’s effects on the child’s peer relationships, I took three measures. Marital conflict was measured through a validated questionnaire of relationship conflict (Dyadic Adjustment Scale). Behavior in peer relationships was measured by combining items from two validated questionnaires to form an aggression scale and reclusion scale (Child Behavior Checklist and Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation). Finally, emotional disposition was measured through affect coding of a series of ten emotion-eliciting episodes (Lab-TAB). Sadness and anger scores are of particular interest as they may be connected with feelings of blame and threat, respectively.

title: The Devil in the Details: Sin, Damnation and Hell in Medieval Consciousness
abstract: Joan of Arc has been studied as a historical figure often and from many perspectives, but one aspect of her life that has not often been considered is the manner in which her story has been less than impartially told by important commentators. My research considered her 15th-century theological defense by University of Paris chancellor Jean Gerson, and a Third Republic biography written by Anatole France. In both cases, I encountered what I call "generous revisionism." Her story was told with a specific, intellectually dishonest goal in mind: Gerson had long opposed affective feminine spirituality, but he excused it in Joan of Arc's case because she served a useful political goal during the Hundred Years' War; and France gave her a revisionist personal history characterized by clerical and monarchical manipulation, in order to reclaim her as a secular national symbol for the Third Republic. These results were at cross purposes with conventional beliefs about the intellectual practice of these two men, as Gerson has the reputation of a consistently archconservative theologian, and France, an ardent secularist, set out to write a faithful biography yet rewrote the fundamental details of Joan of Arc's life to suit his own purposes. Joan of Arc was more complex, and more her own person, than she appears in either depiction.

title: Harmony (Film Cycle #1)
abstract: Harmony (Film Cycle #1), originally an investigation into the relationship between physics and metaphysics, became a study in unique methods of using digital video technology to encode analog physical processes. The first film of the cycle, ROYGBIV, is mathematically modeled on a geometric sequence, the wavelength values of the visible color spectrum, and corresponding digital RGB values. Conceptually, it is based on the process of redshifting and a hypothetical temporal model of the universe. DVI, the second film, demonstrates the decay in resolution that results from using digital means to encode analog rephotography. While it too has a unifying mathematical macrostructure, there are also unruly internal microrhythms based on the acoustic content of the manipulated video sample. The third film in the cycle, A Joke to Go Out On, uses numerical cryptography and the Dewey Decimal system to encode excerpts from my own writings on humor theory. The cycle is still being revised, with a projected completion date of summer 2006.

title: The Influence of Gesture on Children’s Spatial Representation
abstract: Spatial reasoning is fundamentally important to human survival and learning. While adults are capable of walking around a new city and readily knowing the relations between various neighborhoods and landmarks, children have more difficulty integrating information about spaces. It is unclear how this ability to integrate spatial information increases developmentally. Spatial information is often relational; because relations are often difficult to communicate in speech, gestures may be useful for expressing relationships between objects in space. Gestures may also affect the ways in which people think about space. This could be particularly helpful for children attempting to integrate spatial information. In our study, 8- and 10-year-old children navigate a space with six tall boxes, each containing a toy animal, and learn which animal “lives” in each box. They are then taken into a nearby room and asked to describe the space to a parent. Children are finally asked to make a model of the room using six squares with pictures of each animal. Their responses were videotaped for later review. Results have shown that eight-year-old children do not appear to integrate spatial information, nor employ gesture when talking about a space. Ten-year-olds are more likely to produce gestures during spatial descriptions and perform better on the model. In a follow-up study, 8-year-olds who are encouraged to gesture show improvements in the model performance. There appears to be a developmental progression in gesture production and spatial integration. Further research investigates the development of spatial reasoning and gesture in children with learning disabilities.

title: A Nation of Babbitts: French Readings of American Literature in the Interwar Years
abstract: Between the early 1920s and the mid-1930s, articles that heralded the arrival of a “new” American literature began to appear in French journals. Written by prominent French intellectuals, these commentaries almost uniformly concluded that certain works within the American realist school of fiction accurately depicted contemporary American life. They further insisted that such authors represented hope for the successful subversion of their country’s otherwise intellectually empty mass culture. Such concerns revealed an anxiety on the part of French observers over American post-World War I power, its seemingly unmitigated industrial expansion, and its financial hegemony. During this period, a number of books in which French intellectuals expressed their concerns over the postwar Franco-American relationship also appeared. Those who wrote about American literature synthesized the concerns of these books with their readings of the novels. In particular, their embrace of Sinclair Lewis’s Babbitt evidenced a predisposition to viewing American realist fiction as a mirror of the reality in the United States. In identifying realist novels’ pessimism about the future of their country, interpreting them as representative of American life, and linking their creation to novelists’ expatriation to France and their reliance on French literary traditions, intellectuals asserted France’s cultural power at a time of growing anxiety over American political and economic power. In so doing, intellectuals revealed their own fears of American modernization and what it portended for French society even as they engaged to an increasing degree with American cultural products.

title: On Government Borrowing and the US Federal Budget Deficit
abstract: There is a need to address the faults that surround media and outspoken critics who consider the United States’ current fiscal woes unmatched by previous generations.’ Massive government borrowing during World War II and, again, during the Reagan Administration has yielded various interpretations from economists on what deficit levels are optimal as well as achievable for the United States. This paper focuses on the publications and commentaries of economists from the 1980s and 1990s, including James D. Hamilton, Marjorie A. Flavin, Robert Eisner, Alan J. Auerbach, Jagadeesh Gokhale, Laurence Kotlikoff, Douglas Elmendorf and George Mankiw. In particular, an investigation is made into the borrowing constraint of the federal government and its accounting standards, and the effects a surge in borrowing has on the nation’s future prosperity. An understanding of the previous decades approach to fiscal policy will provide a lead-in to today’s dilemmas and shed light on how to plan for the future. This paper will show, as economists suggest, that the budget deficits in 2005 and 2006 do lie within historical ranges and are sustainable going forward. In contrast, these same models in economics clarify why the entitlement spending programs pose a dangerous threat to the future of the United States.

title: Regulation of chondrogenesis by GPI-linked proteins
abstract: The growth of cartilage is regulated by the growth plate chondrocytes. The growth plate consists of distinct zones of differentiated chondrocytes. During bone growth, cells from the resting zone are progressively recruited to the proliferative zone. In the proliferative zone, the cell cycle is upregulated, resulting in a rapid increase in the number of chondrocytes. As the cartilage grows, cells progressively exit the proliferative zone, hypertrophy and die (hypertrophy zone), and are subsequently replaced by bone. To understand the regulation of bone growth, we analyzed the Piga mutant mouse, in which all GPI-linked cell surface proteins were knocked out, resulting in short-limbed mice. Histological analysis failed to detect organized cells consistent with proliferative chondrocytes in Piga mutant mice. However, studies of cell proliferation and gene expression suggest that the disordered cells are proliferative chondrocytes. These data suggest that GPI-linked proteins are important determinants of chondrocyte morphology.

title: Helping Hands: How Hand Gestures May Facilitate Spatial Thinking in Adults
abstract: When people describe space, such as when giving directions, they very often move their hands. Although it is clear that these spontaneous movements would benefit a listener, we wonder whether the production of gesture also benefits the speaker. The current research explored whether people who gesture will have an easier time learning about a new environment. Participants learned the locations of six boxes in a room, each containing a different toy animal, either by exploring the room (study 1), or by hearing a description of it (study 2). After walking through the room, participants in study 1 were asked to describe the space and construct a model of it. Most adults used gesture to communicate spatial information and performed well on the model construction. In order to gain more information about these findings, some adults were instructed to keep their hands on a clipboard while giving their description. These adults, who could not use their hands, performed significantly worse on the model task (p < .05). Study 2 results were consistent with these observations. Adults who produced more hand movements also tended to perform better on the construction task. The notion that hand movements may actually help people think should not be overlooked. Perhaps if people are encouraged use their hands frequently, they will have an easier time acquiring spatial information

title: The 'Malaria Metaphor' in Victorian and Edwardian Britain
abstract: At the beginning of the 20th century, the British Empire was near the height of its power. Yet many of those invested in empire, including scientists studying tropical disease, felt they were not receiving sufficient resources to accomplish their goals. Among these was the eradication of malaria, which these scientists portrayed as a barrier to social and economic “development”. Malaria interested these scientists for its history in limiting European expansion, but also for its metaphorical significance as a disease of “backwards” peoples and blighted places. Even after Ronald Ross showed that malaria was transmitted by mosquitoes, not marshes or immorality, the association between malaria and “development” remained. Ross, like other scientists, felt that Britain’s classically-educated elites were not paying enough attention to factors like disease in the rise and fall of nations — including their own. Motivated by this situation, he encouraged classicists to study the influence of malaria in the history of ancient Greece and Rome. The resulting scholarship reveals much about the rhetoric of science and empire in Edwardian Britain. Writers like Ross and W. H. S. Jones used the “malaria metaphor” to advance their own views about the sort of institutional changes Britain would need to remain an international leader. Yet rhetoric cuts both ways, as these documents also reveal the consequences of applying imperial thought-processes to the metropole. The result is an interesting fragment of intellectual history that can show us how we have changed since the days of empire, and how we have not.

title: Female Cancer Survivors and Infertility: Moving Fertility Preservation from Bench to Bedside
abstract: Thirty years of advancements in cancer treatment have led to unprecedented survival rates. However, life-preserving treatments can cause chronic medical problems, including infertility, which cannot be easily addressed post-treatment. For a number of years, men have been able to preserve their fertility through semen cryopreservation, but women lack an equivalent option. While a woman’s ovary can be cryopreserved before treatment, difficulties in maturing eggs in vitro have prevented the establishment of egg banks. At Northwestern University, a three-dimensional culture system has been developed to mature eggs in vitro, providing the foundation for a method to preserve female fertility. Questions remain regarding the translation of these developments into clinical practice. In order to fill this gap, my project addressed two questions: 1) can eggs be grown in vitro after cryopreservation, a necessary step in fertility preservation?; and 2) what are the opinions of survivors and their families regarding fertility preservation for young women? To answer the first question, I found that eggs can be isolated from cyropreserved mice ovaries, cultured in a 3D system and matured normally. The second question was answered through focus groups with childhood cancer survivors and their parents. Participants reported that they would have seriously considered fertility preservation if it had been an option and believed that it should be presented to all patients, regardless of age. My work unities basic and social sciences within the emerging field of oncofertility and can be applied to fertility preservation options for women.

title: The Relationship between Visual Attention Abilities and Personality
abstract: The ability of the mind to selectively attend to different items in the environment has been a major topic of research. Modern research utilizing brain imaging technology has revealed that attention is not a single process, but rather a number of independent abilities localized in different brain regions. This research examined systematic individual differences in various attention abilities to elucidate relationships among the underlying mechanisms. A computerized attention battery was constructed to characterize each individual’s “attention profile.” For example, a person might be superior at focusing attention, average at switching attention, and inferior at distributing attention with the overall pattern characterizing the person’s attention profile. Regression analyses suggest that the abilities to focus and distribute attention are mediated by opponent mechanisms, meaning individuals superior at focusing, tend to be inferior at distributing. It was also found that the attention mechanisms segregate into two broad categories, those that promote spatial and temporal attention abilities and those that promote global and object-based attention abilities. Further examination of individuals’ attention profiles compared with their scores on a five-factor personality inventory showed multiple relations between attention and personality. Most notably, individuals high in “Neuroticism” tended to be inferior at shifting attention, whereas individuals high in “Openness to Experience” tended to perform better at shifting tasks. Besides these stable individual differences in attention profiles, it was also found that one’s attentional state fluctuates over time between shifting and focusing modes. Overall, these findings help to explain why individuals attend to and perceive the world differently.

title: Colocalization of Estrogen Receptors and Temperature Sensitive Ion Channels in the Mouse Brain: Implications for the Mechanism of Hot Flashes
abstract: The hot flash, an abrupt sensation of heat, is the most common medical complaint among peri- and post-menopausal women. Understood as caused by a disturbance of normal thermoregulation, hot flashes are characterized by vasodilation, increased heart rate, and perspiration. The underlying physiological mechanism remains unknown. The occurrence of the hot flashes is correlated with lowered levels of circulating estrogen, and it is hypothesized that estrogen affects thermoregulation via control of temperature sensitive ion channels of neurons in the hypothalamus and particularly in the preoptic area. Of particular focus in this study is the two-pore-domain potassium ion channel TREK-1, which shows high levels of expression in the preoptic area. Adult female were ovariectomized and half received subcutaneous implantation of a capsule containing estradiol and half received a capsule containing adhesive only. Double-label immunohistochemistry (IHC) was performed on perfused brains to identify regions in which there is co-localization of estrogen receptor and the TREK-1 channel. Aim 1 tested the hypothesis that removal of estrogen alters thermoregulatory responses in mice, as it has been shown to do in rats. Aim 2 optimized IHC procedures. Aim 3 quantified co-localization of estrogen receptors (ERs α and/or β) with temperature sensitive ion channels in the mouse brain. The experiments provide clues to the relationships of estrogen, temperature sensitive ion channels, and thermoregulation as they apply to hot flashes.

title: An Exhibition Without an Equal: Circus Advertising and the Emergence of Mass Culture
abstract: By the 1880s, large circuses exposed audiences to the full gamut of advertising—broadsides, posters, newspaper ads, couriers, trading cards, programs, and the immense street parade—to create a common American cultural link across racial, class and age divisions through mass communication. National advertising visibility for the circus, as a traveling show, hinged in large part to the increasing railroad lines reaching into both rural and urban communities in the west unlike other entertainments—for instance, theaters and zoos had fixed locations. Extensive advertising campaigns of the large railroad circuses from the 1870s to the 1890s, led by newly mass-produced color posters, informed and reminded a national audience of a shared cultural tradition. The ubiquity of flashy posters placed in public spaces—appearing on town walls, chain-link fences, barns and abandoned buildings at a rate of 5,000 per town—fostered the trend of spectator culture. The advertising machine generated a unique cultural form and replaced the performance as the main event, made manifest when occasional brawls broke out between circus companies over advertisement space. After filtering through three lithograph poster archives and reading dozens of first-hand accounts from advertising agents and circus owners, along with ample secondary sources, I conclude that circus advertising served as the prototype of an emerging mass culture—the major exception in an era of cultural elitism—to be improved upon in time with radio programs, movie theaters and television. The existing body of work on the circus almost universally neglects my conclusions or offers only speculation, instead of academic attention, to the possibility of the circus as an emerging mass culture. Most secondary sources present concise histories of circus advertising or allude to its important reflection and representation of circus performances, but fail to explore the implications of advertising as establishing a common culture among a mass audience.

title: The Reverse Hand Orthosis
abstract: This device for use with physical therapy is designed to correct contractions of the hemi paretic hand and fingers, and wrist muscles. The device is generally a glove and incorporated exoskeleton, which consists of four components. The spring steel mechanism provides tensile force to keep the fingers in an open, relaxed position. The spring steel resists contractions of the fingers; as the finger bends further there is an increasing amount of resistant force. Forces are applied axially along both sides the metacarpal phalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints to minimize compressive force applied to each joint. A backbone prevents hyperextension of the fingers and a thermoplastic brace stabilizes the wrist in a fixed comfortable position. The glove includes a zipping mechanism that eases donning of the glove for its user. The user gains voluntary mobility of their hand that is normally restricted by involuntary contractions. Therefore, the newly designed glove and exoskeleton develop an opposing concept of the conventional hand orthosis, which restricts all movement of the hand, by being passive to a user’s voluntary motion, while actively applying a force that overcomes involuntary motion of the hemi paretic hand.

title: Marketing to the Latino Community of Chicago: Exploring Constructed Identity through Conflicting National and Local Images
abstract: The stated goal of advertising is to sell a product, but as any good account executive will tell you, the real goal is to sell a cultural identity that people want to consume. The projection of cultural symbols and images is necessary to persuade audiences to use and purchase the product in question. Often, people remember commercials they view without remembering the marketed product. The products appearing in advertisements are an important piece of the puzzle of the cultural identity being marketed. However, the key to understanding the projected cultural identity of these advertisements lies in using more probing questions to unearth idealized images of people, social relationships and the quality of those relationships as portrayed in commercials. In a society strongly attached to media and consumption the images portrayed are incredibly important in determining an identity. Advertisements for all social and economic groups project an image that people want to consume so that they can possess a certain identity. Analyzing television commercials that appear on the Chicago Univision station and outdoor advertisements in Rogers Park (a northeast community of Chicago), I map out the, at times conflicting, projected identity of Latinos in Chicago: a market targeted because of its’ potential buying power, and yet a community/population that is still struggling for financial, political and social stability. These contradictions are most clearly viewed in the differences between national images and the local images of Chicago-area Latinos. I also explore the tensions between economic realities and idealized situations (which are strongly linked to gender roles) and the real vs. assumed identity of U.S. Latinos.

title: Italia Restituta: Trajan’s Ideological Contributions to the Politics of Roman Road Building
abstract: The project examines the relationship between road building and hegemonic ideology by identifying the significance of the construction of the Via Traiana, a Roman road was built in the early second century CE by the Emperor Trajan (98 C.E.-117 C.E.). My research contextualizes the road within the historical tradition of Roman road building. In December 2005, I went to Italy to travel along the route of the Via Traiana to study the primary artifacts associated with its construction. Field research included visiting the archaeological sites of ancient towns connected by the road, viewing art and architecture erected in its commemoration, and taking photographs for future reference and analysis. Following the field study, I have concluded that, unlike most other Roman roads, the Via Traiana was not constructed for the primary purpose of transporting armies, but rather to function as a symbol of Trajan’s political ideology of Italia Restituta, or “Italy Restored,” through its commemoration of specific Trajanic policies and reforms. In fact, the road was intended to be viewed in conjunction with, and even as a monument to Trajan’s reforms of Rome’s military, economic, judicial and administrative systems. Ultimately, the road enabled Trajan to present himself as a restorer of the Empire as it was before the period of civil unrest preceding his reign, when in fact he was attempting to alter Rome’s hegemonic infrastructure. In the process, Trajan not only drew upon a precedent of utilizing road building for political self-furtherance, but also through the road project uniquely legitimized his widespread changes to the Empire.

title: The Perfect Public Defense: Does it Exist?
abstract: In 1963, the Supreme Court in Gideon v. Wainwright ruled that every indigent defendant should be guaranteed the right to counsel regardless of the crime. A decision one hailed as revolutionary within political, legal and social worlds has now lost its beauty due to the current state of many public defense systems across the country. The idealistic notion of public defense has been crushed under the weight of heavy caseloads, lack of attorney training, and budget cuts. In addition to these problems, tougher sentencing guidelines and more stringent laws have further exacerbated the need for reform. Through research for the project, I found that a statewide pubic defense system can be implemented at little increased cost to the state. By developing certification standards, establishing more oversight, and instituting more attorney support, public defenders can be much more adept at handling their caseloads. Every state has a different public defense model. Some states such as New York rely on a number of legal organizations and private attorneys to handle public defense cases. Other states, such as Georgia, now rely on a statewide agency to oversee public defense. This agency, the Georgia Public Defender Standards Council (GPDSC), has managed to implement successfully many of the reforms I have listed with little or no cost to the state. I have used the GPDSC as support for my claim that a statewide system is the most effective way to increase the efficiency and quality of public defense. The implementation of the GPDSC will provide other states with a model to reform their own public defense systems. This research will contribute to the scholarly literature on law and public defense by illustrating that complacency within the area of public defense will cause many systems nationwide to eventually collapse.

title: Tetrathiomolybdate and its Interaction with Cu(I)-Proteins: Fighting Cancer by Disrupting the Angiogenic Process
abstract: Angiogenesis is the process of blood vessel growth and proliferation. In order for a tumor to exceed a critical size of 2mm, angiogenesis must be stimulated to divert nutrients to feed a tumor's rapid growth. Thus, angiogenesis is an important target in cancer treatment. It is mediated by many different angiogenic promoters that influence the migration, proliferation, and differentiation of cells, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF). Many of these angiogenic factors appear to be dependent on normal levels of copper (Cu). Lowering copper levels moderately with a drug called tetrathiomolybdate (TM) produces strong antiangiogenesis and potential anticancer effects. Our goal is to discover the precise mechanism by which TM binds copper in the body. To study this unknown mechanism, we are using coordination model studies of Cu chaperones, such as Cu(I)Atx1 and Wilson’s Domain 5, with TM. These TM-Cu-chaperone complexes could provide a model for the possible Cu-TM interactions in angiogenic promoters. Our studies will also show if TM is binding to intra or extracellular copper proteins, or both and determine how strong of an affinity it has for copper. Data from EXAFS and FPLC gel filtration as well as the shapes of the faces of the crystals formed when TM reacted with Cu(I)Atx1 all suggest that the TM is forming a trimer complex with Cu(I)Atx1. We will only know for certain once we have resolved the crystal structure. To date, we have obtained diffraction resolutions of up to 1.8 Å on the crystals formed, but have not been able to resolve this data.

title: Analysis of Proteasome-mediated Protein Degradation from Internal Initiation Sites
abstract: Regulated protein degradation is an essential cellular process that controls pathways, such as the cell cycle, signal transduction, gene expression, and the immune response. In eukaryotes, regulated degradation of proteins is accomplished by the proteasome, a multi-subunit, barrel-shaped complex. The proteasome particle encloses the active sites of proteolysis that are accessible through narrow entrances at either end of the cylindrical structure. Folded substrates are unraveled by the proteasome and translocated through the central channel to the proteolytic sites. Substrates are specifically targeted to the proteasome by multiple covalent addition of a small protein called ubiquitin on their side chain lysine residues. Efficient degradation by the proteasome also requires an unstructured or disordered region in the substrate protein. This unstructured region engages the proteasome unfolding machinery and is the site of degradation initiation in the substrate. The initiation site can be located at the N or C terminus or in the middle of the protein. Degradation of proteins from an unstructured region in the middle implies that the region must loop into the proteasome, and effectively two polypeptide chains enter at the same time. I have developed a model substrate to further investigate how the proteasomal machinery unfolds and degrades these types of substrates. Results indicate that the two polypeptides generated from cleavage at an internal initiation site are not degraded simultaneously. I found that the yeast proteasome degrades the polypeptide preceding the initiation site effectively, whereas the polypeptide following the initiation site is degraded more slowly. Experiments are underway to understand the basis of the observed disparity.

title: Model Catalytic Oxide Surfaces: a Study of LaAlO3 Surface
abstract: Insight into the nature of surfaces and the processes that occur on them is of great importance in the study of catalysis. For example, approximately 50% of the total municipal solid waste generated annually in the United States is attributed to the chemical industry in the form of by-product waste. This amounts to more than 100 million tons annually. The goal of this research is to improve the activity and selectivity of catalytic oxidation by identifying catalytically active sites and reaction pathways through atomic scale structure analysis. It is these important prerequisites that will make the engineering of new and more efficient materials possible. The ramifications of the research may result in positive environmental impacts on various industrial activities, including chemical production and fossil fuel consumption for energy generation. While much work has been done on understanding the atomic structure of surfaces on metals, knowledge of transition metal oxide surfaces is minimal. In this poster, we report the discovery of the [equation]R26.6° reconstruction on the LaAlO3 [equation] surface. The approach we take is to stabilize the reconstruction through air anneal treatments and characterize the surface with transmission electron microscopy. Structure solution analysis is performed with Electron Direct Methods on this model perovskite material. We show that the surface exhibits flat [equation] facets and subsurface voids. Our results indicate that simple structural ordering is responsible for the two observed reconstruction domains. We also discuss possible mechanisms for surface stabilization that may be extended to other perovskite materials.

title: Bridge or Barrier?: Judaism's Role in the Acculturation Process of Russian Jews in the United States
abstract: Although various studies across the social sciences have been conducted concerning the psychological battles of identity negotiation and acculturation for immigrants to the United States, few have looked in particular at the post-Soviet immigrant culture of the past decade. This culture is unique because of the inherent similarity it shares with the previously acculturated American Ashkenazi (Eastern European) Jews. The issue analyzed in the two phases of this research is the process of acculturation through the lens of recent Russian-Jewish immigrants to the United States. Two matched sets of participants (recent Russian-Jewish immigrants and third generation and later American Jews) were surveyed regarding their three identities – American, Russian/Eastern European, and Jewish – and measures examined the motivation behind adopting one identity versus another and the values placed upon the different identities. Statistically significant differences between the two groups on many of the measures revealed that while American Jews believe that their Judaism separates them from mainstream America, the post-Soviet Russian Jews are actually employing Judaism as their mechanism for enhanced assimilation, for the strength of their Jewish identity causes them to place less distance between their American and Russian identities. Thus, while American Jews have assimilated to such a degree that emphasizing their Judaism only serves to make them stand out as “different” from the rest and perhaps even prohibits them from merging completely with the mainstream identity, the recent immigrants use their Judaism as a stepping stone, or a bridge, to resemble more adequately the American social identity.

title: The Thirty Years War in Twentieth-Century Opera and Literature
abstract: This project investigates how operatic and literary works may be used to construct both political and historical realities. Specifically, I look at the way the seventeenth-century Thirty Years War was used as a topic and as a metaphor for the two World Wars in twentieth-century German literature and opera. The main examples are works by Bertolt Brecht (Mother Courage) and Günter Grass (Meeting in Telgte) in the field of literature, and operas by Richard Strauss (Friedenstag) and Karl Amadeus Hartmann (Simplicius Simplicissimus), the latter based on the seventeenth-century piece by Grimmelshausen. Written largely in response to the 1939 Hitler-Stalin Pact, Brecht uses the historical subject as a means of critically distancing the observer from what he perceives to be the National Socialist triangle of war/religion/capitalism as well as to construct a Marxist class-consciousness. Published in 1979, Grass’s short novel is a critical assessment of the Group 47 (a literary group that first met in 1947 to discuss the reconstruction of the German language and cultural identity) and its function in post-World-War II Germany; it also reflects Grass’s own political involvement and calls the reader to an active questioning of contemporary events. Strauss wrote his Friedenstag opera following his dismissal as president of the National Socialist Reichsmusikkammer; and, the 1938 premiere’s place within Munich party events may be interpreted as a wish to reconcile with party politics and aesthetics, have his works performed in opera houses again, and to protect his family. Hartmann’s 1934 opera utilizes both the historical text and war as a vehicle for socialist assertions and a Brecht-like aesthetic; further, the piece exemplifies the much debated notion of inner emigration, a term denoting those artists who remained in Third Reich Germany but did not publish due to political or artistic convictions. These examples point to a history that is recreated with each interpretation. Further, they point to the permeable boundary between cultural and political worlds.

title: Expertise Effects on Sorting Strategies of Causal Phenomena
abstract: Psychologists study categorization, the process of grouping some concepts and distinguishing others, in order to understand how people view concepts as similar or different. To the extent that they are similar (e.g. a lemon and a pomelo) people make generalizations and inferences from one concept to another (a pomelo is similar to a lemon, a citrus fruit, and since citrus fruits grow on trees, pomelos probably grow on trees). Research on categorization has mainly focused on entity categories (e.g. citrus fruits). The current study examines how people categorize abstract concepts, specifically, textual descriptions of real-world causal phenomena that vary along two dimensions: domain (e.g. economics) and causal structure (e.g. causal chain). The domain and causal structure dimensions represent two types of similarity. Descriptions in the same domain may share certain features (e.g. money in economics) whereas descriptions with the same causal structure share deep underlying relations (e.g. all causal chains have the form: a causes b which causes c). We compared novices (introductory psychology students) to experts (students in physics and an integrated science program)—students likely to have experience analyzing causal mechanisms. In a structured sorting task, experts sorted more cards into relational categories (matching an exemplar card by causal structure) than into domain categories. In contrast, novices sorted in the opposite pattern. Hierarchical cluster analysis was used to determine dominant sorting strategies of novices and experts. Latent Semantic Analysis, computer software that measures contextual relatedness of words and phrases, was used to explain anomalies in these strategies.

title: Transitive Noun Verb - 18 Months
abstract: Before they utter their first words, infants acquire the ability to process language and thought, making it essential to study infants at younger and younger ages. Previous studies have shown that specific expectations of nouns develop by the age of 14 months. Specifically, at this young age, infants are able to realize that novel nouns refer to object categories and not to salient properties. However, infants’ understanding of words from other lexical categories appears to emerge later. For example, previous research has shown that expectations about verbs develop by the age of 24 months, however no previous research has investigated if this crucial ability may develop even earlier. Since previous research had already demonstrated that 24-month-old subjects were able to understand that verbs refer to actions, the current study used a similar design to investigate whether 18-month-old subjects were also able to understand these verbs. Participants were shown a short video, consisting of a word-learning task designed to teach the subjects new, made-up words. The study consisted of two conditions: one to test infants’ knowledge of verbs and one to test their knowledge of nouns. Essentially, the toddlers were taught a new, made-up word as either a noun or a verb, and then asked to locate the object or action. Data were collected by recording the infants’ eye movements throughout the video to determine how much information they understood.

title: The Effects of Motivational States and Perspective Taking on Automatic and Controlled Prejudice toward Arabs
abstract: In the aftermath of 9/11 and the London subway bombings, the threat of terrorism has heightened people’s awareness of national and personal security. At the same time, these incidents may also have aroused people’s suspicion of Arabs, given the fact that certain members of this group have been associated with terrorism. Upon exposure to a person of Arab descent, it is possible that one may exhibit an automatic negative reaction stemming from a conditioned association between Arabs and threat. However, it is likely that controlled, rational thoughts also factor in when making judgments, which may render one’s initial fears irrational. This research examines different factors that may influence people’s use of stereotyping when making judgments about Arabs. For instance, does a heightened sense of anxiety intensify the use of negative cultural stereotypes? Furthermore, the effectiveness of an intervention strategy called perspective taking is examined. Perspective taking is a process whereby individuals actively attempt to understand another person’s point of view by imagining what they would feel like in the target’s position. This process may evoke feelings of empathy and a perception of similarity with the target, which can have important cognitive, emotional, and social implications. Perspective taking is examined as a potential strategy for decreasing people’s reliance on stereotypes when forming impressions of Arabs.

title: Freedom and Islam: A Case Study of Liberalism in Pakistan’s Islamist Political Parties
abstract: Is Islam anti-freedom? Since the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, the question of Islam’s compatibility with modernity and democracy has become vital. My research questions the widespread assumption that ‘Islam’ necessarily curbs liberty. Much of the Muslim world has adopted non-violent Islamism, which may be a source through which to challenge Islamism’s more radical, threatening manifestations. The United States’ efforts to fight terrorism as a short-term goal and spread liberalism as a long-term goal have clashed in Pakistan, a key strategic ally. Pakistan’s strengthened alliance with the United States and its commitment to fighting terrorism have strengthened the political and social popularity of oppositional Islamist parties, who tend to have ideological platforms that curb individual freedom. Why are there barriers to Pakistan’s Islamist parties adopting ideals that advocate women’s and minorities’ rights and generally a limited role of the ‘religious’ government in people’s personal affairs? Where does this lack of liberalism fall within the dialogue over such freedoms in the legacy of Islamic political thought? Aversion to freedom can be partly attributed to three intellectual barriers prevalent among Islamist parties in Pakistan, and which apply to Islamists in other parts of the world: intensifying anti-Americanism; abuse of the concept of God’s sovereignty as a justification for authoritarian leadership; and a misunderstanding of Islam’s normative position on personal freedom vis-à-vis obedience to God. This thesis analyzes these intellectual barriers and places them within the context of pro-liberal and anti-liberal strains in classical and contemporary Islamic political thought.

title: French Cultural Protectionism Goes Global: A Case Study of Audiovisual Quotas for Television in France
