abstract: Culture was once protected by geography, but today’s split-second communication devices allow cultural products to target a global audience. The idea of cultural imperialism, believed to be imposed by the United States, has threatened Europeans to the extent that they have taken active policy to embargo foreign media products. But France, more than any other European country, has enacted stricter national legislation in a drastic effort to protect its culture. France has championed the notion of cultural protectionism for several decades. The most recent debate occurred at the 2005 UNESCO General Conference Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions. This Convention enshrined the idea of a cultural exception to international trade agreements as a method of protecting local cultures from excessive outside influence. The present research centered on the question: What is the case in favor of cultural protectionism, and what role has France played in developing cultural policies? To answer this question, we pursue the following three goals: (1) understand the arguments made in the controversy over cultural diversity, primarily by exploring the economic and historical contexts on which these opinions are based; (2) support the claim that the French led the movement for cultural protectionism, as evidenced by their regulation of the television medium and the contested European quota system; and (3) demonstrate that the nationalist effort to protect and promote cultural industries has clearly now become an international concern, no longer limited to France and Francophone interests.

title: Determining Tumor Grade Non-invasively Using Quantification of Cerebral Blood Volume through Contrast Enhanced MRI
abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) tumor aggressiveness leads to neovascularity and a subsequent increase in cerebral blood volume (CBV) in the tumor region. Currently, relative CBV (rCBV) found using MRI can differentiate between stable and progressive tumors, but with high variability and overlap. The standard practice for tumor grading is resection, which is very invasive and is limited by tissue sampling error and the lack of a specific tumor marker. We are the first to develop a technique that can quantify CBV and thus vascular proliferation using MRI. We hypothesize that using this technique will lead to a more clear separation in tumor grading. A series of 14 patients scheduled for MRI before surgical resection of CNS tumors were studied. Dynamic susceptibility-weighted contrast-enhanced (DSC) MRI was used to quantify CBV. We compared two complementary quantification techniques: Gradient Recalled Echo (GE) and Spin Echo (SE) MRI acquisitions. A Region of Interest (ROI) analysis was performed to compare qCBV within enhancing regions of the lesion with normal tissue. Vascular proliferation was quantified based on local changes in qCBV, while normal WM served as a control. Statistically significant differences on CBV were observed for both acquisitions. While more patients are needed for this study, current results do not show enough accuracy to diagnose CNS tumors. With better categorization of tumors, this technique could be a great tool for CNS tumor treatment.

title: A “Greener” Solution to Asymmetric Sulfoxidation: Catalysis by [Fe(salen)]2O Complexes
abstract: An increased awareness of environmental issues has lead to the development of green chemistry, a branch of chemistry with the goal of reducing the amount and toxicity of chemical waste. In this sense, environmentally friendly methods for asymmetric sulfoxidation have gained much attention recently, as drugs such as esomeprazole (a chiral sulfoxide found in several acid-reflux drugs) gain popularity. Unfortunately, the current protocols used in the asymmetric oxidation of organic sulfides are far from being environmentally friendly, employing toxic transition metals, corrosive and atom-inefficient oxidants, and volatile organic compound (VOC)-releasing solvents. Our research attempts to integrate the increasing need for asymmetric sulfoxides in the pharmaceutical industry with increasing interest in green chemical methods to produce a catalytic system that is optimized for high enantioselectivity and low environmental impact. In this project, we test the green [Fe(salen)]2O catalyst with several environmentally friendly oxidants (such as hydrogen peroxide) and solvents (including ionic liquids) in the asymmetric sulfoxidation reaction.

title: Perfectionism and its Effect on Academic Performance and Depressive Symptoms in a Middle School Sample
abstract: Perfectionists are described as people who have a tendency to set excessively high standards for themselves while engaging in overly crucial self-evaluations. In their study, Gilman and Ashby (2003) demonstrate that perfectionism, or the setting of excessively high personal standards, leads to higher scores on a number of academic, intrapersonal, and interpersonal variables in middle school students. They examined two types of perfectionists--the normal perfectionist and the neurotic or maladaptive perfectionist. While they show that the normal perfectionist, who sets exceedingly high standards for himself, can accept the idea of not being able to meet that standard, neurotic perfectionists are those who set standards and become extremely distressed when they are not able to meet those standards. For this reason, neurotic perfectionists who are described as being motivated by fear of failure, rather than desire to succeed, were found to be at risk for more psychological disorders. In this exploratory study, we examined the relationship between perfectionism and academic performance, and how this relationship influences mental health. Five middle school students and their parents participated in the study by filling out a number of self report questionnaires, including the MASC, the CDI, the Self Perception Profile for Children, the CBCL and the Parent report of Academic Functioning. Report Cards were also obtained. This project attempts to replicate the findings of Gilman and Ashby (2003), by showing that high levels of perfectionism are related to high academic performance. In addition, we wanted to examine the negative impact that neurotic perfectionism has on the mental health of adolescents. We obtained discrepancy scores by finding the difference between a child’s self concept of performance in school compared to overall GPA, in order to test the hypothesis that neurotic perfectionistic children or those who have negative discrepancy scores experience more depressive symptoms.

title: To Forgive or Not To Forgive: Destiny Beliefs, Attachment Anxiety, and Forgiveness
abstract: One of the most difficult times in a romantic relationship can be during the aftermath of a betrayal, when individuals must decide whether or not to forgive their partners. However, certain individuals may be more willing to forgive their partners than others. I investigated the idea that individuals’ likelihood of forgiving a betrayal is based on their beliefs about the nature of romantic relationships as well as on the level of anxiety one exhibits about their relationships. I suggest that individuals are especially unlikely to forgive a betrayal when they both (a) subscribe strongly to the idea that relationships either are or are not “meant to be” (destiny beliefs) and (b) are experiencing high levels of insecurity in their current relationship (attachment anxiety). Experiencing heightened attachment anxiety after a betrayal may leave individuals especially prone to feelings of vulnerability. These sentiments are likely exacerbated by destiny theorists’ tendency to project current feelings about their relationship onto ideas about the future status of the relationship. In other words, strong destiny theorists experiencing attachment anxiety at the time of the betrayal are likely to conclude that their current vulnerability will last long into the future, a conclusion that will reduce the likelihood of forgiving the transgression. In the experiment, participants completed a self-report scale measuring the strength of their destiny beliefs before experiencing an experimental manipulation of attachment anxiety versus security. They then reported how likely they would be to forgive their partner after various types of betrayals. Results supported the hypothesis that heightened attachment anxiety predicts reduced forgiveness for individuals who subscribe strongly to destiny beliefs, but that it is not associated with forgiveness for those who subscribe weakly.

title: The Internet Connection: Navigating Social and Romantic Relationships through Instant Messenger
abstract: Over the past fifteen years, Instant Messaging (IM) has become a popular form of one-to-one online communication. Although many people use IM, college students in particular are avid users and utilize IM for a variety of reasons. The current study explored the nature of the Instant Messenger environment, as well as how social interaction functions in an online environment. One hundred seven Northwestern undergraduates were surveyed about their IM habits, and several of these respondents were interviewed about those and other topics. Although IM is often considered a lean medium due to the lack of nonverbal social cues typically present in face-to-face interactions, results revealed that intimacy could be created through IM. Results also show how college students utilize IM to develop and maintain romantic relationships, how students display their emotions in IM conversations, and why students choose to flirt, express themselves, and connect with others via IM.

title: A Nice Gesture: Understanding the Messages Our Hands Convey in Forensic Interviews
abstract: This study explores the role of gesture in communication during investigative interviews. Gesture is a ubiquitous aspect of communication, often conveying substantive, iconic information not found in accompanying speech. A previous study using scripted gestures demonstrated that gesture can be a source of suggestibility. We studied the role of gesture in a more naturalistic forensic interview context. Undergraduate students, one interviewer, and one witness participated in mock interviews. We coded all speech and gesture to determine the role gesture played in these interactions. People do rely on gesture to express information not found in speech. Interviewers sometimes convey information in gesture that can cue witnesses about information the interviewer expects to hear. Additionally, witnesses rely heavily on gesture to explain an event, particularly aspects that are difficult to describe verbally. Gestures convey their mental representation of the event and create a visual image for the interviewer. In recounting their understanding of the event, interviewers imitate gestures used by witnesses. Information that witnesses convey through gesture is understood by the interviewers and becomes part of their own mental representation of the event. Details conveyed exclusively in gesture are reported later by the other person, showing that interlocutors pick up on information expressed uniquely through gesture. These data demonstrate the vital communicative role that gesture can play in investigative interviews and have clear practical applications. We recommend that all forensic interviews be videotaped to ensure an accurate record of all the information being conveyed by both witnesses and interviewers in these interactions.

title: Training Visual Attention with Neurofeedback
abstract: Neurofeedback is a technique that provides users with feedback of electrical activity recorded at the scalp. This feedback allows the user to change neural activity in order to obtain a reward signal. The technique appears to be promising, but it is controversial because of the extravagant claims that have been made by proponents. We attempted to demonstrate training of visual attention by using a novel combination of neurofeedback and a method for inducing measurable neural activity that has been shown to be influenced by attention. The method uses steady-state visual evoked potentials, which are produced by flickering a stimulus (in this case a checkerboard) at a particular frequency. The flickering stimulus produces neural activity at the same frequency as that of the stimulus, and this activity provides a continuous record of stimulus-related neural activity. The activity was presented back to the participant so that increases in the frequency-locked activity were rewarded with a tone. Participants attempted to increase both the frequency and the duration of the reward. Two training protocols were used; one in which participants were rewarded whenever the attended frequency exceeded the reward threshold, and another in which participants were rewarded when they simultaneously increased activity related to the attended frequency and decreased activity related to a simultaneously ignored frequency. The results suggest that participants learn to enhance neural activity at the target frequency.

title: Humanitarianism and the Controversy of Bias
abstract: Five months after the December 2004 Tsunami devastated the coastal regions of South India and South East Asia, President Bush used a rhetoric of “becoming saved” through his “mission” to communities in need to announce his Faith-Based Initiative to the public. Much controversy has arisen among academics and experts as a result. In a Frontline debate that followed, Professor Amy Black explained the main concern of opposition groups: “We don’t want people to be coerced to have to follow a particular religious perspective.” Undoubtedly, a majority of humanitarian action involves political, social, cultural, religious, or gender biases that take form in either proselytizing or social-change programs. Such programs can sometimes cause regression within certain societies rather than the progress envisaged by the acting organizations. Still, as President Bush has pointed out, many of these organizations have produced effective results through dedicated voluntarism in troubled communities. During the summer of 2005, I studied the way one organization dealt with these biases while working with tsunami-affected villages South India. Utilizing the resources provided by the Isha Foundation, my host-NGO, I documented the story of Isha’s tsunami relief and rehabilitation operations in the Tamil Nadu region. A non-governmental, non-religious organization teaching Yoga, Meditation, Pranayama, and other Eastern mystical techniques to over 100,000 volunteer-members throughout the world, Isha proved to be a particularly useful lens through which the delicate balance between providing humanitarian aid while still respecting the customs and beliefs of the recipients of aid could be viewed.

title: The Effects of Parasocial Relationships on Emotional Well-Being in the Elderly
abstract: Interpersonal relationships have a positive impact on an individuals’ physical and emotional well-being. Unfortunately, due to limited mobility, failing health, and cognitive degeneration, elderly individuals are prone to losing companions and the interpersonal relationships they afford. Horton and Wohl introduced the concept of parasocial relationships, which are one-sided connections that develop between television viewers and media figures. The goal of this research project was to determine if the elderly benefit from parasocial relationships similarly to the way they benefit from interpersonal relationships. I hypothesized that elderly individuals with strong parasocial relationships will report higher degrees of life satisfaction. Thirty-five senior citizens between 65 and 92 years of age completed a Parasocial Interaction Scale (PSI) and Life Satisfaction Index (LSI) after being primed with discussion about either their favorite television character, their best friend, or with no prime. Additionally, they were interviewed about this character and their best interpersonal relationship. Contradicting the hypothesis raised, elderly individuals with strong parasocial relationships had lower life satisfaction under all priming conditions than participants with low PSI scores. Interview responses revealed that subjects with strong parasocial attachments viewed and described their favorite characters very positively and compared them to the individuals in their lives. This upward social comparison may elicit feelings of disappointment and social frustration, and ultimately yield lower life satisfaction. While similarities exist between parasocial and interpersonal relationships in how they form and develop, this study is the first to demonstrate that in the elderly, parasocial relationships have a negative impact on life satisfaction.

title: Psychotherapy Narratives and the Good Life: Themes Related to Happiness and Maturity
abstract: This study examines former psychotherapy patients’ narratives of their therapy experiences. A community sample of 100 adults completed an extensive questionnaire consisting of short-answer and narrative questions about their therapy or counseling as well as several measures of subjective well-being and psychological maturity. The researchers sought to establish correlations between themes within the narratives of the participants and their current levels of well-being and maturity. Specifically, they hypothesized that lower current well-being among the participants would correlate with narrating the problem for which they entered therapy as being an enduring, long-term issue in their life, and that higher well-being would correlate with narrating the problem as being more of a discrete occurrence. Also, the researchers hypothesized that lower levels of psychology maturity, as measured by Jane Loevinger’s conception of ego development, would correlate with narrating their therapy experiences as ending when they stopped attending sessions. On the other hand, those participants who scored higher in ego development (and were thus more mature) would tend to narrate their therapy experiences as ongoing projects in their lives, despite no longer seeing a therapist. Through the data obtained from this study, we can gain a better understanding of the ways in which former psychotherapy patients narrate and make sense of their experiences in treatment. Eventually, this knowledge will enable clinicians to devise and implement even higher-quality, more effective methods to help their patients re-write their life stories to create happier, more meaningful lives.

title: Framing the Union: European Media Address the Reformation of the European Union
abstract: The news media are some of the most powerful influences in today’s society. Which stories are run, their location in the presentation of news, and the way they are framed (how the use of specific language makes particular facts more or less salient) all effect what individuals take away from each story. The creation of the European Union is one of the most significant political, economic, and cultural changes occurring in the world today. As of 2003, the EU was home to 379.5 million people and in the past two years the Union has added ten new states. Given the magnitude of the political changes in the European Union and the effects that the media have on public opinion of those changes, the stance of the media in various EU countries on the advancement on the Union is worthy of examination. My study observed newspaper coverage of the recent EU Constitution Ratification process in three European countries (France, Spain, and the United Kingdom) to examine potential frames used by the various media. It also looked for a possible correlation between the success of the Constitution Ratification and the frames most frequently employed. The project sheds light on the role of the press in the extension of the European Union through the qualitative and quantitative examination of news stories relating to the EU Constitution Ratification from France, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

title: Negotiating Identity in Kosovo’s Post-Conflict Urban Development
abstract: This paper investigates features of post-conflict development in Kosovo’s capital city, Prishtina, as embodying and defining contemporary the nationalist discourse. Since NATO forced Serbian troops out of the region in June 1999, Kosovo has presented an opportunity for a wide array of international and local interests to realize political goals that are often shrouded in the ambiguous terminology of “nation-building”. Constructions of nationalism shape collective historical memory and define national community, but powerful elite organizations are generally responsible for its formation. The cliché that victors write history is more complicated when the “victors” are international peace-keepers. In a contested city such as Prishtina, seemingly mundane or unrelated issues of urban development, such as publishing maps, zoning, and preserving cultural heritage, become moments of nation-building that try to legitimize certain accounts of the past. The questions this paper asks are how the people of Kosovo, as well as external actors, interpret historical legacy; how they apply those interpretations to decisions about urban development; and how those developments may in turn be affecting Kosovo’s national identity? While it is clear that Kosovo’s government, international administration, and foreign NGOs manifest their political interests by exercising control over the city’s growth, Prishtina’s local population is independently sorting through its urban identity, often asserting cultural and historical affiliations over the dictates of imposed ideologies. Material for the paper comes mainly from two trips to Kosovo, first in July and August and again in December 2005, where I conducted archival research and interviews with UN administrators, government officials, NGOs, architects, and local community members.

title: The Loveliest School: Examining How Present Concerns Influence Recollections of the Foster School in Evanston, Illinois
abstract: The project uses recent scholarly literature on oral histories and narratives to analyze the stories residents of the 5th Ward recount about the old Foster School in Evanston. Starting in the 1960s, African-American students from the 5th Ward were and still are today bused to schools throughout Evanston. Integrated through a special pilot program, the Foster School was later closed, leaving the 5th Ward without a school of its own. That the 5th Ward not only lacks a school, but also is the only Evanston ward without a school, is a central part of residents’ narratives as they discuss memories of the Foster School and current educational issues. When studying oral histories, it is important for researchers to consider the time and place informants tell stories, as present concerns will influence narratives about the past. The paper then combines scholarly literature with research on school-community relationships to understand how current educational concerns shape recollections of the Foster School. When 5th Ward residents discuss how the Foster School contributed to the neighborhood, they not only express happy memories associated with the school. Residents also touch on immediate aspects regarding identity, race, social class, sense of community, desegregation, busing, and the achievement gap arising from perceived deficiencies within the current educational system in Evanston. Imbedded within these concerns then are what community members think are important elements to school-community relationships, physical location of the school building, and perceived formation of community and identity within a school and the neighborhood.

title: Competing Land Uses at Mt. Elgon
abstract: This study examines recent land use conflicts on Mt. Elgon, an extinct volcano on the border of Uganda and Kenya, in light of historical and contemporary land tenure systems on the mountain. Presently, there are two government-owned protected areas (a National Park and a Forest Preserve), a “National Reserve” managed by the minority Ogiek community, and an agricultural area of smallholder plots on this tropical mountain formerly covered by species-rich Alpine forests. Beginning with the resettlement of the forest-dwelling Ogiek community in the 1970s, the dual priorities of economic development and environmental conservation have come into conflict on the mountain. These competing priorities have resulted in not only rapid changes in land use and widespread deforestation on the mountain, but also limited economic opportunities and tensions among forest-adjacent communities. Drawing from a combination of primary interviews completed on Mt. Elgon in July 2005 and secondary research conducted at Northwestern University’s Herskovits Africana Library, this project highlights the role that undefined property rights, border disputes, and political marginalization play in creating economic and cultural disincentives for integrated, sustainable land use on the mountain. It argues that only by enforcing private property rights, changing economic incentive structures, and creating locally-acceptable institutions for integrating the management of Mt. Elgon’s entire ecosystem will local communities and the global conservation community be able to reconcile their sometimes competing, but ultimately interdependent, agendas.

title: The Relationship Between Demographics and Field Tracking in a Substance Abuse Research Study
abstract: Major problems exist during the allocation of funds for research projects. Furthermore, these problems are compounded when dealing with a transient population such as those who participant in a drug-abuse research study. Data was examined from one particular drug-abuse research study in order to further enhance knowledge on how to predict costs. “Field tracking” was identified as the most time consuming and thus resource consuming dependent variable that commonly extended outside of non drug-abuse research conditions. Various demographic variables were analyzed in order to predict individuals who were exceptionally likely to be field tracked and thus costly. The independent variable, Income, was found to significantly correlate with field tracking. Individuals with “low” income and “high” income were found to be more likely to have been field tracked while those with “moderate” income were found to be less likely to have been field tracked. The secondary independent variables, Age and Ethnicity, were then analyzed while controlling for income; these results have thus far been inconclusive. From these results, it can be concluded that the self-reported income of a population in a drug-abuse research study can be used to predict likeliness of field tracking and thus extensiveness of cost. Further research will be proposed to identify more predicting variables.

title: Deontology vs. Consequentialism: Exposing the False Dichotomy in Moral Reasoning Research
abstract: Many of the most remarkable and surprising actions that people commit – actions that range from terrorist acts to self-sacrifice to refusing to compromise certain beliefs under any condition – stem from an individual’s strongly held beliefs about what is right and what is wrong. Many of these values are widely viewed as fixed and irreconcilable, and negotiations involving such beliefs are assumed to inevitably result in deadlock. These values, known as “protected values” in the psychological literature, are conceptualized as moral rules that proscribe certain actions (e.g., utilizing protected wildlife areas for certain purposes). The psychological literature predicts that any type of cost-benefit analysis or attempt to measure the utility of options has no place in the decision making process in people with protected values. Further, most studies suggest that these two types of decision-making strategies are fundamentally incompatible and particularly resilient to change. Based on the shortcomings of prior research, the present study examined the structure and persistence of these types of decision-making strategies in the domains of the environment and animal testing. Individuals were pre-selected based on their reported preference for a certain type of decision-making strategy in each domain. A second, follow-up experiment was employed to assess empirically the malleability and persistence of these preferences. An analysis of participants’ responses to a series of hypothetical scenarios following the presentation of an experimental manipulation revealed key misunderstandings about how strongly held beliefs ultimately manifest themselves in society through individual decision-making. Implications of these findings for future research and policymaking are discussed.

title: Genocide in Rwanda: An Analysis of Domestic Origins
abstract: Research focused on evaluating various explanations that purport to illuminate the domestic causes of Rwanda’s genocide. Genocide, in its most basic manifestation, originates as a concept— a fanatical attraction to demographic purity or an otherwise intangible hypothesis for the maintenance of political power. Regardless of the rationale for its formulation, a project of its magnitude will forever remain unfeasible—confined to the minds of its architects— until endorsement is moved beyond the confines of privileged political circles and into the many disconnected, rural communities of Rwanda’s vast countryside. What is the correct model for grasping how an ideology of violence infiltrated these isolated locales, and once present, how did the slaughter of innocent civilians come to be perceived for teachers, cultivators, businessmen, and health officials as the more viable of two options? Did participants kill because they accepted, and acted upon, the ideas utilized by elites for its justification, or did they make decisions according to a rationale that can be identified only through analysis at the local level? My project has utilized the methodology of social science and political theory to test variables embedded in some of scholarship’s varied, yet nonetheless primary, theoretical perspectives. There is no shortage of prominent explanations, yet this endeavor—testing the accuracy of such claims—is important especially in regard to an issue as delicate and as complex as genocide, humanity’s foremost digression. My work will hopefully shed light on the fundamental question of what drives otherwise rational individuals to commit the most irrational of acts, ruling out those explanations which cannot stand up to a two-pronged thesis methodology composed of regression and case study analysis.

title: Perceptions of Relationship Status: Analyzing the Verbal and Nonverbal Cues
abstract: This project focuses on picking apart the verbal and nonverbal cues associated with romantic partners. Stimuli called “thin-slices” of behavior were used to study the ways in which people make quick judgments about the relationship status of two people. Real life romantic partners and platonic friends were videotaped having a conversation about a random topic and the videotape was trimmed down to a thirty second “thin slice” used as the stimulus. Upon viewing the short video clip, participants were asked to decide whether the couple is dating or if they are just friends. They were further asked to judge the level of intimacy and closeness the couple seemed to have. Participants were in one of three conditions: one in which the pair could be seen and heard, one in which the pair could only be seen, and one in which only the pair’s conversation could be heard with no visual stimulus present. The results lead to the conclusion that people are much better at determining whether a relationship is romantic or not mostly by using visual cues. Participants perform much more poorly if they are given audio cues alone. This same pattern emerges with the ratings of intimacy. When compared to the couple’s self-reported level of intimacy, the conditions most highly correlated were the ones that contained visual cues. Audio cues alone do not seem to provide enough information to make these kinds of judgments.

title: A Soldier's Burden: A Study of Mental Illness during WWII and Now
abstract: In times of war, the American public immerses itself in debates of freedom, liberty, and righteousness. Consumed with beliefs of bettering the world, many times the American public forgets about those that fight for those rights and ideals. Military personnel, academics and physicians have studied the mental health of soldiers since the Civil War, documenting the evolution of what today is known as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The stark contrast of the studies during WWII, when it was labeled as battle fatigue, and today’s term of PTSD is the focus of my research. Contrasting the two periods of war, I have determined that the perception of mental health among soldiers has shifted significantly. What once was understood as a personal weakness or moral defect has transformed today to an environmental problem. Amidst WWII, soldiers were studied as individuals, focusing upon their upbringing, medical history, and family. Today, soldiers’ mental health is analyzed among factors such as actual combat, war stress, and anxiety of death. The shift from the man to the war has mirrored the shift in public perception of the illness as well as the nature of war. As time has passed, the ideals of war have become less black and white, and the stalwart movement to support war has disappeared. The study of mental illness in the military reflects this change. No longer is it the soldier’s fault for his “weak mind,” but it is the nature of war itself that pushes him to the edge.

title: Deception Detection and the P300 Potential: The Brain’s Response to Autobiographical Information
abstract: When one perceives meaningful information, the electrical activity of the brain changes. This change is known in the field of psychophysiology as the P300 potential. Recent studies have shown that the P300 potential has important applications in deception detection. Prior to these studies, the only forensic test available to identify deception was the polygraph, which many experts believe to be inaccurate and easily beaten. During the polygraph test a criminal is presented with facts about a crime he/she is suspected of committing. If he/she recognizes these facts, a physiological change occurs, such as an increase in heart rate. Theoretically, the P300 lie detector works in the same way, but instead of using variables such as heart rate that can be easily manipulated by a perpetrator, the P300 potential is analyzed, leading to a more accurate decision. The experiment currently conducted measures the electroencephalogram (EEG) activity of Northwestern University students, (to date, sixteen experimental and nine control subjects have been run). The experimental group is presented with a series of dates, one of which is their birthday. 81% of the subjects showed a significant P300 in response to their birthdates. Control subjects were run to test for false positives and did not see their birthdates. Of the nine control subjects, only one showed a false positive response, thus, P300 was elicited without the presentation of relevant information. These results, showing significant individual detection, are promising and future research could extrapolate these findings to a real world forensic situation.

title: Effects of Training or Experience on Spatial Ability: A Meta-Analysis
abstract: Spatial ability is important in numerous domains including basic adaptation, reasoning, communication, and performance in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) disciplines (Benbow, 1985; Delgado & Prieto, 2004; Baldwin, 1985). Researchers have also demonstrated that spatial ability can improve with training (Baenninger & Newcombe 1989), schooling (Huttenlocher, Levine, & Vevea 1998), and even videogame playing (Subrahmanyam & Greenfield, 1994). To examine the malleability of spatial ability further, a comprehensive meta-analysis was conducted, specifically looking at whether, and how much, spatial ability measures improve as a result of various types of training and experience. Currently, over 100 studies have been analyzed and synthesized; the magnitude of the different treatments on spatial ability have been measured through computation of effect sizes (using standardized differences between means) yielding a mean effect size of .631. These results indicate that spatial ability is malleable in both children and adults. Many types of training or experience seem to provide a substantial gain in spatial ability, but music-training, task-specific training, and video games appear to produce greater improvement than taking an academic course or listening to music. The current findings also indicate that training diminishes, but does not eliminate sex differences as males and females show approximately equal improvements in spatial ability with training/experience. Overall, children’s spatial ability showed greater improvement with training/experience than that of adults. Repercussion of this meta-analysis may include enhanced performance in STEM disciplines, more comprehensive and beneficial curriculum in school, and the generation of information relevant to the nature-nurture question.

title: Stability, Democracy, and Reform: Determining the Stakes of the Lord's Resistance Army Conflict
abstract: The Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) has fought in Uganda’s north for the twenty years of Yoweri Museveni’s presidency. Previous reports study the roots and costs of the conflict, children abducted by the LRA, and Internally Displaced Persons, but none have determined the weight of the conflict in terms of the country’s governance. My research seeks to understand how Ugandans geographically associated with conflict view the state of Uganda and to decipher conflict’s astonishing longevity. Could the stakes of the conflict ultimately be democracy and Uganda’s tentative nationhood? Survey respondents recruited in Gulu were asked to rate quality of life, governance, and their relation to the conflict. The thirty-five surveys containing sixty-two questions were analyzed. An additional 108 less rigorous interviews discussed military force, peace negotiations, and the conflict’s duration. Interviewees included government officials, military leaders, media figures, academics, and merchants. The survey results show that conflict in the lives of Northerners heavily determines their perception of governance. Respondents affected by the conflict see Ugandan democracy as failing. Yet, interviews also show that Ugandans attribute the conflict’s longevity predominantly to strategic actions of the government to prolong it. This conundrum- a government pursuing a strategy that erodes perceptions of democracy- appears irrational. However, because of donor-dominated finance in Uganda, the NRM government has pursued a rational strategy. In aiding the conflict’s continuation, the government has resisted democratic reforms without alienating the donors. Museveni’s third term suggests this conflict will continue, as will Uganda’s pseudo-democracy, without significant external pressures.

title: The Time Course of Auditory Generalization
abstract: Individuals can improve performance on many perceptual tasks with practice. This improvement is often accompanied by performance on untrained conditions, a phenomenon known as generalization. I investigated the time course over which learning generalizes to untrained conditions, using an auditory task on which listeners were asked to determine which of two time intervals between brief tones was longer (duration discrimination). I trained nine listeners on a single duration-discrimination condition for two days, and eight listeners on the same condition for four days. Before and after training, I tested all listeners on a variety of untrained duration-discrimination conditions to see if learning on the trained conditions generalized to any of them. The results showed that learning on untrained conditions did not occur until learning on the trained condition had begun. Listeners who were trained for two days improved only on the trained condition, while those trained for four days improved not only on the trained condition, but also on an untrained condition sharing the same duration. The finding that learning was initially specific to the trained condition and then broadened over the course of training implies that the neural circuit affected by training is initially stimulus-specific, and becomes less specific only after extended training. These results have implications for the design of perceptual training regimens, including those for the remediation of learning disabilities, since they suggest that maximal generalization may require continued practice on the trained condition even after some learning has occurred.

title: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Andy Warhol and the Mechanisms of Iconographic Reference
abstract: For many theorists and art historians, Andy Warhol (1928-1987) embodies a decidedly postmodernist sensibility—his work referring to, reacting to, and embedded in a surrounding popular culture. However, these hallmark conditions of postmodernism are not entirely unforeseen throughout previous historical periods. Indeed, this sort of cultural interaction was not an entirely new phenomenon in the period of time critics and philosophers once heralded as postmodern. Warhol’s reductive forms and ongoing dialogue with mass culture—both of which are now standards in contemporary advertising—have decisive roots in fin de siècle Paris, and more specifically, in the decidedly modernist work of Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (1864-1901). Lautrec helped elevate the status of poster art while treading the line between fine art and advertising. Through his unique application of iconographic forms, Lautrec remained distinct from his colleagues. In marrying an easily identifiable, yet reductive, iconographic imagery with the newly mastered, lithographic (and thus mechanically reproduced and widely distributed) medium, Lautrec initiated a formal dialogue between artist and masses. Warhol would so heavily rely on this dialogue in his subsequent attempts to create what would ultimately become his notoriously ambivalent cultural critiques. Extensive archival analysis, critical research, close readings, and recent exposure to an incredibly wide range of both artists work in Chicago, New York and Paris allowed me to develop the understanding of celebrity and iconography in these two artists’ oeuvres. I also identified how both artists’ different uses of the celebrity might speak back to the different historical and cultural conditions in which each artist worked. Lautrec may well be the forefather of modern advertising, but—through his use of recognizable iconographic forms—I insist he is also the forefather of Pop.

title: In Virum Perfectum: The Education of African-American Men 'Unto Perfect Manhood' at Hales Franciscan High School, 1962-2000
abstract: Opened by the Franciscan Order’s Sacred Heart Province in 1962, Hales Franciscan was the latest of many single-sex Catholic high schools in the Archdiocese of Chicago. But what set Hales apart from other schools, both private and public, was that it targeted young black men, a group that had largely been kept out of local Catholic high schools that engaged in token desegregation. During a time when African-Americans increasingly pushed for the integration of public schools despite administrative resistance, and as neighborhoods and parishes on the south side experienced rapid racial and economic transformation, Hales Franciscan continually strived toward its motto, “In Virum Perfectum”—Unto Perfect Manhood—eventually sending 100% of its mostly low-income graduates from single-parent homes onto college. It is Hales’s dynamic effort to educate young African-American men, regardless of their circumstances, which is the subject of my research. In particular, my project considers how the demographics of students at Hales Franciscan have affected the school’s mission, educational strategies, and academic performance over time.

title: Development of a Highly Efficient and Selective Catalytic Oppenauer Oxidation System
abstract: The oxidation of alcohols to their corresponding carbonyl containing compounds constitutes one of the most fundamental transformations in organic chemistry. While several oxidation protocols are currently available in the literature, they are plagued by either the use of stoichiometric amounts of heavy metals, selectivity issues (tendency of the oxidant to react with other functional groups besides the alcohol), specificity issues (the inability of the oxidizing reagent to react with only a specific type of alcohol in the presence of another), waste disposal problems, or the employment of highly toxic reagents. Given the rise in interests in environmentally friendly chemical processes over recent years, the development of efficient, clean, and inexpensive oxidation methods that address these aforementioned problems are of utmost importance. One such method is the Oppenauer reaction, a highly selective protocol for oxidizing organic alcohols to the corresponding carbonyls utilizing electrophilic aldehydes and ketones as the oxidants. Although discovered in the mid-1930’s, only recently have Oppenauer oxidation systems implementing catalytic amounts of aluminum, an innocuous metal, been realized. Specifically, we have developed catalytic Oppenauer oxidation method that using catalytic amounts of simple and inexpensive ligand-free aluminum reagents such as trimethylaluminum (AlMe3) and trisaluminum isopropoxide (Al(OiPr)3). Using 3-nitrobenzaldehyde as a readily available and inexpensive oxidizing agent, a variety of highly functionalized alcohols can be selectively oxidized in the presence of these Al-based catalysts. While quantitative oxidation of alcohol was generally achieved in less than 0.5 h using AlMe3 as the catalyst, extended reaction times were generally needed for quantitative conversion when Al(OiPr)3 was employed.

title: Coupling between Unfolding and Dimerization of a Protein-Protein Interaction Domain
abstract: Transcriptional factors are proteins in the nucleus that regulate gene transcription. The Sin3/HDAC corepressor complex is one such protein and is necessary for survival at the embryo stage. The Sin3/HDAC corepressor complex consists of the Sin3 scaffold bound to its transcriptional repressors. Sin3 interacts with its repressors through evolutionarily conserved domains called paired amphiphatic helices (PAHs). We have analyzed the structure and conformation of the PAH2 domain of Sin3 under various conditions. The PAH2 domain of Sin3 is an 89-residue paired amphiphatic helix from residues 295 to 383 for which the solution structures of its complex with Mad1 and HBP1 repressors have already been elucidated by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). (Brubaker et al., 2000; Swanson et al., 2004) We have also found that there is conformational heterogeneity for PAH2 in its free state. By using 15N-labeled PAH2 for 1H-15N correlated spectra at several concentrations ranging from 0.05 mM to 1.0 mM, we have shown that PAH2 exists as an asymmetric dimer at concentrations approaching 1.0 mM. Conformational analysis of both subunits of the PAH2 dimer was performed using 13C/15N-labeled PAH2. We have found significant differences in secondary structure between the two subunits using chemical shift analysis of the peptide backbone. Our ongoing study of PAH2 has continued to focus on identifying possible consequences of this dimerization. In addition, we are identifying the crucial residues in PAH2 needed for binding HBP1 and Mad1 and plan to elucidate the tertiary structure of PAH2 in complex with the KLF family of repressors.

title: Perceptions of Time in Anlo-Ewe Music and Culture
abstract: My research focused on the relationship between perceptions of time in the culture and traditional music of the Anlo-Ewe society of southeastern Ghana. Much research has been done comparing Anlo-Ewe musical time with European musical time, but there has been little research on the connections between perceptions of time in the two cultures and how this relates to the different ways they each perceive time in music. My project sought to fill this gap through simultaneous study of music and culture in the Anlo-Ewe village of Anlo-Afiadenyigba. My research methods included interviews, observation, and participation in cultural events. Before beginning my research, I expected to encounter a radically different set of psychotemporal norms in Ghana because of the dramatic differences between time in Anlo-Ewe music and time in European music. Although I did encounter this in the village, my experiences in the larger towns reflected a more Western concept of time. In fact, I observed a conflict between traditional values and Western values in almost all areas of Anlo-Ewe culture. It is my hope that the findings of my research will not only improve the Western understanding of Anlo-Ewe music, but will also inspire other Westerners to consider the traditional Anlo-Ewe view of time as a healthy alternative to our own narrow, stress-inducing views of time.

title: Pinocchio
abstract: In 1883, Carlo Collodi's famous character Pinocchio appeared in an Italian children's magazine, and since then the iconic marionette and his struggle to become real has been the source material for countless adaptations. Touring around Illinois and Wisconsin, this faithful theatrical retelling of the text features six folk musician storytellers who inventively play, sing, dance, and act this sometimes melancholy, sometimes hilarious and always highly imaginative new musical. In creating this piece, the ensemble researched the stories of Collodi and explored the themes about which he wrote so profoundly. In the story we find a strange and pointed examination of child psychology and development, as the story follows a piece of laughing and crying wood as he develops more and more complex emotion, and finally the ability to love. We have also been interested in issues of gender, particularly in the father son relationship between Geppeto and Pinocchio and ways to stage masculinity. This production is a culmination of that ensemble-based research.

title: Musical Healing of Flamenco: Communication among Performers through Energy
abstract: The main objects of the research were to gain insight into the communicative aspects of flamenco performance and their correlation with heightened energy levels as perceived by the researcher. The latter will deal with the concept of duende and its relation to musical healing. A flamenco triangle, traditionally consisting of a singer, a dancer, and a guitarist, is formed by a continuous exchange of melodic, timbral, and, most importantly, rhythmical ideas among the performers. There exists a particular hierarchy involved in initiation of a musical or rhythmical idea, where the singer always takes the lead. Spontaneity is an essential part of an authentic flamenco execution, though the process seems to oppose the Western improvisatory style. Simultaneity is vital to the release of energy, first from one performer to the other and then from the performers to the audience. The presentation will also address the fundamentals of flamenco necessary for the common ground of communication as well as ethnographic findings of the two different (and mostly opposing) schools of thought regarding flamenco history and authenticity.

title: “Performance as Argument”: Excerpts from Northwestern’s 2008 Showcase Performance Troupe
abstract: Theatre is a method of articulating the ephemeral experience of living, of making manifest human thought, feeling, and behavior. Theatre is embodied experience, which when performed, effects experience and analysis in the spectator. The study of theatre utilizes the language of performance to consider problems of form and function that coincide with matters of cognitive science, neuroscience, sociology, anthropology, and psychology. The performing arts are distinguished by formal elements of coded texts, temporality, and the necessity for additional artists to animate the blueprint. In theatre, actors serve as principal animators in a delicate, complex collaboration with the text, the author, and the audience. An actor has two discrete tasks: 1) to decode dramatic text by isolating and identifying behaviors; and 2) to give those behaviors order and form, translating them into signifiers an audience can perceive and understand. "The problem," said Stanislavski, "is the gift to the actor." A play or text offers a web of questions actors must process as any problem-solver (or researcher or creative thinker) does: defining, gathering information, incubating, and testing multiple options for the most effective or true. At the end of the process, the actor's performance is his or her argument. Each year, Northwestern University’s Theatre Department selects a group of advanced senior actors to present their work in a New York City showcase production. Northwestern is unique as an undergraduate liberal arts program, competing primarily with graduate and conservatory training schools, in presenting the accomplishments of its students to New York’s artistic community and industry representatives. The following three excerpts are from the 2008 Showcase, listed in order of performance: Things You Shouldn't Say Past Midnight, by Peter Ackerman Performed by Northwestern Theatre Students Marco Minichiello and Kenner Bolt Fun, by Howard Korder Performed by Northwestern Theatre Students Kevin Reich and Reggie Gowland Aloha Say the Pretty Girls, by Naomi Iizuka Performed by Northwestern Theatre Students Brian Coleman and Kenner Bolt

title: In Vivo Magnetic Resonance Imaging with a Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agent
abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of mortality in the United States. Synthetic grafts have shown promise in large blood vessel applications, but there has been very little success (43%) in small diameter blood vessels because of early graft occlusion due to thrombosis (i.e. clot formation). One successful approach to overcoming this problem has been to use a poly (1,8-octanediol cocitrate) (POC) based biodegradable scaffold seeded with a layer of endothelial cells. However, there is a need for a non-invasive, in vivo mechanism to assess cell seeded endothelial grafts. Our goal is to investigate the feasibility of using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a noninvasive mechanism for long term in vivo tracking of the cell monolayer. To increase the contrast of the cell layer and allow for a more effective monitoring, cells are labeled with a recently developed Gadolinium-based contrast agent, C6-Gd. This helps to differentiate the cell layer from surrounding tissue, creating an innovative, non-invasive way to monitor the cell monolayer. MRI and relaxivity measurements have indicated that there is suboptimal brightness in the cell mass. This may be due to the subcellular localization of the contrast agent. We have investigated several methods to ensure our agent is more localized in the cytoplasm. This will result in an effective method for cellular labeling that maximizes signal intensity by promoting optimal cellular localization.

title: Essaying the Rust Belt: A Creative Travel Guide
abstract: With a Blickle Undergraduate Travel Fellowship, I set out on a month-long trip visiting Rust Belt places, most of them deindustrialized cities: Gary, Indiana; Cleveland and Youngstown, Ohio; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Sudbury, Ontario; Sault Ste Marie, Michigan. On this route around the Great Lakes, I interviewed local scientists, businesspeople, librarians, curators, and hotel workers. I also took both guided and self-guided “tours” of each individual area in order to better understand its multiple (physical, cultural, spiritual, historical, and political-economic) and intersecting landscapes. The end result of my travel research, when combined with the more traditional academic and literary research I conducted from home, is a creative essay in the form of a travel guide. It is entitled The Shipwreck Museum (named for the final stop on my route, and the final section of the essay). Its narrative arc follows not only my physical journey through the Rust Belt region, but the personal, psychological journey that I simultaneously took as I sought to make sense of what I experienced during my trip—most importantly, as I struggled with the place-specific paradoxes of beauty and tragedy that I found inscribed within each of my destinations. At the essay’s heart is my attempt to illuminate the complexity and value of places, people, and things commonly identified as broken or worthless, and in doing this, to guide the reader toward unexpected places of thought: toward the rediscovery of the spiritual within the material, and of wonder amid the tragedy of the modern world.

title: Clash and Harmony': Painting the Paradoxes of Tibetan Modernity
abstract: Modernization is occurring in Tibet today at an unprecedented rate. Such rapid change is enough to cause ambivalence and confusion anywhere, but in Tibet the case is compounded by the fact that censorship prevents expression of such feelings. Modern artists in Lhasa have discovered ways to use the ambiguity of contemporary art to circumvent censorship and address cultural identity in a modern context. My research with Lhasa artists in fall of 2007 explores the diversity of ways that these artists question what it means to be Tibetan in the twenty-first century. With support from the Kriegbaum and WCAS fellowships, my interviews in both Tibetan and Chinese indicate that the artists are deeply concerned with finding ways to balance change and continuity in their own lives as well as in their society. They use contrast and contradiction in their art to show the absurdity of the dilemma forcing them to choose between being Tibetan and being modern. Some artists focus on the tension between modernization and preservation of tradition. Others are concerned with tensions between collective cultural and individual identities. A few represent the material evidence of modernization in order to highlight the increasing commercialization of Tibetan society and commodification of its culture. I examine the work of several artists who question whether representing ‘Tibetanness’ is even tenable. My research demonstrates how all artists address the issues of language and censorship, and the possibility of expression through omission.

title: Asymmetric Ring-Opening Meso Epoxides with Alcohols Catalyzed by Chiral Aluminum Complexes
abstract: Every living organism is composed of molecules, big and small, with specific chiral orientations that are intricately involved in that organism's ability to control its life processes. Nearly every biochemical process in the human body is associated with specific chiral molecules. As a result, many prescription drugs must possess a particular chiral orientation to be effective. Therefore, great care is taken during the synthesis of these molecules to control their chirality. However, this is not an easy task, and the difficulty in making a chirally pure drug is partially responsible for the rising cost of prescription drugs and health insurance. Therefore, any synthetic advances that can ease this burden or eliminate steps in the manufacturing of chiral drugs have a very high potential to reduce the cost of healthcare. Although synthetic organic chemists have developed numerous methods to control the chirality of a particular molecule, they have not been uniformly successful. To enhance the chiral purity of a particular drug intermediate, expensive starting materials are often required, reaction conditions must be carefully controlled, and an extensive product purification must be carried out. As such, synthetic approaches that can yield chirally pure products without such intensive requirements would be very valuable. To this end, I aim to develop an efficient synthesis of chirally pure B-hydroxyethers, an important class of intermediates for the pharmaceutical and fine chemicals industries, from non-chiral starting materials. This conversion can be achieved under mild reaction conditions in the presence of a highly active but easily accessible aluminum-based catalyst.

title: Electical Characterization of Ferromagnetic/Semiconducting MnGe/Ge Nanowire Heterostructures
abstract: Mn-mediated growth of Ge nanowires (NWs) has been recently reported and shown to have a unique growth mechanism which results in two one-dimensional segments, one of which is a Mn-rich germanide. Such heterostructures are of interest due to their potential for spintronic applications in areas such as computer memory. In this investigation, electrical measurements will be made on individual nanowire heterostructures in order to characterize the electrical properties of the two phases as well as the interface between them. Preliminary I-V behavior suggests that the titanium contacts are not Ohmic and therefore must be improved in order to study these materials. En route to improved contact performance, we have synthesized δ-doped p-type Ge wires, which should provide a simpler system to optimize contact fabrication procedures. In order to observe the behavior of the Mn germanide, which we believe to be a magnetic phase, two contacts must be fabricated on the ~500 µm wire segment. This is a fairly small target, however alignment is possible using atomic force microscopy to precisely locate the region.

title: Grounded Figures, Floating Worlds: Navigating the Works of Kehinde Wiley and Iona Rozeal Brown
abstract: In early 2007, African-American artists Kehinde Wiley and Iona Rozeal Brown looked to art-historical traditions of Japan and China to reinvigorate their painting practices. In the exhibition Kehinde Wiley: World Stage China, Wiley paints wall-sized images of young black American men dressed in hip-hop style against colorful and flowery backgrounds. He also poses the men in the fashion of Maoist propaganda posters of the Chinese Cultural Revolution. Inspired by the popularity of Japanese youth appropriating hip-hop style and culture, Iona Rozeal Brown transforms geishas in "pictures of the floating world" (ukiyo-e woodblock prints) with “bling,” over-the-top hairstyles, and scantily clad attire in her exhibition Epidemic of Excess…Detriment of Denial. Cultural critic Deborah Whaley argues against a similar practice termed as “Black Orientalism,” and problematizes the re-imagining of Asia and the sexualization of Asian bodies in hip-hop visual culture. However, my project situates the ways that Brown and Wiley use Black Orientalism to destabilize seemingly fixed notions of race, class, and gender. While the artists participate in the resurfacing of Asia in the American imaginary, they are also using their paintings to critique black masculinities and black femininities that are circulated globally through mediums like hip-hop visual culture. Accounting for the overwhelming attention to China, Japan, and Asia in the media today, the rapid changes in hip-hop, as well as the resurgence of hip-hop and Asian influences in art practice, my project illuminates the ways that Wiley and Brown place blackness in tension or conflict with seemingly oppositional forces, like Japanese youth, hip-hop, and blackface, or Maoism and black men, revealing a cross-cultural negotiation of identities in the United States and abroad.

title: Second Style Painting in Roman Cubicula
abstract: The Roman villa had a very different function than its contemporary counterpart since it served as both a country retreat and as a place where much work and public entertaining took place. The villa was divided into a public and private sector, which were both clearly delineated based on the status of a visitor. The private sector of a house is more difficult to analyze due to a lack of information about the daily activities, which occurred in restricted rooms such as cubicula or bedrooms. With the help of an Undergraduate Research Grant, I have compared the frescoes of three aristocratic cubicula around Pompeii in an attempt to discover more about the daily life of Romans in the first centuries BC and AD. In doing this analysis it became clear that the typologies used by archaeologists in the past are outdated and they do allow us to understand how versatile rooms in Roman villas were. The frescoes and architectural elements of these three cubicula reveal that “bedrooms” were in fact used for a variety of activities such as sleeping but also dining, reading, studying and small parties. The typologies imposed by archaeologist in the past have been detrimental to the study of Roman villas and this study of “bedrooms” based on décor reveals how multifaceted spaces could be.

title: The Current State of Theatre for Young Audiences
abstract: Based on an updated version of Wesley Van Tassel’s 1968 survey-study entitled “The Views of Theatre for Children,” this research explores the current views of Theatre for Young Audiences (TYA) practitioners and whether or not opinions have changed over time. The current survey, conducted in the fall of 2007, includes Van Tassel’s original twelve multiple-choice questions along with five additional multiple-choice questions and three open-ended responses used to augment the 1968 survey. These twenty questions address such issues as the quality of TYA compared to that of adult theatre, the necessary elements of a TYA production, and the purpose of TYA plays. By focusing on these free-response questions about season selection and play content, this research shows how the historical practice of using education in TYA continues today as well as the limitations that arise from making TYA an educational realm. While a change to make the field of TYA more aesthetically focused rather than educationally focused appears currently implausible from the survey results, a movement towards expanding educational content within the field has more potential. Several of the companies surveyed expressed support for challenging topics in productions, such as sex, drugs, violence, and religion, but more encouragement of these subjects is needed, both by theatre companies and society in general, to make strides in the field of Theatre for Young Audiences.

title: Fragile X Mental Retardation Gene: Interaction with the Circadian Clock
abstract: A loss of function mutation in the human Fragile X Mental Retardation gene (fmr) is associated with a wide range of clinical abnormalities, including sleep defects. Remarkably, a homologous mutation in the Drosophila gene dfmr results similarly in poor circadian rhythms and altered sleep phenotypes. My interest is in what links fmr to sleep and the circadian clock. In order to understand this link, we take advantage of Drosophila and its fmr homologue as our model. My first project investigates a proposed interaction between CKII, a gene associated with the circadian clock, and dfmr. To investigate the possibility of this interaction, I have performed a variety of molecular and genetic experiments. My second project is a screen for enhancers and suppressors of the dfmr mutant phenotype. Mutant dfmr lines are further mutagenized and tested for resultant changes in behavioral phenotype. Lines accruing mutations that enhance or suppress the dfmr phenotype are saved and their mutations mapped. These mutations may help to identify pathways connecting dfmr to the clock, and in doing so help to identify the essential pathways through which fmr gives rise to its variety of symptoms.

title: Music in Real-Time Interactive Video Games
abstract: Interactive, real-time video games have become ubiquitous within Western society over the past two decades. Their many similarities to an improvisational musical environment can be seen by equating repeated button combinations to melodic motives and specific button timing to rhythmic motives. Over the summer of 2007, I conducted a combined academic and compositional research project to shed more light on this connection. Using the software Max/MSP, I modified the human interface device object developed by Hans-Christoph Steiner et. al. and produced a patch which records all data from a USB video game controller with index and time values into a compact text file. Next, Dr. Mercer and I developed a system to play back this data, assigning each button to a distinct pitched oscillator or sound file. Next, I recorded controller data from ten volunteers with varying levels of experience with music performance and real-time video games as they played five matches of Mortal Kombat II for the Super Nintendo and Super Smash Brothers for the Nintendo 64 (each emulated on a computer using USB controllers). Analysis of the results suggests that among participants with large amounts of video game experience, musical experience may denote a slight change in playing style without offering a decisive advantage or disadvantage. Among those unacquainted with video games, however, extensive musical experience lessens ‘button-mashing’ and contributes to a more gradual exploration of multi-button coordination, which requires synchronous motion between different types of controller movements.

title: Racial Disparities in Birth Outcomes of US Infants: An Exploratory Study of Social Factors Relating to the Birth Weights of African-born Women delivering at Stroger Hospital
abstract: In the United States, a great disparity exists between birth outcomes of infants born to white mothers and infants born to black mothers. Epidemiological studies have shown that black mothers give birth to infants with significantly higher rates of low birth weight and infant mortality than those born to white mothers. Geneticists argue that a supposed preterm birth gene can explain these disparities, while anthropologists maintain that race has little to do with genetics; rather, they attribute social, political, and cultural pressures as contributions to this discrepancy. Evidence exists that African-born black mothers give birth to infants of similar weights to those of US-born whites and of greater weight than those of US-born blacks. Despite the disadvantage of giving birth in an unfamiliar country and a foreign health care setting, these mothers have healthy birth outcomes, even better than those of US-born black mothers. These findings support speculations that lifelong minority status, rather than genetic predisposition, may be one of the most important risk factors associated with poor health in infants. Through qualitative, ethnographic interviews of African-born women who have recently given birth, this study aims to explore trends that may account for this unexplained dichotomy.

title: An Exploration of Faith and Politics: What Narratives Reveal
abstract: While faith and politics remain distinct entities in the public sphere, in the minds of many Americans, these concepts cannot be separated. Religious beliefs and practices continually affect how people construct their political worlds. Previous research has documented several trends in the bond between religion and politics, but the literature struggles to explain the trends and achieve consensus regarding how religion comes to influence political beliefs on an individual level. Therefore, studying faith and politics through a life-narrative lens can result in a deeper insight into how people understand the relationship between their religious and political beliefs. The present study examined life-narrative interviews from 115 highly religious and politically active midlife adults to test relationships between faith and politics within the political liberal-conservative paradigm. Previous research and conventional wisdom tend to characterize conservatives as the more religiously influenced group; however, the results provided mixed support for that characterization. Content analysis showed that although conservatives tended to favor greater religious influence in government than liberals, conservatives were no more likely than liberals to cite religious influence in their individual political beliefs. Furthermore, that tendency towards mixing faith and politics on a governmental level related strongly to standardized measures of political and religious belief, but the tendency towards mixing faith and politics on an individual level showed no such relationships. These results suggest a complex and nuanced relationship between faith and politics.

title: Hua Qi, or American Flags Made in China: The Crossroads of Nationalism and Globalization
abstract: From the halls of Congress to the local American Legion, from high-brow magazines to local newspapers, American flags made in China have captured the contempt, the concurrence, or simply the curiosity of the American people. Since September 11, 2001, the American flag made in China has been used as a way to talk about a variety of concerns, including China's human and religious rights violations and its communist government. Most significantly, however, the anxiety about American flags made in China reflects a palpable sense of anxiety about the U.S. economy and its place in the world. Rather than adjudicating the advantages and disadvantages of globalization, as the much of the current literature attempts to do, I analyze the rhetoric surrounding a particularly "loaded" cultural artifact as it circulates through Chinese and American cultures. I conclude that although, in the abstract, globalization and the nation-state can be compatible, if not complementary, the discourses about and images of American flags made in China suggest that nationalism—a commitment to the nation-state as well as hostility toward another nation—is animating much of the opinion in the United States. The implications of this anxiety will continue to influence U.S. economic and trade policy within the Sino-American relationship and, ultimately, how Americans see the United States' role in the world.

title: Making Feedback Work: The Influence of Self-Verifying Feedback on Motivation
abstract: Performance-related feedback is inarguably an integral part of growth and development in organizations. However, these benefits are rarely optimized because feedback recipients do not always utilize such information. In the present study, I draw upon self-verification theory to understand how people respond to feedback. Self-verification theory posits that people desire to be understood for who they are, in terms of both their strengths and weaknesses. Thus, I hypothesize that, regardless of the feedback valence (e.g., positive or negative), when individuals receive self-verifying feedback that confirms their pre-existing self-image, they will be more likely to view the feedback as useful and motivating than will those who receive non-verifying feedback. I am currently testing this prediction on a sample of 150 college undergraduates using a scenario study design. In the scenario, participants are asked to imagine receiving feedback from a superior and complete a short questionnaire assessing their feedback experience. The results of this study will offer exciting and important contributions to the social psychology, organizational communication, and management fields in both the theoretical and practical applications of giving and receiving feedback.

title: Finding Fault: The Role of Comparison in Learning a Geological Structure
abstract: Geoscience education involves learning to identify geological structures. We examined the role of comparison in learning to identify faults (rock fractures showing evidence of movement). Comparison involves structurally aligning two representations (Gentner & Markman, 1997). Learning novel structures may be facilitated by progressive alignment—comparing similar scenes before more distant exemplars (Gentner, Loewenstein, & Hung, 2007). Highly similar items are easier to align structurally, thereby highlighting their common relational structure, and any alignable differences (readily comparable but differing features). In the present study, participants with varying levels of geology course experience were presented with 20 pairs of geological photos, and had to indicate which photo in each pair displayed a fault. We contrasted a similar-first condition, in which perceptually similar pairs preceded dissimilar pairs, and a dissimilar-first condition, which reversed this ordering. Consistent with progressive alignment, similar-first learners were more accurate, especially if they had some background geology experience. Additionally, several participants completed written questionnaires about the information they used to search for and identify faults. High performers were found to utilize evidence of movement and displacement along the fault line. Poor performers, however, tended to focus on fractures, a characteristic but not defining feature of faults. These results suggest that learners may benefit from a progressive alignment sequence of instruction, but may require more initial instruction to prevent common misconceptions before they develop.

title: Jorge Peña Hen, Music Education and Democracy in Chile
abstract: In 1950s and 1960s Chile, musician and educator Jorge Peña Hen proposed and successfully instituted reforms that fundamentally changed the access of everyday Chileans to music performance and education. This thesis will argue that Peña’s musical reforms democratized music education in Chile and analyze the three steps of this process: the decentralization of Western art music in the founding of the Sociedad Bach de La Serena in 1950, the refocus on music education for children in the proposal of the Plan Docente of 1964, and the institutionalization of these changes in the form of the Escuela Experimental in 1965. Peña’s philosophies permeated Chile’s north and successfully resonated throughout the country in the founding of youth symphonies and experimental music schools. In overturning traditional restrictions on access to Western art music his musical work became controversial and ultimately powerfully political, resulting in his brutal silencing by the military coup of 1973. The military regime suppressed information about Peña, and since 1990 only brief biographies have considered his life and works. This thesis is the first English source on Peña, and the first to analyze his work in the context of music reform and democracy. His philosophies have contemporarily found resonance in the Latin American youth symphony movement, a testimony to the timelessness of his visions.

title: Cultural Influences on Neural Responses during Scene Encoding
abstract: How does culture affect our ability to learn novel scenes? Recent behavioral research has shown that culture influences how people process and attend to their physical environment (Miyamoto et al., 2006, Masuda & Nisbett, 2006). In addition to effects of culture on scene perception, we hypothesized that culture also affects the ability to learn novel physical environments. We conducted a behavioral (Experiment 1) and a functional neuroimaging (fMRI) experiment (Experiment 2) to test this hypothesis.
