In Experiment 1, Caucasian-Americans and Asian-Americans viewed Japanese and American scenes and completed familiarity and recognition tests. Results from Experiment 1 indicate that Caucasian-Americans learn unfamiliar Japanese scenes better than American scenes while Asian-Americans learn unfamiliar American scenes better than Japanese scenes. In Experiment 2, these behavioral findings were replicated in a separate Caucasian-American cohort. Moreover, Caucasian-Americans showed greater neural activity to unfamiliar American scenes relative to Japanese scenes in the right hippocampus/parahippocampus, brain regions related to scene perception and recognition, and parietal cortex, parieto-occipital junction and occipital cortex, brain regions related to spatial processing. These results suggest cultural effects on learning and memory processes of physical environments at behavioral and neural levels of analysis.

title: The Political Economy of HIV/AIDS in India: A Comparative State Level Analysis
abstract: In post-1991 India, HIV/AIDS prevalence rates decreased while economic growth increased. One argument on economics and health claims that economic growth increases healthcare opportunities. Yet, when I correlated data on state-level GDP and HIV prevalence in India, I found that many wealthy states experience high prevalence. While poverty alleviation, education development, and gender equity are named as realities required to decrease prevalence, little exploration of the political decisions that affect these realities, specifically in the Indian context, has occurred in either the public health or the political theory spheres. Though it is easy to write off poorer Indian states with high-HIV/AIDS rates as examples of how poverty negatively influences health, further examination of economically developed Indian states needs to occur to understand why, in spite of all the entrenched doctrine on HIV/AIDS that suggests these states have the resources necessary to decrease HIV/AIDS prevalence, they still see high prevalence rates. I hypothesized that the consequences of rapid economic development, when combined with increased sex commodification, create a high-risk HIV/AIDS situation for wealthier states, and that states able to negate high-risk situations with political interventions see lower HIV/AIDS prevalence rates than states that do not. After examining quantitative and qualitative data through a case study analysis of Maharashtra, West Bengal, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu, I determined that states actively forgetting the political and health interests of high-risk, often socioeconomically marginalized groups, were more likely to see high prevalence in those groups and generally throughout the state. Thus, I concluded that what Leela Fernandes coins the politics of forgetting applies to India’s HIV/AIDS scenario in some of its high-wealth states; it is the causal factor that determines how economic development, sex commodification, and high-HIV risk shape HIV/AIDS prevalence via active political disengagement.

title: Conductive AFM Studies of Tin-Doped Indium Oxide Thin Film Surfaces
abstract: Conductive atomic force microscopy was performed on ultrasmooth commercial tin-doped indium oxide (ITO) thin films. Scanning previously scanned areas, even under no applied bias, revealed a patterning effect, visible in the current images as boxes of reduced conductivity with an applied sample bias and in lateral force microscopy (LFM) images. However, no detectable change in the topography signal was observed. Increasing biases across the tip-sample junction and scanning the same area multiple times produces patterns of higher contrast in both current and LFM images. Patterns were successfully made in atmospheres with controlled relative humidity levels from 5% to 50%, these environments were achieved by having the AFM in an environmental control glove-box. Secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) characterization of patterned areas revealed a reduction in surface carbon contamination, which suggests that removal of hydrocarbons may play a role in the apparent or effective reduction in surface conductance. Further characterization is needed to determine the patterning mechanism.

title: Matrix Stiffness Regulates Antrum Formation in a 3-Dimensional Ovarian Follicle Culture System
abstract: Formation of fluid-filled antral cavity has been a defining, yet not well understood characteristic of ovarian follicles’ maturation. It was hypothesized that antrum facilitates oxygen transport in follicle growth, and recent studies found antrum formation to be aided by aquaporin proteins. Using a novel 3-dimensional follicle culture system, we are able to regulate antrum formation via the physical properties of the culture matrix, and study aquaporin and hypoxia-inducible factor alpha (Hif-1α) gene expression in the system. In this system, multilayered secondary follicles isolated from mouse ovaries were placed in droplets of alginate, which were then allowed to cross-link in calcium chloride solution. Studies were performed in 0.5% and 1.5% alginate concentrations, which have significantly different stiffness. RNA was isolated from the follicles after 2-8 days of culture, for RT-PCR analysis of aquaporin and Hif-1α gene expression. Only 5.5% of follicles cultured in 1.5% matrix formed antral cavity, but the follicles showed high expression of aquaporin and Hif-1α genes. Follicles cultured in 0.5% less stiff alginate matrix formed antra in over 85% of follicles, but showed low expressions of aquaporin and Hif-1α genes. It is thus proposed that stiffness of alginate matrix used in 3D in vitro culture system has regulating effects on antrum-regulating gene expression, due to induced hypoxic effect in follicles. Follicles cultured in stiffer alginate matrices are unable to expand in the growth process, and thus antrum unable to form, due to the external pressure of the stiffer alginate matrix. However, because of increasing tissue mass within the follicle, oxygen transportation into the follicle is impeded, causing hypoxic conditions within the follicle. Aquaporin proteins, particularly aquaporin 7 and 8, are then expressed to alleviate the hypoxic effect, thus describing the regulation of alginate matrix stiffness in gene expression related to antrum formation in in vitro cultured ovarian follicles.

title: Don’t Think of a Pink Elephant: Investigating Brain Activity Underlying Mental Image Generation and Inhibition
abstract: What happens to you when you hear the phrase: “pink elephant?” Does a Dumbo-like image quickly pop into your mind’s eye whether you want it there or not? Through sheer will power, could you prevent that elephant from entering your visual consciousness? We conducted two experiments to determine the extent to which people can avoid visual imagery on command. We obtained subjective reports on visual imagery in two conditions. In the IMAGE condition, subjects were asked to form vivid visual images for the referents of 96 concrete, highly imageable spoken nouns. In the REFRAIN condition, subjects were asked to focus attention on the sound of each of 96 similar words and not to think of anything visual at all. In addition, EEG data were collected so that we could analyze a specific brain potential that has been associated with visual imagery in prior experiments. Initial EEG results showed that subjects were largely unsuccessful at inhibiting imagery when completing the IMAGE and REFRAIN conditions in an alternating fashion. In a second experiment, subjects engaged in each condition for an extended period of time, and EEG results showed that subjects were successfully able to inhibit imagery. Although self-report measures indicated some success in the REFRAIN condition in both experiments, EEG evidence suggested that subjects in the second experiment had superior abilities to inhibit the visual imagery that normally comes to mind so swiftly and naturally. These methods are thus suitable for assessing the degree of control people have over mental imagery.

title: A for Apology
abstract: Within the past several years, American universities have begun to follow in the footsteps of such institutions as governments, businesses, and religions by adding to what one scholar has called “a global frenzy to balance our moral ledgers” (Dwyer 41). Scholars have written extensively on the institutional apologies of businesses, governments, and religious institutions. Excluded from this focus, however, stands the institution of the American university. My project, based on a month of research at both the University of Alabama and Brown University, argues that the American university is able to offer an effective institutional apology for events that occurred in the distant past because it has the potential to engage in a process I call active consideration. Roughly, active consideration means the promise of ongoing debate. Such a process of consideration has the potential to be a powerful ameliorating force for victimized groups. Both the University of Alabama and Brown have extensive ties to slavery, and each school has attempted to reconcile with this history. For reasons detailed in my research, the efforts of Brown can be described as successful while those at Alabama cannot be. My case studies demonstrate the viability of original suspicion: the University as an institution apologizes in a fundamentally different manner than other kinds of institutions. The examples provided by Brown and Alabama offer a prescriptive framework for universities that are considering an apology in the future. My research outlines this framework, cautioning universities as to the correct way to perform an apologetic gesture that will be endowed with real sincerity and reconciliatory significance.

title: Optimizing the Shift in Aircraft Control under Trajectory Based Operations

people.major: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences

abstract: Recent initiatives to modernize the nation’s airspace propose allowing aircraft to operate with limited air traffic control for portions of their flight utilizing a trajectory-based operation. Still, aircraft control will transfer from pilots en route to air traffic controllers for final descent. The location of this control shift, a distance from destination airport, is a dynamic value that will change based on flight volumes, weather, and other factors. This research examines the location of the control shift through a regression, which models the impact of the factors such as flight volumes and weather. The model reveals the effect of certain factors on the shift location and suggests an optimal location of control shift given prevailing conditions. Achieving an optimal control shift location is crucial to an effective implementation of these modernization initiatives. Such improvements to the capacity of the airspace and efficiency of the aircraft routings will certainly benefit the entire economy.

title: Celastrol Selectively Binds to Cysteine Residues in the Model Protein Dihydrofolate Reductase
abstract: Heat shock proteins (Hsps) are a group of molecular chaperones whose expression is increased in response to cellular stresses, such as the presence of misfolded proteins. Recent research has implicated the therapeutic benefits of modulating the heat shock response (HSR) through which chaperones are expressed via the activation of the transcription factor HSF1. Small molecule screens for activators of the HSR have produced one molecule in particular, celastrol, which activates the HSR with kinetics similar to those observed with heat shock. Research has demonstrated that celastrol may activate the HSR through inhibition of Hsp90 ATPase activity, although the exact mechanism remains unclear. One potential hypothesis is that celastrol functions as an alkylating agent and binds to cysteine residues, thereby altering the conformation and activity of Hsp90. To test this hypothesis, we investigated the effects of celastrol-binding on the structure, stability, and activity in the model system dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), which is a well-characterized, small 18 kDa protein. To test the hypothesis that celastrol-binding to cysteine is specific and inhibitory, we introduced a cysteine residue within the so-called M20 loop, using a non-cysteine DHFR as a template. Because the M20 loop adopts three different conformations during catalysis, it is hypothesized that celastrol-binding to the cysteine residue will affect the activity. To resolve the mechanism, the kinetics and reversibility of binding will be tested as a function of time and celastrol concentration using absorbance, fluorescence, and circular dichroism spectroscopy. The structure and stability of DHFR will also be assayed using circular dichroism.

title: Age-Related Loss of Calbindin Identifies Basal Forebrain Cholinergic Neurons Destined to Degenerate in Alzheimer’s Disease
abstract: The reasons for the vulnerability of select neuronal populations in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) remain unknown. We have used the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (BFCN), which are vulnerable to degeneration early in the course of AD, to determine the cause. A selective loss of the calcium binding protein, calbindin-D28K, from the human BFCN occurs in the course of normal aging. The calcium dysregulation caused by the loss of calbindin may contribute to the loss of BFCN in AD. Immunohistochemical methods were used in postmortem brains from young (<65 years), old and AD cases. The number of choline acetyltransferase and low-affinity neurotrophin receptor immunoreactive BFCN remained constant in old individuals when compared with the young and displayed a significant decrease in AD. In contrast, the number of calbindin-positive BFCN showed a significant decrease in normal-aged individuals when compared with the young and remained constant in AD. The percentage of calbindin-positive BFCN in the aged was significantly lower when compared with the young. Of great interest, the percentage of remaining BFCN in AD which contained calbindin immunoreactivity displayed a significant increase when compared with the normal aged, indicating that the majority of surviving BFCN in AD are calbindin-positive. These observations indicate that neuron loss in AD occurs preferentially in the BFCN which lose their calbindin in the course of normal aging and that the calbindin-positive BFCN survive the neurodegenerative process. It is likely that loss of calbindin during aging deprives the BFCN of calcium buffering capacity, leaving them vulnerable to degeneration due to calcium toxicity in AD.

title: Analyzing the Correlation between Infiltration Processing Techniques and Electrical Performance in Solid Oxide Fuel Cells
abstract: Fuel cells are becoming an increasingly beneficial alternative to how we consume energy so it is important to understand the characteristics of and means by which we manipulate the properties of fuel cells. There are many different types of fuel cells, but solid oxide fuel cells (SOFC) are a great choice due to their high efficiency. SOFCs are also attractive because of their resistance to corrosion and inexpensive materials. Both the materials that are used in construction and the structure are essential for energy efficiency. The structure dictates the electrical performance through how porous the surface is and how the surface is being maximized. In this investigation, different infiltration techniques are being applied to cells to see how resistance is affected. A fuel cell has three layers, an electrolyte in between a cathode and an anode. The fuel cells in this particular experiment are symmetrical with an electrolyte and a cathode on each side which is made out of yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) and Strontium Doped Lanthanum Manganite (LSM). A total of 4 cells were tested, each infiltrated with LSM with varying volume percentages. Using an impedance analyzer, the cell’s resistances were tested at different temperatures to observe the cell’s performance. The structure of these cells will then be analyzed using a 3D focused ion beam-scanning electron microscope (FIB-SEM).

title: Versions from Occitan and Original Poems
abstract: My project consists of English versions of songs by troubadours, medieval Occitan poets, as well as my own poems that grew out of the experience of translating. I chose songs that, in one way or another, addressed the theme of absence. I used the Blickle Fellowship to travel to France and to see for myself the landscape that gave rise to the songs, and, while this experience led me closer to them, it also revealed a remoteness that I could not overcome. Absence is an important factor in translation. I wanted to occupy the songs, but intimacy is impossible. There is always distance, and though I could not traverse it, I believe the distance itself became productive. My first versions were line-for-line translations that felt impersonal and flat. The songs have an expressive quality that my literal translations lost. Although they would have made tedious finished pieces, by writing them I developed a familiarity with the songs. I found that by writing more compact versions, I could infuse them with the energy lacking in the first versions. My poems were initially exercises to orient myself and find a voice that could approach the issues important to the songs, but it became apparent that these poems were more important than exercises. As I wrote, I discovered the continuum of relationships that existed between the versions and my poems. Ultimately, my project is a dialogue addressing the absence at the heart of the songs, as well as the distance inherent in translation.

title: A Modular Approach to Small Molecule-DNA Hybrid Synthesis
abstract: Over the last two decades, aggregated DNA hybrids have become the materials of choice in the development of new strategies for genetic detection, templated synthesis, programmed self-assembly, and molecular computing. Hybridized mixtures of materials containing multiple DNA strands, such as DNA-functionalized comb polymers and DNA-functionalized gold nanoparticles, have notably sharpened dehybridization, or melting, profiles compared to unmodified DNA:DNA duplexes. This enhanced melting property can be used to improve the selectivity for single-nucleotide polymorphisms and has been attributed to cooperative melting of neighboring duplexes that are within 20-40Å of each other. In this model, the hybridization of complementary multi-DNA materials was proposed to result in a network of ‘parallel’ DNA duplexes where the condensed ion cloud around each duplex can appreciably overlap with those of its neighbors. Under these conditions, the coalesced ion cloud stabilizes the duplexes, causing them to melt as a cooperative unit over a narrow temperature range, instead of participating in partial melting over much broader temperatures. Although aggregated hybrid DNA materials possessing narrow melting transitions are currently used in commercial applications, the fundamental parameters underlying the sharpened melting behaviors of these materials are not well understood. This paper describes the modular, ‘click’ chemistry-based synthesis of a library of small molecule-DNA hybrids (SMDHs) that can be used to unravel the extent that DNA spacing, orientation, and density affect the melting behaviors of hybrid DNA materials.

title: Die Deutsche Gesundheitskrise: Zwangsläufige Auswirkung oder Fehlverhalten der Regierung? (The German Healthcare Crisis: Unavoidable Eventuality or Governmental Mistake?)
abstract: Until recently Germany has boasted one of the most widely acclaimed decentralized, state regulated healthcare systems of the 20th century, yet the past few decades have seen the system steadily decline into an unstable behemoth of increasing costs and lowered care levels. Politicians, academics, and doctors alike agree that there exists an acute crisis, yet no major reform has been undertaken to rectify this situation. Further criticism can be leveled after comparing the current German healthcare crisis with that which gripped Holland until a few years ago. A recent series of major reforms in the Netherlands has led from a previously 'german-esque' system, sharing the same structure and organization with the currently floundering German system, into a new age of lowered costs and broader coverage. This information throws the German inactivity into sharp relief and leaves the educated observer with a burning question: Why hasn't Germany been able to enact a similar reform? This paper provides a semi-historical background of the healthcare systems and crises in both Germany and Holland, before suggesting three hypotheses addressing the specific reasons for the current German political inactivity. The influence of special interest groups, excessive party politics, and the inherent difficulty of mass action afforded through a federalist system were all explored as probable culprits. After an in-depth discussion into each hypothesis, this paper asserts that the current German healthcare crisis stems from an excess of party politics abusing the federalist system, in effect hampering any attempts at unified healthcare policy proposals.

title: Synthesis and Analysis of Spectrally Active Molecularly Imprinted Polymers for the Selective Recognition of Penicillin G-procaine
abstract: Molecular recognition elements in the form of molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) could one day allow rapid, inexpensive screening of infectious diseases to become a simple bedside reality. Recent investigations have also explored the use of MIPs in catalysis, drug delivery, chemical sensing and separation, and screening of drug candidates, among many other applications. Of particular interest in pharmaceutical and environmental applications is the use of MIPs as stationary phases for the selective extraction of specific biomarkers from blood or contaminants from polluted water. To successfully be used in commercial and large scale applications, a reporting system must be coupled to MIPs to report both the successful binding of the specified analyte and the amount of analyte present. With this in mind, monomers were created with the dual abilities to specifically bind a model Penicillin analyte and signal this binding event with changes in their UV-vis and fluorescent spectra. This paper reports the selection of these spectrally active monomers and their subsequent polymerization into MIPs.

title: Tick-Tock Clock: The Effect of Time-Related Stress on Time Management Skills
abstract: The present research examined the effects of academic stress on time management skills. Specifically, a case study was conducted of students from two different universities: Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, United States and the University of Warwick in Coventry, England. It was hypothesized that students from Northwestern University would experience greater level of academic stress resulting from the structure of their courses. It was further hypothesized that this increased stress would result in a greater engagement in time management behaviors. One hundred seventy-nine participants were surveyed. All participants were given a stress survey followed by a time management behavior scale. The surveys were conducted over three different time periods across the semester in order to get a picture of the pattern of stress experienced by students. Results indicated that overall, students at Northwestern University reported greater engagement in time management behaviors than students at the University of Warwick. These results were not significant when averages were compared at the three different time points. Furthermore, differences in stress levels were not statistically significant. However, there were a number of significant effects pertaining to gender, age and time management behavior that are discussed in this paper. Discussion focuses on the basis for these results and the implications for further research.

title: Modeling Meditation Network Structure Using EEG Phase Synchrony and Complex Systems Science
abstract: Neural processing can be visualized as a complex network of interacting systems. Recent graph theoretical analysis of simulated, in vitro and in vivo brain networks has revealed that in many cases, these networks have a discernible small-world hierarchical structure. This study exploited these properties of neural networks by modeling electroencephalogram (EEG) phase synchrony of meditating subjects. Recording electrodes were each represented as ‘nodes’ in a network, with connections between nodes signifying gamma phase synchrony between particular electrode pairs. The resulting network was algorithmically analyzed for underlying modular structure using a recently published hierarchical network module extraction technique. We believe this network-based approach to EEG modeling may offer interesting insights into brain states characterized by functional connectivity via transient phase synchrony.

title: Unnamed Characters in the Tragedies of Sophocles
abstract: Following Aristotle, comments in the works of literary critics Problemata, Vernant and Vidal-Naquet describe the different roles of the Chorus and the individualized characters in Athenian tragedy. These literary critics find that the Chorus represents the views of the fifth-century city-state, while the other characters embody heroes from a mythic past estranged from the typical citizen. This analysis, however, overlooks unnamed characters who appear throughout tragedy, for they play a role that falls somewhere between that of the Chorus and the heroes. The goal of my paper is to analyze the special status of the unnamed characters in the tragedies of Sophocles and the poet’s exploitation of their status in his dramas. I study characters who receive no name throughout the play and are identified only by their profession. Messengers are the most common unnamed characters, but nurses, tutors and priests also make appearances. These characters are typically of low social standing since they are usually household servants. Because Hall studies the disenfranchised characters (e.g. women, slaves and foreigners) of tragedy, she has discussed briefly unnamed characters. She focuses on the social context of these characters, but the goal of this paper is to analyze them in their dramatic context: how they function within the plays themselves.

title: Talking Democracy in Sierra Leone: The 2007 Presidential Election Campaigns and Their Effects on Voter Decision-Making
abstract: For a populace characterized by low levels of literacy and education, but approaching the prospect of democracy, how does the dissemination of political information through electoral campaigns factor into the voting decisions made by citizens? Sierra Leone held its Presidential elections in August and September 2007. In the preceding weeks, 48 interviews were conducted in 8 localities country-wide in order to uncover citizens’ perspectives on the candidates, campaigns, and democracy more generally. While most all voters knew their vote “long before” the campaigns began in early July, thus bringing the significance of this form of political communication into question, survey participants still articulated rational reasoning as to why they would vote for their candidate of choice. Though some respondents cited influences from family, tribe, bribery and intimidation, participants tended, in particular, to base their decisions on performance evaluation of the previous government. Information regarding these results did not come from the campaigns themselves but rather the local and national discussion about the progress made by the previous administration. Although most voters paid “quite a bit” of attention to the campaigns, their influence isolated from other forms of public discourse was limited by the communications infrastructure by which voters are exposed to campaign messages, as well as by cultural norms that discourage criticism of authority figures and the ability to speak to elements of a community that is not one’s own, in this case an opposing party or the environment shaped by an administration that an individual has not yet experienced firsthand.

title: Evaluating Two Pathways for Split Triceps Transfers for Patients with Arthrogryposis: A Computer Simulation Study
abstract: Arthrogryposis is a debilitating congenital condition characterized by multiple joint contractures, including extension contractures of the elbow. Tendon transfer surgeries are indicated if passive elbow flexion is present in an attempt to restore active elbow flexion. However, none of the current tendon transfer surgeries are able restore normal active elbow flexion. In order to address this failure of current surgical interventions, surgeons have proposed a split triceps transfer surgery in which the long head of the triceps is wrapped medially from the posterior to anterior compartment and attached to the ulna or radius. Surgeons are still unaware of the optimal path for the long head of the triceps, so this study sought to determine whether a long or short moment arm would be more successful in restoring active range of motion (ROM) to the elbow. Additional analysis will determine how the preoperative strength of the long head and the force-length properties of the muscle may affect the optimal path for the long head of the triceps. A three-dimensional computer model of the upper extremity was used to simulate two tendon transfer pathways and the biomechanical consequences. The simulated surgeries suggest that a long moment arm for the transferred long head of the triceps would be more effective in restoring active ROM if the transferred muscle is weak and a short moment arm would be more effective if the muscle is stronger. These results appear to be insensitive to where the long head of the triceps operates on the force-length curve.

title: Gender Implications in Hindi Cinema
abstract: In the study of post-colonial Hindi cinema, it is critical to contextualize the impact of Bollywood’s implications with regards to cinema genderfication and the perpetuation of Indian female stereotypes. Very few ‘Westerners’ seem to realize the magnitude of Bollywood, not only as a global influence, but also as an industrial monolith. While Hollywood certainly leads in terms of revenue, it can be argued that Bollywood carries more influence based on audience reach alone. Perhaps even more importantly, the industry has grown alongside India’s invented definition of nationalism, and the two are integrally linked. Sub-continental nationalism has many parallels to Hindi cinema. Both Independent films as well as Bollywood films have played an important role in developing a unique brand of nationalism based on specifically chosen aspects of traditional sub-continental culture. Dr. Vrinda Nabar argues women are often forced to embody aspects of traditional culture when societies are challenged by the strain of globalization. To this effect, women are ‘re-negotiated’ as the country struggles to fully industrialize while maintaining its sense of tradition. Hindi cinema unavoidably plays a role in this negotiation. Although typical Bollywood portrayed women primarily as subsidiary accompaniments to the hero, Hindi cinema is currently going through a rapid transformation with regards to its depictions of women. While Ananda Amritmahal, a professor at the Sophia College in Mumbai argues any change in the portrayal of women in Bollywood films is superficial, director Ram Gopal Varma is trying to inject women with depth and character into films that otherwise cater to the mainstream Bollywood audience.

title: Decision Making Processes in the Market Place
abstract: Individuals do not always make rational decisions in the financial marketplace. A number of factors (for example, self-esteem concerns or emotional processes) can increase the likelihood of irrational decision strategies. These irrational strategies include overweighting ‘sunk costs,’ (i.e., persisting in investing in a previously risky company; Baumeister & Zhang, 2004). The current study will investigate whether these factors increase irrational decision-making (e.g., sunk costs) or risky decision making more generally. This study utilizes a 3 (type of writing task) x 2 (type of investment) to establish the extent to which priming different types of emotional memories influences irrational and risky decision-making. Participants will have the chance to invest hypothetical money in one of two companies. After their initial investment decision, participants will briefly write about either an emotional memory or a control situation. Finally, the participants will have the opportunity to reinvest in one of two companies. Consistent with earlier research, those individuals exhibiting high self-esteem and experiencing an emotional memory are predicted to ultimately lose more money by engaging in risky and potentially irrational decision-making. Specifically, it is predicted that they will overcompensate for any losses they experience in the first round of investments.

title: The Emergency Contraceptive Pill: Knowledge and Attitudes in a University Population
abstract: The emergency contraceptive pill, also known as the morning-after pill or Plan B, is a post-coital regimen used to prevent unintended pregnancy following unprotected intercourse, contraceptive failure, or sexual assault. This study employs the social-psychological Information-Motivation-Behavioral Skills Model as a framework for analyzing the use of the emergency contraceptive pill as a preventive sexual and reproductive health behavior. The purpose of the research is to measure pill knowledge and attitudes among young adults to determine if sex, political affiliation, and religiosity influence knowledge and attitudes and to connect the findings to the current socio-political context and discuss the implications of emergency contraceptive pill use. A comprehensive online questionnaire was used to assess the knowledge and attitudes of a non-random sample of 428 undergraduate students at Northwestern University. While the results show a general lack of detailed, accurate knowledge about the pill, an overwhelming majority of students reported favorable attitudes toward pill use. In addition, chi-square testing found dependent relationships between biological sex and knowledge, political affiliation and attitudes, and religiosity and attitudes. This study concludes that the emergency contraceptive pill is a safe, convenient, and effective contraceptive method that has the potential to reduce the high unintended pregnancy and abortion rates in the United States. To provide young adults with more knowledge about the pill for informed decision-making, the study recommends increased funding for comprehensive sex education, outreach and educational initiatives on college campuses, and strong federal and state policy implementation to promote accurate knowledge about and expanded access to the emergency contraceptive pill.

title: The Impact of Employment and Educational Attainment on Relationships, Career, and Wellbeing: A Possible Selves Study with Undergraduate Women
abstract: Previous research has shown that most female college students expect to pursue a career and raise children in their near future, though many plan to either quit their job or work part time when their children are young. While studies have found that such disruptions can be detrimental to a career, researchers have not considered undergraduate women’s perceptions of possible consequences due to these career paths. Further, since women have increased their presence in graduate and professional schools, it is important to understand the role education might play in women’s future employment plans. In the present study, college women imagined themselves as mothers of young children in one of three different career scenarios: employed full-time, employed part-time, or not employed. They also envisioned having either a bachelor’s degree or advanced degree in their field. In the employed conditions, women rated finance and respect related goals as more likely than the women in the not employed condition. Goals regarding a relationship with the child were more likely for the women in the part-time or not employed conditions than the employed full-time condition. Additionally, women who imagined having an advanced degree or being employed full-time rated employment related goals as more likely than did those who envisioned having a bachelor’s degree or not being employed. Participants in the full-time and part-time employment or advanced degree conditions rated this possible life as more positive than the participants in the condition in which they were not employed or had a bachelor’s degree, respectively.

title: Multicultural Approaches to Learning: An Exploration of a British Academy's Religious Education Curriculum
abstract: Among the educational policies directed at fostering social cohesion in England, the role and purpose of compulsory Religious Education for all British pupils has long been a topic of scholarly debate. This study seeks to examine the process by which a British Academy designs and enacts a Religious Education curriculum and the role of the surrounding community, local government, and school ethos in that procedure. Given the lack of empirical work on current school practices due to frequent changes in national legislation and expectations for schools over the last fifty years, this case study fills the gap in research on present-day programs. Through textual research, student and staff interviews, and field observations, this study aims to understand the political and cultural context within which the curriculum was conceived, how the curriculum is translated in the classroom, and the impact of its teachings on students. On-sight research was performed at Mossbourne Academy during January 2008. Data was analyzed qualitatively guided by themes found in Religious Education literature as well as grounded theory. Analysis confirmed schools’ freedom and lack of accountability in program development as Mossbourne implemented its curriculum independent of government or community oversight. This study concludes that there is a strong relationship between the curriculum’s design, delivery, and effect on students and the school’s ethos. Mossbourne’s ethos, which enforces strict behavior management and discipline, ensures student participation and competency in the course. This research is among the first to explore relationships between school ethos and Religious Education in the UK.

title: Molecular Analysis of the Cadmium-Responsive Gene cdr-1 Expression in Caenorhabditis Elegans
abstract: Many environmental pollutants, such as cadmium, arsenic, and paraquat, have acute effects that result in damage to the genome and proteome and, in humans, are correlated with a wide range of pathologies. In order to protect against or repair the damage caused by these molecules, organisms have a highly conserved array of stress-inducible genes. The goal of this thesis is to elucidate components of the regulatory pathways that govern responses to cadmium in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Utilizing a fluorescent reporter library to visualize cytoprotective gene expression, I observed inducible expression of the following genes with cadmium: mtl-1, mtl-2, and cdr-1. Strong induction of all three genes was observed in the intestine within six hours in response to a broad range of cadmium concentrations (1 µM-1 mM). As the regulatory features of cdr-1, a gene encoding a putative microsomal glutathione transferase, are unresolved on a molecular level, promoter deletions were constructed in order to identify cis-acting regulatory sequences Using truncated promoters, the minimal cdr-1 promoter is no larger than 269 base pairs upstream from the transcription start site. Within this region, there are binding sites for two major intestine-specific transcription factors: ELT-2 and SKN-1. RNA interference of ELT-2, an intestine-specific GATA transcription factor involved in stress resistance, but not SKN-1 reduced cdr-1 expression to control levels, similar to that observed for the known ELT-2 targets mtl-1 and mtl-2. These studies highlight ELT-2 as a critical regulator of cadmium-inducible genes in the intestine and suggest a central function for it in alleviating cadmium toxicity.

title: Buried by the Benta: Cemetery Patterning in Middle Bronze Age Hungary
abstract: In burials lie the transition between life and death. The placement of the dead cross-culturally and throughout history often reflects idealized social stratifications, distributions of wealth and control of resources. In Hungary, Bronze Age cemeteries have been located near tells – gradually built up mounds or hills covering successive remains of ancient communities. At one such tell discovered near Százhalombatta, Hungary, the mortuary practices of the Vatya who occupied the area, and what those practices tell us about this Bronze Age people, remain largely unexplored. This research project focuses primarily on identifying and investigating the relationships between the cemeteries and settlements of the Vatya culture during the Middle Bronze Age in the Benta Valley, Hungary. Using existing research on Middle Bronze Age cemeteries, maps of the Benta Valley, and the current work on settlements conducted by the Benta Valley Project, I created a model to identify Vatya cemeteries in relation to settlements through topographic patterns and survey based on a Vatya burial site signature. Maps created using ArcGIS programs, that include both Middle Bronze Age settlement patterns and density with MBA cemetery patterns, will form a visual representation to develop spatial and topographic relationships of settlement size and location with cemetery size and location in the Benta Valley, to analyze further how the hierarchy of the settlements relates to the hierarchy of the cemeteries. Both located at high elevations transposed across streambeds, Vatya settlements of the dead reflect the settlements of the living with some distortion.

title: Defining the Mechanism of Gene Recruitment to the Nuclear Periphery
abstract: DNA in the eukaryotic nucleus exhibits spatial organization that can rapidly change in response to transcriptional and developmental cues. Studies in yeast and other organisms have found that certain inducible genes are dynamically recruited to the nuclear periphery when transcriptionally active. These findings suggest that proximity of the DNA to the nuclear periphery could play a role in regulating gene expression. Therefore, a fundamental understanding of how genes are recruited to the nuclear periphery can shed insight into how cells target DNA to a specific nuclear location and the functional implications of this controlled targeting event. We are using the yeast GAL1 gene as a model system to dissect the molecular requirements of gene recruitment to the nuclear periphery. Using a candidate approach, we have classified four broad categories of non-essential proteins that might be involved in recruiting genes to the nuclear periphery: which include 1) nuclear pore components, 2) chromatin modifying proteins, 3) nucleoplasmic motor proteins, and 4) other nuclear periphery proteins. Using a gene deletion technique based on homologous recombination, we have generated a collection of null mutants and analyzed the requirement of these protein candidates in GAL1 gene recruitment. By means of a quantitative chromatin localization assay, we have found a subset of nuclear pore components and chromatin modifying proteins to be required for gene recruitment to the nuclear periphery. These results suggest that the nuclear pore complex is the site to which active genes are recruited and that chromatin modifications may play a key role in targeting of active genes to the nuclear periphery.

title: Legacies of Tolerance: Islam and Democracy in Mali
abstract: Since September 11th, 2001, Islam has been increasingly discussed in the media, and one often hears it referred to as being incompatible with democratic forms of government. However, the spotlight has not reached sub-Saharan Africa, and specifically Mali, where evidence appears to support the proposition that a form of nonpolitical Islam peacefully coexists with a democratic government. Scholars such as Samuel Huntington argue that countries with majority Muslim populations are unable to develop into democracies. Mali, the fifth poorest country in the world, has defied this assumption and risen to become one of the most “free” countries in the world, according to Freedom House. This paper seeks to examine why Mali developed into the democratic state it is today. I conducted 100 interviews with Malians, which I analyzed along with books and articles published by academic experts in the fields of Islam, democracy, and Malian history. I have determined four variables that have potentially led Mali to espouse a democratic system of government: Mali’s pre-colonial history, its French colonial legacy, the type of Islam practiced in Mali, and the governing mechanisms currently in place. It is through the examination of these variables that I have come to the conclusion that the “clash of civilizations” hypothesis put forth by Samuel Huntington is flawed and should be reexamined within the African context. Furthermore, it has become clear that Islam and democracy are not in contrast with each other, but have successfully collaborated to develop Mali into the free state that it is today.

title: Divine Representations of Roman Children in Funerary Portraiture
abstract: Children’s funerary monuments provide insight into the ways in which children were viewed and represented in Roman society. Understanding children’s funerary portraiture is especially useful in this regard, as portraits of children often differ significantly from those of adults. In their respective studies of Roman funerary altars and children’s sarcophagi, Diana Kleiner and Janet Huskinson have discussed broader themes of portraiture in funerary iconography. My research examines a particular subset of these depictions - iconographic allusions to divinity in children’s monuments. I suggest that children are often represented with elements of the divine not only to suggest hope for continued life after death, but also as shorthand for unattained stages of adulthood. In this paradox of representation, children can be commemorated in immortal play alongside divine beings, but also in mature roles as an adult god. For this presentation, I will focus upon monuments of girls as Venus and Diana as well as children represented as putti or “baby cupids.” These portrait depictions blend traditional religious and cultural attributes of the divinity represented, such as sexuality or chastity, with allusions to the social norms of adult monuments. In this way, monuments depicting children as divinities emphasize both the child’s young age at death and the adult attainments and characteristics they never lived to fulfill. These depictions can also suggest a class-consciousness, as former slaves often commemorated their free-born children in a manner which suggested the increased social and legal opportunities that their parents lacked.

title: Neural Basis of Social Perception of a Human versus Virtual Human
abstract: Are virtual humans socially understood as human? To investigate this question, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure the neural correlates of perception and social evaluation of two types of agents: an Embodied Conversational Agent (ECA or virtual human) and a real human. Fourteen participants viewed static images of both the human and ECA, rated each image for emotional valence, and completed a post-scan survey on social impressions of the two agents. No significant differences were found in behavioral measures of rating or reaction time, although the real human was rated as more socially relatable in three dimensions. Viewing either kind of agent relative to rest elicited neural activity in a network of brain regions previously associated with social judgments, including left superior temporal sulcus and right fusiform gyrus. Viewing the ECA relative to human resulted in increased activation in superior temporal sulcus, anterior cingulate gyrus, left precuneus, right angular gyrus, and left inferior frontal gyrus, areas associated with social perception, attention, and cognitive control. The condition of human relative to ECA revealed no areas of significant activation. Interestingly, this finding stands in contrast to previous research which suggests passive viewing of humans but not virtual humans elicits greater neural activation in regions associated with social judgment and mentalizing. Our results suggest that while accurate social judgments can be made of either real humans or virtual humans, it appears the latter might require heightened cognitive processing, perhaps because of the novelty and unfamiliarity of virtual humans.

title: Characterizing the Fine Structure of a Novel Protein Processing Signal
abstract: The regulated degradation of proteins by the ubiquitin-proteosome system allows the cell to control processes such as the cell cycle, apoptosis, and cell fate decision. Normally, the proteosome degrades proteins processively to avoid formation of fragments with unwanted functions. Recently, however, two proteins have been identified which are only partially degraded by the proteosome. These proteins include the transcription factors Cubitus interuptus (Ci) and p105, a precursor of NF-κB. As a result of this partial degradation, the fragment assumes functions unique to its partially degraded form. For my project, I characterized the fine structure of the processing signal necessary for fragment formation. The processing signal consists of a sequence of simple amino acid composition followed by a tightly folded domain in the direction of degradation. These elements cause the proteosome to stall at the protein’s folded domain and to cleave the protein upstream of this domain. I investigated the dependence of fragment formation on the length of the simple sequence. I created constructs encoding a tightly-folded domain followed by a complex sequence spacer and then by a simple sequence region of variable length. After transcribing and translating these sequences, I tested processing in in vitro degradation assays. These experiments allowed me to better characterize the fine structure of this novel processing signal. This information will make it possible to identify processing signals in databases and to eventually determine the prevalence of this signal in biology.

title: Ménilmontant: The Loss and Recovery of Internal Experience
abstract: In a post-World War I France disenchanted with the ideals of technological progress and rationality, Dimitri Kirsanoff's 1926 short, experimental film Ménilmontant mirrors this sentiment specifically in its depiction of time: through its content and form it in fact subtly advocates the value of the subjective, internal endurance (that of the central, anonymous young woman played by Nadia Sibirskaïa) over objective, spatialized representations of time. The film displays the overwhelming use of linear temporal measures in running the Parisian workday and their ability to permeate the individual’s mentality, leading to the fragmentation of one’s actual time-as-experienced or what philosopher Henri Bergson deemed as durée. Thus, in opposition to such artificial regulation Kirsanoff includes the equally constant, omnipresent images of flowing water that come to suggest the Bergsonian philosophy of a continuous inner duration that underlies and better represents the overall human experience. Furthermore, Ménilmontant purposely rejects early cinema’s common use of intertitles to indicate the passage of time, not only placing it among the early avant-garde but also directly using film form to indicate the constant stream of life imagery and duration. Finally, it is during the scenes of Sibirskaïa’s solitary moments of self-reflection that further demonstrate film’s capacities in rendering visible the possibility of leaping out of structured time, the coexistence of the past alongside the present, and the inner struggle making up sociologist Georg Simmel’s notion of the metropolis individual in which one’s true interiority becomes oft-lost and suppressed due to socially designated systems and products of modernity.

title: Social Anxiety, Intolerance for Uncertainty, and Interpretive Bias
abstract: Our project investigated the relationship between social anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, and interpretation bias. Previous studies have suggested that socially anxious individuals often interpret ambiguous information in negative ways, but have failed to differentiate between their initial interpretations and more strategic judgments. We predicted that while socially anxious individuals will initially interpret ambiguous situations in negative ways, those individuals with a high tolerance for uncertainty will be more likely to consider multiple explanations on interpretation tasks that allow for strategic thought. To test this hypothesis, 106 Northwestern undergraduates were given two self-report interpretation tasks requiring different degrees of strategic thought. Using a repeated measures regression analysis, the effects of social anxiety and intolerance of uncertainty on different types interpretive biases will be analyzed.

title: Disney’s Broadway Empire: The Intersection of Artistic Ambition and Corporate Synergy
abstract: Since the 1994 opening of "Beauty and the Beast," The Walt Disney Company's presence on Broadway has permanently changed the New York theatrical community. Disney's first stage production was compared to a theme-park attraction, but, following the tremendous artistic and financial success of "The Lion King" in 1997, Disney Theatrical Productions has continued to hire highly respected directors and design teams to develop Disney projects. Disney takes pride in bringing quality family entertainment to diverse audiences, while attempting to match, and ideally exceed, their own prior artistic triumph. Though undeniably benefiting from the power and deep-pockets of the parent company, as well as extraordinary brand recognition, Disney Theatrical Productions has defied naysayers to establish a formidable Broadway presence. Through a variety of published sources and personal interviews, I researched and analyzed the motives and creative process of Disney Theatrical Productions. I also assessed the company's demonstrated artistic ambition and financial success despite intense media bias and prejudice within the theatre industry. My research explored how Disney develops Broadway shows with a sophisticated artistic vision for family audiences; how Disney attracts the talents of visionary creative teams; to what extent critics show bias when confronted with the Disney brand; and the creative development of the Broadway productions of "Aida," "Mary Poppins," and "The Little Mermaid." I concluded that Disney’s Broadway ventures consistently achieve the following three benchmarks for success articulated by Thomas Schumacher, president of Disney Theatrical Productions: audience affection, commercial success, and artistic fulfillment.

title: High Resolution Subwavelength Distance Measurements: a Variable-Angle Standing-Wave Total-Internal-Reflection Optical Microscope
abstract: Over the years optical microscopy has continually evolved and developed into an essential tool for many scientific endeavors. Standing-Wave Total Internal Reflection Microscopy (STIRM), the tool we are developing, is a relatively new strategy for that promises to allow precision measurements of structures and their separations on cell surfaces. We believe that it is possible to achieve resolutions greater than those available with current techniques. STIRM works by exploiting two phenomena that occur in light: the evanescent wave and interference. Evanescent waves are formed when light undergoes Total Internal reflection. These waves are highly attenuated; they decay exponentially over lengths less than a wavelength of light. Interference patterns are formed when two beams of coherent light (derived from a common laser) occupy the same space. Their amplitudes can sum constructively or destructively, giving us an alternating pattern of light and dark fringes. The spacing of these fringes can be calculated from the wavelength of light used, the index of refraction of the material used, and the incident angle of the incoming beams. We have created a prototype that allows us control over the incident angle and the phase angle of our interference pattern. By varying the phase angle at several incident angles, we are able to extrapolate tiny distance measurements of 20nm gold spheres based on the known spacing of the standing wave. When used in conjunction with fluorescence microscopy, STIRM can be an accurate way of making distance measurements smaller than a wavelength of light.

title: Binding State and Society: Taxation and the Development of the Welfare State in Chile and Brazil
abstract: The provision of social benefits and the collection of taxes are two of the most essential and existential functions a state can perform, shaping the relationship between citizens and their state. Yet the interaction of the two elements, and the subsequent implications for how welfare states are financed, has received scant attention, particularly in the developing world. This thesis examines the dramatic divergence of social policy outcomes in two countries with relatively similar economic and political trajectories—Chile and Brazil. While Chile has achieved consistently high levels of universal coverage and benefit provision, Brazil’s system has long been characterized by dramatic inequities and considerable fragmentation. This analysis finds that the initial choice of different finance mechanisms has had profound political, financial, and institutional effects on the creation and evolution of social policy, and concludes that these effects ultimately explain contemporary variation between Chilean and Brazilian welfare regimes. While Brazil relied nearly entirely on payroll taxes through social contributions to fund its nascent social policy regime, Chile was supported by a diverse set of taxes. The heavy and increasing reliance on social contributions in Brazil generated powerful entrenched interests and both power-based and bureaucratic path dependence that ultimately precluded universalization. Chile faced no such opposition to universalization and consolidation due to its diversity of finance sources. This paper also finds that despite supporting massive retrenchment and privatization of the Chilean welfare regime, military dictator Augusto Pinochet’s implementation of a value-added tax ironically facilitated social policy expansion after Chile’s return to democracy.

title: The African Defense Against the Hegelian: Reconciliation of Senghor and Diop
abstract: This piece aims to reconcile the works of two esteemed Senegalese philosophers, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Cheikh Anta Diop through the use of themes as presented in Hegel’s Philosophy of History. Most scholars of these two thinkers agree that the starting point for their individual projects is a rejection of the colonial agenda that had inundated scholarship concerning Africa. However, it is commonly cited that the approaches that Diop and Senghor use—one very scientific, fact-based, systematic one and the other heavily philosophical, culture-based, observational—diverge in defending against the exclusion of Africa from historical and cultural relevance. Current scholarship focuses on how Senghor and Diop differ in two ways: (1) the means through which they engage in their fight against colonialism and (2) their fundamental interpretation of whether the African has any essential differences from the European. I reject this theory of fundamental conflict, arguing that although the process of each is different, the ending principle they each exalt is the same. I chart out this eventual convergence by running the arguments of Senghor and Diop through five themes: Philosophy, Religion, Family Structure, Language, and Aesthetic Contribution. It is through these fundamentally cultural themes that Hegel philosophically attempts to disempower African culture and history. I aim to use these core components of culture not to prove Hegel wrong, but to show that the core parts of Senghor and Diop’s arguments align much more than most are willing to admit.

title: Mechanical Characterization of Self-Assembling Gels for Tissue Regeneration
abstract: The Stupp group is currently investigating a system of molecules, called peptide amphiphiles, which self-assemble into predetermined macromolecular structures under specific environmental cues. For this project, the macromolecular structure of interest is the nanofiber and its self-assembly is induced via changes in pH or via the addition of salts. The formation of nanofibers and their corresponding gels are useful for many applications, most notably those in the field of regenerative medicine. One necessary step in reaching the goal of using peptide amphiphiles in the body is to effectively mimic the mechanical properties, particularly stiffnesses, that naturally occur in our tissues. This requires a precise understanding of how our body's environment affects these properties. Consequently, this project aims to investigate how environmental changes in the body - such as changes in pH, changes in salt concentration, and the presence of other molecules - effects the stiffness of gels formed from peptide amphiphiles.

title: Understanding Gene Recruitment: An Investigation of the Regulatory Elements Involved in Gene Recruitment
abstract: The nucleus is a highly organized structure composed of distinct chromosomal territories. The spatial arrangement of DNA can dramatically influence the transcriptional state of genes in eukaryotic cells. The nuclear periphery was once associated exclusively with silenced genes. However, recent studies find that many genes are actively recruited to the nuclear envelope upon expression, and in some cases this is necessary to promote maximal transcription levels. This inducible association with the nuclear periphery is known as gene recruitment. The INO1 gene in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is one gene that undergoes gene recruitment. Transcription of INO1 is negatively regulated by Opi1. When Opi1 is bound to the INO1 promoter, transcription is repressed and the gene is nucleoplasimic; Opi1 dissociation leads to INO1 activation and recruitment to the periphery. We hypothesize that Opi1 is also involved in regulating gene recruitment of INO1. We have identified an element within the INO1 promoter, known as the Gene Recruitment Sequence (GRS), both necessary and sufficient to target DNA to the nuclear periphery. Integrating the GRS at a distant site in the genome causes targeting of that site to the periphery constitutively. Similarly, cells lacking Opi1 demonstrate constitutive targeting of INO1. Thus, Opi1 may also function as a negative regulator of gene recruitment. I find that targeting Opi1 near either of its two endogenous binding sites in the INO1 promoter is sufficient to repress gene recruitment. These results indicate that Opi1 is involved in regulating gene recruitment and may do so by interrupting the GRS signal.

title: Investigating Mach-IV Scale Facets and Trustworthiness Correlates

people.major: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences & Psychology

abstract: Researching personality correlates of trustworthiness is an important endeavor for psychologists with applications in the working world. Trustworthiness has been shown to be a more powerful behavior than trust, as the former can predict the latter but the opposite does not hold (Chaudhuri & Gangadharan 2007). One scale tested in relation to these two traits, the Mach-IV scale (Christie & Geis 1970), is linked with aspects of personality and has yielded mixed results. While some experimental designs based of the standard Investment game show significant correlations with trust and not trustworthiness, others have found correlation with either both or only trustworthiness (Burkes et al. 2003; Gunnthorsdottir 2002). The proposed study seeks to clarify the relationship of Mach-IV scores on these areas by first investigating the scale’s overall correlations to personality as well as potential multiple factors embedded in the scale. Next, a new Investor game variation involving a confederate and a two-round interaction with the same partner where roles are reversed in each round is tested with the Mach scale as potential predictor of behavior. These modifications are aimed at reducing the variability of responses that were problematic in past experiments as well as magnifying the trustworthiness aspect of the subject’s role during the game. The results of the first part of the study propose that the scale is actually testing two conceptually separate features of Machiavelliansm, internal and external beliefs. The second part of the study fails to lend resolution to the debate in using the scale as a trustworthiness predictor.

title: Bio-Inspired Chitosan Hydrogel Formation
abstract: This study investigates a new method for chitosan hydrogel formation using a catechol-analog crosslinker, 2,4,5-trihydroxybenzaldehyde (Tbz). Chitosan is a well-known polysaccharide with the disaccharide repeat of β-(1,4)-D-glucosamine and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, from chitin deacetylation and has been widely applied for functional biomaterials. Chitin is found in the exoskeleton of arthropods and crustaceans. The use of Tbz to crosslink the chitosan backbone was inspired by the previous study in which dopamine was utilized as a material-independent, chemically active surface adhesive molecule. Dopamine combines the chemical functionality of 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (DOPA) and lysine found in mussel adhesive proteins, Mefp-3 and -5 (Mytilus edulis foot protein-3 and -5), that are specifically located at interfaces between adhesive pads and opposing substrates. Similarly, this chitosan hydrogel system features the amine group functionality in chitosan chains and a catechol-analog crosslinker. However, this system has been designed with multiple forms of chemical reactivity. Under acidic conditions, pH 5.5, the chitosan amine groups covalently bond to the benzaldehyde crosslinker through an imine formation mechanism. The imine is reduced to a secondary amine in the presence of the reducing agent of sodium borohydride. This forms the primary backbone of the hydrogel network. Oxidation of the catechol moieties over time results in further crosslinking between Tbz molecules, facilitating the hydrogel’s unique dynamic phase transition behavior; the hydrogel is first formed in a hydrated phase, and subsequently exhibited a phase transition over time to a dry brittle state. It is hypothesized that the Tbz oxidation “collapses” the hydrogel network.

title: The Race to be Greek: The Distribution of Minority Students Among Greek Letter Fraternities
abstract: This project examines why some minority students at a predominately white university decide to join a fraternity that matches their racial/ethnic background and others join the traditionally "white" fraternities. I analyze three minority groups- African Americans, Hispanics, and Asians. The main variable is which type of fraternity the students joined, and the secondary variables included neighborhood and high school demographics, socialization characteristics, the fraternity selection process, family characteristics, desired qualities of fraternities, and minority students’ consideration of race. This project is not a mere description; it offers a comparative case study between minority students who join fraternities with predominately white memberships and Greek-letter organizations matching their racial/ethnic background. The findings suggest that “race” does play an important role, but they also disprove the argument that claims ethnicity specific organizations promote and encourage self-segregation. Instead of race, factors like support networks along with the knowledge about and connections to Greek-letter fraternities are the most noteworthy influences in minority students’ decisions to join a predominately white fraternity. In addition, minority students are drawn to fraternities matching their race/ethnicity due to the extent to which they are knowledgeable about that organization. At the same time, minority students who join white fraternities are highly critical of the racial/ethnic element of ethnicity-specific fraternities. Finally, the findings also suggest that the notion of culture should be strongly considered as a reason for the decision to join a particular type of fraternity.

title: I temba liyaphilisa: Redefining Development Through the Joe Slovo Anti-Eviction Struggle
abstract: Seeking reconciliation in the post-Apartheid Era, South Africa is faced with addressing massive inequality in a host of areas. Ranked only below Brazil as the most unequal country in the world, suitable housing and employment continue to be detriments to the ruling party African National Congress’s (ANC) quest for ‘development status’. With a substantial constituency living in informal housing, the delivery of effective and sustainable housing for the residents of informal settlements in South Africa is critical. The ANC government, however, has not followed through on its campaign promises, ignoring its urban residents, over half of whom currently reside in informal settlements. In response, thousands of residents, all over South Africa, are currently refusing evictions. This project explores the factors that have led to the mobilization of the anti-eviction movements in informal settlements. More specifically, this project uses interviews and observations of members of the Joe Slovo informal settlement anti-eviction mobilization in Cape Town, South Africa. Attempting to explore the alternative that protesters face if they choose compliance, interviews of Delft residents who have been relocated to Temporary Relocation Areas (TRAs) mandated and organized by the ANC’s Breaking New Ground Initiative. Through analysis of field data, the project seeks to parallel the struggle against evictions and for inclusion with the negritude movement expressed by Aimé Césaire and Leopold Senghor. By presenting the words of Joe Slovo residents themselves, this research contributes to the limited literature on informal settlements and gives voice to those who have often been silenced by legal, administrative, and political actions.

title: That's No Way to Say Goodbye: The Jewish Community in Cochabamba, Bolivia
abstract: “That’s No Way To Say Goodbye” is a documentary film that gives audiences a view into the disappearing Jewish community in Cochabamba, Bolivia and what it means to be a part of it. In 1939, Bolivia was one of the only countries in the world to open their doors to Jews fleeing Nazi Europe. While some tried to establish roots in Bolivia, others thought of it merely as a temporary home, eventually hoping to reach more desirable locations with larger Jewish communities. Over time, this instability has led to a major decrease in the country’s Jewish population. While Bolivia’s Jews are almost completely lacking in research attention, the film hopes to shed light on this unfamiliar story of the Jewish Diaspora. The twenty-one-year-old filmmaker looks to his own generation of Jews living in Cochabamba, and what they think of this disappearance. Their views highlight a major conflict plaguing many young Jews in communities around the world today – the battle of preserving one’s cultural identity versus an inevitable yearning for cultural assimilation. In filming the documentary and exploring this issue, the filmmaker also questions his own Judaism.

title: The Effect of Socioeconomic Status on Empathy and Helping
abstract: Empathy, one person’s emotional reaction that is elicited by and congruent with the emotional state of another person, is fundamental for successful human interaction. In order for people to communicate effectively and coexist peacefully, they must understand one another. Previous research has shown that people who identify themselves as members of a specific group display stronger empathic reactions to other members of that group and are more likely to help them. However, this research has examined groups that tend to be more essential to individuals’ identities, such as sexuality, race, and nationality. My study investigates whether this behavioral pattern applies to a social construct that is secondary to identity: socioeconomic status (SES). We measured the emotional reactions and helping intentions of participants who represented the extremes of the socioeconomic spectrum to targets of both SES groups in positive and negative situations. Our results showed that a three-way interaction between the SES of the participant, event valence and the SES of the target approached significance, and with more power further research would yield significance. In addition to SES group identification, we found that social dominance orientation (SDO), or the belief that there should be societal hierarchy, was a major predictor of empathy and helping behavior. People higher on SDO were much less likely to empathize with the target or help them. The implications of these results can inform us about altruism, charity, philanthropy, and general helping behavior.

title: Water-Sharing, the Punjab, and Indo-Pakistani Disputes: Re-Analyzing the Success of the Indus Waters Treaty
abstract: The Indus Waters Treaty is seen as a symbol of hope for relations between India and Pakistan as well as a sign of water sharing cooperation in the Indus Basin. While internationally the treaty was considered a triumph, the question remains whether this treaty addressed issues at the local level or whether these interests were subjugated to international concerns. The Punjab, almost completely within the Indus Basin, was developed by the British as an agricultural center through the development of irrigation. In 1947, in response to nationalist demands, the Punjab was split into Indian Punjab and Pakistani Punjab. The irrigation system’s integrity was destroyed because the border cut across its canals. As a result of the borders, a water conflict between India and Pakistan emerged, compounded by tensions over Kashmir, refugees, and economic assets. The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960, a seeming success for both water and Indo-Pakistan relations. The treaty, however, again partitioned the Punjab by dividing the Indus Basin rivers between the two countries. This thesis seeks to answer: “On what criteria is the ‘success’ of the treaty based?” It provides insight into how India and Pakistan prioritized demands based on political needs and questions how the treaty might be judged from a local perspective, a perspective ignored by existing literature. This thesis concludes that the treaty’s ‘success’ must be tempered by its failures and thus the treaty may not be a symbol of collaboration for the resolution of water conflict.

title: “In the Bonds of Woman and the Slave”: The Woman/Slave Analogy in Woman’s Rights Discourse before and after the Civil War
abstract: The organized movement for woman’s rights was closely linked with the abolition movement from its birth in 1848. As a result, the rhetoric of antislavery permeated feminist discourse and women frequently compared their lives as married women without legal status to the lives of chattel slaves by deploying an analogy between all women and slaves. This study will argue that the woman/slave analogy first brought the feminist and abolitionist movements together, and then divided them along male-female and black-white lines. To study the analogy before and after the Civil War, this project examines the usage of the analogy in national convention rhetoric including the 1860 Tenth National Woman’s Rights Convention, the 1866 Eleventh National Woman’s Rights Convention, the 1867 First Anniversary of the American Equal Rights Association, and the 1869 Anniversary Convention of the American Equal Rights Association. This study argues that usage of the woman/slave analogy did not disappear throughout post-Civil War national convention debates; rather, the analogy changed. In 1860, women argued that they were bonded to their husbands like slaves to their masters. After the Civil War, women no longer argued they were explicitly enslaved, but understood that women were like slaves because they had similar work to do to secure civil rights. However, by 1869, as the African American civil rights movement and woman’s rights movement experienced growing tension over the priorities of the reform coalition, women again began to argue again in conventions that they were slaves to angry and ignorant men.

title: Using Fluorescence to Characterize Trp-41 and C-terminal Domain Movement during Activation in the Influenza M2 Protein
abstract: Despite medical advances, the influenza virus still results in 36,000 deaths per year in the United States. This has caused researchers to strive to discover alternative strategies in combating the virus. One strategy involves inhibiting the crucial M2 proton channel protein located in the virus membrane. M2 activation occurs when surrounding pH decreases, as in an endosome. The lower pH results in M2 permitting proton conductance, lowering the pH within the virion interior. This in turn causes the release of influenza RNA from the viral membrane protein and allows the RNA to diffuse into the cytoplasm, infecting the cell. Currently, the M2 activation mechanism is unknown. Two residues, His-37 and Trp-41, have been determined to be necessary for M2 function. By understanding how even one of these residues changes conformation when M2 is activated, new methods for disrupting M2 activation can be developed. The indole side chain of Trp-41 is inherently fluorescent. Dyes that undergo quenching by Trp-41 can be placed at particular locations on the protein and the amount of emission quenching can be measured. Quenching directly correlates to the distance between the Trp-41 and the dye and changes in the amount of quenching will show the movement of Trp-41 during activation. This experiment has been conducted from the ecto-domain of M2 and repeating them from the cytoplasmic domain will allow for comparison. By using fluorescence, Trp-41 conformation change during activation and accessibility will be observed. From this new ideas can be developed on inhibiting M2, particularly at Trp-41, and combating the virus.

title: Beyond the Walls: Moroccan Religious Communities and the Fracturing of Martin Buber’s Dialogic
abstract: Religious conflict pervades the world today. The alienation of religious communities from Israel-Palestine to India has produced an international culture of discrimination, violence and fear. By addressing the critical dynamics of religious interaction through a relational framework, this research seeks to envision a more peaceful world system.
