Jewish philosopher Martin Buber forwards a relevant dialogical theory based on the genuine turning toward the other and engagement in relations of mutual subjectivity, manifest in his classification of the primary relations I-It and I-Thou and his exploration of community. This study applies Buber’s philosophy to the Moroccan context in order to understand issues of religious identity and interaction. Morocco is a pertinent illustration of the boundaries and contacts between communities of believers, as it was once home to the largest Jewish community in the Islamic world. Morocco is not only a relevant, but a timely case study, as its Jewish community is rapidly dwindling; the current Jewish population hovers around two thousand, a scant one percent of the number fifty years ago. Using Buber’s theory as an analytical tool alongside socio-historical analysis and interviews with members of the Jewish community in Casablanca, Moroccan Jewry is examined within three paradigms: interdependence of the marketplace, dynamic of the Jewish quarter, or mellah, and competing forces of identity. As the complex inter-religious relations are clarified, analysis reveals that Morocco’s history is marked with moments and places where the dialogic had true potential. However, dialogue became fractured rather than actualized due to mitigating circumstances, most especially third party intervention.

title: Habitability of Planets in Binary Star Systems
abstract: Roughly 20% of the known planetary systems are found within binary stars. A binary companion is known to affect the orbital evolution of a planet through long-term perturbations. These perturbations are capable of inducing high levels of eccentricity onto the planetary orbit, diminishing the planet's prospects for harboring life. As the search for habitable planets elevates, it has become important to understand the conditions that lead to habitable and unhabitable orbital behaviors of planets within a binary system. Although the orbital evolution of a single planet within a binary is easily predicted, multiple planet systems within a binary have not been studied carefully because of the additional interactions and the larger parameter space. Indeed, a study of multiple planets within a binary is more realistic and relevant because both observations and planet formation theories suggest that multiple planet systems are more likely to form. To investigate the habitability of such systems, we simulated the orbital evolution of an extensive set of systems with an Earth-like planet and a gas-giant planet within a binary star. The simulations show that the Earth-like planet will exhibit a variety of orbital behaviors that are sensitively dependent on the location of the gas-giant planet. Furthermore, we find that these behaviors can be predicted by a semi-analytical analysis of the various perturbations involved within the planetary systems. With the physical understanding of the systems in our simulations, we can infer the possible behaviors of planets in binary systems to aid in the search for habitable planets.

title: The Effects of Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance on Memory, Evaluation and Attribution of Social Interactions
abstract: The current study examines the way attachment anxiety and avoidance lead to differences in the processing of social information, influence the evaluation of social interactions and shape the interpretation of ambiguous social situations. Sixty-eight undergraduate psychology students read a series of 30 fictional events described as part of a college student's "daily event diary." Diary events could be categorized as individual, describing a task the diary's writer completed that day, or social, describing an interaction with a friend or classmate. Additionally, each event was positive, negative or ambiguous/neutral in valence. After reading the diary, participants completed three tasks related to social processing: a memory task, an event evaluation task, and an attribution task. In the memory task, participants high in attachment anxiety recalled more events that contained social interactions, especially interactions that were ambiguous rather than clearly positive or negative. In the evaluation task, individuals high in attachment anxiety were significantly more likely to perceive ambiguous social interactions as rejecting while individuals high in attachment avoidance showed a marginal tendency towards interpreting the same interactions as ignoring. Finally, when comparing explanations for the events, individuals high in attachment avoidance were significantly less likely to attribute a negative but ambiguous social experience to the diary writer, while individuals high in attachment anxiety were marginally less likely to attribute the experience to situational causes. These results support previous findings that attachment style influences cognition, as well as identifying specific ways in which attachment anxiety and avoidance modulate perception of the social world.

title: Review of Hispanic Women & HPV: Can Policy Makers Reduce Cervical Cancer Among Those at Highest Risk?
abstract: Hispanic women are among the most susceptible populations to cervical cancer. As such, they are also among those who may benefit most from the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. The future success of HPV vaccination relies on adult women’s acceptance of vaccinations as well as parents’ readiness to have their adolescent child vaccinated. This project systematically reviewed HPV vaccination patterns among the Hispanic population through an analysis of data in PubMed, CINAHL, PsychINFO as well as journals likely to publish information on this topic. I searched for articles in the English language using the following keywords: hispanic, latina, human papillomavirus vaccine, acceptance, and attitude. In addition, germane articles were reviewed that assessed ethnic women’s acceptance patterns towards vaccinations more generally. The data demonstrate that Hispanic women overwhelmingly accept the HPV vaccine. Hispanic women unanimously indicated that they would get the HPV vaccine, and believed that the vaccine was effective compared to other minority groups, such as African Americans, who were more skeptical. Furthermore, Hispanic parents are the most likely ethnic group to vaccinate their daughter before age 13. Still, socio-economic barriers inhibit Hispanic women from getting this immunization. The study concludes that Hispanic women do have the potential to overwhelmingly accept the HPV vaccine; however, the cost, lack of awareness of HPV and its link to cervical cancer, and culturally inappropriate outreach programs compound to construct systematic barriers to HPV vaccination. Thus, effective vaccine programs that help reduce the risk of cervical cancer among Hispanic women should utilize sources trusted by these women to disseminate information.

title: Social Strategies and Rejection Experiences
abstract: Following a rejection experience, individuals may modify their social behavior in order to facilitate future interactions. This exploratory study examined both the verbal and non-verbal strategies employed by individuals during a covertly videotaped interaction with a confederate after either a rejection or inclusion experience. The interactions were unscripted and naturalistic. Verbal strategies coded included self-disclosure and incidence of laughter, while non-verbal strategies included smiling and instances of physical mimicry. Success ratings were also obtained from confederates’ post-interaction and considered with respect to the array of behaviors displayed by participants.

title: Sustaining Peace: Black Electoral Politics and Robert F. Kennedy, Indianapolis 1961-1968
abstract: On April 4th, 1968, Martin Luther King was assassinated in Memphis, TN. That same night in Indianapolis, presidential hopeful Robert F. Kennedy prepared to give a campaign speech in an impoverished black neighborhood. Upon news of King’s death however, Kennedy instead informed the crowd of the assassination; delivering an inspired address imploring the black community to emulate King and embrace wisdom and peace in the face of disorder. Indianapolis, unlike other cities, did not erupt in violence after King’s murder. Many historians and media representations have subsequently attributed the peace in Indianapolis to Kennedy’s words. My research, pursued with a summer 2007 URG, intended to investigate how and why Kennedy’s rhetoric held violence in abeyance that night. Over the course of a year’s worth of archival research at the JFK Library, the Indiana Historical Society, and the Indiana State Library, my project changed considerably. I discovered, significantly, that the Indianapolis black community sustained an engagement with political institutions and non-violent protest throughout the 1960s. The tranquility that characterized the city after King’s death was rooted not in Kennedy’s words but in the belief that electoral politics and non-violence had and would continue to work for civil rights progress. My work led me to write a thesis that complicated the typical late sixties narrative of civil rights radicalism. I demonstrated, through RFK and Indianapolis blacks, that black communities continued to agitate for progress through conventional frameworks at a time when many perceive militant solutions to have dominated the civil rights landscape.

title: Mastering the Feminine Market: Renegotiating Conjugal Debt in Chaucer's 'Shipman's Tale'
abstract: Critics writing about Chaucer’s Shipman’s Tale have long focused upon the frank connection between sexual and mercantile exchange within the tale. The developing market system created deep cultural anxiety about the instability of value, which Chaucer manipulates with his repeated conversion of one hundred francs to sex both within and without a legal marriage. While the majority of criticism has focused on the dubious worth of the merchant’s world, I argue that, regardless of the morality of her actions, the merchant’s wife in the tale has benefited from the new system of economics, taking the lessons learned in the marketplace and using them to rewrite her marriage contract with her husband. The result of this revision is to create an entirely new category of sexual relations within marriage, allowing the tale to indirectly deal with the problematic (and impossible to criminalize) issue of marital rape.

title: The Promise and Pitfalls of Perspective Taking in Intergroup Contexts
abstract: This project sought to better understand recent research that suggests that perspective taking is a viable de-biasing strategy in interracial interactions. However, past research is limited to situations in which there is no potential for the individual to be evaluated by the target. The potential for evaluation is a key element in all types of interactions, as it affects the psychological processes employed during the interaction. Consequently, these effects can have a large impact on the interaction, and, more importantly, the attitudes that each person forms toward the other person following the interaction. The present research examined the effects that perspective-taking has on interactions in which evaluation potential was both present and absent. While watching a short video of a black student, participants were asked to either adopt her perspective or to maintain a neutral perspective. After this perspective-taking manipulation, participants were either led to believe that the other student would or would not hear an audio recording that they would make. The audio was then coded for content and quality in order to evaluate the possibility for both positive and negative effects of evaluation potential on perspective taking. Lastly, participants filled out self-report measures regarding their attitudes toward the target.

title: Structure Determination and Characterization of UCuOP, UCu0.6Sb2, and UFeSe3 Three Uranium Compounds Containing a First-Row Transition Metal
abstract: The oxypnictides UCuOP, LaFeOP, LaFeOAs, and LaNiOP were synthesized in recent yerars. UCuOP shows complex dependence of magnetic behavior on temperature, whereas the other three compounds were found to be superconductors. The aims of the present work were (1) to resynthesize UCuOP and perform in-depth characterization of its single crystals, (2) synthesize uranium analogues of the lanthanum compounds, and (3) substitute other pnictogens (P, As, Sb) and chalcogens (S, Se, Te) to produce new related compounds. Synthesis attempts yielded three compounds: UCuOP, UCu0.6Sb2, and UFeSe3. The compounds UCuOP and UCu0.6Sb2 were synthesized at 1273 K; UFeSe3 was synthesized at 1023 K. UCuOP and UCu0.6Sb2 crystallize in a closely related structure in the space group P4/nmm of the tetragonal system with two formula units per cell. UFeSe3 crystallizes in the orthorhombic space group Cmcm with four formula units per cell. In UCuxSb2, the cell dimensions change as a function of x in accordance with Vegard's law. Magnetic susceptibility measurements on UCuOP show antiferromagnetic ordering at 222(2) K. Magnetic susceptibility measurements on UFeSe3 show a paramagnetic behavior.

title: SCN-enriched Transgenic Expression of Clockwt Restores Circadian Wheel Running Behavior in Clock∆19 Mutant Mice

people.major: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences

abstract: Most organisms possess an endogenous circadian rhythm that drives biological functions and mechanisms to operate periodically, in cycles of approximately 24 hours even in the absence of any environmental cues such as light. Although, most peripheral organs and tissues in mammals have circadian rhythms in isolation, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the brain is recognized as the dominant circadian pacemaker that coordinates the peripheral circadian oscillators. A dominant negative mutation in the Clock (Clock∆19) gene, a primary transcriptional activator in the circadian feedback loop, lengthens the free-running period in mice and results in arrhythmic wheel-running behavior in constant darkness. Previously, a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) was used to drive the transgenic overexpression of wildtype CLOCK to rescue the aberrant circadian wheel-running behavior observed in Clock∆19 mutant mice. In BAC transgenic mice, transgenic overexpression of Clockwt mimics the spatial expression of endogenous Clockwt gene expression, which results in the overexpression of Clockwt in virtually all tissues throughout the body. To investigate the roles of the SCN and the central nervous system in the control of circadian rhythms, we utilized the tetracycline transactivator (tTA) system to conditionally drive the expression of the Clockwt transgene in a brain-specific and temporally-controlled manner in Clock∆19 mutant background mice. Our results show that the phenotypic state of the Clock∆19 mutant animals is dependent on Clockwt transgenic expression and that overexpression of the Clockwt transgene in the SCN and CNS of Clock∆19 mutant mice is sufficient in restoring their free-running period and circadian wheel-running rhythmicity in constant darkness.

title: Visualization of Individual mRNA Transcripts in Single Living Yeast Cells
abstract: Divergent gene pairs—two genes oriented “back-to-back” along a stretch of a chromosome— uniquely focus attention on a fundamental problem in gene regulation. How does a gene regulatory protein obeying only the laws of physics “know” which gene it is supposed to be regulating? Traditional studies of transcriptional regulation—how a gene gets turned on or off—measure average values across cell populations, but do not answer this question. For example, a study might find that each cell in a given population possesses on average 0.7 mRNA molecules of a given gene. A fraction of a molecule cannot exist; some cells must have zero molecules, while others have some or perhaps many molecules. These studies also require killing the cell population and, as such, cannot observe the progression of regulatory events over time. Therefore, we are developing a novel experimental approach based on sequence-specific RNA binding proteins fused to fluorescent reporters, which will allow us to count individual mRNA molecules in single living yeast cells in real time. We are developing two independent such systems, with different RNA sequence specificities and different colors, to simultaneously study the expression of both genes of a divergent pair. By altering the shared promoter site of a divergent pair and literally visualizing the resultant change in transcription, we will tease apart the details of the mechanisms that allow regulatory proteins to regulate only the genes they need to.

title: Probing Electron Capture Supernovae: X-Ray Binaries in Starbursts
abstract: X-Ray binaries are double star systems consisting of a dense compact object, such as a neutron star or black hole, in tight orbit around another star. Stellar material is transferred from the star onto the compact object, creating extremely bright X-Ray emissions, which are easily detected by modern X-Ray telescopes such as the Chandra X-Ray Observatory. Due to their short lifetime, X-Ray binaries are highly correlated with recent star formation activity, and are thus the best tool for determining the recent star formation history of extragalactic sources. Here, I will show theoretical models of the X-Ray binary population resulting from a large burst of star formation activity, focusing on activity between 25-60 million years after star formation. During this interval, the X-Ray binary population is highly impacted by an event known as an electron-capture supernovae, in which electrons merge with the heavy elements inside a massive star to create explosions significantly different from traditional iron core-collapse supernovae. While electron-capture systems may form a significant portion of the observed neutron star population, existing theoretical models dispute both the percentage of systems, which will undergo electron-capture, as well as the energetics of the electron-capture process. I will show how X-Ray binary observations uniquely allow us to constrain the population of electron-capture supernovae and use accepted values of these parameters to explain the overabundance of X-Ray binary sources in the Small Magellanic Clouds.

title: Social Anxiety and Online Communication: A Conservative Strategy for Friendship Formation
abstract: The relationship between social anxiety and a tendency to communicate online as opposed to in person was investigated. Eighty-five Northwestern University undergraduates completed questionnaires about their use of online communication in exchange for credit in an introduction to psychology course. The results indicate that socially anxious individuals tend to prefer online social communication as compared with non-socially anxious individuals. Specifically, socially anxious individuals prefer to meet a new person and continue to communicate with casual acquaintances online, while in-person communication with close friends seems to be a universal preference. This study demonstrates that socially anxious individuals differ in the way they prefer to communicate and suggests that they employ a more conservative strategy with regard to friendship formation.

title: The Urban Garden Project
abstract: Urban community gardens are filled with hope, promise and life. Often found in low-income, high-crime neighborhoods, these gardens offer havens of peace. They serve as outdoor community centers where people meet, work, learn and grow together. People in community gardens connect with the land, with each other, and with the healthy, homegrown, culturally appropriate food they grow. In a country fed by fast food, these Eden’s of fresh, local vegetables are more important than ever. Last summer I worked in, studied and experienced community gardens in San Francisco, Chicago and Boston. I investigated the social and cultural importance of urban community gardens through the eyes of the people that work in them. I chose these cities for their local support of green space, enthusiasm for urban gardening, and for the diversity of people, communities and landscape that they offer. I spent three weeks in each city, focusing on one garden per week. The gardens I worked with were in different neighborhoods and were different sizes. Some grew vegetables, others only flowers. The selection allowed me to work with people of different ages, ethnicities and classes in order to find their common experiences in urban community gardens. I did interviews, conducted research, observed behavior and experienced the communities around the gardens. Throughout the past ten months, I have turned the research, experiences and stories into an original play about one community garden. The Northwestern Theater Department is now producing the play, the GARDEN, which will be performed May 2 & 3, 2008 in the Struble Theatre.

title: Correlates among Regional Brain Activity and Children's Emotions to Structured Tasks
abstract: Current research suggests a lateralization of brain activity when an individual experiences different emotions. This lateralization is split into positive emotions, associated with the left prefrontal cortex (PFC) and negative emotions, associated with the right PFC. These findings come from studies focused on adults in resting states. The current study examines children’s brain correlates of emotion during emotion-eliciting tasks. Three-year-old participants completed 6 structured emotion-eliciting tasks while their brain activity across frontal regions was measured using near-infared spectroscopy (NIRS). They then engaged in several tasks meant to elicit different types of emotion. Both biological and behavioral data was coded. Findings of the correlates of behavioral expressions of different emotions (happiness, anger, sadness, and fear) with brain activity across frontal regions will be discussed. Such findings have important implications for how children develop emotions and could lead to a better understanding of the etiology of mood disorders.

title: Leaving the Number Behind Bars: South African Prison Gangsters in a Struggle for Post-Release Redemption
abstract: I received an Eric Lund Reporting and Research Grant through Medill to return to Cape Town, South Africa, where I worked for the daily Cape Argus newspaper for six months last year. During the last month of my previous stay, I began a regular correspondence with a member of the notorious 28s prison gang who was trying to put his past behind him. I did extensive research on the brutal underworld of South African number gangs, which are based heavily on Zulu mythology. On my return trip, I interviewed three rehabilitated number gangsters, a senior warden at the maximum security Pollsmoor Prison, a rehabilitation group and an academic who was the son of one of my gangster sources. I became especially close with one, named Melvyn Matthews, and after meeting with him on multiple occasions he showed me the house he was building in the Cape Flats. He is now a notable community organizer of the Kaapse Klopse Karnival, an annual Cape Town festival. Another two sources were essentially the "Bonnie and Clyde" of the Cape Flats, a husband-wife crime team who now work to rehabilitate prison gangsters. I have transcripts from our interviews as well as photographs of many of my sources.

title: An Evaluation of Current Medical Treatment Practices in India in a Cultural and Religious Context
abstract: In countries around the world, the popularity and utilization of complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) options has been increasing and is relatively widespread. Two thirds of the population worldwide uses some type CAM method. India's case is particularly interesting because the alternative treatment options are professionalized systems of medicine, often providing primary medical care, particularly for diseases such as cancer, AIDS, arthritis, asthma, diabetes, and epilepsy. The history of complementary and alternative treatment and biomedicine in Indian medicine is complex due to the history of external colonizing forces in India that led to the development of Arabic Unani medicine, European medicine, and homeopathy, in a society in which the indigenous system, Ayurveda, was most prominent. Despite external influences, these four medical systems have remained prominent avenues for treatment. Not only do these forms of medicine provide insight about treatment practices, but they also shed light on how illness is perceived. The purpose of this study was to understand the relationship between the mind-body and alternative medical systems branches of complementary alternative treatment and biomedicine in present-day India using a model of epilepsy to elucidate the conflicts between the two and the roles that each have played in the context of illness. It was found that most patients attempted several different types of treatment options, including both allopathic and CAM. Considerations for treatment selection included religiosity, economic considerations, and psychological understanding of the etiology of epilepsy as an illness. Belief in spiritual possession, punishment due to former sins, and exorcism as a cure for epilepsy were present, particularly amongst patients of lower socioeconomic status.

title: Effects of Half and Half Addition on Antioxidant Power of Coffee
abstract: Recent research has shown that dairy products bind to chlorogenic acid, a major antioxidant present in coffee beans. Samples of coffee were brewed and mixed with half and half, and then high resolution 1H NMR spectroscopy experiments were run on the samples and compared to results with reduction potential to test whether the binding of milk products and chlorogenic acids resulted in a drop of coffee’s antioxidant power. The results show an initial drop in both chlorogenic acid NMR peak height and reduction potential with the half and half addition. With continued addition of half and half, however, a chlorogenic NMR peak with a shift around 7.4 ppm began to rise, corresponding to a similar rise in the reduction potential, implying the production of a novel chlorogenic acid isomer with antioxidant properties through the addition of dairy products to coffee.

title: Possible Selves in Psychotherapy Narratives
abstract: For many individuals, psychotherapy is an important experience which allows people to reassess past goals in favor of new ones. More important than actual goal change is the way in which people perceive their goals to have changed as a function of the psychotherapy process. This perceived personal change and growth speaks to the power of therapy towards providing a healthier view for the future. In the current study, participants who had recently completed psychotherapy were asked to narrate their ideal view of themselves and their goals in the future, also known as their current best possible self. They were then asked to retrospectively recall their best possible self before the start of therapy. These past and present selves were coded on the dimensions of realism, concreteness, valence, approach versus avoidance goals, and six adapted levels of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, belongingness, esteem, self-actualization, and self-transcendence goals. Compared with retrospectively narrated accounts of goals before therapy, post-therapy goals were more realistic, more concrete, more positive and more approach-based. The post-therapy narratives also contained fewer physiological goals, more self-actualization goals, and more self-transcendence goals. These results suggest that individuals think about their goals in a more psychologically healthy way following therapy. Additionally, individuals view the process of psychotherapy as moving them higher up on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs.

title: Effects of Tenure on CEO Performance
abstract: In an ever-changing business environment, companies across all industries are beginning to change their Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) every few years. Possible reasons for this dynamic include the board's desire to hire someone who will steer it in a new direction, the current CEO is not leading the company in a direction that will allow it to financially perform above-par, or the current CEO decides to resign. Regardless of the reason, many people believe that the leadership of its CEO can greatly affect the financial performance of a company. One of the factors that this report investigates is the impact of tenure on the effective leadership of a CEO. Tenure is the amount of time that a CEO has been with a company, both as a CEO and in his or her previous positions. Our project aims to analyze the financial performance of a company (as indicated by long-term stock price) versus the tenure of its CEO and to determine if there really is a correlation. 322 of the Fortune 500 companies’ CEOs were classified as either “insider” or “outsider” CEOs. The average five-year stock price growth between companies in both categories was calculated to determine which category of CEOs performed better.

title: Rural World Gained: The Migration of Farmers into Northeast Louisiana During the Mid-Twentieth Century
abstract: In the late 1950s and early '60s, amidst an overcrowding agricultural landscape, a throng of farmers from Southeast Missouri and Central Arkansas seized opportunity to better their lives and continue their farming tradition for future generations of their families. They migrated to Northeast Louisiana where land was being cleared and new cropland was available in abundance; they overcame numerous hardships; and in the end they transformed Northeast Louisiana into the thriving agricultural region it is today, preserving both their way of life and a small piece of the rural ethos that is so prevalent in the American imagination.

title: Synthesis and Electrochemical Characterization of Metal-Modified Monolayers
abstract: The goal of my research is to observe how various sulfur-based linker groups affect the rate of electron transfer of metal-modified self-assembled monolayers. Numerous experiments have been done to study the rate of electron transfer in monolayers with a thiol linker group as the attachment to an electrode. This study focused on the rate of electron transfer in monolayers of dithiocarbamates, thiocarboxylic acids, and dithiocarbonates as the linker group. Ferrocene-containing molecules with these different linker groups were designed in order to directly compare the electron transfer rates. Cyclic voltammetry and alternating current voltammetry are used to observe the rate of electron transfer.

title: The Determination of the Reactive Oxygen Species Released during the CCS Mediated Copper Loading Mechanism of SOD1
abstract: Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1) is a protein that is associated with the pathogenesis of familial Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (fALS). SOD1 is an enzyme that catalyzes the dismutation of superoxide radicals. SOD1 maturation is mainly facilitated by another protein, a molecular chaperone called Copper Chaperone for Superoxide Dismutase (CCS). SOD1 requires several post-translational modifications to become fully active. These modifications include the binding of Cu1+ to SOD1 and the formation of a stabilizing intramolecular bond within SOD1(1). To activate SOD1 via the addition of copper to the active site, copper has been proposed to be guided to the binding site by CCS in a process that involves an intermolecular disulfide formation between the CCS and SOD1 upon exposure to molecular oxygen and the isomerization of this disulfide bond to an intramolecular disulfide bond within SOD1(1). The requirement for oxygen in the formation of the SOD1 intermolecular disulfide bond to CCS and the ultimate SOD1 intramolecular disulfide bond is known(1). What is not known, however, is the oxygen species that is formed during this process as well as the exact timing of the copper transfer. This project aims to answer these two unknown aspects of the mechanism through the use of various fluorescent dyes and electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy.

title: Effects of Training on Pitch-reflex
abstract: The production of correct vocalization patterns in many birds and mammals, including humans, requires careful monitoring of auditory feedback. Although research has proven that auditory feedback is essential for voice fundamental frequency control, the exact mechanisms of this phenomenon are still unknown. Studies have supported the idea of the audio-vocal system monitoring feedback to control pitch fluctuations. When subjects are asked to vocalize while hearing the sound in near-real time, a computer-shift in the pitch heard in the headphones will result in a change in the pitch of the vocalization. Subjects reflexively alter their pitch in response to the change they hear. Because of the automatic nature of the response and its presence without training, the audio-vocal response to the unexpected change in pitch is termed the pitch-shift reflex. Perceptual acuity (better ability to hear pitch differences) and vocal training (formal singing lessons) have been shown to bring about larger pitch-shift reflexes. Thus, we propose to train naïve subjects to become more attuned to the pitch they are vocalizing at. This heightened awareness will result in higher sensitivity to stimuli during the post-tests compared to the pre-tests, and during the later sessions compared to the earlier sessions. If these results are observed, it would suggest that the pitch-shift reflex, though involuntary, can be trained to react in a particular way. This training regimen could then, in theory, be modified for use in a clinical setting in the treatment of voice disorders relating to pitch-control.

title: Tailored to Fit: A Study of Member States Response to European Social Guidelines
abstract: In 1997, the Member States of the European Union approved further integration of the states through common social policies. This provision of the Treaty of Amsterdam created the foundation for the passage of European soft law, non-binding European guidelines for national policies and institutions. Policy formulation at the European level created discrepancies between European guidelines and existing national policies and institutions. While some Member States’ policy preferences “fit,” or aligned, with European guidelines, other states experienced a “misfit.” The study aimed to identify how three Member States with fit and misfit welfare preferences attempted to comply with European standards by analyzing in the cases of childcare and gender pay gap guidelines. A comparative analysis of Sweden, Germany and England’s efforts to incorporate childcare and gender gap guidelines revealed the type of reform used by Member States to incorporate the policy affected the state’s ability to make progress toward compliance. Member States integrated European social policy into national welfare regimes by adapting existing institutions, recycled reform, or by crafting new institutions to address European policies. Member States with good fits to European guidelines were able to approach compliance by incorporating the standards into existing frameworks. Misfit states that attempted to adapt existing institutions were less successful at making progress than states that tailored their reform to the new European standards. The comparative analysis shows divergent national and European preferences will require some states to tailor existing national preferences to achieve compliance and find a true fit with European policies.

title: Systems Analyses Reveal Tissue Specific Chaperone Networks with Distinct Functions in Eukaryotic Organisms
abstract: Many human neurodegenerative diseases, such as Huntington’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease, are associated with the expression of toxic misfolded proteins that interfere with cellular function. To repair this damage and guide correct folding, misfolded proteins are assisted by helper proteins called molecular chaperones. Molecular chaperones are classified into 16 distinct families corresponding to their roles in protein folding quality control. The function and specificity of chaperone family members are mediated by conserved structural regions called chaperone functional domains. Cross species analysis of five eukaryotic genomes indicates that select chaperone families have expanded subclasses that are functionally diverse. These families have acquired other “non-chaperone” domains whose contribution to chaperone function has not yet been determined. This study elucidated the role of these non-chaperone domains in promoting functional diversity of molecular chaperones. Computational predictions based on established biochemical studies revealed six major functional networks of chaperone involvement, predominantly in signaling and cell structure/protein transport. Understanding the functional consequences of these non-chaperone domains will provide valuable insight into the dynamic role of chaperone networks in diseases of protein misfolding.

title: Identification of Novel Circadian Genes in Drosophila using a Multilevel Approach
abstract: Organisms have evolved complex behaviors to adapt to their natural environments. Circadian rhythms represent one such fundamental behavior common to all living organisms. Circadian rhythms encompass daily biological cycles that govern many aspects of behavior including sleep, metabolism, activity, hormonal levels, etc. The fruit fly, Drosophila, serves as a model organism for the study of circadian rhythms. Our goal was to contribute to the understanding of circadian rhythmicity by utilizing computational, molecular, and behavioral approaches to identify and study candidate circadian genes. A rigorous statistical analysis of large-scale gene expression data identified ~200 rhythmically expressed genes that could potentially interact directly with the circadian molecular clock. A detailed characterization of one of these candidate genes, clockwork orange (cwo), revealed that it plays a critical role in the maintenance of high amplitude circadian oscillations in flies. The presence of mammalian counterparts of cwo suggests a similar mechanism might exist in humans. The use of multilevel analytical approaches to discover additional circadian genes will provide novel drug targets for the treatment of circadian and sleep disorders.

title: The Shot Heard Round the World: News of the American Revolution in 18th Century Venice
abstract: The American Revolution—the war, the ideals it upheld and the formation of a new country—had far reaching consequences on contemporaries across the late 18th century world. For my Senior Thesis, I examined the discourse on the American Revolution in Venice as told through newspapers circulating throughout Venice between 1782-1790. After receiving an Undergraduate Research Grant, I conducted primary research at Princeton University Library’s Department of Rare Books and Special Collections. I focused on a collection of newspapers entitled Notizie del Mondo, which I analyzed to see which events received a lot of attention and coverage in Venice during this period. Although the scholarship of Piero Del Negro examines the discussion of the American Revolution among the social, political and intellectual elites of Venice, my thesis is concerned with the regular literate masses of Venice and the presentation of news within the city’s bustling café culture. With my thesis, I hope to show the interconnectedness of an American event and the longest surviving republic at the time, and to assess the extent to which knowledge of the American Revolution was present in a city-state nearly halfway around the world.

title: Smooth Muscle Myosin Heavy Chain (SMMHC) Structure, Function, and Role in Acute Myeloid Leukemia in the inv(16) Fusion Protein
abstract: Smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (SMMHC) is a protein affected by inv(16), which fuses its C-terminal coiled-coil domain with a majority of the core binding factor b (CBFb) transcription factor. inv(16) is the most common chromosomal inversion found in gene karyotypes of patients diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). SMMHC, a component of a contractile protein complex found in smooth muscle cells of various organs of the body, exists as a bipolar dimer by way of a C-terminal coiled-coil and a globular N-terminal head with ATPase activity. The focus of this project has been to study the C-terminal domain (CTD) of SMMHC using biophysical methods. Here we analyze the nature of the SMMHC domain and provide some insight into the structure of the multimerization domain. NMR analysis of 13C and/or 15N labeled SMMHC suggests that the coiled-coil has a natively unfolded tail. The remaining residues form a rigid structured coil. The structure of the rod-like coil and oligomerization state of SMMHC was studied using analytical ultracentrifugation and crystallography. Velocity sedmientation experiments have been run at varying salt concentrations of 100 mM (low salt), 150 mM (physiological), and 200 mM or 300 mM KCl (high salt) because SMMHC demonstrates a strong salt dependence in vitro in order to multimerize. Unexpectedly, analysis showed that at lower ionic strengths, SMMHC may exist in several heterogeneous dimer conformations or as an aggregated filament. Current models suggest that filaments form as ordered anti-parallel dimers, which aggregate into tetramers, octomers, and so on, but we suggest that formation of filaments may not be as straightforward.

title: Computer Simulations of Gas-Liquid Interfaces: F + Squalane
abstract: Recently there has been significant interest in the chemistry of interfaces, both from a theoretical and practical point of view. Interfacial systems are found in biology, such as the transfer of oxygen in blood vessels and the absorption of drugs, as well as in industrial settings involving manufacturing and catalysis. Despite these important applications, there is no general quantitative or predictive model of how these systems behave. Most recently, there has also been interest in the behavior of polymers in low-Earth orbit, such as the exterior of spacecraft during exit and re-entry of the Earth’s atmosphere. This problem inspired several experiments designed to study gases reacting with the liquid hydrocarbon squalane, a model reaction for such systems. Computational studies are an excellent complement to these experiments because they allow access to variables which are difficult or impossible to measure in the laboratory. Here we present a computational study of the fluorine + squalane system using a new hybrid theoretical technique. This is one of the only reports of direct simulation of bond breaking chemical reactions to date. Our results show qualitative agreement with experiment and add to the developing picture of reactions at the gas-liquid interface. In particular we study the effects of gas collision at different angles, the characteristic time scales of reaction, and the energy transfer between gas and liquid molecules.

title: Shantipatha: An Initiative for Social Empowerment
abstract: Project Shantipatha was funded by the 100 Projects for Peace Grant in 2007. Its goal is to increase social and economic empowerment in rural villages of south India using seed funds for building economic independence, and enhancing education and entrepreneurship. Shantipatha was accomplished in conjunction with the International Human Development and Upliftment Academy, an NGO in Mysore, India. A poverty scorecard was developed based on World Bank Indicators capturing information regarding social stratification, living standards and economic metrics. Over 200 women and 100 schoolchildren participated in detailed interviews. The scorecard garnered facts regarding economic status, sanitation, and healthcare. It captured monthly income, consumption patterns, schooling, agriculture, and other needs. For example, it was found that over 82% lacked sanitation facilities, 50% procured drinking water from the local river, and nearly 60% of interviewees did not own land. Three seed funds were established to alleviate problems. The Book Fund helped to purchase school supplies, using accrued interest from the fixed fund. Two microfinance funds were established to encourage higher education and entrepreneurship. The Small Business Fund enabled allocation of micro-loans to start small businesses, or improve an existing business. Individuals created proposals, planned for finances and seasonal variations, partnered with city institutions to transport goods into rural areas. The Educational Fund provided underprivileged women with high test scores with a two year micro-loan for higher education. Based on current progress, Shantipatha funds are being successfully deployed and modulated with increasing efficiency.

title: Polydopamine: Mussel-Inspired Surface Coating for Metal Removal
abstract: Inspired by the amino acid sequence of mussel adhesive proteins, the Messersmith research group at Northwestern University recently developed a simple one-step chemistry for surface modification called polydopamine coating which has the ability to form on virtually all types of material surfaces (1). One remarkable secondary reaction of polydopamine platform is the formation uniform metal coating onto it by electroless metallization. This high affinity for metals is consistent with the previous findings that natural melanin, which has 5,6-dyhydroxyindole (DHI) as its most abundant subunit, has a high affinity for metal ions including Ca, Mg, Na, K, Fe, and Cu in the body and serves as a metal reservoir or metal sink depending on the specific metal. DHI is the proposed structural unit of polydopamine coating. Inspired by this surface independent coating ability of polydopamine and its high affinity for metal ions, we studied polydopamine coating as a possible adsorption material for heavy metal removal during water treatment. Here we demonstrate that a simple polydopamine coated beads, which can be used as a column of filter, can effectively bind and sequester copper, lead, mercury, barium, cadmium and chromium ions in water with a capacity higher than commonly used adsorption materials. Also we demonstrate that polydopamine metal removal system can be used repeatedly by removing and re-applying polydopamine coating when the coating is saturated with metal ions. This reusability in addition to high capacity and affinity for metal binding of polydopamine coating can lead to developing a cost effective metal removal system.

title: The Effects of Parental Psychopathology: Examining Parenting Behavior as a Mediator between Parental Depression and Anxiety and Child Internalizing Outcomes
abstract: The clinical literature has consistently demonstrated an association between parental psychopathology, specifically anxiety and depressive disorders and symptoms, and child emotional maladjustment. However, the causal mechanisms by which this vulnerability to psychopathology is transmitted from parent to child remains uncertain. Although there is substantial evidence that genetic factors are implicated, they do not fully account for this transmission. Additionally, existing experimental evidence relies primarily on maternal psychopathology; fathers are highly underrepresented. As a result, there is a paucity of scientific evidence demonstrating not only why an association exists between parental psychopathology and child outcomes, but more specifically, whether or how this relationship differs across mothers and fathers. The present research aimed to identify the role that parenting behaviors, as observed in laboratory parent-child interactions, might play to mediate the association between parental depression and anxiety and child internalizing outcomes. Results suggest that parenting behaviors are influential in the relationship between parental psychopathology and internalizing outcomes. In addition, notable differences emerged between mothers and fathers.

title: Carbon Footprint Study
abstract: The transportation of goods and materials presently has negative effects on the environment. These consequences are a result of shippers not taking the effects of carbon emissions into account in their choice of carriers (modes), shipment frequencies and size of shipments. PHILIPS Electronics, a leading manufacturer of electronic consumer products and professional products and services wished to determine and reduce the carbon footprint of their Forwarding and Distribution Department in North America. This research project guides them in understanding the definition of a carbon footprint and how is it measured, and the correlation between carbon emissions and each mode of transportation. I also presented what other leading carriers and customers of PHILIPS are doing to reduce their carbon emissions, and what environmental groups PHILIPS can join to help report their carbon savings. Quantitatively, I developed a user-friendly worksheet that measures the savings for switching modes of transportation. This worksheet was modeled after the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, but made specific for PHILIPS Medical Systems. The user inputs the number of units transported from each destination and the worksheet outputs tons of carbon dioxide and total dollars saved by switching modes from air to ocean, and motor to rail. This project was presented to the PHILIPS General Purchasing, Forwarding & Distribution North America Conference in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on April 9, 2008. PHILIPS will use the worksheet to influence carrier and mode decisions. Also as a result of this project, PHILIPS has joined the EPA SmartWay Transport Partnership at a corporate level.

title: Function of a Novel Cation Current in Drosophila Circadian Pacemaker Neurons
abstract: Circadian rhythms drive metabolic and behavioral rhythms throughout the 24-hour solar cycle, preparing organisms for light and dark transitions. While genetic analysis of circadian function in Drosophila has made significant progress in recent years, electrophysiological study of the transformation of molecular rhythms to behavioral output is a relatively new area of investigation. A voltage-gated divalent blocked cation (DBC) current in circadian pacemaker neurons has recently been discovered, and the amplitude of the current oscillates in circadian pacemakers with circadian time. External calcium ions effectively block inward sodium currents in these neurons, whereas the removal of divalent cations from the external bath allow for the DBC leak current to pass. The newly identified current, however, was recorded only from neurons in flies entrained to a light:dark cycle (12 hr lights on: 12 hr lights off). It is possible that this current is responsive to light conditions rather than regulated by the endogenous circadian clock. My research examines cells from arrhythmic flies at different times of day through voltage-clamp recordings to help determine what exactly drives this current. Finding a lack of fluctuation in this DBC current in per mutants throughout the day would indicate the current is clock-regulated rather than light-responsive. If verified this current will be one of the first electrophysiological links between the clock and circadian output in flies.

title: Foucault on Man and Museums
abstract: In the late sixties the French philosopher Michel Foucault was contracted to write a book about the painter Eduard Manet. Foucault often used examples from art in his philosophy but rarely addressed art itself. This book on Manet, some scholars argue, was to articulate a philosophy of art for Foucault. However, Foucault never finished the book and destroyed all his written materials that related to this work. The only remnant of this work is a recorded lecture delivered in Tunisia in 1971. My research analyzed these recordings from Tunis. Although they are only a small extract from a larger project, they still contain unique ideas about art. By taking these ideas from the lectures and placing them in the context of Foucault’s larger oeuvre, my project developed into a discussion about the relationship between art and museums. To expand on these concepts about museums, I investigated France’s newest art museum, the Musée du Quai Branly. This museum opened in the summer of 2006. From the day it was first proposed, this museum has been a source of controversy in France. Critics, academics, and politicians of all stripes have lambasted it, while others held it up as a model art museum. I examine the controversy in light of the Tunis lectures and Foucault’s thoughts on Manet. In the end I use the Musée du Quai Branly as case study for discussing Foucault’s unique ideas and in turn use the Foucault to provide new perspective on contemporary French culture.

title: Objectification Theory and the Psychological Impact of Sorority Rush
abstract: On college campuses across the U.S., thousands of women join sororities each year through the process of sorority rush. While few studies have been conducted on rush itself, sororities have been criticized for their potential to engender an excessive focus on appearance in their members. Such a focus can lead to self-objectification, a trait-like concept that involves taking a third person’s perspective on one’s body. Objectification Theory posits that women are frequently objectified, which can lead to habitual self-monitoring of one’s body’s appearance. Research has linked this self-monitoring to a number of negative outcomes including body dissatisfaction, negative affect, and cognitive disruptions. The present study investigated the relationship between sorority rush, self-objectification, body image disturbance, eating disordered behavior, and negative affect through a study of women participating in sorority rush at Northwestern University. Results showed that those participating in rush evidenced higher levels of body surveillance and eating disordered behavior during rush. Additionally, those who reported less satisfaction with rush reported significantly more body shame and levels of self-objectification. While women seeking to join sororities may be evaluated on a number of different attributes, the short nature of interactions during rush may make the impact of physical appearance especially salient in the impression formation process. Furthermore, the ongoing interpersonal evaluation associated with sorority rush may lead women to increase the extent to which they focus on their own appearance. Thus, rush may have the potential to have measurable psychological consequences on women – even before they become members of a sorority.

title: Ergodic Theory and Furstenberg’s Conjecture
abstract: Ergodic theory studies the interaction of two fundamental notions of mathematics: transformations and measures. A measure is a way of assigning length to a set-this is necessary for integration. For example, Lebesgue measure l on the real numbers says that the length of an interval [a,b), where a<b, is the distance between the endpoints, that is l([a,b))=b-a. An important example of a measure, the Dirac delta measure, is where an interval on the real line has measure 1 if it contains the point 0, and 0 if it does not. In this case, d([-1/2, 1/3))=1, but d([2, 1000))=0. A transformation is a map from a set to itself. For instance, if we fix some real number a, we have the transformation on the real numbers T(x)=x+a. This transformation then distinguishes certain measures. Lebesgue measure is invariant under this map, while the Dirac delta measure is not. This roughly means applying T to a set does not change its Lebesgue measure, but it can change its Dirac delta measure. Furstenberg’s conjecture states that for two specific transformations, the only measure invariant under both of them is Lebesgue. As Lebesgue measure is in some senses the most natural measure, this result is an important characterization. My project is on Host’s proof of Rudolph’s theorem, which is a weaker form of Furstenberg’s conjecture. I will give a more intuitive sense of what these technical terms mean, explain the tools used in the proof and the heuristics behind them, and discuss the additional hypotheses necessary.

title: Going Green and Staying Green: Changing the Environmental Attitudes of Urban High School Students
abstract: Environmental education programs are one avenue through which to create students who are committed to a sustainable future in the long-term. For urban students, in particular, environmental education can foster a connection to nature that may not otherwise occur in an urbanized setting. The existing body of literature does not clearly address the long-term effects of such programs on urban participants despite the fact that changing ecological attitudes is one of the primary goals of environmental education. Thus, this study addresses how one particular placed-based environmental education program designed for urban youth influences the environmental attitudes of the participating students over time. Using a cross-sectional research design, I conducted surveys and interviews with both current and past participants of the College First environmental education program at the Chicago Botanic Garden in order to understand how the program is experienced and interpreted in the long term. More specifically, surveys and interviews were conducted with 10 current and 10 past participants of College First ranging in age from 16 to 23 to assess differences in ecological attitudes among age groups and to determine why such differences may occur. With a better understanding of the long-term effects of environmental education, educators can develop programs in such a way that will better connect urban youth with their environment and, subsequently, better fulfill the goals of environmental education for all populations by producing more environmentally conscious individuals.

title: Changing Family Structure in Mexico: Women in the Maquiladoras of Ciudad Juarez
abstract: Women working in maquiladoras, American-owned assembly plants based in Mexico, represent the fastest-growing labor force along the U.S.-Mexico border. Each year thousands of families leave their agricultural jobs so that women can acquire these higher-paying assembly-line jobs. For many, migrating north also entails leaving behind family members and unique village cultures. How do Mexican rural migrants make sense of their new lives in the assembly plants of border cities? With the help of a Northwestern Undergraduate Research Grant, I interviewed six families from the southern village of Magdalena Tlacotepec, Oaxaca who migrated to Ciudad Juarez, Chihuahua to secure maquiladora jobs. Previous research describes the sexual competition in maquiladoras—the currency through which shopfloor relations play out—but it fails to disclose working conditions’ effects on womens’ roles as wives and mothers. As the primary components of the maquiladora workforce, efforts to understand womens’ migration, work and wages are central to the story of this great transition in Mexican history. I pursued a research strategy that revealed womens’ life stories and complemented their narratives with responses from other family members. I was particularly interested in how higher wages changed the six families’ lives and how different family members viewed these changes. My research took me to the border city of Ciudad Juarez and to the southern village of Magdalena Tlacotepec, where I was able to gain the perspectives of family members who stayed behind. I developed my research into a Creative Writing Senior Thesis, which took the form of creative non-fiction.

title: Identifying MicroRNA Pathway Genes in Drosophila Melanogaster
abstract: RNA Interference (RNAi) is a technique that uses small interfering RNA molecules to knockdown gene translation of complementary messenger RNA transcripts. MicroRNAs (miRNA) are small single-stranded non-coding RNA transcripts that through a similar mechanism play a major role in endogenous silencing of the translation of genes; miRNAs are also required for normal development in both plants and animals. miRNAs have been implicated in as diverse biological roles as regulation of the cell cycle, response to growth factors, cell fate, and cellular metabolism. Both the molecular pathway controlling the production of miRNAs and the function of the majority of miRNAs, however, are not understood. Understanding how the pathway functions is essential to understand how both miRNAs and RNAi could be used to treat genetic diseases and cancer. My work has utilized a screen previously developed by the Carthew lab that uses green florescent protein expression in the eyes of Drosophila melanogaster to identify mutations in the miRNA pathway. I conducted this screen to identify and understand the function of the genes in the miRNA pathway. Utilizing this system, I have screened over 10,000 flies for mutations in the miRNA pathway and a total of 36 putative miRNA pathway mutants have been identified. The two mutants identified with the strongest phenotype have failed to complement with mutants of the known miRNA gene pasha, which confirms the ability of the screen to identify mutations in the miRNA pathway. This data suggests that novel miRNA pathway genes will likely be identified by this screen.

title: Family Size and Other Biodemographic Correlates of Sexual Orientation in Men
abstract: To better understand sexual orientation from an evolutionary perspective, we investigated whether gay men have larger family sizes than straight men. We also checked to what extent three generally separately studied patterns correlated with each other or with family size, and for evidence of replication of each individual pattern in our sample: handedness, number of biological older brothers, and hair-whorl rotation pattern. A brief anonymous survey was administered in Gay Pride festivals and general community festivals to 863 straight men and 607 gay men. Sexual orientation was assessed via a modified Kinsey Scale by questionnaire. The two samples were demographically similar to each other, and the measured inter-rater reliability for the hair-whorl observation was very high. Results supported the familiarity of male sexual orientation, the fraternal birth order effect and the increased family size in gay men. Compared to straight men, gay men had significantly increased numbers of relatives in numerous categories of relatives, including older brothers. Meanwhile, no correlation was found between handedness, hair whorl orientation and sexual orientation.

title: Walking Forward, But Looking Back: Understanding the Experience of Zimbabwean Refugees in South Africa
abstract: Between one and four million Zimbabweans currently live in South Africa. They flee the political persecution and hunger resulting from recent shifts in the policies of the Mugabe regime. Across the border in South Africa, however, they face violence, xenophobia and discrimination. In March 2008, I traveled to Cape Town and Johannesburg to learn how Zimbabwean refugees in South Africa negotiate the circumstances in both countries. I interviewed about 40 refugees, focusing in particular on stories in which ordinary people sought to make a better life for themselves, often at great personal risk. Prompted by what I was hearing from refugees and the unfolding Zimbabwean elections, I traveled to Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, to learn more. The conditions on the ground were difficult, as is often the case in areas of political turmoil, with poor hospital supplies, uncertain electricity, food shortages and uncontrollable inflation. For Zimbabweans, this was an extreme shift because the country had, at its independence in 1980, been amongst the most developed on the continent with plentiful food, good infrastructure, a highly educated population, and a burgeoning professional class. My research presentation traces my own personal journey through South Africa and eventually Zimbabwe as a way of understanding the plight of refugees in 2008. Through this narrative, I hope to show how refugees see themselves as trapped in a nexus of politics, corruption and incompetence on both sides of the border, while also demonstrating the ways in which African men and women find a way to survive this seeming entrapment.

title: Tracing Galactic Magnetic Fields into Molecular Clouds
abstract: Different types of interstellar objects can generate their own large-scale magnetic fields. Many stars, including our own Sun, have magnetic fields, as do the Earth and several of the other planets in our Solar System. Additionally, the Milky Way Galaxy also has a large-scale magnetic field. The question of whether this Galactic magnetic field penetrates into the molecular clouds where stars are born remains open. Molecular clouds have characteristic sizes that are about 100 times smaller than the scale of the Galaxy itself. Measurements of magnetic fields associated with molecular clouds have been recorded through a variety of methods. One method is to observe the Zeeman splitting patterns of thermal OH line emission in order to calculate the magnetic field. Zeeman patterns in OH emission result when a magnetic field splits one of the spectral lines (caused by the excitation of the atom to a higher energy level) of OH. The magnitude of the splitting is directly related to the magnetic field strength. We have carried out a survey of the literature on OH Zeeman measurements, with the goal of seeing whether these are correlated with the orientation of the large-scale Galactic magnetic field. We will present a progress report on this work.

title: Message Framing Effects in Elective Surgery
abstract: Traditional framing studies present participants with scenarios, requiring them to choose between two options that differ in implied risk. The two options are often presented in a positive frame, emphasizing positive aspects of the options, and in a negative frame, emphasizing negative aspects of the options. Despite the changing frame, the options are fundamentally equivalent. Researchers have investigated framing effects in medical and health behavior decision making. However, there have been few empirical investigations of how individuals make decisions regarding elective procedures. This study investigates the application of framing effects to decisions and perceptions about elective eye surgery. This research differs from other decision making studies because refractive eye surgery is not medically compulsory. One hundred twelve Northwestern undergraduates read a hypothetical scenario in which they were asked to imagine that they suffer from nearsightedness and to choose between getting glasses and eye surgery. Each option was framed in terms of its gains (probability of experiencing corrected vision) and losses (probability of experiencing potential side effects and dependence on glasses). The study discusses the influence of framing, changing references points, and personal issue involvement on perceptions about elective eye surgery.

title: Do Actions Speak Louder Than Words? Correlations between Observer-Rated and Self-Reported Personality and Hypomania Measures
abstract: Current diagnostic criteria define hypomania as a state of elevated or irritable mood that is distinct from an individual’s normal state and persists for at least 4 days. Research has demonstrated the predictive value of the Hypomanic Personality Scale (HPS) in identifying individuals who will eventually suffer hypomanic episodes. The current study further tests the hypothesis that the HPS may be related to personality traits. In this study, participants engaged in 10 tasks that were designed to elicit behaviors relevant to personality traits. In addition to the HPS, participants also completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, worry, and depression, as well as the Big Five Mini-Markers (Saucier, 1994). Observers and experimenters also rated these participants on the Mini-Markers. Correlations among self-reported hypomania, self-reported personality traits, and observer-rated personality traits were examined. Both self- and observer-ratings of Openness and Extraversion correlated significantly with the HPS, while anxiety was found to correlate positively with scores on the HPS. Self-reports of Neuroticism also correlated positively with hypomania. Implications are discussed.

title: Perceptions of Behavior of Ingroup Members
abstract: In general, people are proud of the social groups to which they belong. Such pride is experienced even for groups that have negative stereotypes associated with them. Identifying with a stigmatized group is not without its problems, though. In addition to contending with negative beliefs about the group, people may experience pressure to avoid perpetuating stereotypes by acting in ways that counter negative beliefs about one’s group. This project investigates how people respond to socially deviant behaviors of ingroup members when this behavior occurs in the presence of other ingroup members or in the presence of outgroup members who may see the negative behaviors as confirming their negative views of the group. We hypothesize that socially deviant behavior enacted by ingroup members in the presence of outgroup members will lead people to utilize self-protective strategies in order to distance themselves from the deviant ingroup member. We do not expect that these strategies will be utilized when the same behaviors occur in the presence of ingroup members. We expect these results to be moderated by identification with the group, such that higher identification should lead to increased use of self-protective strategies when encountering socially deviant behaviors by ingroup members.

title: He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not: Misattribution of Arousal in Romantic Interracial Interactions
abstract: This study examined the relationship between political orientation and romantic attraction toward racial minorities of the opposite sex. Previous studies found that White, politically liberal men showed more romantic interest toward a Black dating partner than toward a same-race dating partner. Given that liberals tend to be more physiologically aroused during interracial interactions (Nail, Harton, & Decker, 2003) and that people may misattribute arousal to other sources (Dutton & Aron, 1974), it is possible that liberals are erroneously attributing race-related anxiety to romantic arousal. To test this hypothesis, White, liberal men were recruited for a dating study where they met White and Black dating partners and indicated their romantic interest in each of them. Half of the participants were given information that induced them to misattribute their arousal to a source other than their dating partner. Heart rate was also measured to assess levels of arousal. Although the data did not support the main hypothesis, the present study replicated previous results showing political orientation to predict differences in interracial romantic attraction.

title: Sementics: A Discursive Comparison of Infertile People’s and Doctors’ Understandings of Male-Factor Infertility

people.major: Sociology and Science in Human Culture

abstract: The advent of assisted reproductive technologies enabled medical professionals to examine pregnant women alongside infertile women and men. Drawing on data from 100 infertile person blog entries and 96 doctor blog entries, my research compares how infertile people and doctors make sense of male-factor infertility and uncovers how medicine, culture, and economics shape dominant modes of knowledge production about male-factor infertility. My results show that assisted reproductive technologies used to assess and treat male-factor infertility open up men’s bodies to reproductive scrutiny and challenge men’s reproductive subjecthood. I conclude by addressing the implications of a discourse where infertile men are reduced to their biological processes; where infertile people and doctors privilege biogenetic connections over other forms of parenting; and where infertile people, who are unsuccessful in their quest to form biogenetic families, inscribe alternative family forms with assumptions about ‘biologically’ determined gender and racial differences.

title: Owning the Issues Online and Off
abstract: How does the medium in which a political statement is made affect the content of that statement? This research explores that general question, through content analysis of the statements made by candidates for the United States Senate in daily newspapers during the 2006 midterm election season, compared to data drawn from content analysis of candidates’ websites over the same period. While research exists on candidate behavior and issue ownership in various media, none has yet been undertaken into comparing these behaviors across these media. In doing so, this research also sheds light on various other topics: Do partisans emphasize issues typically associated with one party or the other? Which party’s candidates tended to “go negative” more often over the period in question? How does the medium in which a statement was made (the Internet or a traditional state newspaper) impact the likelihood it will be negative? Do candidates emphasize issues more often on the Internet or in traditional media? In exploring the main question and these offshoots, this thesis adds to the body of research into political communication, and contributes to the emerging literature on political behavior on the Internet, an area of increasing importance in early 21st century campaigns.

title: Investigating Transcription Silencing through TAF Occupancy Analysis
abstract: When mechanisms responsible for the heritable repression of gene expression fail to halt transcription, the result is unregulated cell growth. By understanding the mechanism by which transcription silencing occurs, it is possible to determine which events are responsible for the failure of repression. We are studying the core promoter-recognition complex which consists of TATA box-binding protein (TBP) and TBP associated factors (TAFs) which provide the stability for the core complex to bind to the promoter. This complex is the first transcription factor to bind to the promoter, so its absence prevents subsequent attachment of transcription factors necessary for transcription initiation. Our lab showed transcription silencing takes place at the level of TBP recruitment, as TBP levels were significantly reduced at repressed promoters, compared to active promoters. By analyzing the occupancy of TAFs, we aim to discover which TAFs are responsible for the failure of TBP to bind at silenced genes. Through ChIP assay using strains of Saccharomyces cerevisiae with each TAF TAP-tagged, we assessed the occupancy of TAF6, TAF9, and TAF10 using traditional and Real Time PCR. We analyzed the naturally expressed mating locus (MAT) to determine the degree of occupancy of each TAF at silenced and active promoters. From our results, TAF6 and TAF9 showed no significant trends. However, a strong correlation between relative occupancy of TAF10 and whether the promoter was active or repressed was evidenced. This suggests TAF10 is a key protein in determining whether TBP binds to promoters and transcription is activated.

title: Confounding Criminals: P300 Detection of Deception
abstract: The detection of deception has recently been improved with the use of the P300, an event-related potential evoked by relevant and meaningful information. The P300 is used with the guilty knowledge test (GKT), which allows the investigator to identify guilty items because those that items are relevant and evoke a large P300 compared to irrelevant items. The GKT protocol has undergone many modifications to make it countermeasure-resistant, including the separation in time of attention-forcing target and probe trials. An original asymmetric probability of target to nontargets used to induce a P300 proved to be especially effective. It may have been the asymmetric conditional probability of probe followed by target that led to increased sensitivity. In order to test this hypothesis, three groups were run: a symmetric simple guilty group, an asymmetric simple guilty group, and a symmetric false positive group to identify any difference in detection and false positive rates. Thus far, the symmetric simple guilty group has had a lower detection rate.

title: The Synthesis and Characterization of Multimeric MRI Contrast Agents
abstract: Contrast agents are being used in over 30% of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examinations in hospitals in the U.S. By decreasing proton relaxation time, T1 in human tissues, MR contrast agents can enhance the signal intensity and provide anatomical information of tissue and organ systems. The current clinical compounds utilize the paramagnetic qualities of the gadolinium ion [Gd(III)] to enhance image contrast. These contrast agents are small, single Gd(III) complexes that are limited in their functional diversity and effect on water relaxation. This project investigated the boost to proton relaxation by a Gd(III) agent in relation to the available number of water coordination sites on the molecule as well as its rotational correlation time—the speed at which the molecule rotates in its environment. These parameters were studied via the synthesis of benzene-derived, multimeric contrast agents possessing varied numbers of water coordination sites. The analysis of these novel, multi-Gd(III) compounds showed an increase to the overall molecular relaxivity as well as amplified image contrast per Gd(III) unit. Common clinical MR agents possess relaxivities in the range of 3.5-4.5 mM-1s-1 whereas the macromolecular compounds that were synthesized demonstrated values around 10-12 mM-1s-1 per Gd(III). The total molecular relaxivity peaked at 64 mM-1s-1 for the six-Gd(III) compound, significantly dwarfing the potency of anything that is clinically available. The large effect of rotational correlation time on image enhancement leads to the conclusion that a macromolecular approach has a promising future for MR contrast agent design and synthesis.

title: Bladder Replacement Therapy Utilizing Autologous Sources of Stem and Progenitor Cells
abstract: Spina bifida is the most common disabling birth defect in the United States, occurring in 7 out of 10,000 live births. Approximately 5-10% of spina bifida children have normal urinary control. Patients suffer from immense bladder dysfunction that typically requires self-catheterization for urination. Current surgical techniques to improve bladder function use intestinal lining as a graft, but the diseased bladder still lacks contractile function and can further lead to cancerous ulcers and mucus formation. This research project involves the forced differentiation of bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) that can be used in a bladder regenerative setting. MSCs can be transdifferentiated into cellular components of the bladder wall while EPCs can provide vasculature to nourish developing tissue. Autologous cell sources also alleviate concerns regarding undue immunological responses as well as the use of systemic immunosuppressive therapies.
