Patient derived MSCs were treated with combinations of cytokines including TGF� 1 and HGF in an effort to differentiate MSCs into smooth muscle cell phenotype. Concurrently, EPCs were grown in culture with cytokines that would promote the formation of blood vessels in vivo. Upon examination, the MSCs displayed contractile proteins similar to those found in bladder smooth muscle and were capable of contraction when stimulated by an agonist. Blood vessel formation was evident when utilized in an in vivo chicken chorioamniotic membrane model. Data gathered from this study provides evidence that autologous sources of stem and progenitor cells may be used for bladder replacement purposes.

title: Characterizing the Effects of Aggregation Suppression on Toxicity in C. elegans Models of Protein Aggregation
abstract: Aggregation of misfolded proteins is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative diseases, including Amyotropic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and the polyglutamine (polyQ) disorders. PolyQ disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of a glutamine repetitive tract that induce protein misfolding and aggregation. Aggregates in familial form of ALS arise from unstable, mutant Cu,Zn-superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) proteins that tend to form oligomers and filamentous arrays. Although aggregates have been observed to accumulate in parallel with the clinical course of these neurodegenerative diseases, studies to date have been unable to definitively establish if aggregation is causal, consequential, or incidental to neurotoxicity. A genome-wide RNA interference screen identified 67 suppressors of visible aggregates in polyQ and SOD1 C. elegans models. This study characterizes the consequences of polyQ aggregation suppression on toxicity. Animal movement, characterized by speed and coordination, serves as a readout for organism toxicity, and automated tracking software has been developed to this end. Motility assays suggest that the presence of visible aggregates is uncoupled from toxicity, lending credence to the hypothesis that polyQ-induced toxicity is not directly caused by aberrant protein-protein interactions facilitated by end-stage aggregates. A better understanding of the aggregation process, its regulation, and its link to toxicity will provide insight into the mechanisms by which neurodegenerative disorders are triggered.

title: Insuring All Kids: Risk and Decision-making in Illinois Child Healthcare Policy
abstract: In June 2006, Illinois became the first state to guarantee all children access to affordable health care. Under the All Kids program, children up to the age of 18 can obtain coverage, regardless of income, health status, or citizenship. Despite this guarantee, however, 11% of children in Illinois are still living without health insurance. In this project, data from existing studies, academic journals, newspaper articles, and original interviews is used to examine each step in the process of enrolling in and utilizing All Kids. Anthropological theory of risk and uncertainty is applied to each of these steps in order attempt to understand why individuals do or do not enroll their children in this program. By gaining a deeper understanding of how peoples’ cultural beliefs influence their decision-making strategies, this research proposes improvements in the All Kids program. Ultimately, an improved All Kids program will benefit Illinois families, while at the same time serving as a model for child healthcare policy on a national level.

title: Regulatory Focus and Social Dilemmas: Promotion and Prevention in Strategic Decision Making
abstract: Social dilemmas are scenarios where individuals’ personal interests come into conflict with collective interests. Two experiments attempted to explain decision making in social dilemmas from the perspective of regulatory focus theory. Regulatory focus theory proposes that there are two motivational orientations: promotion and prevention focus. Promotion focus is associated with concerns about personal gains, whereas prevention focus is associated with concerns about obligations to others. Therefore, we hypothesized that when individuals are in a prevention focus, they will act more collaboratively in a social dilemma than individuals in a promotion focus. Participants completed two interdependent decision-making tasks (a public goods game and an ultimatum game). In Experiment 1, we examined single-shot games and in Experiment 2 we looked at multiple-round games. We found that prevention-focused individuals acted more collaboratively than promotion-focused individuals in both single-shot and repeated pubic goods games, but found no significant differences in the single-shot and repeated ultimatum games.

title: Transformations in Éire: How the Troubles Ended
abstract: This thesis argues that discrimination, or perceived discrimination, in Ulster helped to create a society in crisis. However, changes in government policy in Northern Ireland and marked economic, social, and intellectual changes in the Republic helped to bring about an end to the Troubles in the North. The Troubles began in 1968 when demonstrations of the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Movement became violent, and it ended in 1998 with the signing of the Good Friday Agreement. Chapter One explores public housing allocation in Northern Ireland in the 1960s. It demonstrates that, while discrimination in housing allocation did not occur in the whole of Northern Ireland, the Campaign for Social Justice successfully utilized isolated incidents of discrimination to begin the Civil Rights Movement and that the Northern Irish government eventually answered their calls for reform in the 1970s with the creation of the Northern Ireland Housing Executive. Chapter Two discusses employment discrimination. It suggests that an employment differential existed, but the government in Northern Ireland passed fair employment legislation in the 1970s and 1980s. It created the Fair Employment Commission to help combat the issue and assuage the concerns of the Catholics. A third chapter examines the economic, social, and intellectual changes in the Republic in the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s that allay the fears of both the Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland. Little work has been done on the coincidence of a shifting social attitudes and positive economic changes to explain the end of the Troubles. In the 1960s, inequality between the Catholic and Protestant communities caused tensions. However, reforms in the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s in Northern Ireland and marked economic improvement, liberalized social attitudes, and a reinterpretation of history in the Republic helped to calm the concerns of both the Catholic and Protestant communities, facilitating peace.

title: Platelet Size and Age Modify Antiplatelet Effects of Aspirin and Clopidogrel in Patients with Stable Coronary Artery Disease
abstract: The mechanisms for variable antiplatelet effects of aspirin and clopidogrel are poorly described. We evaluated the roles of platelet size and age in modifying the effects of antiplatelet therapy in patients with stable coronary artery disease. Patients (n=90, 74% male, age 64.4 ± 11 years) receiving aspirin and clopidogrel (≥ 1 week) were recruited. Platelet aggregation to 1.5 mM arachidonic acid (AA) was assessed. Platelet gates were established with flow cytometry to define the upper 20% (large) and lower 20% (small) of platelets by size. RPs in each group were measured using thiazole orange. P-selectin and PAC-1 expression (anti-GPIIb-IIIa) were assessed after stimulation with 10 µM ADP. Aspirin resistance (AR) was defined as 1.5 mM AA aggregation ≥ 20%. Compared with smaller platelets, larger platelets had significantly greater expression of P-selectin, GPIIb-IIIa, and % RPs. Large platelets of AR patients (23/90 subjects) had significantly higher expression of RPs and GPIIb-IIIa, but not P-selectin, compared with non-AR patients. No differences were observed between the small platelets of AR and non-AR patients. We can conclude that larger platelets remain more active than smaller platelets after dual antiplatelet therapy. The major difference between patients with or without AR appears to reside in the large platelet fraction. Young platelets (RPs) comprise a significant proportion of large platelets in AR patients, possibly contributing to their activity.

title: Ascorbic Acid Enhances Sonic Hedgehog Signaling between Prostate Cancer Cells and Osteoblasts: Implications for Prostate Cancer Bone Metastasis
abstract: The major cause of mortality from prostate cancer (PCa) is metastatic disease which occurs preferentially in the bone. The key to understanding this proclivity for the bone microenvironment lies in characterizing the interactions between PCa cells and the host bone stroma including bone cell response and extracellular matrix (ECM). Previous studies have implicated Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling in the upregulation of Gli1 expression leading to osteoblast differentiation (OD), a requisite step in the formation of metastatic prostate tumors in bone (Lamm et al., 2005). Additionally, OD is promoted by Ascorbic Acid (AA), a requirement for collagen synthesis in the ECM (Franceschi & Iyer, 1992). The role of the ECM in PCa metastasis is poorly understood. This study hypothesized that AA and Shh play synergistic roles in PCa cell-osteoblast cell interactions leading to collagen synthesis in the ECM and subsequently, OD. Using a co-culture of Shh over-expressing PCa cells, mouse osteoblasts, RT-PCR, ALP staining and microscopy this study was able to demonstrate that 1) AA enhances Shh-Gli1 signaling between PCa cells and osteoblasts 2) AA enhances Shh mediated osteoblast differentiation and 3) AA and Shh result in increased collagen deposition, indicating ECM maturation in preparation for OD. This research tests the idea that a collagenous ECM facilitates Shh-Gli signaling and OD. The data thus far suggest that the combined actions of AA and Shh may be a mechanism to promote osteoblastic tumor growth of metastatic prostate carcinoma and indicate that Shh and AA are potential therapeutic targets against PCa bone metastasis.

title: A “Weighty” Issue in Brazil: Obesity Determinants Associated with Nutrition Transition
abstract: Many developing nations are currently undergoing a nutritional transition, meaning that there have been modifications in the nutritional profile of human populations due to various economic, demographic, environmental, and cultural factors. As undernutrition reduces in prevalence, overnutrition has been rising for the past few decades in many developing nations. A consequence of overnutrition is obesity, which can lead to many other chronic illnesses including heart disease and hypertension. In Brazil between 1975 and 2003, obesity rates increased by 92% and 63% for men and women respectively, with rates being higher for low-income family individuals (Monteiro et al 2007). What once was considered a disease of the socioeconomic elite seems to now be a problem faced by all Brazilians; however, individuals with different socioeconomic status and dietary/physical activity behaviors will have different susceptibilities to becoming obese. For example, urbanization and rural populations are facing different challenges in combating obesity, and individuals who were undernourished early on in life are more likely to become obese (Popkin et al 1996). Therefore, it is important to analyze which parts of the population seem to be most likely to become obese, as well as what determinants should be addressed in national public health policy. Overall, it is clear that the nutritional transition in developing nations is correlated with an increase in obesity, yet it is important to address the specific factors affecting different nations, as well as subpopulations with in the nation based on the factor’s associative risk for developing obesity.

title: ARCAT and the Difficulties of Latin American Immigrants
abstract: ARCAT, an acronym for Association pour la Recherche et la Communication pour L’Accès aux Traitements, is a humble Parisian AIDS and Hepatitis association fighting a nationally pivotal battle. Like so many other French civil rights, GLBT, AIDS and public health organizations, ARCAT has suffered under the reign of Nicolas Sarkozy who has single-handedly made its mission of spreading medical knowledge and granting health treatment more and more precarious everyday. Unlike other associations, ARCAT has taken active steps to adjust to France’s 21st century oppression by creating a Sector of Immigrant Prevention. This small sector has effectively torn down the barrier of language and immigrant trepidation; a daunting task only a few organizations have taken on. As an intern in the Latin American sector of HIV prevention, I witnessed how seemingly just social policies as the CESEDA (Immigrant Code laws) and the LSI (Interior Security Laws) can cause chaos for ordinary people. Prostitutes, transsexuals and the “sans-papiers” (immigrants without papers) compose the majority of the Latino demographic with which ARCAT works. My research delves into ARCAT’s relationship with Latino immigrants and sex-works and sheds light on how France’s obsession with interior security has caused public health catastrophes and a looming sense of dread in the Latin American community. My work adds to the well-established statistics and charts which has caused the CESEDA and LSI’s growing unpopularity but focuses on an overlooked and ignored Latino sex-worker community.

title: Anthropomorphism in Children’s Picture Books and Childhood Anthropocentrism
abstract: This series of studies examined the degree of anthropomorphism in young children’s picture books in an urban majority-culture preschool classroom. It also explored how children’s books with anthropomorphic vs. biological representations of animals affected children's conception of animals and their relationship to humans. A biologically accurate or an anthropomorphic book about bears was read to 3-year-olds and a subsequent experiment was used to determine whether either book was able to shift children's ideas of animals and nature towards a more or less anthropocentric (human-centered) view. I believe that discovering how children learn best about the natural world and what kinds of media affect their conceptions of nature would have significant implications in such areas as science education, as we would be better able to tailor curricula to children’s existing knowledge.

title: Helping Hands: The Role of Gesture in Spatial Processing
abstract: When people talk, they gesture. Gesture complements speech, facilitates understanding, promotes spatial cognition and development, and plays an important role in problem-solving. Previous research has shown that gesture affects how people encode information about a novel environment. The present study set out to explore how gesture relates to the ability to recall spatial information. In particular, we addressed the following questions: Do certain types of story content (spatial vs. non-spatial) elicit more spontaneous gestures; do certain types of probes (route vs. survey) elicit more spontaneous gestures; and lastly, does controlling gesture (limiting vs. encouraging) affect how well a space is encoded and recalled? In order to answer these questions, a set of students was given either a spatial or a non-spatial story to read. Students presented with the spatial story were far more likely to gesture than students who were given the non-spatial story, suggesting that gesture is important when encoding and recalling spatial information. A separate group was given only a spatial story, but was asked questions from either a “route” or “survey” point of view. Students gestured more frequently when probed with route questions. Students were also able to recall information more accurately when asked a route question. A third group of students were assigned to one of two conditions: encouraged or discouraged gesture. Students who were encouraged to gesture answered both route and survey questions more accurately than those whose gesture was restricted. These results demonstrate that gesture contributes to the encoding and recall of novel spaces.

title: Head Of Patient Elevation (HOPE) Monitor
abstract: Ventilator Associated Pneumonia (VAP) is one of the most prevalent and deadly infections acquired in hospitals. Thankfully, VAP incidence can be dramatically reduced by raising the patient’s Head-of-Bed (HOB) angle to at least 30 degrees. Although many hospital beds are capable of adjusting Head-of-Bed angles, compliance rates for this simple procedure are less than 50%. VAP is estimated to cost US hospitals $1 billion and 30,000 lives annually. The Head Of Patient Elevation (HOPE) Monitor is a retrofit bed tilt monitor which sounds an alarm when a bed has been prone for an extended period of time and wirelessly transmits bed angle data to the nurses’ station for analysis. The HOPE Monitor consists of three design modules: hardware, software, and exterior design. The hardware consists of an accelerometer, a Liquid Crystal Display (LCD), Zigbee transceivers, and other electrical components. The software runs on a custom-designed Java Graphical User Interface, which both displays and plots bed angles in real time. The exterior design utilizes a “Lock and Key” mechanism which will allow the monitor to be easily removed from beds and placed onto a charging dock. The HOPE Monitor will be able to operate for approximately 100 days between charges and costs approximately $150 for materials in bulk production. The HOPE Monitor will prevent millions of unnecessary deaths as well as save billions of dollars for hospitals.

title: Home is Where You Make It: The Development of Biases in Students’ Mental Representations of their College Campus
abstract: Previous research has shown that people are prone to making systematic errors in judgment when describing relations between landmarks in multiple geographic regions (Stevens and Coupe 1978). More recent work has demonstrated that where one lives can play a role in the development of subjective representations of superordinate regions (Friedman, Kerkman and Brown 2003). This study aims to further investigate these issues by looking at how Northwestern University undergraduates' subjective representations of their campus differ based on what region of campus they inhabit and how these representations develop over time. Subjects rated their familiarity with a series of 28 highly salient campus landmarks. Then their cognitive mapping of these locations was assessed using a drag and drop computer interface. Data was collected from 154 subjects across 4 academic quarters to analyze the developmental time course of the development of accuracy and bias in their cognitive maps of campus. Utilizing bidimensional regression methodology (Friedman and Kohler 2003) it was found that students’ development of accuracy in their cognitive maps of campus is both region dependent and continuous across their time spent on campus. Region specific bias was also found through analyzing subjects’ intra and inter-region distance estimations. These results serve to validate the application of Friedman and Kohler’s bidimensional regression methodology to the study of cognitive maps, as well as to shed light on the manner in which accuracy and categorical bias develop through subjects’ interaction with a space with implicit geographical categories that are learned primarily via direct navigation.

title: Hot Flashes: Uncovering the Mechanism of Thermo-dysregulation
abstract: Hot flashes commonly occur during menopause – a physiological phenomenon in which women cease to ovulate, and therefore lose the production of endogenous estrogen. It is hypothesized that this loss of estrogen causes the change in thermoregulation, which results in the experience of hot flashes. Thermoregulation takes place primarily in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus via the activity of temperature sensitive neurons. We aim to uncover the mechanism by which estrogen alters the sensitivity of these neurons. We have found that estrogen potentially acts through the modification of activity of the potassium channels known as background-leak or K2P channels. Because these channels can alter the electrical activity of a neuron and because it has been shown that they respond to changes in temperature, we hypothesize that K2P channels mediate the effects of estrogen on thermoregulation. Our experiments have found that the effect of these channels of thermoregulation does indeed differ between animals with estrogen versus animals that lack estrogen. Furthermore, we are working to discover what type of estrogen receptor is involved in this mechanism. The classical model of estrogen receptor is a ligand-activated transcription factor that mediates transcriptional events in response to estrogen. However, because these transcriptional events require a time period of several hours to days, whereas we have found that estrogen can alter thermoregulation within less than an hour, we have, therefore, turned our attention to a third potential estrogen receptor, GPR30, and are currently studying the possibility of its role in the hot flash mechanism.

title: Overweight, Obesity, and Incidence of Heart Failure
abstract: Overweight and obesity have been associated with incidence of heart failure (HF). Few studies, however, have investigated the relation between both abdominal and total obesity and rate of HF in populations that includes both middle-aged and elderly individuals. We examined the association between self-reported anthropometric measures—body mass index (BMI), waist circumference (WC), waist-hip ratio (WHR), and waist-height ratio (WHtR)—and incidence of HF in a population of middle-aged and elderly men and women. Over 7 years of follow-up 522 of 37,457 women and 932 of 44,365 men developed HF. Obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2) compared to normal weight (BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2) was associated with a 58% greater rate of developing HF (95% CI 22%-106%) among women and a more than doubled rate among men (hazard ratio (HR) = 2.27, 95% CI 1.88-2.75). Abdominal obesity was also associated with rate of HF in women (WC ≥ 88.0 cm versus < 80.0 cm HR = 1.48, 95% CI 1.16-1.88; WHR ≥ 0.85 versus < 0.85 HR = 1.36, 95% CI 1.13-1.64; WHtR ≥ 0.50 versus < 0.50 HR = 1.24, 95% CI 1.02-1.50) and in men (WC ≥ 102.0 cm versus < 94.0 cm HR = 1.74, 95% CI 1.47-2.05; WHR ≥ 1.0 versus < 1.0 HR = 1.38, 95% CI 1.16-1.64; WHtR ≥ 0.50 versus < 0.50 HR = 1.32, 95% CI 1.08-1.62). We can conclude that both BMI and measures of abdominal adiposity were associated with incidence of HF in middle-aged and older women and men.

title: Design of Nanoplasmonic Materials using Genetic Algorithms
abstract: Genetic algorithms are applied to design multi-parameter nanoplasmonic devices with optical applications. Lens-like metal structures are designed to spatially focus an incident plane wave to scales much smaller than its wavelength. First, a symmetric nanoscale metal lens is considered. The optimal structure resembles a dipole antenna. Next, a more complex asymmetric lens system is optimized and much greater field enhancement is obtained. Finally, various features of these optimal structures are analyzed to understand their optical properties and functionality. Other methods in nanoplasmonics are also discussed.

title: Avatar Self-Portraiture
abstract: From mirrors guiding the hands of artists to snapshots capturing smiling faces, popular visual technology has always affected the way we depict ourselves in self-portraiture. New virtual world technologies such as Second Life, currently inhabited by 13.2 million resident avatars, offers a new form of self-representation. Although avatar portraiture takes on many characteristics from earlier forms of self-portraiture, it departs from tradition in depicting identities without needing to depict the physical body. The popularization of the avatar presents a new moment in the tradition of self-representation. In this paper I will outline how, historically, popular technology has influenced our understanding and portrayal of our identities. I will then introduce the concept of the avatar, its sudden rise as a popular form of self-representation, and how it is heavily influenced by past technologies. Then, based on my own interviews with Second Life users about their approach to portraiture, I hope to show that avatars present a new moment in self-portraiture because these new virtual representations can sever the connection between identity and the body. Finally, I will explain how this new development can reflexively influence our identities, the way we see ourselves, and even the way we behave.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Novel Diblock and Triblock Copolymer Hydrogels
abstract: Transplantation and surgery are the most effective tools doctors have today for organ replacement. Despite the large number of individuals who do receive a transplant, 21% of individuals pass away without them. Biomaterials research has demonstrated considerable potential in the search for alternatives, especially in tissue engineering. Hydrogel polymers show promise as scaffolds for tissue growth and replacement. However, its practical use has been limited by weak mechanical properties. Recent work has revealed that superimposed networks of polymers enhance mechanical toughness, achieving a modulus (resistance to deformation) more than ten times higher than their single-network counterparts. Extending the concept of these double network hydrogels to another system of polymers, I have conducted axial/compression tests and rheological studies in an effort to gauge the strength of triblock and diblock copolymer gels under various solvent and crosslinking conditions.

title: A Life of Wonder: Winifred Ward
abstract: Winifred Ward, a revolutionary teacher, strove to bring imagination into every child’s education. She invented Creative Dramatics, a process-centered form of educational drama, and established the groundbreaking Children’s Theatre of Evanston, bringing drama to children for the first time. Ward believed in educating the whole child, emotionally and intellectually, by incorporating imagination and storytelling into the curriculum. Storytelling is a human experience in which a child assumes the identity of a character and, through the lens of that character, explores the world. When I began my research in Winifred Ward’s archives, I was struck by the quantity of letters she received from students of all ages repeatedly thanking her for changing their lives. I wanted to bring her amazing character to life for a modern audience by adapting her archives into a solo-performance piece. I made careful selections from her academic writings, personal letters and photographs to create a performance that illustrated her passion and the powerful impact drama has on a child’s life. A solo-performance seemed most appropriate since it would communicate how one woman influenced the lives of so many others: through one actor, the audience hears Ward’s voice, as well as the voices of everyone she affected. A Life of Wonder: Winifred Ward tells Ward's story, but in telling her story, many others emerged: the lives of all of the people she touched who have spread her philosophies throughout the world. Her legacy lives on in the people they have taught.

title: Co-overexpression of Akt and Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) in Mesenchymal Stem Cells Promotes Endothelial Differentiation and Angiogenesis
abstract: It has been previously shown that transplantation of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) co-overexpressing Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) and Akt prevent cell apoptosis, enhance angiogenesis, and improve heart function. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, MSCs were adenovirally transduced with genes encoding for green fluorescent protein (group 1) as control, Akt (group 2), Ang-1 (group 3) and both Akt and Ang-1 (group 4). After 48 hours of transduction, the cell lysate and conditioned medium from each group was collected. I conducted real-time PCR on the samples which showed significant up-regulation (more than 2 fold) of HIF-1α, HO-1, VEGF, VEGFR-1 and PGF in group 4. Exposure to sub lethal anoxia amplified these changes. Gene silencing by HIF-1α siRNA markedly reduced the protein expression of HO-1, VEGF and VEGFR1 in group 4. Concentration of VEGF was the highest in conditioned medium (CM) from group 4 as shown by ELISA and was abrogated by HIF-1α siRNA. Group 4 MSCs showed tube formation upon 4 hours VEGF treatment. In transwell migration assays, VEGF exerts a potent chemoattractant activity on group 4 cells via VEGF/VEGFR1/2-mediated mechanism Real-time PCR array, immunocytochemistry, flow cytometry and immunoblotting showed higher expression of endothelial markers (VEGFR-1, Tie-1 and Tie-2) in group 4 MSCs. In conclusion, the co-overexpression of Ang-1 and Akt potentiates release of HIF-1α dependent angiogenic mediators and promotes endothelial differentiation to enhance angiogenesis.

title: We're Always in a Crisis Here: Outmigration from a Rural Mexican Community
abstract: The prospects for rural areas in Mexico heavily influence outmigration to cities within Mexico and across the border to the United States. Migrants leave in pursuit of jobs and viable opportunities for education and a higher standard of living. The communally-owned land community of El Oro, situated in the state of Nayarit, Mexico, is no different. However, based on ethnographic and oral history interviews with members of the community of El Oro, whose main source of income is cattle ranching, we have observed a significant shift from a permanent outmigration, which characterized the mid-1970’s through the early 1990’s, to seasonal migration. Recent increases in assistance from government programs established to provide supplemental monetary support have instead created economic dependence on these programs. Although government programs have not generated significantly higher standards of living or opportunities for employment in El Oro, they have proven to offer a monetary incentive for remaining in the community. Seasonal migration to supplement this government support has developed as a response to the new financial incentive of remaining part-time in El Oro. The implications of this migratory shift will continue to evolve as government support finances higher education for youth from El Oro and as the support programs themselves evolve, most likely establishing a new pattern of outmigration.

title: A Population Synthesis Analysis of Double Neutron Stars
abstract: The evolutionary history of the few known Double Neutron Star (DNS) systems has been the subject of much controversy over the past four decades. Due to their tight orbits and high velocities, DNS systems are some of the most exotic celestial objects in the universe. Since the discovery of the first DNS system, B1913+16, in 1974, DNS systems have provided astrophysicists with excellent laboratories to learn about stellar evolution. In this talk, I will present the results of a population synthesis study, which investigates a variety of parameters in the formation of neutron stars. I will place constraints on the supernova kick velocities, occurrence of electron capture supernovae, and mass transfer phases in the evolutionary history of DNS systems. Although the mechanics are not well understood, these factors play an important role in determining the characteristics of DNS systems. Finally, I will use these constraints to explain the evolutionary history of several known DNS systems.

title: The Art of Schmoozing: Positive Effects of Information Sharing in Intra-Cultural Negotiations
abstract: The establishment of trust in negotiations is widely regarded as a prerequisite for realizing high joint gains – at least in Western cultures like the United States. Past research suggests that trust underlies the strategic choice of negotiating distributively or integratively. In order to realize joint gains through integrative negotiation, it is beneficial for negotiators to build trust by getting to know the other party, i.e. “to schmooze.” Building on research linking trust, culture, and joint gains, I hypothesized that American managers devote more time to and engage more frequently in behavior best categorized as schmoozing. To test this hypothesis, I analyzed roughly 6,000 statements taken from independently-coded transcripts of an intra-cultural negotiation simulation between two American or two Indian managers. Analysis of the data supported my hypothesis and revealed another interesting finding: Indian managers tend to make more low-quality, single-issue offers compared to their American counterparts. Ultimately, schmoozing provides a simple and often overlooked mechanism for negotiators from low trust cultures like India to improve their joint gains. Conversely, negotiators from high trust cultures like the United States should not assume reciprocal schmoozing in negotiations. This study contributes to the extant research on negotiations by demonstrating the importance of schmoozing in linking culture to behaviors to trust to joint gains in an economy rife with opportunities for inter-cultural exchange.

title: Ironic Effects of Egalitarian Priming on Intergroup Empathy and Altruistic Motivation
abstract: What predicts bias or motivates helping behavior? Modern social psychologists have identified social dominance orientation (SDO) as the degree to which one prefers their own social group to dominate others. Stronger social hierarchy preference has been shown to support political ideologies that promote social hierarchy rather than egalitarianism (e.g., politico-economic conservatism), oppose public policies intended to attenuate group-based social inequality (e.g., civil rights, women’s rights, gay and lesbian rights), and seek societal roles that reify dominance hierarchy within social institutions (e.g., law enforcement rather than social work). Notably, empathy is an important attenuator of preference for social hierarchy. Using social psychological priming techniques and fMRI, I examine how priming abstract political attitudes affects empathic neural response. My hypothesis builds upon recent neuroimaging evidence from my lab, which indicates that a person’s preference for human social hierarchy or egalitarianism predicts neural response within brain regions associated with empathy, such as the anterior cingulate cortex and bilateral insula. Developing a more comprehensive understanding of what leads to active bias against historic and newly-formed outgroups will aid in developing policies correct these imbalances.

title: Breast Milk Rx: Exploring the Effects of Early Life Nutrition Upon Maternal Hemoglobin Status
abstract: Breastfeeding is recommended as the most beneficial method of ensuring health and well-being in infants. As the most bioavailable source of iron for infants, breast milk provides optimal nutrition to establish proper iron metabolism and develop adequate iron stores in early life. Several epidemiological studies performed across global populations have concluded that the risk of developing some chronic non-communicable diseases in adulthood is influenced by nutrition and other environmental stimuli acting in early life. To date, no study has evaluated the role of early life nutrition upon iron status and the risk of developing iron deficiency in adulthood. Iron deficiency anemia, highly prevalent in women and children, is the most common nutritional disorder worldwide. The purpose of this study was to explore the influence of early life nutrition upon maternal hemoglobin status in adulthood. Study participants consisted of young Filipino mothers (n=118) born to the original index population recruited for the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey (CLHNS) in 1983-84. Multivariate analysis revealed a significantly negative association between duration of received breastfeeding and adult hemoglobin levels. Women categorized as breastfed for a long duration (18+ months) during infancy displayed significantly lower levels of hemoglobin in adulthood than those breastfed for a relatively shorter duration (0-18 months). Controlling for present and early life socioeconomic status strengthened this relationship. Interestingly, there were no relationships observed between lifestyle factors like diet, income, or educational level and maternal hemoglobin levels in this population. These findings add to the growing body of research investigating the influence of early life nutrition and specifically the protective role of breastfeeding for offspring throughout infancy and into adulthood.

title: Colorimetric Detection of Short Chain Alcohols by Immobilized Enzymes
abstract: Both enzyme immobilization and detection of short chain alcohols are important in a wide variety of scientific and commercial fields. Certain polymers and resins can effectively bind enzymes while maintaining the enzyme’s catalytic effectiveness. This research focuses on creating a colorimetric indicator for shot chain alcohols by way of immobilized enzymes and indictors in various matrices. Specifically, a coupled reaction of alcohol oxidase, horseradish peroxidase, and 3,3’,5,5’-tetramethyl benzidine (TMB) is utilized in order to create a detection scheme for short chain alcohols. The effectiveness of the reactions in solution is examined first. When ethanol is added to the solution of enzymes and TMB, the solution turns a light blue color, indicating the presence of ethanol. Next, the ability of various resins and polymers to immobilize the reactants is examined. Several different matrices are tested, including polystyrene, pyrrole, and thiole. The effectiveness of each matrix in binding the enzymes while maintaining their catalytic facilities is analyzed. This work is an ongoing process, with new variations in polymer type and concentration, as well as variations in reactant concentrations, being examined at the conclusion of each set of trials. This project builds upon a successful chemical interaction and seeks to identify the best combination of components, concentrations, and chemicals possible for the creation of the final detector.

title: Bringing Theatre to the Classroom for Students Affected by Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: The prevalence of children who have a diagnosis on the Autism Spectrum has increased from one in one thousand in the early 1990s to one in one hundred fifty-two by 2002. Instead of continuing with business as usual, it is imperative that classroom teachers and teaching artists adapt curriculum and expectations to best serve this rising populations of students. Theatre and Drama, though not consistently a priority in classrooms across the country, can be an incredible tool for students on the Spectrum. Drama can provide safe opportunities for students for whom social interaction is an immense challenge, can increase language skills through the games and dramas introduced, and most importantly, can become a real emotional outlet for some students. However, with these wonderful opportunities come intense challenges. Theatre lives in a world that requires a modicum of social engagement and communication skills, a distinct difficulty for children affected by Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Using a detailed examination of Autism Spectrum Disorder that involves classroom observations, interviews and personal experience, blended with a thorough inquiry into what drama tools would serve these students best, I crafted a curriculum that addresses the challenges that ASD brings, while simultaneously creating a safe environment in which these students can play, overcome obstacles, and become more expressive, socially comfortable people.

title: Australia's Stolen Generation: The Legacy of Forcible Child Removal
abstract: For most of the 21st century, government policy in Australia called for the forcible removal of Aboriginal children (usually mixed-race children) from their families. These children were adopted or fostered by white families or placed in institutions in order to integrate them into white society. Members of this “Stolen Generation” often faced physical, emotional and sexual abuse as children. As adults, they suffer from identity issues, loss of culture, high incarceration rates and low employment rates. My research while in Australia focused on the long-term effects of removal on individual members of the Stolen Generation, as well as the changes that have occurred in policy and public opinion since Prime Minister Rudd issued the first federal apology to the Stolen Generation last February. I found that although Aboriginal activists had high hopes for post-apology reconciliation and healing, most are now disillusioned by the inaction of the federal government. Some even feel that today’s high rates of Aboriginal children in out-of-home care and the juvenile justice system represent the formation of a new group of stolen children. Activists today push for financial reparations as the only meaningful form of apology and the sole avenue toward equality. A year after the apology, most non-Aboriginal Australians know of the Stolen Generation, but it remains a controversial issue: in a country plagued by continued racism and marginalization of indigenous people, opinions vary regarding the need for an apology or compensation, as do beliefs about the severity of long-term effects of removal.

title: Healthy to Me: Incorporation of Perspectives on Health and Healthcare among People, Practitioners, and Government Programs in Ho, Ghana
abstract: Medical anthropology has always stressed that the views people are important for understanding health and healthcare in a given setting. Over the last 60 years, the approach to examining the scope of the healthcare system from people’s perspectives has become increasingly complex: more attention is paid to the "pluralistic" healthcare system and the structural circumstances and constraints which shape such a system. This broad view of the elements of a healthcare system necessitates an equally broad definition of what makes such a system “effective.” While a myriad of indicators might be investigated to understand the efficacy of a healthcare system, my work engages with an indicator that is true to the medical anthropology tradition of engaging with people’s views. Understanding the beliefs and actions of people as they tie to those who actually create and distribute healthcare services—practitioners and government programs—becomes crucial in the holistic approach to healthcare. In this paper, I will explore the incorporation of people’s perspectives on health and healthcare by those practitioners and government programs that the people identify as significant, using a case study of women, practitioners, and government program representatives in Ho, Ghana. I suggest that the expanded-descriptive methodology which I use to paint the picture of the healthcare system relevant to these women in Ho could broaden the information gathered by Ghana's Health Information System, provide a ground-up, holistic understanding of Ghana's healthcare system and its efficacy in relation to the incorporation of perspectives, and guide future research and resource development.

title: Trends and Predictors of Menarche in Filipino Girls
abstract: Previous reports suggest that nutritional stressors during childhood may predict menarche, the onset of menstruation. Early life psychosocial stressors may also influence menarche, according to certain developmental theorists. Little is known about the effects of these stressors in non-Western, non-industrialized contexts. Many developing countries have tropical climates, lower food availability, and a greater prevalence of infectious diseases, which may distinctly shape timing of menarche. The present study aimed fill this research gap by analyzing menarche timing and predictors, both nutritional and psychosocial, in the Philippines. Data from the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey (CLHNS), a community-based prospective study in Cebu City, Philippines were used. The representative sample of female singletons (N=1,009) were surveyed and measured during childhood (8.5 +/- 0.04 yrs). Compared to US white girls, Cebu girls had a later mean menarche (12.9 vs. 13.1 years), which was significantly influenced by childhood nutritional status. Multivariate regression analysis indicated significantly earlier menarche in Cebu girls of greater BMI (P ≤ 0.001). After accounting for confounding nutritional variables, girls from smaller households showed significantly earlier menarche (P ≤ 0.01). Father absence, a psychosocial stressor linked to earlier menarche in European industrialized populations, did not predict menarche in Cebu. These results support the notion that early life conditions affect menarche but that the relative influence of psychosocial stressors may depend on the available resources and nutritional stress of the study population.

title: The Cure
abstract: This project explores race, medicine, and belief through a plot in which a mother’s search for her identity and a cure for her sick child are inextricably intertwined. Titled “The Cure,” the novella questions whether a single cure can heal, a single medical choice can offer medical relief, and a single identity can constitute a person and her decisions. The plot of “The Cure” focuses on a mother seeking medical care for her son in Quetzaltenango, Guatemala. Partly due to her indigenous upbringing, she prefers care from a healer, though her husband prefers care from a doctor. The mother, however, has not always preferred healers. The cause of her change in opinion remains a provocative mystery until the novella’s end. As the family seeks medical help from a healer, a doctor, and a natural medicine vendor, the mother struggles to determine whether she identifies herself as an indigenous person (who is supposed to believe in healers) or a non-indigenous person (who is supposed to believe in doctors). The inspiration for this project derived from my own research in Quetzaltenango and its surrounding villages, where I interviewed and observed healers and the users of healers and doctors. The novella, a thesis for the English Major in Writing, developed out of an English 398 senior thesis seminar and an independent study. In order to perfect my writing for the project, I read a variety of fiction writers who employ rich, ethnographic description, dramatize cultural conflict, and create distinct personalities for individual characters.

title: Hybridized Medicines: Trends of Midwifery and Natural Medicine in Guatemala
abstract: The 1996 Guatemalan Peace Accords promised to protect indigenous medicine (“Agreement” 1998). However, contemporary processes of medicalization and professionalization have called the success of this protection into question. Using interviews and observations conducted in Quetzaltenango and its surrounding villages, this study compares how medicalization and professionalization have influenced two important forms of indigenous medicine—midwifery and natural medicine—and what their influences on these medicines signify for the protection of indigenous medicine in Guatemala. Anthropological literature has assessed the effects of medicalization and professionalization on midwifery and natural medicine in the United States and in several developing countries. This study engages with this literature and expands upon it by analyzing how the effects of medicalization and professionalization differ between midwifery and natural medicine in Guatemala. Findings indicate that both midwifery and natural medicine now exist as hybridized biomedical/professional/indigenous medicines. Yet, separate causes of medicalization and professionalization for midwifery and natural medicine have resulted in differently hybridized forms that possess unique threats and assets. Government training that replaces indigenous midwifery knowledge with biomedical knowledge has fostered medicalization and professionalization within midwifery. On the other hand, market pressures to sell indigenous natural medicine knowledge have fostered medicalization and professionalization within natural medicine. These processes of medicalization and professionalization and their negative and positive effects on midwifery and natural medicine demonstrate the complex changes occurring within Guatemalan indigenous medicine today. Furthermore, the analyses carried out in this study provide a means of understanding how indigenous medicine can be better protected in the future.

title: "I Impregnated a Girl, What Should I Do?": A Case Study of Using Theater for Development to Promote Critical Thinking in Uganda
abstract: The Ugandan Ministry of Education and Sports cites significant improvements in the last decade in the areas of access to education, equity in education, and quality and relevance of education, especially in terms of public health education. However, despite these achievements, scholars, educational leaders and pubic health officials are concerned that students lack the critical thinking skills necessary to apply content knowledge to decision making. White and Robinson (2001) present a model for the explicit teaching of critical thinking skills in the arts. Given the cultural importance of Music, Dance and Drama in Uganda and the emergence of Theater for Development as a popular method of spreading public health information, the present author explores a case study using Forum Theater as a viable method for problem-based learning that improves critical thinking skills. The case study consisted of conducting Forum Theater workshops with a local performance troupe focused on creating an environment for participants to work together to define a problem, brainstorm potential solutions, evaluate potential solutions, and then understand the repercussions of the decision in a health care context. The workshops culminated with the performance troupe using Forum Theater techniques to address the multiple components of public health questions in front of an audience. The successful application of White and Robinson's model within the case study provides preliminary evidence that problem-based methods of teaching critical thinking can effectively teach Ugandan students the skills necessary to make healthy decisions.

title: Inside Terrorist Groups: The Role of Organizational Factors in Terrorist Attacks
abstract: Despite the importance of international terrorism to United States national security and the recent proliferation of general information about terrorist groups like al Qaeda, there is still a lack of real understanding of how terrorist groups operate. Although decision-making in covert organizations is often portrayed by the media as shadowy, irrational, and impossible to understand, terrorists are constrained and influenced by tangible organizational factors like funding and resources, operational capabilities, group structure, and the security environment in which they operate. In my thesis, I develop a theoretical model that uses the relative centralization or decentralization of the group’s physical organizational structure and the level of unity or disunity among the group’s top leadership to classify terrorist organizations at different points in time. In general, I argue that as a group becomes more centralized, its attacks increase in scale and sophistication, and that as the leadership becomes more unified, individual attacks are better integrated into the campaign. I then test my model through an examination of the historical trajectories of three terrorist groups – al Qaeda, the IRA and ETA. This analysis demonstrates that changes in the organizational structure and unity among the leadership led to variations in the scale, sophistication and integration of attacks consistent with my model. This correlation between organizational factors and attack characteristics has important implications for counterterrorism policies. While current government efforts focus on limiting the capabilities of terrorist groups, manipulating internal organizational factors could accelerate a group’s demise and cause it to self-destruct.

title: An Argument for the Positive Moral Effects of Taste in Society in Immanuel Kant’s Critique of Judgment
abstract: Immanuel Kant’s Critique of Judgment stands not only as a seminal work of aesthetic theory, but also as a conclusion to his larger critical project. Scholars agree that a key goal of this book is to resolve the apparent disconnect between the worlds of nature and morality—simply put, are our moral aims achievable in the natural world? However, they also acknowledge that Kant’s solution is multifaceted, and addresses both metaphysical and societal worries. I construct Kant’s answer to this later question: how can I hope to be moral in society? Scholars have typically interpreted Kant to take a negative view of the moral effects of taste in society. I argue against this view, and show how taste plays an ambiguous but ultimately positive role in moral achievement in society because taste is fundamentally both social and unsocial. Taste helps to address many of the evil effects that come from society that if left unchecked could lead one to moral despair. Expanding upon Kant’s conception of human society as unsocial sociability, I outline how taste interacts with our social and unsocial natures and show how taste provides a benefit to society. I end by showing the positive moral effects of taste in society: it aids the creation of a civil society and makes human society a place friendlier to moral achievement.

title: Elasticity of Demand for Auto-Travel and Gasoline
abstract: This paper analyzes the short and long-run elasticities of demand for both auto-travel and gasoline. During the 1970’s, this area of economics became the focus of many researchers following the Arab Oil Embargo. The record gasoline prices of the 2008 summer provide another time period of price fluctuation to analyze. Using OLS regression techniques to find coefficients for elasticities, this paper looks at several functional forms including log-linear and a log model. Examining several different variables and using a lagged variable to separate the effects, the regression will abstract the long-term elasticities from the more general, short-term model. The elasticity should change over time because consumers have more ways to modify their behavior in response to price shocks. Looking at elasticities for both travel and gasoline consumption will provide important insight in the realm of policy-making. Several proposals have been made recently for increasing the gas tax or taxing miles traveled to increase revenue for highway construction and maintenance. The results of this study will show whether consumers will change their gasoline consumption or driving more dramatically in response to price shocks.

title: From Machine to Monument: The Multiple Narratives of the Bessemer Converter
abstract: Bessemer Court of Station Square, a downtown entertainment and restaurant complex in Pittsburgh, represents the junction between the city’s past and present. Amid franchise restaurants, shops, and a musical synchronized fountain sits a Bessemer converter, an industrial machine that once turned iron into steel. The Bessemer converter’s transformation from machine to monument explicates the rich industrial heritage and identity of the “Steel City.” The object in its locational context functions as an exemplary lens to study the multiple narratives that preserve the memory of Pittsburgh’s industrial legacy. This American Studies thesis illustrates that Pittsburgh's post-industrial history is comprised of multiple narratives that interact with one another. It examines the preservation and representation of the Bessemer converter in Station Square. From the machine's placement in a public and commercialized venue, multiple historical narratives emerge that retell Pittsburgh's history of deindustrialization in different and sometimes competing ways. The thesis investigates three narrative perspectives on deindustrialization. The Bessemer converter illustrates the ambivalent relationship between the civic elites of Pittsburgh and the city's industrial history. The machine also acts as a lens through which non-Pittsburghers view and remember the city's legacy of steel. Finally, the Bessemer converter functions as a vehicle through which steelworkers’ narrative of deindustrialization can be read. Through the image of Bessemer converter, this thesis argues that these multiple narratives destabilize the idea of a dominant and controllable historical narrative.

title: Death of a Friend: Facebook as a Virtual Site of Mourning
abstract: Facebook boasts over 200 million active users. With this population, it is not an extraordinary occurrence that an account holder passes away, leaving behind their profile. Because the account is not canceled with the account holder’s death, friends of the recently deceased can continue to post messages that express grief. Behaving much like grave or memorial, Facebook becomes a site for real mourning, revealing the importance of virtual space in our contemporary society.

title: Among The Salvages
abstract: This project began as a critical-theory approach to what it means to be a person living in a tourism-dominated society, that is, to be the "Toured," a person responsible for ensuring the pleasure of the visitors. Such is the experience of many who live and work in my hometown of Daytona Beach, Florida. As I pursued this line of inquiry, however, I was drawn farther and farther down the chain of those living in this town, until eventually I arrived at those undeniably at its bottom-most position: the homeless. ("Bottom-most" does not necessarily mean "most servile;" a lot of the time they end up being its most independent and carefree folks). The project evolved into an exploration of a homeless woman's trek across the place's landscape, accompanied only by her small insanities, good faith, and the baby boy to whom she has just given birth. Convinced as I was that there is no more "local" variety of people than a town's homeless, this approach may illuminate some really intriguing aspects of my subject, this city. It is about tourism still, but more tangentially--there's no escaping it here, and I continued to research its economic effects on local conditions. But my focus turned to other aspects of the city's life-blood, for example the Halifax River, where she lives on an improvised raft with her child to escape the mainland's violence and mosquitoes. Eventually, as she must, she leaves this unsustainable life on the river and is taken into an actual community, in a handmade camp on the shore, living outside of any but their own society. I have come to really appreciate this character and I hope that others will too. I should mention that she has a sense of humor.

title: Metallurgical Analysis of Native American Copper Artifacts from Cahokia
abstract: The members of the Mississippian culture inhabiting the Cahokia Mounds site in southern Illinois from 650 to 1400 CE were known for their ability to produce intricately formed decorative and ceremonial copper objects from native copper nuggets. Since North American Indians are not believed to have melted metals, these objects are thought to have been created by hammering copper nuggets into thin sheets. Previous studies of Mississippian copper artifacts, while limited in scope, have revealed that copper workers heat-treated, or annealed, the hammered sheets to reverse the embrittlement that occurs in deformed metals. It is also suspected that multiple sheets may have been hammered together to create layered structures, and that the straight edges of some objects were cut using a standard shearing technique. The unprecedented discovery of a copper workshop at Cahokia, dating to ca. 1200 CE, has provided a novel opportunity to comparatively analyze Mississippian worked copper artifacts. With the goals of more fully explaining the hammering and annealing process and identifying the presence of layering and shearing, eight small copper artifacts from the Cahokia workshop were examined. Cross sections were taken from the objects and the microscopic structure was assessed using optical microscopy, microhardness testing, and scanning electron microscopy in order to determine the processing route. Features seen in these objects were recreated on copper samples, and microstructural findings were compared to confirm the identification of Mississippian metalworking techniques.

title: The "Crisis" of Universalism and the Fight against Discrimination in France
abstract: This study examines the traditional concept of universalism in French political thought. In principle, this concept ensures equality for all individuals before the law without distinction of origin, race or religion. In short, France defines itself as a color-blind state. As such, all citizens retain a neutral identity devoid of all particularities and are thus equals unified in this neutrality. However, the state has encountered problems reconciling its universalistic philosophy with the reality of social inequalities rooted in racial/ethnic discrimination. To investigate this struggle, I interviewed representatives of both state-affiliated and independent organizations that are engaged in the ongoing fight against discrimination. I argue that in order to recognize and punish discriminatory practices, such organizations must inherently operate within a color-conscious mindset. My research thus analyzes how color-conscious organizations combat discrimination in a color-blind state. More specifically, this study concentrates on the chosen tactics and instruments used by these organizations. Further, the study will address how proposed new tactics, notably the collection of racial/ethnic statistics, have fueled debate and tested the boundaries of anti-discrimination policy. Essentially, by tracing indicators of color-consciousness and color-blindness, this study examines the different ways in which state-affiliated and independent anti-discrimination organizations mitigate threats to their respective perceptions of society while fighting for the same cause.

title: Nanoscale Doping of Transparent Conducting Oxides with Focused Ion Beam
abstract: The capability of creation of electronic device display and control functions within an optically transparent medium offers the possibility of dramatically changing both the consumer and scientific sectors of modern optoelectronics. Recently, multiple advances have been reported in the areas of transparent transistors and other optoelectronics components, principally centered on transparent conducting oxides and carbon nanotubes. It is likely that both of these materials systems will play major roles in realizing future display and control functions that utilize transparent circuitry. Curiously, however, effective means for the controlled placement of interconnects, an absolute necessity for transparent device-to-device integration, has remained elusive. Our work involves an effective method for the spatially-controlled writing of embedded, optically transparent, electrically conducting oxide nanowires and other patterns via focused ion beam implantation into highly resistive transparent metal oxide thin films. The resulting doped regions form 110-160 nm wide wires of ~7nm nominal depth, which are theoretically limitless in length, connectivity, and shape. These electrically-active wires are imaged by a combination of conductive atomic force microscopy (c-AFM) techniques, and dopant concentration profiles are characterized with secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS).

title: Matrix Stiffness Regulates Antrum Formation in a 3-Dimensional Ovarian Follicle Culture System
abstract: Using a novel 3-dimensional ovarian follicle culture system, we regulate antrum formation via the physical properties of the culture matrix, and study aquaporin and hypoxia-inducible factor alpha (Hif-1α) gene expression in the system. In this system, multilayered secondary follicles isolated from mouse ovaries were placed in droplets of alginate, which were then allowed to cross-link in calcium chloride solution. Studies were performed in 0.5% and 1.5% alginate concentrations, which have significantly different stiffness. RNA was isolated from the follicles after 2-8 days of culture, for RT-PCR analysis of aquaporin and Hif-1α gene expression. Only 5.5% of follicles cultured in 1.5% matrix formed antral cavity, but the follicles showed high expression of aquaporin and Hif-1α genes. Follicles cultured in 0.5% less stiff alginate matrix formed antra in over 85% of follicles, but showed low expressions of aquaporin and Hif-1α genes. Alginate matrix used in 3D in vitro culture system has regulating effects on antrum-regulating gene expression, due to induced hypoxic effect in follicles. Follicles cultured in stiffer alginate matrices are unable to expand in the growth process, and thus antrum unable to form, due to the external pressure of the stiffer alginate matrix. However, increasing tissue mass within the follicle impedes oxygen transportation into the follicle, causing hypoxic conditions within the follicle. Aquaporin proteins, particularly aquaporin 7 and 8, are then expressed to alleviate the hypoxic effect, thus describing the regulation of alginate matrix stiffness in gene expression related to antrum formation in in vitro cultured ovarian follicles.

title: Generativity and Midlife Child-Free Women
abstract: Personality psychologists are interested in the ways in which adults, during midlife, better both the world around them and the next generation. In recent decades the amount of research on generativity, a psychological term referring to how adults leave a legacy for themselves and positively affect the next generation, has greatly increased. It has emerged as an important part of adult identity development and a critical component of finding contentment with one’s life. Yet, still lacking is a comprehensive study on midlife adults without children and how they may be generative as well. This study begins to explore generativity among these adults, starting with mid-life, child-free women. The study, which used both quantitative and qualitative measures, involved 40 female participants aged 45-60. Several fascinating findings have emerged. These findings include: no significant differences regarding the general levels of generativity of mothers and child-free women; among child-free women, a positive correlation between amount of desire to have had a child in the past and level of generative concern in the present; women who are child-free by choice are significantly more satisfied with their lives than those who are child-free by circumstance, especially in terms of feeling that “my life is close to my ideal;” age is negatively correlated with one’s satisfaction of life for child-free women, but not for mothers. These findings and others begin to fill an existing gap in the body of literature on generativity. They can also serve to better society’s understanding of child-free women and help to decrease the stigma often associated with being child-free.

title: Opium Smoking and the Politics of Association in England, Hong Kong, and Mainland China
abstract: This paper explores British opium use in Hong Kong and, to a lesser extent, mainland China between the years of 1815 and 1895. My goal herein is to interpret an interesting disparity: the confusing fact that while British attitudes toward opium smoking in England were firmly and vehemently opposed to the practice, expatriated British living in Hong Kong and Mainland China almost entirely accepted it. The national revulsion toward smoked opium appears stranger still considering that British opium use in England in all forms but that of smoking was widespread and tolerated. In four sections, I compare the attitudes of the British in England and the British in Hong Kong towards opium, suggesting reasons that might explain this divergence of popular sentiment. I conclude that, because British familiarity with the situation of opium smoking in Chinese life softened Western opinions of it, and because Hong Kong was an island where cultural familiarity was a by-product of life and business, the English who visited or lived in Hong Kong had attitudes that defied traditional conceptions of opium smoking.

title: Learner's Perception and the English as a Second Language Classroom
abstract: My research focused on a homogeneous American Literature high school classroom and its effect on how the English as a Second Language student learns the English language. The quality of English as a Second Language (ESL) education has become more of an issue since the population in the United States is increasingly becoming more diverse, and the immigrant population of students who have little knowledge of English continues to grow. Because of the growing population size in ESL classrooms, this research examines the effectiveness of the ESL homogeneous classroom in helping ESL students learn the English language. It draws from 10 semi-structured interviews and 15 student surveys. The sample is from the ESL classroom at Mather High School. The participants vary in races and range from ages 14 – 18. The interviews focus on language arts activities used in the classroom and the classroom environment. Quantitative data will be employed to measure the students’ opinions about how practices in the ESL homogeneous classroom and the classroom itself help the learner comprehend the English language. Initial findings suggest the importance of the communal environment of ESL learners present in the homogeneous classroom in assisting with language comprehension.

title: Magnetoelectric Cobalt Ferrite/Bismuth Ferrite Hybrid Nanostructures
abstract: Gaining electrical control over the magnetic state of a material is an important step toward the next generation of magnetic memory devices. Composite ferromagnetic/ferroelectric materials exhibit the magnetoelectric effect, an effect that allows for control of the material's magnetization using an external electric field. Such systems are expected to possess superior functionalities on the nanometer length scale. I present detailed analysis of the static and dynamic properties of nanostructures of one artificial magnetoelectric material, cobalt ferrite/bismuth ferrite. The nanostructures are 200 nm in size, far too small to be seen by the naked eye. Several types of imaging and experimentation were carried out, including scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, magnetic force microscopy, SQUID magnetometry, ferromagnetic resonance spectroscopy, etc., to study the physical properties. The results indicated growth of crystalline structures and complex magnetic domains, suggesting progress towards fabrication of a true magnetoelectric composite. If successful, these nanostructures could be used to construct more efficient electronic devices, such as magnetic field sensors, generators, and transformers, to name a few.

title: Candidates for Admiration: Identity and Display in the Art of London’s Public Parks from 1750-1800
abstract: London’s parks were an attractive subject for a wide variety of artists in the late eighteenth-century because of their unique role as sites of social tension and compromise. Parks were newly accessible, only recently relinquished from private royal usage. I contend that the diversity of the park challenges the view held by previous writers that the modern urban public in London was made up entirely of upper-class men. In the park, people of different classes, genders and levels of refinement occupied the same space in a way that was entirely new. People came to the park with the intention of putting themselves on display and achieving social standing or respectability through their behavior. My research focuses on a variety of paintings, prints and drawings, both serious and satirical, and argues that the creation of these works was intended to promote reflection and discourse on the complex issues of the evolving urban society by presenting both positive and negative sides of public behavior. The art works thematize the performance of class, gender and military roles in the city and the anxieties associated with public presence and observation. I focus on the representation of fashion, deportment and spectacle as the key signifiers used by individuals to construct and present their identity. Throughout the selected works, the artists remind the viewer that the novelty of the public park was that it was a democratic space where longstanding attitudes were challenged in the everyday life of modern urban citizens.

title: Small Molecule Activators of the Heat Shock Response as Potential Neurodegenerative Disease Therapeutics
abstract: Environmental and pathophysiological insults that lead to protein misfolding and aggregation activate a highly conserved cellular response, the heat shock response (HSR), which helps maintain protein homeostasis by up-regulating the expression of heat shock proteins (hsps). Hsps function as molecular chaperones and help refold proteins into their native states and promote the degradation of protein aggregates. Several fatal neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, and Huntington’s diseases are characterized by protein aggregates and plaques, which lead to the progressive loss of neuronal cells and eventually to patient death. Since the HSR has a key role in suppressing protein misfolding and aggregation, we hypothesize that finding small molecules that induce the HSR could delay, reduce, or suppress protein aggregation in the cell and might have an immense potential to cure neurodegenerative diseases associated with protein misfolding. Our laboratory has identified more than 300 small molecule activators of the HSR using a high-throughput cell-based assay. Compounds displaying high potency in activating the HSR and low cytotoxicity are being characterized to identify their mechanism of action and cellular specificity. In addition, we show that the small molecules are able to activate the HSR in a living organism, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, suggesting that the small molecules may have in vivo efficacy. The small molecules are currently being evaluated for their potential to reduce protein aggregation and toxicity in C. elegans models of neurodegeneration.

title: The Role of Experience in Preschool Children’s Racially-Based Category Inductions
abstract: What factors affect young children's acquisition of racially-based social categories? By the time they reach kindergarten, children are sensitive to--and make inferences based on --social categories including race and gender. The current study asks whether children's experience affects the developmental trajectory of category-based inferences. Three- to four-year-old White and African-American children were taught a novel property about a particular person and then asked whether they would extend that property to other people of the same and different races. Preliminary results suggest that African-American preschool children are more sensitive to the category race when making inductive inferences than their White counterparts.

title: The History of Brother Titus the Sparrow
abstract: “The History of Brother Titus the Sparrow” is a poetic attempt to provide a compelling account of the formation and maturation of a single character through his relationships. The poem takes seriously an identity philosophy that creates a whole being from the interwoven relationships and connections this being has. This identity philosophy is worked out as a poem to highlight the ambiguous intimacy such a philosophy carries with it hand in hand. Discarding naive notions of cause and effect, the mystery and rough-hewn answers found in the makeup and structure of a poem create the active space within which we can live our full, complex, rarely direct lives. Rufinius is depicted as a young man in his 18th, 19th (briefly), and 20th years. The poem uses occasional Biblical metaphors to progress his relationships and alludes most strongly to the Cain and Abel story from the book of Genesis. Father-son and brother-brother relationships figure strongly into the poem. Poetically, the poem is in free verse, but in such a kind that takes on a reason for its quasi-structure as the poem moves forward. Many of the allusions and much of the symbolic language in the poem is self-referential. Both of these qualities, as well as the atemporal structure of Rufinius' life, are meant to create an enclosed, holistic characteristic: the poem is meant to make most sense on the second read, after each part has been assimilated into a whole.

title: Validation of Schedule for Nonadaptive and Adaptive Personality (SNAP)-Derived Analogues of Primary and Secondary Psychopathy
abstract: Psychopaths have been described as socially dominant, affectively vacuous, and behaviorally impulsive. The prototypical psychopath, first defined by Herbert Cleckley in 1941, has become an intriguing subject for researchers for the following reason: the psychopath’s severe psychopathology is masked by an outward semblance of normalcy, what Cleckley called “the mask of sanity.” In recent decades, there has been a proliferation of psychopathy research, with sustained efforts at conceptualizing the syndrome and inferring its etiology. The present study examines primary and secondary subtypes of psychopathy and their relationship to other psychological variables in an undergraduate population. While primary psychopaths are largely marked by their callous and unemotional affective and interpersonal style, secondary psychopaths are distinguished by high levels of impulsive antisociality. Primary and secondary psychopathy analogues were developed using the Schedule for Nonadaptive and Adaptive Personality (SNAP). These models were correlated with self-, peer-, and observer-reports of Five-Factor Model personality, as well as self-report measures of anxiety, behavioral inhibition and activation, and temperament. The results of this study will assess the validity of utilizing SNAP-derived analogues of psychopathy and will help to better conceptualize primary and secondary psychopathy subtypes.

title: Marriage Medicine: Probing the Influence of Marriage and Cohabitation on Male Cardiovascular Disease Risk in the Philippines
abstract: Live-in arrangements between unmarried couples have become increasingly popular in Western and non-Western countries alike. Although a number of demographic studies correlate marriage with improved health status in males, little is known about the potential health benefits associated with cohabitation. With cardiovascular disease (CVD) as the leading cause of death worldwide, the goal of this study was to examine various biomarkers of CVD risk in married, cohabiting, and single males living in a non-Western population. Data were selected from 859 Filipino males of the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey (CLHNS) with general outcomes including a panel of serum lipids and blood pressure readings.
