On average, cohabiting men exhibit significantly lower total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and diastolic blood pressure than single and even married men. For HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and systolic blood pressure, no significant differences were noted between groups. Adjusting for physical characteristics strengthened these relationships while controlling for lifestyle characteristics diminished the overall effect size suggesting a possible role for behavioral differences. The study offers preliminary evidence for a weak, but suggestive role for testosterone in mediating CVD-risk. As contemporary notions of marriage continue to evolve, future studies should closely monitor health disparities between these expanding marriage categories in order to enrich scholarly debate, family planning, and public policy measures.

title: The Effectiveness of Tax Increment Financing
abstract: Tax increment financing (TIF) is a public finance tool with which local governments offer incentives for economic development in their towns. To implement TIF a municipality declares a certain area a TIF district and then diverts any subsequent increase in property taxes to a TIF fund which is used to finance private development projects in the district. The hope is that the public funds spent in the TIF district will attract new businesses and spur economic growth. If this is indeed the case, TIF should raise property values in the towns that implement it, as the new development should be capitalized into home prices. Using cities from 10 different states, I test to see whether TIF was effective in raising municipal median home values between 1990 and 2000. I also test to see whether differences in the state statutes authorizing TIF have any impact on its effectiveness.

title: "Coming Out" in the Courtroom: Performing Identity in the Space Between U.S. Asylum Policy and Practice
abstract: A successful application for asylum must establish a history of past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution based on race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion. In the mid-1990s, a body of asylum case law began responding to an awareness of persecution based on sexual identification as Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT), which now constitutes “membership in a particular social group.” Despite the shift in case law receptive to LGBT related claims, the evidentiary and corroboratory requirements of the asylum process still pose a resource-intensive challenge to individuals with a valid claim. Sexual minorities face increasingly difficult parameters in the asylum process, as credibility regarding “coming out” as LGBT is often questioned. Someone making an LGBT related asylum claim must demonstrate that the basis for the claim is legally objective. Yet, by nature, sexual orientation is highly subjective and culturally specific. Frequently, in order to be considered credible, asylum seekers must respond in standardized ways. Although from different cultural backgrounds, the asylum seekers must perform a particular, uniform narrative. In the asylum process, there is often much difficulty in interpreting and translating culture for legal purposes. This paper explores the ways in which U.S. immigration policy and practice diverge in determining the status of LGBT asylum seekers and highlights the need within the judicial system to better understand different cultural modes of expression.

title: Women and Redemption in Mexican Cinema
abstract: From its beginnings in the late nineteenth century to its current worldwide renown, Mexican cinema has stood out in Latin America as a powerhouse in terms of financial resources, technical production and international distribution. Despite its cultural importance and rich history, Mexican cinema in many ways reflects a lack of evolution in its characterization of female figures. Women are caught in a traditional, distinctly Mexican double bind: they are expected to be both virgin and whore, the epitome of virtue and the sexual fantasy. Despite these contradictory expectations, women are socially condemned for displaying their sexuality or for rebelling against society’s ideal of the docile, pure figure. In my research, I analyze how Mexican films have served to perpetuate this impossible female position throughout the country’s cinematic history. I chose movies with female protagonists; the films range from Santa in 1931 to 2002’s The Crime of Padre Amaro. All the women in my chosen movies shatter the social ideal of the virginal figure, either of their own volition or through circumstances beyond their control. For this reason, they all must experience redemption by the film’s end in order to absolve them of their contradictory set of characteristics. Although this redemptive process varies and has been challenged by recent filmmakers, it is inescapable – even in films made seventy years apart – which evidences the staying power of the female virgin-whore dichotomy in Mexican society.

title: Ultra-High Porosity Silica Aerogel
abstract: The aim of my project was to develop a modified and improved method to reproducibly synthesize 99% porous aerogel with homogeneous structural properties for superfluid 3He experiment. Prof. Halperin’s lab is interested in studying the physical behavior of 3He when it is introduced into the pores of aerogels. Aerogels act as impurities that change the physical properties of superfluid 3He, and are predicted to stabilize the new 3He superfluid phases. Experiments conducted so far have mainly investigated the superfluidity of 3He in aerogels that are 98% porous, and they have indicated many differences between the properties of pure 3He and that of 3He in aerogels. The investigation of 3He in lower density aerogels (i.e. 99% porous) will help us understand how porosity and impurities affect liquid 3He. Aerogels of 99% porosity are synthesized by the ‘one step’ sol-gel method. They are characterized by measuring their porosity and imaging the samples between crossed polarizers. Imaging the aerogels with polarized light provides information about the distribution of the clusters that make up the backbone of the gel. Depending on the intensity of the light passing through a sample, we can determine whether that sample is structurally homogeneous and isotropic or not. The 99% aerogel samples that I synthesized did not change the polarization of light through them, which indicated that the gel samples have no preferred structural direction. These measurements confirm that the modified synthesis method of 99% aerogel prevents microscopic orientation of the gel structure.

title: Chemotaxonomy and Population Genetics in Pseudotsuga Menzeisii
abstract: In order to investigate past climates, researchers have turned to a variety of biomarkers found in fossils. One such proxy for ancient climates is the average chain length of the n-alkanes found in fossil plants. However, despite its use as a proxy for past climates, little is understood about how climate actually affects average chain lengths. n-Alkanes were sampled from Pseudotsuga menzeisii (Douglas Fir) from various sites in the state of Washington, and the profiles of the n-Alkanes were compared to climatic data with no meaningful correlation found. However, the n-Alkane distribution seemed to indicate that two chemically distinguishable populations of P. menzeisii were present. The same samples were then analyzed for microsatellite data. From this data, the genetic distance was calculated.

title: State Attorneys General and the Bully Pulpit: How State Prosecutors Have Regulated Businesses Without Filing Litigation
abstract: In the 1970's and 1980's the U. S. federal government began to assume a diminished role in the nation's regulatory processes. This "New Federalism" created a void that was filled by state attorneys general who went from being reactive local actors to aggressive national policymakers. These state prosecutors employed a variety of means to expand their authority, including multi-state litigation and the use of the bully pulpit, a relatively newer tactic, to aggressively pressure targets to accept sweeping settlements without the necessity of litigation. This thesis builds on existing research to explain the factors that lead to the pursuit of settlements in lieu of commencing litigation, once the state attorney general has determined to take action. After applying a fuzzy-set analysis to three case studies, Eliot Spitzer’s regulation of Merrill Lynch (2002), Andrew Cuomo’s campaign against child pornography on the internet (2008), and the classic example of litigation, the multi-state tobacco suits (1998), this paper argues that a combination of an unusually strong perceived consumer response to the allegations and some evidence of wrongdoing are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for the aggressive pursuit of a non-litigated settlement. In reaching this conclusion, a number of rival hypotheses are considered and it is demonstrated that none of them adequately explain the basis on which the decision to pursue settlement is made.

title: Nucleosome Positioning Across the Plasmodium Falciparum Genome
abstract: The DNA in a eukaryotic cell is orders of magnitude longer than the cell itself. In order to fit inside cells, protein complexes called nucleosomes tightly wrap the DNA. Previous work has shown that nucleosomes prefer to wrap sequences with specific properties. Plasmodium Falciparum-- the organism that causes the most severe form of malaria--has a genome consisting of nearly 80% adenine and thymine, making it highly skewed towards A and T. Sequencing P. falciparum nucleosomal fragments across the genome will allow us to determine whether the sequence preferences predicted by current models are generalizable to AT-rich DNA. I have isolated nucleosomal fragments from P. falciparum and have begun preparing them for sequencing using the ABI-SOLiD system. I have also begun isolating nucleosomal DNA from synchronized P. falciparum cultures at specific stages in its life cycle. Mapping nucleosome positions in several stages of the P. falciparum life cycle allows us to examine regions of DNA upstream of genes specific to one stage and to identify sequences covered by nucleosomes when the gene is not expressed but free of nucleosomes when it is expressed. Regions upstream of differentially-expressed genes occupied by nucleosomes in one stage but not others are likely to contain regulatory sequences. The P. falciparum genome has low information content due to its skewed composition, making it difficult to identify unique regulatory sequences. Mapping nucleosomes across the P. falciparum life cycle and correlating nucleosome occupancy with gene expression could lead to the discovery of novel P. falciparum regulatory sequences.

title: Individual Differences in Affective Experience
abstract: Most theories of affect (or emotion) predict that affects of opposite valence, such as happiness and sadness, are either negatively correlated (de-synchronous) or independent (asynchronous). That is, a person who experience de-synchronous affect becomes happier as he or she becomes less sad. When a person experiences asynchronous affect, the individual’s level of happiness has no impact on the individual’s level of sadness. The purpose of this study was to further explore momentary affective experience, focusing on individual differences in relationships between types of affect and what factors may explain these differences. Participants were 42 college-aged individuals (36 women). Using a novel cell-phone text messaging technology developed for this research, participants responded six times per day for two weeks to a list of items measuring concurrent affect, personality states, and appraisal of situations. The relationships between affects of opposite valence varied among respondents. Individuals with more positive within-person correlations between two key aspects of personality, state extraversion and state neuroticism, also had more positive relationships between positive affect and negative affect. As the positive affect felt by these individuals increased, they tended to experience more negative affect as well; they reported feeling happier, but at the same time also sadder. Individuals who tended to perceive threatening situations as challenges exhibited greater positive relationships between energetic arousal and tense arousal. These findings suggest that individual differences in routine behavior and reflective cognitions (perceptions of situations) influence patterns of momentary affective experience. Models of affect may benefit from considering behavioral and cognitive variables.

title: The RNA Interference Pathway Regulates Virus-Host Interactions in Drosophila Melanogaster
abstract: Persistent viral infections are commonly characterized by equilibrium between virus and host with few adverse effects for the host. The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster is a great model to study this equilibrium, sharing many conserved components with mammalian antiviral pathways. Nora virus is suggested to cause persistent infections among wildtype (WT) Drosophila stocks, although immunocompromised flies such as Relish mutants display high viral levels. We tested mutant flies that were deficient in the RNA interference (RNAi) pathway and consistently detected high levels of Nora virus that correlated with decreased lifespan. To assess potential pathogenecity of high viral levels, Nora virus was purified from RNAi deficient fly extracts and injected into WT flies. We observed high levels of Nora virus, significantly decreased lifespan, and fewer progeny from injected flies. Our data suggest that Nora virus can cause pathological effects when virus-host equilibrium is disturbed by mutations in the RNAi pathway or by artificial introduction of more virus. Furthermore, sequencing analysis indicated our RNAi deficient flies are infected with a strain of Nora virus different from the virus detected in Relish mutants. We intend to further characterize these viral strains, which potentially originated due to unique pressures imposed by distinct antiviral pathways. Further elucidation of virus-host interactions can aid the development of RNAi-based techniques in a wide array of clinical contexts: from controlling West Nile virus in mosquito vectors to targeting HIV in infected patients

title: Effect of Atomic Structure in Elastic Response of ZnO Nanowires
abstract: Understanding the mechanical properties of ZnO Nanowires and their relationship to the atomic structure is key in their successful wide-range application. Materials in the nano-scale such as thin films and nanowires are envisioned to be key components in the next generation of electronic devices and medical treatment. They are ideal building blocks of nano-electromechanical systems (NEMS), supercapacitors, transistors, and photovoltaic systems (PVs) for use in solar energy conversion, and are being exploited for superior methods of drug delivery and medical diagnostics. In this work the results of Molecular Dynamics simulations of ZnO nanowires of crystallographic orientation [0001] are presented. It was found that the Young’s modulus of such nanowires increases from 169 GPa to 194 GPa as the wire diameter decreases from 20 nm to 5 nm. This size effect originates from surface reconstruction, which becomes more important with increasing surface to volume ratio. These results are in agreement with experimental data showing an increase in the Young’s modulus of ZnO nanowires with a decrease in diameter in a range smaller than 80 nm.

title: Modeling Drosophila Retinal Cells Using Surface Energy Minimization
abstract: Drosophila flies have a compound eye composed of many individual units called ommatidia. Ommatidia have a very specific structure that allows them to capture and focus light to be interpreted by fly's brain. Cadherin molecules that bind on the membranes within the ommatidia are essential to this well-defined geometry. The wild type, or normal, Drosophila ommatidia have a standard number of cadherin molecules that are distributed to each membrane. Mutant Drosophila ommatidia, on the other hand, under or over-express cadherin molecules, which causes their geometries to warp. Using these two parameters, wild type cadherin population and mutant cadherin population, we can explain the changes in geometry by simply following nature's law of energy minimization. Furthermore, the incredible accuracy of this method confirms the importance of the cellular development of the ommatidia and proposes a method of cadherin distribution.

title: BioShield: Biomimetic Ballistic Defense System
abstract: BioShield is a novel bulletproof vest design that provides optimal protection from National Institute of Justice Level III-V ballistic rounds, while offering flexibility for the user’s movement during combat. Our technology uses existing materials arranged in a novel way to create the optimal vest for soldiers and law enforcement personnel. The various sized plates protect the user by taking into account the varying body structure present in the torso. For hard, inflexible areas such as the rib cage, larger plates are used to guarantee that the vest does not deform. The deformation of the vest in this area would endanger the life of the wearer, because any deformation of the rib cage results in a potentially punctured vital organ. For soft, flexible areas such as the stomach, smaller plates will be used to allow for slight deformation and greater flexibility. People do not move the upper torso as much as the lower torso, and because the stomach area can conveniently deform more than the upper torso, so too can the vest, allowing optimal movement and equal protection. The vest is comprised of a cross section of stiff, inflexible, small plates backed by a slightly flexible metal, surrounded by a polyurethane elastomer. The entire vest is encased in Kevlar Aramid Fibre, adding extra protection and stab resistance. Our vest can take four or five hits, as opposed to one or two, because unlike ceramic, the Young’s Modulus of titanium beta alloy and tungsten carbide is high, making them stiff but fairly flexible materials. Their material properties allow the small plates encased in polyurethane inside the vest to come together on impact and encase the bullet. As the material encases the bullet, the bullet is deformed significantly and cannot pass through the other side of the vest. Our vest’s price is comparable to other inferior vests on the market, making it a competitive product. Our business venture is versatile because our product includes the ability to remove the stiff plates, making the vest a Level III. Level III is the optimal level for many SWAT teams and law enforcement personnel.

title: Layers of the Courtroom: Arthur Miller’s Treatment of History in The Crucible
abstract: The selection of evidence to be presented in the courtroom has a tremendous effect on the outcome of the case. This being said, the attorney’s method of selection is a heavy determinant of its worth. Research is concerned with both the attorney’s selection process and how the attorney decides to present it. Because these two processes carry such weight in preparing and executing the case, it is also worth examining how the heavily regulated justice system monitors them. Much like a lawyer in a trial, a playwright decides what information to use in presenting his/her story and arguing the case. This process of selection can be more readily examined in documentary plays or plays based on real events. In writing The Crucible, Arthur Miller could have chosen any number of witchcraft trials to present and many characters to examine. Furthermore, John Proctor had an entire life’s worth of experiences and characteristics to draw upon in creating his character, but Miller chose to illustrate a specific man in a specific setting as a crux of his play. All of the decisions Miller makes about what is relevant to the story, the plot, or the narrative are designed to give the audience a certain perception of the character and narrative. Attorneys make these decisions; actors, directors, and set, lighting, and sound designers also make these decisions. This research analyzes how the dramatist and the attorney select what is relevant and significant, and how their selection processes relate with one another.

title: Can Regular Exercise Protect Women From Development of Endometriosis?
abstract: Endometriosis is a common and serious women’s health issue, afflicting between 3-10% of reproductive-aged women. Its defining feature is ectopic growth of endometrium-like tissue. Symptoms vary, but often include severe period pain, pain with sex, and infertility. The pathophysiology is poorly understood but is known to involve abnormal expression of sex hormones, immune responses, angiogenesis, and apoptosis, leading to promoted survival of miss-placed endometrial tissue. Exercise may potentially have a protective effect on the development of endometriosis considering that it decreases endogenous reproductive estrogen levels in women. This study explores the association between regular exercise history and subsequent development of endometriosis. We utilized 10-year follow-up data from the youngest cohort (18-23 year olds in 1996) of the Australian Longitudinal Study on Women’s Health (ALSWH). We characterized differences in exercise habits between women with and without endometriosis development, and sought to identify candidate confounders of this relationship. Subsequently, adjusted hazard ratios were calculated to determine the long-term effect of exercise history on endometriosis development. The results revealed no impact of prior exercise on diagnosis of endometriosis in surveys 2-4 of ALSWH (P=0.537, HR=1.007). The effect of exercise on endometriosis development is either too small to detect and thus clinically negligible, or lost due to misclassification bias in our study from self-reporting of endometriosis and physical activity. A more rigorous study with primary records review and more detailed exercise recording would be needed to further clarify this issue.

title: The Effects of Non-Biodegradable Donations on Uganda's Waste Removal System
abstract: As Corporate Social Responsibility programs and other forms of global giving increase in popularity, donors send a growing amount of physical material to the developing world. Unfortunately, many donated goods -- sanitary napkins, electronics, shoes -- do not biodegrade, and are sent to countries without the waste management capacity to process them. I received an Eric Lund Reporting and Research Grant to research Uganda's waste removal system and its capacity to process non-biodegradable materials. I met people who make money by salvaging useful goods from the country's only landfill, and environmental activists who are organizing these "scavengers" into a collective in order to achieve recognition, respect, and better working conditions. I also researched sanitary napkins -- a non-biodegradable item that American companies donate to Africa, an item that cannot even burn properly. Sanitary napkins are gaining popularity in Uganda as an expensive, imported status symbol (and a growing waste removal problem). I met with Dr. Moses Musazi, a professor at Makerere University who invented a locally made, biodegradable sanitary napkin made from papyrus.

title: Hemispheric Asymmetry in Visual Receptive/Integrative Field Size: A Crowding Study
abstract: There has been long standing anecdotal evidence of differences between the hemispheres of the brain. The left hemisphere has been described as logical, analytical, and linguistic. The right hemisphere has been described as emotional and creative. Recent empirical evidence has shown actual functional and structural differences between brain hemispheres. Specifically, evidence from language and semantics suggests larger receptive fields in the right hemisphere than the left hemisphere. The current study aims to synthesize knowledge of the receptive/integrative field size from language study with a vision effect called crowding in order to describe a physiologic difference in brain structure.

title: Orthographic and Phonological Consistency Effects in Cortex Differ in Children with Reading Disability During Spoken Language Processing
abstract: Orthographic consistency (sounds in a word may have multiple spellings) and phonological consistency (spelling of a word may have multiple pronunciations) have been fundamental to formulating models of word processing in normal and impaired readers. Although substantial research has investigated the neural basis of consistency effects in visual word processing, little is known about the neural basis of consistency effects in spoken language processing in normal or impaired readers. In the current study, normal children (9- to 12-year-olds) and children with reading disability (impaired readers) were sequentially presented with two spoken words and asked to determine whether they rhyme. Sensitivity of the brain to consistency of the first word in the pair was examined. In line with previous studies, normal readers showed greater activation for lower consistency in medial frontal gyrus and inferior parietal cortex. In contrast, impaired readers showed greater activation for higher consistency in medial frontal gyrus and left middle frontal gyrus. Moreover, higher skill on phonological awareness among impaired readers was associated with greater activation for lower consistency in left middle frontal gyrus. This study suggests that impaired readers only effectively engage their language network for words with consistent mappings between orthography and phonology. The dominant theory of reading impairment implicates a deficit in phonology and treatment often involves training in phonological awareness. Higher phonological awareness in impaired readers may only result in the effective processing of higher consistency words.

title: The Search for a Vaccine: An Investigation of Genes in Neisseria gonorrhoeae
abstract: Every year, there are approximately 800,000 cases of gonorrhea in the United States. Pelvic inflammatory disease, which is caused by gonorrhea, affects about one million women each year as well. The annual cost of gonorrhea and its related complications is almost $1.1 billion dollars. If it is left untreated, this sexually transmitted disease can lead to infertility and severe complications with pregnancy. Gonorrhea is caused by infections of the bacteria Neisseria gonorrhoeae in the genital tract, mouth and anus of both men and woman. The mechanisms of N. gonorrhoeae were the topic of my summer research. The HFQ gene synthesizes an abundant RNA binding protein in many bacteria, and my goal was to further define its role in N. gonorrhoeae by engineering a strain of N. gonorrhoeae that lacks this gene. The creation of this mutant strain would allow for the role of the HFQ gene and the genes that control it in N. gonorrhoeae to be defined. My research also aimed to further investigate N. gonorrhoeae by fusing a pLES94 reporter gene with elements from several genes found in N. gonorrhoeae to study the isolated effects of these genes. The genes investigated, the tonB gene, the fur gene, and the rmp gene, are involved in iron transport within the cell. Iron homeostasis is a key metabolism in N. gonorrhoeae, and the further investigation of the genes that control it might lead to the discovery of a gene that is suitable to be a vaccine candidate for N. gonorrhoeae.

title: Induction of Diabetes Resistance and Prevention of Recurrent Type 1 Diabetes Post-islet Transplantation via Gene Therapy
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease resulting from T cell-mediated destruction of the insulin-producing β cells in the pancreas. Islet transplantation is an experimental treatment that essentially “cures” T1D, ideally allowing the patient an insulin injection-independent method for controlling blood glucose levels. However, transplantation of even syngeneic islets into type 1 diabetics often follows with disease recurrence, as the underlying autoimmunity eventuates in destruction of the transplanted islets. Susceptibility to T1D is shown to be abrogated by inheritance of HLA class II DQ alleles containing a charged amino acid at position 57 of the β-chain, which is noted to confer protection from disease. We attempt to overcome this existing autoimmunity through gene therapy following non-myeloablative islet transplantation. Recombinant retroviruses transfected with T1D protective gene IAβd are transduced into hematopoietic stem cells to achieve molecular chimerism, which effectively abrogates risk of severe graft-versus-host disease following transplantation. These cells are then reconstituted into spontaneously diabetic non-obese NOD mice that received non-lethal irradiation, a pre-operational procedure to islet transplantation. Our results show that disease recurrence can be prevented in NOD mice with pre-existing T1D following islet transplantation, suggesting that molecular chimerism is capable of preventing development of T1D autoimmunity in cases of individuals expressing MHC alleles associated with susceptibility of disease via restoration of protective gene expression. These results are provocative, and in conjunction with current clinical methods, suggest a possible means whereby disease progression can be reversed or overcome.

title: Doing Business Underground: The Informal Economy as Seen From the Buenos Aires Subway System
abstract: This thesis examines the many resources that itinerant vendors on the Buenos Aires subway system utilize to build a sustainable livelihood in an urban setting. The findings of this research may shed light on the motivation of the people actually engaged in informal economic activity, as many studies on this topic fail to incorporate qualitative research on how workers themselves understand their situation. Rather than simply citing marginalization or entrepreneurship as the catalysts for the informal economy, the few scholars who have worked closely with informal workers have found a more complex set of incentives that attract people to this sector. Drawing on interviews with informal workers on the Buenos Aires subway, this study aims to contribute empirical analysis that may broaden the discussion on this type of work and challenge one-sided explanations of the existence of this sector. The heterogeneity of age, sex, background and socioeconomic status of those interviewed demonstrates how difficult it is to characterize "informals" as belonging to one group or another. To tell the story of one such diverse community, this work utilizes textual research, interviews with itinerant subway vendors, and observation of this particular market, a microcosm of the informal economy.

title: High Field Strength MR Imaging Camputes The Microstructure of Mouse Pancreas
abstract: Patients with pancreatic cancer are plagued by poor prognosis due to late diagnosis. Current methods of early detection are unreliable and noninvasive imaging has yet to visualize both the endocrine and exocrine components of the pancreas due to poor spatial resolution. In this study, we employed high field strength MR microscopy as a noninvasive method of imaging pancreas microstructure. Mouse pancreatic tissue samples from 11-month-old, normal mice were imaged ex-vivo using magnetic resonance microscopy. Using high-spatial resolution 3D imaging a 14.1T MR imager and with a voxel size of 70um, we were able to distinguish between different structural components of the pancreas due to structure and relationships of the tissue types, along with comparison to histology. In the reconstructed 3D image, fluid filled tubes and ECM had the greatest signal intensity; acini had the lowest intensity but comprised most of the gland; and islets had moderate intensity and were circular in shape, often localized around tubes, which is consistent with reports in the literature of islets residing around blood vessels. With this data, we have begun to analyze ex vivo pancreata from EL-Kras transgenic mice to identify precancerous lesions. Future work will include an in-vivo longitudinal study to visualize lesion progression. Capturing cellular changes through noninvasive imaging can become a reliable means to identify precancerous lesions. This will allow for screening of high risk populations and potentially treatment at the earliest stages of malignant transformation.

title: Sansalvamide Analogue Induces G1 Cell-Cycle Arrest through the Up Regulation of p21 and Down Regulation of cyclin D1 in Pancreatic Cancer Cells
abstract: Pancreatic cancer survival remains limited due to inadequate chemotherapeutic options. Sansalvamide A, a cyclic depsipeptide produced by a marine fungus, has demonstrated significant anti-cancer activity. We previously tested a series of analogues in pancreatic cancer cells and chose the most potent for this study. Two human pancreatic cancer cell lines (AsPC-1 and CD18) were incubated with increasing concentrations (0.1-100μM) of the Sansalvamide analog. Cell proliferation was then measured by thymidine incorporation and cell counting. Cell cycle analysis was determined by flow cytometry with propidium iodide staining. Western blot analysis was used to evaluate expression of CDK2, cyclin E, cyclin A, cyclin D, E2F, CDK4, CDK6, and p21 at multiple time points. At 20 μM concentration, treatment with the analog caused G1 cell-cycle arrest in both cell lines. Western blot analysis demonstrated up-regulation of p21, down regulation of cyclin D1, cyclin E, cyclin A and cdk4 consistent with G1/G0 cell cycle arrest. Sansalvamide A attenuates pancreatic cancer cell growth and represents a promising anti-cancer therapy.

title: Affective Responses to Objectification: The Importance of Context
abstract: Women in Western cultures are frequently objectified (e.g., whistled or started at). Objectification Theory posits that this can lead to habitual self-monitoring of one’s physical appearance, known as self-objectification. Self-objectification is best described as the adoption of an outsider’s perspective on one’s own body. This is known to have negative consequences, such as body dissatisfaction, eating disordered behavior, negative emotions, and decreased cognitive ability. However, anecdotal evidence suggests that some women may find milder forms of objectification enjoyable (e.g., some women claim to be happier after a guy “hits on them” or “checks them out”). This study examined students’ positive and negative emotional responses to objectification in different contexts. We changed the context by altering two different factors: the person doing the objectification and the situation in which the objectification occurred. Survey items were altered to include objectification by romantic partners, attractive strangers, and unattractive strangers. Additionally, survey items were altered to include objectification alone at night, with multiple friends, and at a party. Surprisingly, results revealed that only objectification by a romantic partner yielded an overall positive response; even objectification by an attractive person elicited negative emotions. However, liking objectification by a romantic partner predicted eating disordered behavior, especially bulimia. Feeling positive towards objectification in general (regardless of the context) also predicted eating disordered behavior. In general, results suggested that enjoying objectification may be problematic, consistent with previous research showing that women who deny sexism and accept traditional gender roles experience heightened distress in response to sexist events.

title: From Stem Cell to Pigment Cell: Elucidating Key Steps in Melanocyte Development
abstract: Melanocytes differentiate from melanoblast stem cells which arise from the neural crest in developing vertebrate embryos. In addition to melanocytes, neural crest stem cells give rise to a diversity of cells types including neurons and glial of the peripheral nervous system, craniofacial bone and cartilage, and neuroendocrine cells of the adrenal gland. The multipotent nature of the neural crest stem cells suggest that distinct molecular events are necessary to restrict a cell’s fate, causing it to develop into a melanocyte rather than another neural crest derivative. Previous studies in a number of model organisms have identified transcription factors that have roles in melanoblast specification. However, the relationship between the expression and function of these factors has yet to be characterized within a single model system. This information is essential to achieve a comprehensive understanding of melanocyte development. To this end, in situ hybridization was used to characterize the temporal and spatial expression of melanocyte regulatory factors in early Xenopus laevis embryos. Additionally, overexpression experiments were carried out to assess the functional capabilities and hierarchical relationship between these factors. Ectopic expression of assessed genes and supernumerary melanocytes were observed in response to each of the overexpressed factors; however, the time and location varied with each factor. These results reveal that the temporal and spatial context of the precursor cells determines their fate and this contributes to a system wide understanding of how neural crest stem cells are specified to become melanocytes.

title: Drivers of Humanitarian Intervention: Exploring the United States' Policy Towards Sierra Leone
abstract: My study explores the drivers behind U.S. policy regarding humanitarian intervention, specifically investigating the motivation behind American responses toward Sierra Leone. I focus on how U.S. policies reflect moments of harmony between Liberal and Realist International Relations Theory and American political objectives. I argue that the policies regarding U.S. humanitarian intervention primarily revolve around considerations of domestic and international political aims as well as U.S. past and present involvement in other conflicts. The culminating decisions occur when these politics and interests suggest the same policy that both Realist and Liberal International Relations theories would propose. When possible, U.S. policies regarding humanitarian intervention reflect Liberal concerns, but they tend to rely upon Realist considerations. The U.S. may claim they will intervene due to normative principles and highlight arguments within the Liberal paradigm, but ultimately will act on Realist motivated strategic interests. Consequently, the U.S. government’s reasons for intervention will not be consistent or overtly obvious over time, but rather they will depend on strategic interests at the moment. Sierra Leone presents an instructional, foundational, and somewhat typical example of the policymaking process that surrounds intervention. Although the U.S. never conducted a humanitarian intervention of Sierra Leone, the lack of intervention is instructive in understanding the policy drivers of intervention. Understanding what factors are necessary for intervention must be balanced with an understanding of what factors prevent it in order to paint a more accurate and complete picture of the motivations and drivers behind humanitarian intervention.

title: Framing Gender-Based Claims in U.S Asylum Law
abstract: 80% of the world’s refugees are women and children. Many of these women seek asylum in the United States in order to escape the gender-based persecution they have faced in their countries of origin. Gender-based claims are defined as having two components: first, those claims focusing on persecution particular to women such as sexual abuse, rape, female genital mutilation (FGM), domestic violence, bride burning etc.; second, those claims focusing on persecution based solely on an applicant's gender such as persecution for disobeying repressive laws or not conforming to social mores (Bahl, 37). Under current U.S asylum law, gender is not a statute upon which persecution can be alleged. I coded 50 gender-based asylum cases from the year 1995 and 2005, exploring how women citing gender-based claims establish credibility in the absence of a gender statute by framing their persecution into one of the existing refugee categories, and seeing how those frames impact the success or failure of a particular claim. From my data analysis it is clear that women face difficulty establishing credibility in asylum law due to conundrums specific to their gender and types of persecution they face.

title: Histidine- and DOPA-Modified Poly (Ethylene Glycol) Hydrogel
abstract: This study aims to improve mechanical properties of 4-armed DOPA-terminated poly(ethylene glycol) hydrogels, hydrophilic polymer networks that swell with water, to make them better suited as surgical adhesives or underwater glues. This study mimics chemistry that is believed to underlie the strong mechanical properties of insect cuticles and squid beaks, whose proteins contain high content of crosslinks between histidine (His) and 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) amino acid residues in their structure. DOPA is also found in high proportion in mussel adhesive proteins that tether marine mussels to underwater surfaces, and has been previously used in biomimetic polymers and hydrogels for biomedical applications. The proposed hydrogel features a two component system: one 4-armed PEG polymer terminated with a DOPA-analog and a second 4-armed PEG polymer terminated with a His-analog. Network formation of the hydrogel relies on crosslinking between oxidized catechols of DOPA and imidazole rings of His in presence of an oxidizing agent to form a strong network of covalent bonds. It is believed that DOPA-His crosslinking will impart stronger mechanical properties than existing DOPA hydrogels, while maintaining their adhesive properties. Modified PEG polymers were synthesized and isolated via standard peptide conjugation chemistry. Products were characterized with UV/vis spectroscopy, MALDI, and 1H NMR. Adducts of modified mPEG polymers from NaIO4-induced crosslinking were characterized with MALDI and GPC to determine degree of polymerization. Rheology was used to assess the mechanical properties of the modified 4-armed PEG gel.

title: Windham, Connecticut and the Origins of the American Revolution
abstract: Americans often mythologize the Founding Fathers as extraordinary leaders who single-handedly changed history. When studying the American Revolution, historians often overlook the people who actually fought the Revolution and instead focus on George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Alexander Hamilton. This approach to understanding the American Revolution is misleading and disenfranchising. The American Revolution was motivated in large part by the economic self-interest and passion of everyday colonists. This project focuses on the political climate of the agrarian eastern Connecticut town of Windham from 1774-1775. With a population of roughly 3,500, Windham boasted some of the most radical behavior in New England. The town sent more troops and funds to the Lexington Alarm -- the first battle of the American Revolution -- than any other town in Connecticut. Yet the Founding Fathers did not shape Windham’s political climate. When the Revolution broke out, the people of Windham focused more on their economic troubles and a land grab with Pennsylvania than the potential of democracy. A study of Windham exemplifies a bottom-to-top approach of inquiry in understanding the American Revolution. Rural towns like Windham each had their own personal version of the Revolution. While the findings in Windham are not necessarily universal among the colonies, a look at the town offers a glimpse into what happened on the eve of the war and why so many men of all ages risked their lives.

title: Des Papiers pour Tous, Divergent Outcomes of the Undocumented Immigrant Movement in France
abstract: In 1996, 300 undocumented African immigrants occupied a Parisian church to protest their inability to reside legally in France. Their action succeeded in drawing public, media, and governmental attention to their cause, resulting in widespread public support for their movement and 80,000 regularizations of undocumented immigrants. Today, once again, 1,300 African immigrants are occupying a public building in Paris, but this time their protest has gone largely unnoticed. These protesters rarely appear in the news and have obtained a minimal number of regularizations. Why have two such similar instances of collective action with similar strategies and participants resulted in such divergent outcomes? This thesis will argue that the reason for this disparity stems from current protesters’ failure to form alliances with other societal actors, such as trade unions and immigrant rights associations. These alliances are crucial to gain access to the media arena, which in turn guarantees public visibility and thus influences government policy. Based on interviews with current protesters and associations, the autobiographies of the 1996 protest leaders, and an analysis of both mainstream press and the movements’ newsletters, I posit that the immigrants of 1996 succeeded due to their close ties to outside support networks that increased their media visibility and political influence. This research reveals that alliances with outside actors, which lead to increased public attention, are crucial to the success of a social movement.

title: Analysis of Human DAZL, DAZ Function Using a Drosophila Model
abstract: The reproductive Deleted in Azoospermia (DAZ) gene family, composed of BOULE, DAZ-Like (DAZL) and DAZ, is one of the most common human infertility factors, with the absence of the DAZ gene alone representing 5 to 10% of infertile men. The DAZ gene family is remarkably conserved: Boule is present in mice, flies and humans, DazL in mice and humans and Daz solely in humans. In Drosophila, boule is required for completion of meiosis. Additionally, it has been established that human Boule (hBOL) can function in meiosis after meiosis resumes in male Drosophila boule-/- samples upon addition of hBOL transgenes. To learn more about the function of human DAZ and DAZL (hDAZ, hDAZL), vectors were created containing hDAZ and hDAZL under the control of a fly specific testis promoter. These vectors will be injected into wild type Drosophila and crossed onto a boule mutant background. Testis samples will then be analyzed to determine if hDAZL and hDAZ have any effect on meiosis in the absence of fly boule. We hypothesize that hDAZL and hDAZ will restore meiotic function in boule mutant flies. The results of this experiment may allow us to definitively state the role that hBOULE, hDAZL and hDAZ have in meiosis which could have enormous ramifications in fertility diagnosis among couples struggling with conception. Furthermore, this project could also provide a better understanding of Daz gene family function as well as clarify the mechanisms of action of these genes.

title: Testing for Holocene Hydroclimatic Change in the Sierras: New Insights from Fallen Leaf Lake, Lake Tahoe Basin, CA
abstract: The Sierra Nevada is the primary source of California’s and northwestern Nevada's water resources. To understand the potential for severe and prolonged drought in the Sierras, it is necessary to study past events recorded by proxy data. Recent studies have discovered submerged and upright trees rooted ~36m below the surface of Fallen Leaf Lake (FLL), suggesting that lake levels were significantly lower during the past. Several of these trees have been dated to ~1200 AD, consistent with the timing of the Medieval Climatic Anomaly observed at other locations in the Sierras. We conducted a field campaign in summer 2008 to acquire a high-resolution sidescan sonar survey of FLL. By using this data in concert with previously gathered seismic CHIRP, sediment cores, and ROV video footage, we have been able to search for additional submerged trees as well as geomorphic and sedimentary evidence for past hydrologic changes. Sidescan sonar provided complete coverage of the lakefloor, imaging 9 upright trees and over 80 downed trees. Examination of the data also reveals numerous submerged paleoshorelines along the entire circumference of FLL to depths >60m below the present lake level. Multiple shoreline fluctuations have allowed the preservation of in-situ ancient trees beneath the lake surface and provide strong evidence for sustained drought during medieval times. The data also demonstrate the feasibility of using high-resolution geophysical methods towards identifying climate proxies and the potential for future inter-disciplinary studies in FLL.

title: No Speed Limits When Tracking Multiple Objects
abstract: As we navigate the visual world, many tasks require us to actively observe multiple objects simultaneously. As we drive we must avoid incoming vehicles and pedestrians, and when we play sports or video games we must track and recognize our teammates. We conducted a study to test the limits of this tracking ability by asking participants to track a set of six target circles moving among six identical distractor circles. Past studies using similar displays have shown that performance decreases when objects move faster. This study tests a counter-intuitive prediction that suggests object speed, per se, may not limit our capacity for tracking objects. Instead, other factors that accompany speed may motivate the performance drop, such as the increased chance of confusion when objects move too close to one another. If so, then we might be able to track objects at surprisingly high speeds once these other factors are controlled. We kept pairs of target and distractor objects far from each other, to maintain large inter-object distances. Under these conditions, faster object speed did not impair tracking ability. Only the total distance traveled by each object predicted whether it was successfully tracked. Despite our intuitions, this study suggests that there is no speed limit in the ability of observers to track multiple objects.

title: Characterizing Meal Timing and Meal-Sleep Alignment in DSPS Patients
abstract: Patients with Delayed Sleep Phase Syndrome (DSPS) are associated with a number of behavioral and physiological characteristics. Like other night owls, people with this circadian rhythm sleep disorder (CRSD) have wake and sleep times that are consistently delayed with respect to the general population. However, DSPS patients can be distinguished by generally unsuccessful attempts to advance their sleep schedule and difficulty awakening to meet occupational or social requirements. Yet prevalence estimates suggest that the syndrome nonetheless remains underdiagnosed clinically. Given the need for these patients to be more thoroughly characterized, recent animal research suggesting a relationship between metabolic and feeding patterns and circadian rhythms provides a new direction of investigation. We examined the timing of meals and their alignment with sleep in three age and gender-matched groups: DSPS patients (N=18), unaffected night owls (N=27), and control subjects (N=12). We hypothesized that DSPS subjects are delayed and misaligned in their food intake with respect to distinctly characterized Owls and Controls. We found that both DSPS and Owls were distinguishable from Controls for select variables; however, there were no significant differences between the former two groups. Further analysis suggested that some aspects of meal timing and alignment are not associated with DSPS status, but rather are correlated with the degree of delay in an individual’s sleep schedule. Although this finding may hold several ramifications, future research must address the caloric distribution across meals for them to be fully understood.

title: Identifying Substrates of Cbk1 in Saccharomyces Cerevisiae Using SDL
abstract: Eukaryotes demonstrate great control over their cellular morphology which is important for cell division, motility, and differentiation. Neurons, for example, have highly specific cell morphology in regard to their axons and branching structures called dendrites. The importance of understanding the molecular mechanisms of cell morphogenesis is apparent from many diseases such as cancer, in which this process is not regulated properly. In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, many signaling pathways are not well understood because the targets of kinases and phosphotases are unknown. One such kinase that is essential for normal cell morphogenesis that could be more closely studied is Cbk1. Although Cbkl’s enzymatic activity is required for polarized cell growth and cell separation, substrates of Cbk1 have not been identified using a systematic approach. In light of this, Synthetic Dosage Lethality (SDL) screen was used to identify substrates of Cbk1. Synthetic Dosage Lethality (SDL) is a new systematic approach for identifying target molecules regulated by signaling pathway. SDL is based on the idea that increasing substrate level has no effect on fitness of the wild-type strain because the kinase of interest is fully functional and can inhibit the overexpressed substrate. In contrast, mutation of the kinase of interest causes a clear phenotype, such as lethality, because the mutant enzyme cannot inhibit the overexpressed substrate. Such synthetic lethality may imply genetic interaction between the overexpressed gene and Cbk1. This work provides possible novel Cbk1 targets and furthers our understanding of the pathways that control morphogenesis.

title: English Speech Recognition in the Presence of Competing Foreign Accented Speech
abstract: It is often hard for listeners to understand speech in noise. One type of noise that is distracting for listeners, and makes it more difficult to understand the target speech, is competing speech noise. If the competing speech noise is spoken in a language other than English (a different language than the speech the listener is trying to attend to, e.g., Mandarin) listeners can often times improve their recognition of the target speech. It is not clear why this occurs. That is, it may be easier to understand English speech in the presence of competing Mandarin speech because the two speech signals are composed of different frequencies. If this were true it would indicate that it becomes easier for listeners because the two signals are more distinguishable in the auditory periphery (i.e., the inner ear). However, listeners may just find the non-English speech less “distracting,” indicating a higher level (e.g., within the auditory cortex) reason for the improvement. This study investigates listeners’ recognition of English speech presented in the presence of five different competing speech signals. The competing speech will consist of two talkers speaking simultaneously in either English, Mandarin-accented English with high intelligibility, Mandarin-accented English with moderate intelligibility, Mandarin-accented English with low intelligibility, and Mandarin. These data will help us understand why listeners are able to improve their recognition of English speech when listening in the presence of competing speech spoken in a language other than English.

title: Habitability of Planets in Binary Star Systems
abstract: Roughly 20% of the known planetary systems are found within binary stars. A binary companion is known to affect the orbital evolution of a planet through long-term perturbations. These perturbations are capable of inducing high levels of eccentricity onto the planetary orbit, diminishing the planet's prospects for harboring life. As the search for habitable planets elevates, it has become important to understand the conditions that lead to habitable and unhabitable orbital behaviors of planets within a binary system. Although the orbital evolution of a single planet within a binary is easily predicted, multiple planet systems within a binary have not been studied carefully because of the additional interactions and the larger parameter space. Indeed, a study of multiple planets within a binary is more realistic and relevant because both observations and planet formation theories suggest that multiple planet systems are more likely to form. To investigate the habitability of such systems, we simulated the orbital evolution of an extensive set of systems with an Earth-like planet and a gas-giant planet within a binary star. The simulations show that the Earth-like planet will exhibit a variety of orbital behaviors that are sensitively dependent on the location of the gas-giant planet. Furthermore, we find that these behaviors can be predicted by a semi-analytical analysis of the various perturbations involved within the planetary systems. With the physical understanding of the systems in our simulations, we can infer the possible behaviors of planets in binary systems to aid in the search for habitable planets.

title: A Prospective Study Linking SASB Profiles to Marital Dissatisfaction and Dissolution
abstract: The present study examined couple interaction patterns leading to adverse marital outcomes with the objective of providing information for improving marital therapy techniques. Past research on couple dynamics has presented conflicting evidence regarding the relative importance of positive versus negative affect, autonomy versus dependence, active listening, introspection, and stonewalling in predicting marital outcomes. The present study therefore used the Structural Analysis of Social Behavior coding system (a circumplex model which explores interactions on the dimensions of focus, affiliation, and interdependence) to shed light on conflict discussions between marital partners and their predictive validity for marital satisfaction and later marital stability. Warmth in interactions predicted marital satisfaction for both husbands and wives. There was also a negative correlation between wife satisfaction and husband autonomy, as well as husband satisfaction and wife control. Furthermore, blaming, defensiveness, and sulking predicted adverse marital outcomes. For wives, active listening on the part of the husband predicted higher marital satisfaction. Trends also indicated that autonomous and positive introspection among wives predicted higher satisfaction. An exploratory 6-month follow-up study examined the relationship between these variables and marital dissolution. This research thus utilized a novel approach to the study of couple dynamics through the exploration of the construct of positive introspection, as well as the inclusion of 6-month follow-up marital assessments.

title: The Use of Comparison in Learning
abstract: Education in earth sciences is important, especially considering the environmental challenges facing future generations. For many students, learning about earth science is difficult because it requires spatial skills to identify geologic features, such as deformations of the Earth’s crust, and to interpret their structural components beneath the surface. An important educational issue is thus how to support students’ learning of spatial concepts. We apply a cognitive theory of analogical comparison to teach students to identify faults – fractures in rock that show evidence of displacement. The act of comparison involves aligning the structural commonalities of two or more items. Highly similar items are easier to align, thereby highlighting their common relational structure, and alignable differences (readily comparable but differing features). This suggests that teaching a student to distinguish faults from other features will be most effective when the student can compare a fault image with a highly similar no-fault image. Participants in this study were assigned to one of two conditions: (1) Paired presentation – participants were shown two similar pictures of geological structures together, where one picture contained a fault and the other did not, (2) Separate presentation – the same images were shown at separate times. Because comparison is expected to support learning of important characteristics of a fault, students in the paired condition should be more accurate when they identify faults in a later task. We discuss results from this research and implications for classroom learning.

title: Behavior as Property: An Examination of the Relationship Between Common and Private Views of Fertility and Observed Outcomes in the United States and Nepal
abstract: This study attempts to investigate motivating factors that influence fertility behavior by specifically attempting to extend past research and theory in the realm of economic property to determine to what level its conclusions can be applied to the understanding of fertility outcomes. The study consists of two regression models constructed from US and Nepalese data using principal-component analysis to generate proxy measures representing variables such as collectivist or individualist social and/or political tendencies and adherence to fertility norms. In addition, it measures the effects of beliefs concerning the ideal number of children for a family and a number of demographic and social control variables. The results of these regressions show that there is evidence for fertility behavior following what would be predicted by property theory. The results also motivate a framework that helps to further hypothesize the connection between social and political views, the degree to which fertility decisions and outcomes are seen as “private” from the perspective of property theory, and finally the number of children actually born to an individual or family.

title: Physical and Psychological Health of First and Second Generation Turkish Immigrants in Germany
abstract: Since the 1960s, the Turkish population in Germany has steadily grown, but despite their large numbers, their health status remains unclear. To evaluate the health of first and second generation Turkish migrants, this paper uses the large and representative German Gender and Generations Study (GGS) to assess three separate health outcomes: chronic illness, self-assessed health, and feelings of emptiness. The paper investigates whether sex, age, socioeconomic status, emotional support, or duration of residence in Germany predict these various dimensions of health. Results establish clear health status differences between Turks and native Germans. First generation Turks tend to have lower chronic illness rates and rate their health as better than Germans at younger ages, but these advantages diminish among higher age strata. In addition, both first and second generation Turks have higher rates of feelings of emptiness compared to native Germans across all age strata. Controlling for socioeconomic status and age reduces these health differences modestly, pointing to their likely role as mediators. These findings suggest that Turkish migrants may have physical and psychological health disadvantages, and that Turkish females of both generations are especially vulnerable.

title: Prevalence and Gradation of Metabolic Syndrome in South India
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) related mortality claims nearly 18 million lives every year. Increased prevalence of CVD predicting factors such as insulin resistance, obesity and hypertension are expressed as a cluster of symptoms called the metabolic syndrome. Asian Indians are known to have a higher risk of CVD than other ethnic groups due to earlier onset and lack of timely detection among other reasons. The objective of this study of two communities is to investigate whether there is a graded difference of prevalence of metabolic syndrome symptoms across rural, semi-urban and urban locations in order to identify any critical stages of onset. The semi-urban location is between the largely untouched rural environment and the nearest urban center and is an example of the ‘transition’ phase of nutrition and urbanization. The study incorporated 146 participants and anthropometric measurements, blood pressure and Glycosylated hemoglobin measurements were obtained. The expected difference between rural and semi-urban habitats was not significant in central adiposity, anthropometric metabolic and blood pressure variables. The prevalence of metabolic syndrome was only 31.75% which is similar to the rural prevalence rates of similar studies. The urban prevalence rate on the other hand, is significantly higher. The stark differences between urban and rural prevalence rates raise questions about whether the instance of exacerbation of symptoms between rural and urban areas can be isolated. This study proves that there is not a well-defined pattern; rather there is a rapid and uneven progression of metabolic diseases from urban to semi-rural to rural areas.

title: Synthesis of Organic Surfactants for Self-Assembly into Nanoscale Buckled Vesicles
abstract: The primary objective of this project is to synthesize anionic and cationic surfactants that self-assemble into buckled vesicles in an aqueous solution. Earlier work in the field has shown that surfactants can self-assemble into micron-sized icosahedral vesicles under optimized conditions. Our goal is to form vesicles on the nanoscale that are stable to a variety of different conditions. The surfactants are designed to have a polar headgroup, a rigid, aromatic section, and a hydrophobic alkyl tail, all of which play vital roles in the self-assembly process. The assembly is driven by noncovalent interactions such as π-π stacking, hydrophobic collapse, and the presence of alternating charged head groups. We have synthesized and purified molecules with biphenyl, azobenzene, and diphenylacetylene aromatic groups, all with varying alkyl tail lengths. All synthesized molecules have been characterized by proton and carbon NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry. The microscopy samples were prepared by quick freeze/deep etch, a technique that makes a platinum replica of a frozen solution. The replica was imaged using transmission electron microscopy. These conditions were used to study different mixtures of anionic and cationic surfactants in a 1:1 ratio or with excess anion. Additionally, the azobenzene compounds with tail lengths of 6, 8, and 10 carbons were all shown to be gelators in a 2 weight percent solution. Thus far, the mixture of anionic and cationic surfactants with an azobenzene aromatic segment and an eight carbon length tail has been shown to produce buckled structures most similar to the goal we are pursuing.

title: Effects of Attribution Style on Depression for Multicultural Asian Americans
abstract: Depression is a condition that affects millions of Americans. Of special interest are any reliable predictors of depression. Attribution style is thought to be one such predictor, as those that are prone to depression or are experiencing depressive symptoms tend to attribute negative events to themselves and positive events to others or their environment. Interestingly, people from collectivist, interdependent cultures, like those in Asia, exhibit these depression prone attribution tendencies; nevertheless, not all such people suffer from depression. Of particular interest are multicultural Asian Americans, because of their ability to adopt either a collectivist attribution style or an independent attribution style dependent on the circumstances of the situation. In this experiment, the fluidity of these attribution styles were tested to see if Asian Americans could be primed to utilize either a collectivist or independent strategy in coping with positive and negative interactions. More importantly, primed subjects were tested to determine if adopting either a collectivist or individualistic attribution style had an effect on a subject’s overall mental health.

title: Pragmatic Encroachment, Defeaters, and Knowledge
abstract: In traditional epistemology, only truth-conducive factors have played a central role in determining whether a given subject has knowledge. That is, an instance of knowledge has been determined exclusively by epistemic considerations. This view, however, has been recently challenged by several philosophers who argue that the practical stakes of a situation can also affect the attribution of knowledge to a given subject. The opposing view, known as pragmatic encroachment, argues that the subject’s practical interests must be considered in addition to all epistemic facts of the situation that are already reflected. This paper examines the arguments presented by proponents of pragmatic encroachment—specifically those of Jason Stanley, Jeremy Fantl, and Matthew McGrath—and presents a critical analysis of their claims. After much consideration of the arguments in favor of pragmatic encroachment, I make the claim that the sole existence of practical stakes in a given situation does not itself affect the attribution of knowledge to a particular subject. Rather, many high stakes situations call for the subject to consider alternative cases, which inevitably give rise to doubts. These doubts, in turn, collectively work to undermine the level of confidence that the subject originally has in high stakes situations below the threshold of knowledge. Thus, for many instances, pragmatic encroachment is simply an issue of the confidence level one has for knowledge, rather than knowledge, itself. I acknowledge, however, that this reaction serves only as a partial response to the problem and not an exhaustive one, as not all high stakes situations generate doubts in the subject. This concern is, therefore, addressed with a complementary argument from stable invariantistism, which presents an additional solution against pragmatic encroachment. Finally, in light of the stable invariantist view, two main issues with pragmatic encroachment are revealed and discussed in detail.

title: Cultural Priming Modulates Emotional Attention and Experience
abstract: Cultures across the world have been categorized as collectivistic or individualistic, and this categorization of cultural values has produced important insights into psychological constructs, such as self-concept and well-being. Previous studies have found that geographical prevalence of pathogens was positively correlated with collectivistic cultures and negatively with individual cultures, suggesting behavioral manifestations of collectivism, such as ethnocentrism and conformity, have developed as a consequence of these pathogenic diseases. Expanding on this concept, the present study was conducted to see if simply priming participants with either one of these cultural values can modulate or heighten emotional attention to fearful or neutral stimuli and emotional experience. After priming the participant with collectivistic or individualistic values, he/she completed a dot-probe task where the participant was asked to locate a dot after being briefly exposed to neutral and fear-inducing pictures. The participants primed with collectivistic cultural values were expected to be more aware of the fearful stimuli, an evolutionary benefit of collectivism, and indeed, the reaction times of those participants were shorter than the reaction times of the participants primed with individualism when the dot replaced the fearful stimuli. The State and Trait Anxiety Inventory, Beck's Depression Inventory, well-being survey, and personality surveys given after the task showed that cultural priming also affected emotional experiences of the participants. Those primed with collectivism showed greater state anxiety levels, less positive affect, and greater neuroticism than those primed with individualism. These findings illustrate the influence of individualistic and collectivistic cultural values on emotional attention and experience.

title: Speech Perception of Korean-English Bilinguals with Korean as L1
abstract: Understanding a language requires that a person be able to perceive the correct speech sound categories for that language. In the current study we focus on pairs of sounds in Korean and English that are difficult for speakers of the other language to differentiate. English utilizes a two-way voicing distinction for its stop consonants: voiced and voiceless (/d/ and /t/, respectively); however, Korean utilizes a three-way distinction: plain, aspirated, and tense consonants (/t/, /th/, and /t’/, respectively). The distinction of these Korean stop consonants is difficult for monolingual English speakers to discriminate (Francis & Nusbaum, 2006). English liquids (/r/ and /l/) are difficult for monolingual Korean speakers to discriminate (Lee & Lee, 2003). We have investigated the perception of English /r/ vs. /l/ and Korean plain vs. aspirated stops by Korean-English bilinguals whose first language is Korean. This research indicates that age of acquisition (AOA) of English and amount of exposure to a language affect bilinguals' ability to perceive phonetic contrasts in their second language (English), but all bilinguals perform equally well in their perception of L1.

title: The Role of Reading Skill in Language Processing
abstract: The word superiority effect (WSE) indicates that readers are better at identifying single letters when they occur within words, as opposed to within a non-word string of letters. This suggests that readers apply knowledge about letter groupings while reading, even when not asked to pronounce or comprehend the meaning of the text. But does the WSE universally describe readers’ performance, or is this robust effect additionally mediated by an individual’s reading skill? Higher reading skill presumes a greater ability to quickly recognize letter strings as words; thus, with reference toward the alternate "missing letter" phenomenon, more skilled readers are expected to show a weaker WSE. In contrast, less skilled readers are expected to show the traditionally reported WSE pattern more strongly, since they may be more prone to processing words letter by letter. Exploring this relation between reader skill and visual word recognition ultimately contributes toward a clearer understanding of language cognition and the factors that influence it.

title: Comparing the Perception of Meaningful Discourse Structure in Music and Language
abstract: Despite common belief that music lacks truth-conditional meaning, recent evidence of similar neural processing of the syntactic and semantic aspects of the music and language suggests that they share much in common (Steinbeis and Koelsch 2007). However, this similarity seems to break down at different structural levels. Music studies have proposed that listeners attend to local but not global structure (Tillman and Bigand 2004, Deliège et. al. 1997). Linguistic data have yet to distinguish the level of meaningful structure perception. Thus, this study aims to make parallel findings for both domains, additionally comparing musicians to nonmusicians. Original musical and textual compositions were analyzed for tree structure by the Generative Theory of Tonal Music (Lerdahl and Jackendoff 1983) and the Rhetorical Structure Theory (Carlson et. al. 2001), respectively. The branches at each tree depth were cut and randomized as audio-visual music clips and visual text slides in iMovie projects. Collegiate native English speakers – 50 musicians and 50 nonmusicians – were asked to recreate what they considered the original work in a puzzle task. The resulting ordered strings were analyzed using edit distance, revealing that successful recreation was overall independent of subject and stimulus type. Musicians performed better than nonmusicians for music only at intermediate tree depths (p=0.03). Cluster analyses suggested that musicians attended to structural (global) cues in their recreation process while nonmusicians relied on surface (local) cues. These novel findings provide empirical support for a differing compositionalistic tendency in music and language as perceived by musicians versus nonmusicians.

title: The Creation of a New Space for Children in 15th- and 16th-Century Florentine Public Images of the Family
abstract: My research project analyzes the space created for children in 15th and 16th century public images of the family. In particular, I focus on Florentine public images due to Florence's status as a center of Renaissance artistic and cultural development. These developments led to significant changes in paintings of and written works regarding the family. Artists developed the skill to accurately portray children with age-appropriate emotional expressions, gestures and physical features. Additionally, the tools needed to record family diaries and daily affairs became widely accessible. The combination of newly developed artistic skill and innovative methods for recording family histories led to the creation of a new space for children in Florentine public images of the family. Through an analysis of the space created for children in public images of the family, my work adds to the ongoing debate regarding the history of childhood. Philippe Aries is credited with initiating this debate in 1962 through his publication, "Centuries of Childhood." According to Aries and his followers, childhood was discovered in the 15th and 16th centuries. It was this discovery that led to changes in the artistic representations of children. In my work, I argue that rather than representing a private, emotional discovery of childhood, changes in artwork reflect a new societal emphasis on the inclusion of children in the public images created of family.

title: A Simple Prescription For Envelope Binding Energy
abstract: Binary star systems can be divided into two evolutionary categories: those with non-interacting members and those where interaction occurs. The latter case can present complicated behavior not seen in the evolution of individual stars. One example of interest is the development of a common envelope. This occurs when one of the two stars, called the primary, outgrows its Roche lobe, resulting in gas flowing from the primary to the secondary star. Under certain conditions this can result in a common envelope of gas around the entire system. Predicting what happens next is difficult. It is generally thought that the two stellar cores spiral inward, releasing orbital energy through friction to the envelope. This process then continues until the envelope is expelled. Assuming this model, the final orbital separation of the stellar pair can be obtained from the value of the binding energy of the envelope. This value requires detailed stellar structure models to calculate, and is usually estimated for large scale studies where these aren’t available. In this investigation, such stellar structure models are generated for a wide range of possible stars, and the binding energy is calculated for each. Then a best fit equation is introduced taking basic stellar parameters such as mass, age, and composition, as input, with the binding energy as the dependent variable. The results are to be published for use in large scale studies of contact binaries, greatly increasing precision beyond the currently relied upon estimations.

title: The Astronomer and the Artist: Galileo Galilei and the Florentine Accademia del'Disegno
