abstract: My research project attempts to demonstrate that Tuscan astronomer Galileo Galilei’s relationship with the Florentine Accademia del'Disegno played a vital role in the development of his ability to interpret and illustrate the rockiness of the Moon’s surface. Research materials include primary sources, secondary sources, and Galileo’s ink wash drawings printed in his treatise Sidereus Nuncius. Galileo is often credited with inventing the telescope and creating the first comprehensive rendering of the Moon’s topography. As a result, he receives most admiration for his work as a scientist. Recently, contemporary scholars have discovered that Galileo was actually not the inventor of the telescope, nor was he the first to observe the Moon’s surface at high magnification. However, he was nevertheless more capable of drawing the Moon’s surface than his peers. Art historians such as Horst Bredekamp argue that Galileo’s relationship with the Tuscan art world contributed to this, as Galileo used art theories of light and perspective in his astronomical observation practices. Galileo’s biographer Vincenzo Viviani suggests that long before Galileo touched a telescope, he pursued a career in the arts, evidenced by his application for a teaching position at the Florentine Accademia del'Disegno at age 25. With further investigation, it becomes evident that this drawing academy played a crucial role in Galileo’s development as an artist and his translation of art theory to the field of astronomy. Italian architect Giorgio Vasari founded the Accademia as an educational institution where painters, sculptors, and architects could meet not just as artisan guild members, but as intellectuals. I strive to illustrate the specific influence of the Accademia in Galileo’s developing knowledge of artistic theory as a result of the Accademia’s effort to unite Tuscan artistic and intellectual figures as well as its instructional emphasis on light and perspective art theory.

title: Spatial Attention Drives Imagination
abstract: We imagine actions and events in the world when we listen to someone telling a story, predict the actions of others while driving, or foresee the outcome of a game. This project explores how our visual system allows us to imagine objects moving, even when they are currently static. Our hypothesis is that when you imagine an object moving, you shift spatial attention around as if you were following that object. To test this idea, we asked subjects to imagine a central static object moving either to the left or to the right, while measuring the locus of spatial attention with brain electrophysiology. With this technique, leftward shifts of attention are reflected by more electrical activity over the back right of the head (which processes the left side of the world), and rightward shifts are reflected by more activity over the back left of the head. Pilot data show that participants do shift attention while imagining motion, suggesting that the motion of spatial attention may underlie our perception of imagined motion.

title: Papaya and the Pill: Perceptions of Birth Spacing and Contraceptive Use Among Women in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India
abstract: The large body of research on family planning programs has focused on the efficacy of these initiatives in relation to the intent of the policy maker. This top-down approach has failed to account for socio-cultural perceptions of fertility and child-bearing. The purpose of this research is to understand how cultural and political factors influence the knowledge and acceptance of a variety of birth spacing methods, from papaya to the pill, among women in rural Andhra Pradesh, India. While family planning in India is motivated by demographic concerns and is designed to reduce population size, women use health as the framework for continuing or discontinuing their reproductive careers. The research is significant because it explores reproductive health decision-making from the perspective of the woman, particularly the level of congruency between cultural beliefs and political motives. This has implications for the field of public health because it emphasizes the needs and expectations of the individual who is grounded in a socio-cultural setting in creating effective programs. Moreover, while there is extensive research in anthropology on cultural and social views of birth spacing, there is little integration between culture and politics - both areas have typically been treated separately. My research looks at the interplay between the two which is critical for anthropology because it enables the field to have concrete applications to real-world issues by integrating other fields.

title: Interactions Along the Fault Lines of Civilizations: Investigating Literary Legacies and Transitions in Russian Accounts of the Caucasian Conquest (1817-1864)
abstract: My project extends the arguments of Susan Layton's 1995 book, Russian Literature and Empire: Conquest of the Caucasus from Pushkin to Tolstoy. While Layton's work examines how the literature of the Caucasian Conquest shaped conceptions of Russian nationality and statehood, this paper probes the Conquest's corollary influences on Russian literature and its associated criticism. Textual presentations of the Caucasian theater contributed to the rise of a literary perspective that emphasized individual consciousness and experiential authenticity within the dynamic progression of the nineteenth-century. By contesting fanciful Caucasian storytelling traditions, these innovative narrative methodologies opposed established conventions of Romanticism affirming instead emerging tenets of Realism. How then did Russian authors experience the Caucasus and how did they convey their impressions to Russia’s educated elite? What sentiments did Bestuzhev-Marlinsky, Lermontov, Pushkin, and Tolstoy express in describing the Caucasian theater and how did their convictions develop noticeably more realistic transcriptions of the individual's unique deliberations within his complex environments? This paper accordingly examines primary source literary accounts of the Caucasian Conquest to investigate how Realist narrative methods evolved within their changing historical contexts. While such contents illustrate the remarkable artistic imaginations of Bestuzhev-Marlinsky, Lermontov, Pushkin, and Tolstoy, they additionally demonstrate more momentous transitions of narrative form and procedure. The succession and consequence of Caucasian works produced by these four prolific authors inspired a critical legacy that endorsed Realism as a preeminent style of modernity while devaluing Romanticism as a subordinate approach of the past.

title: Dysregulation of the Heat Shock Response in the Presence of Mutant Huntingtin
abstract: Cells respond to protein misfolding by inducing the heat shock response (HSR). The HSR is a genetic response in which molecular chaperones (such as the heat shock proteins, or HSPs) are upregulated to restore protein folding homeostasis. In Huntington’s disease, mutant huntingtin protein misfolds and aggregates, and causes disruptions to the cellular protein folding machinery. In theory, this should induce the HSR, but there are discrepancies in the literature as to whether or not the HSR is induced. Our objective is to examine and resolve some of those discrepancies by doing a comprehensive analysis of mutant huntingtin expression and HSR induction in mammalian cells. We used quantitative RT-PCR to measure expression levels of key HSPs in HeLa cells that conditionally express mutant huntingtin and found that HSP expression was not significantly increased in mutant huntingtin-expressing HeLa cells. In Huntington’s Disease, mutant huntingtin aggregates are associated with cellular toxicity. To address the HSR of aggregate-expressing cells in particular, we used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to examine HSP expression in subsets of cells. Our results indicate that the HSR is not significantly induced in cell populations enriched for aggregates. We have also measured HSP expression during mutant huntingtin expression time courses and have examined potential mutant huntingtin-induced blocks to the HSR by measuring HSR induction by a second stress, such as heat shock. It is our hope that this comprehensive analysis of the HSR during mutant huntingtin expression will contribute to an understanding of the pathology of Huntington’s Disease.

title: Network Trends and Characteristics of Online Video Viewership
abstract: Over the past year I have performed extensive research on the mechanisms behind the sharing and viewing of online videos hosted on popular websites like YouTube and MetaCafe. The study has involved interviews and metric-based analysis, which has revealed several interesting characteristics of online video viewership. The interview portion of the study has exposed that online video viewers are becoming increasingly fragmented into unique "sharing networks", defined primarily by interests in similar content. The interviewees expressed that their "sharing networks" are growing to become highly defined and exclusionary. The metric-based portion of the study has explored the activity distribution of online videos. Analysis of activity metrics such as views, comments, and blog posts reveal that online video activity exists in a scale-free distribution found in many other social networks. The distribution is characterized by an exponential curve, where a small minority of online videos receives the vast majority of activity. Recently, much research has been done to explain the existence of similar online network distributions in terms of their long tails. This analysis of online videos explores the existence of the opposite side of the distribution, and postulates that the aggregation systems employed within these websites help support, and even amplify the natural scale-free distribution. This adds another layer to the complexity of why certain online videos quickly reach immense popularity, and become "viral videos".

title: The Relative Impact of Maternal Modeling and Weight-Related Criticism on Daughters' Body Images
abstract: Research has shown that mothers strongly influence their daughters’ eating habits and body images, though the way in which they do so is still debated. There are two main theories that address this issue. The theory of maternal modeling suggests that mothers influence daughters by displaying behaviors and attitudes to adopt, while the theory of direct communication argues that mothers influence their daughters by directly criticizing daughters’ appearance or directly encouraging daughters to lose weight. The current study aimed to clarify which form of maternal influence is most powerful. Participants completed measures of eating attitudes/behaviors (EAT-26; Garner et al., 1982) and body dissatisfaction (the body dissatisfaction subscale of the Eating Disorders Inventory II; Garner et al., 1983), both as themselves and as they believed their mothers would complete them. Participants also completed a questionnaire designed to measure the amount of direct communication they received from their mothers about their weight and appearance while growing up along with a number of open-ended questions about key body image-related events. Participants’ own scores on the EAT-26 and Body Dissatisfaction subscale were positively correlated with how they believed their mothers would have completed these same scales. Scores on the direct communication scale, however, were not significantly correlated with either daughters’ or mothers’ scores. Qualitative analyses indicated that women believed they would have handled body image-related issues in a manner substantially different from how their mothers handled these incidents. Overall, the results of this study show strong support for the theory of maternal modeling.

title: The Comparative Effects of Quarry Blasting and Environmental Factors on Cracks in a Residential Structure
abstract: The notion of blasting, even in a controlled setting such as limestone quarry, can be alarming to residents and business owners within earshot. Because humans are inherently sensitive to these vibrations, they perceive that the structures they live in are adversely affected. The goal of the research is to assuage these concerns by comparing effects caused by ground motions with those caused by everyday events. This project reports the effects of ground motion caused by blast vibrations on the structural response and crack displacements in a one-story house. More importantly, these effects are compared with those caused by thunder, occupant activity, and long-term climatic factors. Hourly, daily, and seasonal variations in temperature and humidity cause cracks to displace orders of magnitude more than the dynamic events by which people are very concerned.

title: The Burning Hive: A Creative Essay on Beekeeping in an Hostile Environment
abstract: A few years ago, articles began appearing in the media about a mysterious circumstance called Colony Collapse Disorder, by which honeybees everywhere were disappearing. Scientists’ attempts at making honeybees resistant to CCD so that commercial crops dependent on pollination would not be harmed seemed to me too narrow. No one was thinking about why, in fact, CCD was happening in the first place. I decided get to the root of the problem, by which I mean I decided to study human beings, and how our actions, our methods of farming, and our re-structuring of the natural landscape have led to the current plight of the honeybee. With a Weinberg Summer Research Grant, I spent three months studying beekeeping in Southern Illinois. Creating immunity to CCD, I confirmed, was only a temporary solution, not an explanation of the problem. My study of bees culminated in a lyric essay that attempts to engage with environmental issues in a comprehensive way. Using bees as a nexus, my essay explores and connects many seemingly unrelated issues. It explains why monoculture farming leaves bees with no forage, and how, starved, they depend on beekeepers to feed them high fructose corn syrup. This syrup, lacking the amino acids and antioxidants of honey, (their natural food), depletes their already fragile immune systems and leaves them incapable of fighting predators such as Varroa mites. Additionally, my essay considers what we can learn from the concept that a hive is actually a highly evolved entity known as a “superorgansim.”

title: Ageism vs. Racism: An Experimental Examination of Interacting Stereotypes About Black Older Adults
abstract: Research suggests that Black Americans are associated with crime and threat while older adults are seen as warm but forgetful. The present work includes two studies examining how these conflicting stereotypes affect perceptions of older Black adults. In Study 1, participants rated perceptions of facial expressions for young White, young Black, older White, and older Black male faces. Results showed age did not attenuate perceptions of anger, a signal of threat, on Black faces. In Study 2, participants read a scenario about either a young or old, Black or White female target who leaves a store without paying for a hat; when confronted by the store manager, the target claims she forgot she was wearing the item. Participants rated how believable the woman’s story was as well as how angry the manager should feel. Participants who read a scenario featuring an older target felt the excuse was more believable than did participants who read about a younger target. There was also an effect of race, however, such that Black targets were seen as less believable than White targets. Additionally, participants thought the store manager would feel less angry toward older targets but would be angrier at the older Black target than the older White target. These results suggest that age and race stereotypes both impact how older Black individuals are perceived, but the warmth and forgetfulness associated with older adults are applied more readily to older White adults than to older Black adults.

title: A Well-Baby Checkup: A Ghanaian Perspective: Maternal Factors and Childhood Health
abstract: Poor nutritional status during childhood has major effects on long-term health. In the setting of rural Ghana, childhood malnutrition is prevalent, despite the fact proper nutrition guidelines have been incorporated into intervention programs. Thus, barriers may be preventing mothers from using their nutritional knowledge to make healthy decisions in the household. This study assesses the prevalence of malnutrition and the factors affecting it as seen in a sample of Ghanaian women and their children aged 3-24 months (n=33). Anthropometric measurements were collected on the children and interviews were conducted with the mothers. Analysis found that malnourished children were more likely to be the offspring of mothers with low nutritional status (p=0.221), single (p=0.012), and to lack national health insurance (p=0.176). Because marital status was related to other variables including nutritional knowledge (p=0.040) and number of people in the home (p=0.201), it is possible that the relationships in the home act as a barrier to proper childhood health. Efforts to improve the home dynamics and increase the use of national health insurance may decrease the level of childhood malnutrition in this setting.

title: Optical Torsional Control of Charge Transfer through Molecular Junctions
abstract: As the physical limitations of silicon chips are exceeded by the need for faster processing power, it becomes necessary to compensate by exploring alternative circuit technology. One strategy applies the evolving field of the optical control of molecules to the manipulation of charge transfer through a junction. A simulation is used to examine a molecular switch formed of a biphenyl molecule adsorbed onto a surface and placed near a scanning tunneling microscope tip. The introduction of a circularly polarized optical field permits torsional control of the phenyl rings about the molecular axis. This optical force may thus transition the skewed geometry of the molecular equilibrium state to a coplanar configuration which facilitates charge transfer events through a system of conjugated pi bonds. The applicability of biphenyl species toward optical control of molecular junctions is assessed through results to be presented at the symposium.

title: That They May Be One: Reconciling Authoritarianism and Commitment to Ecumenism in John Paul II’s Pontificate
abstract: Pope John Paul II’s ecumenical legacy will affect not only future Vatican decisions, but also inter-denominational relations among Christians in an increasingly global society. In his inaugural address, John Paul II promised to further ecumenism, the movement to achieve unity among all Christians. Despite this pledge, several Vatican documents issued during John Paul II’s pontificate reflect confident authoritarianism, sparking public condemnation from both Orthodox and Protestant Christians. I argue that this apparent contradiction, while resolvable, masks a second more serious barrier to ecumenical dialogue. Comparing documents from John Paul II’s pontificate, I first analyze the tension between the Church’s commitment to ecumenism and its authoritative claim to epistemological privilege. I show that ultimately the question creating this tension involves the proper relationship of the Church to various kinds of truth. John Paul II’s authoritarianism is actually a result of his efforts to unify Catholics and render the Church a single-minded “person” as a prerequisite for ecumenical progress. While I conclude that the ecumenical strategy expressed in John Paul II’s writings is ultimately unrealistic, contrary to typical critiques of John Paul II, I show that it is not the authoritarian tone which poses an obstacle to ecumenism. Instead, it is John Paul II’s implicit strategy of holding a dialogue among representatives – each of whom speaks for the “person” of a cohesive church – that makes his vision problematic.

title: Por la libertad de decidir: The Fight for Democracy and the Morning After Pill in Chile
abstract: Chilean social movements have been the focus of several studies, most of them referring to those of the dictatorial era. Since social movements are context and culture specific, it is important to study the new surrounding factors and motivations of current movements. Although Chile is still among the most conservative countries of Latin America, liberal opinions and movements are on the rise. This thesis uses political process model and collective action frame analysis to examine how and why a liberal social movement in favor of the morning after pill was able to form despite a conservative social climate. It also examines how the movement reflects the changing political climate, and how the climate has effected the movement. Due to an open and changing political climate, use of new technology, and strong motivational frames, the movement in favor of the morning after pill managed to attract the attention of the government and Chilean society. This movement is not just about a woman’s right to birth control; it also uses the morning after pill as a symbolic representation of the lack of true democracy in Chile. The movement’s specific objective for true democracy is representative of the relatively new master frame of democratic rights, an idea which resonates with Chilean society and mobilized large numbers of participants.

title: Cognitive and Non-cognitive Development Among Young Children in Chile: Effect of Participation in Public Childcare Centers
abstract: In recent decades, access to early childhood education programs in Latin America has been growing. Yet, little is known, in a systematic way, about the quality of childcare services in the region. This paper examines the issue of quality in a longitudinal study in Chile by carrying out an empirical analysis of the impact of participation in public childcare centers on multidimensional aspects of child development. The results reveal that there are significant gains in non-cognitive areas of development, particularly those concerning the child's expressive abilities, while there are questionable setbacks in the child's cognitive capabilities. Thus, the research suggests that considerations of rigorous program evaluation must be part of every nation's plan of future investment in early childhood education.

title: The Influence of Geographic Software on Education and Spatial Ability
abstract: Student interest and success in the sciences and mathematics has been on the decline in many US schools. Spatial learning is essential in improving educational performance. It is especially helpful in increasing the understanding of physical models, diagrams, and visualizations and can be facilitated through the use of maps. Utilizing maps, children can experience and actively think about their surroundings without having physically experienced it. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) interpret reality effectively by using maps to convey spatial information about geography of the earth. For these reasons, the use of the GIS-based software program My World in conjunction with middle-school curriculum textbook Planetary Forecaster should positively influence spatial thinking and facilitate learning in the science classroom. In the lesson, eighth graders gain content knowledge on the relationship between temperature and tilt of the Earth. They are given pre- and post-tests based on spatial ability and conceptual knowledge that measures their learning in the activity. They are also interviewed about their answers, and many times, the student will spontaneously gesture to indicate the relationship of the tilt of the earth and temperatures in different regions. Eighth graders participating in the experimental condition of using the mapping software should achieve higher scores on a spatial assessment activity than students who learn in the traditional classroom. After subjects are run, an analysis of change in spatial abilities, content knowledge, and use of gesture are coded and statistically evaluated.

title: Genetic Mapping of the Low Psychostimulant Response Mutant Gridlock’d
abstract: Strong genetic components to addiction and a relationship between drug sensitivity and propensity for addiction have been shown in numerous studies. The low psychostimulant response mutant Gridlock’d on a C57BL/6J genetic background was outcrossed with mice from a C3H/HeJ genetic background; the resulting F1 offspring then mated to complete a F2 genetic cross. Various genetic markers of these offspring were genotyped with single sequence length polymorphism polymerase chain reaction and gel electrophoresis. Because the homozygous Gridlock’d was on a C57BL/6J background and was outcrossed to a C3H/HeJ background strain, the extreme low quantitative response offspring were expected to exhibit the homozygous BL6/BL6 genotype across the chosen genetic markers and the extreme high quantitative response offspring were expected to exhibit the C3H/C3H genotype. Accordingly, those of intermediate quantitative response were expected to exhibit the BL6/C3H genotype. Genetic markers that exhibited strong genetic association to a certain phenotype, expected or unexpected, were labeled “hot markers.”As more genetic regions are genotyped, Quantitative Trait Loci (genetic regions responsible for a certain phenotype) will be mapped. Background QTLs will later be separated from mutated QTLs by comparing data between a wild-type control cross and a mutant cross. Chromosome 8 is under further investigation.

title: Motivating the Establishment of Trust Before and After Violations of Trust
abstract: Trust is often difficult to develop because it entails accepting vulnerability for uncertain rewards. Investigating what motivates individuals to accept the risks inherent in trust could thus provide insight into building trust, facilitating cooperation and reducing conflict. Individuals use two strategies when pursuing goals. Promotion motivations encourage strategies of pursuing gains despite risking losses, whereas prevention motivations encourage strategies of guarding against losses despite forgoing potential gains (Molden, Lee & Higgins, 2008). Prevention-focused, compared to promotion-focused, individuals may therefore be less likely to risk vulnerability and trust others in situations from which they both might benefit. The present research examined trust using an investment game. Participants repeatedly decided how much of an initial allotment to “invest” in a partner who, after the experimenter tripled each investment, would supposedly decide how much to return to the investor. The partner’s behaviors were actually simulated such that after a period of fair returns, there was a single round in which the “partner” kept more than their share, after which a period of fair returns resumed. Results showed that a prevention focus leads to more dramatic responses to others’ actions (betrayals and trusting behavior). Promotion-focused individuals did not change their behavior following small betrayals, but like prevention-focused individuals, trusted their partners less immediately after large betrayals. Following large betrayals, unlike promotion-focused individuals, prevention-focused individuals never trusted their partners above their initial level despite the partner’s return to fair behavior. Regardless of betrayal size, as trusting relationships developed, both groups reached similar absolute trust levels.

title: Experimental Evidence That Peer Comments Encourage Restrained Eating in Undergraduate Women
abstract: Two experiments examined the effect of a peer comment that supported restrained eating and the effect of that peer’s appearance on the amount of food participants took in a lab setting. First, we examined sorority members’ potential influence on the eating behavior of prospective sorority members. Forty-six college women completed a study where snacks were provided for the participant and a confederate to eat. Prior to taking any snacks, the confederate made a comment either indicating deliberate restrained eating or a neutral comment. The confederate either wore a t-shirt indicating she was a member of an elite sorority on campus or a plain t-shirt. The second study involved the same procedure and food comments; however instead of the confederate acting as a sorority member, she dressed in either attractive or unattractive clothing/make-up. Results indicated a main effect of the eating comment in both studies, with participants in the restrained eating condition taking significantly less food. Results suggest that women’s eating choices were directly influenced by a restrained eating comment made by a peer, regardless of their previously measured habitual eating behaviors. Several significant interactions suggested that the effect of the eating comment on participants’ mood depended on how much the participant ate. Overall, results point to the potential for even the smallest eating-related comments to influence a peer’s eating behavior. The role that social comparison processes played in women’s eating behavior is also discussed.

title: Maternal Education and Family Functioning as Predictors of Children’s Early Academic Achievement in Low-Income Households
abstract: Children who face economic hardship are less likely to succeed in school than their more affluent counterparts. Most previous research has sought explanations for this achievement gap using nationally representative samples—comparing poor children to middle- or high-income children. However, the effects of poverty are not homogeneous and some poor children overcome socioeconomic risks to succeed academically. Using data from Welfare, Children, and Families: A Three City Study, which has a large sample comprised solely of low-income families, this project examines the variant effects of mothers’ education and family functioning on the academic achievement of poor children. There were three waves of data collection (1999, 2000-2001, 2005) with extensive interviews for mothers and standardized math and reading assessments for children. For this study, we focus on the preschooler cohort (N=772, ages 2-4 years in Wave 1). We utilize regression analyses to explore the relationships between child academic achievement and parental practices and family structure. We found significant effects of increases to maternal education on children’s math achievement. Specifically, mothers who earn educational degrees see their children’s math score increase an average of 9 points (average score = 100), compared to mothers with the same initial educational level who do not return to school. Stable marriages are also positive predictors of math achievement, and increases in the number of children in the household are negative predictors. Reading achievement scores are higher for children in stable marriages, but this relationship is partially mediated by higher levels of family routine in married households.

title: The Effect of Emotion on the Pitch Shift Reflex
abstract: Leading scientists and doctors in the world have not identified the exact neural mechanisms that underlie vocalization and the control of voice pitch. Many speech and communication disorders result in difficulty or inability to control voice fundamental frequency (F0). In order to help treat these patients with the optimal therapy to solve this problem, the specific neural mechanisms that control vocalization must be identified and understood. Previous studies in the speech physiology field have revealed a phenomenon known as the pitch shift reflex. This reflex is the automatic vocal response to a shift in pitch, or voice F0 feedback. Because emotion is an automatic and subconscious response in the human body, much like certain vocal responses, I have hypothesized that affective state (emotional response) may affect vocal control. To test affective state on automatic vocal responses, I have performed a study incorporating pitch-shifted voice feedback. Twenty female subjects looked at emotion-provoking pictures while vocalizing and listening to themselves in real time with computer generated pitch shifts. I measured the response magnitudes of their pitch shift reflex to learn if emotional stimulation has an effect on vocalization. Although the data have not yet been analyzed, I predict that the data will show that the response magnitudes of the pitch shift reflex are significantly different when emotionally stimulated. Hopefully the results of this study will get us closer to understanding more about the mechanisms underlying common speech disorders.

title: Accuracy of the Quantification of Capillary Bed Blood Flow in the Brain Using Magnetic Resonance Imaging
abstract: Quantification of cerebral blood flow (CBF) has an impact on the diagnosis and treatment of neurovascular pathologies. Dynamic Susceptibility-weighted Contrast-enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (DSC-MRI) has the potential to quantify CBF with greater resolution, less patient exposure to ionizing radiation, and lower costs than the standard of reference, [15O]-H2O positron emission tomography (PET). We hypothesize that MRI CBF measurements will correlate with PET CBF. MRI and PET perfusion scans were obtained from seven patients with confirmed neurovascular disease and co-registered for region of interest (ROI) analysis. PET CBF maps were generated using the autoradiographic method. MRI CBF maps were calculated using the “Bookend” technique. We found that there is a significant correlation between MRI and PET CBF; however, there is a systematic offset between flow values measured in PET and MRI, with PET values being greater. Our study shows that the offset between the two methods is potentially a result of the assumptions of tracer kinetic models used in MRI and PET perfusion measurements.

title: Bioengineering Single Crystal Growth
abstract: Sea urchins turn simple ingredients into high-performance materials. The tests, teeth, and spines of the adults are hierarchical organic-inorganic composites based on calcium carbonate single crystals of complex morphology. Even sea urchin embryos grow intricate endoskeletons, called spicules, which are composed of single calcite crystals that elegantly branch and curve. Modern crystal growth techniques do not begin to approach the complexity and intimate control exerted by the primary mesenchyme cells (PMCs) that are responsible for this process of biomineralization. Understanding, controlling, and ultimately re-programming sea urchin embryo PMCs could enable advances in “bottom up”- synthesis of magnetic, optical, and semiconducting materials. Our research efforts focus on forward-engineering spicule development of the sea urchin embryo in vitro. We show our approach to control the direction and shape of calcite single crystal growth by micro-patterning PMCs on cell culture substrates. We developed an efficient approach to pattern wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), a protein that selectively binds spiculogenic PMCs (but not other embryonic cells), directly onto glass substrates in a micro-contact printing (µCP) process. After transferring WGA with patterned PDMS elastomer stamps, we backfill the surface with a non-stick protein. In this way we create a substrate that has patterns that bind PMCs on a non-stick background. We further demonstrate how this approach can be used to isolate and create patterns of PMCs and how we use these patterns to control the spicule growth process.

title: Genetic Structure of Araçari (Toucans) across the Rio Japurá
abstract: Amazonia is often misperceived as a homogenous tropical rainforest with uniform species distributions. In reality, it is heterogeneous and certain species are only found in certain areas. Recognizing this heterogeneity, biologists began defining areas of endemism (AOEs), or regions of unique biodiversity, to divide the Amazon rainforest and understand its patterns of species distributions. Currently, there are eight recognized AOEs, primarily outlined by the major rivers of the Amazon. In addition to these major rivers, it has been suggested that other, smaller rivers, such as the Rio Japurá, may also define AOEs. In this study, we tested this hypothesis by looking at the genetic structure across the Rio Japurá for the widely distributed Amazonian toucan species the Ivory-billed Araçari (Pteroglossus azara). We show that the subspecies of Ivory-billed Araçari on the north bank of the Rio Japurá is genetically distinct from the subspecies on the south bank and therefore supports the hypothesis that the region north of the Rio Japurá and south of the Rio Negro should be considered a unique area of endemism.

title: Semantic Contextual Cues and Listener Adaptation to Foreign-Accented English
abstract: The context surrounding words can facilitate word recognition for native and non-native listeners. However, for degraded speech signals (e.g. with noise), non-natives may lose the ability to take advantage of contextual cues unless the speech is clearly produced (Bradlow and Alexander, 2007). This study investigated whether: 1) foreign-accented speech degrades the signal such that natives show reduced ability to take advantage of context, and, 2) both native and non-native listeners adapt to foreign-accented speech. Native and non-native listeners were exposed to accented speech in two blocks. In each block, half the sentence final words were in high and half in low predictability contexts. Listeners were asked to identify sentence final words. In a single talker condition, natives benefited from context and adapted to the accent; non-natives could not use context but showed adaption. In a multi-talker condition, natives benefited from context and adapted to the accent. Context effects were only seen though in sentences produced by speakers of L1 Chinese, the accent group with the greatest number of talkers. Non-natives benefited from context and adapted, however the context effect was only seen when listener and speaker L1 matched. These results suggest that accented speech disrupts the native ability to take advantage of context, but this can be overcome by adaptation to a specific accent. Non-natives benefit from a talker-listener L1 match, thus allowing them to function at higher processing levels. Both natives and non-natives can adapt to accented speech in general over time, both talker-specific and multi-talker.

title: Property Rights and Incentives: A Plot-Level Analysis of Rural Thailand
abstract: A system of clearly defined property rights is considered one of the fundamental pillars of the world’s developed economies. This study examines how the emergence of formal land rights influences the incentives of economic agents in the developing world, where property rights are characterized by ambiguity, asymmetric information, moral hazard and inconsistent state policy. Using household-level data from rural Thailand, I analyze how two different categories of land right certificates differentially affect plot-level rental and investment decisions. While one title affords unrestricted rights to sell and rent out land, the other allows land to be transferred only via inheritance, although plots of both categories continue to be leased at the same rate. I hypothesize that the moral hazard associated with renting land to potentially negligent tenants provides an added disincentive to leasing plots with limited title, who are in effect intergenerationally bound to their land. Likewise, there is greater incentive to rent out plots with unrestricted title, since there are no restrictions on future transactions. The analysis deals with two sources of potentially confounding heterogeneity bias by employing a unique set of instrumental variables that identify exogenous variation in land title conditional on farmer and village fixed effects. In line with the expectations drawn from economic theory, I find that unrestricted title increases the likelihood of renting out, while the more limited title has the opposite affect. Furthermore, my findings call into question the widely held contention that formal land rights generate greater plot-level investment. From these results I draw some general conclusions regarding land-use management and government policy in the developing world.

title: Rapid Spatial Learning in an Informal Educational Setting through Analogical Comparison
abstract: Comparison is a key process involved in learning and cognition. Learning environments that are geared towards comparison processes can facilitate rapid learning in children. In a natural learning environment at the Chicago Children’s Museum, we studied the role of structural alignment in children’s learning of the diagonal brace principle—a key principle in achieving stable constructions. Children (6-to-8-year-olds) were shown pairs of buildings, one with a diagonal brace and one without, and encouraged to wiggle them to determine which was “stronger”—i.e., more stable. Then they built their own ‘skyscraper’ with their families in a free-form building activity. Children readily noticed that the one with the diagonal brace was more stable. Our question was whether the children would abstract the diagonal brace principle from this brief experience. We predicted that high alignment would lead to the greatest insight into diagonal braces. After the comparison, children engaged in a free-form building activity with their families. Then we showed them a wobbly building and asked where to put another piece to make it stronger. Children who received the comparison training performed better than those who did not; and within the training groups, those in the high-alignment condition performed better than those in the low-alignment condition. These findings confirm our prediction that the alignment process can help children learn the diagonal brace principle.

title: Simulation of Pores Stability in Phospholipid Bilayers
abstract: Self-assembled vesicles consisting of a spherical bilayer of lipids surrounding an aqueous core are known as liposomes. Liposomes have emerged as a promising delivery system for potent chemotherapeutic agents. Modified liposomes on the nanoscale have been shown to have excellent pharmacokinetic profiles for the delivery of nucleic acids, proteins, and chemotherapeutic agents. It is important that the liposome system remain stable until it has reached the desired target site at which point it undergoes triggered release due to changes in pH or temperature. Most temperature sensitive liposomes take advantage of the peak in permeability of the bilayer that coincides with a phase transition. At the phase transition temperature, gel and liquid phases coexist and incompatibilities in molecular packing may assist drug release. Unfortunately, many standard liposome compositions result in liposomes that release drugs slowly at the phase transition temperature, and the use of such systems for drug delivery has been unsuccessful. One method to improve the efficiency is to incorporated lysolipids, which are single chain analogues of standard lipids, into liposomes. Lysolipids tend to form micellar structures in aqueous solution. When incorporated in small amounts into lipid systems, it is postulated that lysolipids help to form stable, long lasting pores in the lipid bilayer as it undergoes phase transition from gel to liquid crystalline. However, the characterization of liposome cargo release is a difficult process to probe experimentally. Hence, computational molecular dynamics could be employed to reduce the experimental complications. The Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics model, which helps simplifying the complicated systems, requires less time to simulate and is efficient enough to help understanding the nature of the pore stability in phospholipid bilayers.

title: Early Aspirants: Unpacking the Flow from Aspirations to Entry in K-12 Teaching
abstract: While the U.S. student body becomes increasingly diverse, our teaching force remains predominately white and female. A wealth of literature in education and labor economics has examined factors affecting teacher labor force demographics. Questions related to early interest in the profession, however, have not been of particular focus. In this study, I use a nationally representative longitudinal dataset, the National Education Longitudinal Study (NELS: 88), to examine ‘Early Aspirants’ to the teaching profession, students who articulate an ‘expected occupation’ of K-12 teaching in high school. I use hierarchical logistic regression, appropriate given the nested data structure and binary outcome variables, to examine two sets of relationships: characteristics and factors associated with odds of early interest in teaching, and characteristics and factors associated with odds of becoming a teacher among early aspirants. In a multivariate regression framework, I explore motivations behind aspirations to teach, and facilitators of and obstacles to persistence on those aspirations. In shedding light on the early aspirants, the study raises questions about how we might better attract and hold onto aspiring teachers, particularly those from under-represented roups.

title: Dependent Relationships between Nucleotide Positions of an Anticodon Indicate Important Positions for Tertiary Structure
abstract: In biological and chemical processes, precision is important. For molecules or compounds to interact with each other properly, the pieces must fit together in a particular manner to achieve the proper result. If some of the molecules do not have the correct shape, they will not fit together, and the appropriate reaction will not occur. Every compound possesses a characteristic shape that allows it to perform its role, and molecules arranged differently will be unable to fulfill the exact same task. In effect: structure indicates function. This concept holds true for Transfer RNA (tRNA), which is responsible for converting Messenger RNA to protein during translation. A single mutation can irrevocably damage the structure, preventing it from working efficiently. Studies have previously focused on distinguishing specific anticodons from others based on the identities of nucleotides at key positions. However, it is also important to determine how nucleotides in a single molecule interact with each other to give the most stable three-dimensional conformation. Positions crucial for the correct tertiary structure are more likely to interact dependently with other positions, as they will need to interact with each other in particular configurations. Comparison between important positions for differing anticodons will make it possible to determine whether the same positions are important for the structure of all tRNA or just for a particular anticodon. The objective of this study is to determine statistically the relationships between pairs of positions in an anticodon as these relationships may indicate positions crucial for the resulting structure.

title: Marketing Our Maladies: Rationalizing Medicine via Direct-to-Consumer Advertising
abstract: In the past decade there has been a rapid increase in the number of direct-to-consumer (DTC) pharmaceutical commercials. By looking at DTC drug advertisements, I seek to understand how medicine has become strategically rationalized by large profit-driven corporations. My study identifies the hegemonic views of the pharmaceutical companies and the rhetoric used to convince consumers to buy into their claim. It also examines consumer dissent by analyzing parodies of commercials made by random users on Youtube.com. The results show that, while pharmaceutical companies have economic power, their marketing tactics have not gone unquestioned. Consumers are able to “see through” their claims. Through parody, consumers have found an innovative way to voice their opposition to DTC drug ads, indicating that medicalization has not been fully accepted.

title: Creation of an MRI Phantom for Quantifying Liver Iron Content in Iron Diseases
abstract: Iron overload diseases like hemochromatosis and thalassemias are serious health issues for millions of people. The current method for diagnosing these diseases uses a liver biopsy that is invasive, expensive, and error prone. Furthermore, 0.5% of patients experience serious bleeding and prolonged hospitalization after these procedures. The current methods for classifying iron deposits are antiquated and require improvements. To improve these procedures, we are developing a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) phantom using ferritin coated beads that will mimic hemosiderin deposits found in the liver. This tool will more accurately and noninvasively allow for the characterization of iron overload diseases by providing a direct comparison of iron concentration in vivo. To develop this tool, we initiated a reaction between polystyrene beads containing surface aldehyde functionalities with lysine amino acid residues on the surface of the iron protein ferritin. Different sized beads were utilized in an attempt to mimic the differently sized hemosiderin deposits- -insoluble iron accretions—that are found throughout the liver. I found the relaxivities of 1µm, 0.4 µm, and 0.02 µm Ferribeads, (ferritin containing polystyrene beads) to be 3.002 mM-1s-1, 2.78 mM-1s-1, and 4.081 mM-1s-1. Alternatively, the control beads had a relaxivity of 0 mM-1s-1, and ferritin protein alone had a relaxivity of 0.137 mM-1s-1. We used Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) to determine the iron concentration of the bead samples. We discovered a linear relationship between iron concentration and relaxation rate. These results demonstrate progress towards the development of an ex-vivo MRI phantom for prognosis of hemochromatosis.

title: Ion Channel Investigations in Drosophila Circadian Neurons
abstract: Electrophysiology is used to study the membrane properties of cell types in a variety of model organisms. Recording current and voltage from neurons with specific internal and external solutions allows for the isolation of ion currents and thus membrane channels. Determining how channels function with temporal and genetic change can lead to insight into what process the channels promote in an organism. My research aims to identify the important ion channels present in Drosophila circadian neurons, and ultimately how the channels contribute to driving circadian rhythms. Previous work has indicated an oscillation in the amplitude of a divalent-blocked cation current (DBC) over the course of the 24-hour day. The DBC current in Drosophila, however, still needs further characterization in terms of function and genetic origin. A voltage-gated calcium channel, cacophony (cac), has been suggested as a candidate channel for this current, and a corresponding RNAi line has been created. Investigations of this and other channels in pdf-Gal4:UASmGFP labeled circadian neurons may unveil the connection between the well established circadian clock and its underlying electrical processes. A more complete understanding of how circadian rhythms work will aid in treatments for circadian disorders such jet lag, and shift work sleep disorder, and familial advanced sleep-phase syndrome.

title: Predictive Modeling of Gentrification in the City of Chicago

people.major: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences

abstract: In the past several decades, the City of Chicago has seen an increased amount of neighborhood revitalization known as gentrification. This process was first initiated from the downtown central business district and the lakeshore area, and has continued to spread to varied extents on the North, South, West, Northwest, and Southwest sides of the city. My research attempts to explain the factors behind the spread of gentrification in Chicago: why certain neighborhoods improve while other are left behind. My explanation focuses on a model that includes a particular neighborhood's characteristics, its accessibility to transit, its proximity to downtown, and its spatial relationship to previously gentrified areas. Using logit and multivariate regression analyses and spatial Geographic Information Systems (GIS) models, the results may help predict the neighborhoods that would gentrify next, leading to more informed urban planning and business decisions.

title: The Skinny on Stress: Maternal Psychosocial Stress and Infant Birth Weight in the Philippines
abstract: Low birth weight, a major cause of perinatal mortality and childhood morbidity, has also been linked to increased risk of adult disease and decreased fecundity. The relationship between birth weight and adult health is based on the theory that prenatal nutrition provides the fetus with a cue to its future environment. In response, the fetus adapts its biological settings to this proposed environment. This study evaluates the reliability of fetal growth rate as a nutritional cue by assessing the extent to which maternal psychosocial stress influences birth outcomes in sample of Filipino women and their infants (n=2891). Measures of maternal psychosocial stress from economic stressors, life event stressors, home stressors and work stressors were collected during pregnancy and used to predict weight, length, BMI, and premature birth. For each measure of psychosocial stress, the number of stressors was found to predict a dose-response decrease in birth weight, length, and BMI caused by a combination of decreased fetal growth rate and decreased duration of gestation. After accounting for potential confounders, medium economic stress and high life event stress were found to significantly decrease birth weight. These findings suggest an effect of maternal psychological health on fetal nutrition and could reduce the value of fetal nutrition as a cue of the fetus’s future environment.

title: The Effects of Linguistic Framing on the Apprehension of Spatial Relationships
abstract: This project examines how the visual system represents spatial relationships among a set of objects. Intuitively, we feel that we perceive these relationships just by paying attention to two objects simultaneously. Instead, we tested the possibility that the visual system represents spatial relationships like language does, as an ordered sequence over time. To describe the spatial relations between the objects on your desk, you might say that "the mouse is to the right of the keyboard". The visual system could represent spatial relationships in a similar ordered sequence, by shifting attention toward one object and then the other. We tested this idea by biasing the subject toward one of two colored circles in a display, by phrasing the question as either, "is red to the left of green" or "is green to the right of red?" The question is logically identical, but should induce subjects to structure their perceptual sequence in a given order. We tested the impact of these instructions in one of two ways. First, we asked subjects to judge the left/right relationship between the two circles, while presenting either color slightly before the other in time. If visual relations are judged by simultaneously attending to both objects, then this manipulation should not affect response times. In contrast, observers were faster when the 'target' object of the sentence (e.g., "Is green...") preceded the 'reference' object (e.g., "...of red"), suggesting that visual relations are coded as a sequence. A second study used an electrophysiological marker of attention to passively track shifts of attention during perceptual judgments, and found a congruent pattern of results. Together, these findings suggest that our understanding of spatial relationships in the visual world may rely on a language-like representation.

title: Archaic Greek Poetry and the Book of Job: Perspectives on the Righteous Sufferer
abstract: In the Biblical world where piety is rewarded and sinners are punished, the Book of Job addresses the problems that arise when these roles are confused. But the question of theodicy, why bad things happen to good people, is not exclusive to Judeo-Christian literature. Solon’s fragment 13 and Simonides’s fragment 542, archaic Greek poems from the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, are just two examples of the extensive literary tradition that addresses the problems of divine justice. As such, the conclusions of these two poems are similar to conclusions made by different characters in the Book of Job. In fragment 13, Solon supports a view of justice akin to that of Job’s God: bad behavior is always punished, but good behavior does not guarantee reward because misfortune is a random force. Hence, the best thing that men can do is to minimize their allotted suffering by avoiding reprehensible actions. Meanwhile, in fragment 542, Simonides sees a view of justice like that of Job’s Satan: men are only good as long as the gods continue to bless them. This project compares how each work comes to its respective conclusion regarding divine justice, and how the conclusions themselves differ.

title: Religious Traditions of the Sea Islands in the Immediate Postbellum Period
abstract: In November 1861, Union troops sailed into the Port Royal Sound, quickly defeating the small garrison of Confederate soldiers stationed there. Their target was the sleepy town of Beaufort, a prosperous planters’ locale nestled halfway between Charleston and Savannah, in the Sea Islands of South Carolina. The Union victory accomplished exactly what Lincoln’s administration had intended: following a summer of military defeat, the Port Royal coup stimulated morale among a weary Northern population; the profitable King’s cotton cultivated on the islands surrounding Beaufort temporarily eased the financial woes of a fast-depleting federal treasury; strategically, Port Royal was the largest deep water harbor between Cape Hatteras and Florida. With all the pieces fitting neatly together in this military, political, and economic victory, Lincoln deliberately ignored what, in hindsight, was Port Royal’s most pressing matter: what to do with the 8,000 slaves who now inhabited the otherwise abandoned Sea Islands. In the months that followed, missionaries -- backed by Northern philanthropists -- flocked to the islands aiming to “prepare the islanders for responsible citizenship,” establishing churches and schools in their wake. Over the next three years, until the “project’s” dissolution in 1865, missionary work on the islands thrived. Now known as the Port Royal Experiment, the missionary project has been studied in mostly social terms; effectively, one scholar describes it as a “rehearsal for Reconstruction.” My research sheds light on an unexplored and important element of the Port Royal Experiment: the religious interaction that occurred between the missionaries and the local African Americans. Possessing a uniquely hybrid cultural form -- designated “Gullah” -- that is directly informed by African traditions, the islanders practiced an especially syncretic Christianity, marrying a “white” theological perspective with a distinctly African worldview. Therefore, the period of intense (white) cultural exposure that accompanied the Port Royal Experiment led to notable changes in the islanders’ Gullah religion. My research -- based on ethnographic research conducted on the islands as well as primary texts contained in the University of North Carolina’s archives -- suggests that the religion of the Gullah islanders with whom the missionaries interacted underwent a process of change; specifically, worship rituals and biblical exegesis, no longer “Gullah” in the traditional sense, more closely resembled the Christianity practiced in more mainstream African American churches.

title: Healthy Defenses: How College Women Resist Normative Body Discontent
abstract: While women’s average body weight has increased over the past four decades, cultural beauty ideals have become increasingly thinner (e.g., Owen et al., 2000). Research suggests that this widening gap between actual and ideal body size exacerbates body image disturbance in women (e.g., Bessenoff, 2006). Indeed, women’s dissatisfaction with their bodies is so common it has been termed normative discontent (Rodin et al., 1985). Little research has focused on women who maintain healthy relationships with their bodies. This study explored these women’s perceptions of how their positive attitudes toward their bodies were shaped. One hundred and six participants completed a preliminary survey, and seventeen women who scored below average on standard measures of eating behavior and body dissatisfaction were selected. Fourteen of these women responded to qualitative questions assessing experiences and attitudes affecting their body image. Three coders identified five types of healthy defenses against normative discontent. The most common defenses (26% and 25% of coded responses, respectively) involved women choosing to value other aspects of themselves over their physical appearance or appreciating their body for its functions instead of its appearance. Other common defenses included focusing on positive role models (20%), deliberately rejecting unhealthy choices of close others (15%), and focusing on positive aspects of one’s appearance (13%). The results point to several ways in which women who are healthy and satisfied with their bodies fight an ongoing battle against their culture’s beauty ideals. These findings can point to methods of intervention for women who struggle with body image disturbance.

title: Safekeeping
abstract: Although I intended to write a creative project—a manuscript of poems—about architecture, research led me to investigate an eclectic set of miniatures. By beginning with Susan Stewart’s On Longing and Gaston Bachelard’s The Poetics of Space, I first considered how a miniature functions as a port and haven for greatness. While writing my earlier poems, I realized that although there is a world inside a miniature, miniatures simultaneously coax the viewer into the larger world. My poems address themes once written about by Sylvia Plath and Elizabeth Bishop while examining what and who operate as miniatures. My research fell within three categories: critical works about collection, secondary materials that explored topics specific to individual poems, and books of poetry. Other subsidiary research that influenced my project include an interview with Gregory Johnson, author of Lessons Learned Living in 140 Square Feet; visits to the Thorne Rooms; and children’s novels. Ultimately, I confronted how the novelty-factor of a miniature masks that its world relies upon being dominated. Miniatures require man to be possessive, like a child, and creative, like a god. Poems in this manuscript encapsulate the crises of aging and faith that miniatures mark or inspire. Since miniatures are memorable for their interiority, the manuscript works to collect personal meditations, that appear to rise out of the depths of things, with the hope that the final spectacle will rouse a reader to do the same. It is a call to reflect and to indulge in collection.

title: Identifying Consensus Among Experts as to What the Average Citizen Should Know About the Supreme Court
abstract: Recent analysis of the fifty state social studies standards reveals that such standards vary widely as to the guidelines they set for education relating to the Supreme Court. Such disparities raise concerns about how well and to what extent students in the United States are educated about the important government organizations, an issue that is of critical concern to research related to civic engagement. This study seeks to identify an expert-formed consensus on what the average citizen should know about the Supreme Court in order to better instruct how the Supreme Court is represented in curriculum. Twenty in-depth interviews were completed for this study; ten with law-related education experts, five with Supreme Court scholars, and five with teachers identified as having strong law-related education curriculum. Initial findings suggest that current focus on high-stakes testing may present a significant obstacle to teaching about the Supreme Court in the classroom. Findings further suggest that in deciding what the average citizen should know about the Supreme Court, experts frame cases and issues in terms of historical significance, interest level and cultural literacy. These findings have important implications for the development of more meaningful state standards and the future of civics and law-related education.

title: Aging Effects on Cortical Network Connectivity During Speech Perception in Noise: A Graph Theoretical Analysis
abstract: I apply graph theory to model the functional human cerebral cortex as a network composed of anatomical voxels sharing functional connections or edges. Cerebral hemodynamic (functional) data were taken from a previous study examining effects of aging on speech perception in noise. This analysis tested the hypothesis that younger adults' more accurate speech perception in noise is associated with stronger network connectivity. Edges between voxels were established when the cross-correlation of any two voxel time series exceeded specified thresholds. Global network data including connection density and average path length were calculated, as well as voxel-wise parameters including degree centrality. T-tests were employed to examine age effects on network connectivity measures. Younger subjects were found to possess significantly higher connection density and shorter average path lengths. Nodes of exceptionally high degree were found clustered near the prefrontal cortex, precuneus, insula and auditory cortex, partially overlapping with our previous analysis based on GLM. T-tests revealed that elderly subjects possessed significantly lower degree specifically in the left superior temporal gyrus (STG), including primary auditory cortex. Global differences in connection density and path length suggest a more efficient network in the young cortex during speech perception tasks. The findings agree with behavioral results, which found younger subjects to be significantly more accurate at identifying speech in high levels of noise. The results further suggest that loss of connectivity in preliminary processing areas of LSTG (e.g., auditory cortex) may be a primary factor driving auditory decline in the elderly.

title: Growth and Optical Birefringence Characterization of Silica Aerogel for Use in Superfluid 3He Experiments
abstract: Silica aerogel is an extremely porous material, chemically identical to glass, which has been used in applications ranging from insulation to trapping cosmic dust. One application in which silica aerogel plays an integral role is in the study of condensed matter physics, specifically the study of superfluid 3He. In superfluid 3He, silica aerogel acts as an impurity, allowing an otherwise pure system to better model real, impure systems, such as superconductors. However, silica aerogel growth methods vary widely, and, consequently, could be a cause of inconsistencies in recent experiments. Therefore, the ability to structurally characterize silica aerogels is essential to understanding experimental results. The previous characterization method used, x-ray scattering, is a time-consuming and difficult process. We have developed an efficient and economical method to characterize aerogels – optical birefringence. Optical birefringence is a property of anisotropic materials which cause an incident wave to produce two refracted waves. Though optical birefringence had been used to characterize a variety of materials, it had not been used to characterize silica aerogels. Using this method, easily interpreted, qualitative results for many aerogel samples have been obtained. Additionally, we have developed aerogels of tunable anisotropy using optical birefringence results and improved growth methods. The implementation of these gels in experiments will also be discussed.

title: Cultural and Linguistic Challenges in Patient-Doctor Communication: The Value of the Spanish-English Medical Interpreter
abstract: This research focuses on the role of the Spanish-English medical interpreter in the patient-provider interaction. With the 2008 US Census reporting that 15% of the population is self-identified Hispanic or Latino, a 3.3% increase from the previous year, finding a means to bridge the gaps between belief systems and languages is becoming increasingly important. This is especially important within the United States' healthcare system, where protocol is often strictly defined. The research focuses on the obstacles to successful patient-provider interaction without any language or cultural barrier, with a language or cultural barrier, and how this barrier is bridged through the use of medical interpreters. The research was done through a literary review of previous studies, as well as with a new component consisting of interviews of 10 Spanish-English medical interpreters, 5 each from Chicago and Boston. The study found that interpreters are often expected to fill a broad spectrum of roles, some of which conflict, leaving them in difficult ethical situations. Since there is no national or generally even a state-wide protocol for the training and certification of medical interpreters, there is no standard for the interpreters' role. Through more careful study of the interpreters' role and a more developed organization to train and certify medical interpreters, as well as training of healthcare providers and patients on how to work with interpreters, many of the cultural and linguistic barriers can be overcome, permitting higher quality healthcare for ethnic and linguistic minorities.

title: Ecological Interactions in Multi-Species Biofilms under Imposed Gradients of Fluid Flow and Nutrient Influx
abstract: Most microbes coexist as complex communities: biofilms, and are spatially structured by external flow conditions. In this study, we aimed to explore the relationship between environmental heterogeneity and the spatial structure of well-defined multi-species biofilms. We hypothesized that each member of a multi-species community would colonize regions of the biofilm where local conditions particularly favored its growth. P. aeruginosa (P.a.) and Flavobacterium spp. (F.s.) were chosen to form the multi-species biofilms. A novel planar flow cell was used to support the biofilm growth under highly controlled imposed flow gradients. The spatial structure of the biofilms was characterized using confocal microscopy. Flow patterns were observed using Particle-Tracking Velocimetry and simulated using a Lattice Boltzmann (LB) model. P.a. and F.s. show distinctly different growth rates and ability to adhere to surfaces. P.a. grew distinctly faster than F.s. and dominated the multi-species biofilm in closed batch experiments. However, F.s. dominated the biofilm community under all flow conditions tested in flow-cell experiments. In experiments with slower inflow, F.s. primarily grew in regions with relatively low nutrient influx (local velocities from 0.08 to 0.11 mm/s), while P.a. mainly grew in regions with higher nutrient influx (velocity ~0.16 mm/s). Under faster inflow, F.s. grew extensively throughout the flow cell, and achieved significantly greater biomass than under the slower inflow condition. In this co-culture, P.a. was unexpectedly able to colonize regions of high hydrodynamic shear, up to local velocities of ~0.6 mm/s, by colonizing the base of the F.s. biofilm. The experiments demonstrated that imposed gradients in flow conditions and nutrient influx strongly influence the distribution of F.s. and P.a. in multi-species biofilms. The greater ability of F.s. to adhere to the substratum allowed it to dominate the biofilm under all fluid flow conditions tested even though it grew more slowly than P.a.. Further, the presence of F.s. allowed P.a. to persist in high-shear regions where P.a. was unable to grow on its own.

title: The Relationship Between the Media and Congressional Action: The Case of International Child Labor
abstract: Across the globe, 200 million child laborers work long hours in egregious conditions producing goods for the mass market. National news media occasionally run stories about child laborers, shocking the conscience of the American public and calling for reform. My research focuses on the relationship between media attention to international child labor and United States Government (USG) attention and action to the issue. Previous research explored the ability of media to influence USG attention and action; however, the literature never addressed the issue of international child labor, reached little consensus evaluating media effectiveness at shaping the political agenda and failed to resolve questions of directionality in the government-media relationship. The present investigation examined the role of the national news media in shaping congressional discourse and policy action about international child labor issues utilizing a 20 year time series analysis. The investigation found significant increases in media mentions of international child labor issues preceded congressional action over 80 percent of time. Although clearly influential, the news media was only one of many factors which helped get international child labor on the congressional agenda from 1989-2008. The present investigation also examined the role of legislative entrepreneurs and the relationship between the actions of said entrepreneurs and the news media. My study concluded media attention played a significant role in getting international child labor on the U.S. policy agenda by creating the policy windows in which legislative entrepreneurs took action.

title: Selective Incentives and Green Leveraging: Explaining Metropolitan Commitment to Climate Change Policy
abstract: This project investigates the varying level of commitment to climate change mitigation policy by the fifty largest cities in the U.S. Using regression analysis and a collection of original data on city sustainability, I explore the ways in which urban form, civic capacity, and existing emission levels effect commitment to climate change mitigation. Surprisingly, I find that urban form and physical infrastructure is the single statistically significant determinant of climate-positive policy. I hypothesize that political processes use existing urban form coupled with climate policy as a lever to garner both economic and political selective benefits in individual metros.

title: Neural Correlates of Emotion in Young Children
abstract: Current research supports a two-dimensional model of affect in which emotions are said to be varying degrees along two different dimensions. Central among these theories is Russell’s (1980) circumplex model, positing that emotions are arranged in a circle around two basic neurophysiological systems or dimensions—Pleasantness versus Unpleasantness (valence), and Activation or Arousal. Watson and colleagues (1999) refined this model and termed the dimensions Positive Affect (PA) and Negative Affect (NA). These independent dimensions are related to the Behavioral Activation System and the Behavioral Inhibition System of motivation, respectively, and are differentially related to the experience of different emotions. The BAS is associated with PA and anger, whereas the BIS is associated with NA. Research suggests that when an individual experiences different emotions, a lateralization of brain activity occurs depending on the emotions’ motivational components and valence. Activation of the left prefrontal cortex is correlated with PA and anger (BAS) whereas activation of the right prefrontal cortex is correlated with NA (BIS). These findings are replicated in a number of EEG studies that examined adults during states of rest. The present study examines the neural correlates of emotions in three-year-old children during active emotion-eliciting tasks. Participants completed six structured tasks while a near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) machine recorded the changes in blood flow in the left and right prefrontal cortex. The design of this study allows us to temporally compare the experience of different emotions to the activation of the left and right prefrontal cortex. Furthermore, this study examines the correlates of emotionality in children in order to gain insight into the development between emotions and the activation of specific brain structures as observed in adults.

title: Examining the Effects of Predator Exclusion Structures Associated with Geoduck Aquaculture on Mobile Benthic Macrofauna in South Puget Sound, Washington
abstract: Intertidal aquaculture of geoduck clams (Panopea abrupta) is a rapidly expanding industry in Puget Sound, Washington, yet little is known about the ecological impacts of disturbances associated with geoduck operations. This study examined the effects of predator exclusion structures associated with geoduck aquaculture on mobile benthic macrofauna in South Puget Sound, Washington. Species abundance and diversity were assessed on both structured and unstructured habitats; surveys revealed significantly more graceful crab (Cancer gracilis) on unstructured habitats, and significantly more Pacific staghorn sculpin (Leptocottus armatus) on structured habitats. Dietary patterns of L. armatus occupying both habitats were evaluated in relation to tide level. Stomachs of L. armatus were significantly more full on ebbing than flooding tides for both habitats, suggesting that sculpin migrate into intertidal areas to forage. However, results for small sculpin (52-81 mm TL) were equivocal, and these fish may use the complex structured habitat for refuge in addition to foraging. A significant difference in prey composition was observed between habitats, which is attributed to increased variability of prey on the structured habitat. Infaunal polychaetes were the main prey in unstructured habitats, while sculpin consumed more epibenthic gammarids in structured habitats. Predator exclusion structures used in geoduck aquaculture appear to alter the composition of macrofaunal communities relative to unstructured areas and affect the dietary patterns of L. armatus.

title: American Literature’s Global Circulation
abstract: My project examines the contemporary translation, re-interpretation, and reception of post-World War II American fiction in Western Europe, the Maghreb, India, and China. The project uses this information to paint a picture of America’s contemporary global image. In this way, my research re-examines America’s place in an increasingly globalized world through the re-publication and reception of some of its most widely read postwar stories. Analyzed works include The Catcher in the Rye (J.D. Salinger), On The Road (Jack Kerouac), Goodbye, Columbus, and The Human Stain (Philip Roth). Through a close reading of these novels’ international editions (cover art, introductions, notes) and evidence drawn from a series of interviews with international publishers and booksellers, this project examines American culture’s international promulgation through a literary lens.
