Research for this project was conducted during a three-month around-the-world trip (June to September, 2008) funded by the Circumnavigators Club Foundation, during which I interviewed numerous publishing executives and booksellers, in addition to visiting various international book fairs and literary festivals. Upon returning from my travels through Western Europe, Morocco, Tunisia, India, and China, I completed a sixty-eight-page report and delivered a speech on my research results to the Circumnavigators Club. Interview questions for publishers, booksellers, and consumers of fiction included: 1. How do you choose which American texts to translate? Which works are most frequently translated and/or re-published? 2. Which work of post-World War II American literature would you consider most popular in your country right now? Or, if not a specific work, which author? 3. What is your favorite American novel? How has it changed your view of America? The answers to these questions, along with a close reading of international editions of originally American texts, point toward certain international views of America, and the ways these views differ from one another.

title: The Dialectic Between Moral and Medical Models of Drug Addiction: An Exploratory Study
abstract: The problem of drug use within the United States is incredibly detrimental to society and especially to those persons, families, and friends directly involved. My research aims to elucidate one of the results of such a problem: the general public's varying views on drug addiction itself. Why do some people hold punitive views towards drug addicts while others are more tolerant? I am closely examining the dynamic found within such varying viewpoints, which is that of the dialectic between the moral and medical models of addiction. To find answers to the question of why some people hold punitive rather than tolerant views toward drug addicts I used a sample of Northwestern University students (located in Evanston, IL) and distributed an online survey (N=248). Using various descriptive statistics I was able to determine some of the reasons for such an attitudinal divide. The independent variables I looked at most closely were direct contact with drug users, direct contact with drug addicts, religiosity, media influence and the framing of questions. Each of these variables showed varying levels of significance in regard to the dependent variable, attitudes toward drug addiction. Some of the basic premises on which my results fell can be found by looking at some of the concepts in social psychological theory, in particular that of exposure effect. Also, the role of consistency in attitude formation, media effects theory and framing theory coupled with the expertise heuristic are considered as explanatory frameworks.

title: Fabrication and Assembly of Nanopyramids
abstract: This project focuses on a new class of nanomaterials with 3D shapes—nanoscale pyramids made via a top-down, nanofabrication approach. These noble metal nanopyramids (NPs) have been observed to cluster into groups of different particle numbers. By dispersing these particles at varying concentrations in diverse solvents, functionalizing them with different ligands, and controlling the conditions of evaporation, we investigated the parameters affecting the self assembly of NPs. We found that clusters of increasing particle number can be formed by greater NP concentration in solution, slower rate of solvent evaporation, and increasing hydrophobicity of the substrate. This assembly can be explained by colloidal aggregation theory and van der Waals (VDW) interactions. This work is significant because the versatile fabrication method allows for a thorough investigation of the parameters governing the assembly of NPs during evaporation, giving control of self assembly on the nanoscale.

title: Comparison of Contraceptive Use in Rural Guangdong Province with the Effect After Migration to the United States
abstract: While the Chinese government's “One Child Policy” (OCP) is one of the most debatable human experiments, many have yet to expose its effect on contraception usage and understanding in rural areas of China. One of the most problematic provinces today is Guangdong, the fifth largest province, where, within 10 months of 2006, 4823 new HIV cases were reported, raising the total to over 40,000. This semi-structured interview-based study is concentrated in rural Guangdong, with purposive sampling adopted to optimize the quality of the findings. From a total of 55 participants (~95% women), 25 in-person in-depth interviews were conducted with U.S. emigrants from Guangdong and 30 were interviews with current residents in the rural areas. All persons interviewed stated that this was the first time they had talked openly about contraception and associated topics. However, despite this lack of discussion, they shared many common views about knowledge of contraception, opinions about OCP policy, and willingness to talk about intercourse. Their willingness to talk appears to have a positive correlation with how far they lived from Chinese rural areas. Abstinence is the predominant method used in prevention because other methods of contraception, such as IUDs, carry negative connotations. Most interviewees in rural China failed to acknowledge the role contraception plays in HIV/AIDS prevention. This study shows a demand for improved dialogue about modern contraception in rural Guangdong. Immigrants to the U.S. suggested further research and methods for counteracting the taboos regarding contraceptive practice and HIV/AIDS.

title: Tracing the Estrogen Receptor Alpha Signaling Pathway Controlling Hot Flashes
abstract: Hot flashes are one of the most common and severe complaints of peri- and post-menopausal women. Previous studies have shown that the drop in estrogen levels associated with menopause is responsible for the disruption in normal thermoregulatory patterns. Using two genetically modified mouse strains, the current study investigated the role of the estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) in modulating thermoregulatory patterns through different signaling pathways: the classical pathway, which requires binding of the estrogen-estrogen receptor complex to an estrogen response element (ERE) on DNA, and non-classical pathway which is ERE-independent. The first mouse strain contained a knockout mutation for the gene encoding the estrogen receptor alpha (the ERαKO mouse). The second strain was the non-classical estrogen receptor knock-in mouse (NERKI, which is an ERα null mutant mouse bearing a mutant ERα containing a deactivated DNA-binding region of the ERα. Estrogen in this NERKI mouse exerts its effects mainly through non-classical ERα signaling. In the present experiment adult mice were housed on a 12L:12D photoperiod and fed a low phytoestrogen diet. Tail skin temperature (TST) and locomotor activity were recorded using G2 eMitters and Vital View Software (MiniMitter Inc., Bend, OR) for eight mice from each genotype (wild type (WT, ERαKO, and NERKI). Data were recorded for 1 week prior to ovariectomy. At the time of surgery 4 females of each genotype were given a silastic capsule with 2.5 μg 17β-estradiol (OVX+E); 4 were given a blank capsule (OVX+C). The experiment was divided into two replicates; 4 mice of each genotype were tested in each replicate. Significant differences were found among the three genotypes (Repeated measures ANOVA, main effects of genotype, time, and interaction between genotype and time, all p < 0.001). Elimination of ERα signaling resulted in a modest increase in average TST over 24 hrs in intact mice (WT 26.5 o F vs ERαKO 26.9o F) which was reduced by the NERKI mutation (26.6o F). However, averaging TST over 24 hr masks differences in the daily patterns of TST. Deletion of ERα reduces the amplitude of the day-night difference in TST (WT 1.4 o F vs. 1.1 o F ERαKO); the NERKI mutation restores the day night difference in temperature (NERKI 1.7 o F). Furthermore, the three different genotypes showed a significant difference with regards to the effect of ovariectomy and estrogen replacement (Repeated measures ANOVA, main treatment effects and interaction for genotype, treatment and time; all p < 0.001). The results of this study suggest that estrogen signaling via the non-classical ERalpha signaling pathway plays a significant role in thermoregulation. Supported provided by an UGRF from NU to JKT and AG030181 to JEL and THH.

title: Investigations into the Efficacy and Specificity of MRI Contrast Agents
abstract: The magnetic properties of biological tissues allow for in vivo imaging via magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Over 30% of the MR examinations performed in the U.S. include specialized organo-metallic compounds known as contrast agents to provide heightened image resolution. These MR agents utilize the paramagnetic qualities of the gadolinium(III) ion [Gd(III)] to shorten the time for nuclear spin relaxation (T1) in water protons following magnetic excitation. A reduction in T1 is interpreted by imagers as increased brightness and a higher degree of contrast between localized areas. The following work represents a two-year investigation into improving the efficacy of Gd-based agents as well as developing a cell permeable agent capable of selective contrast enhancement. The former study analyzed the parameters governing the effectiveness of these compounds in reducing T1. These parameters include the available number of water coordination sites on the Gd(III) chelate as well as its rotational correlation time—the speed at which the molecule rotates in its environment. These properties and their effects on water relaxation were studied via the synthesis of benzene-derived, multimeric contrast agents. The results obtained from these novel, multi-Gd(III) compounds revealed a direct relationship between the rate of molecular rotation and relaxivity. The effects of water coordination on T1, however, were less clear and demonstrated an interesting trend. In addition to investigating the efficacy of Gd(III) agents, work was also done on improving cell permeability in a calcium-sensitive agent. A modification of the existing structure has been determined and its synthetic route reported here.

title: Casements
abstract: My senior thesis is a novella told through the unified voices of five children who have been abandoned by their mother. I used an infrequently-explored narrative technique—the plural “we” narrator—to examine ideas of inhabiting a body, character interaction, and observation. From their cloistered, fifth-floor apartment, the children observe three characters as their actions begin to intertwine. The characters lose control of their fate as their lives—symbolized by windows—fall apart. By the end of the novella, the existence of the five narrators is inexorably linked with the people they have been watching. There is something inherently unnerving about the plural voice. The novella emphasizes this chilling, mysterious quality by characterizing the narrators: their situation, their past, the torturous nature of their surroundings, and ultimately, whether or not they inhabit physical bodies. The conundrum of good and evil is examined: can morality transcend corporeal existence? My narrative strategy proved technically difficult, since the main characters are seen only through the narrators, and so their histories and thoughts can be revealed only if the narrators are aware of and deign to reveal them. Reading and research focused on three primary themes: the concept of interconnected narratives, the nature of evil, and classic works of magic realism. I also researched a city-setting for the work. The novella achieved a sense of reality by being situated on a street corner in Bucktown. Grounding the magic realism of the story in this way proved effective—a specific location lent believability to the most fantastical elements.

title: Urinary Bladder Regeneration Utilizing Mesenchymal Stem Cells Seeded onto Elastomeric Thin Films
abstract: Acquired or developmental disorders affecting urinary bladder function leads to a myriad of pathological conditions, even with advances in surgical intervention. Previous studies have yielded inconclusive results due to inappropriate cell types and primitive scaffold design. An alternative using bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) addresses this shortcoming: MSCs may be transdifferentiated into bladder wall components, suitable for bladder regeneration studies, when combined with poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) thin films (POCf). POCf is a highly reproducible elastomeric material capable of being used as a synthetic scaffold. Human MSCs/Urotsa (an immortalized urothelial cell line), and bladder smooth muscle cells (bSMCs)/Urotsa were seeded on opposing sides of POCfs at 15K cells/cm2, cultured for 1 week. Cell viability was determined in vitro up to 21 days post-seeding. A 30% bladder cystectomy was created in a nude rat bladder augmention model and repaired with the aforementioned cell seeded POCfs or unseeded POCfs enveloped with an omentum. Rats were sacrificed 4 weeks post-implantation and augmented bladders were paraffin embedded for Masson’s Trichrome and anti-human g-tubulin staining. in vitro MSC viability at day 1 and 21 post-seeding was >98% on POCfs. Rat bladders augmented with an MSC/Urotsa seeded POCf grew to thickness levels greater than a comparably seeded cSMC/Urotsa POCf. Collagen to muscle ratio was also comparable between MSC and SMC groups. g-tubulin staining of the MSC/Urotsa POCfs indicated that cell outgrowth was of human origin as also seen with directly labeled cSMCs. Data gathered from this study demonstrate that MSCs, paired with synthetic POCfs, support the regeneration of bladder tissue in vivo.

title: Feasibility of Ovarian Cryopreservation as a Fertility Preservation Method for Patients with Ovarian Malignancies: A Histological Assessment
abstract: With the advent of chemotherapy and other fertility-threatening cancer preventatives, ovarian cryopreservation has arisen as a novel method for fertility preservation in women. Although ovarian cryopreservation has been successful in many cases of cancer, little work has been done to study the effectiveness of cryopreservation in patients with ovarian cancer or other ovarian malignancies. In these cases, effectiveness of cryopreservation may be dependent upon the size of the patient's follicle pool prior to treatment. The objective of this retrospective study was to determine the follicular densities of 55 ovarian mass patients (mean age 34.5+/- 6.5 SD). Patients were diagnosed by pathological analysis as having one of the following: borderline tumor (n=10), BRCA1 mutation (n=12) cystadenoma (n=13), dermoid (n=10), or ovarian cancer (n=10). Follicular densities were used to determine whether ovarian cryopreservation would be an effective fertility preservation method for each malignancy. Patients diagnosed as BRCA1 positive or possessing dermoids had the highest median follicular density (10.43 & 8.64), and most follicles appeared healthy. More irregular follicles and lower follicular densities were found in borderline tumor and cystadenoma ovaries (1.4 & 4.56). Patients diagnosed with ovarian cancer possessed few follicles (0.27), and many were unhealthy. Based on our findings, ovarian cryopreservation would be most beneficial to BRCA1 mutation or dermoid patients as they possess the most follicles. Patients with borderline tumors or cystadenoma should receive individual analysis before a decision for or against cryopreservation is made. Because few follicles remain in the ovaries of ovarian cancer patients, ovarian cryopreservation would not be an effective fertility preservation measure for these patients.

title: Ivy League Mimicry, Selectivity Pressures, and Opaque Admissions Policy: The Jewish Admissions Quota at Northwestern
abstract: The Jewish quotas practiced by institutions of elite American higher education, including Northwestern University, in the 20th century are not a mere historical anomaly of a bygone era; instead, they are a telling historical example of how discrimination in college admissions reflected broader social mores and institutional pressures. My project explores how and why Northwestern chose to institute a Jewish quota, investigates the people involved explicitly and complicity with enforcing the quota, and offers an understanding of the events which contributed to the ultimate unraveling of the quota. The genesis for the Northwestern Jewish quota began as an institutional response to aspirational selectivity pressures coupled with a desire to attract a diverse applicant pool of talented students, albeit through a less codified quota than those implemented by Ivy League peers. The following questions are raised and addressed in my research. How did the institutional religious climate of Northwestern contribute to the quota? What factors, such as selectivity pressures, led to the quota's development at Northwestern? Was the quota formalized in writing or an informal policy? How did the exclusion of Jews extend from the admissions quota into student life, including access to the Greek system? Why did the quota come to an abrupt end in 1963? Can the legacy of the Jewish quotas be instructive to current admission policies which seek selectivity— such as affirmative action and legacy preference—in higher education? The answers to these questions illuminate a cloudy chapter of the history of Northwestern and American higher education.

title: Corporate Characteristics and Boycott Success
abstract: Social movement scholars traditionally posit that boycotters successfully force corporations to alter their behavior or policies through the strength of their movement, their strategy, and/or the political environment in which the boycott occurs. These models downplay the importance of corporate characteristics and the industrial context within which their target organization is situated, instead arguing that when a sufficient amount of external pressure is applied, corporations will make a relatively predictable choice to avoid a loss of profits and a decline in reputation. However, in attempting to precisely map how and why this cost-benefit decision-making occurs, economists and others drawing on an understanding of corporate social responsibility and political economy models have argued that a variety of corporate and industry characteristics can drive and affect the decision to change behavior. This study expands the effort to contextualize the managerial behavior of corporate executives beyond simple cost–benefit analysis by examining whether sources of instability within the corporation or its industry play a significant role in determining the outcome of boycotts. Ultimately, utilizing a dataset of 91 boycotts waged against publicly traded companies between 1996 and 2005, this study shows that corporate characteristics such as the number of recently experienced position shifts and growth opportunities have little effect on the likelihood of capitulation, however companies which experience a high number of controversies and industry wide threats are less likely to capitulate to boycotts.

title: Body Business: Power Through Prostitution in Eighteenth-Century Paris
abstract: Eighteenth-century France witnessed an influx of young single women migrating to Paris in search of work in a labor market that quickly became oversaturated; they were left with no choice but to turn to prostitution, either periodically or permanently, to survive. A substantial portion of the estimated 40,000 prostitutes in the capital worked out of brothels under the supervision of a madam. My project, based on a summer of research in police records stored at the Archives de la Bastille in Paris, argues that the madam occupied a unique position of power in eighteenth-century France. The Bastille documents are more than simple arrest records. Indeed, eighteenth-century Paris witnessed an information-gathering craze in which police gathered comprehensive information reports on various segments of the population; for prostitutes these included anecdotes describing daily events, habits, appearance, requests, clientele, and conversation, as well as short biographies of women. A close examination of the madam is absent from the literature on both eighteenth-century prostitution and female power-wielders. My project fills a void in these literatures by arguing that the madam is different from other powerful women because she does not work in a hierarchy with men and her power was not granted to her by men; moreover, she does not draw on her femininity as the basis of her authority, but rather finds legitimacy for her power in her status as an ungendered professional businessperson. She uses her power to blur lines of social status and control the bodies of both men and women.

title: The Problematic Nature of Treatment Compliance Among Mexican and Mexican-American Type 2 Diabetics: Does Culture Arbitrate Compliance Status?
abstract: Already disproportionately affected by diabetes, Mexican and Mexican-Americans also exhibit a high frequency of diabetes treatment noncompliance. Overall noncompliance among this population is routinely placed at 40% with noncompliance rates well over 60% for diet and exercise recommendations (Hernandez-Roquillo 2003; Bonds 2003). In order to help prevent the development of macro-vascular and micro-vascular complications, the factors influencing these high rates of noncompliance must be thoroughly investigated. In an effort to discern the cultural context of diabetes care among this community in-depth ethnographic interviews were collected from a total of 18 Mexican and Mexican-American type 2 diabetics. These interviews reveal that among this population there is a highly social facet ascribed to the diabetes treatment experience that is notably incongruent with the widely prescribed biomedical models of diabetes treatment. This is a model of health care that fundamentally privileges the individual and not the family and social unit of which that individual is a part. For a community in which familial goals and familial wellbeing are routinely emphasized and prioritized, however, this incongruence presents the diabetic with a serious dilemma. Individual health goals routinely find themselves contending with familial health goals. This project investigates the individual health implications of this dilemma. It also explores the possibility that instead of the individual lifestyle modification strategies described in the US type 2 diabetes mellitus management model, family and community influence can serve as a salient tool for the medical professional to modify management approaches to diet and exercise so that compliance can be improved in these areas.

title: Are the Wealthy Also Born Healthy? Stereotypes about Mental Health, Physical Disfigurement and Socioeconomic Status
abstract: Stigmas regarding high and low socioeconomic status (SES) in America dictate how individuals are treated and affect perceptions of their social and practical skills and abilities. Past research, focusing almost exclusively on adults, has demonstrated that both mental health and physical appearance are associated with public perceptions of an individual’s SES. Those labeled as mentally ill or perceived as physically unattractive are often assumed to have lower SES than their healthy and attractive counterparts. The present study examined whether these same patterns and social perceptions of SES extended to children afflicted with mental disorders or physical unattractiveness, and their families. Do these stigmas take effect early in life, and are these associations also made with children’s families? Assessing family SES may indicate whether participants believe it is the social environment (e.g., family living conditions, financial stability, and household structure) that is to blame for these conditions. Participants were shown picture profiles of elementary school children afflicted with a mental disorder (Autism), a mental condition with a physical component (Down’s syndrome), physical unattractiveness (facial disfigurement), and no condition—the control (healthy children). Then, participants completed a measure of questions indirectly assessing SES. Participants consistently perceived the child with a facial disfigurement to have a lower family SES than healthy children and children with both mental conditions. The results suggest that facial disfigurement is associated with family SES, and participants may attribute its presence to social environments. Children with mental health conditions were less stigmatized and perceived to be of higher family SES.

title: Helping Hands: Gesture and Spatial Learning
abstract: This study explores the relationship between gesturing and spatial learning. We asked: Can story content elicit spontaneous gesture? How does gesture relate to recall accuracy about a space? Does being encouraged to gesture affect recall accuracy? Subjects in Experiment 1 read either a high-spatial (described locations of landmarks and routes) or a low-spatial story (did not include spatial relationships between locations). Results indicated that participants who read the high-spatial story gestured significantly more than the low-spatial story subjects. Experiment 2 tested whether gestures affected reasoning and problem solving. Subjects read the high-spatial story. They were then asked route (“walking north, the school is on your right.”) and survey questions (“the Store is north of the school.”). Subjects spontaneously gestured more while answering route questions, suggesting that gesture is particularly important in the processing and recall of route information. Experiment 3 tested effects of encouraging (or discouraging) gesture while learning spatial information. Subjects were placed in an Encouraged, Discouraged, or a No Instructions condition. They read a spatial story and were then asked route, survey, and non-inference questions. Both the encouraged gesture subjects and discouraged gesture subjects more accurately answered route and survey questions than the No Instructions group. The study of gesture is important because it complements speech, facilitates understanding, and promotes spatial cognition. Currently, an analysis of the size, type, and dimension of gesture is also being performed. Such information can prove to be valuable in determining what particular types of gesture allow people to better learn spatial information.

title: The Institutionalized Role of NGOs in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
abstract: The Convention on the Rights of the Child includes a unique prescribed institutionalized role for Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) that is absent from the eight other United Nations human rights treaties. Many researchers focus on the struggle NGOs face trying to access meetings and most focus on the effect of NGOs on State Parties’ commitments. There is a gap, however, in identifying the causal factors that lead to the creation of a role for NGOs in the convention text. My thesis focuses on two conventions where NGOs played a role during the drafting process. The first is the Convention on the Rights of the Child where NGOs held a permanent spot at the discussions, resulting in their inclusion in the Convention text and reporting process. I argue that because these NGOs advocate for such a vulnerable and politically-neutral population, States Parties would face negative repercussions if they tried to exclude them. A streamlined process for NGO input to the reporting process was created, a status I call an “institutionalized role for NGOs.” The second case, the Convention Against Torture, offers a contrast as NGOs were similarly vocal during the drafting process but were not included in the final text because they were excluded from the drafting sessions altogether. NGOs trying to access existing or future conventions would be able to save valuable resources and would greatly benefit from identifying those factors. Using primary and secondary sources, the study examines the drafting processes and final texts before offering an in-depth contextual analysis.

title: Measures of Dysfunctional Cognition in Depressed Individuals as a Function of Stressful Life Events
abstract: In the study of the clinical etiology of depression, one prominent cognitive theory posits that individuals who have an underlying cognitive vulnerability to depression (e.g. high levels of dysfunctional attitudes) who also experience a stressful life event are at increased risk for developing depression relative to those without such attitudes. Dysfunctional attitudes are rigid, extreme, and counterproductive thoughts such as “If everyone doesn’t love me, then my life is worthless” and “It’s hopeless because things will always be this way” (e.g. Weissman and Beck, 1978). Furthermore, it is theorized that stressful life events activate cognitive vulnerabilities and contribute to the onset of depression. The present study investigates dysfunctional cognition using data from the ongoing Youth Emotion Project by examining changes in measures of dysfunctional attitudes as a function of life stress and depression status. Dysfunctional Attitudes Scale (DAS) scores are compared at three time points for two groups of individuals who experienced a depressive episode: those with a stressful life event within three months prior to onset, and those without such an event. Consistent with previous findings by Monroe et al. (2007), depressed individuals with major stress should exhibit a more marked increase in dysfunctional attitudes between baseline and a current depressive episode and a more marked decrease between a current episode and follow-up. Conversely, individuals without major life events pre-onset should show less pronounced increases in these patterns of cognitive vulnerability between the first and second time points as well as steep declines in dysfunctional attitudes at follow-up.

title: Gandhian Philosophy Turns 100: Nonviolent Resistance in the 21st Century
abstract: In 1909, Mohandas K. Gandhi published his manifesto Hind Swaraj (Indian Self-Rule), where he sets forth the principle of nonviolent resistance upon which he would eventually lead India to its independence from the British Raj. Yet Gandhi was assassinated soon after independence and his vision was never fully realized. Today, many of the problems he worked to eliminate continue to plague India and most of the post-colonial world. My research looks to Dr. Vandana Shiva and Satish Kumar, contemporary "Gandhians" who carry on the Mahatma's legacy through their work on international agricultural policy, environmental education, and human rights. Though they have received much international coverage, little attention has been given to their Gandhian roots. While in India, I conducted extensive interviews with Shiva and Kumar at Bija Vidyapeeth, Shiva's farm-based institute for science, technology, and ecology. They discussed Gandhi's perennial philosophy and, in particular, illuminated the meaning of "Hind Swaraj." "Self-rule," they believe, refers to a continuum from the individual to the society. In the face of climate change, food shortages, and economic devastation, Gandhi would have urged us not to feel powerless or exterior to the solution. Rather, he shows us that to reform a community, an institution, or even an entire country, the individual must begin by reforming him or herself through contemplation and action. Mahatma Gandhi, Dr. Shiva and Satish Kumar show us that embodiment of our values - being the change - is an imperative for anyone concerned about the state of the world today.

title: Associations Between Self-Report and Observational Lab Measures in Personality Traits of Parents
abstract: Previous research suggests that there are associations between the personality traits of parents and children. Research investigating such associations through parent-child temperament studies furthers our understanding of personality development. However, most of these studies rely exclusively on self-report measures of personality and temperament. The aim of the study is to test whether findings from questionnaire methods are consistent with these from observational lab measures of personality. I investigated specific associations between self-report measures and observational lab measures in parent personality. I also examined the stability of parent personality in a marital interaction compared to a parent-child interaction. Observational lab measures included objective coding. Coders viewed the behavior of parents who participated in a study on child temperament. Prior to lab visits, both parents filled out self-report questionnaires assessing Big Five and abnormal personality traits. Coders viewed either the marital interaction or the parent-child interaction that took place during the lab visit. Based on these rather large slices of behavior, coders rated each parent on a Big Five inventory and a questionnaire measuring psychopathological personality traits. Analyses will focus on the degree of association across measures for the Big Five traits of Extraversion, Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to Experience.

title: Progesterone-Induced Blocking Factor (PIBF) is a Novel Interacting Protein with the NR5A Family of Orphan Nuclear Receptors
abstract: In the female reproductive cycle, inhibin made in the ovary inhibits follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in the anterior pituitary gland in a negative feedback loop to keep FSH from continuing to stimulate follicle growth. Inhibin is a dimeric protein made of an α and β subunit. In the inhibin-α promoter, two related nuclear factors, steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1) and liver receptor homologue-1 (LRH-1), compete for the same binding site to activate the gene. These are orphan members of the nuclear receptor superfamily, subfamily NR5A. An LRH-1 specific interacting protein, progesterone induced blocking factor-1 (PIBF-1), was identified in a yeast two hybrid screen of a human ovary library using the ligand binding domain of LRH-1 as the bait. In this study, PIBF-1 is shown to have the greatest interaction with the ligand binding domain of LRH-1 compared to the other domains of the protein, including the N-terminal domain. Further experiments show that PIBF-1 is expressed in the rat ovary in the nucleus of transfected cells. I was particularly interested in determining whether the physical interaction of LRH-1 and PIBF-1 had a functional consequence on the ability of LRH-1 to regulate inhibin gene expression. Using the inhibin-α promoter fused to a luciferase reporter gene, it is shown that PIBF-1 coactivates LRH-1, but not as much as it coactivates the related protein, SF-1. A known LRH-1 coactivator, SRC-1, was used in a GAL4 activation assay as a positive control in order to compare its transcriptional activities with that of PIBF-1; PIBF-1 does not activate LRH-1 mediated transcription in this assay as strongly as does SRC-1. PIBF-1 strongly interacts with LRH-1, but more experiments will be required to determine if it functions as a transcriptional coactivator.

title: A Simple and Fast Test to Determine X Chromosome Number by MLPA
abstract: Fragile X Syndrome is caused by an expansion of a trinucleotide repeat sequence in the 5’ untranslated region of the FMR1 gene. This expansion results in hypermethylation of this region and shuts down expression of this gene which results in the characteristic phenotype. The ‘gold standard’ test for detection of this expansion remains Southern blot hybridization. However, Southern Blot is time consuming and costly so many clinical laboratories screen patients by polymerase chain reaction first and reserve Southern blot hybridization for those patients in which normal size repeat regions cannot be confirmed. However, to use this approach, the number of FMR1 genes has to be known. Females normally have 2 X chromosomes and therefore 2 gene copies, whereas males normally have one copy. However, some females may have 3 or more X chromosomes (e.g. 47, XXX female) and some males may have 2 or more X chromosomes (47, XXY male or Kleinfelter’s Syndrome). Therefore it is essential to have another method to determine the number of X chromosomes (and more specifically, the number of FMR1 genes). We have developed a test based on a technique called multiplex ligation probe amplification that is designed to determine the number of X chromosome copies as well as the number of FMR1 gene copies. This test is accurate, simple and cost-effective. We have validated this test for clinical use in conjunction with PCR for FMR1 expansion mutation.

title: Not Your Grandma's Debate: Public Forum and its Role in the Forensics Community
abstract: A style of interscholastic debate called “Policy Debate” has always been a prominent high school extracurricular activity. It has been shown to increase academic achievement, critical thinking skills, and self-confidence in high schoolers, among other benefits. However, as Policy Debate has become more fast-paced and laden with archaic terms, participation numbers have dwindled. An alternative form of debate called “Public Forum Debate” was introduced in the early part of this decade, and though it has gained popularity, some Policy enthusiasts are reluctant to support this “lesser” form of debate. This study examines this bias by seeking to understand how students and coaches conceive of their experiences with Public Forum. I surveyed over 50 Public Forum debaters and 70 debate coaches about the benefits and drawbacks they attribute to Public Forum. Many different suggestions emerged, but there was a consensus that Public Forum functions best when it does not deviate from its design: forcing students to speak slowly, accepting a wide variety of research sources, and only allowing lay judges to moderate the contests. This result is significant because it implies that Public Forum Debate can be just as beneficial as Policy Debate, given the right circumstances. It also suggests that, if participation in debate is ever going to increase (especially among low-income students and other non-traditional debaters), then Public Forum should be promoted as a simpler entry-point into the activity.

title: The Effect of Hospital Ownership Conversion on Surrounding Hospitals

people.major: Mathematical Methods in the Social Sciences

abstract: As primary providers of health services, the hospital industry is a critical component of the United States’ health care system. Hospitals can be classified based on their ownership type: for-profit or not-for-profit. While not-for-profit hospitals provide a significant source of charitable care to local communities under favorable tax incentives, for-profit hospitals have induced greater efficiency and have greater access to capital through stocks. The competitive nature of the hospital industry has subjected hospitals to financial pressures that force them to undergo conversion in order to remain sustainable amidst the changing health care market. Between 1985 and 1999, over 700 hospitals have changed their ownership status; these conversions have raised public concerns, particularly conversions from not-for-profit to for-profit. Most of the previous research has focused on the difference between for-profit and not-for-profit hospitals and on the effect of ownership conversion on the converted hospital itself. The results have contributed to changes in government regulations on conversions. However, no empirical study has examined the effect on rival hospitals. In this research, I have analyzed how hospital ownership conversions have affected the surrounding hospitals, where surrounding hospitals are determined using the fixed-radius approach. In particular, I have investigated the changes in financial performance and uncompensated care of the surrounding hospitals. Public policy implications of this research include reevaluation of state regulatory standards to account for effects of conversion on the performance of the entire market rather than the performance of individual hospitals.

title: Unraveling Musical Training's Impact on Neural Mechanisms of Selective Auditory Attention
abstract: Musical practice and performance requires the ability to pay attention to a specific melody or harmony line in the presence of other simultaneous competing lines. Musicians’ abilities to perceive specifics in music transfer to their abilities in speech. Although musicians have enhanced auditory attention abilities, the neural underpinnings of this enhancement are uncertain. To determine how musical training impacts neural indices of selective auditory attention, we recorded cortical auditory-evoked potentials to simultaneous attended and ignored acoustic streams in adult musicians (n=11) and non-musicians (n=11), ages 18-32. Participants attended to one of two simultaneously-occurring stories, which differed in speaker voice, direction of presentation and story content, while ignoring the competing story. A 32 channel electrode cap recorded neural responses to the speech stimulus /da/, which was embedded in the stories and alternated between the attended and ignored ears. This paradigm produced average neural responses to both the attended and ignored speech streams, which could then be compared within and across subjects. Although musicians and non-musicians performed the task equally well, musicians demonstrate a decreased impact of attention on cortical responses to the speech stimulus, compared to non-musicians. Specifically, musicians demonstrate a decreased negative amplitude 100 ms post-stimulus onset to attended speech. Correlation analyses show that more years of musical training relate with less of an impact of attention on cortical responses to speech. These outcomes reveal a decreased impact of selective auditory attention on the cortical processing of speech in musicians, compared to non-musicians. Results are interpreted to indicate more efficient cortical attention mechanisms in musicians, which may account for behavioral advantages when listening to competing musical or speech streams.

title: The Cruel Colony
abstract: "The Cruel Colony" is a manuscript of poetry, consisting of five lyrics and one narrative verse-opera. It began as an attempt to write the landscape of Southern Utah. I am drawn to this landscape, with all its shadowy recesses, its rocks, its deceptive emptiness, its thin hot atmosphere. I wanted to render it in verse without trivializing it, to do it, and everything associated with it, justice. The goal was to make it more than simple, and often reductive, nature poetry. I found that if I approached the landscape looking through a personal lens I would be able to give it meaning, to make its physical beauty resonate through the eyes of a speaker articulates his memory through nature. I also became attracted to the idea of “sacred space,” the way in which a physical environment gains profound, sublime importance through elements of spirituality, myth and, again, personal memory. The second part of the project, the opera, is my attempt at writing a family myth that relates to and incorporates Southern Utah as sacred space. My foundation was the tradition in poetry of divine sublimation through nature. It is a vibrant tradition, established by Romantic poets like John Keats and Percy Bysshe Shelley, but continued by modern and postmodern poets like Wallace Stevens and Gary Synder. To internalize and personalize this tradition, I incorporated aspects of the divine unique to Southern Utah, like sacred Hopi and Navajo fables. The result is a verse all my own.

title: From Our Feet to the Beat & the Page to the Stage
abstract: My senior honors thesis focuses on Chicago Filipino American youth and the creation of social movements through performance. Specifically, I attempt to answer the question of how and why hip hop dance and spoken word are so important and/or useful to post-2000 Chicago Filipino youth in creating social movements. Throughout my research, I have examined how these youth utilize and transform these art forms to develop their own sense of space within their communities. Furthermore, I am exploring how Chicago in particular is an understudied site of Asian American lives. My research exists at an intersection between Asian American Studies, Filipino American Studies, African American Studies, Latina/o Studies, as well as Performance Studies. The examination of these youth arts and social movements is important because it chronicles an emerging and collective history not yet fully explored in academia. My project proposes an analysis of hip hop separate from that of the dominant African American cultural form and offers a new look at how these social movements are ever-changing. In post-2000, several key community performance figures stand out— Young Asians with Power (YAWP!), ReDefinition, Impulse, and Non Stop dance crews. My approach utilizes personal interviews, participant/observer interaction, pop cultural texts analysis, and the emergence of technology/user-generated websites. I also discuss subjects such as generational differences, postcoloniality, post-civil rights, and the constantly changing/fluid sense and construction of identity. Since there has not yet been a coherent study of this topic, these resources are pioneer source materials to document this pioneer study.

title: Effects of Amusia on Chinese Language Processing
abstract: Language and music are closely associated in that they are universal and specific to humans. Amusia, commonly known as tone-deafness, is a musical disorder that cannot be explained by mental retardation, deafness, or lack of exposure. Due to the similarities in language and music, the cognitive and neural relations between the two raise the question whether individuals with music deficiencies also have language deficiencies. In tonal languages such as Mandarin and Cantonese, tones are defined both by their pitch heights and by their pitch contours. Thus, it is important to examine tonal languages since tone distinction is a critical feature in language comprehension. Currently, the Montreal Battery of Evaluation of Amusia (MBEA) is the best tool available to detect Amusia. However, the MBEA is designed for Western listeners who speak atonal languages. In this study, the MBEA is modified to evaluate Amusia for Chinese subjects who speak tonal languages, specifically Mandarin and Cantonese. In particular, the test is designed with novel musical phrases that are composed according to the rules of the pentatonic scale so that the musical stimuli are most relevant to Chinese subjects. With this test, Amusia in Chinese subjects will be examined to see if there is a correlation between music and language and also to see if Amusia will have a greater impact on Chinese subjects since they speak tonal languages.

title: Determining Sequence Specificity in the Interaction Between Cbk1 and Ace2 in Saccharomyces Cerevisiae.
abstract: Protein kinases are critical regulatory proteins that control diverse processes like cell morphogenesis, cell fate, and cell separation through cell signaling. Protein kinases phosphorylate target proteins by adding phosphate groups to specific amino acids on those targets. Cell-signaling is a communication system that governs cellular activity; therefore, the deregulation of cell signaling is responsible for many diseases, one of which is cancer. In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, many cell-signaling pathways are poorly understood because the targets of these kinases are still unknown. In budding yeast, cell division is asymmetric because in the final step before cell separation, the daughter cell is responsible for degradation of the septum shared between mother and daughter. Ace2 is a daughter-specific transcription factor that promotes the expression of genes that degrade the septum. The phosphorylation of Ace2 by Cbk1 leads to an accumulation of Ace2 in the daughter nucleus, directly resulting in asymmetric cell division. This process emphasizes the ability of Cbk1 to regulate cell division in budding yeast through interaction with Ace2. We have been able to identify a 15 amino acid region on Ace2 that is critical for binding with Cbk1 and used an alanine scan to identify Cbk1’s sequence specificity in interacting with Ace2. Amino acids in the Ace2 sequence were individually mutated to alanine to see if interaction was abrogated. We hypothesize that similar sequences bind to Cbk1 and can therefore be used to find other Cbk1-binding partners, helping us further understand the role of Cbk1 in cell signaling pathways.

title: Contextualizing Oppositional Defiant Disorder and Conduct Disorder in Latino Youth
abstract: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) and Conduct Disorder (CD) are two of the most commonly diagnosed mental health disorders in children. While prevalence rates vary depending on the sample population they are generally estimated to be between two and sixteen percent for ODD and between one and ten percent for CD. With the recent rise in interest in cross-cultural and minority mental health issues one might expect that these two disorders would be a significant focus of current scholarship. While these disorders appear to be generally well studied, scholarship that examines these disorders within minority communities is incredibly scarce. The goal of this project is to better understand ODD and CD in Latino youth. An extensive review of existing literature from fields such as psychology, psychiatry, anthropology and sociology led to identification of several sociocultural factors that influence the diagnosis and expression of symptoms of both disorders among Latino youth. This project studies the influence of racial/ethnic bias on the diagnosis of the disorder as well as how the effects of discrimination, neighborhood context and acculturative stress may influence the presentation of ODD and CD in Latino youth. By combining multiple bodies of scholarship this project contextualizes ODD and CD in Latino youth. Furthermore, this project demonstrates that in order for researchers to fully understand cross-cultural and minority issues in mental health it is necessary to adopt an interdisciplinary approach to scholarship that allows one to study disorders within the social and cultural contexts they present themselves in.

title: Stranded in Jordan: A Study of Jordan's Iraqi Refuge Policy
abstract: The refugee policies of first world countries or the international refugee regime have been popular topics in refugee studies. This research often overlooks that most refugees flee to neighboring countries in the third world and minimizes the impact that these countries’ domestic policies have on the refugees. The literature on host countries’ responses to a refugee influx is based on a different context than is most often found in practice. With one of the highest ratios of refugees to total population in the world, Jordan challenges the standard assumptions and theories in the literature. Jordan has an authoritarian regime, a chronic lack of natural and economic resources, an insular and homogeneous society, a complex diplomatic position in the region and vis-à-vis the U.S., and a complicated history of hosting Palestinian refugees. Furthermore, the Iraqi refugee population is not in camps, but dispersed in Jordan’s urban centers, adding another layer of complexity to responding to the refugees. This thesis traces the historical trajectory of Jordanian policy on Iraqi refugees, explains causes of the policies, and evaluates the availability of durable solutions. This study employs elements of process tracing, content analysis, and discourse analysis to analyze how Jordan perceives Iraqi refugees as a security/stability threat and how such perceptions affect its refugee policies. Its findings suggest that despite discourse on treating Iraqis as “welcomed guests,” the Jordanian regime’s evolving policies reveal increasing concern that their presence is a threat to the security and stability of the regime and Jordanian society.

title: Interwoven: The Economics, Politics and Sociology behind Reshaping Hmong Generations and Gender through Craft
abstract: The Hmong practice a traditional embroidery and stitchery craft called pa ndau, or ‘flower cloth.’ The craft has been reshaped and redefined as the Hmong have experienced radical periods of war, displacement and relocation. Originally, pa ndau was an intricate form of embroidery and cross-stitching that produces squares of abstract, geometric patterns to create decoration for traditional dress. Since the violent persecution of the Hmong in Laos, pa ndau also refers to storycloths, which typically depict the Hmong’s role in the “Secret War” in Laos. In addition to this literal transformation of the craft, I study the changing nature of pa ndau in America. Traditionally, pa ndau was passed down from generation to generation and done in one’s spare time, providing women with a means of relaxation and creativity. However, in the United States, younger Hmong women are finding new outlets for self-expression and group cohesion and pa ndau is practiced less and less. For the older generation, pa ndau is becoming a more formalized process; it used as a means of income and often structures social group meetings. Through participant-observation and interviews, I investigate theories of material culture and second-generation assimilation to examine how Hmong women are using this craft to assimilate to, or disassociate from their new American surroundings and how a younger generation of Hmong girls are defining what it means to “be Hmong-American.”

title: Purification and Characterization of in vitro Tools to Study Huntingtin Aggregation Kinetics
abstract: Huntington’s disease is an autosomal dominant genetic disease caused by an expansion of the CAG repeat in the huntingtin (Htt) gene. This mutation is translated into an elongated polyglutamine (polyQ) stretch, which destabilizes the native folding of the protein and leads to aggregation. Htt with a polyQ length greater than 35 residues aggregates at a rate that strongly correlates with Q-length. The elongated polyQ region has been suggested to disrupt Htt’s native function and to sequester other cellular proteins into aggregates, causing impairment of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, transcription control, and axonal transport. This indicates that Htt toxicity may arise from multiple pathways, rather than one major cause. However, the exact mechanism is still unknown. Over the past 2 years, I have constructed and characterized fluorescently labeled Htt with various polyQ lengths. The purification of Htt is a major challenge to study the protein in vitro because the protein easily aggregates and causes toxicity to the host organism during expression. The conventional purification method had a low yield of full-length Htt and contained many Htt fragments. I have tested multiple expression conditions and purification methods to optimize both the yield and purity. The finalized protocol yields the full-length protein at both a higher concentration and improved purity compared to the initial protocol. I confirmed the purified Htt binds the fluorescent dye Flash, and aggregates in a polyQ- and time- dependent manner. This fluorescent protein can be used to observe huntingtin aggregation kinetics and its interaction with other cellular proteins in vitro.

title: To Give or Not to Give: Effects of Socioeconomic Status and Ethnicity on Willingness to Make a Directed Donation
abstract: Every day, people are forced to make sacrifices to varying degrees. While a sacrifice may be personal and something as small as giving up an hour of sleep, of special interest are sacrifices that involve the saving of a human life. One such type of sacrifice is an organ donation. Previous research on the motivations behind people making organ donations has been limited in scope to research about non-directed donations. For instance, blood donations are typically non-directed donations because they do not have any particular recipient in mind. The purpose of this research is to understand how people judge when it is appropriate to make a directed sacrifice, specifically, a kidney donation or bone marrow transplant, and what factors influence a person’s decision about whether or not to donate his/her kidney or bone marrow to another person. My research examines the effects of social relationships, socioeconomic status (SES), and ethnicity of both the donor and the recipient on these sorts of judgments. This research is significant because it examines how people think about issues relating to personal sacrifice: Is it a moral decision? Do people feel a sense of obligation to donate? Or is it more of a practical decision? The research is conducted with the hope that the results will be helpful in the formation of health policy, especially as it relates to people’s motivations to make donations and sacrifices for others.

title: The Statue Garden
abstract: What I initially proposed for this project, my senior project, and what it has in fact turned out to be are, at least to my mind, two wholly different things. My initial intent was to write a collection of poems about a location, a small town in Connecticut, in which I spent the formative summers of my childhood. While it could be argued that it is still a collection of poems about nature, it has expanded to include not only the exterior landscape, but also the interior landscape of the family and home. I explored the work of various poets, mining their work for stylistic and thematic similarities. Among the poets who served useful, Seamus Heaney, Herbert Morris, Robert Wrigley, and Stanley Kunitz were perhaps the most indispensable. The collection I wrote makes memory believable as metaphor. The recollection and metaphors are held up to one another as two mirrors, giving back to the eye not the original, but a reflection, an opposite that deepens ever inward. While some of the poems explore the sense of loss associated with this place and childhood and some explore the complexity of family relationships, all of them work to find a language for the unsayable.

title: Gender Disparity in the 2008-2009 Recession: A Look at Role Reversals
abstract: My thesis explores gendered role reversals that have occurred as a result of the 2008-2009 recession. I sought to understand whether, or how, role-reversals occur as a result of a huge economic change such as a recession. I gathered my data through interviews with people that I recruited from different sources, including unemployment support groups and employment networks based in the Chicago area. I interviewed twenty-four people, including men and women who had lost their jobs, and women whose husbands had lost their jobs. Based on my interviews, this thesis will show what happens to couples when sudden economic changes arise. Whether or not a role reversal occurs varies from couple to couple, as does the nature (positive or negative) of their experience; nevertheless, this thesis will conclude that role reversals are prevalent in the recession. It will show that in the few cases where reversals are absent, or the reversals are not a positive experience, underlying factors—such as existing gender ideologies, traditional upbringings, or the length of time spent searching for a job—are the likely cause or excuse. This study will provide useful research on role-reversals and can help us understand this phenomenon and how people cope with such a major change.

title: Repression and the Gulag in Kazakhstan
abstract: Thanks to Northwestern's Undergraduate Research Grant, I was able to spend the summer of 2009 in Kazakhstan interviewing people who had been repressed during the 1940's and 50's. I recorded thirteen heart-rending stories of deportation, labor camps, and arrest. I unearthed a community of Ukrainian nationalists who served me countless cups of tea while they told me stories of torture and loss. I talked a spy, to a daughter of a general, to a woman who married someone whose life had been broken by a labor camp. I returned to the United States with fifteen hours of recorded narrative, telling stories of people whom no one had dared to talk to before. Then, in the fall, I took an independent study with the History Department in which I transcribed and translated all of my interviews (since they were originally recorded in Russian). I wrote introductions to my interviews and annotated them, making them suitable for the average person to pick up and read. I produced 50 pages of material, based off of my summer research. This spring, I am taking an independent study with Medill in which I am taking a few of my interviews and turning them into audio documentary stories. This ongoing project is a quest for me to make the stories of the people of Kazakhstan known. I first became inspired to talk to the repressed people in Kazakhstan when I realized how little was actually known about these people. There are very few books published on the Gulag labor camps, though Stalin affected the lives of as many people as Hitler did. My project is about unearthing these stories, about bringing unknown facts and dirty truths into the light. I am combining my fluent Russian with my journalism major to produce this unique project.

title: Froissart: Herodotus of the Middle Ages
abstract: Deemed the Herodotus of the Middle Ages, Jean Froissart left four books documenting heroic acts and feats of honor during the Hundred Years War. The rediscovery of Jehan LeBel’s chronicles, however, indicates that a large portion of his first book was taken directly from LeBel. Indeed, unlike the topics of the later three books, the first book covers a period from before Froissart’s time or during his youth, thus he had to rely on other sources. Contemporary historical work on Froissart has reversed his long held reputation of being The Medieval Historian. He is defamed for plagiarism, wild fancies of invention, and, often times, being downright wrong. He is held responsible for the incorrect facts that he wrote, and the facts that he failed to write. Although his attackers may uphold a valid claim, they fail to take into account Froissart’s actual achievements within the chronicling tradition. Uncommon among medieval writers, Froissart revised his works multiple times throughout his lifetime. In particular, he developed and adapted the material borrowed from LeBel. This can especially be seen when viewing how he incorporated information from a second source, Chandos Herald’s Life of the Black Prince which often conflicts with LeBel. By analyzing how Froissart attempted to resolve the disparities between his sources we gain new insight on how he worked as a chronicler and as a creative agent. Furthermore, by considering his work within the context of the time period, a more balanced view of his heritage and value can be appraised.

title: Full Wallets and Empty Hearts: Hetairai in Greek Literature and Culture
abstract: Classicists fight a constant battle against their primary sources. How many texts do we not have? How close are the texts we do have to the original works? How far can we trust the original works to reflect the society in which they were writtten? Especially problematic is the limited perspective afforded by our authors: upper class men composed nearly all extant Classical literature. My thesis attempts to give a voice to one silent subset of Greek society, or at least to show why the voice that was given to this group was not its own. The hetaira, or courtesan, was a high-class sex worker not unlike the geisha of Japan. She received much attention in ancient literature, and many hetairai are named and discussed across genres and centuries. Yet these hetairai are suspiciously alike: they all seem to be the same basic character, renamed and altered slightly. My project traces the centuries of character formation that resulted in this composite identity, in which various stereotypes about the behavior of hetairai coalesced into the figure of The Hetaira. A mercenary, promiscuous, manipulative temptress, The Hetaira became a stock character in Classical literature. I argue that several qualities made hetairai unique among women and contributed to a reversal of gender roles in their associations with men, and that the phthonos—envy, resentment, general ill will—inspired by their appropriation of male privileges helped to create the archetypal Hetaira, whose faults are based upon misuse of these very privileges.

title: Power and Dependency: Interactions between Informal Caretakers and Patients with a Mental Illness in Uganda
abstract: This research examines the role of informal caretakers, such as family members and friends, in caring for individuals with mental illness in Uganda. Previous studies describe the role of informal caretakers of the mentally ill in Western countries, and the research on mental health in sub-Saharan Africa is growing. This paper builds on such previous work by exploring the effects of informal care in a context which has yet to be studied. In Uganda, individuals with mental illness typically hold a devalued place in society. As a result, when adults suffering from mental illness are placed under the care of an older relative (usually female), they are often treated like children. Rather than being given the opportunity to perform the normative adult social roles existing in Uganda, patients rarely live independently or hold jobs while under the care of a family member. The dynamics of power and dependency between caretaker and patient may have negative effects on treatment outcomes and the well-being of the patients. Although social support is often heralded as a positive force in the African context, I argue that this assumption needs to be examined critically. In the case of mental illness in Uganda, clients could benefit from a reordering of the relationship with caretakers and changes to societal perceptions that allow clients to interact with others on a more equal basis.

title: The Effects of Chinese Commercial Investment on Governance in African States
abstract: Chinese economic engagement with African states has expanded rapidly throughout the past decade via trade, foreign direct investment, loans, and direct development financing. This project explores theories of governance in modern Africa and investigates the effects of Chinese commercial investment on governance in African states. I use the cases of Angola and Ethiopia in order to evaluate how regime type, degree of institutionalization, sector of investment, and financial mechanisms associated with Chinese projects affect African governance. Even if the types of financing options employed by China create growth or align with positive development indicators, there are still effects on governance that may cause a perpetuation of the same economic problems financing aims to fix. My research indicates that instead of shrinking the African state, increasing Chinese commercial investment has the effect of reinforcing executive authority and patrimonial structures of governance that allow the state to thrive off the co-option of the private sphere. In a region where presidential power is increasingly consolidated by strong executives, Chinese investment may be supporting elements of informal governance which allow the perpetuation of patrimonial tendencies and political patronage networks.

title: Mechanical Properties of Bis-leucine Oxalyl Amide
abstract: Bis-leucine oxalyl amide is a low molecular weight gelator capable of forming gels with polar and organic solvents through self-assembly. A fundamental understanding of self-assembled systems can lead to new methods in drug delivery and the design of new soft material systems. An important feature of these self-assembled systems is the intermolecular forces between solvent and gelator molecule. By changing the solvent the gel is formed with, the mechanical properties also change. In this project two variables were considered: the degree of neutralization present for the gelator molecule ranging from neutral to completely ionized, and the concentration of the gelator molecule, changing from 1 weight percent to 8 weight percent in 1-butanol. Mechanical properties were studied using displacement controlled indentation techniques and temperature sweep rheometry. It has been found that properties such as the storage modulus, gelation temperature and maximum stress allowed increase with bis-leucine oxalyl amide concentration. The results from this study will establish a 2-D contour map between the gelator concentration, the gelator degree of ionization and mechanical properties such as storage modulus and maximum stress before failure. The intermolecular forces between the bis-leucine low molecular weight gelator and 1-butanol govern the mechanical properties of the gel system, and understanding these interactions will be key to implementing rationally designed self-assembled systems based on these or similar molecules.

title: Roles of Mitf and SoxE Factors in Melanocyte Development
abstract: Melanocytes are specialized cells derived from the neural crest that are responsible for producing melanin. The neural crest is a multipotent cell population in chordate embryonic development that differentiates into a diverse range of cell types depending on received molecular signals. Within the melanocyte lineage, numerous molecular players in the differentiation process have been identified, including the transcription factors Mitf and members of the SoxE family. Although studies have shown that both of these proteins are needed for activating transcription of genes critical to melanocyte function and survival, the genetic relationship between Mitf and SoxE factors remains to be precisely described. Some studies show that the primary role of SoxE factors is turning on Mitf, while others suggest that SoxE factors have other essential downstream roles. To clarify this relationship, morpholino oligonucleotides were used to inhibit translation of Mitf protein, and the effects were assessed using in situ hybridization to visualize changes in expression of key melanocyte-specific genes. Additionally, animal caps were dissected from embryos injected with mRNA of Mitf and SoxE mutant constructs, which were also subjected to in situ hybridization. The results show that Mitf is required for expression of melanocyte-specific genes, but this activity is dependent on the presence of SoxE factors even after Mitf is turned on. Moreover, SoxE factors may inhibit or enhance this activation in a dose-dependent manner. These findings contrast with work showing that activation of Mitf is the primary role of SoxE factors, and sheds light on alternative regulatory functions of SoxE factors.

title: Home Gardens, Migration, and South Asian Immigrant Women in a Chicago Neighborhood
abstract: Home gardens are small enclosures in which people from many societies grow plants for food, medicine, and ornament. In the global South, home gardening is a traditional practice, and women commonly keep home gardens in both rural and urban areas. Many migrants to the North, however, give up gardening. In this study, I interview 25 South Asian immigrant women at a community center in Chicago’s Rogers Park. Each interviewee kept a home garden in her home country but does not keep one in Chicago. I ask how the interviewees valued home gardening before migration and whether they intentionally chose to avoid it after migration. The results demonstrate that nearly all found home gardening satisfying for a variety of reasons; lament the loss of this activity; and take creative steps to cope with the loss of their gardens, find substitutes for them, or partially recreate them when circumstances allow. Still, many interviewees stated or implied that their efforts to adapt to new circumstances in the U.S., especially economic pressures, take precedence over gardening. I make two arguments: First, home gardens are important not just as biological or economic systems of production, but as arenas in which women exercise agency. Second, in this study women’s choices about gardening interact with contextual factors, most notably economic environment. This study supports a research paradigm that conceptualizes women's agency as dynamic and contextualized.

title: Regulation of the Induction of the Cellular Cadmium Stress Response by Chemonsensory Neurons in Caenorhabditis elegans
abstract: Cadmium is a teratogenic, mutagenic, and potentially lethal heavy metal to which humans are regularly exposed. To address cadmium toxicity, cells rely upon a well-established cellular stress response. The stress response is a transcriptional response wherein specific genes are activated in order to combat the deleterious effects of a particular environmental stressor. Although the stress response confers cytoprotection to cells facing cadmium, stress response induction can have inhibitory effects on growth and division of single cells. Since multicellular organisms depend on coordinated cellular activity, one might expect multi-cellular organisms to have developed systemic mechanisms for regulating the cellular stress response. Indeed, there is evidence that in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans), the function of the heat-sensing AFD neurons can modulate induction of the cellular stress response to heat (the heat shock response). C. elegans have an extensive chemosensory network devoted to cadmium sensation. It is therefore possible that chemosensory input might regulate the cellular cadmium stress response, just as thermosensory input regulates the heat shock response. We show that in C. elegans the activity of a chemosensory neuronal network responsible for cadmium sensation modulates cellular heavy metal stress response activation. Mutations in genes affecting these neurons cause the induction of some, but not all, cadmium stress response genes to be altered in mutant animals. More specifically, our data suggests that the chemosensory neuronal network regulates the cadmium-induced activation of genes that are regulated specifically by the master stress response regulator, the transcription factor Heat Shock Factor 1 (HSF1).

title: Faculty and Student Perceptions of College Students with ADHD
abstract: This research project consists of a survey designed to examine the perceptions and attitudes that exist towards students with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), a neurobehavioral, developmental disorder characterized by a failure of inhibition and often accompanied by symptoms of inattentiveness, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. Psychosocial factors, such as the attitudes and perceptions of other people, play a role in the success of a college student. Students with ADHD may be particularly vulnerable in this area; as growing numbers of individuals with ADHD attend colleges and universities across the country, it is necessary to measure the success of these students in higher-level education. The questions in this survey consider the perceptions that students with ADHD enrolled in a four-year postsecondary institution of education have of themselves academically, and to compare and contrast these beliefs with the perceptions and attitudes that faculty members and students without ADHD enrolled in the same institution have towards students with ADHD. The survey consists of questions regarding personal and educational background, past experiences with individuals with ADHD, as well as other factors that may influence perceptions of students with ADHD.

title: The Political Self: Self-Agency in Liberal and Conservative Christian Adults
abstract: This study examines the different modes of self-agency described in the life narratives of liberals and conservatives. Interview responses obtained from 50 highly religious and politically active Christian adults were content analyzed for themes of self-regulation and self-exploration. Conservatives, as predicted, exhibited a stronger degree of regulation of the self, while liberals expressed a greater tendency towards exploration and discovery of the self. Consistent with findings relating political orientation to motivated social cognition, this hypothesis associates political ideology with the development and maintenance of the self. Conservatives seek to control the self, ordering their thoughts and behavior to align with conceptions of a dangerous and threatening world. Liberals, in contrast, tend towards exploration, emphasizing personal growth in light of an exciting world filled with numerous resources.

title: Development or Dependence? The China Factor in Senegal's Tertiary Sector in the 21st Century
abstract: The purpose of this research is to determine, on one side, whether or not China’s economic presence in Senegal's tertiary sector has had developmental impacts, which I define in terms of promoting an autonomous Senegalese capacity to produce and compete in the global economy (a neo-liberal expectation). On the other side, my research attempts to explain whether this presence has created a strong dependency on Chinese goods, either at the expense of Senegalese economic capacity or the autonomy of its commercial class to protect its own interests (a dependency approach expectation). The tertiary sector in this case represents the service sector where merchants sell finished goods and services to the local population. The academic debate that revolves around my research question concerns the relationship between developed and developing countries and whether China’s economic presence in Africa today repeats features of Senegal’s experience with Western powers such as France, Britain, and the US. The two conflicting theories in this academic debate are Dependency theory and Neoliberal Globalization economic theory. While there is strong evidence for dependency theory predictions in China’s economic behavior in Senegal, a Neo liberal prevailed in the tertiary sector. To better understand China’s economic impact on this sector, this research draws on local surveys, and interviews, and observations to highlight how China’s involvement has become beneficiary for a nation.

title: The Meaning of/in Difference: The Infinite Prison of Literature and Genet's Freedom in the Future Aesthetic
abstract: This thesis argues for a Blanchotian conception of literature that, under analysis, is capable of providing an explanation for the totality of Jean Genet’s work in the form. The argumentation herein will begin by presenting Jean-Paul Sartre’s understanding of literature in What is Literature? as a form of aesthetic communication which is categorically distinct from other modes such as painting and musical composition. The paper will then show how Jean Genet’s literature poses a special kind of problem for Sartre’s category distinction by exercising a form of expression in which meaningful communication is problematized by the absence of any stable object of reference that can subsist across subjective differences of essentially distinct spectators.
