Since spina bifida is a developmental defect with unknown genetic and environment influences, we speculate that certain molecular mechanisms may be one of many causative agents responsible for this condition. Specifically, we hypothesize that aberrant microRNA (miRNA) expression may fall under this category. We anticipate that our results will demonstrate differences in miRNA expression profiles in control samples versus their disease counterparts. Differential miRNA expression may shed light upon the molecular mechanisms that are involved with the neurogenic bladder and may eventually lead to therapies to correct the dysfunction and restore proper bladder function to patients.

title: Education Systems in Chicago and Santiago: The Comparison and Why it Matters
abstract: Of any school systems to examine, why would one choose Chicago, U.S., and Santiago, Chile? The modern political contexts of both the Chicago and Santiago school systems are much more interconnected than one might think. In the early 1980’s, The Chicago Boys, a group of young and influential economists in Chicago, made an agreement with the Chilean dictatorial government where Universidad Catolica Economy students could do their graduate work with the University of Chicago. “El Ladrillo” was created: a development plan that was based on rapid liberalism and monetaristic reform, and caused the almost immediate decentralization of health care and education. My paper focuses on how this irrefutable connection led to several similarities between the current Chicago and Santiago school systems. I explain several of the main historical factors which have led to the current education systems: 1) less focus on pedagogy and more focus on structural reform; 2) flexibility in curriculum; 3) establishment of per student subsidies by the government; 4) decentralization of school management; and 5) the replacement of government education centers with NGO and Business Associations and interests. After discussion of these factors, my paper analyzes two existing models of schools: the Community or Municipality driven school, and the Preparatory Institute model. I then critique the models and make recommendations for future reform. My research is based on school visits, interviews, and secondary sources.

title: Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1 Mice
abstract: Spinocerebellar Ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is a neurodegenerative disease caused by the expansions of a glutamine repeat track in ATXN1; it belongs to the family of polyglutamine disorders, that also includes Huntington's and Kennedy's diseases. ATXN1 has been shown to play a role in gene regulation, a process that is altered in the cerebella of SCA1 knock in mice, the most precise animal model of SCA1. We have found that Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF-a chemical signal released by cells that stimulates the growth of new vessels) mRNA is down regulated in the Purkinje neurons (cerebellar neurons that are most susceptible to SCA1) of SCA1 mice and that ATXN1 directly suppresses VEGF transcription by binding to the VEGF promoter. Furthermore over expressing VEGF improved the SCA1 phenotype. In order to explore the effect of reduced VEGF levels on the vasculature in SCA1 mice, we quantified capillary density in the cerebellum of SCA1 mice compared to their wild type littermates. Interestingly we have found that SCA1 mice have decreased density of blood vessels in the cerebellum; replenishing VEGF significantly increased the density. These findings indicate there is an important role in communication between a degenerating nervous system and the vascular system around it that still has to be explored in more detail. These findings also indicate future avenues of research, including finding a VEGF related biomarker to indicate the advancement of SCA1 in patients and creating a therapeutic delivery mechanism to rescue VEGF in the brain in hopes of ameliorating the SCA1 phenotype.

title: Regulation of the Inhibin-alpha Subunit Gene by the NR4A Family of Orphan Nuclear Receptors
abstract: Nuclear receptors play an important role in dynamically regulating gene expression. One family of nuclear receptors, the NR4A subfamily, has been shown to regulate gene expression in several tissues, specifically in liver and skeletal muscles. Our lab has previously demonstrated that the NR4A protein nerve growth factor inducible-B (NGFI-B) can act to inhibit inhibin-alpha subunit gene expression in ovarian granulosa cells. Due to its integral role in the synthesis and secretion of the gonadotropins follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), inhibin-alpha gene regulation is essential for maintaining normal, reproductive estrous cycles. To more broadly study this class of nuclear receptors, we sought to investigate the remaining two NR4A members, nuclear receptor related 1 (Nurr-1) and neuron-derived orphan receptor 1 (NOR1), and examine their roles in regulating inhibin-alpha gene expression. In this study, I have demonstrated that all three NR4A messenger RNAs are rapidly and robustly induced in rat ovaries after human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG, an LH analog) treatment and that this expression is associated with a decrease in inhibin-alpha messenger RNA levels. This pattern was also observed in mouse granulosa cells after stimulation by the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin. Furthermore, luciferase reporter gene assays suggest that NGFI-B, Nurr-1, and NOR-1 are all able to repress inhibin-alpha promoter activity. We generated mutations within the DNA binding domains of these proteins and found that these mutants were still able to repress inhibin-alpha promoter activity although they were unable to bind to DNA. These data suggest that the NR4A family of orphan nuclear receptors is able to repress inhibin-alpha gene expression and that the mechanism of repression does not require DNA-binding.

title: Plant Community Responses to the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
abstract: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) is a dramatic, but transient global warming event that occurred 55 million years ago. It is associated with a sea surface temperature increase of 5°C and rapid ocean acidification. This makes the PETM an excellent natural experiment for current anthropogenic global warming. Previous studies in the Bighorn Basin, Wyoming have observed dramatic migrations of the plant community in response to PETM warming. However, these migrations are not observed in the Williston Basin, North Dakota. I hypothesized that this is because the PETM is not fully preserved in the Williston Basin. The PETM is usually identified by a negative carbon isotope excursion, or period where the concentration of the light isotope 12C increases relative to the heavy isotope 13C. However, the organic material present in the Williston Basin is highly degraded, complicating interpretation of the isotope record. To avoid these degradation effects, I extracted and isolated plant waxes from sediment samples collected at Williston Basin. By focusing on individual compounds I hoped to avoid the systematic enrichment of 13C that accompanies degradation. I did not find an isotope excursion, suggesting that the PETM is not preserved at Williston Basin. However, in samples from the “orange zone”, where previous studies have placed the PETM based on the location of plant fossils, the degradation is so extreme that no plant waxes are preserved. Thus, this study cannot conclusively determine if the PETM is preserved in the orange zone, but it can conclude that it is not present outside the orange zone.

title: Something To Get Off My Chest: Bras and Binders in the Construction of Genders
abstract: Feminist thought disagrees on whether the bra is restrictive or not. The majority of historic and popular accounts render the bra constrictive to women’s bodies. Corroborating this view is the idea that signs of femininity (including the bra) conform to normative, hegemonic, idealized womanhood, and lead women to understand themselves as inadequate, docile, and subject to men’s wills. This school of thought exposed the problematic systemic treatment of women in society and enabled intelligent critique of and protest against it. However, this strictly oppressive hypothesis applies larger systemic meanings indiscriminately to all subjects within that system, ignoring positive considerations of individuals who use bras in daily life, the contradictory practices they employ, and the empowerment and positivity they sometimes feel. Many women actively choose to wear bras. The oppressive hypothesis paints these people as either naïve victims of the culture or as aware of their oppression but lacking the courage or agency to challenge it. If that view fails to align with the lived experience of many women, we must flirt with the possibility that there are legitimate reasons why intelligent, self-aware, even feminist-identified people wear bras. My work combines post-modern theory with personal interviews of eight non-heteronormative subjects. I complicate the argument against feminine dress by comparing it with its masculine counterpart – the chest binders that transgender men use. Furthermore, I examine what purpose bras serve for the people I interviewed, and how their use of bras, rather than being oppressive, is actually subversive.

title: Where the Streets Have a Name: Exploring Public Space, Identity Formation and Authenticity in Buenos Aires' Carnaval
abstract: For murgueros, the sweltering summer month of February is perhaps the most important time of the year; Carnaval is a chance to express collective identity, to perform the unison of sweeping movements and pounding bass drum beats that they have practiced. Akin only in origin to the famed Brazilian Carnaval, Argentine Carnaval assumes its own form in streets of Buenos Aires. La murga, a form of dance characteristic to Buenos Aires’ Carnaval, is danced in a group formation according to barrio [neighborhood]. The practice of la murga creates a sense of community within working and middle class barrios as the multigenerational social spaces it forms emerge as a rich addition to public neighborhood life. Murga is strongly tied to place both because it utilizes public space, such as parks and plazas, for practice and performance, and because participation in la murga strengthens murgueros’ sense of pride in their barrios. Murga is cultura popular, produced in the streets, by the people, for the people; it works outside the confines of the commercialization of spectacle seen in the Carnavales of other Latin American countries. In this way, la murga is symptomatic of the greater social, economic and political tensions that exist in an urban landscape recently impacted by neoliberal globalization; it is a multi-layered art form expressive of a social conscience through which murgueros negotiate collective identity construction and their own relationships to public space, and fight to maintain the authenticity of their art form in the streets of Buenos Aires.

title: On The Absence of Celluloid in the Digital Age: Liveness, Lost Cinema and the Case for Catch My Soul (1974)
abstract: Is it possible to engage with something that is already gone? If so, how? Patrick McGoohan’s 1974 rock musical adaptation of Othello, entitled Catch My Soul (AKA: Santa Fe Satan) is a film that, thirty years ago, disappeared. Since 1979, neither a 35mm nor 16mm print has been said to exist. Despite its absence as a celluloid print, its memory lives on in the form of memorabilia such as posters, newspaper ads and soundtrack recordings available on both vinyl and 8-track recordings. Additionally, the memory lives on through obituaries of the recently deceased McGoohan (January 13th, 2009) and through the writings of amateur authors on cult cinema weblogs about the film’s seeming ephemerality, ostensibly “missing in action.” But if we can preserve the memory of the film’s experience, does it not still exist to us? Or, must we see the celluloid itself in order to truly experience the film? The questions posed here are not limited solely to Catch My Soul, but rather represent a historian’s quest to understand what engaging in a live, although asymptotic, relationship (ie. an example of Zeno’s Paradox) with a supposedly nonexistent entity (an object of lost cinema) means for film history in the Digital Age, an area of film studies hitherto wholly unexplored.

title: The Effect of Acculturation on Risk Factors for Type II Diabetes among Indian Immigrant Women
abstract: The rate of diabetes among Indian immigrants in America is increasing rapidly, facilitated in part by acculturation to western life. This study attempts to elucidate the relationship between duration of time lived in the US and increased risk factors for diabetes. The study population consists of low socioeconomic status Indian immigrant women recruited from a Chicago-based health clinic (n=90). This study explores the biological or lifestyle factors that contribute to why Indian immigrants are more susceptible to Type II diabetes in America. Also, this study explores the quality of how Indian diabetics care for their disease. We found a significant relationship between duration of time lived in the US and abdominal obesity (p=0.01), and a somewhat significant relationship between body fat percentage (p=0.09) and body mass index (p=0.09). The female Indian subject population had higher rates of diabetes, overweight/obesity, hypertension, high cholesterol, and more sedentary lifestyle when compared to the rest of the US population. Finally, diabetics within this female Indian sample population (n=39) did not take care of their diabetes well in accordance to current standards of biomedicine, with 53.8% having an a1c hemoglobin measurement above 7.0% and 64.1% reporting less than 2 hours of weekly exercise. This study calls for a focus on educational interventions about Type II diabetes and ways to control it and prevent its onset while living in the US.

title: Saving Space
abstract: This collection of stories, “Saving Space,” works with the overlapping difficulties of constriction and isolation – often self-imposed. In these thematically linked stories, the characters attempt to fulfill unmet emotional needs. Some miss lost loved ones, one longs for a girlfriend. Some try to remember and some try to forget. The characters often react to their loss or restriction by directing their anger outwards, whether it is onto animals or other people. The pieces strive to reveal the range of human reactions to such moments, but also their similarities. Each story details a unique and surprising setting, from an Alzheimer’s home in “Long for Gone” to the research laboratory in “Tissue Analysis.” And although each character grapples with his or her situation differently, when read together, the stories reveal the universal nature of pain. Many of the characters struggle with limited perspective and all battle personal flaws. Because of these problems, some of them are unable to find whatever it is they are searching for. But in these sometimes pale, lonely stories, there are moments of hope also. Even while one woman cannot grab hold of an opportunity for change, another character finds quiet joy in a clean room and a shared sunrise. Painful memories are not only inhibiting, but can also be agents of transformation.

title: The God Squad: Social Outreach and the Rise of Evangelical Protestantism on College Campuses
abstract: Over the last four decades, mainline Protestant campus ministries, once the spiritual home of most American undergraduates, have faced sharp decreases in attendance. The blame for this decline is often placed on the perceived “secularization” of the American university; many commentators on modern religion seem to believe that faith is no longer important or relevant to college students. At the same time, non-denominational evangelical ministry groups have become increasingly prevalent on college and university campuses across the country. Although these simultaneous trends seem incongruous and invite further investigation, an analysis of the issues behind this shift in campus religious ecology is absent in current literature about college students and religion. My project is based partially on my own interviews with mainline and evangelical college students and religious leaders. It examines these two types of ministry and outreach to provide an explanation for the rise in non-denominational evangelical campus ministries’ popularity. Surprisingly, these ministries’ outreach to students focuses very little on theological claims; instead, evangelical ministries’ events are presented as opportunities for socialization and fellowship. Moreover, pressure to join evangelical ministries that cater to niche populations on college campuses often comes from students’ peers; students who are part of visible social groups gravitate to ministries that serve these groups in part out of simple homophily. This analysis of the social and psychological factors in evangelical campus ministries’ outreach complicates the theory of secularization to provide a more complete explanation for the reasons behind the trend toward evangelization on college campuses.

title: Space Invaders: Street Art, Site-specificity, and the Contest for Urban Space
abstract: Street artists appropriate urban space for aesthetic interventions, acts that imply opposition to the prescribed structures and pathways of the city. Analyzing the works of Vhils and Banksy, two prominent street artists who practice in London, I examine the ways in which street art engages the city as a site of critical inquiry, a space to be celebrated and interrogated, fought for and fought. In making artworks that critique the city from within its streets, these artists make visible hidden aspects of the urban condition: the economic and political forces that shape urban space and prescribe its uses; the populations of city dwellers who are subjected to the structuring of urban space and the everyday experience of urban living; and the possibility of alternative uses of urban space—the ways in which spatial structures and strictures can be subverted by urban spatial interventions. Informed by field research and building upon urban spatial theory and models of site-specific art making, I argue that the visual interventions of street art encourage a rethinking of urban space by those who occupy it but have little influence over its production. Making art that confronts the forces of urban spatial structuring in the space of the city, these artists not only expose the city to the mechanisms of its own contentious production, but site it as ground zero of the contest over the control of urban space.

title: The Effects of Drawing on Children's Understanding of Spatial Relationships
abstract: This study investigates how children think about spatial environments and the strategies they use to communicate spatial information. It aims to determine how drawing influences their mental representations. We hypothesized that drawing would allow children to communicate more spatial relations, and would improve their scores on a spatial inference test. Participants were six-year-olds and eight-year-olds who were volunteered by their parents. Each child walked through a “playhouse” with six rooms in a 3x2 grid. Each room had a different toy animal in it, and they were asked to memorize where all the animals lived. After the initial learning stage, the children described the playhouse to their parent. The control group verbally described the playhouse twice; the children in the experimental groups first verbally described it, and then were asked to draw on a whiteboard while they verbally described it again. Next, they were brought back to the playhouse and were asked to make inferences about the spatial relationships between the rooms. The results show that eight-year-olds performed significantly better on the inference task than the six-year-olds. Neither age group used much spatial language in their verbal descriptions, but the six-year-olds who drew scored higher on the task and showed a better understanding of the relationships between the rooms than those children who only gave a verbal description. For children this age, drawing may provide a more accessible way of communicating relations, and may also lead to a more integrated mental representation of the space.

title: It’s All About How You Use It: The Relationship between Directive Memory Function and Life Satisfaction
abstract: This study examined whether there was a relationship between directive memory function, emotional valence of memories, and life satisfaction. Previous autobiographical memory research has found that people generally use their memories in three ways. These include self, social, and directive functions. When people use the self-function, they tell memories primarily for identity management. When they use the social function, they wish to facilitate social connections. Finally, when they use the directive function, they hope to learn from their pasts in order to make future actions. In this study, 65 participants provided vivid single-event memories of a high point, low point, childhood, adolescent, adult, and virtue scene (a time when someone taught them a lesson) via an online survey. For each memory, these participants gave a six-point rating designed to measure the principal ways they used their memories. After conducting statistical analyses, the most important findings were that there was a significant correlation between directive memory function and life satisfaction, and that people generally use the memory scenes that are most relevant and recent to their lives. The more people used directive functioning, the higher they rated their life satisfaction. Moreover, the memories that they drew from were the adult scenes as reflected by their high, low, adult, and virtue scenes. Memory valence was important only if the particular memory scene was positive. These findings are significant because they add more depth to the under researched areas of autobiographical memory function and life satisfaction.

title: Friendship Performance in the Music of Nico Muhly
abstract: The music of the young postminimalist Nico Muhly features an unusual amount of collaboration between composer and performers. Muhly’s mature collaborations embody an aesthetic which heavily combines his compositional style with the unique skills of his performers. “The Only Tune,” a deconstruction of a folk ballad written for singer Sam Amidon and small ensemble, draws on both Muhly’s musical influences and Amidon’s folk music background. The work represents a true collaboration between equals. Drawing on careful analysis of recorded performances of “The Only Tune,” as well as interviews with Muhly and his collaborators, this paper examines the extent to which Muhly and Amidon blend their disparate styles to create a unified work with a multiplicity of authorship. Interviews, as well as a close scrutiny of Muhly’s writings in print and on his blog, bring to light an important secondary aspect of Muhly’s music: the performance of friendship. Muhly portrays his close ties to his collaborators within the music itself. His works embrace a sentimentality which defies the archetypical, autobiographical idea of the composer-as-hero in his own music. This sentimentality indicates a larger trend in 21st-century postminimalist music, which channels the techniques of classic minimalism towards a dramatic, often purposefully emotional, narrative. By alluding to the personal and musical histories of his friendship within works like The Only Tune, Muhly explores the relationship between himself and his collaborators, creating music as performed, shared biography.

title: ¿Leyes Malditas o Leyes Benditas? An Examination of the 1990s Legal Reforms in Bolivia
abstract: In the 1990s, the Bolivian government formally recognized its indigenous majority for the first time. The government declared Bolivia a "multiethnic, pluricultural" nation, breaking with the historical tendency of the state to marginalize, assimilate, homogenize, and subordinate its highly diverse population. This affirmation of indigenous identity was accompanied by a multitude of legislative changes, including educational reform, administrative decentralization, the recognition of traditional forms of indigenous organization as political units, a change in the forestry laws, agrarian reform, partial privatization of state-owned enterprises, and social security reform. The new laws were all part of the Plan de Todos (Plan for All), a series of comprehensive reforms that sought to drastically restructure the Bolivian state. Many of these reforms have been touted as substantial gains for Bolivia's indigenous majority. Others, including many organizations of indigenous people, argue that the reforms were constructions of the elite institutions to maintain their power and dominance. This paper seeks to explore the intentions of the reforms and the relationship between the reforms and contemporary social and political movements and indigenous organizations. It asks: How did the legal reforms of 1994 come about, and precisely what relationship did it have to the indigenous social and political movements? What motivated the state to enact these reforms at that particular moment in history? What was the intent of the reforms intend, and how were they received by indigenous organizations and peoples?

title: Mitterrand's Third Way: Class Collaboration and the Auroux Laws
abstract: Francois Mitterrand’s presidency transformed the system of labor relations in France. After he was elected in 1981, Socialists held both the presidency and an absolute majority in the National Assembly for the first time since the inception of the Fifth Republic. With such a strong ability to effect change, it comes as no surprise that Mitterrand wasted no time in passing a series of sweeping labor reforms that rewrote a third of the famously complex Code du travail. But instead of stacking the deck in the favor of workers and unions, as one might expect from a Social Democratic party, the new laws - named the Auroux Laws after the Minister of Labor Jean Auroux - liberalized French labor relations, moved labor regulation away from the state and into the firm, and seemed to lie more towards the Right of the political spectrum than the Left. And all this from a party that called themselves Socialists. This project seeks to explain these policy choices. Through analysis that focuses on the political structure of the French "split-Left," this essay argues that the Auroux Laws were not as large a departure from the rest of Mitterrand's early policies as they might seem. Instead, these apparently right-leaning laws provided a deeply institutional role for labor negotiations that most scholars credit as the primary source of strength for contemporary organized labor in France.

title: Not So Different After All: A Comparitive Analysis of the Cognition of Full Term Versus Premature Infants
abstract: Full term neonates know a lot about the world around them. However, it remains to be seen how infants who are born prematurely understand how the world works. In labs that study typically developing infants it is common procedure to eliminate data from premature infants in an effort to reduce error variance. The current study challenges the validity of this practice. We examined how premature infants differ from full term infants in looking time studies. The results show that premature twins showed a significant familiarity preference during tests while premature single children showed a significant novelty preference similar to what is observed in full term infants. This suggests that premature single infants more closely resemble full-term infants in cognitive tasks than previously thought. This also suggests a difference between premature twins and single infants which warrants further investigation.

title: Linguistically Grounding "Queer": Infidel Heteroglossias in the Globalized Genderscape
abstract: Queer theory demands destabilization of terms and rejection of essentializing categorization as a means to approach gender equality. While it is theoretically useful to understand the range of gender identities as existing on a spectrum, linguistic research maintains that speakers nevertheless continue to make linguistically-based categorizations in order to facilitate interpersonal communication and make sense of a diffuse continuum of experience. Rather than another reformation of the a priori queer theory philosophy, the current study suggests a documented philosophy built from the ground up-- an "empirically responsible" account of how and why the embodied mind functions in gender identity labeling. In imagining the future of an empirically responsible gender theory, it is critical to examine the range of possibilities offered by transnational case studies. The interdisciplinary nature of linguistic analysis allows us to analyze various manifestations of gender queering across transnational third-gender identities. Anthropological evidence from Thailand, Brazil, and India highlights the arbitrary division of sexuality and gender continuums based on language customs and cultural socialization. Regardless of how the particular distinctions were drawn, these categorizations were nevertheless invariably called upon in creating coalition and petitioning for rights. Drawing on cognitive linguistic theory and Donna Haraway's 'A Cyborg Manifesto', this project explores how embodied linguistic theory can help understand transnational accounts of third gender identities. Admitting the nature of categories and recognizing the cognitive and social need for categorization can be used to open up novel and liberating political identity spaces through heteroglossic integration of differing transnational gender ontologies..

title: Fat Talk Among College Women Reflects and Creates Body Dissatisfaction
abstract: Women’s dissatisfaction with the size of their bodies is so common that it has been termed “normative discontent.” Though women’s body dissatisfaction has been heavily researched for decades now, only recently have researchers begun to investigate a phenomenon known as fat talk. In general, fat talk is characterized by women (typically peers) engaging in mutual disparagement about the size and shape of their bodies. These two studies explored college women’s fat talk both qualitatively and quantitatively in order to better elucidate the ways in which fat talk may act as an injunctive norm, reinforcing women’s body-related distress. Study 1 explored college women’s perceptions of and participation in fat talk, and the link between fat talk and body dissatisfaction. Engaging in fat talk was associated with greater body dissatisfaction. However, there was no association between a woman’s actual body size and how often she complained about her body size. Fat talk may be less about being fat than about feeling fat. In study 2, fat talk was experimentally manipulated. Hearing a confederate fat talk made the participants more likely to fat talk themselves and increased body dissatisfaction. Engaging in fat talk mediated the relationship between hearing fat talk and increased body dissatisfaction. Together, these results suggest that fat talk is a phenomenon that both reflects and creates body dissatisfaction.

title: Characterization of Mesenchymal Stromal Cells and Axonal Growth for Studying Spinal Cord Injury
abstract: Recent research suggests that multipotent mesenchymal stromal stem cells (MSCs) may have clinical applications in the nervous system. Primary MSCs are thought to lose their therapeutic capacity with prolonged culture, thus one aim of this study was to characterize human bone marrow-derived MSCs (hMSCs) and determine how long they retain their “stemness,” i.e., differentiability. For successful application of hMSCs to central nervous system pathology such as spinal cord injury, it is also necessary to develop animal models of injury, implantation, and repair. To date, neurological stem cell research has primarily used neural stem cells (NSCs); models developed in these studies can likely also be applied to MSCs, which are more easily extracted from patients. Thus, the second purpose of this study was to generate an NSC model as a foundation for a future study applying hMSCs to the treatment of spinal cord injury. This experiment showed that MSCs maintain their viability and proliferation ability at higher passages, but differentiation ability does begin to decrease. Rubrospinal tracing served as a good measure of spinal cord repair after hNSC transplantation, and a similar experiment should be attempted with MSCs. This experiment showed that hMSCs have potential therapeutic uses in the nervous system and applications using NSCs may possibly be expanded to MSCs.

title: Rethinking the Teaching Profession: How to Address the Implementation Gap and Improve Teacher Quality in Chicago Public Schools
abstract: Education reform is stuck. Decades of research reveal vast disparities in access to high- quality schools, and the persistence of achievement gaps squanders our collective human capital to a degree equivalent to a permanent national recession. Systemic education reform is truly needed, but it cannot advance without addressing the fundamentals of instruction: teaching and learning. Providing teachers with better on-the-job training has immense potential to translate into better school environments. A wealth of research has delineated the characteristics of effective professional development; however, the implementation of these ideas has been scattershot. This implementation gap occurs, in part, due to the derailing effects of a kaleidoscope of educational narratives that fail to converge on how to implement existing research on improving teacher quality. This project utilizes a multifaceted and interdisciplinary approach to document these educational narratives on the stage of Chicago Public Schools, including national and local policy platforms and speeches; interviews with local teachers and principals; and public opinion polls, news media, and fictional media characterizations of teachers in action. Untangling areas of contention among these educational stakeholders and realizing shared goals are critical steps to translating theory into practice. Moving forward, to address the implementation gap, teacher idealizations of reform and existing pockets of successful innovation should be considered, examined, and productively injected into school structures. Policymakers and school leaders must seriously consider reform efforts that refashion the existing the educational infrastructure, rethink the nature of teachers' work, and create both better working conditions and support systems for teachers.

title: Moral Reasoning in Applied Ethics
abstract: There has been much debate among moral philosophers and practitioners about what method of moral reasoning should be used to best address the issues that arise in applied ethics. Moral reasoning can be understood as the process by which one is able to determine the most morally justifiable action in a particular situation. Therefore, understanding and evaluating this process is very relevant to applied ethics, the study of moral questions within a specific context. Casuistry is a method of moral reasoning that has been a topic of interest in bioethics. It is referred to as having a "case-based" approach to moral reasoning in that moral judgments are arrived at through the use of analogical reasoning with "paradigm cases". Casuistry has been contrasted with the model of principlism (and more recently, specified principlism), which is considered a "principle-based" approach since moral judgments are arrived at deductively through normative principles. I assess the effectiveness of these models, focusing on two criteria: justification and practicality. I argue that none of these models adequately addresses both of these criteria and therefore cannot be considered a unitary account of moral reasoning. I find that justification and practicality often conflict within these models, and some models attempt to strike a balance between the two. I argue that such a balance is not of much use in some areas of practice, and so I propose the conjunction of multiple models with different models being selected depending upon the justificatory or practical requirements of a particular situation.

title: The Politics of Assimilation: Generational Differences in Gay Activism
abstract: Since the emergence of a post-Stonewall gay movement, gay identity politics have become inextricably linked to the sexual subculture that helped foster it. But starting in the 1990s, that subculture has undergone profound shocks as openly gay men and women have rapidly entered American public life. This research examines how the mainstreaming of gay culture affects political identity, using surveys and interviews of self-identified gay activists in Illinois across generational groups. I wanted to know both the quantitative effects of mainstreaming on political identity as well as its qualitative implications for the strategies and goals that drive political action. I found that mainstreaming does not necessarily decrease political identity—while activists tend to think gay people are culturally similar to non-gay people, they believe they are still politically different—but how political action is framed changes significantly. The generational effect is such that younger activists tend to feel less oppressed in their daily lives, but they feel that gay people as a group are just as oppressed. They also orient political goals toward institutional demands for equality, while older activists espouse personal needs for protection.

title: Inverse Relationship between Maternal Blood Pressure and Offspring Birth Weight in Cebu, Philippines
abstract: Low birth weight has been linked to an increased risk of adult cardiovascular disease and high blood pressure. The inverse relationship between birth weight and adult blood pressure is based on the hypothesis that a mother provides her fetus with cues to its future environment, and that the fetus responds by adapting its physiological settings to best suit the expected environment. Recent research has shown that the opposite relationship also holds true, and that high maternal blood pressure predicts low offspring birth weight. This study examines the influence of maternal cardiovascular health on infant birth weight and evaluates intergenerational effects between blood pressure and birth weight in a sample of Filipino women and their infants (n=323). After accounting for potential confounders, including maternal height, BMI, and nutritional status, as well as primiparity and infant gestational age, higher maternal blood pressure was found to decrease birth weight, with a stronger relationship seen in male than female offspring (for males, β-coefficient =-6.586 and p=0.090; for females, β-coefficient =-4.395 and p=0.348). Intergenerational analyses showed that blood pressure does not likely play a strong role in the intergenerational transmission of birth size. Variations in energy requirements for male and female intrauterine growth might account for gender differences in birth weight. These findings suggest that the inverse relationship between birth weight and blood pressure is self-propagating, and that the unique intrauterine environment experienced by a fetus influences the expression of adult disease.

title: Unguided Tour
abstract: “Unguided Tour” is a novella that tells the story of a newlywed American couple who end up visiting Auschwitz on their honeymoon. The bride is Jewish-American, and the groom is an atheist immigrant from Nepal. The trip to the concentration camp tests their relationship when the two react differently, and they are forced to reevaluate the way they see each other and the world because of it. It also tells the story of when they fell in love, much to the dismay of their Jewish friend who loved the eventual bride. Using Auschwitz as a catalyst, the novella questions the effects of personal background, race, and religion on love and life.

title: Analysis of Multiple Species Population Systems with Nonlocal Coupling
abstract: My research project entails analyzing a specific population model which represents a competition for resources between two interacting species over a fixed spatial domain. The model originally consisted of a pair of differential equations with a nonlinear coupling to represent interaction between the two species. I added an integral term, so that the model now consists of a pair of integrodifferential equations. The integral term represents a non-local coupling between the two species. I first found the critical points of the model, i.e., constant solutions that represent a coexistence of the two species. I then did a linear stability analysis of these critical points and found conditions under which the critical points were stable. I found that one important factor in determining stability was the extent of the nonlocal coupling. A large extent of coupling tended to be destabilizing. Finally, I developed a computer program to solve the integrodifferential equation system. My computations validated my stability analysis and also determined new, nonlinear states, which the system evolves to when the critical points are unstable.

title: Context Effects and the Nature of Moral Judgments
abstract: Past research has demonstrated that humans tend to rely on emotions and intuitions to drive moral judgments. Furthermore, some researchers have concluded that certain moral intuitions are universal and innate. It is believed that these emotional and intuitive responses generally involve rapid, automatic, and unconscious cognitive appraisals. Proponents of this intuitionist approach say that moral intuitions come first and directly cause moral judgments, and that moral reasoning is usually an ex post facto process. The current study sought to demonstrate that reasoning is not simply a retroactive process, but that it plays an important role in moral judgment. One hundred twenty-eight participants were assigned to one of three conditions, each group receiving a unique moral dilemma. Participants were asked to provide either a positive or negative rating of potential outcomes. We were able to demonstrate strong context effects, shifting average approval ratings of an action by simply adding an additional alternative to initial choice dyads. These findings are important because if universal and innate moral intuitions are the primary drive behind moral judgments, we should have failed to demonstrate context effects. The findings support the initial hypothesis that reasoning is not an entirely retroactive process, and that it plays a significant role in moral judgment.

title: Visual Cluster Inspection Using Google Sky
abstract: My work at Dearborn has concerned galactic clusters. Clusters of galaxies are the largest gravitationally bound systems in the universe. We study clusters because, in addition to them being interesting themselves, they can tell us much about cosmology. Knowledge of the origin and evolution of clusters can be used to help answer the cosmological problems facing astronomers today: What is the nature of dark energy? What is the distribution of cold dark matter in the universe? An extensive catalog of clusters has been compiled at Fermilab by running an algorithm on data from the sky. However, before this catalog can be used to help answer questions, it must be cleaned up. No software is perfect; even the best algorithms can be expected to falsely identify non-existent clusters. So, we need a way of cutting out all of the bad outputs from the catalog. My job has been to develop software to visually inspect the clusters in the catalog. The program converts catalogs of clusters into files readable by Google Earth. Google Earth offers a fluid, user-friendly atmosphere. It allows users to quickly view any portion of the sky at any magnification. In this way, clusters can be viewed and evaluated individually.

title: Lost in Translation: Overcoming Linguistic Hurdles in Education in Rural Morocco
abstract: The question of the language of instruction in schools is a contentious one in many communities in the US as well as internationally. In Morocco, a movement has formed to elevate the status of the three major indigenous languages (Tarifit, Tamazight, and Tashelhit), most critically in educational settings in rural areas where a majority of indigenous Moroccans or Imazighen live. Outside of Marrakech, the Ait Iktel Association of Development (L’Association Ait Iktel de Développment) confronted this dilemma by founding, managing, and staffing their own schools and setting the language of instruction for elementary-aged students as Tashelhit, the indigenous Amazigh language of southern Morocco. I offer this case study since it illustrates the value of natal language instruction to further the awareness of Amazigh languages, to reverse language shift by creating subsequent generations of speakers, and chiefly, to improve education in rural communities. I examined the effectiveness of this approach to language and education in the context of research conducted in 2008 and 2010. I argue that natal language instruction at the primary school level can succeed in building a stronger foundation in basic education than if the language of instruction differed from students’ home language. In the context of recent work in international development on language instruction in schools, I suggest that the education model of the Ait Iktel Association of Development and other approaches may offer a useful model for other national associations, international organizations, and national ministries of education.

title: Fabrication of Charge Transport Measurement Devices on Graphene
abstract: Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms in a planar, honeycomb crystal lattice, is a material currently enjoying a huge surge in popularity. Believed to be the strongest material in existence, graphene has also been shown to possess unique electronic, magnetic, and optical properties. Despite progress already made, however, there is still much work left to be done in the characterization of this fascinating material. This project focuses on the unique techniques employed to create charge transport measurement devices on graphene, from the initial steps of synthesizing single-layer sheets to design and fabrication of electrical contacts on the order of nanometers in size. Furthermore, basics of charge transport will be discussed, as will information on the experimental setup required to probe physics at millikelvin temperatures.

title: Experiencing the Culture of College Major and Religion
abstract: College is a time for students to encounter new ideas, challenge their beliefs, and form their identities and worldviews. Religion and college major are parts of this self-exploration, and investigating how these two factors interact could improve understanding of young adults’ development. Thirty-one undergraduate students were recruited through student groups, religious organizations, and academic departments. They were interviewed according to a semi- structured guide of questions about major choice, religious life, and the interaction between academics and religion. The study intended to find if religion affects choice of major, if major affects religiosity, and how students experience the relationship between the two. No clear correlation was found between major and religion. However, three different ways of experiencing the relationship between major and religion were identified. The first group had chosen majors so that the values and beliefs of their religion and majors aligned. For the second group, religion and major remained entirely separate. The third group had chosen majors that did not necessarily align with their religion, but they explored the conflicts and tried to reconcile them. The first group experienced major and religious culture according to one sociological model: culture as a latent variable. The second group experienced major and religious culture according to another sociological model: culture as a toolkit. The third and largest group, however, did not fit neatly into either model of culture. These findings have implications for the sociological view of culture beyond the fields of college academics and religion.

title: Age Effects on Social Motivation in Children with Autism
abstract: The current study examined whether children with autism prefer to interact with adults or children and compared this preference to their typically developing (TD) peers. The mixed-design study required ten children with autism and ten age-matched typically-developing peers to complete a task where pushing either of the two available buttons disbursed a treat under each of the following two minute conditions: adult vs. child, adult vs. gumball machine, and child vs. gumball machine. We analyzed the proportion of adult pushes over total social pushes (adult + child) and the proportion of child pushes over total social pushes. We hypothesized that the children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) would demonstrate less motivation overall, prefer the machine to adults or children, and display significantly less social motivation to interact with children than adults (machine > adult > peer). The results from this study may yield important implications for autism remediation given the current emphasis on peer-mediated intervention. In addition, the results may support the advances seen in children with autism using structured venues such as music and simple technology.

title: Seeing Thigh to Thigh? An Investigation of the Femoral Bicondylar Angle in Humans
abstract: Investigations of the primate bicondylar angle (BA) have historically centered on the interspecific distinction between humans, nonhuman primates and hominid ancestors. The literature cites no single standard osteometric definition; it is not a common measure in forensic or human variation studies. The goal of this project is to introduce a method for measuring the femoral bicondylar angle, tested through inter- and intra-observer analyses, as well as investigate variation by sex, age and ancestral group. Four populations, male and female of a broad age range, were analyzed - Terry Black (n=50), Terry White (n=50), Arikara (n=50) and Native Alaskan (n=50). Femoral bicondylar angle was assessed by placing a compass against the board above the femur lining up the attached wire (positioned at the base of the compass) with the previously measured midshaft marks. This method provided readings of between 3° and 17.5 ° for this sample. To implement the inter- and intra-observer analyses, the bicondylar angle was measured independently, twice on separate occasions, by each observer (author and Dr. EB Waxenbaum of Northwestern University's Anthropology Department) for 100 of the individuals. Inter-observer comparisons resulted in non-significant variation (p>0.8032; p>0.8284); similar results were found for the intra-observer analyses (EBW, p>0.9007; MKS, p>0.9281). With this project, I will demonstrate the efficacy of this metric assessment of the human bicondylar angle by offering a pilot study of this methodology. Additionally, this project investigates intraspecfic human variation within the BA, prompting future research deepening investigation of variation in this feature by sex, age and ancestry.

title: Screening Nanopyramid Assemblies to Optimize Surface Enhanced Raman Scattering
abstract: This project describes how gold pyramidal nanoshells (nanopyramids) can be assembled into two architectures with different optical properties. We have demonstrated control over the assembly of nanopyramids into low-order (side-to-side) and high-order (stacked) structures by decreasing both the rate of solvent evaporation and surface wettability. Literature and modeling suggested the presence of an intense electromagnetic field in the region between particles which could be used to enhance Raman scattering, an effect used to identify molecules by a vibrational signature. To test which assembled architecture supported the most Raman scattering, we compared the scattering intensity of the resonant Raman molecule methylene blue (λex = 633 nm). We discovered that high-order structures exhibited more Raman scattering compared to low-order assemblies. Hence, measurements and modeling suggest that high-order assemblies are more promising than low-order assemblies as surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) substrates because they support a larger geometric region of high electric field intensity. This work has demonstrated that the local spatial arrangement of assembled nanoparticles is an important design parameter for optimizing nanoparticle-based SERS sensors.

title: dpNSOM: A Novel Nanoscale Refractive Index Measurement Technique
abstract: To diagnose and treat cancers at an early stage, research focuses on early detection using imaging as well as techniques to characterize cells, structures, and molecules. Optical microscopy is a widely used technique to analyze cell structure. However, the resolution of conventional optical microscopy is diffraction-limited. This poses a roadblock to detecting cancer at an early stage, as studies have indicated that nanoarchitectural changes, significantly smaller than the diffraction limit, precede histologically noticeable events such as dysplasia. These changes are invisible to optical microscopy techniques that are currently considered the gold-standard. My research is aimed at demolishing this roadblock. I am using a near-field scanning optical microscope, NSOM, to develop a novel means to quantify optical refractive indices within biological cells. Probing in the depth direction, depth probing NSOM, dpNSOM, has a resolution of 50 nm or finer, fully one order-of-magnitude below the diffraction limit. The techniques that I am developing could be used to analyze cells that are potentially in the earliest stages of cancer. From the basic-science perspective, the data obtained in this manner would serve to increase basic knowledge of fundamental nanoarchitectural changes in a cell that accompany cancer progression. From the public health perspective, the techniques I am developing would potentially facilitate a robust and life saving cancer screening methodology.

title: Priming Pathogen Prevalence: Effects on Individualism-Collectivism in Relation to the Culture-Gene Coevolution Theory
abstract: The culture-gene coevolution theory describes how genetic physiology, environmental pressures, and cultural behavior influence each other and evolve together. The theory clarifies three positive correlations between three factors: the short allele frequency for the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) in populations, geographical pathogen prevalence, and the cultural value of collectivism). Compared to those who are more individualistic, collectivistic individuals tend to identify themselves with their in-group and favor preservation of their in-group’s well-being. Collectivistic behavior that protects the in-group’s health, such as avoidance of unfamiliar pathogens and infected individuals, could reduce introduction and transmission of new pathogens into one’s group, which could be particularly evolutionarily adaptive in regions with high pathogen prevalence. The current study examined the directional relationship between pathogen prevalence and the cultural values of individualism-collectivism by manipulating pathogen prevalence with an explicit pictorial pathogen prime and by measuring the participants’ levels of individualism-collectivism. Asian Americans were randomly assigned to receive either neutral or pathogen-salient pictorial primes and then completed paper and online surveys measuring their cultural values. The pathogen prime consisted of twenty-four images of body parts with visible symptoms of infectious diseases while the neutral prime consisted of twenty-four images of corresponding healthy body parts. Participants primed for pathogen prevalence were expected to display more collectivistic behaviors than would subjects in the neutral condition. The current study’s investigation of how pathogen prevalence influences development of culture contributes to our understanding of diversity and global health.

title: Partial Urinary Bladder Regeneration Utilizing Mesenchymal Stem Cells Seeded onto an Elastomeric Thin Film
abstract: The need for a novel bladder augmentation model is long overdue. Patients with dysfunctional neurogenic bladders, such as those with spina bifida, undergo extensive surgery to augment the bladder in order to increase the capacity to hold urine. Yet this surgical intervention does not improve bladder function as urodynamics of the augmented bladder remain unchanged. This study takes advantage of the plasticity of bone marrow derived stem cells and the elasticity of recently developed biomaterials towards bladder regeneration efforts. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) and poly(1,8-octanediol-co-citrate) thin films (POCfs) were evaluated. MSCs demonstrated a high viability and proliferation capacity in vitro and when cultured on POCfs, and even expressed contractile proteins in an undifferentiated state akin to bladder smooth muscle cells (SMCs). To replicate the bladder augmentation surgery, MSCs seeded onto POCfs were implanted into a nude rat bladder, resulting in robust MSCs growth in vivo. MSCs post-implantation had an enhanced contractile protein expression as well. This protein profile allowed for carbachol-induced in vitro contraction, clearly confirming MSC candidacy in bladder smooth muscle regeneration. EPCs, when cultured in a CAM model, developed branched vasculature. Additionally, ureteral SMCs (spared of neurogenic pathology) had a high proliferation capacity and expressed contractile proteins found in SMCs as well. These findings suggest that POCfs cradle the growth of MSCs and EPCs, developing into the smooth muscle and vascular network of the bladder wall, respectively. This novel approach to bladder reconstruction may contribute towards eradicating the need for self-catheterization and improving bladder functionality in spina bifida patients.

title: Macrophage Influence on Pre-pubertal Follicle Development in Mice
abstract: Macrophages secrete over 100 different molecules, including growth factors and cytokines that have been proposed to be involved in several ovarian processes, including follicular development, ovulation, and corpus luteum involution, but the interplay of the known cytokines and their roles in the pre-pubertal ovary has not been well-studied. To examine the role of macrophages on pre-pubertal follicle development, we examined both the localization of these cells in relation to different subclasses of follicles and the effect of co-culturing macrophages and follicles in our established in vitro culture system. Localization studies demonstrate an increasing number of macrophages present in the ovary over the pre-pubertal period, with no significant association with a particular follicle class on day 2, a strong association with primordial/primary follicles on day 6 which changes to a more significant association with secondary/antral follicles on days 10 and 19, and a re-association with primordial/primary follicles on day 26. Co-culturing experiments demonstrate that a feeder layer of macrophages cause an increase in follicular growth and survival in low or no FSH media. Together, these data suggest a model in which macrophages are in close association with growing follicles in vivo and secrete molecules that directly aid in follicle growth.

title: Mirrored Malinches: Gender and Geopolitics in Lone Star and Their Dogs Came with Them
abstract: La Malinche became the Indian translator for Hernán Cortés and the Spanish Conquistadors after they arrived in Mexico in the early sixteenth century. Because of her role as both translator for the Spanish and as Cortés’s concubine, La Malinche has traditionally been considered a traitorous figure in Mexican and Chicano/a culture. Chicana feminists have attempted since the 1970s to redeem the figure of La Malinche by framing her as a symbol of female agency oppressed by Chicano nationalist patriarchy. My thesis analyzes two fictional works – the film Lone Star by John Sayles and the novel Their Dogs Came with Them by Helena María Viramontes. Both works use doubled representations of La Malinche to reflect the pervasive misogyny of Chicano nationalism and broader American society. I argue that that these two works situate discussions of gender within a broader geopolitical context that is often ignored by Chicana authors referring to La Malinche. As a woman who translated between languages and symbolically blended the races of indigenous Amerindians and Europeans by bearing Cortés’s child, La Malinche crossed ethnic and political borders. The unstable identity boundaries which these works depicts between the doubled Malinche figures function as a metaphor for other permeable boundaries, such as those between Mexico and the United States and between racially segregated communities in the United States. By analyzing how both works use La Malinche to critique traditional understandings of both gender and geopolitics, I aim to contribute to an emancipatory politics of literary interpretation that simultaneously addresses gender oppression and divisions between racial, ethnic, and national groups.

title: Causal Thinking vs Perceptual Alignment in Determining Preservation of Identity
abstract: What allows us to identify unique individual objects? The primary criterion that comes to mind is appearance. To gage what types of changes people would allow to occur to an individual object and still have it retain its original identity, studies have been performed with transformation machines which alter the appearance of the post-transformational object. Rhemtulla and Hall (2009) performed such a transformational study in which an object (Fido the dog) was transformed into an identical looking object (Fido the dog), an object of the same basic kind (different looking dog), or across basic kind (cat). They found that people were more likely to say that the cat (across kind) could be Fido than a different looking dog (within basic kind), thus resulting in a non-linear progression (Identical dog>cat > different looking dog). In my pilot study I performed a very similar experiment; however, I also manipulated the function of the object so that the post-transformation object either had the same function, a different function, or was broken. I hypothesized that function is a strong causal factor which helps define the identity of an object, and therefore manipulating the function would drive subjects to perform more casual thinking than simple aligning of appearances. Thus I would see a linear progression in identity ratings (Identical dog> different dog> cat). I did in fact find this trend, but my methodology was somewhat different from the Rhemtualla and Hall's study. I am now addressing these methodological differences in a second baseline study.

title: Theatre for Community Development in the Context of Mass Atrocity and Genocide
abstract: Since the turn of the century, the Lord's Resistance Army insurgency has - like a virus - clogged the veins of communities in Central-Eastern Africa and oppressed the people of Uganda. Despite issued arrest warrants for leader Joseph Kony in 2005 from the International Criminal Court, the LRA has continued to violate several human rights violations including child abduction, sexual harassment, and murder. This is not the first time that mass atrocity has plagued this area, for example the Rwandan Genocide of 1994. The short-term effects are devastatingly visible, but the lasting effects that mass atrocity has on these communities is often left unaddressed. In this study, my research focuses on existing Theatre for Community Development projects in Uganda and comparing this work to the body of theatre at large that addresses mass atrocity. Theatre for Community Development finds its roots in Augusto Boal's Theatre for the Oppressed, which is art that focuses on shared experience, on taking the power out of the hands of the few and giving it back to the individuals - to the communities - in order to create sustainable empowerment. With this study I address the long-term effects of mass atrocity by looking through a lens of theatre with the purpose of restoring community by opening dialogue for Ugandans. This study has urgent implications today as the LRA continues to infect and attack communities in Uganda.

title: Determination of Specific Receptor Involvement in Aβ-Induced Toxicity Using Gold Nanoparticle Oligonucleotide Complexes
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease is a neurodegenerative condition marked by initial loss of the ability to learn and recall information and followed by the gradual onset of severe dementia. At the molecular level, the disease begins with the assembly of toxic oligomers from the metabolically generated amyloid β peptide. Binding of these neurotoxins, called amyloid-derived diffusible ligands (ADDLs), to some unknown surface receptor induces changes in synaptic composition and structure, thereby disrupting cell-communication and memory formation. We have attempted to identify the crucial proteins that facilitate ADDL synaptotoxicity by silencing potential receptor genes with gold nanoparticle oligonucleotide complexes (GNOs). This recently developed technology has proven to be a highly effective delivery system for antisense DNA or siRNA in many cell types, and here, its use is demonstrated in neurons. Identification of these proteins will lead to a better overall understanding of Alzheimer’s pathogenesis and will provide new targets for therapeutics that can block or modify disease-causing interactions.

title: Help Wanted?: Exploring the Relationships Between Street Youth and Their Service Providers in Cochabamba, Bolivia
abstract: More than 31 organizations working to support the needs of street youth exist in Cochabamba, Bolivia, yet the number of kids living and working on Cochabamba’s streets continues to multiply. My thesis explores this situation from two perspectives: those of Bolivian street youth and those of directors and staff of organizations intending to benefit these kids. Using ethnographic research conducted with street-living youth groups and staff from street youth program centers, my thesis investigates the priorities and self-defined needs of kids along with the objectives and challenges faced by organizations. I argue that insufficient funding for organizations results in programs that provide short-term benefits instead of investing in kids’ long-range futures. This short-term attitude within programs is replicated by street youth who exercise their agency by strategically choosing what they view as the most desirable services offered by various organizations rather than committing to forming a relationship with a single service provider. As noted in anthropological literature, recognition that youth possess agency and are not passive victims of their circumstances disputes the Western notion of a “proper” childhood based on children’s supposed dependency on adults. Although anthropological theories contribute to an understanding of street youth and their experiences, research is lacking which considers both the views of youth and the views of organizations. I attempt to explore the situation in Cochabamba by utilizing these two perspectives in order to suggest that street youth and their service providers must each contend with limitations that influence their interactions with one another.

title: The Bearded Woman on the Cross: St. Ontcommer and Medieval Popular Piety
abstract: According to legend, St. Ontcommer was a young princess of Portugal who renounced paganism and refused to marry. When God sent her a full beard to help her escape a suitor, her own father had her crucified in anger. In northern Europe during the late Middle Ages, versions of this legend circulated widely and hundreds of works of devotional art were dedicated to the androgynous virgin saint. In over five centuries since her legend first emerged, the bearded woman on the cross has been recognized as the patron saint of prisoners, the sick and dying, soldiers, fertility, childbirth, livestock, musicians, bakers, travelers, marriage, incest survivors, and women seeking escape from bad relationships. This paper investigates the emergence of the cult of St. Ontcommer, seeking to explain the significance of this seemingly unusual popular figure within her own late-medieval context. I use art and textual evidence to show that the cult of St. Ontcommer became widespread in part because she encompassed both an ideal of bodily women’s spirituality and a tendency towards the feminization of Christ important to art and literature of the later Middle Ages. Additionally, her ambiguous representation suggests multiple possibilities for access to the divine, allowing her to serve as an adaptable and powerful symbol to her diverse supplicants. Finally, her transgression of boundaries between male and female, “disfigured” and transcendent, reflects both the fluidity and the paradox important to late medieval conceptions of gender and the body, particularly as they apply to perceptions of the holy.

title: Biological Control of Strontium and Barium Uptake by Desmid Green Algae
abstract: The sequestration of 90Sr from radioactive waste is complicated by the chemical similarity between alkaline earth metal cations Ca2+, Sr2+, and Ba2+. Additionally, this chemical similarity leads to indiscriminate transport of Ba2+ and Sr2+ with the biologically relevant Ca2+ in most organisms. However, desmid green algae of the genus Closterium have shown a unique ability to sequester barium and strontium by precipitating (Ba,Sr)SO4, indicating they possess a mechanism to select between Sr2+, Ba2+, and Ca2+. Using Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-AES), we examined the mechanism by which this selectivity occurs by quantifying the intracellular concentrations of these metal ions. The results from protein binding assays using native protein extractions suggested that binding of Sr2+, Ba2+, and Ca2+ to proteins does occur, but the level of binding selectivity remains in question. Whole cell digestion competition experiments revealed that Sr2+ and Ca2+ compete for uptake at the plasma membrane. Therefore, we conclude that selectivity is not in uptake, but additional work is needed to determine the specific roles of selective binding and selective precipitation.

title: What's New in Sex Since the Seventies?: A Historical Analysis of the Portrayal of Sex and Relationships in Feminist and Popular Women's Magazines
abstract: During the 1960s and 1970s, the second wave feminist movement fought for sexual liberation and equality of genders in sexual intimacy and expression. How have media portrayals of sexuality, sexual health and relationships changed from the sexual revolution of the 1970s to now? To assess this research topic, I reviewed both feminist magazines and mainstream magazines from 1970 to 2009. I examined all articles in the feminist publications Off Our Backs and Ms. from this four-decade time period, and all articles from Cosmopolitan and Glamour for the years 1970, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1985, 1989, 1990, 1995, 1999, 2000, 2005, and 2009. I coded each article that mentioned sex, sexuality, or sexual acts, as well as articles discussing related topics such as relationships and dating, sexual danger, sexual health, pornography, prostitution, and sex in media – all set within the United States. My results indicate that feminist publications have greatly decreased the number of articles about sex and sexuality, while in mainstream magazines the topic of sex has proliferated. A content analysis shows that sex issues are no longer framed in a considerably feminist light. Additionally, the integration of feminist topics on sex and relationships has not occurred to a large extent in mainstream media, with the exception of several specific topics. The implications of this data include the absence of a critical perspective on sex in periodical sources. This may give women a limited perspective on how to view sex and heterosexual relationships, which could have a negative effect on gender equality in sexual relationships.

title: A Study of the Discrepancies between Feminist Attitudes and Feminist Self-Identification
abstract: The research question was, “How does the label feminist affect the likelihood of young females identifying as feminists?” The aim of this study was to attempt to understand some of the reasons why some young women have feminist attitudes and beliefs while not always identifying with the label. Prior research has recognized stereotypes, media representation, and exposure to feminism as factors affecting identification as feminists. This study sought to expand the number of participants, include mixed-methods, and study sorority women. It was hypothesized that (1) the term “feminist” is defined inconsistently, (2) the label is stigmatizing, and (3) there is a lack of knowledge about the feminist movement. Using the Attitudes Toward Women Scale (Spence & Helmreich, 1978) and the Self-Identification as a Feminist Scale (Syzmanski, 2004), 271 female students shared their beliefs about women and their tendency to identify as feminists privately and publicly. Interestingly, 43% of participants held feminist attitudes, but did not label themselves as feminists. Next, thirteen one-on-one semi-structured interviews were conducted. Reasons why women are hesitant to identify as feminists are (1) negative stigma, (2) media portrayal of feminists, (3) little experience with feminists, (4) no personal connection with feminism, (5) ambiguous definition of feminists/feminism, (6) lack of information about the feminist movement, (7) fear of not meeting expectations of feminists, (8) fear of peer judgment, and (9) fear of not acquiring a mate. Based on these findings, recommendations were created for new strategies, programs and advocacy endeavors to increase activism to reduce prejudice and to generally encourage greater work toward gender equality.

title: The Cultural Politics of WMD Terrorism in Post-Cold War America
abstract: Analysts across the political spectrum often portray September 11, 2001, as marking a clear divide in American history, creating a sort of before- and after-9/11 approach to our interpretation of that event. My research questions this premise through readings of two popular culture texts from the 1990s. I focus on the motifs of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and terrorism in the 1996 blockbuster Independence Day and Tom Clancy’s 1998 techno-thriller novel Rainbow Six to argue that national security politics underwent a more continuous evolution between the Cold War and 9/11. I look at how the representations of destruction and terrorism contained in these works reflect concerns about terrorism voiced by national security analysts in the 1990s. I draw upon psychoanalytic political theory, most notably that of Michael Rogin, and historical studies of the interactions between American cultural politics and militarism, especially Michael Sherry’s work on Cold War and 1990s history, to examine how these texts stage fears about WMD terrorism in the midst of the culture wars of the 1990s. At a time when militarism’s social role was in question, the threat of WMD terrorism justified maintaining and updating the American national security complex. It became a way to counter the growing influence of private sector actors and resolve anxieties over shifting gender politics. I show that this complex web of political issues functioned around a trend towards non-statist militarism that anticipated extralegal practices in the War on Terror, such as extraordinary rendition and indefinite detention.

title: Environment Detection for Mobile Eye-Tracking
abstract: Eye-tracking, a technology which tracks the direction of a person’s gaze, provides unique and valuable insights into how we communicate, collaborate, and think as well as the potential to change how we interact with our world. This potential has traditionally been restrained in part by the difficulty of determining what a person is looking at given the direction of their gaze, which in eye-tracker data is disconnected from their environment. This work is a software system called Gaze Collision Detection (GCD), which correlates a person’s gaze and environment by using simple augmented reality and computer graphics techniques to determine the subject of someone’s gaze. It is designed to support research and application in communication and human-computer interactions. GCD’s capabilities for deriving object-under-gaze from saved eye-tracking data are accessed through their bindings to the Python programming language. Currently, GCD is making its first research appearance in a communication study on how people use language in shared visual spaces through a tool that codes eye-tracker data significantly faster, though less reliably, than could be done by research assistants. A second application allows GCD to act as a helper, speeding human coding while maintaining accuracy. GCD is also packaged as an extension to the Applied Sciences Laboratory’s EyeVision software, providing object-under-gaze data during eye-tracker use. EyeTunes, a system where looking at an album’s cover plays music from it, leverages this to demonstrate how future glanceable input could easily allow for that to open for people with disabilities at a literal glance.

title: Political Currency and the Lasting Legacy of Alexander Hamilton
abstract: This project is presented as a short essay with accompanying images, distilling and synthesizing several months of research done into the life and political legacy of Alexander Hamilton. Of specific interest to the project is Hamilton's involvement in political scandal, and how the legacy of that scandal is remembered and appropriated for varying political purposes. In addition, the project also examines the significance of the design choices of United States currency, and how those choices can influence the character of political legacy. The significance of this project lies in its attempt to illuminate the very deliberate, non-neutral choices which go into the creation of U.S paper money, and how those choices can be tied back to the (at times tawdry) histories of this country's founding fathers.

title: Tuberculosis Infection Control in Tanzania: Evaluating the Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices of Key Stakeholders
abstract: Once thought to be on the path to global eradication, tuberculosis (TB) is making a swift and deadly re-emergence in Africa where general health conditions, HIV/AIDS prevalence, and new multi-drug and extreme drug resistant strains have provided favorable conditions for the disease's rapid spread. While attention has been focused on medicinal remedies to TB for years, social interventions are still in early stages of gaining traction.
